evidence.title: Deployment protocol and base model jointly determine residual risk in rule-based clinical LLM supervision

In the multisite Llama 70B extension, deploy violation rate was 0.0% under handoff-on (strict VR 2.0%) versus 2.4% under handoff-off.

evidence.quote: A multisite extension (Llama 70B, N =2935 encounter-derived scenarios, three sites) confirmed 0.0% deploy violation rate under handoff-on (strict VR 2.0%) and 2.4% under handoff-off.

evidence.effect: Scope-matched KG retrieval (notably G2) yielded the most consistent gains; indiscriminate graph unions often introduced distractors that reduced accuracy; larger models frequently matched or exceeded KG-RAG with a No-RAG baseline on Probe 1; smaller/mid-sized models benefited more from well-scoped retrieval. No numeric values reported in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Indiscriminate graph unions introduce distractors that reduce accuracy.
evidence.quote: Larger models frequently match or exceed KG-RAG with a No-RAG baseline on Probe 1, indicating strong parametric priors, whereas smaller/mid-sized models benefit more from well-scoped retrieval.

evidence.title: An agentic AI framework connecting language models to electronic health records and a biomedical knowledge graph for real-world evidence
evidence.comparator_used: Same LLMs without knowledge-graph access/SPOKE grounding
evidence.outcome: 100-task clinical research benchmark mean scores
evidence.effect: Knowledge-graph access improved mean scores overall for GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8; no numeric score delta reported in the provided text.
evidence.quote: Across the 100-task benchmark, knowledge-graph access improved mean scores overall for GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, though the pattern differed between models; on BiomixQA, SPOKE grounding raised multiple-choice accuracy for both models, without changing true/false accuracy.

evidence.title: Quantum Knowledge Graph: Modeling Context-Dependent Triplet Validity
evidence.comparator_used: No validator baseline (reasoner only); also KG validation without context matching
evidence.outcome: Medical QA accuracy on KG-grounded MedReason subset (2,788 questions), Haiku-4.5 as Reasoner and Validator
evidence.effect: KG-backed validation +0.61 pp over no-validator baseline; QKG with context matching +0.79 pp over KG validation without context matching and +1.40 pp over no-validator baseline (paired McNemar, all p<0.05). With stronger validator (Qwen-3.6-Plus), raw QKG gain over no-validator baseline +5.96 pp; context-matching gap p=0.73 on raw set, p=0.05 after adjustment.
evidence.quote: With Haiku-4.5 as both the Reasoner and the Validator, KG-backed validation significantly improves over a no-validator baseline ($+0.61$ pp), and QKG with context matching yields the largest gain, outperforming both KG validation without context matching ($+0.79$ pp) and the no-validator baseline ($+1.40$ pp; paired McNemar, all $p<0.05$).

evidence.title: Cosine Similarity Conflates Clinically Distinct Cancer Variants: A Case for Typed-Graph Retrieval in Precision Oncology Decision Support
evidence.comparator_used: Cosine-similarity vector retrieval over text embeddings (PubMedBERT, MedCPT, BGE-large-en-v1.5), including with an exact variant-ID guardrail
evidence.outcome: Wrong-variant retrieval for clinically distinct cancer variant pairs
evidence.effect: Cosine retrieval put the wrong paired variant in the top 5 for 75% to 100% of queries under the biomedical encoders (52-document corpus). The typed-graph pipeline gave a 0% wrong-variant retrieval rate with 95.8% normalization accuracy.
evidence.tradeoff: Depends on a normalization layer that resolves variant strings to canonical nodes (95.8% normalization accuracy, so some strings were not resolved correctly). Evaluated on only 9 variant pairs.
evidence.quote: Adding an exact variant-ID guardrail to cosine retrieval, and routing retrieval through an end-to-end typed-graph pipeline, both reduced wrong-variant retrieval to zero.

evidence.title: Systematic Evaluation of Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Gastrointestinal Tumor Board Decision Support
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline configurations with broader corpus scope (not curated guideline retrieval)
evidence.outcome: Concordance with multidisciplinary team recommendations
evidence.effect: Baseline concordance 79–85%; curated guideline retrieval combined with query rewriting improved concordance to 93–95% (p < 0.01). Corpus curation had greater influence than model selection. The effect of corpus curation alone is not separated in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Among residual discordant cases in optimal configurations, approximately 60% were clinically inappropriate recommendations, so expert oversight is still required.
evidence.quote: Combining query rewriting with curated guideline retrieval improved concordance to 93–95% (p < 0.01), with prompt design and corpus curation exerting greater influence than model selection.

evidence.title: Reducing Hallucinations and Trade-Offs in Responses in Generative AI Chatbots for Cancer Information: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: RAG over general Google internet search results (open web search)
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate (medically harmful or misinformation) rated by 2 clinicians
evidence.effect: CIS-based chatbots 0% (GPT-4) and 6% (GPT-3.5) vs Google-based 6% and 10%; for questions not covered by CIS, Google-based chatbots 19% (GPT-4) and 35% (GPT-3.5); Google vs CIS OR 9.4 (95% CI 1.2-17.5, P<.01)
evidence.tradeoff: CIS chatbots declined to answer questions not covered by CIS content, whereas Google chatbots responded in 52% (GPT-4) and 71% (GPT-3.5) of those cases; overall response rates for RAG chatbots fell (36% to 81%).
evidence.quote: Using reference data from Google searches generated more hallucinations than using CIS data, with an OR of 9.4 (95% CI 1.2-17.5, P<.01); the OR for the conventional chatbot was 16.1 (95% CI 3.7-50.0, P<.001).

evidence.title: Effects of Cross-lingual Evidence in Multilingual Medical Question Answering
evidence.comparator_used: Web-retrieved content (open web) versus curated specialized medical repositories such as PubMed
evidence.outcome: Multilingual medical QA accuracy by evidence source
evidence.effect: No numbers in the abstract. Web-retrieved English data was most beneficial for high-resource languages, while curated sources such as PubMed were described as limited.
evidence.tradeoff: Curated sources such as PubMed provide authoritative expert knowledge but lack adequate multilingual coverage.
evidence.quote: When incorporating external knowledge, web-retrieved data in English proves most beneficial for high-resource languages.

evidence.title: Precision Grounding: augmenting large language models with evidence-based databases for trustworthy genetic variant summarization
evidence.comparator_used: Web-search grounding (open web search); MedRAG over its own databases was also tested
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and completeness of genetic variant summaries (5-point Likert scale), and clinically significant hallucinations
evidence.effect: Accuracy 4.76 (+0.74) and completeness 4.94 (+0.84) versus web-search grounding; fewer hallucinations such as incorrect pathogenicity classification and summarizing the wrong variant
evidence.tradeoff: Limited coverage in the corpus hurts: MedRAG failed to generate clinically useful summaries because its databases held limited relevant information, and it did worse than web search.
evidence.quote: Precision Grounding outperformed web-search grounding, achieving significantly higher accuracy and completeness scores, which were based on a 5-point Likert-Scale of 4.76 (+0.74) and 4.94 (+0.84), respectively.

evidence.title: Demo: Guide-RAG: Evidence-Driven Corpus Curation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Long COVID
evidence.comparator_used: Large-scale literature databases (unfiltered primary literature) and a narrow single-guideline corpus
evidence.outcome: LLM-as-a-judge scores for faithfulness, relevance and comprehensiveness on Long COVID clinical questions (LongCOVID-CQ)
evidence.effect: The guidelines plus high-quality systematic reviews corpus 'consistently outperformed' both the single-guideline and the large-scale literature database configurations. The abstract reports no numeric scores.
evidence.quote: Our RAG corpus configuration combining clinical guidelines with high-quality systematic reviews consistently outperformed both narrow single-guideline approaches and large-scale literature databases.

evidence.title: Evaluating Web Retrieval-Assisted Large Language Models With and Without Whitelisting for Evidence-Based Neurology: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Open-web retrieval (no domain restriction) with the same Perplexity Sonar, Sonar-Pro and Sonar-Reasoning-Pro models
evidence.outcome: Correct-answer rate and mean accuracy (0-2 scale) on 130 AAN guideline-derived neurology questions
evidence.effect: Correct-answer rates open vs whitelisted: Sonar 60% vs 78%, Sonar-Pro 80% vs 88%, Sonar-Reasoning-Pro 81% vs 89%. Mean accuracy gain from whitelisting: 0.23 for Sonar (95% CI 0.12-0.34), 0.08 for Sonar-Pro (95% CI 0.01-0.16), 0.08 for Sonar-Reasoning-Pro (95% CI 0.02-0.13). Including ≥1 nonprofessional source halved the odds of a higher rating in Sonar (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.37-0.66), whereas citing an AAN or neurology document doubled it (OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.64-2.89). Whitelisting also halved output variability.
evidence.quote: Restricting retrieval to authoritative neurology domains yielded a clinically meaningful 8 to 18 percentage-point gain in correctness and halved output variability, upgrading a consumer search assistant to a decision-support-level tool that at least performed on par with a specialized literature engine.

controls.question: Should the LLM answer from retrieved trusted passages, from full content placed in its prompt, or from training knowledge alone?
controls.control: Retrieve relevant passages from guidelines, institutional documents, literature or the record and supply them to the LLM before it answers.
controls.comparator: Training knowledge alone, or full content in a long-context/static prompt
controls.aim: Reduce hallucinations and outdated answers while balancing accuracy, cost and simplicity
variants: Retrieved EHR excerpts versus full patient record in long-context model
Static structured knowledge table in prompt for small closed domains versus vector RAG
controls.family_label: retrieval-augmented generation, source citation, knowledge graphs, EHR grounding

Severity did not differ significantly (P=.17), and 2 of the 5 RAG hallucinations (40%) were rated alarming vs 1 of 15 with native ChatGPT. The physician had to check and correct outputs. Slightly reduced understandability (linguistic accessibility) of answers for Claude3.7 and Qwen3 with RAG.

evidence.title: Exploring Patient Perspectives, Engagement, and Output Quality in Doctor-Supervised Use of Artificial Intelligence During Informed Consent Consultation With ChatGPT and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG): Quantitative Exploratory Study
evidence.comparator_used: Native ChatGPT (GPT-4o) without retrieval, relying on training knowledge alone, with a physician present in both arms
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate and physician-rated response quality; patient satisfaction with information delivery and informedness
evidence.effect: Hallucinations 5/52 (10%) with ChatGPT+RAG vs 15/39 (38%) with native ChatGPT (P=.002). Quality was higher in every dimension (all P<.001), e.g. accuracy 4.625 vs 3.910 and evidence-based 4.961 vs 3.346. Patients reported higher satisfaction with information delivery (P=.01) and perceived informedness (P=.01). Patients asked more questions with RAG (52 vs 39 total, not significant between the two groups). Responses were about 3 times shorter with RAG.
evidence.tradeoff: RAG did not eliminate hallucinations. 4 of the 5 RAG hallucinations came from information missing in the FAQ document. Severity did not differ significantly (P=.17), and 2 of the 5 RAG hallucinations (40%) were rated alarming vs 1 of 15 with native ChatGPT. The physician had to check and correct outputs. This was a small, non-randomised pilot with 12 patients per arm.
evidence.quote: We observed significantly fewer hallucinations in the RAG group versus in the native ChatGPT group (5 out of 52 [10%] vs 15 out of 39, 38%; Table 8 ).

evidence.title: Generative AI Is Not Ready for Clinical Use in Patient Education for Lower Back Pain Patients, Even With Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence.venue: AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science proceedings. AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science
evidence.comparator_used: Traditional LLMs without retrieval (no RAG)
evidence.outcome: Physical therapist Likert ratings of accuracy, completeness and redundancy, plus Flesch Reading Ease readability of LBP patient education materials
evidence.effect: RAG-based LLMs rated more accurate, more complete, more readable and less redundant than traditional LLMs; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Generated materials were still judged not ready for clinical practice; significant challenges remain in clinical relevance and granularity of content.
evidence.quote: The findings demonstrate that RAG-based LLMs outperform traditional LLMs, providing more accurate, complete, and readable patient education materials with less redundancy.

evidence.title: Guideline-Integrated Large Language Models Improve Decision Support for Acute Ear, Nose and Throat Emergencies
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline ChatGPT and Gemini responses without guideline retrieval (model knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, guideline adherence and safety of LLM decision support for acute ENT emergencies, rated by five blinded otolaryngologists on a nine-domain rubric
evidence.effect: Significant improvement in diagnostic accuracy, diagnostic workup quality, management planning, referral appropriateness and guideline adherence; reduced misleading recommendations; modestly decreased overtreatment; overtesting rates unchanged. No numeric values given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Compared with baseline models, RAG-enabled models demonstrated significantly improved diagnostic accuracy, diagnostic workup quality, management planning, referral appropriateness, and guideline adherence.

evidence.title: Multi-Agent Dynamic Refinement Outperforms Static RAG in Clinical Reasoning for Complex Nephrology Cases
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline frontier LLM without retrieval (Model A)
evidence.outcome: Clinical reasoning score across nine cognitive steps in longitudinal nephrology cases
evidence.effect: Human evaluation (20-point scale): Model B 16.2 (SD 1.2) vs Model A 16.1 (SD 1.3), no significant improvement. AI panel (15-point scale): Model B 14.3 vs Model A 14.2.
evidence.quote: Implementing static RAG (Model B) yielded no significant improvement over the baseline.

evidence.title: Beyond Arrow's Impossibility: Fairness as an Emergent Property of Multi-Agent Collaboration
evidence.comparator_used: Unaligned or adversarially prompted agent (no ethical-framework RAG)
evidence.outcome: Bias moderation and access for marginalized groups in triage allocation
evidence.effect: Qualitative: RAG-aligned agents partially moderated bias and restored access for marginalized groups, but did not fully convert a biased counterpart; no numbers reported in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Even explicitly aligned agents exhibited intrinsic biases toward certain ethical frameworks, consistent with known left-leaning LLM tendencies
evidence.quote: Aligned agents partially moderate bias through contestation rather than override, acting as corrective patches that restore access for marginalized groups without fully converting a biased counterpart.

evidence.title: A Chatbot for the Management of Bipolar Disorder: Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation with an Open-Weight Large Language Model to Answer Clinical Questions Based on the CANMAT and ISBD 2018 Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder
evidence.comparator_used: Base Llama 3.3 70B model without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Guideline consistency of responses rated by six expert psychiatrists (3-point scale), plus preference ratings
evidence.effect: RAG: 80 answers (63.5%) fully consistent vs 24 (19.0%) for baseline; major deviation 10 (7.9%) vs 48 (38.1%); OR = 9.1, 95% CI 5.3–16.3, p < 0.001; 110/126 (87.3%) rated as more or as correct as baseline; preference favored RAG in 78.7% of cases
evidence.tradeoff: Performance varied by vignette, with some errors in both retrieval and reasoning.
evidence.quote: The RAG system produced 80 answers (63.5%) rated fully consistent with the guidelines versus 24 (19.0%) for baseline, and only 10 answers with major deviation (7.9%) versus 48 (38.1%) for baseline.

evidence.title: Performance and usability of retrieval-augmented large language models for stroke patient and caregiver support
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot LLM (no retrieval) for GPT-4o, Claude3.7 and Qwen3
evidence.outcome: Exam-question accuracy and clinician-rated accuracy, relevance, completeness and understandability of open-ended answers
evidence.effect: RAG improved accuracy, relevance, and completeness across all three LLMs, with GPT-4o under RAG achieving the highest overall mean score; RAG slightly reduced understandability for Claude3.7 and Qwen3. No numeric values given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Slightly reduced understandability (linguistic accessibility) of answers for Claude3.7 and Qwen3 with RAG.
evidence.quote: RAG integration improved accuracy, relevance, and completeness across all three LLMs, with GPT-4o under RAG configuration achieving the highest overall mean score.

evidence.title: ChatGPT on guidelines: Providing contextual knowledge to GPT allows it to provide advice on appropriate colonoscopy intervals
evidence.comparator_used: Standard GPT4 without the guideline knowledge base (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Correct colonoscopy screening/surveillance advice across domains (high-risk feature identification, correct interval, guideline citation) on 62 case scenarios, each tested three times
evidence.effect: Contextualized model outperformed standard GPT4 in all domains; no high-risk features missed; a correct interval was given in the majority of cases; guidelines were cited appropriately in almost all cases. Numeric values are not given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Hallucination of additional high-risk features occurred in two cases; the interval was not correct in all cases.
evidence.quote: The contextualized GPT4 model outperformed the standard GPT4 in all domains.

evidence.title: Deriving the OTA/AO fracture classification from routinely collected radiology reports using a large language model
evidence.venue: OTA international : the open access journal of orthopaedic trauma
evidence.comparator_used: zero-shot prompting and zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting (no retrieval)
evidence.outcome: OTA/AO classification agreement (Cohen kappa and accuracy) against expert ground-truth labels
evidence.effect: On radiology report descriptions, RAG performed similarly to the other strategies. The best result was RAG with ideal fracture descriptions, where full-label agreement remained only moderate.
evidence.tradeoff: Errors were largely due to imprecise descriptions, hallucinated information, or incorrect application of factually correct information.
evidence.quote: The 3 prompting strategies tested yielded similar classification performance on radiology report fracture descriptions

evidence.title: Performance of large language models in interventional cardiology: the ILLUMINATE blinded model-comparison study
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT (ChatGPTd) relying on training knowledge alone
evidence.outcome: Composite expert-rated score (appropriateness, accuracy, relevance, clarity, clinical utility) for complex interventional cardiology cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT with ESC guidelines (ChatGPT-gl) 7.7 (95% CI 7.4-7.9) vs default ChatGPT 6.9 (6.6-7.3); differences across LLMs P<.001 and consistent across all scoring dimensions
evidence.quote: Performance significantly varied across LLMs (P less than .001), with ChatGPTi (7.8 [7.5-8.0]) and ChatGPT-gl (7.7 [7.4-7.9]) outperforming others.

evidence.title: Retrieval-augmented generation elevates local LLM quality in radiology contrast media consultation
evidence.comparator_used: Same local Llama 3.2-11B baseline without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate and mean rank of replies in synthetic iodinated contrast media consultations
evidence.effect: Hallucinations 0% vs 8% (χ²(Yates) = 6.38, p = 0.012); mean rank improved by 1.3 (Z = -4.82, p < 0.001)
evidence.tradeoff: Performance gaps with cloud-based models persisted despite RAG.
evidence.quote: Under controlled conditions, RAG eliminated hallucinations (0% vs 8%; χ²₍Yates₎ = 6.38, p = 0.012) and improved mean rank by 1.3 (Z = -4.82, p < 0.001), though performance gaps with cloud models persist.

evidence.title: Large language models as clinical decision-support tools in multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders: A comparative study of ChatGPT-4o and neurologists
evidence.venue: Multiple sclerosis journal - experimental, translational and clinical
evidence.comparator_used: Practicing neurologists (290 respondents); the study also ran ChatGPT-4o without RAG, but the abstract reports no numbers for that arm
evidence.outcome: Guideline-adherent decision-making at item level across 21 clinical vignettes
evidence.effect: 80.5% vs. 66.5%; p = 0.001 for ChatGPT-4o with RAG vs neurologists. Multivariable GEE odds ratio for ChatGPT-4o as predictor of evidence-based decision-making was 3.17 (95% CI 2.05-4.88; p < 0.0001).
evidence.tradeoff: Performance was no better than neurologists in emerging biomarker scenarios (e.g., serum neurofilament light chain) where clinical consensus is still evolving.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4o with RAG achieved significantly higher guideline adherence in decision-making than neurologists (80.5% vs. 66.5%; p = 0.001).

evidence.title: Decreasing Administrative Effort Related to Non-Approval of Image-guidED Procedures Using Large Language Models - The DENIED-AI Pilot Study
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting without retrieval
evidence.outcome: Reviewer-rated content and grammar quality of insurance appeal letters
evidence.effect: Mean content and grammar scores were 3.9 ± 0.95 and 4.3 ± 0.9 (out of 5), with no significant differences by model or technique (p >.05)
evidence.quote: Mean content and grammar scores were 3.9 ± 0.95 and 4.3 ± 0.9 (out of 5), with no significant differences by model or technique (p >.05).

evidence.title: Diagnostic Accuracy Masks Outdated Reasoning: Evaluating LLMs on Evolving Clinical Guidelines
evidence.comparator_used: No corpus access (no-context baseline, relying on training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Superseded-guideline vocabulary density in model responses
evidence.effect: Injecting guideline context of any kind increased superseded-vocabulary use for every model relative to the no-context baseline.
evidence.tradeoff: One biomedically fine-tuned model showed a distractor-driven accuracy collapse to 17.9–25.0% under injected context. Stated rationale was valid in only 53.7% of responses despite near-ceiling conclusion accuracy.
evidence.quote: First, injecting guideline context of any kind increased superseded-vocabulary use for every model relative to the no-context baseline.

evidence.title: Adaptive Fast-Slow Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional Classification of Prenatal Ultrasound Reports: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Same DeepSeek-V3.2 models (base and reasoning) without RAG, assessed on internal retrieval datasets and external test datasets
evidence.outcome: Classification performance on the subjective severity tasks
evidence.effect: RAG significantly improved both models on internal retrieval datasets (P<.05) but not on external test datasets (P>.05). Adding RAG to V3.2-R lowered accuracy to 81%, versus 86% without RAG.
evidence.tradeoff: Adding RAG to V3.2-R degraded performance on external data, suggesting potential noise interference. The authors say the finding is tied to their setup and current retrieval implementation.
evidence.quote: Crucially, while RAG significantly improved both models' performance on internal retrieval datasets (P<.05), this benefit did not generalize to external test datasets (P>.05).

evidence.title: Authoritative Textbook-Augmented Large Language Models for High-Altitude Public Health Medical Education in the Xizang Autonomous Region: Cross-Sectional Comparative Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline DeepSeek R1 without textbook retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Multidimensional expert-rated scores (comprehensiveness, accuracy, clarity, relevance) on an 80-question high-altitude public health benchmark
evidence.effect: HPHME-Xplus-RAG median 8.00 [IQR 7.88-8.00] vs baseline DeepSeek R1 median 7.63 [IQR 7.38-7.88]; P<.001, r_rb=0.68 (large effect)
evidence.quote: The deployed retrieval-augmented model integrating the authoritative textbooks and the optimal LLM DeepSeek R1, HPHME-Xplus-RAG, achieved remarkable improvement in multidimensional scores compared to baseline DeepSeek R1 (median 8.00 [IQR 7.88-8.00] vs median 7.63 [IQR 7.38-7.88]; P<.001, r_rb=0.68, indicating a large effect).

evidence.title: Implementing Generative Artificial Intelligence in a Tertiary Hospital Health Screening Center
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose AI models (without institution-specific retrieval)
evidence.outcome: Completeness, safety, and overall preference of chatbot responses
evidence.effect: Institution-specific RAG chatbot outperformed general-purpose AI models in completeness, safety, and overall preference; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: An institution-specific retrieval-augmented generation chatbot showed favorable preliminary usability and outperformed general-purpose AI models in completeness, safety, and overall preference.

evidence.title: Almanac: Retrieval-Augmented Language Models for Clinical Medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Standard LLMs without retrieval (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Bing) answering the same clinical scenarios
evidence.outcome: Factuality, completeness and safety of answers to clinical scenarios (n = 130) rated by a panel of 5 physicians
evidence.effect: Significant increases in factuality (mean of 18% at p-value < 0.05) across all specialties, with improvements in completeness and safety
evidence.quote: Performance on a novel dataset of clinical scenarios (n = 130) evaluated by a panel of 5 board-certified and resident physicians demonstrates significant increases in factuality (mean of 18% at p-value < 0.05) across all specialties, with improvements in completeness and safety.

evidence.title: Generating guideline-concordant and safe recommendations for diabetic kidney disease management via a hierarchical retrieval-augmented large language model
evidence.comparator_used: unaugmented baseline LLMs (no retrieval)
evidence.outcome: accuracy and guideline compliance of DKD recommendations, and safety-critical errors (e.g., medication contraindications by renal function stage), rated by 12 blinded physicians
evidence.effect: RAG-enhanced system significantly outperformed unaugmented models on accurate, guideline-compliant recommendations and substantially reduced safety-critical errors; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Our evaluation reveals that the RAG-enhanced system significantly outperforms unaugmented models in providing accurate, guideline-compliant recommendations.

evidence.title: Development and Evaluation of an Augmented Artificial Intelligence Model for Urogynecology Queries
evidence.comparator_used: Standard ChatGPT-4.0 without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Total QAMAI quality score (accuracy, clarity, relevance, completeness, usefulness, sources) rated by six urogynecologists for 10 common patient questions
evidence.effect: Median total QAMAI 22 (IQR 19-25) vs 16 (IQR 13-18), p < 0.01; higher in all six domains; sensitivity analysis excluding unblinded Source domain 18 (IQR 16-20) vs 14.5 (IQR 11-17), p < 0.01; raters preferred retrieval-augmented model in 81% of responses
evidence.quote: The retrieval-augmented model demonstrated significantly higher total QAMAI scores than the standard model (median 22 [interquartile range, IQR, 19-25] vs 16 [IQR 13-18], p < 0.01) and outperformed the standard model in all six domains.

evidence.title: Low-energy small language models with retrieval-augmented generation can surpass large-model performance in rheumatology
evidence.comparator_used: Same models without RAG (training knowledge alone), also compared with and without a predefined diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic and therapeutic accuracy (F1) and RAGAS factual consistency/relevance on ten rheumatology cases
evidence.effect: Mixtral-8x7b with RAG had the highest diagnostic F1 (72%), therapeutic F1 (73%) and RAGAS score (81%). Nemotron-70b without RAG reached 71% diagnostic F1, and Qwen-Turbo without retrieval reached 72% therapeutic F1. Performance varied substantially across models and configurations.
evidence.tradeoff: Clinically relevant errors persisted across all models, so expert oversight is still needed.
evidence.quote: Mixtral-8 × 7b-32768 with RAG achieved the highest diagnostic (72%) and therapeutic (73%) F1 scores.

evidence.title: Evaluation of large language models and retrieval-augmented generation for clinical reasoning in pediatric myopia: a 50-case real-world study
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline LLMs without RAG (GPT Base, Gemini Base, Grok Base) relying on training knowledge alone
evidence.outcome: Clinician consensus alignment, automated Accuracy/Utility/Safety scores, and high-risk recommendation rate in pediatric myopia cases
evidence.effect: RAG models achieved 90-94% consensus alignment vs 68-82% for baselines; high-risk recommendation rate 0% in all RAG models vs 6-14% for baselines; GPT-RAG weighted automated score 7.46 vs GPT Base 7.37
evidence.quote: Crucially, the probability of high-risk recommendations-those capable of causing severe vision loss-was eliminated (0%) in all RAG models, whereas baseline models exhibited high-risk error rates of 6-14%.

evidence.title: Representation Before Retrieval: Structured Patient Artifacts Reduce Hallucination in Clinical AI Systems
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline LLM without retrieval (C0), compared with RAG over raw clinical text (C1)
evidence.outcome: Unsupported claim rate
evidence.effect: Unsupported claims rose from 5.0% (95% CI: 3.8–6.4%) at baseline to 43.6% (95% CI: 40.1–47.2%) with RAG, an 8.7-fold increase (p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 2.31)
evidence.tradeoff: RAG added a new failure mode: sharply more unsupported claims than the baseline LLM.
evidence.quote: Contrary to prevailing assumptions, RAG increases rather than decreases hallucination in clinical text generation.

evidence.title: A Chatbot for the Management of Bipolar Disorder: Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation With an Open-Weight Large Language Model to Answer Clinical Questions Based on the CANMAT and ISBD 2018 Guidelines for Bipolar Disorder: Un dialogueur pour la prise en charge du trouble bipolaire : utiliser la génération augmentée par récupération avec un grand modèle de langage (GML) à poids ouverts pour répondre aux questions cliniques fondées sur les lignes directrices de 2018 de CANMAT et de l'ISBD relatives au trouble bipolaire
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of psychiatry. Revue canadienne de psychiatrie
evidence.comparator_used: Base Llama 3.3 70B model alone (training knowledge only, no retrieval)
evidence.outcome: Guideline consistency of answers to bipolar disorder clinical vignette queries, rated by expert psychiatrists (3-point scale); preference ratings
evidence.effect: 110/126 (87.3%) RAG responses rated as correct as or more correct than baseline; fully consistent 80 (63.5%) vs 24 (19.0%); major deviation 10 (7.9%) vs 48 (38.1%); OR = 9.1, 95% CI [5.3-16.3], P < 0.001; RAG preferred in 78.7% of cases
evidence.tradeoff: Performance varied by vignette, with some errors in both retrieval and reasoning; 10 RAG answers still had major deviation.
evidence.quote: Ordinal regression showed RAG responses were significantly more likely to be more correct (OR = 9.1, 95% CI [5.3-16.3], P < 0.001), which was consistent across all raters.

evidence.title: Incorporating information retrieval into AI chatbots for patient education on thyroid eye disease
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose ChatGPT (GPT-4o-mini) answering without retrieval
evidence.outcome: Clinical quality (relevance, accuracy, balance, scope) and non-clinical quality (empathy, understandability, readability) of patient-education answers on thyroid eye disease
evidence.effect: Clinical mean score 5.55 for ChatGPT-RAG vs 4.94 for ChatGPT. ChatGPT-RAG was intermediate overall, trailing ChatGPT on non-clinical metrics (g = 0.44) and trailing OpenEvidence clinically (g = 0.53).
evidence.tradeoff: The RAG model scored lower than plain ChatGPT on non-clinical metrics (empathy, understandability, actionability).
evidence.quote: Across both domains, ChatGPT-RAG achieved intermediate performance, more closely trailing OpenEvidence clinically (g = 0.53) and ChatGPT with respect to non-clinical metrics (g = 0.44).

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model for Angiographic Prediction of Coronary Physiology
evidence.comparator_used: Same GPT-5.2 model without retrieval-augmented generation (No-RAG), given identical angiographic frames and structured clinical text
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM-predicted and invasively measured iFR (MAE, RMSE, correlation) and threshold-based classification accuracy
evidence.quote: With RAG, point estimates favored improved continuous agreement, with MAE decreasing to 0.029, RMSE to 0.038, and correlation increasing to r = 0.830 (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Development of retrieval-augmented generation-based large language model for drug-induced liver injury using Livertox data
evidence.comparator_used: Non-RAG GPT-4o variants (unconstrained, and soft-constrained with a prompt to reference LiverTox), relying on training knowledge
evidence.outcome: Hepatologist-rated accuracy and completeness (5-point Likert) and hallucination rate for DILI questions
evidence.effect: RAG-LLMs outperformed non-RAG in accuracy (p<0.001) and completeness (p<0.01); effect sizes d=0.778 (accuracy) and d=0.526 (completeness); no hallucinations observed in RAG-LLM outputs vs several hallucinated responses in both non-RAG GPT-4o variants; GPT-4o (RAG) highest overall score 4.47±0.10
evidence.quote: RAG-LLMs outperformed non-RAG GPT-4o variants in accuracy (p<0.001) and completeness (p<0.01).

evidence.title: [Can ChatGPT Responses Be Improved by Incorporating S3 Clinical Practice Guidelines?]
evidence.comparator_used: Same GPT-4 questions answered without the guideline, relying on the model's training knowledge alone
evidence.outcome: Response accuracy and conciseness, rated 1-3 by three ENT specialists
evidence.effect: Accuracy 1.77 vs. 1.26 (p = 0.003); conciseness 1.96 vs. 1.50 (p = 0.004)
evidence.quote: Providing the guideline as a PDF together with the respective question resulted in a significant improvement in accuracy (1.77 vs. 1.26; p = 0.003) and conciseness (1.96 vs. 1.50; p = 0.004).

evidence.title: Enhanced LLM-supported instructions for medication use through retrieval-augmented generation
evidence.comparator_used: Llama3 with a standard prompt (model1) and with an enhanced structured prompt without retrieval (model2)
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated adequacy and clarity of generated patient medication instructions; critical errors
evidence.effect: Adequacy median (IQR) 93.0 (40.0) vs 94 (53.3) vs 100 (15.0), p = 0.001; clarity 90.0 (60.0) vs 92 (55.0) vs 95.0 (24.0), p = 0.012, for model1, model2, model3 (RAG on PIL). Enhanced prompt plus RAG reduced critical errors such as incorrect and incomplete instructions and factual inaccuracies.
evidence.quote: RAG introduction significantly improved instructions adequacy: median (interquartile range) 93.0 (40.0) vs. 94 (53.3) vs 100 (15.0), p = 0.001, and clarity 90.0 (60.0) vs. 92 (55.0) vs 95.0 (24.0), p = 0.012, for model1, model2, and model3 respectively.

evidence.title: EndoBot: An LLM Workflow-Driven Agent for Intelligent Gastrointestinal Endoscopy Consultation
evidence.comparator_used: Standalone LLM without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and safety of AI-driven GI endoscopy consultation
evidence.effect: Reported as significantly improved accuracy and safety versus standalone LLMs; no numerical values given in the text
evidence.tradeoff: Challenges persist in edge cases and non-Chinese inquiries; clinician oversight remains essential.
evidence.quote: This study demonstrates that RAG-enhanced Agent significantly improve the accuracy and safety of AI-driven GI endoscopy consultations compared to standalone LLMs.

evidence.title: Fine-Tuning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Hybrid Large Language Models for Postoperative Decision Support: Comparative Analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline Gemini 2.5 Flash without retrieval (training knowledge alone); also compared with fine-tuning and hybrid
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy on 150 postoperative queries (expert-rated)
evidence.effect: baseline 68% vs RAG 91.3% (P<.001, all knowledge-enhanced models vs baseline); fine-tuning 92.7%, fine-tuning+RAG 97.3%; fine-tuning and RAG broadly comparable on most secondary outcomes
evidence.tradeoff: Knowledge-enhanced models had lower readability than baseline, partly attributed to standardized safety boilerplate; baseline lacked equivalent safety/deferral instructions, which likely influenced safety findings.
evidence.quote: All knowledge-enhanced models significantly outperformed baseline in overall accuracy (baseline 68% vs fine-tuning 92.7%, RAG 91.3%, fine-tuning+RAG 97.3%; P<.001).

evidence.title: Assessment of Large Language Models in Colorectal Cancer Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Decision-Making: A Retrospective Single-Center Comparison of Guideline-Integrated General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specialized Models
evidence.comparator_used: MedGemma 27B operating without external guideline retrieval
evidence.outcome: Concordance with MTB decisions and clinical safety rate
evidence.effect: Guideline-integrated Gemini 2.5: κ = 0.792, 85.0% exact concordance, 83.7% safety. MedGemma without retrieval: κ = 0.566-0.610, accuracy 70.3-73.5%, safety 62.3-62.7%; p < 0.001.
evidence.tradeoff: Retrieval was not isolated. The arms differ in both model and guideline access, so the effect cannot be attributed to retrieval alone.
evidence.quote: A guideline-integrated general-purpose LLM demonstrated superior concordance and safety compared with a domain-specialized model operating without external retrieval, supporting its adjunctive use within MTBs while preserving expert clinical judgment.

evidence.title: ARTEMIS: a pilot study comparing AI-based and expert therapeutic decisions in simulated clinical cases of neuroendocrine neoplasms
evidence.comparator_used: Customised GPT with static domain knowledge (GPTs)
evidence.outcome: Agreement with expert benchmark for systemic therapy recommendations
evidence.effect: RAG and GPTs both 70.0% agreement vs expert benchmark 63.8%; both met the -10% non-inferiority margin but not the -5% threshold. RAG tended to propose fewer additional tests and lower costs.
evidence.quote: RAG and GPTs achieved 70.0% agreement versus the expert benchmark (63.8%), meeting the exploratory -10% non-inferiority margin but not the stricter -5% threshold.

evidence.title: An antibiotic chatbot: Evaluation of a retrieval-augmented generation approach for providing guideline-based antimicrobial advice
evidence.comparator_used: Same locally-deployed LLM (gpt-oss-20b) without RAG-based local guideline context, and a frontier model (gpt-5.4) without RAG
evidence.outcome: Proportion of answers to simulated antimicrobial advice questions judged fully correct
evidence.effect: With RAG, 162/186 (87%) attempted answers were fully correct. Without RAG, 21/186 (11%) were fully correct with the same local LLM and 92/200 (46%) with gpt-5.4.
evidence.tradeoff: RAG still produced occasional errors (5% incorrect, 8% partially correct), performance was lower in complex scenarios such as renal impairment, and only 5/9 (56%) out-of-scope questions were correctly identified. Median generation time was 12 s (single-stage).
evidence.quote: LLMs without RAG-based local guideline context had lower performance: 21/186 (11%) answers to simulated questions fully correct with the same locally-deployed LLM and 92/200 (46%) with a current frontier model (gpt-5.4).

evidence.title: Concordance between GPT-4 and a multidisciplinary tumor board in pancreatic cancer: A prospective pilot study
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4 recommendations before additional prompting with the abstracts (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Concordance of treatment and diagnostic recommendations between the multidisciplinary tumor board and GPT-4
evidence.effect: Overall concordance was 73.3% (κ = 0.64, p < 0.0001) and did not improve following literature prompting with 41 high-ranking abstracts. No post-prompting figure is given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The overall concordance rate between the MDT and GPT-4 was 73.3% (κ = 0.64, p < 0.0001) and did not improve following literature prompting.

evidence.title: Comparison of Large Language Model-Based Systems and Prompt Engineering for Internal Medicine Clinical Pharmacy Cases
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Clinical Pharmacy : JACCP
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose ChatGPT 4o without RAG (2x2 factorial with prompt template)
evidence.outcome: Composite of response accuracy and completeness
evidence.effect: Predicted probabilities for meeting primary outcome: GPT no Template 0.54, GPT with Template 0.60, OpenEvidence no Template 0.64, OpenEvidence with Template 0.52; no statistically significant interactions
evidence.quote: Neither the use of health care provider domain-specific LLM with RAG nor a prompt engineering template was found to improve LLM-based system accuracy and completeness.

evidence.title: Improving Accuracy and Source Transparency in Responses to Soft Tissue Sarcoma Queries Using GPT-4o Enhanced with German Evidence-Based Guidelines
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4o without RAG (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy, comprehensiveness and safety, and error rate, for soft tissue sarcoma queries
evidence.effect: RAG outperformed non-RAG across all evaluated areas (p < 0.05); error rate 40% without RAG reduced to 10% with RAG
evidence.tradeoff: The model still produced incorrect responses in certain complex scenarios, and caution is advised in clinical use, particularly for rare diseases like sarcoma.
evidence.quote: GPT-4o with RAG outperformed the model without RAG across all evaluated areas (p < 0.05).

evidence.title: Large Language Model-Generated Patient Instructions for Prescriptions in Primary Health Care: Preclinical Algorithm Validation
evidence.comparator_used: Llama3.1-8B without retrieval (base model, training knowledge alone); ChatGPT-4.0 also compared
evidence.outcome: Overall quality score of generated medication instructions, plus incorrect-use and hallucination frequency
evidence.effect: Overall median 79.9 (IQR 34.4) for Llama3.1-8B-RAG vs 66.5 (IQR 50.9) for Llama3.1-8B, post hoc P=.44. Incorrect-use instructions: 22.8% (n=19) in both. Hallucinations: 9.1% (n=6) with RAG vs 13.6% (n=9) without, chi-square P=.67 across models. RAG vs ChatGPT-4.0 overall P=.05.
evidence.tradeoff: Llama3.1-8B-RAG scored lower than ChatGPT-4.0 on language simplification (mean 5.44, SD 2.6 vs 7.05, SD 1.5; P<.001). RAG did not reduce incorrect-use instructions (22.8% in both).
evidence.quote: Llama3.1-8B-RAG received evaluations with similar overall scores to ChatGPT-4.0 (post hoc test, P=.05) and similar to Llama3.1-8B (post hoc test, P=.44).

evidence.title: Development and validation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and GraphRAG for complex clinical cases
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline LLM (GPT-4o) without retrieval
evidence.outcome: Clinical correctness and guideline adherence of CKD decision-support answers
evidence.effect: RAG-based methods outperformed the baseline LLM in clinical correctness and guideline adherence (no numeric values given in the abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: All RAG systems were limited by the scope of the indexed guideline and performed poorly when essential information was missing.
evidence.quote: RAG-based methods outperformed the baseline LLM in clinical correctness and guideline adherence.

evidence.title: Optimizing the Clinical Application of Rheumatology Guidelines Using Large Language Models: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework Integrating EULAR and ACR Recommendations
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline ChatGPT-o3-mini answering without context retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Answer quality (relevance, factual accuracy, safety, completeness, conciseness) and preference, rated by LLM-as-a-judge (Gemini 2.0 Flash) and by two blinded rheumatologists on a 15% sample
evidence.effect: RAG significantly outperformed baseline across all criteria (p<0.001) in LLM judge evaluation; rheumatologists confirmed (p<0.001 for accuracy, safety, completeness); RAG preferred by LLM judge in 92.8% of comparisons (p<0.001) and by human evaluators in 71.2%-74.8% (p<0.001)
evidence.quote: Analysis revealed that the RAG system significantly outperformed the baseline system across all criteria (p<0.001) in the LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT-4o and Four Open-Source Large Language Models in Generating Diagnoses Based on China's Rare Disease Catalog: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: qwen2.5:7b without retrieval augmentation (model knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy for rare diseases
evidence.effect: RAG raised qwen2.5:7b accuracy to 79.3% (χ²1=31.11, P<.001), with 85.9% retrieval precision
evidence.quote: RAG implementation enhanced qwen2.5:7b's accuracy to 79.3% (χ²1=31.11, P<.001) with 85.9% retrieval precision.

evidence.title: Locally deployed context-aware chatbot outperforms generic large language models for guideline-concordant pediatric imaging recommendations
evidence.comparator_used: Same Llama-3.1-8B without RAG (training knowledge alone); also GPT-4o and Claude Opus without RAG
evidence.outcome: Share of recommendations rated 'Usually appropriate' per ACR criteria, and run-to-run consistency
evidence.effect: ped-Llama (RAG) 80% (40/50) 'Usually appropriate' vs Llama-3.1-8B without RAG 46%, GPT-4o 54%, Claude Opus 46%; 90% when 'May be appropriate' also accepted; consistency across runs 72% vs 44-50% for generic LLMs
evidence.quote: ped-Llama achieved 80% (40/50) "Usually appropriate" recommendations, outperforming Llama-3.1-8B (46%), GPT-4o (54%), and Claude Opus (46%), and matching the specialist radiologist (76%).

evidence.title: Clinical decision support in hematological malignancies using a case-grounded AI agent
evidence.comparator_used: Plain LLM with no tools or retrieval (training knowledge only)
evidence.outcome: Tumor board concordance in the ablation (15 cases) and mean expert Likert rating (Q1-Q6) across 45 cases
evidence.effect: Ablation: plain LLM 0% concordance (mean score 4.1) vs full agent 86.7% (mean score 9.0). gpt-oss-120b mean Likert 4.22 ± 0.063 with HemaGuide vs 3.21 ± 0.39 plain (P = 0.0015).
evidence.tradeoff: Median latency 39 s per case (p95 62 s) on commodity hardware. Hallucinations still occurred in 2/664 cases (0.3%), so confabulation risk is mitigated but not eliminated. Plain models showed a 'stable but wrong' pattern.
evidence.quote: The plain LLM baseline achieved 0% concordance across all 15 cases (mean score 4.1); the full agent achieved 86.7% concordance (mean score 9.0).

evidence.title: Multimodal Large Language Model With Knowledge Retrieval Using Flowchart Embedding for Forming Follow-Up Recommendations for Pancreatic Cystic Lesions
evidence.comparator_used: Default knowledge and flowchart embedding; the T026 arm was plain-text RAG from the ACR IFC algorithm PDF document.
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLM follow-up recommendations for pancreatic cystic lesion management
evidence.effect: Radiologist 1: default knowledge 42.4%, plain-text RAG 23.7%, flowchart embedding 89.9% (p < .001); radiologist 2: 39.9%, 24.2%, and 91.9% (p < .001); radiologist 3: 40.9%, 25.3%, and 91.9% (p < .001).
evidence.quote: The accuracy of the LLM follow-up recommendations based on default knowledge, plain-text RAG, and flowchart embedding for radiologist 1 was 42.4%, 23.7%, and 89.9% (p < .001), respectively; radiologist 2 was 39.9%, 24.2%, and 91.9% (p < .001); and radiologist 3 was 40.9%, 25.3%, and 91.9% (p < .001).

evidence.title: Detecting emergencies in patient portal messages using large language models and knowledge graph-based retrieval-augmented generation
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt-only LLM without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Emergency triage performance of patient portal messages
evidence.effect: Models with RAG outperformed the LLM without retrieval; the best RAG model (knowledge graph, global search) reached accuracy 0.99, sensitivity 0.98, specificity 0.99
evidence.quote: The traditional LLM without any retrieval mechanism underperformed compared to models with RAG, which aligns with the expected benefits of augmenting LLMs with domain-specific knowledge sources.

evidence.title: First, do NOHARM: a medical safety benchmark and randomized study of physician and AI teaming on clinical consultations
evidence.comparator_used: Generalist LLMs without retrieval augmentation
evidence.outcome: Harm potential / safety performance of consultation recommendations (NOHARM benchmark)
evidence.effect: RAG-based clinical AI tools outperformed generalist LLMs; no numeric effect given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Even the RAG clinical AI tools carried potential for severe harm, with errors of omission accounting for more than 80% of severe errors across systems
evidence.quote: Harm potential was not uniform across systems, with clinical AI tools outperforming generalist LLMs, and multi-agent AI teaming further improving performance in generalist models.

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence-Generated Multiple-Choice Questions in Wilderness Medicine: Quality, Feasibility, and Time Savings for Educators
evidence.comparator_used: General Gemini AI without grounding (training knowledge alone), with human-written questions as a reference
evidence.outcome: Quality ratings of generated MCQs (accuracy, clarity, complexity, relevance) and respondent correct-answer rates
evidence.effect: General AI differed significantly from human-written questions on accuracy, clarity and complexity but not relevance. Grounded AI showed no significant difference from human-written questions on any of the 5 metrics. Respondents were significantly more likely to answer both general and grounded AI questions correctly than human-written ones. The abstract reports no direct grounded vs general AI test.
evidence.tradeoff: AI-generated questions were easier to answer correctly than human-written ones, so the authors say difficulty must be sufficiently high and questions should be edited by a human expert.
evidence.quote: No statistically significant differences were found between grounded AI and human-written questions on any of the 5 metrics.

evidence.title: Evaluating the appropriateness and safety of generative AI in delivering lifestyle guidance for atrial fibrillation patients
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4o without retrieval (training knowledge alone), with electrophysiologist responses as a further reference
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated quality of lifestyle guidance for AF patients (error rate, specialized content, empathy, helpfulness, accuracy)
evidence.effect: Against electrophysiologists, GPT-4o had a lower error rate and significantly higher specialized content, empathy and helpfulness. DB GPT and PubMed GPT (RAG) were only similar to electrophysiologists on these dimensions, with strengths in exercise-related specialized content and diet-related accuracy. No numeric values are given in the abstract, and no direct RAG vs GPT-4o test is reported.
evidence.quote: DB GPT and PubMed GPT showed similar error rates, proportions of specialized content, empathy, and helpfulness compared to electrophysiologists, but exhibited strengths in specialized content in exercise-related and accuracy in diet-related dimensions.

evidence.title: Applying generative AI with retrieval augmented generation to summarize and extract key clinical information from electronic health records
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with the Llama 2 13B model alone, without RAG
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of generated structured summaries about clients' nutritional status from EHR data
evidence.effect: overall accuracy improved from 93.25% to 99.25%, a 6% increase
evidence.quote: The addition of RAG improved the summarization process, leading to a 6% increase and achieving an accuracy of 99.25%.

evidence.title: Blinded Expert Evaluation of Large Language Models for Osteoporosis Case Management in Older Adults: Impact of Direct Guideline Integration
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT 4.5 base model without guideline loaded (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated quality score (5 domains, max 25) incl. scientific accuracy and guideline compliance
evidence.effect: ChatGPT 4.5 base 22.76/25 (95% CI 22.30–23.22) vs ChatGPT 4.5 + guideline 21.42 and NotebookLM + guideline 21.56; base model significantly superior to three panels (Friedman χ²=18.377; p = 0.0004); differences only in scientific accuracy (p = 0.0006) and guideline compliance (p < 0.0001)
evidence.quote: While ChatGPT 4.5’s performance aligns with findings, the lack of benefit from guideline uploading suggests unstructured presentation may be inadequate for integration.

evidence.title: MTS-Bench: A Manchester Triage System Benchmark for Language Model Triage Safety
evidence.comparator_used: OpenAI GPT-5.1 general-purpose model answering without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Undertriage rate on the ordered MTS scale across 156 prompts per system
evidence.effect: GPT-5.1 undertriaged 44.2% (69/156; 95% CI 36.7 to 52.1), including 75.0% of Red and 73.4% of Orange prompts. Both DR. INFO configurations undertriaged 11.5% (18/156; 95% CI 7.4 to 17.5), Fisher's exact p = 1.0e-10. With the misleading GP anchoring statement, GPT-5.1 undertriaged 8/8 Red prompts and DR. INFO undertriaged none.
evidence.quote: On this benchmark, replacing a general purpose language model with an agentic retrieval augmented system over a curated clinical knowledge base substantially reduced the undertriage rate.

evidence.title: ChatGPT in Occupational Medicine: A Comparative Study with Human Experts
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT answering without legislative context (training knowledge alone); human physician answers served as the reference
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated answer completeness and accuracy on a 5-point Likert scale, plus user preference
evidence.effect: No numbers in the abstract. ChatGPT with legislative context was comparable to professional doctors on completeness. Physicians still outperformed ChatGPT on accuracy. The abstract does not report the with-context versus without-context difference directly.
evidence.tradeoff: Users tended to prefer human-generated answers even when ChatGPT had legislative context.
evidence.quote: Occupational physicians perform better than ChatGPT in generating accurate questions on a 5-point likert score, while ChatGPT with access to legislative context is comparable to professional doctors in providing complete answers.

evidence.title: Augmenting Large Language Models With National Comprehensive Cancer Network Guidelines for Improved and Standardized Adjuvant Therapy Recommendations in Postoperative Breast Cancer Cases
evidence.comparator_used: Unaugmented general LLMs Claude-2 and GPT-4, evaluated against expert multidisciplinary tumor board recommendations as the reference
evidence.outcome: Accuracy/concordance of adjuvant therapy recommendations for postoperative breast cancer cases across seven treatment modalities
evidence.effect: TSB overall accuracy 0.89, Claude-2 0.86, GPT-4 0.78; GPT-4 had lower accuracy in genetic testing recommendations (OR, 0.05 [95% CI, 0.015 to 0.149]; P < .001), and Claude-2 was less accurate in radiotherapy recommendations (OR, 0.41 [95% CI, 0.17 to 0.98]; P = .040).
evidence.quote: TSB demonstrated the highest overall accuracy (0.89), followed by Claude-2 (0.86) and GPT-4 (0.78).

evidence.title: Training ChatGPT for surgical decisions: Bariatric surgery analysis using algorithms and evidence
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT without context (training knowledge alone), before exposure to the 412 articles
evidence.outcome: Concordance of recommended bariatric surgery technique with actual clinical decisions (percentage agreement and Cohen's Kappa)
evidence.effect: Concordance 20.0% (Kappa = 0.003; p = 0.96) without context vs 25.8% (Kappa = 0.068; p = 0.29) after exposure to the articles; significant shift in the distribution of recommended procedures (p < 0.00001). SG recommendations fell from 56.8% to 35.7%, RYGB rose from 26.8% to 30.3%, SADI-S emerged at 17.1%, and dual options appeared in 4%.
evidence.quote: Concordance improved modestly to 25.8 % (Kappa = 0.068; p = 0.29), with a significant shift in global distribution (p < 0.00001).

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Language Models for Patient-Centered Periprocedural Anticoagulation in Interventional Radiology
evidence.comparator_used: Base Claude (same model without RAG integration, relying on training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Guideline concordance of periprocedural anticoagulation recommendations (withholding, withholding/reinitiation timeframes, INR thresholds), scored 0-2 by a human assessor
evidence.effect: RAG integration significantly improved Claude's performance across all categories, except platelet thresholds; RAG Claude achieved the highest overall guideline concordance (1.51/2). Base Claude numbers not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: RAG integration significantly improved Claude's performance across all categories, except platelet thresholds.

evidence.title: Optimization of hepatological clinical guidelines interpretation by large language models: a retrieval augmented generation-based framework
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline GPT-4 Turbo without guideline context (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy of answers on HCV guideline questions
evidence.effect: Accuracy improved from 43 to 99% (p < 0.001) when guidelines were provided as context in a coherent text corpus with non-text sources converted to text
evidence.quote: The results showed a significant improvement in accuracy from 43 to 99% (p < 0.001), when guidelines were provided as context in a coherent corpus of text and non-text sources were converted into text.

evidence.title: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation for guideline-grounded textual planning in implant dentistry: A comparative study
evidence.comparator_used: Standard GPT-4o (no retrieval) vs RAG-LLM using a knowledge base of international consensus reports and clinical treatment guides, on 40 vignettes processed twice each (160 plans)
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated clinical accuracy overall, plus domain scores for evidence traceability, citation precision and biomechanical spatial planning
evidence.effect: Overall clinical accuracy: no significant difference (P = 0.642). Evidence traceability and citation precision: RAG-LLM significantly better (P = 0.046). Biomechanical spatial planning: standard LLM better (P = 0.025). Neither model showed severe literature fabrication.
evidence.tradeoff: RAG showed 'retrieval bias' in soft-tissue complication scenarios, leading to inappropriate hard-tissue augmentation (overtreatment). Its advantage diminished in out-of-distribution synthetic cases lacking thematic overlap with the knowledge base. Continuous expert oversight is still needed.
evidence.quote: However, domain-specific analysis revealed that the RAG-LLM significantly outperformed the standard model in evidence traceability and citation precision (P = 0.046).

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of medication recommendation workflows: Retrieval augmentation, physician-RAG collaborative workflow, and prescribing quality
evidence.comparator_used: Base LLM without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Prescription-parameter accuracy (all-correct rate) and coverage of the expert reference standard
evidence.effect: All-correct rate 0.948 for Retrieval-augmented LLM vs 0.494 for Base LLM. The abstract reports improved coverage but gives no separate recall figures for the RAG-only arm.
evidence.quote: Retrieval augmentation improved coverage and prescribing accuracy, while Physician-RAG collaborative showed the highest agreement with the expert reference standard across completeness, safety screening, prioritization, and structured prescribing quality.

evidence.title: Evaluation of a cornea-specialized large language model for diagnostic and management accuracy in complex corneal cases
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose GPT-4o without the cornea-specific RAG corpus (and unaided clinicians)
evidence.outcome: Clinician diagnostic accuracy and next-step management accuracy in 39 complex corneal cases
evidence.effect: Diagnostic accuracy was 69.2%, 46.2%, 59.0% with general GPT-4o and 71.8%, 48.7%, 74.4% with the cornea-specialized RAG GPT-4o. Unaided it was 48.7%, 20.5%, 38.5%, and the specialized model improved on unaided for all clinicians (p<0.01). Management: unaided 76.9%, 87.2%, 59.0%; with the specialized model Ophthalmologist 3 improved to 71.8% (p<0.05), Ophthalmologist 1 stayed at 82.1%, Ophthalmologist 2 declined to 64.1% (p<0.05).
evidence.tradeoff: Management accuracy fell for Ophthalmologist 2, from 87.2% to 64.1% (p<0.05). Effects on management were inconsistent across clinicians.
evidence.quote: A cornea-specialized LLM enhanced with RAG improved diagnostic accuracy in complex corneal cases, particularly among clinicians with lower baseline performance.

evidence.title: Development and Testing of a Novel Large Language Model-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Medication Safety in 12 Clinical Specialties
evidence.comparator_used: LLM alone without RAG
evidence.outcome: Drug-related problem (DRP) / medication error identification performance across accuracy, precision, recall, and F1
evidence.effect: No numeric performance values reported in the abstract; reported as better with RAG-LLM than LLM alone, with accuracy improved in several categories.
evidence.tradeoff: Lower precision reported for RAG-LLM.
evidence.quote: RAG-LLM performed better compared to LLM alone.

evidence.title: From Guidelines to Real-Time Conversation: Expert-Validated Retrieval-Augmented and Fine-Tuned GPT-4 for Hepatitis C Management
evidence.venue: Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline GPT-4 Turbo without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy and clarity on open-ended HCV questions; correct DAA regimen selection in 25 simulated scenarios
evidence.effect: RAG-Top10 vs baseline: accuracy 91.7% vs 36.6% (p<0.001); clarity 91.7% vs 46.6% (p<0.001). RAG-Top1: 81.7% accuracy, 86.6% clarity (both p<0.001). Correct DAA regimen in 76% of cases with RAG-Top10 vs 24% for baseline (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: On open-ended questions, RAG-Top10 outperformed baseline in accuracy (91.7% vs. 36.6%; p < 0.001) and clarity (91.7% vs. 46.6%; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence-Driven Responses to Acute Liver Failure Queries: A Comparative Analysis Across Accuracy, Clarity, and Relevance
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT 4 without RAG (training knowledge alone), plus ChatGPT 3.5, BARD, CLAUDE and COPILOT
evidence.outcome: Likert ratings (1-5) of accuracy, clarity and relevance for responses to 16 acute liver failure questions or scenarios, rated by 4 independent investigators
evidence.effect: ChatGPT 4 + RAG scored 4.70 (accuracy), 4.89 (clarity) and 4.78 (relevance), against 3.67, 4.04 and 4.01 for ChatGPT 4 without RAG. The order of the three RAG scores is inferred from the abstract's ordering for ChatGPT 4.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT 4, augmented with RAG, demonstrated superior performance compared with others, consistently scoring the highest (4.70, 4.89, 4.78) across all 3 domains.

evidence.title: Empowering Personalized Pharmacogenomics with Generative AI Solutions
evidence.comparator_used: OpenAI's ChatGPT 3.5 (no retrieval from the CPIC knowledge base). The RAG assistant also used GPT-4, prompt engineering and guardrails, so the comparison is confounded.
evidence.outcome: Performance on a specialized PGx question catalog, especially provider-specific queries needing specialized data and citations
evidence.effect: Reported qualitatively as better performance than ChatGPT 3.5; no numeric effect given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy, relevancy and representative language still need improvement; ethical, regulatory and safety concerns remain.
evidence.quote: Compared with OpenAI’s ChatGPT 3.5, it demonstrated better performance, especially in provider-specific queries requiring specialized data and citations.

evidence.title: Retrieval-augmented generative AI enhances clinical reasoning in odontogenic sinusitis versus maxillary sinus mucositis
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Clinical text-only prompting and other prompting strategies without structured literature excerpts.
evidence.outcome: Clinical reasoning quality; diagnostic accuracy and safety were not significantly different.
evidence.effect: Clinical reasoning scores: F(3,123) = 4.32, p = 0.0058; ranked first or second in six of seven evaluation domains; no significant differences in diagnostic accuracy or safety.
evidence.quote: Combining structured literature and imaging with clinical text significantly improved clinical reasoning scores (F(3,123) = 4.32, p = 0.0058), ranking first or second in six of seven evaluation domains.

evidence.title: Rethinking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine: A Large-Scale, Systematic Expert Evaluation and Practical Insights
evidence.comparator_used: non-RAG variants (model without retrieved evidence)
evidence.outcome: Factuality and completeness of responses; relevance of retrieved passages and evidence selection
evidence.effect: Factuality and completeness dropped by up to 6% and 5% vs non-RAG; only 22% of top-16 passages relevant; evidence selection precision 41-43%, recall 27-49%
evidence.tradeoff: Standard RAG introduced a new failure mode: poor retrieval and evidence selection that contributed to the overall performance drop.
evidence.quote: Contrary to expectation, standard RAG often degraded performance: only 22% of top-16 passages were relevant, evidence selection remained weak (precision 41-43%, recall 27-49%), and factuality and completeness dropped by up to 6% and 5%, respectively, compared with non-RAG variants.

evidence.title: Evaluation of the integration of retrieval-augmented generation in large language model for breast cancer nursing care responses
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4 answering directly without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Overall satisfaction (primary), accuracy and empathy of responses to breast cancer nursing care questions
evidence.effect: Overall satisfaction 8.4 ± 0.84 vs. 5.4 ± 1.27 (p < 0.01); accuracy 8.6 ± 0.69 vs. 5.6 ± 0.96 (p < 0.01); empathy 8.4 ± 0.85 vs. 7.8 ± 1.22 (p > 0.05, no inter-group difference)
evidence.quote: The RAG-GPT group showed significantly higher overall satisfaction than that of the GPT-4 group (8.4 ± 0.84 vs. 5.4 ± 1.27, p < 0.01) as well as an improved accuracy of responses (8.6 ± 0.69 vs. 5.6 ± 0.96, p < 0.01).

evidence.title: Evaluating Adherence to Canadian Radiology Guidelines for Incidental Hepatobiliary Findings Using RAG-Enabled LLMs
evidence.venue: Canadian Association of Radiologists journal = Journal l'Association canadienne des radiologistes
evidence.comparator_used: Same LLMs (GPT-4o and o1-mini) without RAG, relying on training knowledge alone
evidence.outcome: Adherence to Canadian radiology guidelines for incidental hepatobiliary findings (319 clinical cases)
evidence.effect: GPT-4o: 97.2% with RAG vs 81.7% without; o1-mini: 95.1% with RAG vs 79.3% without; RAG-enabled configurations outperformed non-RAG counterparts (P < .05). RAG outputs also had improved reading ease and lower grade level scores, though still at advanced comprehension levels.
evidence.tradeoff: Response times for RAG-enabled models increased slightly due to additional retrieval processing but remained clinically acceptable.
evidence.quote: Model performance differed significantly across groups, with RAG-enabled configurations outperforming their non-RAG counterparts (P < .05).

evidence.title: EyeGPT for Patient Inquiries and Medical Education: Development and Validation of an Ophthalmology Large Language Model
evidence.comparator_used: Best fine-tuned model alone, without retrieval
evidence.outcome: Response quality score and hallucination proportion
evidence.effect: Mean 13.08 (SD 5.43) vs mean 15.14 (SD 4.64), P=.001; hallucinations 71/120 (59.2%) vs 57/120 (47.4%), P=.02 (as reported)
evidence.quote: Incorporating information retrieval from reliable sources, particularly ophthalmology textbooks, further improved the model's response compared with solely the best fine-tuned model (mean 13.08, SD 5.43 vs mean 15.14, SD 4.64; P=.001) and reduced hallucinations (71/120, 59.2% vs 57/120, 47.4%, P=.02).

evidence.title: Multi-Evidence Clinical Reasoning With Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Emergency Triage: Retrospective Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt-only baseline LLM (DeepSeek-V3) relying on training knowledge without retrieval
evidence.outcome: Triage accuracy and agreement with expert consensus; overtriage; weighted harm index
evidence.effect: QWK 0.902 vs 0.801; accuracy 0.802 vs 0.542 (P<.001); overtriage 28.8% to 12.7%; weighted harm index 13.7 vs 20.3 per 100 patients for baseline LLM
evidence.quote: In 3‑group analysis, MECR‑RAG reduced overtriage from 68/236 (28.8%) with the baseline LLM to 30/236 (12.7%) and maintained low undertriage from 4/236 (1.7%) to 3/236 (1.3%), with the largest gains in the diagnostically ambiguous yet operationally important categories 3 and 4.

evidence.title: Enhancing pancreatic cancer staging with large language models: the role of retrieval-augmented generation
evidence.comparator_used: Gemini 2.0 Flash given the guideline without RAG (REK+/RAG−), and Gemini 2.0 Flash without the guideline (REK−/RAG−, training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Staging accuracy for 100 fictional pancreatic cancer cases (overall, and TNM classification)
evidence.effect: Overall staging accuracy 70% with REK+/RAG+ vs 38% REK+/RAG− and 35% REK−/RAG−; TNM accuracy 80% vs 55% and 50%
evidence.quote: The REK+/RAG+ group achieved 70% staging accuracy, outperforming REK+/RAG− (38%) and REK−/RAG− (35%).

evidence.title: Evidence-Graded Decision Authorization for Safe Clinical AI: A Constrained Reasoning Framework
evidence.comparator_used: Unconstrained LLM relying on its own knowledge (no retrieval)
evidence.outcome: Unjustified inference rate and appropriate refusal rate
evidence.effect: Unjustified inference 47.7% (RAG) vs 48.7% (unconstrained), p=0.870; appropriate refusal 56.9% vs 56.9%, p=1.0; factual correctness 74.5% vs 69.8%
evidence.quote: An unexpected finding was that retrieval-augmented generation without an authorization gate failed to reduce unjustified inference relative to the unconstrained baseline (47.7% vs. 48.7%, p = 0.870) and produced no improvement in appropriate refusal (56.9% vs. 56.9%, p = 1.0), showing that information supply alone is not sufficient for inferential governance.

evidence.title: Precision Oncology in Non-small Cell Lung Cancer: A Comparative Study of Contextualized ChatGPT Models
evidence.comparator_used: Base GPT-4 and GPT-4o without guideline PDF context (training knowledge alone); prompt-only contextualization also tested
evidence.outcome: Agreement with NCCN guideline-preferred therapies and rate of guideline non-concordant therapy recommendations for NSCLC
evidence.effect: Agreement 23/24 for PDF+Prompt vs 17/24 for GPT-4 (P = 0.040) and 18/24 for GPT-4o (P = 0.089). Non-concordant therapies: 0 for PDF+Prompt vs 4/12 for GPT-4 (P = 0.093) and 5/12 for GPT-4o (P = 0.037). Prompting alone did not significantly improve agreement or reduce non-concordant recommendations. PDF+Prompt responses had lower word count and lower SMOG and Gunning Fog scores.
evidence.quote: The PDF+Prompt contextualized model demonstrated elevated agreement scores of 23/24 versus 17/24 for GPT-4 (P = 0.040) and 18/24 for GPT-4o (P = 0.089).

evidence.title: Transforming the Landscape of Clinical Information Retrieval Using Generative Artificial Intelligence: An Application in Machine Fault Analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Less source data context supplied to NotebookLM (varying amounts of background linear accelerator troubleshooting material)
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated response quality (hallucination, relevancy, correctness, completeness) for linear accelerator troubleshooting
evidence.effect: Responses improved with increasing source data context; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Results indicated that responses improved with increasing source data context and more specific prompt construction.

evidence.title: [A retrieval-augmented generation-based clinical decision support system for the restoration of endodontically treated teeth]
evidence.venue: Zhonghua kou qiang yi xue za zhi = Zhonghua kouqiang yixue zazhi = Chinese journal of stomatology
evidence.comparator_used: Same three LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen 2.5-72B-Instruct, GPT-3.5-turbo) in non-RAG mode, without guideline retrieval
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated decision accuracy, logical coherence and professional readability (Likert), plus ROUGE-L F1 and BERTScore F1 against expert-drafted standard restorative reports, for 30 post-endodontic restoration cases
evidence.effect: All models improved on all evaluation metrics in RAG mode versus non-RAG mode, with statistically significant differences. Highest BERTScore F1 in RAG mode was 0.91 (DeepSeek-V3). Significant model-by-RAG interactions for decision accuracy (χ2=10.11) and ROUGE-L F1 (χ2=8.57), so the size of the gain differed by model.
evidence.quote: The RAG-based CDSS-RAG-Pro improves the accuracy and interpretability of general-purpose LLM in decision-making for post-endodontic tooth restoration.

evidence.title: Reducing Hallucinations and Trade-Offs in Responses in Generative AI Chatbots for Cancer Information: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional chatbots with no reference information (LLM training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate of GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 chatbots
evidence.effect: Conventional chatbots about 40% hallucination vs CIS-RAG 0% (GPT-4) and 6% (GPT-3.5) and Google-RAG 6% (GPT-4) and 10% (GPT-3.5); conventional vs CIS OR 16.1 (95% CI 3.7-50.0, P<.001)
evidence.tradeoff: Conventional chatbots answered every question, but RAG chatbots sometimes declined to answer when information was lacking, with response rate falling to 36%-81%.
evidence.quote: Using RAG with reliable information sources significantly reduces the hallucination rate of generative AI chatbots and increases the ability to admit lack of information, making them more suitable for general use, where users need to be provided with accurate information.

evidence.title: Reliability and readability of five AI chatbots for concussion health advice across retrieval augmented and pretrained models
evidence.comparator_used: Standard pre-trained LLM chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini) answering from training knowledge, compared with RAG-based Perplexity Pro; zero-shot protocol on 11 concussion queries
evidence.outcome: Reliability and information quality of concussion advice (DISCERN, EQIP), scored by two blinded neurosurgeons against the 2023 Amsterdam Consensus Statement
evidence.effect: Perplexity Pro DISCERN 47.36 ± 4.84 and EQIP 65.00 ± 5.48, higher than ChatGPT and Gemini (p < 0.01); DISCERN and EQIP differed across models (p < 0.001). GQS did not differ significantly (p = 0.373).
evidence.tradeoff: JAMA transparency stayed uniformly low across all models (p < 0.001). All models exceeded the 6th-grade reading level, and most exceeded 10th-grade; Perplexity Pro was lowest at FKGL = 7.46. The RAG attribution is inferred ("likely") from a cross-platform comparison, not an isolated ablation. Human-in-the-loop verification is advised.
evidence.quote: Perplexity Pro secured the highest DISCERN (47.36 ± 4.84) and EQIP (65.00 ± 5.48) values, statistically surpassing foundational models like ChatGPT and Gemini (p < 0.01) - a performance gap likely driven by its RAG design.

evidence.title: A multimodal evidence-driven framework for clinical decision support in cognitive impairment
evidence.comparator_used: mHC classifier alone, without retrieval-augmented LLM reasoning
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance under progressive feature masking (missing data)
evidence.effect: Performance declined with increasing missingness for the mHC alone, whereas RAG-LLM correction mitigated this effect, especially under severe sparsity
evidence.quote: When the mHC was evaluated under progressive feature masking, performance declined with increasing missingness, whereas RAG-LLM correction mitigated this effect, especially under severe sparsity.

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Decision-Making in Emergency Care
evidence.venue: Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. Annual International Conference
evidence.comparator_used: Mixtral-8x7B Instruct without a retrieval mechanism (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Physician ratings of medical and content accuracy, case relevance, factual integrity and overall usability
