evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Long-context prompting with the most recent clinical notes (varying amounts of context) across GPT-5.4-mini, Mistral Medium 3 and DeepSeek V3.1
evidence.outcome: Task performance (F1 for imaging procedure extraction, Jaccard for antibiotic timelines, diagnosis generation) and token use
evidence.effect: Imaging Procedures: RAG exceeded long-context performance by 0.17-9.83 F1 across all models using fewer than 8K tokens. Antibiotic Timelines: <8K retrieved tokens matched long-context recent-notes performance (between -3.26 and +3.24 Jaccard). Diagnosis Generation: performance largely static across methods and models.
evidence.tradeoff: No gain for diagnosis generation, the hardest task. Missing information in the notes, often from inter-hospital transfers, limited performance to some extent.
evidence.quote: For Imaging Procedures, RAG strongly outperformed recent-note inputs and exceeded long-context performance (by 0.17-9.83 F1 across all models) using fewer than 8K tokens.

evidence.title: First, Do No Harm (With LLMs): Mitigating Racial Bias via Agentic Workflows
evidence.comparator_used: Standalone DeepSeek V3 without the retrieval-based agentic workflow
evidence.outcome: Explicit racial bias in differential diagnosis ranking (mean p-value, median p-value, mean difference)
evidence.effect: Improvement of 0.0348 in mean p-value, 0.1166 in median p-value, and 0.0949 in mean difference relative to the standalone model; improvement not uniform across every metric
evidence.quote: When embedded in an agentic workflow, DeepSeek V3 showed an improvement of 0.0348 in mean p-value, 0.1166 in median p-value, and 0.0949 in mean difference relative to the standalone model, although improvement was not uniform across every metric.

evidence.title: Extraction of Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) Concepts from Clinical Notes Utilizing Large Language Models (LLM) with Model Context Protocol (MCP)
evidence.comparator_used: No Tools baseline (internal knowledge only)
evidence.outcome: HPO extraction F1, precision and mapping error rate with real-time HPO ontology retrieval
evidence.effect: Mean aggregate F1 0.46 to 0.72 (p<0.001); Mapping Error Rate 40.9% to 7.8% (p<0.001); Precision 56% to 90%
evidence.quote: Mean aggregate F1-score increased from 0.46 (SD 0.22) in the baseline condition to 0.72 (SD 0.15) with tools (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation vs. Long-Context Input for Clinical Reasoning over EHRs
evidence.comparator_used: Long-context prompting with the most recent clinical notes (and smaller amounts of recent-note context)
evidence.outcome: Extraction and reasoning performance over inpatient EHR notes (F1 for imaging procedures, Jaccard for antibiotic timelines, diagnosis generation) and token use
evidence.effect: Imaging Procedures: RAG exceeded long-context performance by 0.17-9.83 F1 across all models using <8K tokens. Antibiotic Timelines: <8K retrieved tokens matched long-context recent-notes performance (-3.26 to +3.24 Jaccard). Diagnosis Generation: performance largely static across methods and models.
evidence.quote: For Imaging Procedures, RAG strongly outperformed recent-note inputs and exceeded long-context performance (by 0.17-9.83 F1 across all models) using fewer than 8K tokens.

evidence.title: Assessing the utility of large language models for phenotype-driven gene prioritization in the diagnosis of rare genetic disease
evidence.comparator_used: LLM without retrieval-augmented generation (baseline prompting)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of identifying diagnosed genes within top-50 predictions
evidence.effect: RAG did not improve accuracy (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Advanced techniques such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and few-shot learning did not improve the accuracy.

evidence.title: MAM-AI: An On-Device Medical Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Nurses and Midwives in Zanzibar
evidence.comparator_used: Same 4B generator without retrieved context (oracle-context vs no-context generator evaluation)
evidence.outcome: Answer quality of the small on-device generator
evidence.effect: Adding retrieved context did not improve the generator's answers (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: adding retrieved context does not improve its answers

evidence.title: Intelligent Framework for Adverse Drug Event Identification Using Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Nonaugmented generation (NAG, no retrieval) and static-augmented generation (SAG, fixed content in the prompt)
evidence.outcome: ADE identification F1-score and recall at the L3 (overlap) matching level across DeepSeek-V3, ERNIE 3.5-8K and GPT-4o
evidence.effect: RAG yielded higher F1-scores than NAG and SAG at L3 across the tested LLMs; best configuration DeepSeek-V3 with RAG had L3 F1 0.9638 (95% CI 0.9541-0.9727); GPT-4o recall rose from 0.6419 (NAG) to 0.9241 (RAG), FDR P=.003
evidence.quote: Across the tested LLMs, RAG yielded higher F1-scores than NAG and SAG at the L3 level.

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Reducing Hallucinations in Drug-Related Question Answering Systems
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline Llama 3.2 without retrieval (training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate, Faithfulness and Factual Accuracy on 150 drug-related question-answer pairs
evidence.effect: Hallucination rate fell from 47.8% to 12.3% (74.3% relative reduction); Faithfulness rose from 0.52 to 0.87; Factual Accuracy rose from 0.54 to 0.89
evidence.quote: Evaluated on a purpose-built dataset of 150 drug-related question–answer pairs spanning ten commonly used medications and multiple information categories, our RAG system reduces the hallucination rate from 47.8% to 12.3% — a 74.3% relative reduction — while improving Faithfulness from 0.52 to 0.87 and Factual Accuracy from 0.54 to 0.89.

evidence.title: Evaluating approaches of training a generative large language model for multi-label classification of unstructured electronic health records
evidence.comparator_used: Same Llama 3.1-8B without retrieval augmentation (model knowledge and prompt only), in zero-shot and few-shot settings
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall and F1 across four clinical tasks
evidence.effect: RAG improved performance only in few-shot learning, with no improvement reported for zero-shot. No numeric values given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Notably, PEFT significantly enhances model performance in both zero-shot and few-shot learning; however, RAG improves performance only in few-shot learning.

evidence.title: Evaluating Retrieval Augmented Generation-enhanced Large Language Models for Question Answering On German Neurovascular Guidelines
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4o-mini without RAG (pretrained model knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Answer correctness on questions about two German neurovascular guidelines, rated by two experts in consensus
evidence.effect: GPT-4o-mini with RAG: 57.6% correct, 15.3% wrong. GPT-4o-mini without RAG: 20.0% correct, 32.9% wrong. The other RAG-enhanced LLMs scored 56.6% to 70.6% correct.
evidence.tradeoff: Error rates stayed significant with RAG. Retrieval errors caused 80% of incorrect answers.
evidence.quote: GPT-4o-mini without RAG performed significantly worse (20.0%, 32.9% wrong).

evidence.title: Benchmarking large language models for question answering on German clinical practice guidelines
evidence.comparator_used: Same LLMs without retrieval (no RAG, training knowledge alone)
evidence.outcome: Multiple-choice accuracy on the cpgQA-DE benchmark of German guideline questions
evidence.effect: RAG substantially improved accuracy across all tested models and for most retrievers; best configuration GPT-5 with multilingual-e5-large reached 95% accuracy; gpt-oss-120b reached 90% with RAG
evidence.quote: RAG integration substantially improved accuracy across all tested models and for most retrievers.

evidence.title: Evaluating the performance of general vs retrieval-augmented generation large language models on oral and maxillofacial surgery board examinations
evidence.venue: International journal of oral and maxillofacial surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Non-tuned GPT-4o baseline using training knowledge alone, without retrieved examination materials
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on oral and maxillofacial surgery Phase A board examination questions (788 questions, 2017-2024)
evidence.effect: GPT-4o with RAG 50.9% vs GPT-4o non-tuned 51.4%; pairwise comparison P = 0.788
evidence.quote: Direct comparison between GPT-4o variants revealed no difference (P = 0.788), indicating that RAG with direct access to examination materials provided no benefit over baseline architecture.

controls.question: Should we invest in cleaning, restructuring and regularly updating the retrieval knowledge base?
controls.control: Restructure, deduplicate and conflict-check source documents before indexing, and regularly refresh the indexed corpus.
controls.comparator: Raw documents ingested once without curation or updates
controls.aim: Prevent retrieval of outdated, duplicate or conflicting content
variants: Preprocessing (deduplication, conflict checking) versus raw ingestion, same source snapshot
Scheduled refresh versus static corpus, same preprocessing
controls.family_label: retrieval-augmented generation, source citation, knowledge graphs, EHR grounding
tradeoffs: Organizations must invest in preparing well-structured knowledge documents. The B-line was only a proof of concept (6 chunks, one document section) with no statistical comparison. Level 1 inter-rater agreement was only fair (Fleiss kappa 0.269).
Rollback has a cost: p95 rollback takes 5.13 s at 78M assertions. No other burden is reported in the abstract.

evidence.title: Measurement of retrieved chunk quality from real-world knowledge in retrieval-augmented generation: A Phase 1 foundational study
evidence.comparator_used: A-line baseline: four institutional manuals ingested as-is, without restructuring
evidence.outcome: Retrieved chunk quality across five LLM-as-a-Judge metrics (including Faithfulness) in a proof-of-concept comparison
evidence.effect: A-line (594 chunks): median scores of 2.0 or below on all five metrics, with fewer than 20% of chunks scoring 4 or higher. B-line (6 chunks from one restructured section): perfect scores across all metrics.
evidence.tradeoff: Organizations must invest in preparing well-structured knowledge documents. The B-line was only a proof of concept (6 chunks, one document section) with no statistical comparison. Level 1 inter-rater agreement was only fair (Fleiss kappa 0.269).
evidence.quote: The B-line optimization achieved perfect scores across all metrics, demonstrating potential for improvement.

evidence.title: EviLedger: governing clinical AI with a verifiable evidence ledger
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-based retrieval without the evidence ledger layer (baseline not detailed in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Stale citations and unverifiable citations in LLM retrieval outputs
evidence.effect: Stale citations fell from 14.7% to 1.2%. Unverifiable citations fell from 28.4% to 2.3%.
evidence.tradeoff: Rollback has a cost: p95 rollback takes 5.13 s at 78M assertions. No other burden is reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: As an auditable memory layer for LLM-based retrieval, EviLedger reduces stale citations from 14.7% to 1.2% and unverifiable citations from 28.4% to 2.3%, while supporting p95 rollback in 5.13 s at 78M assertions.

controls.question: Should our RAG pipeline split documents by structure and meaning rather than fixed length?
controls.control: Use structure- or semantics-aware chunking based on headings, HTML structure or semantic boundaries with micro-headers.
controls.comparator: Fixed-length or naive sentence chunking
controls.aim: Keep clinically coherent passages intact to improve retrieval quality
controls.family_label: retrieval-augmented generation, source citation, knowledge graphs, EHR grounding

evidence.title: Comparative Evaluation of Advanced Chunking for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models for Clinical Decision Support
evidence.comparator_used: Fixed token-dependent chunking baseline in otherwise identical RAG pipelines (Gemini 1.0 Pro, 30 postoperative rhinoplasty questions)
evidence.outcome: Medical accuracy, clinical relevance, and retrieval precision/recall/F1
evidence.effect: Adaptive vs baseline: accuracy 87% (Likert 2.37 ± 0.72) vs 50% (1.63 ± 0.72; p = 0.001); relevance 93% (2.90 ± 0.40); precision 0.50 vs 0.17, recall 0.88 vs 0.40, F1 0.64 vs 0.24. Proposition and semantic chunking also improved all metrics over baseline, though less than adaptive.
evidence.quote: Adaptive chunking achieved the highest accuracy-87% (Likert 2.37 ± 0.72) versus baseline 50% (1.63 ± 0.72; p = 0.001)-and the highest relevance (93%, 2.90 ± 0.40).

controls.question: For medical coding and terminology mapping, should we retrieve candidate codes and have the LLM choose only among them?
controls.control: Retrieve candidate codes or ontology terms and constrain the LLM to select from that shortlist.
controls.comparator: Free LLM code generation, dictionary tools or embedding classifiers alone
controls.aim: Reduce invalid or hallucinated codes and improve coding accuracy
controls.family_label: retrieval-augmented generation, source citation, knowledge graphs, EHR grounding
tradeoffs: Fine-tuned and RAG models struggled with specificity of the mapped terms
The abstract says the additional effort of RAG needs to be justified, but it reports no cost or latency figures.

evidence.title: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT-4 for Automated Mapping of Local Medical Terminologies to SNOMED CT
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.comparator_used: Fine-tuned GPT-4 (also compared with baseline and prompt-engineered GPT-4 without retrieval)
evidence.outcome: Valid SNOMED CT term match rate and exact match rate when mapping local diagnostic terms; structural error rate
evidence.effect: RAG: 96.2% valid term match and 57.6% exact match vs fine-tuned 69.2% valid term match and 47.2% exact match; RAG structural errors 14%, significantly lower than other models
evidence.tradeoff: Fine-tuned and RAG models struggled with specificity of the mapped terms
evidence.quote: The RAG model achieved the highest performance with a 96.2% valid SNOMED CT term match rate and a 57.6% overall exact match rate, surpassing the fine-tuned model (69.2% valid term match, 47.2% exact match).

evidence.title: To RAG, or Not to RAG? A Comparative Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for ICD Coding of German Tumor Diagnoses
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-based coding without RAG (base LLM)
evidence.outcome: ICD-10 and ICD-O code prediction accuracy (exact and partial match)
evidence.effect: RAG improved base LLM performance; with Llama 3.3 70B, partial-match accuracy was 80.6% for ICD-10 and 75.0% for ICD-O. The abstract gives no base-LLM figures.
evidence.tradeoff: The abstract says the additional effort of RAG needs to be justified, but it reports no cost or latency figures.
evidence.quote: RAG improved base LLM performance and outperformed embedding-based approaches on partial-match accuracy (80.6% partial-match accuracy for ICD-10 and 75.0% for ICD-O with Llama 3.3 70B), but not on exact-match accuracy.

evidence.title: Evaluating Clinical Concept Extraction and Evidence-Bounded Terminology Linking: Multisite Model Comparison and Pilot Ablation Study
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-only inference with no retrieved terminology evidence (and matched-concept masking)
evidence.outcome: Exact linking to the reference UMLS concept for known-concept spans (28 spans)
evidence.effect: Complete retrieval returned a reference-matched link for 28/28 spans (100%; 95% CI, 87.9%-100%). With masking, all 28 were assigned POSSIBLE_CANDIDATES. LLM-only inference assigned POSSIBLE_CANDIDATES to 25/28 (89.3%) and LINKED to 3/28 (10.7%). Decisions on the 28 unsuitable-extension spans were identical across all three conditions.
evidence.quote: In Study 2, complete retrieval returned a reference-matched link for 28/28 known-concept spans (100%; 95% CI, 87.9%-100%).

controls.question: Which response policy should patient-facing chatbots use: library-only vetted answers, vetted answers with LLM fallback, or fully generative?
controls.control: Answer from a clinician-validated content library via LLM intent matching, with explicit unmatched-query behavior: decline/escalate, or labeled generative fallback.
controls.comparator: Fully generative LLM responses, with or without RAG
controls.aim: Prevent unsafe or inaccurate free-text answers to patients
variants: Library-only: only clinician-vetted answers; unmatched queries declined or escalated
Library-first with generative LLM fallback for unmatched queries
controls.family_label: retrieval-augmented generation, source citation, knowledge graphs, EHR grounding
tradeoffs: After active clinical promotion ceased, off-codebook queries rose from 2.4% to 26.7%, so community use drifted from the cancer codebook without clinician curation. The governance contract still rejected every adversarial probe.

evidence.title: Community Learning Ledgers for Cancer Navigation in Small Island Developing States
evidence.comparator_used: Same foundation model (Claude Haiku 4.5) without governance, plus three other ungoverned AI systems (ChatGPT GPT-4o, DeepSeek-Chat, OpenEvidence)
evidence.outcome: Caribbean facility citation and actionable navigation across 28 cancer screening queries
evidence.effect: Same model scored 100% with governance vs 54% without (P≤.001). CaribChat cited verified Caribbean facilities in 28/28 (100%) vs 10/28 (35.7%) for ChatGPT and 9/28 (32.1%) for OpenEvidence. Actionable navigation was 28/28 (100%) vs 2/28 (7.1%) for OpenEvidence (P≤.001).
evidence.tradeoff: After active clinical promotion ceased, off-codebook queries rose from 2.4% to 26.7%, so community use drifted from the cancer codebook without clinician curation. The governance contract still rejected every adversarial probe.
evidence.quote: The same model scored 100% with governance and 54% without (P≤.001).

controls.question: Should we use an LLM as a judge to score clinical AI outputs instead of having expert clinicians review everything?
controls.control: Use an LLM judge with a clinician-defined rubric to score AI-generated content at scale, calibrated and spot-checked against expert ratings.
controls.comparator: Expert clinician or physician review of every output
controls.aim: Scale quality, safety, and compliance evaluation while keeping agreement with expert judgment
variants: Auto-generated case-specific rubrics via retrieval and multi-model consensus, expert-audited
Small fine-tuned, distilled, or local-language judge model instead of a general-purpose large model
Judge from a different model family than the generator
Judge blinded to which model produced each answer
Periodic spot-check calibration against expert ratings
controls.family_label: LLM-as-judge, self-consistency, second-model or second-vendor verification, ensembles, multi-agent debate
tradeoffs: Judge is not shown to be accurate: moderate concordance on consensus cases and fair human reliability preclude an accuracy claim. One asymmetry: removed-confirmed 56% vs 42%, so the screen over-removes more on clinician notes. Genuine-error rate can only be reported as an interval (68%, 94% credible interval 48 to 83).

evidence.title: Are automated documentation-error judges fit to measure ambient AI scribes? A pre-registered, blinded human-validation study
evidence.comparator_used: Inter-clinician agreement among expert reviewers adjudicating the same flagged items (clinician-to-clinician envelope), since no gold standard exists
evidence.outcome: Agreement on whether flagged items were genuine documentation errors
evidence.effect: Judge-clinician agreement 64% (95% CI 60 to 68) vs inter-clinician raw agreement 59% (95% CI 50 to 67; AC1 0.24); pipeline concurred on 70% (95% CI 59 to 79) of 77 consensus items; kept-precision 74% for AI vs 81% for clinician notes
evidence.tradeoff: Judge is not shown to be accurate: moderate concordance on consensus cases and fair human reliability preclude an accuracy claim. One asymmetry: removed-confirmed 56% vs 42%, so the screen over-removes more on clinician notes. Genuine-error rate can only be reported as an interval (68%, 94% credible interval 48 to 83).
evidence.quote: Judge-clinician agreement was 64% (95% CI 60 to 68), overlapping that interval.

evidence.title: A Multi-Stage Validation Framework for Trustworthy Large-scale Clinical Information Extraction using Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Subject matter expert review of high-uncertainty cases
evidence.outcome: Agreement between the judge LLM's assessments and expert review
evidence.effect: Gwet's AC1=0.80 (substantial agreement)
evidence.quote: For high-uncertainty cases, the judge LLM's assessments showed substantial agreement with subject matter expert review (Gwet's AC1=0.80).

evidence.title: Blinded Radiologist and LLM-Based Evaluation of LLM-Generated Japanese Translations of Chest CT Reports: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Blinded radiologist (board-certified radiologist and radiology resident) pairwise evaluation of the same report pairs
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM judges with radiologist ratings on translation quality (terminology accuracy, readability, overall quality, radiologist-style authenticity)
evidence.effect: Radiologist-LLM judge agreement QWK=-0.04 to 0.15 (near zero); the two radiologists also agreed poorly (QWK=0.01 to 0.06). All 3 LLM judges favored the LLM translation on all criteria (70%-99%) and rated it more radiologist-like in >93% of cases.
evidence.tradeoff: LLM judges showed a strong preference for LLM-generated output and negligible agreement with radiologists, so automated evaluation alone was insufficient. The two radiologists also differed substantially from each other.
evidence.quote: Agreement between radiologists and LLM judges was near zero (QWK=-0.04 to 0.15).

evidence.title: AI Assessment and Management of Visceral Aneurysms Using ChatGPT-4o-mini: A Pilot Study Examining the Feasibility of Automating the AI Validation Process
evidence.comparator_used: Human evaluators independently assessing the same responses (expert review of every output)
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM self-assessment with a four-tier rubric and human grading of response correctness
evidence.effect: LLM self-assessed 89% of responses as correct (scores 1-2) vs 67% by human evaluators (chi-square, P < 0.0001); greatest discrepancy in the partially correct category; 80 scenarios
evidence.tradeoff: Systematic AI self-overestimation of correctness, so the automated judge was not a reliable substitute for expert oversight
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4o-mini self-assessed 89% of responses as correct (scores 1-2), compared to 67% by human evaluators (chi-square, P < 0.0001), with the greatest discrepancy in the partially correct category.

evidence.title: Physicians and artificial intelligence diverge in evaluating large language models on real clinical cases
evidence.comparator_used: Physician evaluation of LLM free-text responses to real clinical cases (more than 400 physicians across seven specialties), compared with an equal number of AI agents configured to mirror physician characteristics
evidence.outcome: Agreement of automated AI-agent evaluation with physician evaluation of LLM responses, and efficiency of the evaluation
evidence.effect: No numeric effect given in the text. AI agents gave 'highly efficient, directionally aligned assessments' but did not fully capture the nuances of human clinical judgment and could not substitute for physician evaluation.
evidence.tradeoff: AI evaluators missed nuances of human clinical judgment and could not replace physician-centered evaluation. They are suggested only as assistive tools to triage or pre-screen outputs and reduce human burden.
evidence.quote: While AI agents delivered highly efficient, directionally aligned assessments, they did not fully capture the nuances of human clinical judgment and could not substitute for physician-centered evaluation.

evidence.title: Assessing Llm Hallucinations And The Reliability Of Using LLms For Automated Hallucination Detection
evidence.comparator_used: Human rater (expert) annotation of hallucinations in the same outputs
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM-as-judge and human raters on hallucination presence and subcategorization
evidence.effect: Up to 65.7% agreement on hallucination presence and 64.7% agreement on hallucination subcategorization
evidence.quote: Across automated hallucination detection, LLJs demonstrate reasonable alignment with human raters, achieving up to 65.7% agreement on hallucination presence and 64.7% agreement on hallucination subcategorization.

evidence.title: Evaluating Medical Text Summaries Using Automatic Evaluation Metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge Approach: A Pilot Study
evidence.comparator_used: Expert clinician evaluation of the same summaries using the same criteria (relevance, completeness, redundancy, coherence and structure, grammar and terminology, hallucinations)
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM-judge/automatic metric scores and expert ratings of medical summary quality
evidence.effect: Pearson correlation between summary quality score and expert opinions was 0.688 for relevance; neither metrics nor LLM judges were reliable for hallucinations (no other numbers in the abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: New failure mode: LLM judges and automatic metrics missed factual errors and semantic distortions (hallucinations), so full automation of evaluation remains challenging and expert review is still needed for flagged cases.
evidence.quote: In terms of relevance, the Pearson correlation between the summary quality score and the expert opinions was 0.688.

evidence.title: Optimizing Order Sets With a Large Language Model-Powered Multiagent System
evidence.comparator_used: Unaligned LLM-as-a-judge scores (before calibration to expert ratings); not a comparison with expert review of every output
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM judge and expert ratings (Cohen κ) and filtering of suggestions by aligned usefulness score
evidence.effect: Cohen κ improved from 0.06 to 0.41 after expert alignment; filtering with aligned scores reduced total suggestions by 29% while retaining 92% of useful suggestions
evidence.tradeoff: Filtering discarded about 8% of useful suggestions; agreement remained moderate (κ 0.41)
evidence.quote: After expert alignment, Cohen κ improved from 0.06 to 0.41.

evidence.title: Fact-Checking Large Language Model Responses to a Health Care Prompt: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Expert clinician fact-checking (3 clinical experts) of the same responses and statements
evidence.outcome: Accuracy (agreement with experts) and time to complete fact-checking
evidence.effect: Acne scenario: GPT-4o and OpenBioLLM-70B both 86% agreement with experts. 20 claims: GPT-4o 100%, OpenBioLLM-70B 95%. Time: experts mean 18 (SD 3.74) min, GPT-4o 42 s, OpenBioLLM-70B 33 min.
evidence.tradeoff: LLM fact-checks missed some safety messages (urgency of stopping isotretinoin, folic acid). OpenBioLLM-70B was slower than the experts and omitted 1 key safety item. The authors conclude that human experts still need to perform additional checks for accuracy and safety.
evidence.quote: The expert fact-checks took a mean time of 18 (SD 3.74) minutes, GPT-4o took 42 seconds, and OpenBioLLM-70B took 33 minutes.

evidence.title: Reliability of Large Language Model Generated Clinical Reasoning in Assisted Reproductive Technology: Blinded Comparative Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Blinded review by senior ART clinicians
evidence.outcome: Ability to discern quality differences between prompting strategies for generated chains-of-thought
evidence.effect: GPT-4o evaluator failed to discern the performance differences that the clinician experts detected
evidence.tradeoff: AI evaluation missed differences between strategies, so it could not replace human expert evaluation for high-stakes clinical AI
evidence.quote: Notably, the AI evaluator failed to discern these critical performance differences.

evidence.title: Can ChatGPT Aid Clinicians in Educating Patients on the Surgical Management of Glaucoma?
evidence.comparator_used: Manual DISCERN quality scoring of the webpages
evidence.outcome: Agreement between ChatGPT-based DISCERN quality scores and manual scores
evidence.quote: ChatGPT scored the quality of health resources with high precision ( r =0.725).

evidence.title: General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specific Large Language Models in Antibiotic Clinical Decision-Making: A Double-Blind Evaluation with a 2×2 Factorial Design
evidence.comparator_used: Senior clinician expert ratings of the regimens
evidence.outcome: Agreement between ChatGPT 5.2 automated scores and expert clinician scores
evidence.effect: Overall Kendall τ=0.153 (p=0.003); subgroup τ=0.06-0.20, all p>0.05
evidence.tradeoff: Automated evaluation reliability was poor, so it could not replace senior clinical expertise
evidence.quote: ChatGPT–expert correlation was negligible (overall Kendall τ=0.153, p=0.003; subgroup τ=0.06–0.20, all p>0.05).

evidence.title: Human Evaluators vs. LLM-as-a-Judge: Toward Scalable, Real-Time Evaluation of GenAI in Global Health
evidence.comparator_used: Six expert human clinicians rating the same responses across 11 criteria (Med-PaLM 2-adapted framework)
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM-judge scores with human expert evaluations across 11 criteria
evidence.effect: Best LLM-judge (Claude-4.1-Opus) achieved human-equivalent evaluations on only 4 of 11 criteria; GPT-5 was consistently overcritical and Gemini-2.5-Pro overly lenient
evidence.tradeoff: Performance and cost-effectiveness deteriorated substantially when moving from English to Kinyarwanda inputs; sensitivity to linguistic and cultural context
evidence.quote: Our results show that even the highest-performing LLM-judge (Claude-4.1-Opus) achieved human-equivalent evaluations on only four of eleven criteria.

evidence.title: PhysiCase: Development and dual-layer validation of synthetic cases for health professional education: A pilot study leveraging Generative AI
evidence.comparator_used: Expert educator ratings of the cases (physiotherapy educators rated medical accuracy, realism, fidelity, relevance and usability), used as the reference for the automated DeepEval LLM-as-judge scores
evidence.outcome: Agreement between automated LLM-judge metrics and expert ratings of synthetic case quality
evidence.effect: Completeness metric vs expert usability ρ ≈ 0.393 (moderate); answer relevance and prompt alignment showed weak or negative correlations with clinical correctness. 90 of 128 cases (70.3%) passed automated screening.
evidence.tradeoff: The LLM judge missed subtle clinical reasoning failures (reductive logic, biomechanical inconsistency, administrative/contextual gaps), so expert review was still needed to protect clinical accuracy.
evidence.quote: Cross-layer correlation analysis revealed that automated completeness metrics moderately aligned with expert usability ratings (  ρ ≈ 0.393), while answer relevance and prompt alignment showed weak or negative correlations with clinical correctness.

evidence.title: A Quality Assessment Rubric for Artificial Intelligence-Generated Patient-Friendly Radiology Reports
evidence.comparator_used: Prespecified reference-standard grades (human lay and radiologist grading); lay participants' agreement with the same reference was κ=0.43
evidence.outcome: Agreement of ChatGPT-5 rubric grading and rubric-based distribution decisions with reference-standard grades for AI-generated patient-friendly radiology reports
evidence.effect: AI vs reference-standard grades: κ=0.44 (moderate) across 480 reports; rule-based distribution decisions from AI-assigned grades agreed 88.1% with those from reference-standard grades. Lay participants (n=80): κ=0.43, with 73.5% agreement between subjective and rule-based distribution decisions.
evidence.quote: Across 480 reports, AI had moderate agreement (κ=0.44) with prespecified reference-standard grades; rule-based distribution decisions using AI-assigned grades had 88.1% agreement with rule-based distribution decisions using reference-standard grades.

evidence.title: What Users Cannot See: Evaluating LLM Emotional Support Beyond User Preference
evidence.comparator_used: Clinically trained human raters (expert review), and lay raters
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM judges with clinically trained raters when scoring emotional-support responses
evidence.effect: Two independent LLM judges substantially agreed with clinically trained raters. No agreement statistics in the abstract. Lay raters detected only 60% of expert-confirmed Endorse instances.
evidence.quote: Two independent LLM judges substantially agreed with clinically trained raters, yet lay raters detected only 60% of expert-confirmed Endorse instances and rated the personas similarly helpful and desirable.

evidence.title: Evaluating Safety-Critical Communication Behavior of Large Language Models Using Workflow-Embedded Multi-Agent Clinical Simulation
evidence.comparator_used: Independent review by experienced intensive care nurses on a subset of transcripts (human consensus)
evidence.outcome: Agreement between the automated rubric-based LLM evaluator and human assessment
evidence.effect: Agreement was limited across several domains. The automated evaluator had high sensitivity but low specificity for omission detection and differed systematically from humans on actionability and overall safety risk. Human reviewers themselves showed only moderate agreement for omission detection.
evidence.tradeoff: The automated evaluator may prioritize communication structure and fluency differently from clinicians assessing clinical completeness and safety, so expert oversight is still needed.
evidence.quote: Agreement between the automated evaluator and human consensus was limited across several domains, with the automated evaluator showing high sensitivity but low specificity for omission detection and systematically differing from human assessments of actionability and overall safety risk.

evidence.title: Human evaluators vs. LLM-as-a-Judge: toward scalable evaluation of GenAI in global health
evidence.comparator_used: Six human clinicians evaluating responses to Rwandan health workers' questions (five LLM judges compared against them)
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM judges with human clinician ratings across 11 evaluation criteria
evidence.effect: Best LLM judge (Claude-4.1-Opus) matched human evaluators on only 4 of 11 criteria; Gemini-2.5-Pro scored too leniently and GPT-5 too harshly
evidence.tradeoff: Performance and cost-effectiveness fell when moving from English to Kinyarwanda
evidence.quote: The highest-performing LLM-judge (Claude-4.1-Opus) matched human evaluators on only four of eleven evaluation criteria, with other models scoring too leniently (Gemini-2.5-Pro) or too harshly (GPT-5).

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Colonoscopy Preparation Assistance: Correctness and Diversity in Synthetic Dialogues
evidence.comparator_used: Human rater evaluation, including three medical experts
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM-as-a-judge automatic evaluation and human judgments of response correctness
evidence.effect: Automatic evaluation results closely aligned with human judgments; no agreement statistic given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Automatic evaluation results closely aligned with human judgments: leading models approached but did not achieve adequate performance.

evidence.title: Can LLMs Accurately Score Medical Diagnoses and Clinical Reasoning?
evidence.comparator_used: Expert clinician panel scores and independent expert re-scoring panels scoring the same diagnoses
evidence.outcome: Agreement with expert panel scores, ranking of diagnosing agents, and severe-risk error probability
evidence.effect: Uncalibrated LLM Jury scores preserved ordinal agreement with the expert panel but were systematically lower. After isotonic regression calibration, scores and rankings showed excellent agreement with the primary expert panels. Severe-risk error probability was lower for the LLM Jury than for the human expert re-score panels. No self-preference bias was found. No numeric values are given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Uncalibrated scores were systematically lower, so post hoc calibration was needed. Findings come from LMIC hospital cases and need confirming in other clinical settings.
evidence.quote: Together, these results provide evidence that a calibrated LLM Jury is a trustworthy and reliable proxy for expert clinician evaluation in medical AI benchmarking.

evidence.title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
evidence.comparator_used: Expert radiologist ratings of the same summaries (consistency measured with Kendall's coefficient of concordance); LLM-judge prompt variants compared by scale size and scale description detail
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM-as-a-Judge ratings with radiologist expert ratings of LLM-generated clinical summaries
evidence.effect: No numeric values in the abstract. No definitive association between scale size and consistency. For most criteria, consistency was highest when the judges had a detailed description of extreme scale values or no detailed scale description.
evidence.tradeoff: Criteria that work for human evaluation were not always suitable for an LLM judge. Development needed choices about rating scale, criteria and prompt granularity, and a diverse expert team.
evidence.quote: No definitive association was identified between scale size and the consistency of ratings between radiologist experts and LLMs-as-a-Judges.

evidence.title: Evaluating Methods for Assessing LLM-Translated Clinical Discharge Instructions: A Comparison of Automated Metrics, MQM-Based Evaluation, and Clinician Review
evidence.comparator_used: Blinded bilingual clinician review (reference standard) of a randomly selected subset of translations
evidence.outcome: Agreement of MQM-based LLM-as-a-judge scores with clinician assessment of Spanish discharge instruction translations (Cohen's kappa)
evidence.effect: LLM MQM vs clinician kappa -0.18 to 0.20 (slight); clinician-clinician kappa -0.11 to 0.49 (slight to moderate)
evidence.quote: Agreement between LLM-based MQM scoring and clinician assessment was generally slight across domains (κ = −0.18 to 0.20), whereas inter-rater agreement between clinicians ranged from slight to moderate (κ = −0.11 to 0.49), highlighting the inherent subjectivity of clinical translation assessment.

evidence.title: Enhancing the quality and trustworthiness of large language model-generated summaries of clinical oncology literature
evidence.comparator_used: Human expert panel review (3 human experts), assessed via inter-human agreement
evidence.outcome: Agreement on faithfulness verification of summaries
evidence.effect: LLM panel vs human panel kappa 0.67, versus inter-human 0.43 (95% CI 0.34-0.52) and inter-LLM 0.40 (0.38-0.42)
evidence.quote: LLM panel vs human panel agreement was substantial (kappa 0.67), outperforming agreement among the interhuman (0.43 [95% CI, 0.34-0.52]) and inter-LLM (0.40 [0.38-0.42]) panels.

evidence.title: Healthier LLMs: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Public Health Question Answering
evidence.comparator_used: Dual human annotations (expert review) used to validate the rubric-based LLM judge
evidence.outcome: Judge-human agreement across rubric dimensions (faithfulness, completeness, clarity, factual consistency)
evidence.effect: Agreement strongest for faithfulness and completeness; factual consistency and clarity less reliably reproduced
evidence.tradeoff: Caution needed when interpreting factual consistency and clarity scores at scale
evidence.quote: Judge-human agreement is strongest for faithfulness and completeness, while factual consistency and clarity are less reliably reproduced, motivating caution when interpreting those dimensions at scale.

evidence.title: Validating LLM judges for automated oversight of patient communication
evidence.comparator_used: Clinician reference ratings (expert review) of the same outputs
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM judges with clinician ratings on a seven-criterion rubric (safety, reliability, communication quality)
evidence.effect: Spearman ρ > 0.80 for safety screening and factual verification; ρ < 0.60 for communication quality; 19 LLM judges benchmarked
evidence.tradeoff: Patient advocates rated communication quality lower than both clinicians and LLM judges, so recalibration to patient-centered standards is needed.
evidence.quote: LLM judges achieved strong clinician agreement for safety screening and factual verification (Spearman  ρ > 0.80) but weaker agreement for communication quality (  ρ < 0.60).

evidence.title: Judge-dependent safety gains and model-specific helpfulness costs of evidence-sufficiency prompting in clinical LLMs
evidence.comparator_used: Blinded three-clinician review of outputs, plus a different-family LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 5)
evidence.outcome: Agreement of the primary LLM judge (GPT-5.4-nano) with clinician ratings, and cross-judge consistency of the measured effect
evidence.effect: Primary judge sensitivity 1.00 and specificity 0.55 against clinicians. The Sonnet judge agreed on direction but nearly halved the effect (+13.1 points).
evidence.tradeoff: The judge over-flags unsafe answers, so its rates are not calibrated absolute rates. Results were one-directionally judge-dependent, so human anchoring is needed.
evidence.quote: Blinded clinicians characterized the primary judge as a high-sensitivity (1.00), low-specificity (0.55) screen, not a calibrated rate.

evidence.title: K-Bench: a clinically calibrated benchmark for evaluating large language models in high-risk mental health conversations
evidence.comparator_used: Clinician consensus ratings of transcripts
evidence.outcome: Agreement between frozen GPT-4o judge and clinician consensus on item-level ratings
evidence.effect: 94.2% exact agreement across 6,751 eligible item comparisons from 151 clinician-rated transcripts
evidence.quote: A frozen GPT-4o judge achieved 94.2% exact agreement with clinician consensus across 6,751 eligible item comparisons from 151 clinician-rated transcripts.

evidence.title: Rater choice determines measured fidelity: a multi-model evaluation of large language model raters for AI-generated plain-language biomedical summaries
evidence.comparator_used: Human coder review of ten randomly selected articles, used as the reference for four LLM raters (Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek V3.2, Llama 3.3-70B, GPT-4o) applying the same source-anchored rubric
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM rater error and safety-omission detection with the human coder
evidence.effect: Measured error density varied about 4-fold across raters (0.150 to 0.557 errors per 100 words; Friedman p < 0.001). Of 28 sections with a source safety warning, the warning was judged missing in 22 by the strictest rater and in 4 by the most lenient. Claude Sonnet 4.6 agreed well with the human coder, while the lenient raters identified only 3 and 2 of the 9 safety omissions.
evidence.tradeoff: Lenient LLM raters missed most safety omissions, so the choice of rater model changed the conclusion. A rubric alone did not make a rater trustworthy.
evidence.quote: Cross-validation showed that the divergence was directional: Claude Sonnet 4.6 alone agreed well with the human coder, whereas the lenient raters identified only 3 and 2 of the 9 safety omissions.

evidence.title: MedMeta: A Benchmark for LLMs in Synthesizing Meta-Analysis Conclusion from Medical Studies
evidence.comparator_used: Human expert ratings of the same outputs
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM-as-a-judge scores and human expert ratings
evidence.effect: Pearson's r = 0.81; Bland-Altman analysis showed negligible systematic bias
evidence.quote: Our evaluation framework is validated by a well-structured analysis showing our LLM-as-a-judge protocol strongly aligns with human expert ratings, as evidenced by high Pearson's r correlation (0.81) and Bland-Altman analysis revealing negligible systematic bias, establishing it as a reliable proxy for scalable evaluation.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-loop validation of a sequential multi-LLM medical education pipeline
evidence.comparator_used: Same evaluators' ratings of cards before versus after seeing stage-5 (S5) automated LLM feedback (single-arm two-phase design); human expert evaluation served as the reference for the text-level PASS cards
evidence.outcome: Blocking-error detection and technical accuracy and educational quality scores after S5 critic feedback; evaluation-level false-negative rate of text-level PASS cards
evidence.effect: S5 feedback associated with blocking-error flags rising from 39 to 54 evaluation-level observations (McNemar p = 0.003) and lower technical accuracy and educational quality scores (both p < 0.001). Evaluation-level FNR for blocking errors among PASS cards was 1.00% (95% CI 0.50-1.78%), above the pre-specified 0.3% threshold.
evidence.tradeoff: The single-arm design cannot separate useful cueing from anchoring or re-review effects. The pipeline's own PASS gate missed blocking errors above the safety threshold, so the authors do not support fully automated deployment.
evidence.quote: S5 feedback was associated with increased blocking-error flags (39-54 evaluation-level observations, McNemar p = 0.003) and decreased technical accuracy and educational quality scores (both p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Many-to-One Adversarial Consensus: Exposing Multi-Agent Collusion Risks in AI-Based Healthcare
evidence.comparator_used: Unprotected multi-agent system with no verifier agent, relying only on the doctor agent's own decision

evidence.effect: Collusion drove ASR and HRR up to 100% in unprotected systems; the verifier agent checking decisions against clinical guidelines restored 100% accuracy
evidence.quote: In contrast, the verifier agent restores 100% accuracy by blocking adversarial consensus.

evidence.title: PAIR-SAFE: A Paired-Agent Approach for Runtime Auditing and Refining AI-Mediated Mental Health Support

evidence.quote: We find that Judge-supervised interactions show significant improvements in key MITI dimensions, including Partnership, Seek Collaboration, and overall Relational quality.

evidence.comparator_used: Unfiltered LLM responses (no automated evaluator-based filtering)
evidence.outcome: Overall response error rate and harmful responses
evidence.effect: Reduced overall error rates but did not eliminate harmful responses (no numbers in abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: Harmful responses persisted; flagged responses were replaced with a deferral message telling patients to contact their provider.
evidence.quote: Applying an automated safety filter reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses.

evidence.title: Risk Governance for Generative AI Mental Health Support: A Multi-Turn Safety Architecture
evidence.comparator_used: Base LLMs (GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B) responding without the safety governance architecture, as implied by the reported gain in clinician-preferred escalation responses

evidence.effect: Specificity 0.85 (95%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity 0.92 (95%CI: 0.88;0.95); clinician-preferred escalation responses increased by 25.6–59.2 pp; rapport and connection preserved; stable across conversation length and across proprietary and open-source models
evidence.quote: increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6–59.2 pp while preserving rapport and connection

evidence.comparator_used: Unfiltered model responses delivered as generated, with no automated evaluator filter

evidence.quote: Applying an automated safety filter reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses.

evidence.title: CareGuardAI: Context-Aware Multi-Agent Guardrails for Clinical Safety & Hallucination Mitigation in Patient-Facing LLMs

evidence.effect: Reported only as consistently outperforming strong baseline models including GPT-4o-mini across the benchmarks; the abstract gives no numeric effect sizes

evidence.quote: Across these benchmarks, the framework consistently outperforms strong baseline models, including GPT-4o-mini, demonstrating the importance of context-aware, risk-based, inference-time safety mechanisms for reliable deployment in healthcare.

evidence.title: Multimodal Large Language Model Passes Specialty Board Examination and Surpasses Human Test-Taker Scores: A Comparative Analysis Examining the Stepwise Impact of Model Prompting Strategies on Performance
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4 with prompt engineering, RAG and five-shot learning but without the LLM-powered answer validation revision model (AVRM)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on the 300-question ACG self-assessment examination
evidence.effect: Adding the AVRM to prompt, RAG and 5-shot increased GPT-4's accuracy by 4.4%; the full strategy stack raised GPT-4 from 60.3% to 80.7%
evidence.quote: The addition of the AVRM to prompt, RAG and 5-shot increased GPT-4's accuracy by 4.4%.

evidence.title: Expert of Experts Verification and Alignment (EVAL) Framework for Large Language Models Safety in Gastroenterology
evidence.comparator_used: Responses without reward-model rejection sampling (baseline model output as generated)
evidence.outcome: Answer accuracy on upper GI bleeding questions after reward-model rejection sampling
evidence.effect: Accuracy improved by 8.36% overall; the reward model replicated human grading in 87.9% of cases across temperature settings
evidence.quote: The reward model replicated human grading with 87.9% of cases across temperature settings and significantly improved accuracy through rejection sampling by 8.36% overall.

evidence.title: Standard guardrails impose a safety-critical omission tax on clinical large language models that a downstream verification layer reverses: a retrospective multi-cohort evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Standard guardrail stack alone (and the same layer added only as advisory text)
evidence.outcome: Safety-critical omission rate (and commission when placed as advisory text)
evidence.effect: Verification layer that modified the response lowered omission to bare-model level (paired reduction 16.46 percentage points; 95% CI 10.93 to 21.86; McNemar exact P = 1.32 × 10⁻²³), detected 49.0% of omissions the guardrails missed (per-model 39.8% to 73.3%)
evidence.tradeoff: When added only as advisory text rather than modifying the response, the layer raised commission (paired difference 4.44 percentage points; P = 0.0015)
evidence.quote: A downstream verification layer that modified the response before it was returned lowered omission to the bare-model level (paired reduction 16.46 percentage points; Newcombe 95% confidence interval 10.93 to 21.86; McNemar exact P = 1.32 × 10⁻²³), detected 49.0% of the omissions the guardrails missed, and missed none that the guardrails caught (per-model 39.8% to 73.3%; P < 10⁻⁴).

evidence.title: Detecting and Preventing Harmful Behaviors in AI Companions: Development and Evaluation of the SHIELD Supervisory System
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline LLM companion output without the SHIELD supervisory system (five LLMs tested on a 100-item synthetic conversation benchmark)
evidence.outcome: Rate of concerning content in AI companion conversations (over-attachment, boundary violations, ethical roleplay violations, manipulative engagement, isolation reinforcement)
evidence.effect: Baseline concerning content 10–16% reduced to 3–8% with SHIELD (50–79% relative reduction); 95% of appropriate interactions preserved; sensitivity 59%, specificity 95%
evidence.tradeoff: Sensitivity was only 59%, so some concerning content was still missed. About 5% of appropriate interactions were not preserved. The evaluation used synthetic conversations only.
evidence.quote: Testing across five prominent LLMs (GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemma 3 1B, Kimi K2, Llama Scout 4 17B) showed that the baseline rate of concerning content (10–16%) was significantly reduced with SHIELD (to 3–8%), a 50–79% relative reduction, while preserving 95% of appropriate interactions.

evidence.title: Toward Reliable Clinical Coding with Language Models: Verification and Lightweight Adaptation
evidence.comparator_used: LLM code prediction without a verification step
evidence.outcome: LLM-based medical coding accuracy, including hierarchically near-miss errors
evidence.effect: Described as an effective and reliable step; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Our results highlight verification as an effective and reliable step toward improving LLM-based medical coding.

evidence.title: Multispecialty Dental EMRs from Chairside Audio: An Exploratory Study

evidence.outcome: Robustness (variability of EMR quality scores) across specialties; medical accuracy and consistency
evidence.effect: Standard deviation reductions of 33.8% (periodontics), 55.9% (orthodontics), and 42.6% (prosthodontics), with the largest gains in complex prosthodontic cases
evidence.quote: System 2 improved robustness with standard deviation reductions of 33.8% (periodontics), 55.9% (orthodontics), and 42.6% (prosthodontics), with the largest gains in complex prosthodontic cases.

evidence.title: Counterfactual Fairness Audits of Multi-Step Clinical LLM Agents Require a Measured Per-Action Instability Floor

evidence.outcome: Per-action instability floor (rate at which the agent's action changes on identical re-runs)
evidence.effect: Majority-vote aggregation over five draws removes 39% of the instability floor, then the gain flattens; the baseline pooled floor was 8.7% of outcome-vignette cells.
evidence.tradeoff: Mitigation is only partial: the gain flattens and residual instability remains, attributed to heterogeneous per-cell rates. The five-fold sampling cost is implied but not quantified.
evidence.quote: Majority-vote aggregation over five draws removes 39% of it and then flattens, and a null simulation attributes the residue to heterogeneous per-cell rates, so replication mitigates without eliminating.

evidence.title: Assessing and mitigating demographic bias in large language models for diagnostic radiology
evidence.comparator_used: Basic prompting (single response per query)
evidence.outcome: Number of significant race- or sex-related differences in diagnostic accuracy (bias); overall diagnostic accuracy was also compared
evidence.effect: Basic prompting: 10 significant race- or sex-related differences; self-consistency: 4. Overall accuracy did not differ across prompting strategies (p = 0.78 text-only, p = 0.95 vision).
evidence.quote: Text-only and vision models showed no statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy across prompting strategies (p = 0.78 and 0.95, respectively); basic and self-consistency prompting produced ten and four significant race- or sex-related differences, respectively, whereas no significant differences were observed with chain-of-thought prompting.

evidence.title: Burn Extent and Fitzpatrick Skin Tone Assessment from Clinical Photographs: Systematic and Random Error in Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence.quote: Across repeated queries, the median within-image range was 5.0-25.0 pp; averaging the five answers reduced error by only 0.24-2.22 pp.

evidence.quote: Finally, we evaluate a practical mitigation, self-consistency via majority voting, which improves κ substantially and often improves or preserves F1-score, at the cost of additional inference.

evidence.quote: Enhanced versions of both DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1 achieved significant accuracy improvement compared with their base versions in Chinese-language multiple-choice questions (C-MCQs) (P < .001).

evidence.title: Evaluation of LLMs accuracy and consistency in the registered dietitian exam through prompt engineering and knowledge retrieval

evidence.quote: The majority voting strategy, particularly with GPT-4, demonstrated the highest overall score across all cases from the diagnostic complex case collection, surpassing that of other LLMs.

evidence.title: Bias Evaluation and Mitigation in Retrieval-Augmented Medical Question-Answering Systems

evidence.quote: Permutation voting recovers 4 percentage points over single-ordering inference.

evidence.quote: Source-only transfer performed similarly (AUC 0.725), with no significant difference (p = 0.454), and both outperformed target-only logistic regression (AUC 0.628; p < 0.001).

Lower coverage. Mechanically valid quotes occurred in 83.3% to 91.2% of runs, but only 48.0% to 78.8% of evidence-bearing predictions were judged semantically supported.

evidence.title: Atomic Fact-Checking Increases Clinician Trust in Large Language Model Recommendations for Oncology Decision Support: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Recommendation only, explanation, source citation, and explanation plus citation (pooled controls)
evidence.outcome: Clinician trust in AI-generated oncology recommendations (5-point Likert)
evidence.effect: Mean trust 3.80 (3.76–3.84) with AFC vs 2.59 recommendation only, 2.84 explanation, 3.01 citation, 3.09 explanation+citation; Cohen's d = 0.94 (95% CI 0.88-1.00; P < .001) vs pooled controls; trust (score ≥4) rose from 26.9% to 66.5% (+39.5 points; NNT 2.53)
evidence.quote: AFC produced significantly higher trust than all control conditions.

evidence.title: Improving Reliability and Explainability of Medical Question Answering Through Atomic Fact-Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models: Creation and Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Same RAG-generated LLM answers without atomic fact-checking and correction (uncorrected original answers)
evidence.outcome: Factual accuracy and hallucination reduction in medical long-form Q&A, assessed by expert readers and the AMEGA benchmark
evidence.effect: Up to 50% overall answer improvement and 80% hallucination detection rate; the gain was strongest on real tumor-board questions, the most challenging dataset
evidence.quote: The framework significantly reduced hallucinations and inaccuracies.

evidence.title: CardioAgent: A Traceable Agentic and Retrieval-Augmented Architecture for Cardiovascular Clinical Decision Support
evidence.comparator_used: No comparator; functional safety test of the numerical consistency checker on correct and intentionally altered values
evidence.outcome: Detection of altered numerical values and verification of correct numerical claims
evidence.effect: Verified 9/9 correct numerical claims and detected 5/5 intentionally altered values; 4 anomalous inputs handled correctly
evidence.tradeoff: Small synthetic test; no comparison against unverified output.
evidence.quote: Functional safety checks correctly handled four anomalous inputs, verified nine of nine correct numerical claims, and detected five of five intentionally altered values.

evidence.title: Show Your Work: Verbatim Evidence Requirements and Automated Assessment of Large Language Models for Biomedical Text Processing of Trial Eligibility Criteria
evidence.comparator_used: All predictions released without filtering on whether the quote supports the label
evidence.outcome: Macro-F1 when restricted to predictions whose quote was verified (mechanically as an exact substring and by LLM judge as supporting the label)
evidence.effect: Restricting to supported predictions increased macro-F1; no numbers were given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Lower coverage. Mechanically valid quotes occurred in 83.3% to 91.2% of runs, but only 48.0% to 78.8% of evidence-bearing predictions were judged semantically supported.
evidence.quote: Restricting to supported predictions increased macro-F1 at the cost of lower coverage.

evidence.title: Show Your Work: Verbatim Evidence Requirements and Automated Assessment for Large Language Models in Biomedical Text Processing
evidence.comparator_used: all predictions released without checking the quote against the source (unrestricted predictions)
evidence.outcome: macro-F1 versus coverage when restricting to predictions with supported quotes
evidence.effect: Mechanically valid quotes occurred in 83.3% to 91.2% of runs, but only 48.0% to 78.8% of evidence-bearing predictions were judged semantically supported. Restricting to supported predictions raised macro-F1.
evidence.tradeoff: Lower coverage. Valid substring quotes were often not semantically supportive of the label.
evidence.quote: Restricting to supported predictions increased macro-F1 at the cost of lower coverage.

evidence.title: Quantum Knowledge Graph: Modeling Context-Dependent Triplet Validity
evidence.comparator_used: No-validator baseline (reasoner output released without KG-based validation)
evidence.outcome: Medical QA accuracy on KG-grounded MedReason subset (2,788 questions)
evidence.effect: KG-backed validation +0.61 pp over no-validator baseline; QKG with context matching +1.40 pp over baseline (p<0.05); with Qwen-3.6-Plus validator, raw QKG gain grew from +1.40 pp to +5.96 pp.
evidence.quote: Under a stronger validator (Qwen-3.6-Plus), the raw QKG gain over the no-validator baseline grows from $+1.40$ pp to $+5.96$ pp; the context-matching gap is non-significant ($p=0.73$) on the raw set but becomes borderline significant ($p=0.05$) after adjustment for knowledge leakage and suspicious questions, consistent with a benchmark-gold ceiling rather than a QKG limitation.

evidence.title: Citation Hallucination Determines Success: An Empirical Comparison of Six Medical AI Research Systems
evidence.comparator_used: Same best-performing system without the citation verification and repair pipeline (no source-level citation verification)
evidence.outcome: Citation integrity score and weighted total score
evidence.effect: Citation integrity improved from 40.0 to 90.9; weighted total rose from 68.9 to 81.8
evidence.quote: Adding a multi-agent citation verification and repair pipeline to the best-performing system improved its citation integrity score from 40.0 to 90.9 and raised the weighted total from 68.9 to 81.8.

evidence.title: Architectural Hallucination Mitigation in Multi-Agent Document Intelligence: Domain-Isolated RAG and Dual-Channel Claim Verification
evidence.comparator_used: Releasing LLM output without source-level verification (hallucination rate before verification)
evidence.outcome: Delivered hallucination rate
evidence.effect: Delivered hallucination fell from 10.0% to 0.29% at 97.1% claim precision, calibrated on 1,240 documents (8,431 claims)
evidence.tradeoff: Claims without grounding in the source channel are refused rather than delivered, so some claims are withheld.
evidence.quote: Calibrated on 1,240 documents (8,431 claims), C2 reduces delivered hallucination from 10.0% to 0.29% at 97.1% claim precision.

evidence.title: VaaS is a Multi-Layer Hallucination Reduction Pipeline for AI-Assisted Science: Production Validation and Prospective Benchmarking
evidence.comparator_used: Unguided LLM output with no citation verification (C1 condition in the 640-run ablation)
evidence.outcome: Type I (fabricated citation) and Type II (wrong-topic citation) hallucination rates
evidence.effect: Live PMID verification alone (C3) gave 0.0% Type I and 0.0% Type II, versus 95.9% Type II for unguided output. The full VaaS protocol (C4) gave 0.0% Type I and 6.5% Type II, a >14-fold reduction.
evidence.tradeoff: The full pipeline cost less than ~$1 per comprehensive gene review. No latency or new failure modes are reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: live PMID verification alone (C3) eliminated both error types entirely (0.0%/0.0%)

controls.question: Should we combine or require agreement among several distinct LLMs rather than rely on one LLM?
controls.control: Query several distinct LLMs in parallel and accept outputs by consensus or a combined result.
controls.comparator: Single LLM
controls.aim: Improve reliability of accepted outputs
variants: Optional implementation detail: source models from different vendors
controls.family_label: LLM-as-judge, self-consistency, second-model or second-vendor verification, ensembles, multi-agent debate
tradeoffs: Selective manual review is still needed for the discordant cases. Total cost of both LLMs was US $0.76.

evidence.title: Improving reliability and accuracy of structured data extraction using a consensus large-language model approach-a use case description in multiple sclerosis
evidence.comparator_used: Individual single LLMs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) with the same final prompt
evidence.outcome: Error rate in structured data extraction from MS outpatient reports
evidence.effect: The consensus of three LLMs overcame a ceiling effect in error reduction seen with single LLMs. True-error rate was 1.48%, similar to neurologists (around 2%). No single-LLM error rates were given in the text.
evidence.quote: By creating an LLM consensus with the final prompt design, we were able to overcome a ceiling effect in reducing the error rate.

evidence.title: Human Evaluators vs. LLM-as-a-Judge: Toward Scalable, Real-Time Evaluation of GenAI in Global Health
evidence.comparator_used: Individual LLM-judges used alone
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM-judge evaluations after combining several LLMs into “LLM juries”
evidence.effect: LLM juries improved agreement on only one additional criterion.
evidence.quote: Constructing “LLM juries” to balance model-specific biases improved agreement on only one additional criterion.

evidence.title: A Multi-agent Large Language Model Framework to Automatically Assess Performance of a Clinical AI Triage Tool
evidence.comparator_used: Single LLM (HIPAA-compliant GPT-4o) rating ICH presence from radiology reports
evidence.outcome: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) for LLM-derived ground truth of ICH presence, used to evaluate the AI triage tool, against manual review of 1,726 examples
evidence.effect: MCC (95% CI): Full-9 Ensemble 0.571 (0.552-0.591), Top-3 Ensemble 0.558 (0.537-0.579), Consensus 0.556 (0.539-0.574), GPT-4o 0.522 (0.500-0.543). No statistically significant differences among Top-3, Full-9 and Consensus (p > 0.05). Best single-model AUC 0.78 (llama3.3:70b and GPT-4o).
evidence.quote: Using MCC (95% CI) the ideal combination of LLMs were: Full-9 Ensemble 0.571 (0.552-0.591), Top-3 Ensemble 0.558 (0.537-0.579), Consensus 0.556 (0.539-0.574), and GPT4o 0.522 (0.500-0.543).

evidence.title: Human evaluators vs. LLM-as-a-Judge: toward scalable evaluation of GenAI in global health
evidence.comparator_used: Individual LLM judges / single-model LLM-as-judge evaluations
evidence.outcome: Agreement with human evaluators across evaluation criteria
evidence.effect: LLM-juries improved agreement on only one additional criterion.
evidence.quote: Constructing LLM-juries to balance model-specific biases improved agreement on only one additional criterion.

evidence.title: Extracting Clinical Guideline Information Using Two Large Language Models: Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Each single LLM (GPT-4o or Gemini-1.5-Pro) alone versus expert labels
evidence.outcome: Classification error against expert-annotated labels for guideline recommendations
evidence.effect: Single-model accuracy was 93.5% (GPT-4o) and 92.7% (Gemini-1.5-Pro). Where the two models agreed (341/385), only 1 case (0.3%) diverged from expert labels.
evidence.tradeoff: Selective manual review is still needed for the discordant cases. Total cost of both LLMs was US $0.76.
evidence.quote: Among these agreed-upon cases, only one (0.3%) diverged from expert labels.

evidence.title: RadOncRAG: A Novel Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework Improves Large Language Model Benchmark Performance in Radiation Oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Individual LLM performance
evidence.outcome: Aggregate accuracy of majority vote across models
evidence.effect: Majority voting boosted aggregate accuracy when individual model performance exceeded 50%; no numbers given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Majority voting boosted aggregate accuracy when individual model performance exceeded 50%.

evidence.title: Introducing Answered with Evidence - a framework for evaluating whether LLM responses to biomedical questions are founded in evidence
evidence.comparator_used: Individual LLMs grounded in single evidence sources (PubMed, general online content, or the Atropos Alexandria library); no formal single-LLM accuracy comparison is reported in the abstract
evidence.outcome: Share of physician-submitted biomedical questions answered reliably, and agreement across LLMs
evidence.effect: Two or more LLMs agreed on an answer 49% of the time; the ensemble combined with the Alexandria custom source gave reliable answers to over 64% of biomedical queries. General-purpose LLMs grounded in public information varied greatly in their answers, even when sourced from the same publication.
evidence.quote: Using an ensemble approach, we observed that 49% of the time, two or more LLMs agreed on an answer.

controls.question: Should we use disagreement among multiple models to decide which cases get human review?
controls.control: Use disagreement or uncertainty across ensemble members as a case-level confidence signal and route disagreeing items to human reviewers first.
controls.comparator: Single-model confidence, or random or exhaustive human review
controls.aim: Focus limited human review on uncertain, error-prone cases

tradeoffs: Requires 15 LLM calls per model per patient (five temperatures x three repeats); seizure needed a larger review share (19.6%) than the other targets.
Less stable for open-ended, highly subjective tasks, where Reasoning Support Mode was more stable and practical.
Fewer missed hazards but more alerts for clinicians to review (878 versus 729 per 1,000 messages).
With the threshold strategy, the error rate rose slightly to 0.5% (2/374).
Accuracy is projected, not observed, and assumes experts correct all flagged cases. The validation was retrospective and prospective randomized validation is still underway.

About 6.3% of errors were not flagged. Agreement among all systems does not guarantee correctness, because shared errors go undetected. The threshold was post hoc and illustrative, validation used a single annotator, and the corpus was a proxy medical-education set rather than clinical encounters.

evidence.title: Multi-LLM Disagreement as a Scalable Detector of Human Annotation Errors in Structured Data from Clinical Free-Text
evidence.comparator_used: Single LLM models (single-model agreement) for error detection; the lowest-agreement stratum is implicitly compared with exhaustive review
evidence.outcome: Detection of human annotation errors to prioritize annotations for targeted review
evidence.effect: Human error rates rose from 0% at agreement scores 3-4 to 76% at score 0. The lowest-agreement stratum was 6.5% of annotations but held an estimated 80% of errors. Prevalence-adjusted AUC-ROC was 0.991 (95% CI 0.987-0.994) and AUC-PR was 0.893 (95% CI 0.851-0.929).
evidence.quote: Multi-LLM disagreement outperformed single models and provided graded operating points for risk-stratified review.

evidence.title: Uncertainty-aware extraction of clinical findings from Finnish EHRs using open large language models
evidence.comparator_used: Exhaustive manual review of all patients (simulated selective-review workflow ranked by uncertainty)
evidence.outcome: Proportion of patients needing expert review to capture all LLM extraction errors
evidence.effect: Complete error coverage by reviewing 8.3% of patients for hemiplegia, 8.2% for headache and 19.6% for seizure
evidence.tradeoff: Requires 15 LLM calls per model per patient (five temperatures x three repeats); seizure needed a larger review share (19.6%) than the other targets.
evidence.quote: Entropy-based triage achieved complete error coverage by reviewing <10% of patients for hemiplegia (8.3%) and headache (8.2%), and 19.6% for seizure.

evidence.title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
evidence.comparator_used: Human review in modes not triggered by disagreement between the two LLMs (M1 and M2)
evidence.outcome: Human intervention rate and assessment efficiency when disagreement between DeepSeek V3 and Qwen-plus triggers human review
evidence.effect: M3 markedly reduced intervention rates; accuracy under M2 and M3 ranged from 0.633 to 0.900
evidence.tradeoff: Less stable for open-ended, highly subjective tasks, where Reasoning Support Mode was more stable and practical.
evidence.quote: Disagreement Trigger Mode exhibited high cost-effectiveness in structured and moderate-reasoning tasks, enhancing assessment efficiency, while Reasoning Support Mode was more stable and practical for open-ended and highly subjective tasks.

evidence.title: AI safety evaluation in an underrepresented population: real-world performance of clinical decision support and frontier language models on Medicaid patient messaging triage
evidence.comparator_used: high-recall first-stage screen (the other configuration that met the sensitivity floor)
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and missed hazards per 1,000 messages under clinician review of flagged messages
evidence.effect: Disagreement-stratified clinician-review workflow: sensitivity 0.939, 5.0 missed hazards and 878 alerts per 1,000 messages. High-recall first-stage screen: sensitivity 0.855, 12.0 missed hazards and 729 alerts per 1,000 messages.
evidence.tradeoff: Fewer missed hazards but more alerts for clinicians to review (878 versus 729 per 1,000 messages).
evidence.quote: Two configurations met the sensitivity-floor target: a high-recall first-stage screen (sensitivity 0.855; 12.0 missed hazards and 729 alerts per 1,000 messages) and a disagreement-stratified clinician-review workflow (sensitivity 0.939; 5.0 missed hazards and 878 alerts per 1,000 messages).

evidence.title: Extracting Clinical Guideline Information Using Two Large Language Models: Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Exhaustive manual review of all 385 guideline items
evidence.outcome: Manual review workload when disagreeing items are prioritised for human review
evidence.effect: Consistent predictions for 341 of 385 items reduced the need for manual review by 88.6%. The agreement-threshold strategy cut priority review to 2.9% (11/385).
evidence.tradeoff: With the threshold strategy, the error rate rose slightly to 0.5% (2/374).
evidence.quote: The models generated consistent predictions for 341 of 385 guideline items, reducing the need for manual review by 88.6%.

evidence.title: Development and retrospective validation of SCOUT: scalable clinical oversight of large language models via uncertainty triangulation
evidence.comparator_used: Clinician review of every LLM output (exhaustive human review)
evidence.outcome: Volume of cases requiring human review, and projected final accuracy
evidence.effect: Human review volume reduced by 45% to 83%; projected final accuracy 99.1% to 100.0% assuming expert correction of all flagged cases
evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy is projected, not observed, and assumes experts correct all flagged cases. The validation was retrospective and prospective randomized validation is still underway.
evidence.quote: SCOUT reduced the volume of cases requiring human review by 45% to 83%, with projected final accuracy of 99.1% to 100.0% assuming expert correction of all flagged cases.

evidence.title: Cross-model disagreement as a reference-free signal for prioritizing human review in medical speech transcription
evidence.comparator_used: No explicit comparator arm; the implicit baseline is exhaustive review of all transcript tokens
evidence.outcome: Share of human-verified transcription errors recovered by flagged positions versus share of tokens flagged for review
evidence.effect: Flagging positions where six or fewer of eight ASR systems agreed selected 28.6% of tokens and recovered 93.7% of single-annotator HC-verified errors. Errors rose monotonically as agreement fell. Only 2.5% of positions were high-risk (0-3 systems agreeing).
evidence.tradeoff: About 6.3% of errors were not flagged. Agreement among all systems does not guarantee correctness, because shared errors go undetected. The threshold was post hoc and illustrative, validation used a single annotator, and the corpus was a proxy medical-education set rather than clinical encounters.
evidence.quote: At an illustrative post hoc threshold, flagging positions where six or fewer systems agreed selected 28.6% of tokens while recovering 93.7% of single-annotator HC-verified errors on this proxy corpus.

evidence.title: Comparative benchmarking of failure detection methods in medical image segmentation: Unveiling the role of confidence aggregation
evidence.comparator_used: Other failure detection methods, including single-model pixel confidence aggregation metrics, evaluated with risk-coverage analysis
evidence.outcome: Segmentation failure detection performance under test-time distribution shift
evidence.effect: Pairwise Dice score between ensemble predictions showed superior performance; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Our findings highlight the importance of pixel confidence aggregation and we observe superior performance of the pairwise Dice score (Roy et al., 2019) between ensemble predictions, positioning it as a simple and robust baseline for failure detection in medical image segmentation.

controls.question: Should we cross-check AI output with clinician judgment, rule engines, or conventional tools rather than act on the AI alone?
controls.control: Pair AI output with clinician scores, clinical risk tools, rule engines, conventional software, or task-specific models that independently verify it.
