evidence.title: A comparative study of ChatGPT 4o and DeepSeek in addressing CIED infection-related questions: Accuracy and readability assessment
evidence.comparator_used: Same 30 CIED infection questions asked without additional context (generic prompt relying on built-in model knowledge)
evidence.outcome: Proportion of comprehensive answers (expert-graded accuracy); also word count and Flesch-Kincaid readability
evidence.effect: Comprehensive answers rose from 80.00% (24/30) to 93.33% (28/30) for ChatGPT 4o and from 80.00% (24/30) to 90.00% (27/30) for DeepSeek. Word count fell with guidelines (ChatGPT 4o 859.10 to 624.00; DeepSeek 526.27 to 549.43 as reported), not significant (P = .13). Readability improvements were slight and not significant (P = .11). No significant difference in overall accuracy between models (P = .34).
evidence.quote: The use of guideline-based prompts significantly improved the completeness of their responses.

evidence.title: ChatGPT for automating lung cancer staging: feasibility study on open radiology report dataset
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt without the TNM classification rule (generic prompt relying on the model's built-in knowledge), tested with GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of clinical TNM (T, N, M) category assignment from CT radiology reports
evidence.effect: The best accuracy was achieved by GPT-4 when presented with the TNM classification rule: 52.2% (T), 78.9% (N), 86.7% (M). The abstract gives no accuracy figures for the no-rule condition.
evidence.quote: It was beneficial to present the TNM classification rule to ChatGPT to improve the performance.

evidence.title: AI Rater Discrimination Depends on Scoring Protocol in Complex Clinical Decision-Making
evidence.comparator_used: Rubric-free Non Gold Rubric (Non-GR) scoring protocol
evidence.outcome: AI rater discriminative power for distinguishing DRG versus Baseline CDSS outputs in T2D pharmacotherapy evaluation
evidence.effect: GR amplified the AI rater's discrimination between DRG and Baseline CDSS outputs by factors of 1.76 to 5.10; under GR, mean scores were 7.69 to 49.64 points lower and interquartile ranges were 1.68 to 3.67 times wider than under Non-GR.
evidence.quote: Within each question, GR amplified the AI rater's discrimination between DRG and Baseline CDSS outputs by factors of 1.76 to 5.10, while also revealing substantial behavioral variation across rater models that Non-GR suppressed.

evidence.title: Reasoning Before Disposition: A Model-Agnostic Cannot-Miss Discipline for Quiet Emergencies and the Case for Deterministic Enforcement
evidence.comparator_used: Base model with no governance prompt (generic prompt relying on built-in knowledge)
evidence.outcome: Under-triage (failure to escalate to the top acuity tier) in subtle or atypical emergencies
evidence.effect: Across 76 stems, under-triage fell from 13.2% (95% CI 7.3 to 22.6) to 3.9% (1.4 to 11.0); McNemar 7 to 0, p = 0.016; RR 0.30; NNT 11. Across eight models, 19 stems favoured governance and 5 favoured control (sign test p = 0.007). Named-guideline citation rose from 65.6% to 96.9%. MedQA was unchanged at 95.8% in both arms.
evidence.tradeoff: Moved some ROUTINE non-emergency stems to same-day URGENT (17 added vs 2 removed, p < 0.001). HealthBench fell 3.6 points on a single seed. Residual failures stayed concentrated in a few conditions, and some model/elicitation cells were neutral or reversed.
evidence.quote: Across 76 subtle or atypical emergencies, each adjudicated by a blinded, LLM-simulated three-physician panel and each mapped to a published guideline that names its cannot-miss diagnosis, the base model failed to escalate 13.2% (95% CI 7.3 to 22.6) to the top acuity tier; the governance prompt cut this to 3.9% (1.4 to 11.0; paired exact McNemar 7 to 0, p = 0.016; relative risk 0.30; number needed to treat 11).

evidence.title: Extracting Cardiorespiratory Symptoms From Clinical Notes Using Open-Weight Large Language Models: Method Development and Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Instruction-only prompt without ICD-10-CM definitions (Llama 3.3-70B, 93 development notes)
evidence.outcome: ICD-10-CM coding accuracy
evidence.effect: Incorporating ICD-10-CM definitions improved coding accuracy over instruction-only prompting; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Incorporating ICD-10-CM definitions improved coding accuracy, and assumption-free prompting further balanced precision and recall.

evidence.title: MIRA: A Bilingual Benchmark for Medical Information Response Audit
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompts without the knowledge-guided mitigation prompt (original user phrasings)
evidence.outcome: Information dilution, including underinformative simplification, in responses to low health-literacy signals
evidence.effect: Reduced information dilution for most models; largest reductions in underinformative simplification for Claude (~8%) and Qwen (~6%)
evidence.quote: A knowledge-guided mitigation prompt reduces information dilution for most models, with the largest reductions in underinformative simplification observed for Claude (~8%) and Qwen (~6%).

evidence.title: Is this neonate feeling pain? Leveraging clinical knowledge towards high-precision Large Language Model-based neonatal pain assessment
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompts without the specific criteria/facial-feature instructions; the abstract also reports a latent-clinical-knowledge prompt arm.
evidence.outcome: Neonatal automatic pain assessment precision, recall, and withdrawal rate
evidence.effect: Specific criteria/facial-feature prompting reached precision 100% and recall 40.1%; latent clinical knowledge prompting achieved precision 82.3% and recall 73.2%; withdrawal rates were reported as significantly reduced compared to baseline prompts, with no number given.
evidence.tradeoff: Lower recall with the facial-feature/criteria prompt: 40.1%.
evidence.quote: When instructed with specific criteria and facial features, it achieved high precision with significantly reduced withdrawal rates compared to baseline prompts, highlighting the feasibility of this novel approach as a real-world evaluation of state-of-the-art technology through all its steps of development.

evidence.title: Investigating the Ability of Large Language Models to Analyze Recipes for Diabetes
evidence.comparator_used: Direct Query Prompt without dietary guidelines (relying on the model's built-in knowledge)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy in classifying recipes as suitable or not suitable for diabetes
evidence.effect: No numbers in the abstract; models able to reason with the guidelines performed better, and most LLMs were cautious in predicting recipes as suitable
evidence.tradeoff: Most LLMs were overly cautious, avoiding 'suitable' predictions to prevent detrimental outcomes
evidence.quote: Further, the models that can reason using the dietary guidelines performed better in predicting the suitability of recipes for diabetes.

evidence.title: MedCalc-Bench Doesn't Measure What You Think: A Benchmark Audit and the Case for Open-Book Evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Generic direct prompting without the calculator specification, relying on the model's built-in knowledge (closed-book)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on MedCalc-Bench clinical calculator tasks
evidence.effect: Accuracy rose from ~52% to 81-85% on GLM-4.6V and GLM-4.7, surpassing all published results including RL-trained systems, without fine-tuning
evidence.quote: Second, we show that a simple intervention-providing the model with the calculator specification at inference time ("open-book" prompting)-raises accuracy from ~52% to 81-85% on GLM-4.6V and GLM-4.7, surpassing all published results including RL-trained systems, without any fine-tuning.

evidence.title: Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs
evidence.comparator_used: CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM baseline without the injected ECG Interpretation Guide
evidence.outcome: Semantic quality of generated ECG impressions (BERTScore against reference reports) and perceived consistency
evidence.effect: Average BERTScore of generated impressions increased from 0.818 to 0.953; classification performance remained competitive
evidence.quote: In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports.

evidence.title: Prompt-engineering improves clinical safety of large language models for opioid equipotency conversion
evidence.comparator_used: Naive prompts without reference tables or unit explanations (models tested in their native state)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of opioid equipotency conversions within tight (0.85-1.15x) and broad (0.6-1.7x) expected-dose ranges
evidence.effect: Naive models generally had low tight-range accuracy; with reference-based augmentation, over half of models achieved high proportions of conversions within tight accuracy for morphine equivalent conversions (significant improvement; no exact figures in abstract)
evidence.quote: Reference-based prompt augmentation significantly improved performance, with over half of models achieving high proportions of conversions within tight accuracy for morphine equivalent conversions.

evidence.title: Danger, Danger, Gaston Labat! Does zero-shot artificial intelligence correlate with anticoagulation guidelines recommendations for neuraxial anesthesia?
evidence.comparator_used: Minimal-guidance prompt relying on the model's built-in knowledge (baseline prompt without explicit guidelines)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy/AUC of neuraxial bleeding risk assessment versus ASRA guideline-based truth table
evidence.effect: Baseline GPT-3.5 performance was slightly above chance; with detailed prompts and explicit guidelines, performance improved significantly (AUC 0.70, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.77)
evidence.quote: With detailed prompts and explicit guidelines, performance improved significantly (AUC 0.70, 95% CI (0.64 to 0.77)).

evidence.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models in Evidence-Based Medicine
evidence.venue: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (generic prompt relying on the model's built-in knowledge)
evidence.outcome: PICO extraction performance of GPT-4
evidence.effect: Knowledge-guided prompting improved GPT-4 performance by 13.10% over zero-shot in PICO extraction
evidence.quote: Promoting strategies such as knowledge-guided prompting proved highly effective (e.g., improving the performance of GPT-4 by 13.10% over zero-shot in PICO extraction).

evidence.title: A decision-basis contract for auditable LLM-assisted medical billing verification: deterministic rules, verbatim evidence, and fail-closed abstention
evidence.comparator_used: Ablation of the contract without explicit documentation requirements
evidence.outcome: Identification of missing required information in documentation
evidence.effect: Improved for all four models; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Explicit documentation requirements improved identification of missing information for all four models.

evidence.title: How DISCERNing is ChatGPT? An Evaluation of Models and Prompt Engineering in Assessing Patient Education Materials
evidence.comparator_used: Naïve zero-shot prompt without DISCERN guidance (the Combined split-plus-augmented approach was the reported result)
evidence.outcome: Agreement with human DISCERN scores (correlation, absolute error)
evidence.effect: Combined prompting modestly improved agreement and reduced absolute error. Agreement was still weak to moderate, and prompt engineering did not correct calibration bias. Results for Augmented prompting alone are not given separately.
evidence.tradeoff: Systematic score compression persisted (low-quality pages overestimated, high-quality pages underestimated). Run-to-run variability was substantial, with a mean score range of 17.5 points and up to 43 points for one webpage.
evidence.quote: Combined prompting modestly improved agreement and reduced absolute error, particularly for the o3 model, which consistently outperformed GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o.

controls.question: Should we include worked examples in the prompt instead of instructions alone?
controls.control: Provide a set of labeled example cases in the prompt showing expected inputs and answers.
controls.comparator: Zero-shot prompt with instructions only
controls.aim: Improve task accuracy and output consistency
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Higher over-triage with prompting (53.15% to 65.62%)
Critical clinical items showed poor validity; agreement was only moderate, limiting use to initial screening rather than detailed assessment.
One-shot prompting doubled the proportion of protocols with critical errors (risk of patient harm) and shifted errors from language toward factual errors. This was seen for a single model only.
Few-shot prompting increased costs per correct diagnosis for GPT-4o by approximately ¥4.54.

Overall reproducibility, consistency and reliability still judged inadequate despite basic prompting; high variability between repeated runs persisted, and the LLMs could not access the scientific databases needed to include recent literature.
GPT-5e produced more mistakes than the rules-based GPT-5r (35 vs 21; GPT-5r had fewer, p = 0.034). Building the phrases required 50 additional operative reports.

evidence.title: Diagnosis and Triage Performance of Contemporary Large Language Models on Short Clinical Vignettes
evidence.comparator_used: No prompt (zero-shot, no exemplar cases) on the same eight LLMs
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy, triage accuracy, and safety of advice
evidence.effect: Mean diagnostic accuracy 89.84% to 91.67%; mean triage accuracy 76.82% to 86.20%; safety of advice 89.06% to 94.53%
evidence.tradeoff: Higher over-triage with prompting (53.15% to 65.62%)
evidence.quote: Structured prompting improved performance across models: mean diagnostic accuracy increased from 89.84% to 91.67%, and mean triage accuracy increased from 76.82% to 86.20%.

evidence.title: Automated Suicide Risk Factor Monitoring in Crisis Text Line Users: Comparative Study of AI and Human Ratings Using Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompting styles
evidence.outcome: Human-AI agreement for very high suicide risk and classification performance
evidence.tradeoff: Critical clinical items showed poor validity; agreement was only moderate, limiting use to initial screening rather than detailed assessment.
evidence.quote: Zero-shot prompting at temperature 0 yielded perfect inter-rating reliability (α=1.00, 95% CI: [1-1] for high & very high risk), while few-shot prompting showed best human-AI agreement for very high risk (α=0.78, 95% CI: [0.67-0.89]) and strongest classification performance (balanced accuracy 0.54-0.71).

evidence.title: Decreasing Administrative Effort Related to Non-Approval of Image-guidED Procedures Using Large Language Models - The DENIED-AI Pilot Study
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (also compared with RAG) across four LLMs
evidence.outcome: Reviewer-rated content and grammar quality of insurance appeal letters
evidence.effect: Mean content and grammar scores were 3.9 ± 0.95 and 4.3 ± 0.9 (out of 5), with no significant differences by model or technique (p >.05)
evidence.quote: Mean content and grammar scores were 3.9 ± 0.95 and 4.3 ± 0.9 (out of 5), with no significant differences by model or technique (p >.05).

evidence.title: Reliability of Large Language Model Generated Clinical Reasoning in Assisted Reproductive Technology: Blinded Comparative Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with no examples; also Random Few-shot using shallow examples
evidence.outcome: Senior-clinician ratings of LLM-generated clinical Chains-of-Thought across human evaluation metrics
evidence.effect: Selective Few-shot significantly outperformed other strategies across all human evaluation metrics (p < .001); Random Few-shot offered no significant improvement over Zero-shot baseline
evidence.quote: The Selective Few-shot strategy significantly outperformed other strategies across all human evaluation metrics (p < .001).

evidence.title: LLM-Generated Lay-Language Protocols for Molecular Tumor Board Patients: Evaluation of Quality and Clinical Usability
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (A1) versus one-shot prompting (A2) with constrained decoding in both arms
evidence.outcome: Automatic text-quality metrics (ROUGE-1, BERTScore-F1, readability, complexity) versus expert-rated critical errors in lay-language MTB protocols
evidence.effect: Across models, A2 significantly improved most automatic metrics compared to A1. For Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, protocols with at least 1 critical error rose under A2 (10/25, 40% vs 5/25, 20% under A1). The dominant error type shifted from language errors (40/108, 37%) to factual errors (69/145, 48%). The expert differences were directionally consistent but not individually significant (n=25 pairs).
evidence.tradeoff: One-shot prompting doubled the proportion of protocols with critical errors (risk of patient harm) and shifted errors from language toward factual errors. This was seen for a single model only.
evidence.quote: However, expert usability evaluation of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct showed the opposite picture: the proportion of protocols containing at least 1 critical error doubled under A2 (10/25, 40% vs 5/25, 20%) compared with A1, and the dominant error type shifted from language (40/108, 37%) errors to factual errors (69/145, 48%).

evidence.title: Implementing a Resource-Light and Low-Code Large Language Model System for Information Extraction from Mammography Reports: A Pilot Study
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Default zero-shot prompts
evidence.outcome: Data extraction accuracy
evidence.effect: Few-shot prompting led to decreased accuracy (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Chain-of-thought prompting yielded mixed results, while few-shot prompting led to decreased accuracy.

evidence.title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting of the LLMs for new vertebral fracture prediction
evidence.outcome: New vertebral fracture (NVF) prediction after PKP
evidence.effect: Zero-shot LLM performance was poor (F1-score 0.309; MCC 0.044) but improved with few-shot learning; post-few-shot numbers not given in the abstract
evidence.quote: For NVF prediction, the zero-shot LLM performance was poor (F1-score, 0.309; MCC, 0.044) but improved with few-shot learning.

evidence.title: Comparing the accuracy of large language models and prompt engineering in diagnosing realworld cases
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot base prompting of the same model (GPT-4o)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy (hit1) on real-world inpatient records
evidence.effect: GPT-4o hit1 85.9% with few-shot vs 82.4% base (p = 0.02); outperformed other models (all p < 0.05)
evidence.tradeoff: Few-shot prompting increased costs per correct diagnosis for GPT-4o by approximately ¥4.54.
evidence.quote: Few-shot prompting significantly improved GPT-4o's hit1 (85.9 %) compared to its base model (p = 0.02), outperforming other models (all p < 0.05).

evidence.title: Assessing Large Language Models for Clinical Coding in Hand Surgery: Effect of Note Authorship, Prompt Design, and Diagnosis/Procedure Type
evidence.venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompt (instructions only) vs one-shot and multishot prompts
evidence.outcome: Correctness of ICD-10 and CPT codes assigned by LLMs
evidence.effect: No difference between prompt types: P = 0.27 for ICD-10, P = 0.62 for CPT
evidence.quote: No differences in LLM coding performance were observed between note authors ( P = 0.09 ICD-10, P = 0.48 CPT) or prompt types ( P = 0.27 ICD-10, P = 0.62 CPT).

evidence.title: Annual updates of the European Association of Urology - European Society for Pediatric Urology (EAU-ESPU) paediatric urology guidelines: Are large-language models (LLM) better than the usual structured methodology?
evidence.comparator_used: Unstructured 'humane' dialogue without prompt engineering, versus structured conversation with minor prompt engineering (few-shot prompting)
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM responses when updating the hydrocele and varicocele guideline chapters
evidence.effect: Improved consistency with basic prompting versus humane dialogue; no numerical effect reported (60 conversations analysed)
evidence.tradeoff: Overall reproducibility, consistency and reliability still judged inadequate despite basic prompting; high variability between repeated runs persisted, and the LLMs could not access the scientific databases needed to include recent literature.
evidence.quote: The use of basic prompting in the structured conversations compared to the humane responses improved the consistency of the responses.

evidence.title: Optimizing GPT-5 for Operation-Procedure-Code-Extraction from Operative Reports in Meningioma Surgery: Feasibility and Comparison of Context-Enhancements
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-5 with no additional context (GPT-5s), and GPT-5 with the OPS catalogue only (GPT-5o)
evidence.outcome: OPS-code extraction accuracy, hallucinations and mistakes
evidence.effect: Code-triggering sample phrases from 50 additional reports (GPT-5e): accuracy 70% vs 44% for GPT-5s; hallucinations 2 vs 105; mistakes 35 vs 132 (p < 0.001)
evidence.tradeoff: GPT-5e produced more mistakes than the rules-based GPT-5r (35 vs 21; GPT-5r had fewer, p = 0.034). Building the phrases required 50 additional operative reports.
evidence.quote: Non context enhanced GPT-5s showed the lowest rate of correct coding (44%) and highest number of hallucinations (105) and total mistakes (132).

evidence.title: Optimization of hepatological clinical guidelines interpretation by large language models: a retrieval augmented generation-based framework
evidence.comparator_used: Same setup without few-shot examples
evidence.outcome: Overall answer accuracy
evidence.effect: Few-shot learning did not seem to improve overall accuracy (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: In addition, few-shot learning did not seem to improve overall accuracy.

evidence.title: Preclinical Dialogue Simulation: Evaluating Response Accessibility in Conversational Artificial Intelligence for Aphasia Therapy
evidence.venue: Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with instructions only
evidence.outcome: Accessibility of simulated clinician responses to simulated aphasic patient speech, measured by Flesch Reading Ease, Dale-Chall and a composite of 16 readability measures
evidence.effect: Few-shot prompting generally yielded more accessible clinician responses; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Few-shot prompting and advanced reasoning generally yielded more accessible clinician responses, whereas Gemini demonstrated superior accessibility under zero-shot, standard reasoning.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering does not universally improve Large Language Model performance across clinical decision-making tasks
evidence.comparator_used: Out-of-the-box prompting without MedPrompt dynamic few-shot learning
evidence.outcome: Accuracy across clinical decision-making tasks
evidence.effect: Significantly improved relevant diagnostic testing (lowest baseline accuracy) but was counterproductive for other tasks
evidence.tradeoff: Performance worsened on other tasks; impact was model- and task-dependent
evidence.quote: While it significantly improved the performance on the task with lowest baseline accuracy (relevant diagnostic testing), it was counterproductive for others.

evidence.title: Enhancing the CAD-RADS™ 2.0 Category Assignment Performance of ChatGPT and DeepSeek Through "Few-shot" Prompting
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompt without examples, same models (ChatGPT o1 and DeepSeek-R1), 100 modified MIMIC-IV reports
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of CAD-RADS 2.0 category assignment (stenosis categories and modifiers) versus reference radiologist, and hallucination rate
evidence.effect: Accuracy rose from 14% to 98% for ChatGPT and from 8% to 93% for DeepSeek (both P<0.001). Hallucinations fell from 19% to 0% for ChatGPT and from 54% to 0% for DeepSeek. Kappa with the radiologist was 0.979 for ChatGPT and 0.916 for DeepSeek. Repeat-run kappa was 0.957 for ChatGPT and 0.873 for DeepSeek.
evidence.quote: Few-shot prompting significantly improved accuracy to 98% for ChatGPT and 93% for DeepSeek (both P <0.001) and eliminated hallucinations.

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Provide Emergency Medical Help Where There Is No Ambulance? A Comparative Study on Large Language Model Understanding of Emergency Medical Scenarios in Resource-Constrained Settings
evidence.comparator_used: Other prompt engineering techniques tested across 4 LLMs: chain-of-thought, self-questioning, and stacked self-questioning plus chain-of-thought (no zero-shot arm is described in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Clinician-rated quality and contextual applicability of LLM emergency medical responses
evidence.effect: No numeric effect given in the abstract. The study reports 'benefits' of 5-shot in-context learning from 428 responses rated by 22 clinicians.
evidence.quote: Our study highlights the benefits of In-Context Learning with few-shot prompting, and the utility of the relatively novel self-questioning prompting technique.

evidence.title: Leveraging large language models for information extraction from free-text liver MRI reports and assessment of clinical utility: a multicenter study
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (instructions only) vs global few-shot and center-specific few-shot prompting with 2-12 examples, on DeepSeek-V3 and ChatGPT-4o
evidence.outcome: Field-level macro F1 for information extraction from free-text liver MRI reports
evidence.effect: Largest macro F1 gain when k rose from 0 to 2 (DeepSeek-V3: global +0.106, center-specific +0.127; ChatGPT-4o: global +0.086, center-specific +0.107). Performance plateaued at k=4 (DeepSeek-V3 global 0.848, center-specific 0.865; ChatGPT-4o global 0.835, center-specific 0.861), with adjacent-k gains <0.01.
evidence.quote: Few-shot prompting significantly outperformed zero-shot prompting for both LLMs, with the largest gains in macro F1 observed when k was increased from 0 to 2 (∆DeepSeek-V3: global 0.106, center-specific 0.127; ∆ ChatGPT-4o: global 0.086, center-specific 0.107).

evidence.title: Large-Scale assessment of ChatGPT's performance in benign and malignant bone tumors imaging report diagnosis and its potential for clinical applications
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot ChatGPT without few-shot examples (baseline ChatGPT diagnosis of bone tumor imaging reports)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for benign vs malignant bone tumor classification
evidence.effect: Accuracy 0.73 to 0.87; sensitivity 0.95 to 0.99; specificity 0.58 to 0.73 after few-shot learning
evidence.quote: After few-shot learning, ChatGPT demonstrated significant improvement, achieving an accuracy of 0.87, sensitivity of 0.99, and specificity of 0.73, bringing it much closer to the level of physician diagnostics.

evidence.title: Automating the triage of rheumatology outpatient referrals: a comparative evaluation of 23 large language models under simple and advanced prompting
evidence.comparator_used: Simple prompt with instructions only (no worked examples)
evidence.outcome: Between-model variance in triage accuracy across 23 LLMs, size-accuracy and accuracy-cost associations
evidence.effect: Between-model variance in accuracy fell 5.3-fold (0.014 to 0.003; Levene P=.01). Size-accuracy association went from rho=0.42 (P=.047) to rho=-0.05 (P=.83), and the accuracy-cost relationship was removed.
evidence.tradeoff: Under-triage errors persisted with some LLMs. Worked examples were bundled with explicit triage expectations in the advanced prompt, so their separate contribution is not isolated.
evidence.quote: Advanced prompting minimised between-model variance in accuracy 5.3-fold (0.014 to 0.003; Levene P=.01), abolished the size-accuracy association (rho=-0.05; P=.83) and removed the accuracy-cost relationship.

evidence.title: The Effect of Structured Context on Chest Radiograph Interpretation by a Multimodal Large Language Model: A Pilot Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline zero-shot prompt only: "Diagnose this X-ray image." with no example cases
evidence.outcome: Overall chest radiograph diagnostic accuracy (percent-correct with partial credit) on 50 images
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy rose from 28% to 62%. It reached 100% for COPD, pulmonary edema and foreign body, and 80% for pneumothorax, cardiomegaly and pleural effusion. This was a bundled intervention: the 100 labeled example radiographs were combined with the radiologic framework, so the example effect cannot be isolated.
evidence.tradeoff: Atelectasis accuracy fell from 40% to 20%. Lung cancer (20%) and feeding tube placement (40%) stayed poor, and rib fractures were missed in both conditions. Overall reliability stayed inadequate for independent clinical use. Pilot study with 50 images.
evidence.quote: Overall accuracy improved from 28% at baseline to 62% after the structured-context intervention.

evidence.title: LLM Reasoning Does Not Protect Against Clinical Cognitive Biases - An Evaluation Using BiasMedQA
evidence.comparator_used: Base prompt (zero-shot) and debiasing prompt
evidence.outcome: Biased responses on BiasMedQA vignettes
evidence.effect: Statistically significant reduction in biased responses, greater than debiasing prompt (OR 0.1 vs. 0.6 for Llama-3.3-70B; OR 0.25 vs. 0.6 for Qwen3).
evidence.quote: In contrast, the debiasing and few-shot prompting approaches demonstrated statistically significant reductions in biased responses across both model architectures, with the few-shot strategy exhibiting substantially greater effectiveness (OR 0.1 vs. 0.6 for Llama-3.3-70B; OR 0.25 vs. 0.6 for Qwen3).

evidence.title: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA
evidence.comparator_used: Base prompt without example cases
evidence.outcome: Rate of biased responses
evidence.effect: Statistically significant reductions in biased responses across all three model architectures (no numeric effect sizes given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: The debiasing and few-shot prompting approaches demonstrated statistically significant reductions in biased responses across all three model architectures.

evidence.title: Aligning Probabilistic Beliefs under Informative Missingness: LLM Steerability in Clinical Reasoning
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting without in-context examples (the baseline that does not natively use informative missingness)
evidence.outcome: Alignment of verbalized probabilistic beliefs with the target distribution (log-loss) for ICU prognostic inference
evidence.effect: Reported qualitatively: in-context learning can improve probabilistic alignment; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Using a real-world intensive care testbed, we find that while explicit structural steering and in-context learning can improve probabilistic alignment, the models do not natively leverage informative missingness without careful interventions.

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for information extraction from gastroscopy and colonoscopy reports through multi-strategy prompting
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with instructions only
evidence.outcome: Information extraction performance on gastroscopy and colonoscopy reports (entity extraction, pattern recognition, diagnostic assessment)
evidence.effect: Effectiveness of few-shot learning varied across models and tasks; larger models showed more consistent improvement. No numeric values reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The effectiveness of few-shot learning varied across models and tasks, with larger models showing more consistent improvement patterns.

evidence.title: From text to data: Open-source large language models in extracting cancer related medical attributes from German pathology reports
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting
evidence.outcome: Baseline extraction accuracy for oncological attributes from German pathology reports
evidence.effect: Few-shot prompting improved baseline accuracy relative to zero-shot; no numeric values given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Prompting strategy significantly impacted performance: few-shot prompting improved baseline accuracy, and RAG further enhanced performance, particularly for models with fewer than 24B parameters.

evidence.title: A Reproducible Framework for Safe LLM-Based Simplification of ICU Discharge Summaries in Clinical Information Systems
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (and chain-of-thought prompting) with GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini
evidence.outcome: Automated balance of simplification and preservation (similarity, lexical overlap, medication and diagnosis omission); blinded human faithfulness, readability and actionability
evidence.effect: GPT-4o few-shot: similarity 0.844 ± 0.071, lexical overlap 0.638 ± 0.072, medication omission 2.2%, diagnosis omission 0.4%; best combined human-rated faithfulness, readability and actionability
evidence.quote: GPT-4o few-shot provided the strongest automated overall balance of simplification and preservation (similarity 0.844 ± 0.071, lexical overlap 0.638 ± 0.072, medication omission 2.2%, diagnosis omission 0.4%).

evidence.title: Clinician expertise and prompt engineering enhance cancer information extraction in electronic health records by small language models
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with instructions only (also compared with annotated few-shot prompts)
evidence.outcome: Information extraction performance and hallucination rate
evidence.effect: Few-shot prompting significantly improved performance and reduced hallucinations; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Few-shot prompting and native-language inputs significantly improve performance and reduced hallucinations.

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Reliably Extract Physiology Index Values from Coronary Angiography Reports?
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (also few-shot with implausible examples)
evidence.outcome: Extraction performance of physiology index values from CAG reports
evidence.effect: Changes in prompt technique showed no significant improvement across models; best results were obtained with Llama using zero-shot prompting
evidence.quote: Changes in the prompt techinique and adding a RegEx layer showed no significant improvement across models, while using constrained generation decreased performance, although having the benefit of allowing the usage of specific models that are not able to conform with the templates.

evidence.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Extract and Translate Medical Information in Doctors' Notes for Health Records and Diagnostic Billing Codes
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic code generation performance (ICD-10-CM) with local open-weight models
evidence.effect: Few-shot prompting degraded performance; no numbers reported in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Overfitting and hallucinations
evidence.quote: Contrary to common prompt-engineering guidance, few-shot prompting degraded performance through overfitting and hallucinations.

evidence.title: Multilingual LLM Prompting Strategies for Medical English-Vietnamese Machine Translation
evidence.comparator_used: zero-shot prompting
evidence.outcome: Medical En-Vi translation performance on MedEV
evidence.effect: Few-shot prompting yielded only marginal improvements over zero-shot; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Results show that model scale is the primary driver of performance: larger LLMs achieve strong zero-shot results, while few-shot prompting yields only marginal improvements.

evidence.title: Towards Transparent Reasoning: What Drives Faithfulness in Large Language Models?
evidence.comparator_used: Varying the number and type (quality) of few-shot examples, including fewer examples, across GPT-4.1-mini, LLaMA 70B and LLaMA 8B on BBQ and MedQA
evidence.outcome: Explanation faithfulness
evidence.effect: Reported only as 'significantly impact model faithfulness'; the abstract gives no numbers or direction
evidence.quote: Our results show: (i) both the quantity and quality of few-shot examples significantly impact model faithfulness; (ii) faithfulness is sensitive to prompting design; (iii) the instruction-tuning phase improves measured faithfulness on MedQA.

evidence.title: When Prompts Mislead: Textual Dominance and Diagnostic Bias in MLLMs
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot inference
evidence.outcome: Direction of predictions (bias toward the prompted finding)
evidence.effect: One-shot textual prompts biased predictions toward the prompted finding; no numbers reported in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Prediction bias toward the prompted finding
evidence.quote: (ii) Compared with zero-shot inference, one-shot textual prompts bias predictions toward the prompted finding.

evidence.title: Comparative Performance of Large Language Models in Ophthalmology Referral Triage
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with instructions only (phase one baseline), same models and vignettes
evidence.outcome: Classification accuracy and consistency of ophthalmology referral triage into 16 symptom-based categories
evidence.effect: Mean accuracy across models rose from 68.7% to 73.4% after exposure to 957 labeled examples; ChatGPT 4o consistency rose from 66.8% to 93.8% with net improvement in 933 cases (p < 0.001); ChatGPT 5.1 peak accuracy 79.5%
evidence.tradeoff: Performance remained lower for rare or ambiguous referral categories; human oversight and further clinical validation still needed
evidence.quote: Baseline classification accuracy averaged 68.7% across models, improving to 73.4% post exposure.

evidence.title: Performance of Enhanced Large Language Models on Prosthodontic Multiple-Choice Questions
evidence.comparator_used: Base OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1 without enhancement (ICL tested only as part of a combined RAG + ICL + majority voting package)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on prosthodontic multiple-choice questions (Chinese C-MCQs and English E-MCQs)
evidence.effect: C-MCQs: significant accuracy improvement for both enhanced models (P < .001). E-MCQs: higher accuracy but not statistically significant (P = .145). Knowledge-based errors in C-MCQs were significantly reduced (P < .008) but only non-significantly reduced in E-MCQs (P = .604).
evidence.quote: Enhanced versions of both DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1 achieved significant accuracy improvement compared with their base versions in Chinese-language multiple-choice questions (C-MCQs) (P < .001).

evidence.title: The Performance of Large Language Models in Extracting Intestinal Symptoms From Electronic Health Records: Retrospective Observational Study
evidence.comparator_used: Few-shot prompting compared with zero-shot and no-role prompting
evidence.outcome: Intestinal symptom extraction performance, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, balanced accuracy, and inference time
evidence.effect: Some pairwise differences reached statistical significance (P<.05), but the absolute gains in F1-score were small; no single prompting strategy consistently outperformed the others.
evidence.quote: Although some pairwise differences reached statistical significance (P<.05), the absolute gains in F1-score were small.

evidence.title: Natural Language Processing and Large Language Model-Based Automated AO/OTA Classification of Proximal Femoral Fractures: A MIMIC-IV Retrospective Study
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompt with instructions only
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and F1 for AO/OTA 31A vs 31B classification on a balanced test set of 70 cases
evidence.effect: Few-shot (5 examples per class) accuracy 88.57% (F1 = 88.53%) vs zero-shot accuracy 94.29% (F1 = 94.28%)
evidence.tradeoff: Few-shot performance dropped unexpectedly relative to zero-shot
evidence.quote: Zero‑shot prompting attained the same accuracy (94.29%, F1 = 94.28%), while few‑shot learning unexpectedly dropped to 88.57% (F1 = 88.53%).

evidence.title: Benchmarking transformer-based models for medical record deidentification: A single centre, multi-specialty evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting of general-purpose LLMs for de-identification
evidence.outcome: De-identification performance and hallucinated or added text in LLMs with 1, 5, 10 in-context examples
evidence.effect: GPT-4-0125 with ten shots reached F1 0.898 (0.876-0.915), precision 0.874, recall 0.924; hallucinatory output persisted in Phi-3-mini and Llama-3-8B at zero-, one- and five-shots, and universally for Gemma-7b-IT
evidence.tradeoff: Few-shot examples did not remove hallucination in all models; Gemma-7b-IT hallucinated at every shot count; zero-shot figures for direct comparison were not given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Low-adaptation strategies may improve the performance of generalist LLMs and task-specific models.

evidence.title: Predicting emergency mortality risk in traumatic brain injury: comparative analysis of machine learning and large language model GPT-5
evidence.comparator_used: zero-shot GPT
evidence.outcome: Closeness of LLM predictive performance to the SVM model
evidence.effect: Few-shot GPT most closely matched SVM (SVM AUC = 0.920; all LLMs 0.902-0.919 after threshold adjustment); no numeric zero-shot contrast given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Few-shot GPT most closely matched SVM, CoT + few-shot achieved highest sensitivity, and CoT-only favored specificity.

evidence.title: Detecting stigmatizing language with large language models: mind the settings
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompt without example prompts, across Llama 3.2 3B and Llama 3.1 8B at temperatures 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of stigmatizing language detection in clinical notes
evidence.effect: Examples improved accuracy across all configurations. Best configuration was 8B, temperature 0.25, with examples: accuracy 70.2%, TPR 94.1%, TNR 47.4%. The 3B model without examples had TNR 99.7% but TPR 2%.
evidence.tradeoff: The best configuration with examples had a low TNR (47.4%), so it flags many non-stigmatizing notes. The 3B model without examples almost never detected stigmatizing language (TPR 2%).
evidence.quote: The inclusion of examples improved model accuracy across all configurations, while temperature settings had a variable impact, with smaller models benefiting from higher temperatures and larger models performing better at lower temperatures.

evidence.title: When Chain-of-Thought Backfires: Evaluating Prompt Sensitivity in Medical Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Prompting without few-shot examples (zero-shot baseline)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and position bias
evidence.effect: Few-shot examples degraded performance by 11.9% and increased position bias from 0.14 to 0.47
evidence.tradeoff: Increased position bias from 0.14 to 0.47
evidence.quote: Few-shot examples degrade performance by 11.9% while increasing position bias from 0.14 to 0.47.

evidence.title: Assessing the utility of large language models for phenotype-driven gene prioritization in the diagnosis of rare genetic disease
evidence.comparator_used: Prompting without few-shot examples (zero-shot)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of identifying diagnosed genes within top-50 predictions
evidence.effect: Few-shot learning did not improve accuracy (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Advanced techniques such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and few-shot learning did not improve the accuracy.

evidence.title: A Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models with RAG-enabled Dynamic Prompting for Medical Error Detection and Correction
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (instructions only)
evidence.outcome: Recall and false-positive rate in error detection
evidence.effect: SPR improved recall over zero-shot, which had low recall in both detection tasks, but increased FPR; no numbers reported for this comparison
evidence.tradeoff: Increased false-positive rate with static random exemplars
evidence.quote: SPR improved recall but increased FPR.

evidence.title: Evaluating approaches of training a generative large language model for multi-label classification of unstructured electronic health records
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with neither PEFT nor RAG applied
evidence.outcome: Multi-label EHR classification performance across accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 score
evidence.effect: Few-shot learning consistently outperformed zero-shot learning; no numeric scores reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Few-shot learning consistently outperforms zero-shot learning when neither PEFT nor RAG is applied.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Large Language Models in Converting Clinical Data to FHIR Format
evidence.comparator_used: zero-shot prompting without examples
evidence.outcome: LLM performance converting clinical reports to FHIR bundles
evidence.effect: Few-shot learning enhanced performance; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Risk of overreliance on the provided examples
evidence.quote: While few-shot learning enhanced performance, it also introduced a risk of overreliance on examples.

controls.question: Should we have the model reason step by step before answering, via prompting or its native reasoning mode?
controls.control: Prompt for stepwise reasoning or a reasoning scaffold; for reasoning-capable models, enable reasoning mode or higher effort.
controls.comparator: Direct-answer prompt, or standard mode or lower effort on the same model
controls.aim: Improve accuracy on complex clinical reasoning tasks
variants: Native thinking mode vs standard mode
Higher vs lower reasoning effort setting
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Computational cost and the need for human oversight were named as implementation considerations; all methods, including CoT, sometimes hallucinated ECOG status.
Scaffolding reduced top-1 accuracy from 60% to 40% (Convergence Hesitancy Paradox). Retention and convergence appear to be distinct reasoning tasks.

Reasoning output had a low error rate (0.4 per report). Ophthalmologists found incompleteness, misinformation and hallucinations in it, with English prompts producing less of each (incompleteness 44.31%, misinformation 1.96%, hallucinations 0.59%).
Vigilant human oversight remains essential; no cost or latency tradeoff was reported.
CoT performance degraded significantly as table size increased, with limited accuracy and poor scalability
Reasoning increased vulnerability to several bias types in Llama-3.3-70B, including frequency and recency bias.

evidence.title: ChatGPT Exhibits Gender and Racial Biases in Acute Coronary Syndrome Management
evidence.comparator_used: Direct-answer prompt without asking ChatGPT 3.5 to explain its reasoning first
evidence.outcome: Clinical accuracy and gender/racial bias in ACS management recommendations
evidence.effect: Reported qualitatively as improved clinical accuracy and mitigated instances of gender and racial biases; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Finally, we find that through asking ChatGPT 3.5 to explain its reasoning prior to providing an answer, we are able to improve clinical accuracy and mitigate instances of gender and racial biases.

evidence.title: Deriving the OTA/AO fracture classification from routinely collected radiology reports using a large language model
evidence.venue: OTA international : the open access journal of orthopaedic trauma
evidence.comparator_used: zero-shot prompting without chain-of-thought
evidence.outcome: OTA/AO classification agreement (Cohen kappa and accuracy) against expert ground-truth labels on radiology report fracture descriptions
evidence.effect: Similar performance across strategies: almost perfect agreement at bone and bone-and-location levels, declining to slight agreement at the subgroup level.
evidence.quote: The 3 prompting strategies tested yielded similar classification performance on radiology report fracture descriptions

evidence.title: Adaptive Fast-Slow Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional Classification of Prenatal Ultrasound Reports: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: High-speed base model V3.2-B, which answers directly without CoT reasoning
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and F1-score on subjective severity assessment
evidence.effect: V3.2-B reached 56.6% accuracy on severity grading, with recall of 0 for minor anomalies. V3.2-R with CoT reached 86% accuracy and F1-score=0.75 on external data without RAG.
evidence.quote: In contrast, the V3.2-R model utilizing CoT reasoning achieved superior robustness (86% accuracy and F1-score=0.75) on external data without RAG; notably, introducing RAG to V3.2-R degraded performance to 81%, suggesting potential noise interference.

evidence.title: Evaluation of performance of generative large language models for stroke care
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (ZSL) compared with Chain of Thought (COT) and Talking Out Your Thoughts (TOT) prompting across stroke care stages
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy, hallucinations, specificity, empathy and actionability of LLM outputs across stroke care stages
evidence.effect: No numeric values in the abstract. COT was strong in structured reasoning during diagnosis. TOT did well in empathy and actionability. ZSL gave concise, accurate responses with fewer hallucinations, especially in the Treatment stage. None consistently met high clinical standards.
evidence.quote: Each prompt engineering method showed strengths in specific areas: TOT does well in empathy and actionability, COT was strong in structured reasoning during diagnosis, and ZSL provided concise, accurate responses with fewer hallucinations, especially in the Treatment stage.

evidence.title: MDT-guided language-model reasoning for spinal infection diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Matched minimal zero-shot baseline on the same patient record, model and clinical question
evidence.outcome: Balanced accuracy for infection identification (three locally deployed open-weight models, two centres)
evidence.effect: Balanced accuracy increased in all six model-by-centre comparisons; mean differences of 3.63 percentage points at Centre A and 1.48 percentage points at Centre B
evidence.quote: For infection identification, balanced accuracy increased in all six model-by-centre comparisons, with mean differences of 3.63 percentage points at Centre A and 1.48 percentage points at Centre B.

evidence.title: General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specific Large Language Models in Antibiotic Clinical Decision-Making: A Double-Blind Evaluation with a 2×2 Factorial Design
evidence.comparator_used: Standard direct prompting (no chain-of-thought) on the same model, for both MedGo and DeepSeek
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated comprehensive antibiotic regimen score (1-5)
evidence.effect: MedGo 4.25±0.16 to 4.58±0.09 with CoT (Holm-adjusted p=0.024); DeepSeek 3.98±0.20 to 4.41±0.11 with CoT (Holm-adjusted p<0.001); score dispersion reduced
evidence.quote: CoT improved both models (Holm-adjusted p<0.001 for DeepSeek; p=0.024 for MedGo) and reduced score dispersion.

evidence.title: Implementing a Resource-Light and Low-Code Large Language Model System for Information Extraction from Mammography Reports: A Pilot Study
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompts without chain-of-thought
evidence.outcome: Data extraction accuracy
evidence.effect: Chain-of-thought prompting yielded mixed results (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Chain-of-thought prompting yielded mixed results, while few-shot prompting led to decreased accuracy.

evidence.title: The Value Sensitivity Gap: How Clinical Large Language Models Respond to Patient Preference Statements in Shared Decision-Making
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompt without mitigation (direct recommendation, no decision-matrix scaffold), as implied by the Phase 2 evaluation
evidence.outcome: Directional concordance with patient-stated preferences
evidence.effect: Decision-matrix mitigation improved directional concordance by 0.125 (78-trial Phase 2 evaluation)
evidence.quote: Decision-matrix and VIM self-report mitigations each improved directional concordance by 0.125 in a 78-trial Phase 2 evaluation.

evidence.title: Ethical implications of using general-purpose LLMs in clinical settings: a comparative analysis of prompt engineering strategies and their impact on patient safety
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting
evidence.outcome: Transparency of reasoning (explicit reasoning steps) and ethical reasoning score
evidence.effect: 4.2 vs 1.8 explicit reasoning steps (p < 0.001); mean ethics score 78.3 ± 9.1; 13.0% performance gain
evidence.quote: The study highlighted critical gaps in ethical decision-making transparency, with meta-cognitive approaches providing 4.2 explicit reasoning steps compared to 1.8 in zero-shot methods (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: MedVoiceBias: A Controlled Study of Audio LLM Behavior in Clinical Decision-Making
evidence.comparator_used: Audio LLM prompted without chain-of-thought (direct answer), with bias measured across voice profiles
evidence.outcome: Voice-based demographic bias in surgical recommendations (gender, age, emotion)
evidence.effect: Explicit reasoning eliminated gender bias; age disparities of up to 12% between young and elderly voices persisted in most models despite chain-of-thought prompting; emotion effect could not be detected because emotion recognition was poor
evidence.quote: While explicit reasoning successfully eliminated gender bias, the impact of emotion was not detected due to poor recognition performance.

evidence.title: Comparing the accuracy of large language models and prompt engineering in diagnosing realworld cases
evidence.comparator_used: Base model prompting without chain-of-thought
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy (hit1) on real-world inpatient records
evidence.effect: Chain-of-thought prompting showed no significant improvement; no numbers reported
evidence.quote: Chain-of-thought prompting showed no significant improvement.

evidence.title: Bridging the outcome documentation gap in epilepsy surgery: Validating large language model agents for automated Engel and International League Against Epilepsy scoring from clinical notes
evidence.comparator_used: Concise definition-based prompt
evidence.outcome: Exact Engel subclass agreement, exact ILAE agreement, and ordinal distance against human-adjudicated consensus
evidence.effect: Definition-based prompt: 56.5% exact Engel subclass agreement (95% CI = 49.0-63.7) and 60.6% exact ILAE agreement (95% CI = 53.1-67.6); context-aware prompt: 94.7% for Engel (95% CI = 90.2-97.2) and 93.5% for ILAE (95% CI = 88.8-96.3), with lower ordinal distance for both scales (paired sign tests p < .001).
evidence.quote: The context-aware prompt improved exact agreement to 94.7% for Engel (95% CI = 90.2-97.2) and 93.5% for ILAE (95% CI = 88.8-96.3), with lower ordinal distance for both scales (paired sign tests p < .001).

evidence.title: Will AI keep you out of trouble? An expert panel review of LLMs for hazardous regional anesthesia consults
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot (basic) prompting without chain-of-thought
evidence.outcome: Hazard detection rate in hazardous regional anesthesiology scenarios, as scored by expert panel
evidence.effect: Gemini 75% zero-shot vs 84% chain-of-thought; ChatGPT 56% vs 50%; CoPilot 32% vs 45%; no meaningful overall improvement with chain-of-thought
evidence.quote: There was no meaningful improvement in overall LLM performance with chain-of-thought over zero-shot prompting.

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering for Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Status Extraction: Comparing Large Language Model Techniques
evidence.comparator_used: Simple LLM prompting (and a rule-based NLP algorithm) using the same domain-tuned LLM (LLAMAv3.2)
evidence.outcome: ECOG status extraction accuracy (binary any-ECOG-documented vs none); also sensitivity and the three-class outcome
evidence.effect: CoT accuracy 94% vs simple prompting 86% (rule-based 91%); CoT had the highest sensitivity (0.98); three-class accuracy CoT 0.87 (DFT 0.91); in the QUEST human evaluation CoT scored higher than the simple prompt on output quality, reasoning, bias reduction and user satisfaction
evidence.tradeoff: Computational cost and the need for human oversight were named as implementation considerations; all methods, including CoT, sometimes hallucinated ECOG status.
evidence.quote: Both CoT and double filtering technique (DFT) achieved 94% accuracy, outperforming the rule-based method (91%) and simple prompting (86%).

evidence.title: Assessing and mitigating demographic bias in large language models for diagnostic radiology
evidence.comparator_used: Basic (direct-answer) prompting
evidence.outcome: Number of significant race- or sex-related differences in diagnostic accuracy (bias); overall diagnostic accuracy was also compared
evidence.effect: Basic prompting: 10 significant race- or sex-related differences; chain-of-thought: none. Overall accuracy did not differ across prompting strategies (p = 0.78 text-only, p = 0.95 vision).
evidence.quote: Text-only and vision models showed no statistically significant differences in diagnostic accuracy across prompting strategies (p = 0.78 and 0.95, respectively); basic and self-consistency prompting produced ten and four significant race- or sex-related differences, respectively, whereas no significant differences were observed with chain-of-thought prompting.

evidence.title: Assessing Large Language Models for Clinical Coding in Hand Surgery: Effect of Note Authorship, Prompt Design, and Diagnosis/Procedure Type
evidence.venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
evidence.comparator_used: Chain-of-thought prompt vs zero-shot, one-shot and multishot prompts
evidence.outcome: Correctness of ICD-10 and CPT codes assigned by LLMs
evidence.effect: No difference between prompt types: P = 0.27 for ICD-10, P = 0.62 for CPT
evidence.quote: No differences in LLM coding performance were observed between note authors ( P = 0.09 ICD-10, P = 0.48 CPT) or prompt types ( P = 0.27 ICD-10, P = 0.62 CPT).

evidence.title: Artificial Intolerance: Stigmatizing Language in Clinical Documentation Skews Large Language Model Decision-Making
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompting without chain-of-thought reasoning, on clinical vignettes with stigmatizing language
evidence.outcome: Mitigation of stigmatizing-language-induced skew toward less aggressive patient management
evidence.effect: Reported only as 'limited efficacy'; no numeric effect given in the abstract
evidence.quote: These approaches show limited efficacy; models struggle to explicitly identify SL while remaining implicitly influenced by it.

evidence.title: Measuring the Unmeasurable: A Diagnostic Sensor for AI Reasoning Pathology in Sequential Clinical Decision-Making
evidence.comparator_used: Unstructured sequential information delivery without the scaffold (the same model receiving staged case information)
evidence.outcome: Retention of the correct diagnosis, final accuracy and Convergence Regression across staged clinical information; top-1 accuracy
evidence.effect: Unstructured: 90% access, 60% retained (30% access-stability gap). SIPS scaffold: 80% access, 80% final accuracy, 0% Convergence Regression. Top-1 accuracy fell from 60% to 40% with scaffolding.
evidence.tradeoff: Scaffolding reduced top-1 accuracy from 60% to 40% (Convergence Hesitancy Paradox). Retention and convergence appear to be distinct reasoning tasks.
evidence.quote: A structured scaffold, the Sequential Information Prioritization Scaffold (SIPS), eliminates this gap entirely through forced hypothesis accountability: 80% access, 80% final accuracy, 0% Convergence Regression.

evidence.title: Comparative performance of large language models in structuring head CT radiology reports: multi-institutional validation study in Japan
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompting (direct answer) with the same LLMs
evidence.outcome: Accuracy in structuring head CT reports for intracranial hemorrhage and skull fractures
evidence.effect: Gemini's performance improved notably with Chain of Thought prompting; no numeric values reported in the abstract, and the effect of prompting method on Claude and GPT was not stated separately
evidence.quote: Gemini's performance improved notably with Chain of Thought prompting.

evidence.title: Uncovering Language Disparity of ChatGPT on Retinal Vascular Disease Classification: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.comparator_used: Direct-answer diagnosis prompt (no step-by-step reasoning), in Chinese and English
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic F1-score for retinal vascular disease classification from Chinese FFA reports
evidence.effect: English direct diagnosis gave the best F1 (80.05%) of the 4 prompting strategies, so step-by-step reasoning did not beat direct diagnosis. The abstract gives no F1 for the reasoning arms. Chinese direct diagnosis scored 70.47%.
evidence.tradeoff: Reasoning output had a low error rate (0.4 per report). Ophthalmologists found incompleteness, misinformation and hallucinations in it, with English prompts producing less of each (incompleteness 44.31%, misinformation 1.96%, hallucinations 0.59%).
evidence.quote: Compared with ChatGPT using Chinese prompts for direct diagnosis that achieved an F<sub>1</sub>-score of 70.47%, ChatGPT using English prompts for direct diagnosis achieved the best diagnostic performance (80.05%), which was inferior to ophthalmologists (89.35%) but close to ophthalmologist interns (82.69%).

evidence.title: Evaluation of Prompt Design and Internal Reasoning in Chatbot-Based Medical History Taking: Simulation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Nonthinking mode on the same Qwen3-14B model (2×2 factorial with prompt detail)
evidence.outcome: Information coverage (%) on OSCE-inspired checklist across 66 simulated primary care cases
evidence.effect: Internal reasoning significantly associated with improved coverage in the 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA, with a significant prompt detail × reasoning interaction; detailed+thinking 72.3% (SD 14.3%) vs about 60% for thinking or detailed prompt alone and about 51%-54% for minimal nonthinking. Differences most pronounced for past medical and family history domains.
evidence.quote: In the factorial analysis of the 4 LLM configurations, both prompt detail and internal reasoning were significantly associated with improved information coverage, with a significant interaction between prompt detail and internal reasoning interaction.

evidence.title: Preclinical Dialogue Simulation: Evaluating Response Accessibility in Conversational Artificial Intelligence for Aphasia Therapy
evidence.venue: Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
evidence.comparator_used: Standard reasoning mode on the same models
evidence.outcome: Accessibility of simulated clinician responses to simulated aphasic patient speech, measured by Flesch Reading Ease, Dale-Chall and a composite of 16 readability measures
evidence.effect: Advanced reasoning generally yielded more accessible clinician responses; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Few-shot prompting and advanced reasoning generally yielded more accessible clinician responses, whereas Gemini demonstrated superior accessibility under zero-shot, standard reasoning.

evidence.title: Prompting is All You Need: How to Make LLMs More Helpful for Clinical Decision Support
evidence.comparator_used: Simple direct-answer question prompt (“Should this patient be offered thrombolytics?”) versus a five-step CARDS reasoning scaffold guiding information extraction, timing analysis, contraindication checking, decision-process explanation, and risk-benefit discussion; this was tested as part of the structured prompt package, not isolated from the required-fields/template component.
evidence.outcome: Overall helpfulness domains, especially guideline grading accuracy and conversational reasoning, in acute stroke thrombolysis clinical decision support.
evidence.effect: Structured prompting yielded the largest improvements in guideline grading accuracy and conversational reasoning across multiple models. Reported examples: GPT-4o/o3 guideline adherence 83.3% to 100%, unsafe recommendations 16.7% to 0%, grading 0% to 100%; R1-1776 grading and conversation improved from 0% to 100%.
evidence.tradeoff: Vigilant human oversight remains essential; no cost or latency tradeoff was reported.
evidence.quote: Overall, structured prompting yielded the largest improvements in guideline grading accuracy and conversational reasoning across multiple models.

evidence.title: Clinician input steers AI toward accurate and harmful recommendations
evidence.comparator_used: Standard mode or lower reasoning effort on the same models (non-scaled inference)
evidence.outcome: Harmful echoing of clinician-introduced recommendations across WHO harm-severity tiers
evidence.effect: Reduced by 62.7% for mild, 57.9% for moderate, 76.3% for severe, and 83.5% for death-tier recommendations
evidence.quote: Inference-time scaling reduced harmful echoing of clinician-introduced recommendations across WHO harm-severity tiers by 62.7% for mild, 57.9% for moderate, 76.3% for severe, and 83.5% for death-tier recommendations.

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for diagnostic reasoning from unstructured clinical narratives in epilepsy
evidence.comparator_used: other prompt strategies in the study's prompt-engineering ablation (specific comparators not named in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy for mapping seizure descriptions to seizure onset zone
evidence.effect: Clinician-guided chain-of-thought reasoning gave the most consistent improvements; no numbers reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Specifically, clinician-guided chain-of-thought reasoning leads to the most consistent improvements.

evidence.title: Large Language Models for Classifying Usual Interstitial Pneumonia from Radiology Reports: Native Reasoning Versus Structured Prompting
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Other prompting strategies tested on the same models (the abstract does not name them), without a structured reasoning scaffold
evidence.outcome: Classification performance for UIP pattern on HRCT reports (Cohen's kappa, four-class accuracy)
evidence.effect: Improved all Llama models but degraded all models with native reasoning capability (Qwen 3.5 and Gemma 4); no per-model numbers in the abstract. Best overall configuration: kappa 0.70, 82% four-class accuracy.
evidence.quote: Structured reasoning prompting improved all Llama models but degraded all models with native reasoning capability (Qwen 3.5 and Gemma 4), revealing an architecture-dependent interaction.

evidence.title: Bias Patterns in the Application of LLMs for Clinical Decision Support: A Comprehensive Study
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting
evidence.outcome: Biased outcomes across protected patient attributes in clinical vignette question answering
evidence.effect: Chain of Thought 'effectively reduced biased outcomes' (no numeric values given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Furthermore, specific prompt phrasing significantly influenced bias patterns, whereas reflection-type approaches like Chain of Thought effectively reduced biased outcomes.

evidence.title: Large language models are poor clinical administrators: An evaluation of structured queries in real-world electronic health records
evidence.comparator_used: Direct prompting (no reasoning) on the same models
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on structured EHR table tasks (numerical answers)
evidence.effect: CoT prompting moderately improved performance versus uniformly low direct-prompting accuracy, particularly for logical filtering; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: CoT performance degraded significantly as table size increased, with limited accuracy and poor scalability
evidence.quote: CoT prompting moderately improved performance, particularly for logical filtering, but results degraded significantly as table size increased.

evidence.title: LLM Reasoning Does Not Protect Against Clinical Cognitive Biases - An Evaluation Using BiasMedQA
evidence.comparator_used: Non-reasoning base model (Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen3-32B) vs. reasoning-enhanced variants
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy on BiasMedQA vignettes and susceptibility to cognitive bias
evidence.effect: Reasoning models had better overall performance (OR 4.0 for Llama-3.3-70B, OR 3.6 for Qwen3-32B) but did not consistently prevent cognitive bias. In Llama-3.3-70B, reasoning increased vulnerability to frequency bias (OR 0.6, p = 0.006) and recency bias (OR 0.5, p < 0.001).
evidence.tradeoff: Reasoning increased vulnerability to several bias types in Llama-3.3-70B, including frequency and recency bias.
evidence.quote: In neither of the two models, reasoning capabilities were able to consistently prevent cognitive bias, although both reasoning models achieved better overall performance compared to their respective base model (OR 4.0 for Llama-3.3-70B, OR 3.6 for Qwen3-32B).

evidence.title: Performance evaluation and benchmarking across 16 large language models on a comprehensive real-world emergency department triage data set
evidence.comparator_used: Other prompting strategies and other LLMs among the 16 models benchmarked, without a stepwise scaffold
evidence.outcome: Agreement between LLM-predicted and nurse-assigned ESI levels (quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa)
evidence.effect: Structured stepwise prompting reached kappa_qw = 0.747; other models ranged from 0.18 and mostly showed moderate or lower agreement
evidence.quote: Only a structured stepwise prompting strategy achieved substantial agreement (κ_qw = 0.747), approaching reported human inter-rater reliability.

evidence.title: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA
evidence.comparator_used: Non-reasoning variant of the same model (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-32B, Gemini-2.5-Flash), standard mode
evidence.outcome: Rate of correct responses on BiasMedQA bias-inducing vignettes
evidence.tradeoff: Reasoning did not reliably reduce bias susceptibility; Gemini-2.5-Flash accuracy fell to 47.4-86.1% on four unpublished bias prompts, suggesting possible training-data contamination and brittleness.
evidence.quote: In all three models, the reasoning-enhanced variant achieved higher rates of correct responses (Llama-3.3-70B: 72.5-82.1% vs 61.0-73.4%, Qwen3-32B: 71.7-78.7% vs 55.5-64.1%, Gemini-2.5-Flash: 81.8-88.6% vs 80.0-83.7%).

evidence.title: EQUITRIAGE: A Fairness Audit of Gender Bias in LLM-Based Emergency Department Triage
evidence.comparator_used: Direct-answer baseline prompting for ESI assignment (one of four prompt strategies), same five models
evidence.outcome: ESI triage accuracy
evidence.effect: Chain-of-thought prompting degraded accuracy for all five models (no numeric values given in the abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: Lower triage accuracy with chain-of-thought prompting
evidence.quote: Chain-of-thought prompting degraded accuracy for all five models.

evidence.title: Why Chain of Thought Fails in Clinical Text Understanding
evidence.comparator_used: Direct-answer prompting (non-CoT setting) on the same models
evidence.outcome: Performance on 87 real-world clinical text tasks across 95 LLMs, 9 languages and 8 task types
evidence.effect: 86.3% of models suffer consistent performance degradation in the CoT setting; more capable models remain relatively robust, while weaker ones suffer substantial declines
evidence.tradeoff: CoT enhances interpretability but may undermine reliability in clinical text tasks
evidence.quote: Contrary to prior findings in other domains, we observe that 86.3\% of models suffer consistent performance degradation in the CoT setting.

evidence.title: Clinical reasoning from real-world oncology reports using large language models
evidence.comparator_used: Same Gemma models without structured reasoning prompts
evidence.outcome: F1-score on RECIST tumor response and TNM staging reasoning tasks
evidence.effect: Gemma 12B showed substantial improvements with structured reasoning prompts (F1 81.5 tumor response, 74.3 T-stage, 87.1 N-stage, 90.8 M-stage); Gemma 4B performance was inconsistent and sometimes degraded.
evidence.tradeoff: Reasoning prompts sometimes reduced the performance of the smaller 4B model.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, when guided by structured reasoning prompts, it also showed substantial improvements in reasoning tasks, achieving an F1-score of 81.5 (95% CI: 79.8-83.3) for tumor response, 74.3 (95% CI: 70.8-77.8) for T-stage, 87.1 (95% CI: 85.1-89.0) for N-stage, and 90.8 (95% CI: 89.1-92.2) for M-stage.

evidence.title: A Reproducible Framework for Safe LLM-Based Simplification of ICU Discharge Summaries in Clinical Information Systems
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting without stepwise reasoning
evidence.outcome: Blinded human-rated faithfulness and hallucination; combined faithfulness, readability and actionability
evidence.effect: GPT-4o with chain-of-thought achieved perfect faithfulness and 0% hallucination, but GPT-4o few-shot had the best combined faithfulness, readability and actionability
evidence.quote: In blinded human evaluation, GPT-4o with chain-of-thought prompting achieved perfect faithfulness and 0% hallucination, while GPT-4o few-shot showed the best combined faithfulness, readability, and actionability.

evidence.title: Evaluating performance of large language models for atrial fibrillation management using different prompting strategies and languages
evidence.comparator_used: Input-output (IO) direct prompting compared with 0-shot chain-of-thought (0-COT) and performed chain-of-thought (P-COT) prompting, across three LLMs
evidence.outcome: Consistency of LLM-generated recommendation classifications with ESC 2024 AF guideline classifications
evidence.effect: Claude 3.5 with P-COT had the highest recommendation classification consistency (60.3%); Fleiss kappa across LLM-prompt combinations ranged from 0.449 to 0.763 (moderate to substantial agreement). The abstract gives no IO vs COT numbers for the other models.
evidence.quote: Claude 3.5 with P-COT prompting had the highest recommendation classification consistency (60.3%).

evidence.title: Answer Engineering: Local Trajectory Editing for Protocol-Constrained Decision Making in Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Unguided generation (no step-by-step reasoning)
evidence.outcome: Protocol-compliant outcomes for SSNHL versus acceptance on the conductive contrast condition
evidence.effect: SSNHL compliant outcomes fell from 54.5% to 25.1%. Acceptance on the conductive contrast condition rose from 1.6% to 58.9%.
evidence.tradeoff: Step-by-step reasoning shifted errors rather than eliminating them. SSNHL compliance fell, and the conductive condition was accepted more often.
evidence.quote: In the benchmark, step-by-step reasoning shifted rather than eliminated errors: compliant outcomes for SSNHL decreased from 54.5% under unguided generation to 25.1%, while acceptance on the conductive contrast condition increased from 1.6% to 58.9%.

evidence.title: Automated RECIST tumor response classification through prompt-guided large language models
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting (direct classification without a chain-of-thought scaffold)
evidence.outcome: RECIST category classification performance (micro F1) against expert labels
evidence.effect: Chain-of-thought prompting gave the best results, with micro F1 of 0.81 across all RECIST categories; comparator scores are not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The best results were obtained with chain-of-thought prompting, reaching micro F1 scores of 0.81 across all RECIST categories.

evidence.title: Beyond the Flag: Clinical Framing Closes the Moderation Gap in Suicide Risk Measurement
evidence.comparator_used: Prompting without added reasoning
evidence.outcome: Severity classification performance, by text register (long noisy Reddit posts vs short clinician-authored statements)
evidence.effect: Reasoning hurt on long, noisy Reddit posts and helped on short, clinician-authored statements; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Reasoning reduced performance on long, noisy Reddit posts
evidence.quote: The value of reasoning depends on register: it hurts on long, noisy Reddit posts and helps on short, clinician-authored statements.

evidence.title: Judge-dependent safety gains and model-specific helpfulness costs of evidence-sufficiency prompting in clinical LLMs
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without the structured evidence-sufficiency wrapper (same four models, paired cells)
evidence.outcome: Unsafe overconfident answers under incomplete evidence (primary judge), and correct diagnosis as the helpfulness outcome
evidence.effect: Unsafe overconfidence fell from 49.3% to 24.7% (paired reduction 24.7 points, 95% CI 21.8-27.7; p<0.001). Correct diagnosis fell from 80.3% to 50.3%. The second judge (Sonnet) gave a smaller reduction of 13.1 points.
evidence.tradeoff: Model-specific helpfulness cost: near-free for GPT-5.5, near-total for Gemini (-58 points correct diagnosis). The safety effect was judge-dependent.
evidence.quote: Unsafe overconfidence fell from 49.3% to 24.7%, a paired reduction of 24.7 points (95% CI 21.8-27.7; p<0.001), robust in direction across models and paraphrases.

evidence.title: Mitigating medical bias in large language models by prompt engineering: an empirical study of effectiveness and trade-offs
evidence.venue: Philosophical transactions. Series A, Mathematical, physical, and engineering sciences
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompting without chain-of-thought (standard prompt), compared with four other prompting strategies across five LLMs on a medical bias benchmark
evidence.outcome: Bias gap between privileged and unprivileged groups (accuracy gap in percentage points); significant bias reduction cases by McNemar test
evidence.effect: Average gap across all scenarios lowered by 2.4 percentage points; largest reduction 6.2 percentage points (DeepSeek-V3.1-sex); significant bias reduction in 8/15 cases, primarily by improving performance on unprivileged groups
