evidence.tradeoff: Effectiveness and inference overhead varied substantially across models; no strategy was universally effective and some exacerbated bias. The abstract gives no chain-of-thought-specific overhead figures.
evidence.quote: Chain-of-thought prompting yields the largest reduction, lowering the average gap across all scenarios by 2.4 percentage points, where the largest reduction is 6.2 percentage points, obtained in the DeepSeek-V3.1-sex case.

evidence.title: K-Bench: a clinically calibrated benchmark for evaluating large language models in high-risk mental health conversations
evidence.comparator_used: Standard or lower reasoning settings on the same models
evidence.outcome: Average benchmark performance in high-risk mental health conversations
evidence.effect: No average improvement with elevated reasoning
evidence.quote: Therapeutic prompting produced configuration-specific gains concentrated among weaker models, while elevated reasoning produced no average improvement.

evidence.title: Assessing and enhancing the reliability of Chinese large language models in dental implantology
evidence.comparator_used: Same model (Qwen 2.5, Group D) without chain-of-thought prompting, compared before and after applying CoT
evidence.outcome: Recall and hallucination rate
evidence.effect: Recall improved by 0.0621 ± 0.1474 (P < 0.05); hallucination rate rose by 0.0390 ± 0.1639 (P > 0.05, non-significant)
evidence.tradeoff: Potential increase in hallucination rate; the rise was not statistically significant
evidence.quote: Among enhancement strategies, chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improved Group D’s recall by 0.0621 ± 0.1474 (P < 0.05) but caused a non-significant increase in hallucination rate (0.0390 ± 0.1639, P > 0.05).

evidence.title: Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Direct-answer prompt (standard chain-of-thought and direct prompting of GPT-4 without diagnostic reasoning structure)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of GPT-4 when prompted to mimic clinical reasoning
evidence.effect: No numeric values reported in the text; GPT-4 mimicked clinical reasoning processes without sacrificing diagnostic accuracy
evidence.quote: We find that GPT-4 can be prompted to mimic the common clinical reasoning processes of clinicians without sacrificing diagnostic accuracy.

evidence.title: Are Large Language Models Dynamic Treatment Planners? An In Silico Study from a Prior Knowledge Injection Angle
evidence.comparator_used: Direct-answer zero-shot prompt without chain-of-thought reasoning
evidence.outcome: Insulin dosing behaviour/clinical performance in in silico Type 1 diabetes simulator
evidence.effect: CoT prompting led to overly aggressive insulin dosing (no numeric values reported in the abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: Failure modes including arithmetic hallucination, temporal misinterpretation, and inconsistent clinical logic
evidence.quote: However, LLMs exhibit notable limitations, such as overly aggressive insulin dosing when prompted with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, highlighting critical failure modes including arithmetic hallucination, temporal misinterpretation, and inconsistent clinical logic.

evidence.title: Advancing Question-Answering in Ophthalmology With Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Benchmarking Open-Source and Proprietary Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot direct-answer prompting on the same models
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on ophthalmology multiple-choice questions
evidence.effect: Zero-shot-CoT had overall no significant improvement on the models' performance
evidence.quote: Zero-shot-CoT had overall no significant improvement on the models' performance.

evidence.title: The Potential Clinical Utility of the Customized Large Language Model in Gastroenterology: A Pilot Study
evidence.comparator_used: Customized GPT without Chain of Thought prompting
evidence.outcome: Reasoning performance on judgment-based questions
evidence.effect: No improved reasoning with Chain of Thought prompting; no numbers reported
evidence.quote: Even with the implementation of 'Chain of Thought' prompt engineering, the customized GPT did not achieve improved reasoning.

evidence.title: When Prompts Mislead: Textual Dominance and Diagnostic Bias in MLLMs
evidence.comparator_used: Prompting without Chain-of-Thought reasoning (inconsistent text and contour condition)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy under conflicting text and visual cues
evidence.effect: CoT was associated with further degradation rather than self-correction; no separate numbers given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: CoT did not correct the model's textual override and was associated with worse performance
evidence.quote: When an overlaid lesion contour is paired with an inconsistent textual claim, the textual prompt overrides the correct visual cue: overall accuracy drops from 75% to 46% relative to the visual-only condition, and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is associated with further degradation rather than self-correction.

evidence.title: Evaluating and enhancing the performance of large language models in thyroid eye disease through customization and Chain-of-Thought strategies
evidence.comparator_used: Original GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 without Chain-of-Thought prompting
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on TED multiple-choice questions
evidence.effect: GPT-4 76.2% vs CoT-GPT 86.1%; Claude 3.5 83.2% vs CoT-Claude 87.1%
evidence.quote: The addition of CoT, along with customization into GPT-4 and Claude 3.5, led to improvement in the accuracy (CoT-GPT 86.1%, CoT-Claude 87.1%, TED-GPT 86.1%, TED-Claude 89.1%), outperforming all other newer LLMs.

evidence.title: Real-world performance of open-source large language models in diabetes diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Other prompting strategies tested in the study (four strategies in total); the abstract does not name the baseline, though direct prompting is presumably among them
evidence.outcome: F1-score for MetS and DKD binary classification
evidence.effect: Improved MetS classification but degraded DKD performance; no numeric effect sizes in the abstract (overall best MetS F1 0.650, DKD F1 0.570)
evidence.tradeoff: Degraded DKD performance with Chain-of-Thought prompting
evidence.quote: Chain-of-Thought prompting improved MetS classification but degraded DKD performance.

evidence.title: Reasoning Before Disposition: A Model-Agnostic Cannot-Miss Discipline for Quiet Emergencies and the Case for Deterministic Enforcement
evidence.comparator_used: Forced immediate single-shot disposition (direct answer) vs reasoning-permitted elicitation on the same models
evidence.outcome: Baseline under-triage hazard by elicitation mode
evidence.effect: Forcing an immediate single-shot disposition raised baseline hazard by roughly ten percentage points in two of four Claude models.
evidence.quote: Elicitation mattered: forcing an immediate single-shot disposition raised baseline hazard by roughly ten percentage points in two of four Claude models, and the governance increment in the Claude family was largest under that elicitation.

evidence.title: Evaluation of LLMs accuracy and consistency in the registered dietitian exam through prompt engineering and knowledge retrieval
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot (direct-answer) prompting
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on Registered Dietitian exam questions (GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet)
evidence.effect: CoT improved accuracy for GPT-4o and Claude 3.5; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: For GPT-4o and Claude 3.5, CoT improved the accuracy, and CoT-SC improved both accuracy and consistency.

evidence.title: Evaluating a Multi-Modal Large Language Model for Ophthalmology Triage
evidence.comparator_used: Image-assisted diagnosis without chain-of-thought prompting
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic alignment (dissimilarity score), especially when imaging cues were ambiguous
evidence.effect: CoT gave further gains when imaging cues were ambiguous; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Incorporation of image assistance reduced this to 5.234 +/- 1.305, while CoT prompting provided further gains when imaging cues were ambiguous.

evidence.title: Predicting emergency mortality risk in traumatic brain injury: comparative analysis of machine learning and large language model GPT-5
evidence.comparator_used: zero-shot and few-shot GPT without chain-of-thought
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of LLM mortality prediction
evidence.effect: CoT + few-shot achieved highest sensitivity; CoT-only favored specificity; AUCs comparable (0.902-0.919) after threshold adjustment
evidence.tradeoff: Strategies traded sensitivity against specificity rather than improving both
evidence.quote: Few-shot GPT most closely matched SVM, CoT + few-shot achieved highest sensitivity, and CoT-only favored specificity.

evidence.title: Augmenting large language models with clinical knowledge graph for personalized perioperative fluid therapy question answering
evidence.comparator_used: Vanilla direct-answer prompting
evidence.outcome: Average accuracy on the retrospective case-based question set
evidence.effect: CoT 54.20% vs Vanilla 52.67%
evidence.quote: On the retrospective case-based question set, GraphRAG also showed the strongest overall performance, with an average accuracy of 71.12%, compared with 62.47% for DocRAG, 54.20% for CoT, 52.67% for Vanilla, and 52.54% for RoT.

evidence.title: Not One Size Fits All: The Selective Effect of Reasoning Processes for Multimodal Body Language Emotion Recognition in GAI
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot direct-answer prompting on the same model
evidence.outcome: Chance-corrected recognition of emotion from body language (EU-Emotion Stimulus Set)
evidence.effect: CoT improved Gemini Pro 2.0 (OR = 3.97, p < .001) and mitigated its positivity bias. It impaired Gemini Flash 2.0 (OR = 0.40, p < .001).
evidence.tradeoff: In the smaller Gemini Flash 2.0, CoT created a specific blind spot for negative emotions, which may compromise clinical safety.
evidence.quote: We conclude that CoT is not a universal facilitator for emotion recognition; rather, its effectiveness is contingent on model capacity, and its misapplication to smaller models may compromise clinical safety.

evidence.title: When Reasoning Hurts: Source-Aware Evaluation of Frontier LLMs for Clinical SOAP Note Generation
evidence.comparator_used: Same models with provider-native reasoning disabled (non-reasoning configuration), in a 2x2 design crossed with same-source RAG
evidence.outcome: Overall SOAP note quality (seven automatic metrics and two reference-aware LLM judges) across OMI Health, ACI-Bench and PriMock57
evidence.effect: Enabling reasoning significantly degraded GPT-5.4 performance across all three datasets; the non-reasoning GPT-5.4 configuration achieved the highest overall quality under both evaluation approaches. No numeric effect sizes given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Enabling reasoning significantly degrades GPT-5.4 performance across all three datasets, whereas same-source RAG yields smaller, model-dependent improvements.

evidence.title: When Chain-of-Thought Backfires: Evaluating Prompt Sensitivity in Medical Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Direct answering (no chain-of-thought) on MedGemma 4B and 27B
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on MedMCQA and PubMedQA
evidence.effect: CoT decreased accuracy by 5.7% compared to direct answering
evidence.quote: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting decreases accuracy by 5.7% compared to direct answering.

evidence.title: Increasing Large Language Model Accuracy for Care-Seeking Advice Using Prompts Reflecting Human Reasoning Strategies in the Real World: Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt that only asked the LLM to classify the case vignettes, with no reasoning scaffold
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of care-seeking advice (emergency, nonemergency, self-care) across 45 real patient vignettes and 10 ChatGPT models
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy was 67.6% (recognition-primed) and 66.7% (data-frame) vs 63.3% (default). Self-care accuracy rose from 13.4% (default) to 29.8% (recognition-primed) and 24.6% (data-frame). Performance on the 2 emergency and 30 nonemergency cases stayed high across all prompts.
evidence.quote: Both NDM-inspired prompts increased overall model accuracy (recognition-primed: 67.6%; data-frame: 66.7%) compared to the default prompt (63.3%).

controls.question: Should we fund iterative, expert-led prompt refinement and testing on pilot cases before go-live?
controls.control: Refine prompts through repeated rounds of error analysis on pilot cases, clinician review, or automated optimization before deployment.
controls.comparator: Single initial prompt used without refinement
controls.aim: Reduce errors and improve agreement with clinicians before deployment
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Message use decreased despite better sentiment. Providers may have already formed opinions about draft usefulness. Use rose to 35.8% only after nurses were added with extra in-servicing and education, which was outside the primary analysis. The authors say workflow and human-factors integration is needed.
Overall utilization remained low (19.4%)
New failure mode: prompt optimization regressed the assembly agent, so deterministic post-processing or removing the LLM call was needed instead
Rounding discrepancies increased, though described as minor numerical differences without clinical relevance. Evaluated only in simulated scenarios.
Accuracy remained low even after the update; the authors conclude public-facing LLMs are not ready for independent use
Even with the enhanced prompt, GPT made errors regarding location of stenosis, description of prior spine surgery, and other spine pathologies

evidence.title: Poetic or Prosaic? Evaluating the Linguistic Quality of AI-Generated Draft Replies to Patient Portal Messages
evidence.comparator_used: Initial Phase 1 prompt compared with refined prompts in Phases 2-4
evidence.outcome: Token retention of GDR text in final messages
evidence.effect: Prompt refinements increased token retention (no numeric effect reported in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Prompt refinements increased token retention.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering with a large language model to assist providers in responding to patient inquiries: a real-time implementation in the electronic health record
evidence.comparator_used: Original customized prompt written by informaticians and tested in the Epic test environment (pre-period), versus the engineered prompt (post-period) built with perplexity-based selection, few-shot examples and self-consistency scoring against ground truth
evidence.outcome: Provider use of GPT-4 draft replies (primary) and provider negative sentiment ('thumbs down')
evidence.effect: Negative sentiment fell from 12.0% (n=468) to 8.2% (n=307), OR 0.43 (95% CI 0.36-0.52, P<.01). Unadjusted use did not differ (778 vs 549, P=.89). In the mixed model the engineered prompt was associated with lower use (beta -0.10; 95% CI -0.11 to -0.09, P<.01). Only 2.6% of messages were left identical or nearly identical.
evidence.tradeoff: Message use decreased despite better sentiment. Providers may have already formed opinions about draft usefulness. Use rose to 35.8% only after nurses were added with extra in-servicing and education, which was outside the primary analysis. The authors say workflow and human-factors integration is needed.
evidence.quote: In mixed-effects logistic regression, the odds ratio of having a negative sentiment was lower with the engineered prompt versus the original prompt with an odds ratio of 0.43 (95% CI, 0.36-0.52, P < .01).

evidence.title: Utilization of Generative AI-drafted Responses for Managing Patient-Provider Communication
evidence.comparator_used: Earlier version of the draft-generation prompt before refinement
evidence.outcome: Draft utilization rate by healthcare professionals
evidence.effect: Usage rose from 12% to 20% after prompt refinements, particularly among physicians
evidence.tradeoff: Overall utilization remained low (19.4%)
evidence.quote: Overall utilization was low (19.4%), though prompt refinements improved usage (from 12% to 20%), particularly among physicians.

evidence.title: Closed-Loop Quality Assurance for Production Clinical AI Documentation
evidence.comparator_used: Unoptimized initial prompts for reasoning versus assembly agents
evidence.outcome: Quality of agent output after iterative prompt optimization
evidence.effect: Optimization worked on reasoning agents but not on the assembly agent: four consecutive attempts on one assembly agent produced 18–28 point regressions
evidence.tradeoff: New failure mode: prompt optimization regressed the assembly agent, so deterministic post-processing or removing the LLM call was needed instead
evidence.quote: In our pipeline, prompt optimization worked on the reasoning agents but did not work on the assembly agent: four consecutive optimization attempts on one assembly agent produced 18–28 point regressions.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering on leveraging large language models in generating response to InBasket messages
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Initial merged prompt (V1) used without refinement, compared with the optimized prompt (V3) after 3 iterations of clinician- and patient-informed refinement
evidence.outcome: Physician acceptance of draft suitability and patient preference for tone and overall quality
evidence.effect: Physician acceptance of draft suitability rose from 62% to 84% (P<.001) in the validation set (N=200). Patients preferred the optimized prompt for tone (62%) and quality (62%) versus <15% for the first prompt (P<.001). Positive sentiment in patient comments was 68% versus 23%. Hallucinations appeared in 6% (7/116) of original training-set messages and in none of the validation-set messages.
evidence.quote: When comparing responses created from the final prompt to the initial prompt, patient preference shifted to the optimized prompt (V3) based LLM-generated responses for tone ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%) and quality ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%), significantly higher than preference to the first iteration of prompt based LLM-generated response (<15% for both tone or overall quality) with P -value less than .001.

evidence.title: A Guideline-Concordant Chatbot Framework for Structured Colorectal Cancer Screening: Multistage Feasibility Study
evidence.comparator_used: Initial role-based prompt V1 used as baseline without refinement, compared with iteratively refined prompts V2 and V3 on 45 simulated dialogues rated by 4 gastroenterologists
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated dialogue quality across 6 dimensions (information gathering, judgment timing, recommendation accuracy, personalization and clarity, safety and fairness, actionability)
evidence.effect: Kruskal-Wallis P<.001 for all 6 dimensions; V3 scored higher than V1 on all dimensions (adjusted P<.05); median scores rose progressively from V1 to V3, with no decrease in mean scores on any dimension
evidence.quote: Post hoc analyses using Dunn test with Bonferroni correction showed that prompt V3 scored higher than prompt V1 across all dimensions (adjusted P <.05).

evidence.title: An Artificial Intelligence Oracle for Proactive Population Health Quality Improvement
evidence.venue: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt before iterative refinement (baseline alert performance at the start of the 12-week period)
evidence.outcome: Actionable true-positive rate of safety alerts
evidence.effect: Improved from 68% of 147 alerts to over 95% of 203 alerts over 12 weeks
evidence.quote: Iterative refinement of the AI prompts, driven by clinical leadership review, improved the actionable true-positive rate of safety alerts from 68% of 147 to over 95% of 203 over 12 weeks.

evidence.title: Automated HEART score determination via ChatGPT: Honing a framework for iterative prompt development
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt design before iterative refinement (same models, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of numerical HEART subscore responses (mean error vs physician assessment) and rate of erroneous non-numerical responses
evidence.effect: For both models, the rate of erroneous, non-numerical subscore answers decreased from initial to final prompt. For GPT-4, mean error decreased from 0.16 to 0.10 points (95% CI 0.07-0.14) on a 0-2 point scale.
evidence.quote: Accuracy of numerical responses for HEART subscores (discrete 0-2 point scale) improved for GPT-4 from the initial to final prompt iteration, decreasing from a mean error of 0.16-0.10 (95% confidence interval: 0.07-0.14) points.

evidence.title: Leveraging ChatGPT for thematic analysis of medical best practice advisory data
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompt before dialogue-based (pulse-check) calibration
evidence.outcome: Agreement with human coding (Cohen's kappa) for deductive coding of BPA comments
evidence.effect: Calibration improved agreement for both categories; final kappa with structured prompts and calibration was 0.76 (Category 1) and 0.78 (Category 2). Baseline kappa values were not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Baseline agreement was higher for Category 1 than Category 2, reflecting differences in comment type and complexity, but calibration improved both.

evidence.title: Improving reliability and accuracy of structured data extraction using a consensus large-language model approach-a use case description in multiple sclerosis
evidence.comparator_used: Earlier prompt versions, starting from the initial prompt, across 9 iterations
evidence.outcome: Error rate of LLM structured data extraction versus a reference
evidence.effect: Clear reduction in error rate of the various LLMs over 9 prompt iterations. No numeric values were given in the text.
evidence.quote: Through 9 iterations of improving the structure and content of the prompt, we have seen a clear reduction in the error rate of the various LLMs.

evidence.title: Protocol-constrained AI enhances tacrolimus dosing accuracy in kidney transplant care
evidence.comparator_used: Initial TacroDose AI prompt before refinement (single initial prompt)
evidence.outcome: Protocol adherence, sentinel errors and reproducibility of tacrolimus dosing recommendations in 300 simulated scenarios
evidence.effect: Adherence 72.9% to 91.7%; sentinel errors 13.9% to 1.0%; reproducibility 77.3% to 86.7% (all p < 0.01)
evidence.tradeoff: Rounding discrepancies increased, though described as minor numerical differences without clinical relevance. Evaluated only in simulated scenarios.
evidence.quote: Prompt refinement substantially improved performance: TacroAI 2.0 achieved 91.7% adherence, reduced sentinel errors to 1.0%, and improved reproducibility from 77.3 to 86.7% (all p < 0.01).

evidence.title: Deficiencies in clinical reasoning of LLMs in low back pain management and remediation via prompt engineering: from performance evaluation to error diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Original baseline prompts without the targeted safety-oriented prompt added (same questions, n = 7)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, completeness, practicality, readability and safety scores (linear mixed models, Hedges' g as effect size)
evidence.effect: Deepseek-V2.5 improved significantly on all five dimensions (p < 0.001), with the largest gains in safety and completeness. GPT-4o improved significantly on four dimensions but not safety (p = 0.227). Model × condition interaction was significant only for safety (p = 0.002).
evidence.quote: Targeted prompt engineering produced significant improvements for Deepseek-V2.5 across all five evaluation dimensions (p < 0.001), with the largest gains in safety and completeness.

evidence.title: Assessing Large Language Models for Clinical Coding in Hand Surgery: Effect of Note Authorship, Prompt Design, and Diagnosis/Procedure Type
evidence.venue: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
evidence.comparator_used: Original prompts before updating to emphasize ICD-10 laterality (after error analysis)
evidence.outcome: ICD-10 coding accuracy, where laterality was the most common error
evidence.effect: Prompts updated to emphasize ICD-10 laterality demonstrated improved accuracy (40%), compared with 23.9% correct ICD-10 codes overall
evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy remained low even after the update; the authors conclude public-facing LLMs are not ready for independent use
evidence.quote: Prompts updated to emphasize ICD-10 laterality demonstrated improved accuracy (40%).

evidence.title: Assessing the ability of large language models to simplify lumbar spine imaging reports into patient-facing text: a pilot study of GPT-4
evidence.comparator_used: Initial single prompt used without refinement
evidence.outcome: Omission rate of clinically relevant information in simplified reports
evidence.effect: Enhanced prompt maintained reading level while significantly improving omission rate (p < 0.0001)
evidence.tradeoff: Even with the enhanced prompt, GPT made errors regarding location of stenosis, description of prior spine surgery, and other spine pathologies
evidence.quote: An enhanced prompt model using high scoring reports-maintained reading level while significantly improving omission rate (p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering Enables Open-Source LLMs to Match Proprietary Models in Diagnostic Accuracy for Annotation of Radiology Reports
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt for Llama3-8b before prompt engineering on the 600 pilot cases
evidence.outcome: Match-score for annotating Danish trauma radiology reports (Llama3-8b)
evidence.quote: Prompt engineering improved the  Match -score for Llama3-8b from 77.8% (95% CI: 74.4% – 81.1%) to 94.3% (95% CI: 92.5% – 96.2%).

evidence.title: Patient Triage and Guidance in Emergency Departments Using Large Language Models: Multimetric Study
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt before prompt engineering (pre-engineering baseline) for MEWS-based triage
evidence.outcome: MEWS-based triage accuracy (and consistency) on 1854 simulated scenarios
evidence.effect: Accuracy improved after prompt engineering; post-engineering GPT-4-Turbo reached 100% vs GPT-4o 96.2%. Pre-engineering figures not given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Gains differed by model: GPT-4o performed better before prompt engineering but gained less afterwards, so adaptability to prompt optimization varied. No cost or latency reported.
evidence.quote: In the first phase, ChatGPT's triage accuracy, based on MEWS, improved following prompt engineering.

evidence.title: Feasibility of Tailoring Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ambient Scribes for Intensive Care Unit Rounds: Algorithm Development and Validation
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt before iterative refinement (same transcript, phase 1)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and error rate of LLM-generated ICU progress notes
evidence.effect: Iterative prompt improvements increased accuracy and reduced errors in phase 1; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Iterative improvements to the prompt increased accuracy and reduced errors during phase 1.

evidence.title: Evaluating cognitive performance: Traditional methods vs. ChatGPT
evidence.comparator_used: Original GPT-3.5 scoring prompts and interaction protocol before refinement, compared against physician scoring
evidence.outcome: Agreement of GPT-3.5 scores with physician scores on memory and language assessments
evidence.effect: Before refinement, GPT-3.5 differed from physicians in memory (8 of 21 sections, P<0.05) and language in healthy subjects (P=0.009), and in language in stroke subjects (P=0.002). After refinement, differences remained only in memory sections 8 and 14 (P<0.05), with no significant differences in the rest (P>0.05).
evidence.tradeoff: Refinement needed extra conversations (two for healthy subjects, one for stroke subjects). Memory differences in sections 8 and 14 remained. Refinement was tuned on the same discrepancies it was then tested on, and no cost or latency was reported.
evidence.quote: After testing, optimizing the interaction process and scoring rules can reduce most of the differences, with only differences observed in 8th and 14th sections of memory ( P < 0.05), and no significant differences observed in the rest ( P > 0.05) ( Figure 6 ).

evidence.title: Optimizing Large Language Models for Hospital Discharge Prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Automated prompt optimization compared with the basic prompt for GPT-5 discharge prediction on the hold-out test set.
evidence.outcome: Same-day hospital discharge prediction performance: F1 score, sensitivity, PPV, and specificity.
evidence.effect: Baseline GPT-5 prompt achieved an F1 score of 0.48 and sensitivity of 0.37 on the validation set; automated prompt optimization had higher F1 score and sensitivity than the basic prompt on the hold-out test set, with lower PPV and specificity.
evidence.tradeoff: Lower PPV and specificity with automated prompt optimization.
evidence.quote: Automated prompt optimization had higher F1 score and sensitivity than the basic prompt on the hold-out test set, with lower PPV and specificity; test-time scaling and expert-led prompt engineering showed minimal improvement.

evidence.title: Performance evaluation of 9 large language models in anticoagulation decision-making for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
evidence.venue: Research and practice in thrombosis and haemostasis
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt before optimization (baseline HAS-BLED scoring accuracy of 8%-51% across models)
evidence.outcome: HAS-BLED scoring accuracy
evidence.effect: Accuracy reached 95% with ChatGPT-4o Deep Research and 89% with DeepSeek-R1 after prompt optimization (P < .001), versus baseline accuracy of 8%-51% across all models
evidence.quote: Notably, prompt optimization markedly improved HAS-BLED scoring accuracy, reaching 95% with ChatGPT-4o Deep Research and 89% with DeepSeek-R1 (P < .001).

evidence.title: Evaluation of large language models for antimicrobial classification: implications for antimicrobial stewardship programs
evidence.comparator_used: Initial unguided classification (single prompt, no feedback) versus feedback-informed reclassification after feedback on 20% of misclassified cases
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of classifying medications as antimicrobial vs non-antimicrobial (7,239 entries, against manual reference standard)
evidence.effect: All accuracies improved significantly (P < .001) postfeedback: Gemini 99.6%, Claude Sonnet 4 99.4%, ChatGPT-3.5 81.0%, Copilot 79.7%; Gemini had the highest error reduction rate (69.2%) and macro-F1 of 98.9% (95% CI: 98.4-99.3). Baseline accuracy values were not reported in the text.
evidence.quote: Postfeedback, all accuracies improved significantly (P < .001) to Gemini (99.6%), Claude Sonnet 4 (99.4%), ChatGPT-3.5 (81.0%), and Copilot (79.7%).

evidence.title: Hazard-aware adaptations bridge the generalization gap in large language models: a nationwide study
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompt without error-driven adaptation
evidence.outcome: Generalizability of smoking history extraction across institutions (VA vs MIMIC-III)
evidence.effect: Adapted prompts achieved better generalizability across institutions than zero-shot prompts; macro-F1 with the adapted prompt was 0.86 in VA and 0.85 in MIMIC
evidence.tradeoff: Errors remained where task-specific requirements conflicted with pre-trained model behavior, and these were more frequent in the untrained institution (p adj=0.007); hazard distributions varied significantly between institutions
evidence.quote: We demonstrate that adapted prompts, engineered to address observed errors, achieve better generalizability across institutions compared to zero-shot prompts.

evidence.title: Optimizing ChatGPT's Interpretation and Reporting of Delirium Assessment Outcomes: Exploratory Study
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt before iterative optimization (earlier prompt versions of the same ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 models)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy in detecting delirium symptoms and assigning Sour Seven Questionnaire scores against human expert scores
evidence.effect: Described as notable improvement after iterative prompt engineering; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Performance notably improved through iterative prompt engineering, enhancing the models' capacity to detect delirium symptoms and assign scores.

evidence.title: A framework to assess clinical safety and hallucination rates of LLMs for medical text summarisation
evidence.comparator_used: Earlier/initial prompt and workflow configurations in the iterative experiments (no refinement)
evidence.outcome: Major errors (hallucinations and omissions) in LLM-generated clinical notes
evidence.effect: Refining prompts and workflows reduced major errors below previously reported human note-taking rates; overall across 18 configurations (12,999 annotated sentences) hallucination rate was 1.47% and omission rate 3.45%. No per-configuration numbers given in the text.
evidence.quote: By refining prompts and workflows, we successfully reduced major errors below previously reported human note-taking rates, highlighting the framework's potential for safer clinical documentation.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering enables open-source large language models to match proprietary models in diagnostic accuracy for annotation of radiology reports
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt before prompt engineering (Llama3-8b baseline prompt) vs prompt refined on 600 pilot cases
evidence.outcome: Match score for annotating trauma radiology reports (Llama3-8b)
evidence.quote: Prompt engineering improved the Match score for Llama3-8b from 77.8% (95% CI: 74.4%-81.1%) to 94.3% (95% CI: 92.5%-96.2%).

evidence.title: Automated extraction of ESGO operative report fields from free-text surgical notes using large language models in advanced ovarian cancer
evidence.venue: International journal of gynecological cancer : official journal of the International Gynecological Cancer Society
evidence.comparator_used: Basic (unenhanced) form of each model with the initial prompt
evidence.outcome: F1 score for extracting disease involvement across 35 ESGO anatomical sites
evidence.effect: Top two models' F1 rose from 0.851 (95% CI 0.841 to 0.861) and 0.864 (95% CI 0.854 to 0.873) at baseline to 0.897 (95% CI 0.888 to 0.906) and 0.875 (95% CI 0.866 to 0.884) after optimization. Optimization also improved distinction between closely related sites and reduced left/right errors. The enhancements were a bundle (terminology list, clearer instructions, few-shot examples), so their effects are not separated.
evidence.quote: Following optimization strategies, accuracy increased further, reaching 0.897 (95% CI 0.888 to 0.906) and 0.875 (95% CI 0.866 to 0.884).

evidence.title: Securing Safety and Quality in AI-generated Patient Education: A Nurse-led Methodological Framework Integrating Kolcaba's Comfort Theory
evidence.comparator_used: Initial prompt output versus outputs after clinical refinement and theoretical alignment stages of the iterative prompt process
evidence.outcome: Readability (Ateşman's Readability Index) and mitigation of AI hallucinations
evidence.effect: Readability scores improved from 48.5 to 66.8; expert panel CVI 0.93-0.95; hallucinations reported as mitigated
evidence.quote: Readability scores significantly improved from 48.5 to 66.8.

evidence.title: Human-Machine Agreement in Medical Ethics: Patient Autonomy Case-Based Evaluation of Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Foundational LLMs (ChatGPT, LLaMA, Gemini) at baseline, before iterative improvement
evidence.outcome: Agreement with physician panel consensus (Cohen κ)
evidence.effect: Baseline slight to fair agreement rose to substantial or higher (Cohen κ 0.73-0.82); improvement significant (P=.006 ChatGPT, P<.001 Gemini, P<.001 LLaMA)
evidence.quote: With iterative improvement techniques, this agreement evolved to be substantial or higher (Cohen κ of 0.73-0.82).

evidence.title: Institution-Specific LLM Prompting Recovers PHI That De-identification Systems and Their Gold Standards Both Miss
evidence.comparator_used: Initial HIPAA-aligned baseline prompt (prompt 1) before refinement
evidence.outcome: Recovery of missed institutional PHI and precision after prompt refinement based on missed categories
evidence.effect: Recovered 79% (48/61) of missed categories; the over-redaction instruction restored precision
evidence.quote: Naming the missed categories recovered 79\% (48/61) of them, and discouraging over-redaction restored precision.

evidence.title: A Reproducible Protocol and Framework for Large Language Model (LLM)-Assisted Estrogen and Progesterone Receptor (ER/PR) Scoring
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline performance before the recursive prompt engineering and zero-state reset (fresh chat session) protocol
evidence.outcome: Concordance with CAP ER/PR scoring
evidence.effect: Accuracy improved from a 70-80% baseline to ≥95% CAP concordance; final concordance exceeded 83% across all models
evidence.quote: The ZSR protocol proved essential, improving accuracy from a 70-80% baseline to ≥95% CAP concordance.

evidence.title: Developing artificial intelligence tools for institutional review board pre-review: A pilot study on ChatGPT's accuracy and reproducibility
evidence.comparator_used: Standard (non-customized) prompts with GPT-4o
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and consistency of extracting ethically relevant information from clinical research protocols and informed consent forms
evidence.effect: No figures given for this comparison; customized Japanese-prompt GPTs were reported as more accurate and consistent than standard prompts.
evidence.quote: GPTs with customized prompts produced more accurate and consistent outputs than standard prompts.

evidence.title: Comparative performance of large language models and Drugs.com versus Lexicomp for antiseizure medication drug-drug interactions: A cross-sectional study with iterative prompting analysis
evidence.venue: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
evidence.comparator_used: Single initial (zero-shot) prompt without iterative refinement
evidence.outcome: Specificity for clinically relevant (major/moderate) ASM drug-drug interactions, assessed in false positive cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT specificity 0.358 with single prompt vs 0.77 after iterative prompting; DeepSeek 0.200 vs 0.42
evidence.tradeoff: Post hoc analysis run exclusively on false positive cases, so effects on sensitivity and true positives were not assessed. DeepSeek specificity stayed low even after iteration.
evidence.quote: Iterative prompting substantially improved specificity for ChatGPT (0.77) and DeepSeek (0.42), correcting many false positive classifications.

evidence.title: Evaluating Prompt Strategies for LLM-Based De-Identification of German Discharge Letters: A Feasibility Study Using GraSCCo
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompt and structurally modified setups (session-isolated, structured-input) without prompt refinement
evidence.outcome: De-identification F1-score on synthetic German discharge letters (GraSCCo)
evidence.effect: F1 0.93 for the optimized prompt (GPT-4o) vs 0.81 session-isolated and 0.79 structured-input; the baseline setup was unsuitable due to excessive text loss; GPT-OSS with the optimized prompt reached 0.90
evidence.quote: Results indicate that prompt refinement has a stronger impact on de-identification quality than structural preprocessing.

evidence.title: MAM-AI: An On-Device Medical Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Nurses and Midwives in Zanzibar
evidence.comparator_used: Original prompt before redesign
evidence.outcome: Deflection rate (loss of helpfulness) of the deployed generator
evidence.effect: Deflection cut from 33% to 3%
evidence.quote: recover its helpfulness with a redesigned prompt that cuts deflection from 33% to 3%

controls.question: Should we split the task into a chain of smaller prompts instead of one large prompt?
controls.control: Break the task into sequential or atomic sub-prompts where each step's output feeds the next.
controls.comparator: One combined prompt performing the whole task
controls.aim: Improve accuracy and traceability on complex multi-step tasks
variants: Merging prompts when classifier routing errs
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Prompt engineering did not correct calibration bias or reproducibility limitations. Run-to-run variability was substantial, with a mean score range of 17.5 points and up to 43 points for one webpage.

evidence.title: Editing Physicians' Responses Using GPT-4 for Academic Research
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.comparator_used: Combined prompting (one prompt performing the whole editing task)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of editing physicians' responses (removing identifiable and irrelevant content while keeping medical advice)
evidence.effect: Incremental prompting proved more accurate than combined prompting; no numeric comparison reported in the abstract (overall, 31 of 40 responses were accurately modified)
evidence.quote: Challenges included misclassification and incomplete removal, with incremental prompting proving more accurate than combined prompting.

evidence.title: Summarize-then-Prompt: A Novel Prompt Engineering Strategy for Generating High-Quality Discharge Summaries
evidence.comparator_used: Direct concatenation of clinical notes in one combined prompt (M1)
evidence.outcome: Completeness and correctness of LLM-generated hospital course summaries (physician Likert ratings); conciseness also rated
evidence.effect: Completeness 4.28 ± 0.63 vs 4.01 ± 0.69 (p < 0.001); correctness 4.37 ± 0.54 vs 4.17 ± 0.57 (p = 0.002); conciseness no significant difference (p = 0.308)
evidence.quote: The summarize-then-prompt strategy outperformed direct concatenation strategy in both completeness (4.28 ± 0.63 vs. 4.01 ± 0.69, p < 0.001) and correctness (4.37 ± 0.54 vs. 4.17 ± 0.57, p = 0.002) of the summarization of the hospital course.

evidence.title: Automating standardization of prostate cancer biopsy and histopathology reports with privacy-preserving local large language models
evidence.comparator_used: Single-stage prompt performing the whole procedure-report extraction
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of structured data extraction from procedure reports versus human-extracted data
evidence.effect: Multistage workflow 98.0% (1314/1341) vs single-stage 95.3% (991/1040 discrete data points)
evidence.quote: The multistage LLM-NLP pipeline reached 98.0% accuracy (1314/1341) for ultrasound procedure reports.

evidence.title: Prompt Architecture as a High-Impact Design Factor in Expert-Rated Clinical Documentation Quality: A Controlled Comparative Study in Inpatient Rehabilitation
evidence.comparator_used: Single prompt (SP) generating the whole discharge report in one pass
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated quality of AI-generated inpatient rehabilitation discharge reports (structural integrity, clinical coherence, completeness, readability; 4-point ordinal scale)
evidence.effect: Section-based prompt (SBP) had the highest median performance and strongest regression effect, but differences among LLM prompting strategies were not statistically significant after correction. No numeric values are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: SBP demonstrated the highest median performance and strongest regression effect, although differences among LLM-based strategies were not statistically significant after correction.

evidence.title: An Evaluation of Six Artificial Intelligence Tools for Formulary Management
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Clinical Pharmacy : JACCP
evidence.comparator_used: Initial broad single prompt requesting a complete drug monograph
evidence.outcome: Quality of AI-generated monograph content (detail, accuracy, scholarliness)
evidence.effect: Broad prompts gave vague, incomplete, or inaccurate responses across all tools; section-specific prompts substantially improved output quality in all six tools (qualitative, no numbers reported)
evidence.quote: Refined prompt engineering strategies using targeted, section-specific requests substantially improved output quality, with all AI tools producing more detailed, accurate, and scholarly responses.

evidence.title: Structured Clinical Reasoning Prompt Enhances LLM’s Diagnostic Capabilities in Diagnosis Please Quiz Cases
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional zero-shot chain-of-thought prompt performing the whole task in one step
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy (primary diagnosis and top three diagnoses) on 322 Diagnosis Please quiz cases
evidence.effect: Primary diagnosis accuracy 60.6% for two-step vs 56.5% for baseline (p=0.042); top three accuracy 70.5% vs 66.5% (p=0.005). Summary-only: 56.3% primary, 65.5% top three, with no significant difference from baseline.
evidence.quote: Primary diagnosis accuracy was 60.6% for the two-step approach, compared to 56.5% for baseline (p=0.042) and 56.3% for summary-only (p=0.035).

evidence.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Gates for Multimodal Large Language Models in Dental Image Interpretation: A Prompt-Level Protocol for Improving Accuracy
evidence.comparator_used: P1 zero-shot natural language prompt (and P2 structured sections with local checks)
evidence.outcome: Total Score and Full Accuracy on five dental image-interpretation variables vs radiology report
evidence.effect: Mean Total Score 3.47 ± 1.33 (P1) to 4.77 ± 0.68 (P3 HRG); Full Accuracy 23.3% to 86.7%; failures involving three or more variables 20.0% to 3.3%; significant differences for Tooth Number, Tooth Angulation, Anatomical Relationship
evidence.quote: Mean Total Score increased from 3.47 ± 1.33 for P1 to 4.77 ± 0.68 for P3, while Full Accuracy increased from 23.3% to 86.7%.

evidence.title: Benchmark evaluation of large language models for clinical decision support in headache management
evidence.venue: Journal of oral & facial pain and headache
evidence.comparator_used: ask-at-once (AO) prompting
evidence.outcome: supplementary value
evidence.effect: Supplementary value was generally higher with ask-in-sequence (AS); no numerical effect size reported.
evidence.quote: Overall, supplementary value was generally higher with AS, while strategy-related differences in diagnostic accuracy were observed only for Grok-3.

evidence.title: Extracting Cardiorespiratory Symptoms From Clinical Notes Using Open-Weight Large Language Models: Method Development and Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Single-prompt strategies (instruction-only, ICD-10-CM definition-based, assumption-free) on Llama 3.3-70B
evidence.outcome: Precision, recall and F1 for symptom/sign extraction and ICD-10-CM code generation during prompt development
evidence.effect: Multimodule approach with postprocessing achieved the highest performance during prompt development; no numeric values for this comparison in the abstract
evidence.quote: The multimodule approach with postprocessing achieved the highest performance during prompt development.

evidence.title: Evaluating privacy leakages in LLM-driven ambient clinical documentation
evidence.comparator_used: Single combined prompt that generates the note and applies privacy requirements in one step
evidence.outcome: Leakage of third-party personal information in LLM-generated clinical notes
evidence.effect: Decomposing generation and privacy editing into separate steps could further reduce leakage, but only when privacy was defined with contextual specificity; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Decomposing generation and privacy editing into separate steps could further reduce leakage, but only when privacy was defined with contextual specificity.

evidence.title: How DISCERNing is ChatGPT? An Evaluation of Models and Prompt Engineering in Assessing Patient Education Materials
evidence.comparator_used: Naïve zero-shot single prompt scoring the whole DISCERN instrument (the Combined split-plus-augmented approach was the reported result)
evidence.outcome: Agreement with human DISCERN scores (correlation, absolute error)
evidence.effect: Combined prompting, which includes item-level Split scoring, modestly improved agreement and reduced absolute error. Agreement was still weak to moderate. Results for Split scoring alone are not given separately.
evidence.tradeoff: Prompt engineering did not correct calibration bias or reproducibility limitations. Run-to-run variability was substantial, with a mean score range of 17.5 points and up to 43 points for one webpage.
evidence.quote: Prompt engineering did not correct calibration bias or reproducibility limitations.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Large Language Models in Converting Clinical Data to FHIR Format
evidence.comparator_used: single-step prompting (comparator not explicitly described in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and completeness of FHIR conversion
evidence.effect: Two-step approach significantly improved accuracy and completeness; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: The findings demonstrate the critical role of prompt engineering, with the two-step approach shown to significantly improve accuracy and completeness.

controls.question: Should we have the model review and revise its own answer before it is used?
controls.control: Add a step asking the model to critique and revise its own answer before release.
controls.comparator: Single-pass answer without self-review
controls.aim: Catch and correct errors before outputs reach users
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Self-reflection could introduce new errors or leave errors uncorrected; the abstract reports negative benefit on some datasets but no figures.

evidence.title: Multidisciplinary expert evaluation of large language models on questions regarding bariatric surgery: a comparative analysis of ERNIE Bot 4.0, ChatGPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, and Gemini Pro
evidence.comparator_used: Single-pass initial answers (original responses before any review); basic review prompt as the minimal self-review baseline
evidence.outcome: Self-correction of bariatric surgery answers after a review prompt
evidence.effect: Reported only as 'significant self-correction capabilities'; no numeric effect given in the abstract
evidence.quote: However, they showed significant self-correction capabilities, especially when using internet searches and evidence-based resources.

evidence.title: Enhancing diabetic retinopathy query responses: assessing large language model in ophthalmology
evidence.comparator_used: Single-pass answer without self-review (initial responses before the self-correction prompt)
evidence.outcome: Average accuracy score of LLM responses to DR questions
evidence.effect: Average accuracy score increased from 6.4 to 7.5 after the self-correction prompt (reported as a significant improvement)
evidence.quote: After introducing a self-correction prompt, the average accuracy score demonstrated a significant improvement, increasing from 6.4 to 7.5.

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Self-Correct in Medical Question Answering? An Exploratory Study
evidence.comparator_used: Standard chain-of-thought prompting (single pass) vs iterative self-reflection loop, GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on medical multiple-choice QA (MedQA, HeadQA, PubMedQA)
evidence.effect: Modest gains on MedQA; limited or negative benefits on HeadQA and PubMedQA; more reflection steps did not guarantee better performance; no numeric values in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Self-reflection could introduce new errors or leave errors uncorrected; the abstract reports negative benefit on some datasets but no figures.
evidence.quote: Our results show that self-reflective prompting does not consistently improve accuracy and its impact is highly dataset- and model-dependent: it yields modest gains on MedQA but provides limited or negative benefits on HeadQA and PubMedQA, and increasing the number of reflection steps does not guarantee better performance.

evidence.title: Augmenting large language models with clinical knowledge graph for personalized perioperative fluid therapy question answering
evidence.comparator_used: Vanilla single-pass prompting
evidence.outcome: Average accuracy on the retrospective case-based question set
evidence.effect: RoT 52.54% vs Vanilla 52.67%
evidence.quote: On the retrospective case-based question set, GraphRAG also showed the strongest overall performance, with an average accuracy of 71.12%, compared with 62.47% for DocRAG, 54.20% for CoT, 52.67% for Vanilla, and 52.54% for RoT.

evidence.title: Med-HEAL: Analyzing and Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical LLMs with Hallucination-Aware In-Context Learning
evidence.comparator_used: Original first answer from the model without self-critique
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on open-ended EHR clinical question answering
evidence.effect: Self-critique improved accuracy for three of five models (p < 0.05); no parameter updates required
evidence.quote: Experiments across five open-source LLMs-BioMistral, Llama-3.1, DeepSeek, Qwen2.5, and Qwen3, show that the self-critique strategy improves accuracy for three of five models (p < 0.05) without requiring parameter updates.

controls.question: Should we add prompt instructions that guard against cognitive bias and clinically irrelevant demographic cues?
controls.control: Instruct the model to ignore clinically irrelevant demographic or socioeconomic information, avoid stereotyping, and counter cognitive biases such as base-rate neglect.
controls.comparator: Standard prompt without debiasing instructions
controls.aim: Reduce biased or stereotyped outputs
variants: Ignore clinically irrelevant socioeconomic or demographic information
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Responses were 50% longer; responses appeared thoughtful and deliberate despite persistent bias, which risks false reassurance
Poor sensitivity after adding prevalence cues: 30.4%.
Effects varied by model: Sonnet 4.5 showed paradoxical worsening, and residual disparities remained.

evidence.title: Forewarning Artificial Intelligence about Cognitive Biases
evidence.venue: Medical decision making : an international journal of the Society for Medical Decision Making
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without the forewarning (control group, no debiasing instruction)
evidence.outcome: Overall cognitive bias in GPT responses across 10 clinically nuanced cases; length of response; frequency of discussing cognitive biases
evidence.effect: Forewarning decreased overall bias by only 6.9%; no bias was extinguished completely; responses were 50% longer and discussed cognitive biases more than 100 times more frequently
evidence.tradeoff: Responses were 50% longer; responses appeared thoughtful and deliberate despite persistent bias, which risks false reassurance
evidence.quote: Despite these differences, the forewarning decreased overall bias by only 6.9%, and no bias was extinguished completely.

evidence.title: Simulated evaluation of large language model stepwise diagnostic reasoning with real-world chest pain encounters and Bayesian networks
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompting without disease-prevalence cues
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and false alarms for life-threatening chest-pain etiologies
evidence.effect: Baseline prompting: sensitivity 79.3%; specificity 45.2%. Adding prevalence cues: specificity 83.0%; false alarms reduced by 107 per 500; sensitivity 30.4%.
evidence.tradeoff: Poor sensitivity after adding prevalence cues: 30.4%.
evidence.quote: With baseline prompting, GPT-4o systematically over-predicted rare conditions (sensitivity 79.3%; specificity 45.2%); adding prevalence cues or removing diagnostic category constraints respectively increased specificity (83.0% and 94.7%) while reducing false alarms by 107 and 140 per 500, but at the cost of poor sensitivity (30.4% and 8.8%).

evidence.title: Is it possible to vaccinate AI against bias? An exploratory study in epilepsy
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without the inoculation (debiasing) instruction, same vignettes and six LLMs
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic and treatment accuracy and the socioeconomic bias gap (high vs low SES accuracy difference) in epilepsy vignettes
evidence.effect: Diagnosis: accuracy 36% (43/120) to 55% (66/120); bias gap 45 to 27 percentage points. Treatment: accuracy 51% (61/120) to 63% (75/120); bias gap 25 to 8 percentage points. Gemini 3 Pro diagnostic low SES accuracy 0% to 100%.
evidence.tradeoff: Effects varied by model: Sonnet 4.5 showed paradoxical worsening, and residual disparities remained.
evidence.quote: A simple prompt-based intervention overall reduced socioeconomic bias and improved accuracy in LLM clinical recommendations, though effects varied across models.

evidence.title: Contextual Cue Susceptibility in Clinical AI: A Randomized Controlled Clinician-Comparator Study
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline LLM prompting without a base-rate guardrail, on the cue versions of the cases
evidence.outcome: Cue-linked lure diagnosis selection by LLMs
evidence.effect: Lure selection fell to 28.4% with base-rate guardrail prompting, from 84.9% for baseline LLMs on matched cue responses. Clinician participants selected the lure in 27.8%.
evidence.quote: Base-rate guardrail prompting reduced lure selection to 28.4%; rare-or-serious prompting raised it to 93.2%.

evidence.title: Algorithmic fairness in AI-based fitness advice: evaluating socioeconomic bias in county-contextualized physical activity prescriptions
evidence.comparator_used: Standard (baseline) prompt without accessibility-aware instructions, in the DeepSeek model panel
evidence.outcome: Access-cost proxy gap between high- and low-SES counties in AI-generated physical activity advice
evidence.effect: Gap reduced from 0.306 to 0.139 with accessibility-aware prompting
evidence.quote: In the full DeepSeek model panel, accessibility-aware prompting reduced the access-cost proxy gap between high- and low-socioeconomic status (SES) counties from 0.306 to 0.139.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Model-Supported Instructions for Medication Use: First Steps Toward a Comprehensive Model
evidence.comparator_used: Generic prompt (prompt 1) and prompt calibrated for content enhancement and personalization without bias mitigation (prompt 2)
evidence.outcome: Gender bias in generated medication instructions (and adequacy scores)
evidence.effect: Gender bias found with prompts 1 and 2; prompt 3 (bias mitigation) was bias-free. Adequacy scores for prompt 3 outperformed prompts 1 and 2; full or partial acceptability in 94.3% of texts with prompt 3.
evidence.quote: Gender bias was found in our closed-source LLM's output for the first and second prompts, with the third one being bias-free.

evidence.title: Artificial Intolerance: Stigmatizing Language in Clinical Documentation Skews Large Language Model Decision-Making
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without self-debiasing instruction, on clinical vignettes with stigmatizing language
evidence.outcome: Mitigation of stigmatizing-language-induced skew toward less aggressive patient management
evidence.effect: Reported only as 'limited efficacy'; no numeric effect given in the abstract
evidence.quote: These approaches show limited efficacy; models struggle to explicitly identify SL while remaining implicitly influenced by it.

evidence.title: Socioeconomic Inference in LLM Medical Triage: Same Symptoms, Different ZIP Code
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without a debiasing system-prompt instruction (Gemini, low- vs high-income ZIP pairs)
evidence.outcome: Gemini's ER referral rate gap between low- and high-income ZIP codes
evidence.effect: Gap fell from 11.4 to 5.8 percentage points with a single-sentence system-prompt instruction; reduced but not eliminated
evidence.quote: A single-sentence system-prompt instruction reduces but does not eliminate the effect (Gemini's gap between low- and high-income ZIPs falls from 11.4 to 5.8 points).

evidence.title: Prompt-Induced Diagnostic Bias in Large Language Model Classification of Echocardiography Reports
evidence.comparator_used: Bias-injected prompts (three conditions embedding diagnostic expectations) without the explicit mitigation instruction; baseline prompt as reference
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy of LVEF classification from echocardiography reports under bias-injected prompts
evidence.effect: The instruction-based mitigation strategy restored overall accuracy near baseline in all 3 bias conditions (no numeric values given in the abstract).
evidence.quote: The instruction-based mitigation strategy restored overall accuracy near baseline in all 3 conditions.

evidence.title: LLM Reasoning Does Not Protect Against Clinical Cognitive Biases - An Evaluation Using BiasMedQA
evidence.comparator_used: Base prompt without debiasing instruction
evidence.outcome: Biased responses on BiasMedQA vignettes
evidence.effect: Statistically significant reduction in biased responses across both model architectures (OR 0.6 for Llama-3.3-70B and for Qwen3).
evidence.quote: In contrast, the debiasing and few-shot prompting approaches demonstrated statistically significant reductions in biased responses across both model architectures, with the few-shot strategy exhibiting substantially greater effectiveness (OR 0.1 vs. 0.6 for Llama-3.3-70B; OR 0.25 vs. 0.6 for Qwen3).

evidence.title: Exposing the fragility of LLM reasoning through bias-inducing prompts: evidence from BiasMedQA
evidence.comparator_used: Base prompt without debiasing instruction
evidence.outcome: Rate of biased responses
evidence.effect: Statistically significant reductions in biased responses across all three model architectures (no numeric effect sizes given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: The debiasing and few-shot prompting approaches demonstrated statistically significant reductions in biased responses across all three model architectures.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Generate Stigmatizing Language During Reasoning Over Real-World Clinical Data
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without destigmatizing prompt engineering
evidence.outcome: Stigma rate in LLM reasoning text and task performance
evidence.effect: Effect varied across models; stigma rates reduced by up to 91.91% without compromising model performance
evidence.quote: The effectiveness of prompt engineering as a destigmatizing approach varied across models, with stigma rates reduced by up to 91.91% without compromising model performance.

evidence.title: Assessing Algorithmic Bias in Language-Based Depression Detection: A Comparison of DNN and LLM Approaches
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompting without ethical framing in LLM few-shot (N-shot) settings
evidence.outcome: Gender and race/ethnicity disparities in LLM depression classification
evidence.effect: Guided prompting with ethical framing helped mitigate gender bias in the 1-shot setting. Neither the prompting strategy nor more shots effectively reduced race/ethnicity disparities. No numbers are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: In LLMs, guided prompting with ethical framing helps mitigate gender bias in the 1-shot setting.

evidence.title: Caught in the Web of Words: Do LLMs Fall for Spin in Medical Literature?
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompting without an instruction to mitigate spin (implied baseline; details not given in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Impact of spin on LLM outputs
evidence.effect: No numbers reported in the abstract; it states only that prompting can mitigate spin's impact on LLM outputs
evidence.quote: We also find, however, that LLMs are generally capable of recognizing spin, and can be prompted in a way to mitigate spin's impact on LLM outputs.

evidence.title: Enhancing Fairness in Large Language Models for Clinical Artificial Intelligence Applications Through Fine-Tuning and Prompting
evidence.comparator_used: standard prompts without debiasing instructions (six of twelve prompt variants were debiased), tested on Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B and Dolly-7B
evidence.outcome: Bias score across gender, race, profession and religion categories (lower score means better fairness and interpretability)
evidence.effect: Debiased prompts reduced bias; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: We also note that debiased prompts reduce bias, and fine-tuning the model performs even better.

evidence.title: Patient Cognitive Bias in Large Language Model-Supported Health Consultations: Simulation-Based Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without mitigation instructions under biased consultations
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy under patient cognitive bias
evidence.effect: Limited and inconsistent improvements; did not reliably prevent bias-induced performance loss (bias-induced declines were approximately 7 to 39 percentage points)
evidence.quote: Prompt-based mitigation strategies and decoding temperature reduction yielded limited and inconsistent improvements and did not reliably prevent bias-induced performance loss.

evidence.title: Cognitively Biased Prompt Effects on Large Language Model Accuracy for Radiology Board–style Examination Questions
evidence.comparator_used: Cognitive-bias-mimicking prompts without mitigation (biased prompt without debiasing instructions)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on radiology board-style questions
evidence.effect: No numbers reported in the provided text; prompt-level mitigations were effective but only partially restored accuracy lost to biased prompts
evidence.quote: Large language model accuracy for radiology board–style questions was reduced by prompts that mimicked cognitive biases, especially on image-based tasks, and prompt-level mitigations, although effective, only partially restored accuracy.

controls.question: Should we instruct the model not to abandon a justified answer just because a user pushes back?
controls.control: Instruct the model to avoid changing a justified answer solely because of user pressure, while still updating on new clinical information.
controls.comparator: Standard prompt without anti-sycophancy instructions
controls.aim: Reduce sycophantic capitulation to unfounded user pushback
variants: Hold justified position under patient pushback
Re-evaluate only when new evidence is given
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Mitigation did not eliminate harm: about 10% of responses remained potentially harmful, and authority or responsibility-transfer pressure still produced the most harmful responses. No cost or latency data were reported.

evidence.title: MedPRESS: A Multi-turn Benchmark for Patient-Pressure-Induced Medical Sycophancy in LLMs
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt without anti-sycophancy instructions
evidence.outcome: Robustness to patient-pressure-induced sycophancy (unsafe agreement under repeated pressure) across 20 LLMs
evidence.effect: Anti-sycophancy prompting improved robustness for several models but did not eliminate unsafe agreement; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Anti-sycophancy prompting improves robustness for several models, but does not eliminate unsafe agreement.

evidence.title: Obedience to Unsafe Clinical Instructions: How Large Language Models Respond to Authority Cues
evidence.comparator_used: Same scenarios without the short mitigation cue (no instruction to verify or escalate if unsafe), under a neutral control and six social-pressure conditions
evidence.outcome: Proportion of potentially harmful outputs (selection or endorsement of an unsafe clinical decision)
evidence.effect: Overall 16.6% unmitigated vs 10.1% mitigated (absolute reduction 6.5 percentage points; p < 0.001). Synthetic vignettes 10.6% to 7.2% (3.4 points). Real-world discharge cases 46.6% to 24.5% (22.1 points).
evidence.quote: Harmful decisions occurred in 16.6% of unmitigated versus 10.1% of mitigated conditions (absolute reduction, 6.5 percentage points; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: LLMs Can Do Medical Harm: Stress-Testing Clinical Decisions Under Social Pressure
evidence.comparator_used: Same clinical scenarios under neutral and six Milgram-style social-pressure conditions without the brief mitigation cue ('verify or escalate if unsafe')
evidence.outcome: Proportion of potentially harmful responses
evidence.effect: Mitigation reduced harmful decisions from 16.6% to 10.1% (p < 0.001); under pressure conditions harmful output was mitigated 8.3–9.6% vs unmitigated 14.3–16.0%
evidence.tradeoff: Mitigation did not eliminate harm: about 10% of responses remained potentially harmful, and authority or responsibility-transfer pressure still produced the most harmful responses. No cost or latency data were reported.
evidence.quote: Mitigation reduced harmful decisions from 16.6% to 10.1% (p < 0.001).

controls.question: Should we use zero or a validated low temperature rather than the default or a higher setting?
controls.control: Set sampling temperature to zero or a validated low value for clinical tasks.
controls.comparator: Default or higher temperature settings
controls.aim: Improve reproducibility and consistency of clinical outputs
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions

evidence.title: Automated Suicide Risk Factor Monitoring in Crisis Text Line Users: Comparative Study of AI and Human Ratings Using Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Higher temperature settings (three temperature settings compared, including default/higher values)
evidence.outcome: Inter-rating reliability and accuracy of LLM-generated NGASR suicide risk ratings
evidence.effect: Zero-shot prompting at temperature 0 yielded perfect inter-rating reliability (α=1.00, 95% CI: [1-1] for high & very high risk); lower temperatures consistently improved reliability and accuracy.
evidence.quote: Lower temperatures consistently improved reliability and accuracy.

evidence.title: Multi-model assurance analysis showing large language models are highly vulnerable to adversarial hallucination attacks during clinical decision support
evidence.comparator_used: Default temperature settings (standard settings) across six LLMs, 300 vignettes
evidence.outcome: Rate of elaborating on fabricated clinical details (adversarial hallucination)
evidence.effect: Temperature 0 offered no significant improvement; overall hallucination rates ranged from 50% to 82% across models and prompting methods
evidence.quote: Temperature adjustments offer no significant improvement.

evidence.title: Safety Audit of a Large Language Model for Lay Self-Triage Using Japanese Symptom Vignettes: Persistent Red-Flag Under-Triage Despite Improved Reproducibility Under Near-Deterministic Decoding
evidence.comparator_used: Stochastic decoding (temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95)
evidence.outcome: Run-to-run modal agreement and urgent red-flag primary-action safety (hard under-triage)
evidence.effect: Modal agreement improved under near-deterministic decoding. Red-flag hard under-triage was 100.0% for both prompts under near-deterministic decoding, versus 100.0% for P1 and 99.7% for P2 under stochastic prompt-only decoding.
evidence.quote: Near-deterministic decoding improved run-to-run modal agreement, but this reproducibility gain did not improve urgent-case safety.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Are Highly Vulnerable to Adversarial Hallucination Attacks in Clinical Decision Support: A Multi-Model Assurance Analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Default temperature settings (standard model settings)
evidence.outcome: Rate of adversarial hallucination (elaboration on fabricated clinical detail)
evidence.effect: Temperature adjustments offered no significant improvement; hallucination rates ranged from 50% to 82% across models and prompting methods
evidence.quote: Temperature adjustments offered no significant improvement.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering does not universally improve Large Language Model performance across clinical decision-making tasks
evidence.comparator_used: Default temperature setting
evidence.outcome: Clinical decision-making task performance across five sequential tasks
evidence.effect: ChatGPT performed better at zero temperature; Llama performed better at default temperature (no numbers given in abstract)
evidence.quote: Furthermore, ChatGPT performed better under the zero temperature, whereas LIama showed stronger performance under the default temperature.

evidence.title: Drug or Pokémon? Large language model performance in identification of fabricated medications
evidence.comparator_used: Standard (default) decoding
evidence.outcome: Confabulation rate for fabricated medications
evidence.effect: Deterministic decoding (temperature = 0) did not substantially change confabulation rates; no specific numbers reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Deterministic decoding did not substantially impact confabulation rates.

evidence.title: Reproducibility and Robustness of Large Language Models for Mobility Functional Status Extraction
evidence.comparator_used: Higher sampling temperature settings
evidence.outcome: Reproducibility (agreement across repeated runs) in mobility information extraction
evidence.effect: Increasing temperature generally degrades agreement; magnitude depends on model and task (no numbers in abstract)
evidence.quote: Results show that increasing temperature generally degrades agreement, but the magnitude depends on model and task; furthermore, prompt paraphrasing can substantially reduce stability, with particularly large drops for the MoE model.

evidence.title: Rapidly Benchmarking Large Language Models for Diagnosing Comorbid Patients: Comparative Study Leveraging the LLM-as-a-Judge Method
evidence.comparator_used: The other of the 2 tested temperature settings
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic hit rate across LLMs
evidence.effect: Changes in temperature generally had little effect; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Significant variation in diagnostic hit rates was observed across different prompts, while changes in temperature generally had little effect.

evidence.title: Detecting stigmatizing language with large language models: mind the settings
evidence.comparator_used: Higher temperature settings (0.5, 0.75) versus lower (0.25), compared within each model size
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, TPR and TNR of stigmatizing language detection
evidence.effect: Impact varied by model size: the larger 8B model performed better at lower temperature (best overall accuracy 70.2% at 0.25 with examples), while smaller models benefited from higher temperatures.
evidence.quote: The inclusion of examples improved model accuracy across all configurations, while temperature settings had a variable impact, with smaller models benefiting from higher temperatures and larger models performing better at lower temperatures.

evidence.title: Patient Cognitive Bias in Large Language Model-Supported Health Consultations: Simulation-Based Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Default or higher decoding temperature settings (4 temperature settings tested)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy under patient cognitive bias
evidence.effect: Limited and inconsistent improvements; did not reliably prevent bias-induced performance loss
evidence.quote: Prompt-based mitigation strategies and decoding temperature reduction yielded limited and inconsistent improvements and did not reliably prevent bias-induced performance loss.

evidence.title: Case-matched retrieval improves textual alignment of LLM-generated radiology impressions
evidence.comparator_used: higher sampling temperatures (0.7 and 1)
evidence.outcome: Textual similarity of generated impressions to reference impressions (ROUGE, BERTScore F1)
evidence.effect: The highest scores were at temperature 0 (with k = 10); lower temperature was associated with higher similarity scores.
evidence.quote: Lower temperature and larger k were associated with higher similarity scores.

controls.question: Where and when should instructions and key information go in the prompt or conversation?
controls.control: Choose instruction placement, repetition and evidence timing deliberately: system role, periodic restatement, or staged evidence introduction, each assessed against its own baseline.
controls.comparator: User-message placement, once-only instructions, or all evidence upfront, respectively
controls.aim: Improve instruction adherence and reasoning across long or multi-turn interactions
variants: System role vs user message placement
Deferring diagnostic questions or salient evidence to later turns vs upfront
controls.family_label: role, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured, or optimized prompts and system instructions
tradeoffs: Recovery was only partial under the adversarial MSJ context (38%), so restating instructions did not fully restore baseline performance there.

evidence.title: Conversational trajectory degrades large language model detection of suicidal ideation relative to clinicians: a preregistered study
evidence.comparator_used: Once-only instructions (no instruction restatement) across conversational trajectories up to 1,500 turns, tested in 12 top models
evidence.outcome: F1 for suicidal ideation detection at extended conversational depth
evidence.effect: Therapy transcripts: median ΔF1 +0.12 (p<0.001), 89% median recovery to near baseline. MSJ (adversarial) trajectories: ΔF1 +0.08 (p=0.04), 38% recovery.
evidence.tradeoff: Recovery was only partial under the adversarial MSJ context (38%), so restating instructions did not fully restore baseline performance there.
evidence.quote: Restating instructions increased F1 on therapy to near baseline (median ΔF1 +0.12; p<0.001; 89% median recovery) versus MSJ (ΔF1 +0.08; p=0.04; 38% recovery).

evidence.title: Benchmarking Multi-turn Medical Diagnosis: Hold, Lure, and Self-Correction
evidence.comparator_used: Diagnostic question posed at the start of the multi-turn case (no deferral of the question)
evidence.outcome: Premature answering and accuracy at the first point of commitment
evidence.effect: Deferring the diagnostic question to later turns reduces premature answering and improves accuracy at the first point of commitment by up to 62.6%
evidence.quote: We translate these findings into clinically actionable guidance: deferring the diagnostic question to later turns reduces premature answering and improves accuracy at the first point of commitment by up to 62.6%, while reserving salient clinical evidence for later turns prevents a catastrophic accuracy drop of up to 23.3% caused by premature commitment.
