evidence.title: Schema Enforcement and Structured-Output Stability in Locally Deployed LLMs for Clinical Admission-Note Editing: A Proxy-Based Pre-Deployment Evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Embedding system instructions in the user message (Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct)
evidence.outcome: First-attempt invalid outputs
evidence.effect: Separate system/user roles: 12/700 (1.7%) invalid vs. embedded in user message: 55/700 (7.9%)
evidence.quote: In a message-format sensitivity analysis using Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, embedding system instructions in the user message increased first-attempt invalid outputs compared with separate system/user roles (55/700, 7.9% vs. 12/700, 1.7%).

controls.question: Should the system prompt restrict what the chatbot may advise and require history-taking before advice?

evidence.title: Multimodal Large Language Models and Dental Students in Radiographic Landmark Identification: A Novel Grid-Based Assessment
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting (image with plain prompt, no guidance)

evidence.effect: Guided prompting had heterogeneous effects, improving localisation of some landmarks and causing severe regression on others. Gemini 3.1 Pro approached student parity only on cephalometric points under guided prompting. No numeric effect sizes are given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: New failure mode: GPT-5.4 directed the majority of lower-left canine apex predictions to the incorrect lower-right molar region, a prompt-resistant mislocalisation pattern absent in Gemini 3.1 Pro.

evidence.title: When Prompts Mislead: Textual Dominance and Diagnostic Bias in MLLMs
evidence.comparator_used: Visual-only condition (image with overlaid lesion contour, no conflicting text)
evidence.outcome: Overall diagnostic accuracy on hemorrhage versus drusen discrimination when the contour was paired with an inconsistent textual claim
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy dropped from 75% to 46% relative to the visual-only condition
evidence.tradeoff: The inconsistent textual cue overrode the correct visual cue, a new failure mode of textual dominance
evidence.quote: When an overlaid lesion contour is paired with an inconsistent textual claim, the textual prompt overrides the correct visual cue: overall accuracy drops from 75% to 46% relative to the visual-only condition, and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is associated with further degradation rather than self-correction.

evidence.title: Is this neonate feeling pain? Leveraging clinical knowledge towards high-precision Large Language Model-based neonatal pain assessment
evidence.comparator_used: baseline prompts without clinically relevant facial feature information
evidence.outcome: Precision, recall and withdrawal rate for neonatal pain assessment from facial images
evidence.effect: Facial-feature prompts reached precision 100% with recall 40.1% and significantly reduced withdrawal rates versus baseline prompts. The latent-knowledge prompts reached precision 82.3% and recall 73.2%.
evidence.tradeoff: Recall was much lower (40.1%) with the facial-feature prompts than with the latent-knowledge prompts (73.2%).
evidence.quote: When instructed with specific criteria and facial features, it achieved high precision with significantly reduced withdrawal rates compared to baseline prompts, highlighting the feasibility of this novel approach as a real-world evaluation of state-of-the-art technology through all its steps of development.

Post hoc threshold or calibration correction as alternative comparator

evidence.title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Direct modeling on the original (raw) data without SMOTE, under-sampling or cost-sensitive learning
evidence.outcome: Recall of MLP and RF donor-willingness models on the test set
evidence.effect: Recall of both MLP and RF reached above 0.58 with sampling plus cost-sensitive processing, 'significantly outperforming' direct modeling on original data (comparator values not given in the text; see Fig. 2 and Table S2)
evidence.quote: Experimental results show that after processing with both methods, the recall rates of both the MLP and RF models reached above 0.58, significantly outperforming the results of direct modeling on the original data (see Fig. 2 and Table S2 ).

evidence.title: Tipping the balance: impact of class imbalance correction on the performance of clinical risk prediction models
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Models trained on original data without class-imbalance correction (SMOTE, random undersampling and random oversampling at 1:1 compared against no resampling)
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (ROC-AUC, PR-AUC) and calibration (Brier score, calibration intercept and slope) on held-out data
evidence.effect: ROC-AUC change -0.002 to -0.01; PR-AUC change -0.10 to -0.03; no method showed systematic improvement. Resampled models had higher Brier scores (increase 0.029-0.080) and marked deviations in calibration intercept and slope.
evidence.tradeoff: Resampling altered the implicit class prior learned during training, producing miscalibrated and distorted predicted risks despite preserved ranking performance. Gains from imbalance correction can typically be reproduced by threshold adjustment without distorting probabilities.
evidence.quote: Common 1:1 class-imbalance correction techniques do not improve discrimination and may substantially degrade calibration, limiting their suitability for clinical risk prediction where accurate probabilities are essential.

evidence.title: Cross-Sensor and Cross-Population Generalization of Deep Learning Models for Digital Mammography: A Controlled Four-Country Benchmark of Five Backbone Architectures with Statistical Significance Testing

evidence.quote: The density-aware focal loss degraded both AUC and calibration at every weight tested.

evidence.title: Improving Fairness and Mitigating Bias in Multicenter Electronic Health Records Models to Predict Glaucoma Outcomes
evidence.comparator_used: Same model architectures trained without bias-mitigation methods (baseline), plus preprocessing and postprocessing mitigation approaches
evidence.outcome: FairOdds-AUC (AUROC adjusted by equalized odds gaps for sex and race/ethnicity) on internal and external test sets
evidence.effect: IPW improved FairOdds-AUC from 0.562 (95% CI 0.540, 0.581) to 0.600 (0.575, 0.629) for the transformer and from 0.556 (0.534, 0.577) to 0.5922 (0.53, 0.61919) for a fully connected network; adversarial fairness classifier reached up to 0.613 (0.595, 0.629) for the fully connected network; preprocessing/postprocessing FairOdds-AUC changes ranged from -0.009 to +0.021
evidence.tradeoff: Discrimination was essentially unchanged with IPW; postprocessing and preprocessing methods gave more variable changes and weaker generalizability across external sites
evidence.quote: Inprocessing methods, particularly inverse propensity weighting (IPW) and the adversarial fairness classifier, achieved more favorable fairness-performance tradeoffs than baseline and other mitigation approaches across all evaluation sets.

evidence.title: Divergent impacts of explainable AI for dermatological diagnosis on clinicians versus lay people
evidence.comparator_used: AI assistance without fairness-constrained training (comparator not explicitly described in the abstract; implied baseline/unconstrained model and unaided diagnosis)
evidence.outcome: Final diagnostic accuracy and skin-tone-related performance disparities among lay people and primary care physicians
evidence.effect: Assistance from the fairness-constrained AI model improved final diagnostic accuracy and reduced skin-tone-related performance disparities in both lay people (n=623) and PCPs (n=153); no numeric effect sizes given in the abstract
evidence.quote: With fairness-constrained model training, assistance from an AI model that achieved balanced performance across skin tones improved final diagnostic accuracy and reduced skin-tone-related performance disparities among both lay people and PCPs.

evidence.title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline PPD model without debiasing, and 5 debiasing approaches compared (fairness through blindness and reweighing variants)
evidence.outcome: Model fairness (disparate impact, equal opportunity, predictive parity) and predictive performance
evidence.effect: Fairness through blindness yielded the best overall performance and fairness among the debiasing approaches; the baseline model showed some unfairness in AMC data. No numeric values reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: We revised the model by fairness through blindness, a debiasing approach that yielded the best overall performance and fairness, while considering clinical appropriateness suggested by the expert reviewers.

evidence.title: Evaluation Framework for Bruise Detection: Systematic ALS/White-Light Training and Skin-Tone Balancing with Deep Learning
evidence.comparator_used: training without skin-tone balancing (unbalanced skin-tone distribution)
evidence.outcome: failure rates and overprediction across skin-tone subgroups in bruise detection
evidence.effect: Reduced failure rates for darker skin tones; increased overprediction in some demographic subgroups (no numbers in abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: Increased overprediction in some demographic subgroups
evidence.quote: Skin-tone balancing reduced failure rates for darker skin tones but increased overprediction in some demographic subgroups.

evidence.title: Trustworthy AI for radar vital signs: detecting and mitigating gender bias in healthcare
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline models trained without the multilevel mitigation framework (pre-mitigation bias score)
evidence.outcome: Bias score across gender subgroups in radar-based vital sign estimation
evidence.effect: Bias score reduced from 0.0261 to 0.00005 (p<0.001) with F1 score maintained >0.98
evidence.quote: This approach reduced the bias score from 0.0261 to 0.00005 ( p<0.001 ) while maintaining a high F1 score ( >0.98 ).

evidence.title: Gender Bias When Using Artificial Intelligence to Assess Anorexia Nervosa on Social Media: Data-Driven Study
evidence.comparator_used: Classifiers without bias mitigation (original predictors showing gender disparities)
evidence.outcome: Gender disparity in predictive performance (false negative rate gap between female and male users)
evidence.effect: Baseline FNR was 0.082 for female vs 0.005 for male samples; the mitigation strategies reduced disparities but did not eliminate them (no mitigated figures in the abstract)
evidence.quote: We also proposed techniques for bias mitigation, and we could see that, even though disparities can be mitigated, they cannot be eliminated.

evidence.title: Mitigating Algorithmic Bias in AI-Driven Cardiovascular Imaging for Fairer Diagnostics
evidence.comparator_used: Same models before bias mitigation (baseline without fairness-specific mitigation)
evidence.outcome: Fairness metrics (disparate impact, equal opportunity difference, false favourable rates by sex)
evidence.effect: Disparate impact 0.80 to 0.95; equal opportunity difference 0.20 to 0.05; false favourable rate for males 0.0059 to 0.0033 and for females 0.0096 to 0.0064
evidence.tradeoff: No accuracy cost reported; the authors note computational complexity in large-scale data processing as a limitation.
evidence.quote: Bias mitigation improved disparate impact (0.80 to 0.95), reduced equal opportunity difference (0.20 to 0.05), and decreased false favourable rates for males (0.0059 to 0.0033) and females (0.0096 to 0.0064) through balanced probability adjustment.

evidence.title: Exploring Bias Assessment and Strong Calibration in AI-based Medical Risk Prediction Models
evidence.comparator_used: Same models trained without bias mitigation (no reweighting)
evidence.outcome: Disparity in model performance across subgroups
evidence.effect: Disparity was reduced with reweighting; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: When we employed the bias mitigation strategy of reweighting, however, the disparity was reduced.

evidence.title: Assessing Algorithmic Bias in Language-Based Depression Detection: A Comparison of DNN and LLM Approaches
evidence.comparator_used: Fairness-regularized loss versus worst-group loss, applied to DNN-based embedding models. The abstract does not describe the baseline without fairness objectives.
evidence.outcome: Balance between depression classification performance and fairness across gender and race/ethnicity groups
evidence.effect: Worst-group loss achieved a better balance between performance and fairness. Fairness-regularized loss minimized loss across all groups but performed less effectively. No numbers are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Among fairness-aware techniques for mitigating bias in DNN-based embeddings, the worst-group loss, which is designed to minimize loss for the worst-performing demographic group, achieves a better balance between performance and fairness.

evidence.title: Single-Axis Fairness Interventions Produce Asymmetric Cross-Axis Effects in Clinical Prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Models trained without demographic balancing (implied unbalanced baseline; the abstract does not state it explicitly), across 7 architectures and 6 gender- or race-targeting balancing strategies
evidence.outcome: Cross-axis fairness (AUC, TPR, Brier score) on non-targeted demographic axis in one-year mortality prediction
evidence.effect: Gender-targeting largely preserved race fairness; race-targeting consistently disrupted gender fairness across all methods and most architectures. No numeric values reported in abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Race-targeting incurred greater performance costs and calibration loss; fairness gains may reflect leveling down rather than genuine improvement; the same intervention could look successful under TPR but fail under AUC.
evidence.quote: Gender-targeting interventions largely preserved race fairness, while race-targeting consistently disrupted gender fairness across all methods and the majority of architectures.

evidence.title: On the trade-off between fairness and performance in glioma grade prediction using pre-processing and post-processing techniques to mitigate bias
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline classifiers (e.g., logistic regression) without fairness-specific mitigation
evidence.outcome: Prediction performance and fairness for the under-represented racial group (most severe bias)
evidence.effect: Reweighting (pre-processing) was reported to worsen prediction outcomes for the under-represented group and to increase unfairness; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Deterioration in prediction performance for the under-represented group and increased unfairness
evidence.quote: In the case of the most severe bias (race), the pre-trained logistic regression model using the reweighting algorithm shows some deterioration in prediction outcomes for the under-represented group and even an increase in unfairness, while the post-processing approach improves results for the under-represented group and provides significant fairness gains.

evidence.title: Accounting for racial bias and social determinants of health in a model of hypertension control
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: single pooled model trained on all patients without race-specific training
evidence.outcome: Racial bias in error rates (FPR/FNR) for predicting uncontrolled hypertension (SBP >160 mmHg)
evidence.effect: Black patients had a 4.7x higher FPR and a 0.58x lower FNR than White patients; the authors conclude race-specific models were not sufficient to resolve the bias. No numeric results for the race-specific models are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Race-specific models are not sufficient to resolve such biases and require further decision threshold tuning.

evidence.title: Enhancing Fairness in Large Language Models for Clinical Artificial Intelligence Applications Through Fine-Tuning and Prompting
evidence.comparator_used: non-fine-tuned models given the same debiased and standard prompts
evidence.outcome: Bias score across gender, race, profession and religion categories
evidence.effect: Fine-tuning performed even better than debiased prompting alone; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: We also note that debiased prompts reduce bias, and fine-tuning the model performs even better.

evidence.title: Addressing the balance between fairness and performance in glioma grade prediction using bias mitigation techniques
evidence.comparator_used: Same classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost) without bias mitigation, i.e. baseline models trained without fairness-specific objectives
evidence.outcome: Prediction performance and fairness for the under-represented racial group (reweighting pre-processing)
evidence.effect: Reweighting with pre-trained logistic regression showed some deterioration in prediction outcomes for the under-represented group and an increase in unfairness for race, the most severe bias; no numeric values are given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Worse performance for the under-represented group and greater unfairness, so a fairness-accuracy trade-off.
evidence.quote: For the most severe bias (race), the pre-trained logistic regression model using the reweighting algorithm shows some deterioration in prediction outcomes for the under-represented group and even an increase in unfairness, while the post-processing approach improves results for the under-represented group and provides significant improvements in fairness.

evidence.title: Gender bias in the diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline models trained without bias mitigation (no fairness-specific objectives), using the same four algorithms on ADNI data
evidence.outcome: Sex-related bias (disparate impact) and classification performance (balanced accuracy) in AD classification
evidence.effect: Disparate impact decreased from 1.167 to 0.823; adversarial debiasing achieved the highest balanced accuracy (88.91%); LR/DIR improved performance while maintaining fairness
evidence.quote: These findings demonstrate that fairness-aware ML can reduce sex-related bias in AD classification without loss of performance and improve interpretability through more balanced representation of disease determinants.

evidence.title: Survival After Radical Cystectomy for Bladder Cancer: Development of a Fair Machine Learning Model
evidence.comparator_used: Naive XGBoost model trained without unfairness mitigation (best naive model), compared against 3 algorithm unfairness mitigation techniques
evidence.outcome: Model fairness measured by equalized odds ratio (eOR) across sex and racial subgroups, with F1-score as the performance metric
evidence.effect: Naive XGBoost: F1 0.860, eOR 0.619. All mitigation techniques increased eOR; correlation remover gave the highest, final eOR 0.750. Mitigated model F1 was 0.86 in the full test set, 0.904 in Black male and 0.824 in Asian female test sets.
evidence.quote: All unfairness mitigation techniques increased the eOR, with correlation remover showing the highest increase and resulting in a final eOR of 0.750.

controls.question: Should we fine-tune or adapt a model to our own data, guidelines, and context instead of using an off-the-shelf model with prompting?

Training needs a GPU, and LoRA was used for the larger models. Accuracy fell to 73.5% for a new, unseen hospital, with wide variation between hospitals (hospital 2 reached only 25% top-1 in the hold-out test).

Specificity dropped to 64.7%, which the authors partly attribute to cataracts and media opacity increasing false positives. DME sensitivity stayed low. Comparison is confounded by different settings, populations and graders between phases.
Required manual coding of a subset of comments and iterative retraining at each trust; thematic saturation was reached after the fifth organization, so no further coding was needed for the last 4.
Required local site-specific labeled training data (at least 25% of the MIMIC training set); the study was a simulated external site, not a real deployment.
External validation and retraining revealed performance and utility shifts across subgroups, with systematic shifts in net-benefit across threshold probabilities.

evidence.title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.comparator_used: Co-designed PreA (GPT-4o mini with prompting and agent techniques, no additional fine-tuning) versus the same model further fine-tuned on local primary care dialogues
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated quality of referral reports (history-taking, diagnosis, test ordering) in a simulation with 300 virtual patient profiles
evidence.effect: Co-designed (not fine-tuned) vs local data-tuned: history-taking 4.56 ± 0.65 vs 3.86 ± 0.81; diagnosis 4.67 ± 0.55 vs 2.47 ± 1.44; test ordering 4.23 ± 1.09 vs 2.21 ± 1.12; all P < 0.001
evidence.tradeoff: The fine-tuned model replicated real-world primary care deficiencies. It omitted guideline-recommended history elements and demographics, failed to give diagnoses in 30.0% (90/300) and to suggest tests in 39.3% (118/300) of cases when needed, and mimicked an unfriendly clinician tone.
evidence.quote: The co-designed model achieved significantly higher-quality rating scores than the data-tuned counterpart (the co-designed model further fine-tuned on the primary care dialogues) group across all domains: history-taking (without data-tuned 4.56 ± 0.65 versus data-tuned 3.86 ± 0.81; P < 0.001; Fig. 4b ), diagnosis (without data-tuned 4.67 ± 0.55 versus data-tuned 2.47 ± 1.44; P < 0.001) and testing order (without data-tuned 4.23 ± 1.09 versus data-tuned 2.21 ± 1.12; P < 0.001).

evidence.title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
evidence.comparator_used: Off-the-shelf (non-finetuned) BioLORD and Claude 3.7 used as-is for laboratory test concept mapping
evidence.outcome: Top-1 accuracy of laboratory test concept mapping
evidence.effect: Top-1 accuracy was 37.0% for non-finetuned BioLORD, 43.8% for Claude 3.7 and 91.6% for fine-tuned BioLORD on the hold-out test set. When a new hospital was held out and the model was trained on the other hospitals, top-1 accuracy was 73.5%, with the hospital's own data excluded. Other embedding models rose from 11.7-27.9% to 65.8-75.2%.
evidence.tradeoff: Training needs a GPU, and LoRA was used for the larger models. Accuracy fell to 73.5% for a new, unseen hospital, with wide variation between hospitals (hospital 2 reached only 25% top-1 in the hold-out test).
evidence.quote: For example, top-1 accuracy was 37.0%, 43.8%, and 91.6% for non-finetuned BioLORD, Claude 3.7, and fine-tuned BioLORD respectively.

evidence.title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Nanjing-trained MLP and RF models applied directly to Suzhou and Yangzhou without fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Recall on local test data after fine-tuning with 10% of local data
evidence.effect: Without fine-tuning, recall was Suzhou RF 0.67 / MLP 0.63 and Yangzhou RF 0.63 / MLP 0.58. Fine-tuning raised Suzhou RF to 0.77 and Yangzhou MLP to 0.68 (abstract: 0.70 and 0.77 in Suzhou, 0.68 and 0.64 in Yangzhou)
evidence.quote: Subsequent fine-tuning with 10% local data further enhanced performance on top of direct generalization (Suzhou RF recall increased to 0.77, Yangzhou MLP to 0.68), rather than compensating for any shortcomings of generalization.

evidence.title: Real-World Evaluation of AI-Driven Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Public Health Settings: Validation and Implementation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Same AI-3 algorithm as validated off-the-shelf in the validation phase, before retraining on DR stages, DME grading and referral guidelines (compared across phases, not a concurrent arm)
evidence.outcome: Diabetic retinopathy detection sensitivity and specificity versus reference standard
evidence.effect: Sensitivity rose from 68.4% to 99.6%; specificity fell from 96% to 64.7%. After training, DME sensitivity was 26.5% and referable DR sensitivity was 78.9%.
evidence.tradeoff: Specificity dropped to 64.7%, which the authors partly attribute to cataracts and media opacity increasing false positives. DME sensitivity stayed low. Comparison is confounded by different settings, populations and graders between phases.
evidence.quote: The AI-3 algorithm’s sensitivity increased significantly from 68.4% to 99.6%, while specificity decreased from 96% to 64.7% between the validation and implementation phases.

evidence.title: Leveraging AI to Drive Timely Improvements in Patient Experience Feedback: Algorithm Validation
evidence.comparator_used: The algorithm developed in an adult inpatient setting at one London trust, applied as-is to other organizations without trust-specific coding templates
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of theme and sentiment prediction in FFT free-text comments
evidence.effect: Accuracy was lower initially in pediatrics and mental health settings and 'significantly improved' with trust-specific coding templates; overall accuracy was >75%. No specific post-adaptation figures were given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Required manual coding of a subset of comments and iterative retraining at each trust; thematic saturation was reached after the fifth organization, so no further coding was needed for the last 4.
evidence.quote: However, the accuracy of our algorithm significantly improved when individual trust coding templates were applied.

evidence.title: Behind the Curtain: Comparing Predictive Models Performance in 2 Publicly Insured Populations
evidence.comparator_used: Unadapted model: Medicare model coefficients applied as-is to the Medicaid population, compared with the model trained on Medicaid data
evidence.outcome: Predictive performance for avoidable hospitalization in the Medicaid population
evidence.effect: Unadapted Medicaid model displayed poor performance relative to the adapted model; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: The unadapted Medicaid model displayed poor performance relative to the adapted model.

evidence.title: Development, deployment, and continuous monitoring of a machine learning model to predict respiratory failure in critically ill patients
evidence.comparator_used: Off-the-shelf UCSD-trained Vent.io model applied as-is to MIMIC-IV data (external site) without local fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC) at the external site (MIMIC-IV)
evidence.effect: AUC 0.73 without fine-tuning (below the PCCP minimum of 0.85) vs 0.873 after fine-tuning; acceptable performance reached with 25% or more of the MIMIC training data used for fine-tuning
evidence.tradeoff: Required local site-specific labeled training data (at least 25% of the MIMIC training set); the study was a simulated external site, not a real deployment.
evidence.quote: Vent.io had an AUC of 0.73 on the MIMIC-IV dataset, triggering model fine-tuning per the PCCP as the AUC was below the minimum of 0.85.

evidence.title: External validation and update of the J-ACCESS model in an Italian cohort of patients undergoing stress myocardial perfusion imaging
evidence.venue: Journal of nuclear cardiology : official publication of the American Society of Nuclear Cardiology
evidence.comparator_used: Original J-ACCESS model applied as-is to the Italian cohort, without recalibration or update
evidence.outcome: Prediction of three-year major adverse cardiac events (discrimination C-statistic and Brier score)
evidence.effect: C-statistics increased from 0.664 to 0.666 and Brier score decreased from 0.075 to 0.073 after recalibration and update. The updated model performed superimposably to the calibration slope model.
evidence.quote: The recalibrations and updated of the model slightly improved the initial performance: C-statistics increased from 0.664 to 0.666 and Brier score decreased from 0.075 to 0.073.

evidence.title: Evaluating the impact of data biases on algorithmic fairness and clinical utility of machine learning models for prolonged opioid use prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Original model trained on internal data and applied unchanged to the external VHA cohort
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUROC) for prolonged opioid use prediction in the VHA cohort
evidence.effect: AUROC fell from 0.74 (internal test) to 0.70 (full external cohort) with the original model; retraining on VHA data improved AUROCs to 0.82
evidence.tradeoff: External validation and retraining revealed performance and utility shifts across subgroups, with systematic shifts in net-benefit across threshold probabilities.
evidence.quote: Retraining on VHA data improved AUROCs to 0.82.

evidence.title: External Validation of a Machine Learning Model to Predict Postpartum Hemorrhage in a US Northeastern Healthcare System
evidence.comparator_used: Original CSL PPH model applied as-is to the local EHR data (external validation without local refitting)
evidence.outcome: Discrimination for predicting postpartum hemorrhage (AUC)
evidence.effect: Original CSL model AUC 0.60 (95% CI 0.58-0.61) vs refit XGBoost model AUC 0.75 (95% CI 0.74-0.76); PPH incidence 7.7% among 87,662 deliveries
evidence.tradeoff: The refit model remained poorly calibrated and overestimated PPH risk across a range of predicted probabilities.
evidence.quote: Refitting a new model with XGBoost resulted in improved discrimination with an AUC of 0.75 (95% CI, 0.74–0.76).

evidence.title: A TyG-UHR-based machine learning model for screening lean MAFLD: development and external validation
evidence.comparator_used: Post hoc recalibration on an external calibration subset compared with the same model before recalibration
evidence.outcome: Hold-out external validation discrimination and probability accuracy/calibration
evidence.effect: AUC 0.826 vs. 0.810; Brier score decreased from 0.286 to 0.109; log loss from 1.253 to 0.388; calibration intercept 0.103; slope 0.684
evidence.tradeoff: Discrimination was slightly lower after recalibration (AUC 0.810 vs. 0.826 before recalibration).
evidence.quote: In the hold-out validation subset, discrimination remained robust both before and after recalibration (AUC 0.826 vs. 0.810), while probability accuracy improved significantly (Brier score decreased from 0.286 to 0.109; log loss from 1.253 to 0.388).

evidence.title: Multi-Institutional Evaluation and Training of Breast Density Classification AI Algorithm Using ACR Connect and AI-LAB
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.comparator_used: Base breast density model (trained on a single dataset) used as-is, compared with locally fine-tuned versions at each hospital
evidence.outcome: Breast density classification performance of locally fine-tuned models, at the local site and on the holdout test dataset
evidence.effect: Fine-tuned models had mixed performance locally and performed poorly on the holdout test dataset. No numeric performance values are given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Considerable deployment burden: median 66 days to IRB approval, 157 days to install Connect and AI-LAB locally, and 216 days to complete testing and training.
evidence.quote: The fine-tuned models had mixed performance locally and performed poorly on the test dataset.

evidence.title: Validation of a prediction model for postpartum hospital use in geographic contexts with greater rural representation
evidence.venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
evidence.comparator_used: Original NYC-derived model coefficients applied as-is to South Carolina and Florida births, without local recalibration or re-estimation
evidence.outcome: Calibration and discrimination of the 30-day postpartum hospital use prediction model in new states
evidence.effect: Original coefficients: AUC 0.68 (95% CI 0.67-0.68) in SC and 0.69 (95% CI 0.68-0.69) in FL, with overestimated and extreme risk predictions. Intercept updating corrected calibration. Re-estimating coefficients gave AUC 0.69 (0.68-0.69) in SC and 0.70 (0.70-0.71) in FL. AUC also increased within Black, Medicaid-insured, and rural subgroups.
evidence.quote: Updating model intercepts corrected calibration, and additionally re-estimating coefficients resulted in an AUC of 0.69 (95% CI 0.68-0.69) in SC and 0.70 (95% CI 0.70-0.71) in FL.

evidence.title: Testing the Transportability of the Psychosis Metabolic Risk Calculator in Canada (Quebec): International External Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Original UK-developed PsyMetRiC applied to the Canadian sample before updating the race and ethnicity predictor to locally representative categories
evidence.outcome: Discrimination and calibration of metabolic syndrome risk prediction
evidence.effect: Before updating: full model C = 0.74, 95% CI, 0.70-0.77; intercept = 0.225; slope = 1.278; partial model C = 0.70, 95% CI, 0.67-0.74; intercept = -0.555; slope = 0.993. After updating: full model C = 0.74, 95% CI, 0.71-0.77; intercept = 0.000; slope = 1.001; partial model C = 0.71, 95% CI, 0.68-0.74; intercept = 0.001; slope = 1.005.
evidence.quote: After updating the model with a race and ethnicity predictor calibrated to locally representative categories, performance improved slightly (full model C = 0.74, 95% CI, 0.71-0.77; intercept = 0.000; slope = 1.001; partial model C = 0.71, 95% CI, 0.68-0.74; intercept = 0.001; slope = 1.005).

evidence.title: Computed tomography and radiation dose images-based deep-learning model for predicting radiation pneumonitis in lung cancer patients after radiation therapy
evidence.venue: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline trained model applied to external cohorts as-is, without adjusting CT and RD weights
evidence.outcome: Discriminative ability (AUC) for predicting radiation pneumonitis in external RTOG 0617 cohorts
evidence.effect: Test-set-2 (60 Gy) AUC 0.55 to 0.65; test-set-3 (74 Gy) AUC 0.63 to 0.70 after adjustment
evidence.tradeoff: Adjustment needed 40 labelled patients from each external cohort. Post-adjustment AUCs (0.65, 0.70) stayed below the 0.83 on the internal prospective test-set-1.
evidence.quote: After adjusting CT and RD weights of the model using a subset of the RTOG-0617 subjects, the discriminatory power of test-set-2 and 3 improved to AUC 0.65 and AUC 0.70, respectively.

evidence.title: Incremental retraining, clinical implementation, and acceptance rate of deep learning auto-segmentation for male pelvis in a multiuser environment
evidence.comparator_used: Vendor built-in (off-the-shelf) DLAS model used as-is, without institutional retraining
evidence.outcome: Segmentation accuracy (Dice similarity coefficient) for prostate, seminal vesicles and rectum
evidence.effect: Retrained custom model mean DSC 0.82 prostate, 0.48 SV, 0.92 rectum vs built-in model 0.73, 0.37, 0.81; reported as a significant improvement
evidence.tradeoff: Custom model still had failures (91.3% acceptance and 8.7% consensus unacceptable vs 96.5% and 3.5% for manual contours); failure modes included cystogram, hip prosthesis, brachytherapy seeds, air in endorectal balloon, non-iodinated spacer, giant bladder. Retraining required 100 institutional patients.
evidence.quote: This represents a significant improvement over the built-in model with DSC of 0.73, 0.37, and 0.81 for the corresponding structures.

evidence.title: External validation of the PREVENT risk score: performance and clinical utility in an Iranian population
evidence.comparator_used: Original PREVENT model applied as-is, before recalibration to the local population
evidence.outcome: Calibration, sensitivity, net reclassification improvement and net benefit for 10-year ASCVD risk
evidence.effect: In men, predicted risk improved from 4.2 to 7.6% and sensitivity from 62% to 80%. NRI was +61% in men and +79% in women. Net benefit increased slightly.
evidence.quote: The model initially underestimated risk in men, which was corrected by recalibration, improving predicted risk from 4.2 to 7.6% and sensitivity from 62% to 80%.

evidence.title: Can the generalizability issue of artificial intelligence be overcome? Pneumothorax detection algorithm
evidence.venue: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
evidence.comparator_used: PDA-Alpha (trained at center 1 only) applied as-is at center 2, without adaptation to local data
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value and false-positive predictions for pneumothorax detection on the center 2 test set (n=200)
evidence.effect: PPV rose from 0.525 to 0.886 (p = 0.041). False positives fell from 7 to 1. Sensitivity was unchanged (49/50 for both). AUC was 0.993 for PDA-Alpha and 0.986 for PDA-Beta.
evidence.tradeoff: Needed 50 locally obtained pneumothorax radiographs. AUC was slightly lower after adaptation (0.986 vs 0.993, overlapping CIs). The optimal amount of local data is still undetermined.
evidence.quote: The positive predictive value increased from 0.525 to 0.886 after external validation (p = 0.041).

evidence.title: Validating predictive models on EHRs data : lessons learnt from the NCDR-IMPACT-score applied on a French cardiac catheterization cohort
evidence.comparator_used: Original NCDR IMPACT-score applied as-is to the hospital cohort, without local recalibration
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC) for predicting adverse events in the cardiac catheterization cohort
evidence.effect: IMPACT-score-Necker AUC 0.719 vs original IMPACT-score AUC 0.642 (original AUC in the NCDR-IMPACT validation cohort was 0.752)
evidence.quote: Local calibration of the IMPACT-score on our cohort enhanced predictive accuracy, improving the AUC from 0.642 to 0.719, and addressing differences between our population and the original NCDR-IMPACT cohort.

evidence.title: Fine-Tuning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Hybrid Large Language Models for Postoperative Decision Support: Comparative Analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline Gemini 2.5 Flash without fine-tuning (off-the-shelf model); baseline did not receive equivalent safety/deferral instructions
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy on 150 postoperative queries (expert-rated)
evidence.effect: baseline 68% vs fine-tuning 92.7% (P<.001, all knowledge-enhanced models vs baseline); fine-tuning+RAG 97.3%
evidence.tradeoff: Knowledge-enhanced models had lower readability than baseline, partly attributed to standardized safety boilerplate; baseline lacked equivalent safety/deferral instructions, which likely influenced safety findings.
evidence.quote: All knowledge-enhanced models significantly outperformed baseline in overall accuracy (baseline 68% vs fine-tuning 92.7%, RAG 91.3%, fine-tuning+RAG 97.3%; P<.001).

evidence.title: Performance Assessment of ChatGPT-4.0 and ChatGLM Series in Traditional Chinese Medicine for Metabolic Associated Fatty Liver Disease: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGLM4 with internet connectivity but no knowledge base pretraining
evidence.outcome: TCM syndrome differentiation and treatment principles; comprehensive evaluation of answer texts (87 MAFLD cases)
evidence.effect: ChatGLM4+Knowledge base ranked 1st vs ChatGLM4 2nd for syndrome differentiation and treatment principles; ranked 1st vs ChatGLM4 3rd in the comprehensive evaluation. No numeric scores given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, pretraining LLMs with TCM-specific knowledge bases while maintaining internet search capabilities substantially enhanced their diagnostic and therapeutic performance in TCM applications.

evidence.title: Testing Transferability of a Mortality Risk Model for Interhospital Transfer Using Real-World Electronic Health Records: External Validation and Model Enhancement
evidence.comparator_used: Published SafeNET model applied as-is with its original 14-variable schema, without modification, versus locally trained gradient-boosting models (CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost) built on the health system's own EHR data
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC-ROC), F1 and calibration (Brier score) for post-transfer mortality
evidence.effect: CatBoost AUC-ROC 0.92 vs 0.87 for SafeNET; F1 0.74 (95% CI 0.72-0.78) vs 0.73 (95% CI 0.69-0.77); Brier 0.04 vs 0.055
evidence.tradeoff: Functional status variables were missing in 85% of encounters, which limited use of the original feature set. Precision stayed below 0.80 in several local configurations even though recall exceeded 0.70 across most models.
evidence.quote: Locally trained CatBoost models outperformed SafeNET (AUC-ROC, 0.92; F1, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.72-0.78) and demonstrated improved calibration (Brier 0.04 vs. 0.055).

evidence.title: Metabolic syndrome risk prediction in an Australian sample with first-episode psychosis using the psychosis metabolic risk calculator: A validation study
evidence.venue: Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
evidence.comparator_used: Original PsyMetRiC model applied as-is (without recalibration or updating) to the Australian first-episode psychosis sample
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (C-statistic), calibration (observed vs predicted risk), and clinical usefulness (decision curve analysis) for predicting incident metabolic syndrome
evidence.effect: Original partial model C = 0.71 (95% CI 0.64-0.75) and full model C = 0.72 (95% CI 0.65-0.77) with consistent under-prediction of risk; after recalibration and updating, C-statistics slightly improved, agreement between observed and predicted risk greatly improved, and the window of likely clinical usefulness improved significantly (specific post-update values not given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Recalibration and updating led to slightly improved C-statistics, greatly improved agreement between observed and predicted risk, and a narrow window of likely clinical usefulness improved significantly.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop-A Deep Learning Strategy in Combination with a Patient-Specific Gaussian Mixture Model Leads to the Fast Characterization of Volumetric Ground-Glass Opacity and Consolidation in the Computed Tomography Scans of COVID-19 Patients
evidence.comparator_used: 3D-UNet pretrained on an international dataset, before HITL refinement with local data
evidence.outcome: Dice Similarity Coefficient for normal lung parenchyma and COVID-19 pneumonia segmentation
evidence.effect: DSC improved by 0.2 (normal lung parenchyma) and 0.5 (COVID-19 pneumonia); after three HITL cycles DSC was >0.96 for lung and >0.81 for COVID-19 pneumonia
evidence.tradeoff: Needed manual delineation by seven teams of interns, residents and radiologists, with repeated retraining cycles until the quality criteria were met
evidence.quote: The HITL strategy improved the DSC by 0.2 and 0.5 for the normal lung parenchyma and COVID-19 pneumonia segmentation, respectively.

evidence.title: Postpartum readmission for hypertension: Validating a predictive model with incorporation of neighborhood-level social determinants of health
evidence.comparator_used: Original published calculator applied as-is to each hospital cohort (external validation without recalibration)
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (c-statistic) for postpartum HDP readmission
evidence.effect: c-statistic with original calculator 0.71 (BTH) and 0.61 (PFW) vs 0.84 and 0.74 after local recalibration; original cohort 0.80. Decision curve analysis showed net benefit of recalibrated calculators at average risk 0-3%.
evidence.tradeoff: Calculators need local recalibration for each context, which adds a per-site refitting burden.
evidence.quote: Refitting a pre-existing risk prediction model on our hospital cohorts showed improved model performance compared with using the original calculator as published.

evidence.title: Validating and Updating the OHTS-EGPS Model Predicting 5-year Glaucoma Risk among Ocular Hypertension Patients Using Electronic Records
evidence.comparator_used: Original OHTS-EGPS model applied as-is (externally validated) to English EMR data, versus the model refitted (baseline hazard and coefficients re-estimated) on the local data
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (pooled c-index) for 5-year conversion from ocular hypertension to glaucoma
evidence.effect: Pooled c-index 0.67 (0.65-0.69) for the refitted model vs 0.61 (0.60-0.63) for the original OHTS-EGPS model; the original model's pooled calibration slope was 0.45 (0.38-0.51). The authors describe the improvement as modest.
evidence.quote: The overall refitted model performed better than the OHTS-EGPS model, with a pooled c-index of 0.67 (0.65-0.69), ranging from 0.65 to 0.75 between hospitals.

evidence.title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
evidence.comparator_used: Off-the-shelf pre-trained ECG foundation model fine-tuned elsewhere and applied to ICU data as-is, versus targeted fine-tuning on curated public datasets with or without weakly labelled in-house ICU data
evidence.outcome: F1 for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification on ICU continuous monitoring data
evidence.effect: Off-the-shelf: F1 0.68 (SR) and 0.52 (AF). After fine-tuning on consistent public datasets: F1 0.91 (SR) and 0.82 (AF). Adding weakly labelled ICU data further improved recall.
evidence.tradeoff: Adding weakly labelled in-house ICU data improved recall at some cost to precision.
evidence.quote: Fine-tuning on consistent public datasets achieved robust performance (F1 = 0.91 for SR, 0.82 for AF), while adding weakly labelled ICU data further improved recall at some cost to precision.

evidence.title: Clinical Characteristics of Gastrointestinal Malignancy and Validation of the IDIOM Model Among Patients With Iron Deficiency Anemia in Thailand
evidence.venue: JGH open : an open access journal of gastroenterology and hepatology
evidence.comparator_used: Original IDIOM model applied as-is (external validation without local updating)
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AuROC) for predicting gastrointestinal malignancy in Thai IDA patients
evidence.effect: AuROC 62.9% (95% CI, 56.8%-68.9%) for the original model vs 67.2% (95% CI, 61.1%-73.3%) after recalibration/refitting to local data
evidence.quote: After updating, the AuROC improved to 67.2% (95% CI, 61.1%-73.3%).

evidence.title: Tailoring Risk Prediction Models to Local Populations
evidence.comparator_used: Original AHA-PREVENT equations applied as-is to the local population (also compared with a traditional recalibration approach)
evidence.outcome: Calibration (modified Hosmer-Lemeshow) in the test set; also discrimination (Harrell C index) and risk reclassification
evidence.effect: MLM-PREVENT was better calibrated overall (χ23 = 2.2; P = .53 vs χ23 > 16.3; P < .001), in men (χ23 = 2.1; P = .55 vs χ23 > 16.3; P < .001) and in women (χ23 = 6.5; P = .09 vs χ23 > 16.3; P < .001). It also surpassed traditional recalibration. Discrimination was equal (approximate ΔC index, ±0.01). At the 7.5% risk threshold, 11.5% of patients were reclassified.
evidence.quote: The interpretable ML approach presented in this article enhanced the accuracy of the AHA-PREVENT model when applied to a local population while still preserving the risk associations found by the original model.

evidence.title: From Guidelines to Real-Time Conversation: Expert-Validated Retrieval-Augmented and Fine-Tuned GPT-4 for Hepatitis C Management
evidence.venue: Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline GPT-4 Turbo used off-the-shelf without fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy and clarity on open-ended HCV questions
evidence.effect: SFT reached 71.7% accuracy and 88.3% clarity (p<0.001) vs baseline 36.6% accuracy and 46.6% clarity.
evidence.quote: RAG-Top1 achieved 81.7% accuracy and 86.6% clarity (both p < 0.001), while SFT reached 71.7% accuracy and 88.3% clarity (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Prospective Multicenter Validation of Machine Learning Models for Mortality Prediction in Adult Critically Ill Patients using Transfer Learning
evidence.comparator_used: Models trained on MIMIC-IV and applied to the target hospitals without adaptation (baseline implied by the abstract), compared with Domain Adaptation and Inductive Transfer Learning using limited target-domain data
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC and AUPRC) for mortality prediction in a prospective multicenter ICU cohort of 539 patients
evidence.effect: DA improved discrimination across all evaluated models; LightGBM had the largest AUC gain (p = 0.0010) and XGBoost the largest AUPRC gain (p = 0.0419). Random Forest reached 90.7% AUC with DA and 81.3% AUPRC with ITL. Domain-adapted models outperformed APACHE II (p = 0.0044) and SOFA (p = 0.0077).
evidence.quote: DA consistently improved discrimination across all evaluated models, with LightGBM showing the most significant gains in Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) (p = 0.0010), and XGBoost yielding the largest improvements in Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) (p = 0.0419).

evidence.title: EyeGPT for Patient Inquiries and Medical Education: Development and Validation of an Ophthalmology Large Language Model
evidence.comparator_used: Original off-the-shelf Llama2 model
evidence.outcome: Quality of informed advice (rated score) and hallucination proportion
evidence.effect: Informed advice mean 9.30 (SD 4.42) vs mean 13.79 (SD 5.70), P<.001; hallucinations 97/120 (80.8%) vs 53/120 (44.2%), P<.001 (as reported)
evidence.quote: The best fine-tuned model significantly outperformed the original Llama2 model at providing informed advice (mean 9.30, SD 4.42 vs mean 13.79, SD 5.70; P<.001) and mitigating hallucinations (97/120, 80.8% vs 53/120, 44.2%, P<.001).

evidence.title: Deploying machine learning models in clinical settings: a real-world feasibility analysis for a model identifying adult-onset type 1 diabetes initially classified as type 2
evidence.comparator_used: National model (trained on national US EMR data) tested on the regional HIE dataset without retraining, after compatibility adjustments
evidence.outcome: Identification of adult-onset T1D initially coded as type 2 (AUROC and precision at 5% recall)
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.751 (national model) vs 0.774 (localized model); PR5 25.5% vs 35.4%
evidence.tradeoff: Localization added complexity and may impact scalability; data inconsistencies across HIE member organizations could undermine accuracy and providers' trust.
evidence.quote: The national model performed well on HIE data (AUROC = 0.751; precision at 5% recall [PR5] = 25.5%), and localization further improved performance (AUROC = 0.774; PR5 = 35.4%).

evidence.title: The recalibration and redevelopment of a model to calculate patients' probability of completing a colonoscopy following an abnormal fecal test
evidence.comparator_used: Original multi-FQHC model applied/recalibrated as-is in the single large FQHC, versus redevelopment on that FQHC's local data
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (c-statistic) for predicting colonoscopy completion after abnormal FIT
evidence.effect: Original model c-statistic fell from 0.66 to 0.61 on recalibration in the single FQHC (failed recalibration); redeveloped local model c-statistic 0.65
evidence.quote: The model was redeveloped in the same FQHC in a cohort of 1401 patients with a c-statistic of 0.65.

evidence.title: Foundation models enable wearable signal screening for cardiovascular disease among people living with HIV
evidence.comparator_used: Strictly zero-shot NormWear applied to PPG without any local training or labels (also NormWear with a locally trained classifier, and unsupervised PCA features)
evidence.outcome: CVD detection from wearable PPG (AUROC, average precision)
evidence.effect: Frozen PaPaGei embeddings plus a locally trained calibrated Random Forest: AUROC 0.769, AP 0.489, recall 1.000. Zero-shot NormWear: AUROC 0.560, AP 0.226 (abstract reports 0.610 and 0.226). NormWear zero-shot with a supervised classifier: AUROC 0.667, AP 0.322. PCA features: AUROC 0.689, AP 0.208.
evidence.tradeoff: Needs local labels to train the classifier, though not encoder fine-tuning. The comparison is confounded by different models (PPG-specific PaPaGei vs ECG-pretrained NormWear) and different preprocessing, so the authors call NormWear a lower bound and not a fair head-to-head. Only 13 CVD cases, so results are tentative and need validation.
evidence.quote: Our zero-shot baseline (NormWear, AUROC 0.560) represents truly label-free deployment but yields insufficient discrimination, highlighting that some local labels substantially improve utility.

evidence.title: Evaluating a predictive model of tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy failure in a European-type cohort: a step towards population-specific tools
evidence.comparator_used: Original Chinese-cohort predictive model applied as-is (without local adaptation) to the French cohort
evidence.outcome: Risk stratification of patients at risk of TKI therapy failure in the French CP-CML cohort
evidence.effect: The original model did not discriminate risk groups effectively in the French cohort; the model rebuilt on the French cohort identified other predictive variables (sex, leukocytosis, comorbidities, high-risk additional chromosomal abnormalities) that better stratified patients. No numeric metrics reported in the text.
evidence.quote: However, the model reconstruction using this cohort identified other predictive variables (sex, leukocytosis, comorbidities, high-risk additional chromosomal abnormalities) that better stratified patients at risk of therapy failure.

evidence.title: Performance of PREVENT Cardiovascular Risk in Electronic Health Record-Based Clinical Practice
evidence.comparator_used: Published PREVENT equations used as-is, compared with locally fitted Cox, discrete-time neural network, and recalibrated PREVENT models
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (C-index) and calibration (expected vs observed 5-year CVD event rates)
evidence.effect: Local adaptation minimally affected discrimination and modestly improved calibration. The abstract gives no numeric effect for the adapted models.
evidence.quote: Local adaptations minimally affected discrimination and modestly improved calibration.

evidence.title: Calibrating Deep Learning Classifiers for Patient-Independent Electroencephalogram Seizure Forecasting
evidence.comparator_used: Patient-independent deep learning model without calibration (not fine-tuned on any data from the new patient)
evidence.outcome: Seizure forecast accuracy in independent patients
evidence.effect: Forecast accuracy of deep learning methods increased on average by more than 20%, and performance improved systematically in all independent patients
evidence.tradeoff: Calibration requires at least one epileptic event recorded from each new patient.
evidence.quote: We evaluate our calibration procedure using two datasets containing EEG signals recorded from a large cohort of epileptic subjects, demonstrating that the forecast accuracy of deep learning methods can increase on average by more than 20%, and that performance improves systematically in all independent patients.

evidence.title: Evaluation and tuning of a commercial automated planning system for prostate radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Manufacturer-provided baseline model used as supplied (off-the-shelf) before local tuning
evidence.outcome: Rectum sparing (rectum V50 Gy) and plan consistency of automatically generated prostate plans
evidence.effect: Baseline model had inferior rectum sparing to human plans. After two tuning iterations rectum sparing was comparable (0.02 mean difference in rectum V50 Gy) while much of the improved consistency was kept.
evidence.tradeoff: Only much, not all, of the improved consistency was maintained. Tuning needed two further model iterations produced in collaboration with the manufacturer.
evidence.quote: Further iterations of the model resulted in comparable rectum sparing, a 0.02 mean difference in rectum V50 Gy, was achieved whilst maintaining much of the improved consistency.

evidence.title: Structural Findings Transfer, Texture Findings Do Not: An Adaptation Ladder for Cross-Center Dental Diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Source-center model used as-is on the target center (no adaptation), compared with a ladder of ten adaptation techniques across three backbones
evidence.outcome: Cross-center AUC for structural findings (impacted teeth) versus texture findings (caries)
evidence.effect: Impacted teeth AUC 0.71 to 0.92 after adaptation; caries stays near chance. Cheap adaptation (a few thousand trainable parameters, sixteen labeled teeth) recovers most of the achievable benefit for structural findings. Across all 126 configurations the guarantee never breaks.
evidence.tradeoff: Texture findings such as early caries were not recovered by any adaptation, budget or backbone tested. Source performance was largely preserved.
evidence.quote: Adaptation recovers structural pathology strongly (impacted teeth, AUC 0.71 to 0.92) but not texture pathology (caries stays near chance), independently of technique, budget, or backbone.

evidence.title: Local adaptation of a chest radiograph AI model for pulmonary tuberculosis triage in Uzbekistan: Pooled and site-stratified internal validation and exploratory workstation integration
evidence.comparator_used: Public baseline pulmonary TB classifier used without local adaptation
evidence.outcome: Held-out ROC AUC (paired difference between adapted model and public baseline)
evidence.effect: Adapted model ROC AUC 0.9902 (95 % CI 0.9694-1.0000), F1 0.9375, PR AUC 0.9557 on held-out n=76 (15 TB-positive); paired AUC difference from public baseline 0.0054 (95 % CI -0.0077 to 0.0230; p = 0.4864)
evidence.quote: The paired AUC difference from the public baseline was 0.0054 (95 % CI -0.0077 to 0.0230; p = 0.4864), showing no statistical superiority.

evidence.title: Generalisability of fetal ultrasound deep learning models to low-resource imaging settings in five African countries
evidence.comparator_used: Fetal plane classifier trained on the Spanish high-resource centre and applied as-is to the African low-resource centres, without adaptation
evidence.outcome: Recall and precision of fetal plane classification in African centres (Egypt, Algeria, Uganda, Ghana, Malawi)
evidence.effect: Transfer learning for domain adaptation increased recall to [Formula: see text] (value not given in the text) while maintaining high precision across centres; only 25 patients per African centre were used
evidence.quote: In particular, the model can be re-aligned and optimised to boost the performance on African populations by increasing the recall to [Formula: see text] and at the same time maintaining a high precision across centres.

evidence.title: Improving Health Literacy through Lay Summarization of Radiological Reports: An Evaluation of BioNER and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence.comparator_used: Few-shot prompting variants of the same models
evidence.outcome: Overall performance and readability of lay summaries
evidence.effect: Fine-tuned BioBART with NER achieved the best overall performance. Adding RAG to NER degraded few-shot results but improved readability when fine-tuned (no numbers in the abstract).
evidence.quote: Fine-tuned BioBART with NER achieves the best overall performance, highlighting entity-aware extraction as the primary driver of improved patient-friendly summaries.

evidence.title: Diagnosing and remediating harmful data shifts for the responsible deployment of clinical AI models
evidence.comparator_used: Models that use all available hospitals
evidence.outcome: Model performance across hospital sites
evidence.effect: Hospital type-specific transfer-learning models “perform better”; no quantitative effect size reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: We found hospital type-specific models that leverage transfer learning, perform better than models that use all available hospitals.

evidence.title: Assessment of the CLOT (children's likelihood of thrombosis) real-time risk prediction model of hospital-associated venous thromboembolism in children with congenital heart disease
evidence.comparator_used: Original CLOT model applied as-is to the CHD cohort, without refitting
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUROC) for HA-VTE in children with CHD
evidence.effect: AUROC original 0.80 (95% CI 0.75-0.85) vs refit on CHD cohort only 0.85 (0.81-0.89); updated model with added cardiac covariates 0.86 (0.81-0.90)
evidence.quote: The AUROC for the original (0.80 95% CI [0.75-0.85]), refit (0.85 [0.81-0.89]), and updated (0.86 [0.81-0.90]) models demonstrated excellent discriminatory ability within the CHD cohort.

evidence.title: Comparison of Vendor-Pretrained and Custom-Trained Deep Learning Segmentation Models for Head-and-Neck, Breast, and Prostate Cancers
evidence.comparator_used: Vendor-pretrained segmentation models used as-is, without institutional training
evidence.outcome: Auto-segmentation accuracy (average DSC and MSD) against clinically approved contours for head-and-neck, breast and prostate OARs
evidence.effect: Average DSC vendor-pretrained vs custom-trained: 0.81 vs 0.86 (HN), 0.67 vs 0.80 (breast), 0.87 vs 0.92 (prostate). Average MSD: 0.81 vs 0.76 mm (HN), 4.85 vs 2.42 mm (breast), 2.17 vs 1.21 mm (prostate). Significant improvement for 14 of 24 OARs.
evidence.tradeoff: Custom training required institutional data: 30-39 training and 5 validation patients per model, with clinically approved contours.
evidence.quote: Notably, custom-trained models showed significant improvements over vendor-pretrained models for 14 of 24 OARs, reflecting the influence of data/contouring variations in segmentation performance.

evidence.title: Boosting GPT models for genomics analysis: generating trusted genetic variant annotations and interpretations through RAG and Fine-tuning
evidence.comparator_used: Off-the-shelf GPT-4 without fine-tuning, and RAG as an alternative way to inject knowledge
evidence.outcome: Model performance on variant annotation fields
evidence.effect: Fine-tuning GPT-4 improved performance in some annotation fields, but accuracy across more fields remained suboptimal; RAG outperformed fine-tuning for factual knowledge injection
evidence.tradeoff: Fine-tuning was less cost-effective and handled less data volume than RAG; accuracy across many fields remained suboptimal
evidence.quote: Additionally, fine-tuning GPT-4 on variant annotation data also improved model performance in some annotation fields, although the accuracy across more fields remains suboptimal.

evidence.title: Deployment protocol and base model jointly determine residual risk in rule-based clinical LLM supervision
evidence.comparator_used: Non-fine-tuned model under the same supervision
evidence.outcome: Allow rate under supervision
evidence.effect: Fine-tuning increased the allow rate sixfold when combined with supervision (on HealthBench Hard, N=1000; 0.0% deploy VR under C2).
evidence.quote: Moreover, a separate test on HealthBench Hard (N =1000, an independent benchmark with different scenarios and grading) also reached 0.0% deploy VR under C2, and fine-tuning increased the allow rate sixfold when combined with supervision.

evidence.title: Assessing equitable use of large language models for clinical decision support in real-world settings: fine-tuning and internal-external validation using electronic health records from South Asia
evidence.comparator_used: Models fine-tuned only to public clinical datasets (I2B2/N2C2, emrQA) and externally validated on the local Pakistani EHR data, without local fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Medical concept extraction performance (3-label precision, recall, F1, accuracy) on the local EHR dataset
evidence.effect: 3-label precision, recall, F1 score, and accuracy improved by 21-31%, 11-21%, 16-27%, and 6-10% amongst GatorTron, BioMegatron, BioBert and ClinicalBERT; 9-label trends similar. ChatGPT was an exception, performing better on the local EHR dataset by 10% for precision and 13% for recall, F1 and accuracy.
evidence.quote: Fine-tuning the LLMs to the local EHR data improved model performance.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Cardiac Function Estimation from Phone Videos of Echocardiograms
evidence.comparator_used: Pretrained models (primary model and public EchoNet-Dynamic) applied to phone-recorded videos without phone-video fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: LVEF estimation accuracy on phone-recorded echocardiogram videos (MAE, R², AUROC for EF >50%)
evidence.effect: Primary model without fine-tuning on phone videos: MAE 7.00 pp, R² 0.49, AUROC 0.91; after fine-tuning on the 2396-video evaluation cohort: MAE 6.96 pp, R² 0.61, AUROC 0.93. EchoNet-Dynamic: MAE 9.36 to 7.86 pp, R² 0.37 to 0.50, AUROC 0.84 to 0.89.
evidence.quote: On the 2396-video fine-tuning evaluation cohort, fine-tuning improved primary model performance to a mean absolute error of 6.96 percentage points, coefficient of determination of 0.61, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.93.

evidence.title: Assessing generalizability of an AI-based visual test for cervical cancer screening
evidence.comparator_used: Out-of-the-box inference of the SEED-trained classifier on external (EXT) data without retraining
evidence.outcome: Classification performance on external data (% extreme misclassifications) and repeatability
evidence.effect: Strong classification performance on EXT achieved with retraining: 4.0% extreme misclassifications with n = 26 EXT individuals added to SEED (2n normal : 2n indeterminate : n precancer+), with incremental improvement as images from more individuals were added. Repeatability (95% limit of agreement range 0.2-0.4) carried over to EXT even without retraining.
evidence.tradeoff: Retraining needs images from new individuals in the new setting. Device-level heterogeneity affected performance more than geography-level heterogeneity, so retraining needs to be optimized, e.g. when moving to a new device.
evidence.quote: Our results indicate strong repeatability of our multiclass model utilizing Monte-Carlo (MC) dropout, which carries over well to “EXT” (95% limit of agreement range = 0.2 - 0.4) even in the absence of retraining, as well as strong classification performance of our model on “EXT” that is achieved with retraining (% extreme misclassifications = 4.0% for n = 26 “EXT” individuals added to “SEED” in a 2n normal : 2n indeterminate : n precancer+ ratio), and incremental improvement of performance following retraining with images from additional individuals.

evidence.title: Benchmarking domain adaptation methods for cross-site antimicrobial resistance prediction from MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry data
evidence.comparator_used: Source-only baseline (model trained at one site and applied at another without adaptation), and unsupervised domain adaptation methods that use no target labels
evidence.outcome: Cross-site AMR prediction performance from MALDI-TOF spectra (share of the domain gap closed)
evidence.effect: Fine-tuning with target-site labels closed 92%-97% of the domain gap; unsupervised DA yielded only 0%-6% improvement over source-only baselines; with 25% of target labels, 81%-94% of full supervised performance was recovered on cross-site scenarios
evidence.tradeoff: Requires collecting labeled samples at the target site, though a modest number (about 25% of target labels) suffices for competitive transfer methods
evidence.quote: The results demonstrate that simple fine-tuning with target-site labels closes 92%-97% of the domain gap and dominates all unsupervised DA methods, which yield only 0%-6% improvement over source-only baselines.

evidence.title: Local retraining mitigates domain shift in sepsis prediction: Lessons from translating a neonatal model to mixed intensive care data
evidence.comparator_used: CHOP-trained model weights applied directly to GOSH ICU data without local retraining
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC) for sepsis prediction on the mixed GOSH ICU population
evidence.effect: Retraining on GOSH data restored discrimination (AUC range 0.69–0.86). Gradient Boosting reached AUC 0.86 vs 0.87 at CHOP, and KNN reached 0.80 vs 0.79 at CHOP. DeLong's test showed statistically significant gains across all classifiers (p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Retraining on GOSH data restored discrimination (AUC range 0.69–0.86), with Gradient Boosting (AUC 0.86 vs AUC 0.87 at CHOP) and KNN (AUC 0.80 vs AUC 0.79 at CHOP) models performing comparably to their CHOP benchmarks.

evidence.title: TurkishMedLLM: A Source-Grounded and Safety-Aware Turkish Medical LLM for Clinical Decision Support and Digital Health Applications
evidence.comparator_used: Base (off-the-shelf) LLM and base RAG without QLoRA fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Generation quality: RAGAS faithfulness, response relevancy, DeepEval answer relevancy, clinical caution score
evidence.effect: Fine-tuned (QLoRA) RAG: faithfulness 0.91, response relevancy 0.88, DeepEval answer relevancy 0.90, clinical caution 0.93; reported as outperforming base LLM and base RAG (comparator scores not given in abstract)
evidence.quote: In generation-stage evaluation, the fine-tuned RAG configuration achieved a RAGAS faithfulness score of 0.91, response relevancy of 0.88, DeepEval answer relevancy of 0.90, and clinical caution score of 0.93, outperforming the base LLM, base RAG, and fine-tuned non-RAG configurations.

evidence.title: Evaluating and enhancing the performance of large language models in thyroid eye disease through customization and Chain-of-Thought strategies
evidence.comparator_used: Original off-the-shelf GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 without customization
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on multiple-choice questions, and QUEST ratings (accuracy, readability, comprehensiveness, likelihood of harm, reasoning) on short-answer and case questions
evidence.effect: Multiple-choice accuracy: TED-GPT 86.1% vs GPT-4 76.2%; TED-Claude 89.1% vs Claude 3.5 83.2%. Customized models also performed better on case and short-answer questions, with TED-Claude best overall.
evidence.quote: For case and short-answer questions, the customized TED-GPT and TED-Claude also performed better than their original versions.

evidence.title: Evaluating Deep Learning Sepsis Prediction Models in ICUs Under Distribution Shift: A Multi-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.comparator_used: Retraining, fusion training and supervised domain adaptation (fine-tuning was the adaptation strategy tested)
evidence.outcome: Sepsis prediction performance of fine-tuning a source model on target-site data
evidence.effect: Fine-tuning consistently underperformed across all target data sizes (adjusted p < 0.05 vs. DA, fusion, and retraining).
evidence.quote: Key results demonstrate that fine-tuning consistently underperforms across all data sizes (adjusted p < 0.05 vs. DA, fusion, and retraining) even though it has been the go to method in many prior studies that explored this direction.

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for clinical note processing: local fine-tuning and internal-external validation using electronic health records from South Asia
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Same medical LLMs fine-tuned only on public clinical datasets (I2B2/N2C2, emrQA) and applied to local Pakistani EHR data without local fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Medical concept extraction (F1) and medical question answering (ROUGE-L, BLEU) on local EHR notes
evidence.effect: Without local fine-tuning, external validation on local data fell by at least 15% in F1 (MCE) and 35% in ROUGE-L and BLEU (MQA) versus internal validation. Local fine-tuning gave a 7.5% to 15% increase in F1 for MCE and a 27% to 53% increase in ROUGE-L and BLEU for MQA.
evidence.tradeoff: Local fine-tuning needs appropriate clinical and technical expertise and curated local data. The authors describe it as substantially less resource-intensive than training LLMs from scratch.
evidence.quote: However, fine-tuning the LLMs with local EHR data significantly improved model performance across both tasks, yielding a 7.5% to 15% increase in the F1 score for MCE and a 27% to 53% increase in ROUGE-L and BLEU scores for MQA.

evidence.title: Cross-Institutional Five-Class Kellgren-Lawrence Grading of Knee Osteoarthritis via Multitask Deep Learning
evidence.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot transfer of the model to the external Chinese cohort without adaptation
evidence.outcome: External accuracy and QWK on the independent Chinese cohort for KL grading
evidence.effect: External accuracy rose from 66.1% (zero-shot) to 80.0% after selective fine-tuning; QWK reached 0.950; AUC 0.984 for KL≥2
evidence.quote: While external zero-shot deployment revealed a domain gap, with accuracy dropping to 66.1%, our selective fine-tuning protocol significantly bridged this divide, boosting external accuracy to 80.0% and QWK to 0.950, with an AUC of 0.984 for clinically significant osteoarthritis (KL≥2).

evidence.title: Benchmarking transformer-based models for medical record deidentification: A single centre, multi-specialty evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Untuned (off-the-shelf) AnonCAT without concept alignment or fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Word-level PII classification F1 (de-identification) on site-specific data
evidence.effect: AnonCAT F1 increased from 0.851 (0.843-0.859) to 0.910 (0.905-0.914) after fine-tuning; fine-tuned precision 0.978 (0.973-0.982), recall 0.850 (0.843-0.858); least performance shift across datasets
evidence.tradeoff: Fine-tuned AnonCAT recall (0.850) was lower than the best tool, Azure DeID (0.950), despite high precision; fine-tuning requires site-specific annotated data
evidence.quote: AnonCAT showed significant improvement in performance on fine-tuning (F1 increase from 0.851; 0.843-0.859 to 0.910; 0.905-0.914).

evidence.title: Toward Reliable Clinical Coding with Language Models: Verification and Lightweight Adaptation
evidence.comparator_used: Off-the-shelf LLMs without adaptation (prompting only), as well as search-based methods
evidence.outcome: Clinical coding accuracy
evidence.effect: Reported qualitatively as improved accuracy; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: We show that lightweight interventions, including prompt engineering and small-scale fine-tuning, can improve accuracy without the computational overhead of search-based methods.

evidence.title: Escitalopram Adverse Events in Real-World Databases: Signal Detection, Prediction Modeling, and Network Toxicology
evidence.comparator_used: FAERS-trained XGBoost model applied as-is to JADER (cross-database application without retraining)
evidence.outcome: Prediction of suicide-related adverse events (AUC)
evidence.effect: Cross-database application to JADER: AUC 0.6379 (FAERS native 0.8578); retraining on JADER: AUC 0.8365
evidence.quote: Retraining on JADER restored performance (AUC = 0.8365), comparable to native-dataset performance.

evidence.title: Localized fine-tuning and clinical evaluation of deep-learning based auto-segmentation (DLAS) model for clinical target volume (CTV) and organs-at-risk (OAR) in rectal cancer radiotherapy
evidence.comparator_used: Vendor-provided pretrained model (VPM) used as-is, without localized fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Auto-segmentation accuracy for CTV and OARs (DSC, 95HD, sensitivity, specificity, target volume) against ground truth contours
evidence.effect: LFT significantly improved CTV delineation accuracy (p < 0.05), outperforming VPM in target volume, DSC, 95HD and specificity; significant enhancement in small intestine segmentation; both models adequate for bladder and femoral heads. No performance degradation seen for either model on the GenEva dataset from a different CT simulator. Numeric values not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: LFT significantly improved CTV delineation accuracy (p < 0.05) with LFT outperforming VPM in target volume, DSC, 95HD and specificity.

evidence.title: Transferring healthcare risk prediction models between Medicaid populations: a transfer learning evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: source-only transfer to Virginia without target adaptation
evidence.outcome: Race/ethnicity equalized odds difference
evidence.effect: Target-adapted models 0.132-0.157 vs source-only transfer 0.897.
evidence.tradeoff: Disparities persisted; not all complex target-adapted methods improved discrimination (Enhanced MAML AUC 0.677 did not improve over naive transfer).
evidence.quote: Fairness analyses showed lower race/ethnicity equalized odds differences for target-adapted models (0.132-0.157) than source-only transfer (0.897), though disparities persisted.

evidence.title: Clinical-ShiftEval: a framework for simulating and evaluating model adaptation in dynamic clinical NLP tasks
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Off-the-shelf LLM with in-context learning (no adaptation to new data)
evidence.outcome: Recovery of baseline F1 after shift
evidence.effect: Continual training only surpassed in-context and hybrid approaches after incorporating at least 30% of data from the second period; below that, in-context learning was better
evidence.tradeoff: Requires labeled data from the new period and retraining; in-context learning needs no new labeled data
evidence.quote: Continual adaptation with incremental retraining gradually restored performance, but only surpassed in-context and hybrid approaches after incorporating at least 30% of data from the second period.

evidence.title: An infection prediction model developed from inpatient data can predict out-of-hospital COVID-19 infections from wearable data when controlled for dataset shift
evidence.comparator_used: Pretrained inpatient infection model applied directly to wearable data without adaptation
evidence.outcome: AUROC for predicting COVID-19 infection from wearable physiological data
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.52 for the baseline (direct application) vs 0.74 after controlling for contextual effects and applying the dataset shift transformation; detection on average 2 days before diagnostic testing
evidence.tradeoff: Required a small set of wearable data from healthy individuals to derive the transformation, and the gain was combined with controlling for contextual effects.
evidence.quote: After controlling for contextual effects and applying an unsupervised dataset shift transformation derived from a small set of wearable data from healthy individuals, we found that the model performance improved, achieving an AUROC of 0.74, and it detected COVID-19 infection on average 2 days prior to diagnostic testing.
