evidence.title: External validation of predictive models for antibiotic susceptibility of urine culture
evidence.comparator_used: Algorithms trained on the original cohort and applied to the geographically-distant hospital without additional training
evidence.outcome: Discriminative accuracy (AUC) for predicting antibiotic susceptibility at the external hospital
evidence.effect: AUC 0.70-0.93 after training on the distant hospital's antibiogram vs AUC 0.69-0.87 without additional training
evidence.quote: When the algorithms were trained on the antibiogram from the geographically-distant hospital, the accuracy improved (AUC 0.70-0.93).

evidence.title: Evaluating approaches of training a generative large language model for multi-label classification of unstructured electronic health records
evidence.comparator_used: Off-the-shelf Llama 3.1-8B without parameter-efficient fine-tuning, in both zero-shot and few-shot prompting
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall and F1 across four clinical tasks (agitation in dementia, depression in dementia, frailty index, malnutrition risk factors)
evidence.effect: PEFT significantly enhanced model performance in both zero-shot and few-shot learning. No numeric values given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Notably, PEFT significantly enhances model performance in both zero-shot and few-shot learning; however, RAG improves performance only in few-shot learning.

evidence.title: The pediatric transfer gap: How adult-ICU-trained machine-learning models degrade on pediatric intensive care patients
evidence.comparator_used: Source-trained model applied to the target without adaptation (also compared with pooled training and calibration-only updating)
evidence.outcome: ROC-AUC and Expected Calibration Error on younger children (Experiment A); mortality prediction from vital signs
evidence.effect: Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.725 (0.703-0.746) without adaptation vs 0.867 (0.842-0.890) after target-domain retraining; ECE 0.142 vs below 0.01. Retraining on only 5% of the target pool (about 180 patients) recovered most of the gap. Calibration-only updating corrected ECE but did not restore discrimination.
evidence.tradeoff: Requires labelled target-cohort data (50% of target data in the main analysis). Calibration-only updating was insufficient for discrimination.
evidence.quote: The strongest discrimination evidence comes from the fully observed Experiment A: Random Forest ROC-AUC fell from 0.940 (95% CI 0.912-0.968) on older children to 0.725 (0.703-0.746) on younger children, and target-domain retraining recovered 0.867 (0.842-0.890); ECE rose from ≤0.010 to 0.142 and was restored below 0.01.

evidence.title: Generalisation capabilities of machine-learning algorithms for the detection of the subthalamic nucleus in micro-electrode recordings
evidence.venue: International journal of computer assisted radiology and surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Network trained on the largest database and tested directly out-of-distribution on the smaller databases, without fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Balanced accuracy for MER classification (STN detection) on new-centre databases
evidence.effect: Out-of-distribution testing reduced balanced accuracy by 6.5% to 16.0%; fine-tuning on the new database ameliorated this reduction (no per-model numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: This reduction can be ameliorated through fine-tuning the network on the new database through transfer learning.

evidence.title: Enhancing Precision in Rectal Cancer Radiotherapy: Localized Fine-Tuning of Deep-learning based Auto-segmentation (DLAS) Model for Clinical Target Volume and Organs-at-risk
evidence.comparator_used: Vendor-provided pretrained model (VPM) used as-is, without localized fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Auto-segmentation accuracy for rectal cancer CTV and organs-at-risk (DSC, 95HD, sensitivity, specificity, target volume)
evidence.effect: Localized fine-tuning significantly improved CTV delineation accuracy (p < 0.05), with LFT outperforming VPM in target volume, DSC, 95HD and specificity. LFT significantly improved segmentation of the small intestine. Both models were adequately accurate for bladder and femoral heads. No performance degradation was seen on the GenEva dataset from a different CT simulator for either model. No numeric DSC or HD values are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Localized fine-tuning significantly improved CTV delineation accuracy (p < 0.05) with LFT outperforming VPM in target volume, DSC, 95HD and specificity.

evidence.title: End-to-End Machine Learning based Discrimination of Neoplastic and Non-neoplastic Intracerebral Hemorrhage on Computed Tomography
evidence.comparator_used: The same pipeline applied to the external cohort as-is, without fine-tuning on external data
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance (AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity) for neoplastic vs non-neoplastic ICH on the external validation cohort
evidence.effect: Without fine-tuning: AUC 68%, Acc 66%, sensitivity 64%, specificity 67%. After fine-tuning on a small external subset: AUC 70%, Acc 70%, sensitivity 70%, specificity 71%.
evidence.quote: Fine-tuning on a selected small subset of the external cohort enhanced performance, achieving an AUC and accuracy of 70% (sensitivity 70%; specificity 71%).

evidence.title: Deep learning for freezing of gait assessment using inertial measurement units: a multicentre validation study
evidence.comparator_used: The locally developed DL model applied as-is to external cohorts without fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Model-expert agreement on percentage-of-time-frozen (ICC) in external cohorts
evidence.effect: ICC rose from 0.562 ± 0.141 (no fine-tuning) to 0.732 ± 0.138 after fine-tuning with 50 min of external cohort data; local ICC was 0.886
evidence.tradeoff: Fine-tuning needs about 50 min of annotated data from each external cohort, which means expert annotation and human-in-the-loop review. Agreement only approached the lower boundary of inter-rater agreement (ICC 0.73-0.99).
evidence.quote: Fine-tuning the DL model with just 50 min of external cohort data improved the ICC to 0.732 ± 0.138, approaching the lower boundary of the inter-rater agreement between two clinical raters using video annotation (ICC = 0.73-0.99).

evidence.title: Detecting and Remediating Harmful Data Shifts for the Responsible Deployment of Clinical AI Models
evidence.comparator_used: Model without transfer learning to the community hospital data (comparator not explicitly named in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Mortality prediction performance (AUROC, AUPRC) at community hospitals
evidence.effect: Delta AUROC [SD], 0.05 [0.03]; Delta AUPRC [SD], 0.06 [0.04]
evidence.tradeoff: Benefit depended on hospital type
evidence.quote: Transfer learning improved model performance of community hospitals in a hospital type-dependent manner (Delta AUROC [SD], 0.05 [0.03]; Delta AUPRC [SD], 0.06 [0.04]).

controls.question: Should we require models trained on data from multiple sites and devices, including through federated learning?
controls.control: Train or adapt models on multi-institution, multi-device data, pooled and harmonized or via federated or swarm learning when data cannot be shared.
controls.comparator: Model trained on single-site or single-device data
controls.aim: Improve generalizability across sites, scanners, and populations while protecting patient data
variants: Federated learning sharing model updates only
Federated vs centralized pooled training comparison
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment
tradeoffs: SARS-CoV-2+ detection was slightly lower after retraining (88.0% vs 91.0%). The authors note that clinical lab implementation will need continuous optimization as respiratory infections evolve.
Only 50 additional radiographs from center 2 were used. AUC was slightly lower (0.986 vs 0.993). The amount of external data needed to fully address generalizability remains unknown.

Detection of SARS-CoV-2+ samples fell slightly (91.0% to 88.0%). Authors note continuous re-optimization will be needed as respiratory infections evolve. The two arms also used different top-performing algorithms (random forest vs SVM-RBF).
Pooling did not remove platform dependence: direct cross-platform application without recalibration caused a substantial performance decline.
This was an oracle experiment, described as a non-deployment setting, so the gain is not shown to be achievable in real deployment.

evidence.title: Application of MALDI-MS and Machine Learning to Detection of SARS-CoV-2 and non-SARS-CoV-2 Respiratory Infections
evidence.comparator_used: Model trained only on South American (single-source) public spectra and applied to Kazakhstan samples as-is, versus retraining on pooled South American plus Kazakhstan data
evidence.outcome: Detection accuracy on Kazakhstan samples by class (SARS-CoV-2+, NCARI, asymptomatic controls)
evidence.effect: Single-source pipeline as-is: 91.0% SARS-CoV-2+, 48.0% NCARI, 67.0% AC (random forest). Pooled SA-Kaz retraining: 88.0% SARS-CoV-2+, 95.0% NCARI, 78% AC (SVM-RBF), SARS-CoV-2 vs rest ROC AUC 0.983 [0.958, 0.987]; high accuracy maintained for South American samples.
evidence.tradeoff: SARS-CoV-2+ detection was slightly lower after retraining (88.0% vs 91.0%). The authors note that clinical lab implementation will need continuous optimization as respiratory infections evolve.
evidence.quote: After re-training of the ML algorithms on the SA-Kaz peak intensity matrix, the accuracy of detection by the top-performing Support Vector Machine with radial basis function kernel model was at 88.0, 95.0 and 78% for the Kazakhstan SARS-CoV-2+, NCARI, and AC subjects, respectively with a SARS-CoV-2 vs. rest ROC AUC of 0.983 [0.958, 0.987]; a high differentiation accuracy was maintained for the South American SARS-CoV-2 and NCARI.

evidence.title: An artificial intelligence prediction model for optimizing patient selection for cardiac imaging for the investigation of suspected coronary artery disease
evidence.comparator_used: Local model trained on data from two cardiac centres, tested on the other 20 Ontario centres
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUROC), sensitivity and specificity for predicting obstructive CAD
evidence.effect: Local two-centre model on geographical validation: AUROC 0.714, sensitivity 0.73, specificity 0.57; model updated on province-wide data (N = 319,012): AUROC 0.794, sensitivity 0.708, specificity 0.699
evidence.quote: However, following updating, performance recovered (AUROC = 0.794 [95% CI: 0.794, 0.795], Sensitivity = 0.708, Specificity = 0.699).

evidence.title: External evaluation of the Dynamic Criticality Index: A machine learning model to predict future need for ICU care in hospitalized pediatric patients
evidence.comparator_used: Institution-specific CI-D models re-developed on single-site data with identical variables and modeling methods, versus multi-institutional CI-D models applied to the single site
evidence.outcome: Prediction of future care location (routine vs ICU) at >6-12, >12-18, >18-24 and >24-30 hours, measured by AUROC and AUPRC
evidence.effect: Multi-institutional models applied to the single-site test set: AUROC 0.493-0.545, AUPRC 0.262-0.299. Single-site models: AUROC 0.906-0.944, AUPRC 0.754-0.824.
evidence.quote: The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for the multi-institutional CI-D models applied to a single-site test dataset was 0.493-0.545 and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.262-0.299.

evidence.title: Can the generalizability issue of artificial intelligence be overcome? Pneumothorax detection algorithm
evidence.venue: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
evidence.comparator_used: PDA-Alpha trained on single-site data (center 1 only)
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value and false-positive predictions at the second center after adding data from that center
evidence.effect: PPV rose from 0.525 to 0.886 (p = 0.041). False positives fell from 7 to 1. Sensitivity was unchanged (49/50). AUC was 0.993 vs 0.986.
evidence.tradeoff: Only 50 additional radiographs from center 2 were used. AUC was slightly lower (0.986 vs 0.993). The amount of external data needed to fully address generalizability remains unknown.
evidence.quote: Both algorithms successfully detected the presence of pneumothorax on 49/50 radiographs; however, PDA-Alpha had seven false-positive predictions, whereas PDA-Beta had one.

evidence.title: Application of MALDI-TOF MS and machine learning for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 and non-SARS-CoV-2 respiratory infections
evidence.comparator_used: ML models trained only on South American public spectra (published pipeline applied as-is) vs models retrained on pooled South American plus Kazakhstan spectra
evidence.outcome: Detection accuracy for Kazakhstan samples (SARS-CoV-2+, NCARI, asymptomatic controls)
evidence.effect: SA-only random forest: 91.0% SARS-CoV-2+, 48.0% NCARI, 67.0% AC. Pooled SA-Kaz SVM-RBF: 88.0% SARS-CoV-2+, 95.0% NCARI, 78% AC; SARS-CoV-2 vs rest AUC 0.983 [0.958, 0.987]; high accuracy maintained for South American samples.
evidence.tradeoff: Detection of SARS-CoV-2+ samples fell slightly (91.0% to 88.0%). Authors note continuous re-optimization will be needed as respiratory infections evolve. The two arms also used different top-performing algorithms (random forest vs SVM-RBF).
evidence.quote: Incorporation of spectral signatures from Kazakhstan substantially increased the accuracy of detection.

evidence.title: Data Diversity vs. Model Complexity in the Prediction of Pediatric Bipolar Disorder: Evidence from Academic and Community Clinical Samples
evidence.comparator_used: Models trained on a single-setting (academic) dataset and validated externally in the community dataset (cross-dataset approach)
evidence.outcome: External discrimination and calibration in pediatric bipolar disorder prediction
evidence.effect: Mixed-dataset training gave 'much stronger external discrimination and calibration' than the cross-dataset approach, whose external discrimination 'substantially declined'. No numeric values appear in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Models trained on mixed datasets exhibited much stronger external discrimination and calibration.

evidence.title: Structural Findings Transfer, Texture Findings Do Not: An Adaptation Ladder for Cross-Center Dental Diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Model trained on the source center only and applied cross-center
evidence.outcome: Caries AUC when trained with target-center labels versus transferred across the acquisition gap
evidence.effect: Caries AUC 0.79 from the target's own labels versus 0.60 when transferred across centers
evidence.quote: Joint two-center training shows this is non-transfer, not unlearnability: caries is recoverable from the target's own labels (0.79) yet does not cross the acquisition gap (0.60).

evidence.title: Diagnosing and remediating harmful data shifts for the responsible deployment of clinical AI models
evidence.comparator_used: Hospital type-specific models (community or academic) adapted with transfer learning, compared with a model trained on all available hospitals pooled
evidence.outcome: Model performance across hospital sites
evidence.effect: Hospital type-specific transfer-learning models performed better than models using all hospitals; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: We found hospital type-specific models that leverage transfer learning, perform better than models that use all available hospitals.

evidence.title: A data-driven consensus framework for Ct interpretation in real-world multi-assay qPCR diagnostics
evidence.comparator_used: Single-assay models trained on one assay's data (tested for cross-assay generalization)
evidence.outcome: Cross-assay robustness of Ct prediction (MAE)
evidence.effect: Pooled multi-assay training improved cross-assay robustness compared with single-assay models; no numeric effect for this comparison in the abstract. Separately, models applied across platforms without recalibration had MAE 2.62, versus 0.0419 for XGBoost within-platform.
evidence.tradeoff: Pooling did not remove platform dependence: direct cross-platform application without recalibration caused a substantial performance decline.
evidence.quote: Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) achieved the most accurate and stable predictions under data-sufficient, within-platform conditions with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0419, while pooled multi-assay training improved cross-assay robustness compared with single-assay models.

evidence.title: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Distributional Shift and Concept Drift Across Preprocessing Configurations, Domain Adaptation, and Representation Learning in GDM Prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Models trained on the single primary cohort only and tested cross-cohort on the independent set
evidence.outcome: AUPRC on GDM prediction (mixed-domain training vs single-cohort training with cross-cohort testing)
evidence.effect: Mixed-domain (oracle) training AUPRC recovered to 0.944-0.978, versus cross-cohort AUPRC of 0.180-0.266 for classical models and 0.167-0.216 for contrastive models trained on one cohort
evidence.tradeoff: This was an oracle experiment, described as a non-deployment setting, so the gain is not shown to be achievable in real deployment.
evidence.quote: In an oracle mixed-domain experiment (non-deployment setting), when training includes data from both cohorts, AUPRC recovers to 0.944-0.978, confirming that model capacity is not the bottleneck.

evidence.title: Evaluating Deep Learning Sepsis Prediction Models in ICUs Under Distribution Shift: A Multi-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.comparator_used: Supervised domain adaptation with maximum mean discrepancy (DA MMD) compared with fusion training on merged datasets
evidence.outcome: AUROC and normalized AUPRC for sepsis prediction in medium-sized target datasets
evidence.effect: DA MMD: AUROC = 0.720 and nAUPRC = 2.352; fusion training: AUROC = 0.712 and nAUPRC = 2.215; p = 0.02, adjusted p = 0.07
evidence.quote: For example, DA with maximum mean discrepancy (DA MMD) achieves superior performance in both area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC = 0.720) and normalized area under the precision-recall curve (nAUPRC = 2.352) compared to fusion training (AUROC = 0.712, nAUPRC = 2.215; p = 0.02, adjusted p = 0.07).

controls.question: Should we host AI models within our own environment rather than sending patient data to an external vendor cloud API?
controls.control: Host model inference on-premise, on-device, or embedded in scanner, PACS, or viewer infrastructure under health-system control, keeping patient data local.
controls.comparator: Comparable-capability model accessed through an external vendor cloud API
controls.aim: Protect patient data, control cost and latency, and increase institutional control over models
variants: Inference embedded in scanner, PACS, or viewer
Local inference server vs cloud-only inference
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment
tradeoffs: Performance gaps with cloud models persist; the radiologist ranked GPT-4o mini higher than the local RAG model.

Edge needs about $2561 CAD upfront hardware (Cloud $0). Edge had lower deployment task completion and the most interface complaints (mobile app). It also had lower FPS (19.02 vs 28.05), although its latency was lower (52.57 ms vs 101.68 ms end-to-end for Cloud). The Cloud setup used a secondary monitor, which may account for the ergonomic differences. Idle Edge energy use can be avoided by unplugging overnight.
Local deployment was not tested directly; the authors say larger prospective validation is needed.
Numerically lower concordance for the local model, though it stayed within the feasibility thresholds set for this study
The local open-weight model was not of comparable capability: accuracy dropped in most domains, with database retrieval the exception.
Much lower accuracy with the smaller local model, so the comparison is confounded by model size. Cloud DeepSeek-R1 also had longer latency (median 26.54 s).

evidence.title: Retrieval-augmented generation elevates local LLM quality in radiology contrast media consultation
evidence.comparator_used: Cloud-based models (GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude 3.5 Haiku) accessed via external vendor APIs
evidence.outcome: Response latency and quality ranking of the RAG-enhanced local model vs cloud models
evidence.effect: Local RAG model faster (2.6 s vs 4.9-7.3 s); LLM judges preferred it over GPT-4o mini, but the radiologist ranked GPT-4o mini higher
evidence.tradeoff: Performance gaps with cloud models persist; the radiologist ranked GPT-4o mini higher than the local RAG model.
evidence.quote: The RAG-enhanced model remained faster (2.6 s vs 4.9-7.3 s) while the LLM-based judges preferred it over GPT-4o mini, though the radiologist ranked GPT-4o mini higher.

evidence.title: Optimizing AI implementation for surgery: recommendations for infrastructure and deployment in the operating room
evidence.comparator_used: Institution-built AWS cloud system (remote GPU servers, web app on a laptop secondary monitor) versus the on-site Edge system (local GPU workstation overlaying AI on the main surgical monitor), both running GoNoGoNet in a simulated OR
evidence.outcome: Usability (task completion, SUS), ergonomics (NASA-TLX, Borg CR-10), cost, and carbon footprint of Edge vs Cloud AI deployment
evidence.effect: Task completion: Cloud median 100% vs Edge 80% (p = 2.16e-5). SUS: Edge 69.67 vs Cloud 65.33, not significant (p = 0.214). NASA-TLX physical difference 17.33 (p = 0.0004) and frustration difference 14.33 (p = 0.0036), both higher with Cloud. Neck strain higher with Cloud (p = 0.0067); strain in any body part 60% Cloud vs 6.7% Edge. Operational cost about $6.50/h Cloud vs 2.84 cents/h Edge, with equal total cost after ~396 h. Carbon 26.22 g CO2e/h Cloud vs 6.84 g/h Edge when running AI (3.8 g/h idle).
evidence.tradeoff: Edge needs about $2561 CAD upfront hardware (Cloud $0). Edge had lower deployment task completion and the most interface complaints (mobile app). It also had lower FPS (19.02 vs 28.05), although its latency was lower (52.57 ms vs 101.68 ms end-to-end for Cloud). The Cloud setup used a secondary monitor, which may account for the ergonomic differences. Idle Edge energy use can be avoided by unplugging overnight.
evidence.quote: Results showed greater deployment task completion with Cloud but increased physical strain, carbon emissions, and operational costs compared to Edge after 396 h of use.

evidence.title: Evaluating open-source LLMs for dental EMR generation
evidence.comparator_used: Proprietary cloud-accessed models (GPT-4o, GPT-4, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Grok-3) vs open-source locally deployable DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA-3.1-405B
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated 7DI score under optimized (CRISPE) prompting
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-V3 mean 7DI 28.76 ± 2.04 vs GPT-4o 29.22 ± 2.25 (p>.05); one-way ANOVA across models F = 0.54, p=.744; authors state non-significance is not equivalence
evidence.tradeoff: Local deployment was not tested directly; the authors say larger prospective validation is needed.
evidence.quote: Under optimized prompting, DeepSeek-V3 achieved a mean 7DI score of 28.76 ± 2.04, and we did not detect statistically significant differences versus GPT-4o (29.22 ± 2.25; p>.05) in this expert-rated sample.

evidence.title: A Reproducible Protocol and Framework for Large Language Model (LLM)-Assisted Estrogen and Progesterone Receptor (ER/PR) Scoring
evidence.comparator_used: Cloud-hosted models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.0), which are not of comparable capability to the local model
evidence.outcome: CAP concordance of ER/PR scoring for the locally hosted Gemma 3.0 12B versus cloud models
evidence.effect: Gemma 73-93% concordance vs Claude 90-98% and Gemini 85-100%; local model approached cloud-level performance
evidence.tradeoff: Numerically lower concordance for the local model, though it stayed within the feasibility thresholds set for this study
evidence.quote: The locally hosted model approached cloud-level performance within a clinically meaningful range, achieving concordance rates that, while numerically lower, remained within acceptable feasibility thresholds for a protocol development context.

evidence.title: BiomechAgent: AI-Assisted Biomechanical Analysis Through Code-Generating Agents
evidence.comparator_used: Frontier cloud-based LLM
evidence.outcome: Benchmark performance across domains (retrieval, visualization, classification, segmentation, clinical reasoning)
evidence.effect: Performance substantially diminished with the local open-weight model in most domains other than database retrieval (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: The local open-weight model was not of comparable capability: accuracy dropped in most domains, with database retrieval the exception.
evidence.quote: We also tested BiomechAgent using a local open-weight model instead of a frontier cloud based LLM and found that perform was substantially diminished in most domains other than database retrieval.

evidence.title: On-premise medical AI agents for reliable clinical decision-making
evidence.comparator_used: Cloud-based baseline model on the primary MIMIC-IV benchmark
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy on MIMIC-IV-derived benchmarks
evidence.effect: On-premise agent achieved 90.04% accuracy (seven-disease task) and 83.8% (four-disease task), approaching the cloud baseline on the primary benchmark
evidence.quote: Across two Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV)-derived benchmarks, the agent achieved 90.04% accuracy on a seven-disease task and 83.8% accuracy on a four-disease task, approaching a cloud baseline on the primary benchmark.

evidence.title: Locally-deployed vs. cloud-based AI in healthcare: evaluating DeepSeek-R1:8b, DeepSeek-R1, and ChatGPT o3-mini-high for complex medical diagnostics
evidence.comparator_used: Cloud-based DeepSeek-R1 (and ChatGPT o3-mini-high) accessed externally; the local model is a distilled 8B variant, so capability is not matched
evidence.outcome: First-attempt connection reliability versus diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: Local DeepSeek-R1:8b had a connection failure rate of 0.2% (95% CI 0.0%-0.5%) versus 4.6% for cloud DeepSeek-R1, but accuracy was 55.0% (95% CI 51.9%-58.5%) versus 89.5% for DeepSeek-R1 and 78.2% for o3-mini-high.
evidence.tradeoff: Much lower accuracy with the smaller local model, so the comparison is confounded by model size. Cloud DeepSeek-R1 also had longer latency (median 26.54 s).
evidence.quote: The locally deployed DeepSeek-R1:8b demonstrated markedly stronger connection reliability (failure rate 0.2%, 95% CI: 0.0%-0.5%) but substantially reduced accuracy (55.0%, 95% CI: 51.9%-58.5%).

evidence.title: MAM-AI: An On-Device Medical Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Nurses and Midwives in Zanzibar
evidence.comparator_used: Cloud-based retrieval systems (seven retrievers compared)
evidence.outcome: Retrieval ranking quality of the on-device 300M embedder
evidence.effect: The on-device 300M embedder ranks third of seven retrievers and rivals cloud systems
evidence.quote: the 300M embedder ranks third of seven retrievers and rivals cloud systems

controls.question: Should we keep updating deployed models, through scheduled retraining, clinician-correction loops, or targeted edits, rather than leaving them static?
controls.control: Update deployed models at set intervals or from clinician-corrected errors, or apply targeted editing or steering, guarding against forgetting.
controls.comparator: Static model trained once and never updated
controls.aim: Maintain performance as data and practice drift and correct known errors or biases
variants: Scheduled retraining on recent local data
Expert review and correction loop feeding retraining
Test-time adaptation instead of full retraining
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment
tradeoffs: Human-in-the-loop learning risks propagating incorrect user confirmations into later model updates. The authors mitigate this by restricting edit permissions to trained users. Distribution shift needs monitoring and was not evaluated. Session-specific accuracy varied widely (56.7-98.15%).
In simultaneous recruitments in different settings, a single updated model could not optimize performance across both settings.
Expanding to new clinics correlated with performance decline, so retraining was needed to mitigate model drift.

Architectural updates required repeat calibration testing. Technical defects still spiked in months 12 and 19. The clinical score dipped in months 15-16 when the expert reviewer changed. The calibration set had only 100 studies and there was no non-updated control arm.
Population-level model updating could exacerbate fairness gaps in some cases, and fairness drift occurred in both the original and updated models.
Retraining on data shaped by model-driven interventions degraded performance. No universally effective model-updating approach was found, and model use may need to be recorded to keep models viable.

evidence.title: Real-world clinical impact of implementing and updating a deep learning-based automatic contouring system in rectal cancer radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
evidence.comparator_used: First-generation DeepLab V3 system left in place (post-implementation cohort and Auto1-assisted contouring) versus the updated second-generation nnU-Net V2 system
evidence.outcome: Geometric agreement between unedited auto-contours and final treatment contours, failure rate, contouring time, inter-observer consistency, accuracy, and blinded clinical acceptability
evidence.effect: Mean DSC improved from 0.88 to 0.93 for CTV (P<0.001) and from 0.88 to 0.95 for OARs (P<0.001). Mean failure rate fell from 3.30% to 0.64% (about 80.6% reduction). Total contouring time was 16.97 vs 21.74 min (about 21.9% less than Auto1) and 41.15 min for manual. CTV inter-observer DSC was 0.95 vs 0.93. Mean Likert score was 4.02 vs 3.26 (P<0.001), with 95.2% vs 28.6% of contours scoring >=4.
evidence.quote: Auto2 demonstrated significantly better clinical acceptability than Auto1, with a higher mean Likert score (4.02 ± 0.25 vs. 3.26 ± 0.49, P < 0.001).

evidence.title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
evidence.comparator_used: Static fine-tuned model at the start of deployment (session 1), before further updates from expert-validated mappings
evidence.outcome: Top-1 accuracy on the static hold-out test set over ten mapping sessions
evidence.effect: Top-1 accuracy rose from 89.43% in session 1 to 94.22% by session 9. Linear regression gave β=0.367, p=0.021, R²=0.50. Top-5 accuracy stayed at 99-100%.
evidence.tradeoff: Human-in-the-loop learning risks propagating incorrect user confirmations into later model updates. The authors mitigate this by restricting edit permissions to trained users. Distribution shift needs monitoring and was not evaluated. Session-specific accuracy varied widely (56.7-98.15%).
evidence.quote: On the hold-out test set, top-1 accuracy displayed a gradual linear increase, starting at 89.43% in session 1 and increasing with further fine-tuning to 94.22% by session 9, reflecting the benefits of continuous learning.

evidence.title: Research on the generalization of a blood donor recruitment framework based on machine learning
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Previous version of the model (before incremental fine-tuning with newly collected recruitment data)
evidence.outcome: Identification of high-willingness donors and recruitment efficiency (success rate per SMS) across recruitment rounds
evidence.effect: Updated models consistently outperformed their predecessors overall (no numbers in main text; see Tables S9 and S10), with exceptions in simultaneously conducted rounds (1st and 2nd, 4th and 5th, 6th and 7th)
evidence.tradeoff: In simultaneous recruitments in different settings, a single updated model could not optimize performance across both settings.
evidence.quote: As shown in Tables S9 and S10 , the updated models consistently outperformed their predecessors in terms of identifying high-willingness donors and improving recruitment efficiency (measured by success rate per SMS).

evidence.title: The incremental design of a machine learning framework for medical records processing
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Document classification model before retraining, after performance declined as new clinics were onboarded
evidence.outcome: Document classification accuracy
evidence.effect: Retraining document classification increased accuracy by 10.2%
evidence.tradeoff: Expanding to new clinics correlated with performance decline, so retraining was needed to mitigate model drift.
evidence.quote: Retraining document classification increased accuracy by 10.2%.

evidence.title: Using Optimal Feature Selection and Continuous Learning to Implement Efficient Model Arrays for Predicting Daily Clinical Radiology Workload
evidence.comparator_used: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the implied comparison is model quality over time with weekly retraining on live data, against the originally trained model without retraining.
evidence.outcome: Model quality (forecast accuracy) over time during live use
evidence.effect: Weekly retraining on live data resulted in high, and sometimes increased, model quality; no numeric comparison given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Retraining the model on a weekly basis using live data resulted in high, and sometimes increased, model quality.

evidence.title: Evolution of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Application for Mammography
evidence.comparator_used: Initial model version (0.14.0/first calibrated version) before developer updates, within a before-after lifecycle design; there was no separate static-model arm
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy (AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity), technical defect rate and clinical assessment score across successive updated versions
evidence.effect: AUC 0.73 to 0.91 (+24.7%), accuracy 0.77 to 0.89, sensitivity 0.62 to 0.85, specificity 0.84 to 0.93; technical defects 9.0% to 1.0%; clinical assessment score 63.4 to 72.0
evidence.tradeoff: Architectural updates required repeat calibration testing. Technical defects still spiked in months 12 and 19. The clinical score dipped in months 15-16 when the expert reviewer changed. The calibration set had only 100 studies and there was no non-updated control arm.
evidence.quote: Specifically, the AUC rose by 24.7% (from 0.73 to 0.91), the accuracy improved by 15.6% (from 0.77 to 0.89), sensitivity grew by 37.1% (from 0.62 to 0.85), and specificity increased by 10.7% (from 0.84 to 0.93).

evidence.title: Emerging algorithmic bias: fairness drift as the next dimension of model maintenance and sustainability
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Original static random forest model trained on 2013 data and never updated, compared with temporally updated models, 2014-2023
evidence.outcome: Fairness gaps (metric parity between disadvantaged and advantaged groups by race and sex) and overall performance (discrimination, calibration, accuracy) for 30-day post-surgical readmission, mortality, and pneumonia
evidence.effect: No numeric effect sizes reported in the text. Updating had a larger impact on overall performance than on fairness gaps. During stable fairness periods, updating increased, decreased, or did not change fairness gaps. During fairness drift, updating restored fairness in some cases and exacerbated gaps in others.
evidence.tradeoff: Population-level model updating could exacerbate fairness gaps in some cases, and fairness drift occurred in both the original and updated models.
evidence.quote: During periods of fairness drift, updating models restored fairness in some cases and exacerbated fairness gaps in others.

evidence.title: Implications of the Use of Artificial Intelligence Predictive Models in Health Care Settings : A Simulation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Original model before retraining (model not updated after deployment), with performance compared at fixed 90% sensitivity
evidence.outcome: Specificity of the mortality prediction model at fixed 90% sensitivity after retraining on EHR data affected by model use
evidence.effect: Mortality model lost 9% to 39% specificity after retraining once; a mortality model created after an AKI model was implemented lost 8% to 15% specificity; simultaneous AKI and mortality models reduced each other's effective accuracy by 1% to 28%
evidence.tradeoff: Retraining on data shaped by model-driven interventions degraded performance. No universally effective model-updating approach was found, and model use may need to be recorded to keep models viable.
evidence.quote: At fixed 90% sensitivity, in scenario 1 a mortality prediction model lost 9% to 39% specificity after retraining once and in scenario 2 a mortality prediction model lost 8% to 15% specificity when created after the implementation of an acute kidney injury (AKI) prediction model; in scenario 3, models for AKI and mortality prediction implemented simultaneously, each led to reduced effective accuracy of the other by 1% to 28%.

evidence.title: Real world deployment of a pancreatic cancer risk model: impact of refitting, imputation, and computational burden
evidence.comparator_used: Original random survival forest model trained on 2007-2017 data and not refit (static), evaluated on the 2020 cohort
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (C-index) and calibration on the 2020 cohort
evidence.effect: Without refitting, C-index ranged from 0.69 to 0.84 depending on imputation method; with refitting, it ranged from 0.79 to 0.83. Calibration improved markedly with refitting.
evidence.quote: Refitting improved discrimination and calibration.

evidence.title: Analyzing and Mitigating Model Drift in Acute Kidney Injury Prediction for Hospitalized Patients
evidence.venue: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium
evidence.comparator_used: Static model without updating, whose performance drifted over the ten-year period
evidence.outcome: Area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) for AKI prediction, i.e. mitigation of performance drift
evidence.effect: OPU increased average AUPRC by 0.14 in the overall population and 0.11 across subgroups; SSU improved average AUPRC by 0.10 among subgroups
evidence.quote: Our results demonstrated significant reductions in drift, with OPU increasing the average area-under-the-precision-recall-curve (AUPRC) by 0.14 in the overall population and 0.11 across subgroups, and SSU improving the average AUPRC by 0.10 among subgroups.

evidence.title: Disc Diffusion Reader: an AI-powered potential solution to combat antibiotic resistance in developing countries
evidence.venue: Journal of infection in developing countries
evidence.comparator_used: Model before HITL correction and retraining (static model without technician-corrected updates)
evidence.outcome: Model performance (accuracy) after technician corrections and retraining
evidence.effect: Accuracy of 92.95% for inhibition zone detection and 96.92% for antibiotic disc identification, with a performance improvement of 99.28% following HITL corrections
evidence.quote: The application achieved 92.95% accuracy for inhibition zone detection and 96.92% accuracy for antibiotic disc identification, with a performance improvement of 99.28% following HITL corrections.

evidence.title: External Validation and Recalibration of a Mortality Prediction Model for Patients with Ischaemic Stroke
evidence.comparator_used: Original model with its initial coefficients applied unchanged to the later 2016-2018 cohort (external validation, no updating)
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC) for in-hospital mortality after ischaemic stroke
evidence.effect: Recalibrated model AUC 0.743 vs external validation of original coefficients AUC 0.726
evidence.quote: Rigorous external validation slightly decreased the AUC but confirmed the validity of the baseline model for the chronologically later cohort.

evidence.title: Multicenter validation and updating of the ELDER-ICU model for severity assessment in elderly critical illness
evidence.comparator_used: Original static ELDER-ICU model without updating (external validation as-is)
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUROC) and calibration for in-hospital mortality prediction in critically ill older adults across 12 international centers
evidence.effect: Incremental training enhanced performance in most centers; retraining improved AUROC by 0.066 (South Korea) and 0.076 (China) versus original AUROC of 0.753 and 0.698; isotonic regression and Platt scaling improved calibration globally
evidence.quote: Incremental training enhanced performance in most centers, while retraining significantly improved AUROC by 0.066 and 0.076 in the two Asian sites (South Korea and China, respectively).

evidence.title: Implementation of a dynamic model updating pipeline provides a systematic process for maintaining performance of prediction models
evidence.comparator_used: Model that was not updated (static model)
evidence.outcome: Calibration and discrimination of 5-year survival prediction in cystic fibrosis over a 10-year dynamic updating period
evidence.effect: Both proactive and reactive updating pipelines gave overall better calibration and discrimination than the non-updated model; no numerical values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Both the proactive and reactive updating pipelines produced survival prediction models that overall had better performance in terms of calibration and discrimination than a model that was not updated.

evidence.title: Dynamic Updating of Psychosis Prediction Models in Individuals at Ultra-High Risk of Psychosis
evidence.venue: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
evidence.comparator_used: Static logistic regression prediction model (original) trained once and not updated
evidence.outcome: Predictive performance (calibration, discrimination, clinical net benefit) for predicting psychosis onset at 1 year in UHR individuals
evidence.effect: All 3 updating methods improved performance vs the original model (recalibration p = .009; refitting p = .020; dynamic updating p = .001). Dynamic updating performed best: Harrell's C-index 0.71 (95% CI 0.60 to 0.82), calibration slope 1.12 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.87), and best clinical net benefit over the validation period. The original model was poorly calibrated throughout.
evidence.quote: All 3 updating methods improved the predictive performance compared with the original model (recalibration: p = .009; refitting: p = .020; dynamic updating: p = .001).

evidence.title: Stability of Suicide Risk Prediction Models During Changes in Health Care Delivery
evidence.comparator_used: Static model developed on 2009-mid-2015 visits and applied unchanged to late 2015-2019 visits, compared with new models retrained for each calendar year 2015-2019
evidence.outcome: Classification performance (AUC), sensitivity, positive predictive value and calibration for predicting self-harm within 90 days; predictors selected
evidence.effect: Static model AUC 0.840-0.849 in the new sample versus 0.851 in the original sample; new yearly models AUC range 0.790-0.853, with sensitivity and PPV similar to the previously developed model
evidence.quote: New models did not yield superior performance or identify different predictors.

evidence.title: Simulation of covariate and concept drift in machine learning hospital admission prediction from emergency triage
evidence.comparator_used: Static base model trained on 2016-2017 data and not updated, tested on rolling quarterly data from 2018 to 2023
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUROC) and mean daily bed error for hospital admission prediction
evidence.effect: Base model mean AUROC 0.875 (range 0.844-0.887) and mean daily bed error 7.42 beds (range 0.47-13.1); retrained models mean AUROC 0.892 (quarterly) and 0.893 (half-yearly), bed error 4.02 (quarterly) and 4.48 (half-yearly) beds per day; calibration and classification performance similar
evidence.quote: Retrained models demonstrated improved discrimination (mean AUROC 0.892 and 0.893) and reduced bed error (4.02 and 4.48 beds per day) for quarterly and half-yearly retraining, respectively, with similar calibration and classification performance.

evidence.title: Diagnosing and remediating harmful data shifts for the responsible deployment of clinical AI models
evidence.comparator_used: Locked static model that is not updated after deployment
evidence.outcome: Mitigation of data-shift-related deterioration over time (model performance, including during COVID-19)
evidence.effect: Continual learning reported to mitigate data shifts over time and improve model performance; no numeric effect given in the abstract
evidence.quote: We used continual learning, the process of learning from a continual stream of data in a sequential manner, to mitigate data shifts over time and improve model performance.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-driven forecasting and shift optimization for pediatric emergency department crowding
evidence.comparator_used: Models without MLOps-based updating and model selection during the simulation (median R2 of all models, no automated retraining)
evidence.outcome: Forecast accuracy (R2) for PED overcrowding during the simulation period
evidence.effect: Median R2 was 44% across all models, and improved to 60% after MLOps-based model selection
evidence.quote: Throughout the simulation, the median R<sup>2</sup> score for all models was 44% after MLOps-based model selection, the median R<sup>2</sup> improved to 60%.

evidence.title: Application of concept Drift Detection and Adaptive Framework for Non Linear Time Series Data from Cardiac Surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Models without a drift adaptive framework (static, non-adapted models)
evidence.outcome: Predictive performance (error) for hospital stay and ICU stay after drift
evidence.effect: Models with a drift adaptive framework (adaptive, incremental, ensemble learning) performed better than models without one; no numeric difference given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Furthermore, the models that incorporate a drift adaptive framework exhibit superior performance compared to the models that do not include such a framework.

evidence.title: Discovery of an Artificial Intelligence Label Feedback Loop: How the Success of a Clinically Implemented Artificial Intelligence Algorithm Has Created an Unforeseen Challenge to Algorithm Retraining
evidence.comparator_used: Original deployed model V1 (not retrained), versus retrained model V2 trained on 6 times more data
evidence.outcome: Concordance with reported labels across three evaluation sets: recent production hold-out, original pre-AI human-labeled validation set, and recent human-only or human-corrected labels
evidence.effect: V2 had 10% lower concordance than V1 on the recent production hold-out set (mostly AI-influenced labels). Performance was similar on the pre-AI validation set. V2 outperformed V1 on recent cases with human-only or human-corrected labels, particularly for less-common stone types.
evidence.tradeoff: An AI label feedback loop, in which AI-influenced labels contaminate the retraining and evaluation data, confounded retraining and evaluation. Ongoing human annotation and careful validation set construction are needed.
evidence.quote: V2 demonstrated a 10% lower concordance rate than V1 when evaluated on the recent production hold-out set, despite a much larger training dataset.

evidence.title: Dynamic Updating of Clinical Survival Prediction Models in a Rapidly Changing Environment
evidence.comparator_used: One-time discrete model updating (refitting, recalibration or Bayesian update applied once)
evidence.outcome: Predictive performance of survival prediction models in simulated rapidly changing environments (changing survival rates, new treatment, rare predictors)
evidence.effect: Dynamic updating outperformed one-time discrete updating in the simulations; no numeric estimates reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: We found that a dynamic updating process outperformed one-time discrete updating in the simulations.

evidence.title: ReclAIm: A Multi-Agent Framework for Monitoring and Correcting Performance Decline in Medical Imaging AI
evidence.comparator_used: Deployed model before fine-tuning (static model with the performance decline on inference data)
evidence.outcome: Recovery of image classification performance metrics after a detected decline
evidence.effect: Performance discrepancies between test and inference data were detected in 8 of 18 models; for declines of up to 40.6% (cardiomegaly dataset, InceptionV3), fine-tuning restored metrics to within 2% of baseline values.
evidence.quote: In cases with declines of up to 40.6% (cardiomegaly dataset, InceptionV3), fine-tuning restored performance metrics to within 2% of baseline values.

evidence.title: Clinical-ShiftEval: a framework for simulating and evaluating model adaptation in dynamic clinical NLP tasks
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional supervised model trained on the first period and not updated (static), also benchmarked against in-context learning and hybrid approaches
evidence.outcome: F1 drop under label-set incompatibility and task definition evolution after incremental retraining
evidence.effect: Static supervised models dropped up to 82% F1 in LSI and 43% in TDE; continual adaptation with incremental retraining gradually restored performance and surpassed in-context and hybrid approaches after at least 30% of second-period data
evidence.tradeoff: Needs newly labeled data from the second period (at least 30%) to surpass in-context and hybrid approaches; with little new data it performs worse than them
evidence.quote: Continual adaptation with incremental retraining gradually restored performance, but only surpassed in-context and hybrid approaches after incorporating at least 30% of data from the second period.

evidence.title: ReclAIm: A Multiagent Framework for Monitoring and Correcting Performance Decline in Medical Imaging AI
evidence.comparator_used: Deployed model without fine-tuning, i.e. the static model's declined performance on inference data
evidence.outcome: Recovery of classification performance metrics after a detected decline
evidence.effect: Declines were detected in 8 of 18 models; in cases with declines of up to 40.6% (cardiomegaly dataset, InceptionV3), fine-tuning restored performance metrics to within ±2% of baseline values.
evidence.quote: In cases with declines of up to 40.6% (cardiomegaly dataset, InceptionV3), fine-tuning restored performance metrics to within ±2% of baseline values.

evidence.title: Can SAEs reveal and mitigate racial biases of LLMs in healthcare?
evidence.comparator_used: Same Gemma-2 model without SAE latent steering (unsteered baseline)
evidence.outcome: Reduction of race-related bias in model outputs via SAE latent steering
evidence.effect: Improvements in simple settings; less successful for more realistic and complex clinical tasks (no numeric effect given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: We find that this offers improvements in simple settings, but is less successful for more realistic and complex clinical tasks.

controls.question: Should we train on supervision derived from reports, outcomes, routine data, or unlabeled data instead of full expert annotation?
controls.control: Use weak, proxy, or objective outcome labels, or self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled data, instead of full manual expert labels, holding case selection constant.
controls.comparator: Full manual expert annotation of the same cases
controls.aim: Reduce annotation cost and label subjectivity while keeping model performance
variants: Workflow-derived or routine charted proxy labels
Report text or slide-level weak labels
Semi- or self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled data
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment
tradeoffs: Hybrid supervision still needed expert pixel-level annotation of MIA WSIs (180 for training), so annotation cost was reduced rather than removed. Weak labels alone performed far worse, and the hybrid model also added slide-level labels to the manual annotations.

evidence.title: Hybrid supervised deep learning for lung adenocarcinoma diagnosis to optimize surgical strategies
evidence.comparator_used: Fully supervised ResNet-50 + FC classifier trained on manual pathologist patch-level annotations; also slide-level-label-only weakly supervised MIL methods
evidence.outcome: Lung adenocarcinoma subtype classification accuracy (AIS/MIA/IA) on internal and external test sets
evidence.effect: Internal test ACC 95.62% (HSFLA, hybrid) vs 90.51% (fully supervised ResNet50+FC) and 70.80% (best weak MIL, DTFD-MIL); AIS recall 94.74% vs 84.21%. External test ACC 91.67% vs 86.67%. 3D patient-level ACC 94.29% vs 88.57%. With 50% of manual annotations masked, HSFLA kept 89.05% ACC internal and 78.33% external.
evidence.tradeoff: Hybrid supervision still needed expert pixel-level annotation of MIA WSIs (180 for training), so annotation cost was reduced rather than removed. Weak labels alone performed far worse, and the hybrid model also added slide-level labels to the manual annotations.
evidence.quote: Despite the availability of more precise supervision signals, the performance of the standalone ResNet-50 + FC remained inferior to that of HSFLA, achieving only 90.5% ACC and 92.2% AUC.

controls.question: Should we choose a specialized model variant, domain-specific or reasoning-enhanced, rather than a standard general-purpose model?
controls.control: Select a domain-specific, task-specific, or reasoning-enhanced model variant matched to the clinical task and users, validated against the standard alternative.
controls.comparator: Standard general-purpose model version used zero-shot
controls.aim: Improve accuracy and reliability on specialized or complex clinical reasoning tasks
variants: General multimodal LLM zero-shot as alternative
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment
