evidence.title: Evaluating real-world deployment of an HL7-CDA-aligned LLM for ICD-10-CM coding
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose base models (Mistral-7B instruct, Llama2-7B), fine-tuned and evaluated under identical settings
evidence.outcome: ICD-10-CM coding F-score after fine-tuning (internal test set)
evidence.effect: Full-code F: BioMistral 0.780 vs Mistral-instruct 0.760; MedLlama2 0.774 vs Llama2 0.749. Top-50 F: BioMistral 0.906 vs Mistral-instruct 0.877; MedLlama2 0.880 vs Llama2 0.868. The advantage persisted on the KMUH RCT dataset (BioMistral 0.754 vs Mistral 0.736 full-code F). No significance testing was reported for the comparisons.
evidence.quote: BioMistral achieved the highest downstream performance (F 1 -score = 0.78; win rate = 69.2%), followed by MedLlama2 and Mistral.

evidence.title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose embedding models (Qwen3-0.6B, EmbeddingGemma-300M) and the general LLM Claude 3.7 Sonnet, all used zero-shot without finetuning
evidence.outcome: Baseline top-1 accuracy for medication and laboratory test concept mapping
evidence.effect: Domain-specific BioLORD reached 92.9% top-1 for medications and 37.0% for lab tests, against 85.6%/23.7% for Qwen3 and 71.9%/11.7% for Gemma (the lab-test column of Table 1 pairs Qwen3 with 23.7% and Gemma with 11.7%). Claude 3.7 was better on lab tests (43.8% top-1, 86.7% top-5) but worse on medications (76.6% top-1).
evidence.tradeoff: Claude 3.7 carries substantially higher computational and hardware cost, which the authors say makes it unjustifiable for this task. After finetuning, differences between embedding models largely vanished.
evidence.quote: Overall, the BioLORD model outperforms other embedding models, achieving an acc top1 of 92.9% for medications and 37.0% laboratory test names, compared to 91.2% and 27.9% obtained by the next highest embedding model (SapBERT).

evidence.title: Beyond Simulations: What 20,000 Real Conversations Reveal About Mental Health AI Safety
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose frontier LLMs/general-purpose LLMs on published mental-health safety benchmarks
evidence.outcome: Harmful content production across suicide/NSSI, eating disorder, and substance-use benchmarks
evidence.effect: suicide/NSSI: .4-11.27% vs 29.0-54.4%; eating disorder: 8.4% vs 54.0%; substance use: 9.9% vs 45.0%
evidence.quote: The purpose-built AI was significantly less likely than general-purpose LLMs to produce harmful content across suicide/NSSI (.4-11.27% vs 29.0-54.4%), eating disorder (8.4% vs 54.0%), and substance use (9.9% vs 45.0%) benchmarks.

evidence.title: Blinded two-phase evaluation of large language models in complex cardiac surgery: task-specific performance and human-AI collaboration
evidence.comparator_used: Standard general-purpose model GPT-4 (and the domain-specific Llama3-OpenBioLLM-70B), all prompted with the same multi-agent strategy
evidence.outcome: Median normalized expert-rated score on open-ended complex cardiac surgery reasoning tasks (15 scenarios, 10-dimension weighted framework)
evidence.effect: Median normalized scores: O1 0.896, O3-mini-high 0.854, DeepSeek-R1 0.792 vs GPT-4 0.667 and Llama3-OpenBioLLM-70B 0.521; relative rankings stable across scenarios
evidence.tradeoff: Even the reasoning-optimized models were weak on patient safety (0.507), hallucination avoidance (0.549) and clinical efficiency (0.597) across models. Evaluators over-accepted plausible but incorrect or harmful model reasoning: 7.57% of ratings were revised from affirmative to negative after seeing the reference answers.
evidence.quote: Reasoning-optimized LLMs outperformed all other models.

evidence.title: Adaptive Fast-Slow Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional Classification of Prenatal Ultrasound Reports: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Standard high-speed base model DeepSeek-V3.2-B
evidence.outcome: Performance on subjective severity assessment, with factual extraction tasks as a contrast
evidence.effect: The reasoning-enhanced V3.2-R reached 86% accuracy and F1-score=0.75 on external data. V3.2-B scored 56.6% accuracy on severity but above 90% accuracy and F1-score on factual tasks.
evidence.tradeoff: The base model remains efficient for factual classification, so the authors recommend a fast-slow split rather than replacing it.
evidence.quote: In contrast, the V3.2-R model utilizing CoT reasoning achieved superior robustness (86% accuracy and F1-score=0.75) on external data without RAG; notably, introducing RAG to V3.2-R degraded performance to 81%, suggesting potential noise interference.

evidence.title: Characterising liver lesions from free-text computer tomography reports - A real-world multicentre analysis
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose GPT-4 given the same simple and optimised prompts on the same CT reports
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of lesion classification against radiologist-assigned LI-RADS scores, and malignant vs benign classification
evidence.effect: LI-RADS accuracy ranged from 40.8% (Med-LMsp) to 61.3% (Med-LMop) at lesion level and from 27.7% (Med-LMsp) to 52.4% (Med-LMop) at patient level. Malignant vs benign accuracy ranged from 56.1% (GPT-4sp) to 82.3% (Med-LMop) at lesion level and from 71.3% (Med-LMsp) to 86.5% (Med-LMop) at patient level. Med-LMop was statistically superior to the other models (all p < 0.001). Non-classification rates ranged from 12.7% (Med-LMop) to 40.5% (GPT-4sp).
evidence.tradeoff: Both models had high misclassification rates and inconsistent repeatability (12.7% to 39.0%), which the authors say hinder clinical use. Both models were better at detecting malignancy than at full LI-RADS classification.
evidence.quote: Med-LM outperforms GPT-4 in classifying liver lesions from unstructured CT reports with both models better at detecting malignancy than full LI-RADS classification.

evidence.title: Fact-Checking Large Language Model Responses to a Health Care Prompt: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose GPT-4o compared with the domain-specific biomedical model OpenBioLLM-70B
evidence.outcome: Fact-checking agreement with human experts, speed, and omissions of safety information
evidence.effect: 20 claims: GPT-4o 100% vs OpenBioLLM-70B 95% agreement with experts. Acne scenario: both 86%. Time: GPT-4o 42 s vs OpenBioLLM-70B 33 min.
evidence.tradeoff: The domain-specific model was much slower, diverged from experts on 1 pediatric antihistamine question, and omitted 1 key patient-safety information item.
evidence.quote: For the set of 20 medical claims, GPT-4o fact-checking had 100% agreement with that of human experts, whereas OpenBioLLM-70B had 95% agreement.

evidence.title: Comparative Assessment of Performance of Domain-Specific and Primed Versus Non-Primed Artificial Intelligence Chatbots for Clinical Decision-Making in Injuries to the Primary Dentition: An Exploratory Pilot Study
evidence.venue: Dental traumatology : official publication of International Association for Dental Traumatology
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose chatbots (ChatGPT 5.2, Perplexity Pro), non-primed and primed with a guideline summary
evidence.outcome: Accuracy versus IADT guidelines for immediate management, follow-up interval and radiographic recommendations
evidence.effect: The domain-specific chatbot reached 100% accuracy in immediate management, with minor inaccuracies in the general-purpose models. All chatbots had complete diagnostic accuracy. For follow-up interval and radiographic recommendations, the primed general-purpose models showed greater agreement with IADT guidelines than the domain-specific chatbot.
evidence.quote: The domain-specific chatbot achieved 100% accuracy in immediate management decisions, while minor inaccuracies were observed among general-purpose models.

evidence.title: General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specific Large Language Models in Antibiotic Clinical Decision-Making: A Double-Blind Evaluation with a 2×2 Factorial Design
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose model DeepSeek V3.5 (both under direct prompting and under CoT prompting)
evidence.outcome: Physician-rated comprehensive antibiotic regimen score, plus individualized adjustment and dosing precision sub-scores
evidence.effect: Base mode: MedGo 4.25±0.16 vs DeepSeek 3.98±0.20 (Holm-adjusted p=0.040). With CoT: MedGo 4.58±0.09 vs DeepSeek 4.41±0.11, better on individualized adjustment (adjusted p<0.001) and dosing precision (adjusted p=0.005)
evidence.tradeoff: Deficiencies persisted in antimicrobial stewardship ecological awareness, and real physicians still scored higher (4.76±0.04)
evidence.quote: In base mode, MedGo significantly outperformed DeepSeek (Holm-adjusted p=0.040).

evidence.title: Incorporating information retrieval into AI chatbots for patient education on thyroid eye disease
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose ChatGPT (GPT-4o-mini) and the ChatGPT-RAG model
evidence.outcome: Clinical ratings (accuracy, relevance and others) versus non-clinical ratings (empathy, understandability, actionability)
evidence.effect: Clinical mean score 5.96 for OpenEvidence vs 4.94 for ChatGPT (Hedges' g = 1.21, P < 0.001) and vs 5.55 for ChatGPT-RAG (g = 0.53, P < 0.001). On non-clinical metrics ChatGPT scored 18.4 vs 14.96 for OpenEvidence (g = 1.25, P < 0.001).
evidence.tradeoff: The medicine-specific model scored worse on empathy, understandability and actionability than the general-purpose model.
evidence.quote: OpenEvidence significantly outperformed both ChatGPT (mean clinical score 5.96 vs 4.94; Hedges' g = 1.21, P < 0.001) and ChatGPT-RAG (5.96 vs 5.55; g = 0.53, P < 0.001) in clinical rankings and across most clinical metrics, including accuracy and relevance.

evidence.title: More AI, Less Care-Seeking? A National Survey Experiment on the Impact of AI Intensity on Patient Care-Seeking Intention in Chinese Family Doctor Services
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose large language model, as described in the vignette, at the same AI integration level
evidence.outcome: Patient intention to seek care from family doctors
evidence.effect: Medical-specific AI framing gave higher care-seeking intention than general-purpose AI at all intensity levels; the interaction with AI intensity was not significant (p = 0.508). No effect sizes are reported in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: The medical-specific model was a label in a vignette, not a validated model. The label did not buffer the decline as AI intensity rose, since the interaction was not significant.
evidence.quote: Across all intensity levels, framing the system as a medical-specific AI consistently resulted in higher care-seeking intention than a general-purpose model.

evidence.title: Assessment of Large Language Models in Colorectal Cancer Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Decision-Making: A Retrospective Single-Center Comparison of Guideline-Integrated General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specialized Models
evidence.comparator_used: Domain-specialized MedGemma 27B (no external guideline retrieval) compared with general-purpose Gemini 2.5 (guideline-integrated)
evidence.outcome: Concordance with MTB decisions and clinical safety rate in 300 CRC cases
evidence.effect: Gemini 2.5: κ = 0.792, exact concordance 85.0%, safety 83.7%. MedGemma: κ = 0.566 (T=0.0) and 0.610 (T=1.0), accuracy 70.3% and 73.5%, safety 62.3% and 62.7%; p < 0.001 for the difference.
evidence.tradeoff: The comparison is confounded: Gemini had guideline integration and MedGemma had none, which the authors call a predefined asymmetry in knowledge augmentation. Discordance clustered in complex scenarios such as surgical planning, recurrent disease and poor performance status.
evidence.quote: A guideline-integrated general-purpose LLM demonstrated superior concordance and safety compared with a domain-specialized model operating without external retrieval, supporting its adjunctive use within MTBs while preserving expert clinical judgment.

evidence.title: A workflow utilizing general-purpose large language models for efficient structuring and data mining of bone scintigraphy narratives
evidence.comparator_used: Standard general-purpose LLMs under the same prompt: DeepSeek-V3 (non-reasoning sibling), GPT-o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro
evidence.outcome: Structured extraction accuracy and cross-center stability on 384 ground-truth lesion entities
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-R1 total error rate was 3.9% (n=15), against 12.0% (n=46) for DeepSeek-V3, 9.3% (n=36) for GPT-o3 and 14.8% (n=57) for Gemini 2.5 Pro. Its global quality score did not differ significantly across centers (P=.277), whereas DeepSeek-V3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro did differ (P<.001). R1 F1 scores were 0.969-0.989 across the three centers.
evidence.quote: For data from ZS and XH, the four LLMs exhibited varying performance, with statistically significant differences in global quality scores across models (ZS: P <.001; XH: P =.002), with DeepSeek-R1 performing the best.

evidence.title: Comparison of Large Language Model-Based Systems and Prompt Engineering for Internal Medicine Clinical Pharmacy Cases
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Clinical Pharmacy : JACCP
evidence.comparator_used: OpenEvidence, a health care provider domain-specific LLM with RAG features, compared with ChatGPT 4o, a general-purpose LLM, with and without the prompt engineering template.
evidence.outcome: Primary composite of response accuracy and completeness
evidence.effect: Predicted probabilities for meeting the primary outcome: GPT no Template 0.54, GPT with Template 0.60, OpenEvidence no Template 0.64, and OpenEvidence with Template 0.52; no statistically significant interactions reported.
evidence.quote: Neither the use of health care provider domain-specific LLM with RAG nor a prompt engineering template was found to improve LLM-based system accuracy and completeness.

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT-4o and Four Open-Source Large Language Models in Generating Diagnoses Based on China's Rare Disease Catalog: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: standard general-purpose qwen2.5:7b
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy for rare diseases
evidence.effect: Deepseek-R1:7b scored 9.9% versus qwen2.5:7b (χ²1=42.19, P<.001)
evidence.tradeoff: The low-parameter distilled reasoning model showed substantial performance limitations.
evidence.quote: The distilled model Deepseek-R1:7b markedly underperformed (9.9% vs qwen2.5:7b; χ²1=42.19, P<.001).

evidence.title: Grounding Large Language Model in Clinical Diagnostics
evidence.comparator_used: Other general LLMs evaluated in the same clinical diagnostic procedures: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Claude-3-Haiku, Qwen2.5-72b, Qwen2.5-34b, and Qwen2.5-14b
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and procedural performance
evidence.effect: ClinDiag-GPT was trained on over 8,000 real-world cases; no numerical performance effect reported in the abstract, only that it “significantly outperformed” other LLMs.
evidence.quote: It significantly outperformed other LLMs in both diagnostic accuracy and procedural performance.

evidence.title: First, do NOHARM: a medical safety benchmark and randomized study of physician and AI teaming on clinical consultations
evidence.comparator_used: generalist LLMs
evidence.outcome: NOHARM clinical consultation safety/performance; potential for severe harm in recommendations
evidence.effect: Compared 4 widely used RAG clinical AI tools with 20 notable LLMs; clinical AI tools outperformed generalist LLMs; no between-arm numerical effect size reported in the supplied text.
evidence.quote: Harm potential was not uniform across systems, with clinical AI tools outperforming generalist LLMs, and multi-agent AI teaming further improving performance in generalist models.

evidence.title: Correctness, Harmfulness, and Diversity of Large Language Models for Colonoscopy Preparation Assistance: Comparative Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Standard non-reasoning and open-weight models (GPT-4.1, Llama 3.3 70B, Mistral Large-2411)
evidence.outcome: Response correctness in colonoscopy preparation dialogues
evidence.effect: Reasoning models (GPT-5.1, o3) performed best on correctness (no numbers in abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: All models, including the reasoning models, still produced harmful errors, mainly omissions or misinterpretations of prep instructions.
evidence.quote: Closed-weight models (GPT-5.1, GPT-4.1, and o3) outperformed open-weight models (Llama and Mistral) on correctness, with the reasoning models (GPT-5.1 and o3) performing best.

evidence.title: A systematic comparison of ChatGPT and DeepSeek for guideline-based question answering in obstetric anesthesia
evidence.comparator_used: DeepSeek-R1 (reasoning-enhanced) compared with DeepSeek-V3 (standard general-purpose) and the ChatGPT-4o models, zero-shot on obstetric anesthesia guideline questions
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, Overconclusiveness and Completeness ratings (5-point Likert) across models
evidence.effect: No significant differences across models for Accuracy, Overconclusiveness or Completeness (p > 0.05). The only readability contrast involving R1 was DeepSeek-V3 under BP outperforming R1 under IP on FKGL (p = 0.0294), a comparison that also differs in prompting strategy.
evidence.quote: No significant differences were found across models for Accuracy, Overconclusiveness, or Completeness (p > 0.05).

evidence.title: Grounding Large Language Models in Clinical Evidence: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Querying UK NICE Clinical Guidelines
evidence.comparator_used: RAG-enhanced general-purpose model (O4-Mini) compared with the medical-focused Meditron3-8B
evidence.outcome: Faithfulness on 70 curated question-answer pairs
evidence.effect: Meditron3-8B scored 43% versus 99.5% for RAG-enhanced O4-Mini
evidence.quote: Faithfulness, the measure of whether an answer is supported by the source text, was increased by 64.7 percentage points to 99.5% for the RAG-enhanced O4-Mini model and significantly outperformed the medical-focused Meditron3-8B LLM, which scored 43%.

evidence.title: Drug or Pokémon? Large language model performance in identification of fabricated medications
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose LLMs (GPT-5-Chat, GPT-4o-mini, Gemma-3-27B-IT, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B) under standard decoding, versus the domain-specific DrugGPT
evidence.outcome: Confabulation rate (failure to recognize and reject a fabricated Pokémon medication) at baseline
evidence.effect: DrugGPT baseline confabulation 2.7-6.4% vs 47.2-99.6% for the other models
evidence.quote: DrugGPT demonstrated the lowest baseline confabulation rates (2.7-6.4%), whereas other models demonstrated substantially higher rates (47.2-99.6%).

evidence.title: Investigating LLM Capabilities on Long Context Comprehension for Medical Question Answering
evidence.comparator_used: LLMs of different sizes and capabilities, standard non-reasoning models
evidence.outcome: Long-context medical QA comprehension
evidence.effect: Benefits of reasoning models reported; no numbers in the abstract
evidence.quote: We reveal insights on model size effects and their limitations, underlying memorization issues and the benefits of reasoning models, while demonstrating the value and challenges of leveraging the full long patient's context.

evidence.title: Bias Patterns in the Application of LLMs for Clinical Decision Support: A Comprehensive Study
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose LLMs
evidence.outcome: Social bias across protected patient attributes in clinical decision support vignettes
evidence.effect: Medical fine-tuning 'did not consistently outperform' general-purpose models (no numeric values given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Notably, larger models were not necessarily less biased, and medical fine-tuning did not consistently outperform general-purpose models.

evidence.title: PanCanBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Pancreatic Oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Other non-reasoning or earlier general-purpose LLMs, including other GPT-family models
evidence.outcome: Factual accuracy (hallucination rate) and rubric-based completeness
evidence.effect: o3 achieved the highest rubric score but produced inaccuracies more frequently than other GPT-family models; reasoning-optimized models did not consistently improve factuality.
evidence.tradeoff: Higher factual error rate (hallucinations) in o3 despite the top completeness score.
evidence.quote: Importantly, newer reasoning-optimized models did not consistently improve factuality: although o3 achieved the highest rubric score, it produced inaccuracies more frequently than other GPT-family models.

evidence.title: Automated Tumor and Node Staging from Esophageal Cancer Endoscopic Ultrasound Reports: A Benchmark of Advanced Reasoning Models with Prompt Engineering and Cross-Lingual Evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4o (standard general-purpose model), zero-shot; Qwen3 and Grok-3 were also compared
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of automated T and N staging from esophageal cancer EUS reports
evidence.effect: Average T-staging accuracy: DeepSeek-R1 91.4% vs GPT-4o 84.2% (Qwen3 89.5%, Grok-3 81.3%). Average N-staging accuracy: 84.2% vs 65.0% (Qwen3 68.4%, Grok-3 51.9%). Chinese without-prompt T-staging: OR 7.84 (95% CI 4.62-13.30, p<0.001) vs GPT-4o.
evidence.quote: In both T and N-staging tasks, DeepSeek-R1 demonstrated superior overall performance compared to the competitors.

evidence.title: LLM Reasoning Does Not Protect Against Clinical Cognitive Biases - An Evaluation Using BiasMedQA
evidence.comparator_used: Standard general-purpose base models (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-32B) vs. their reasoning-enhanced variants
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy and bias susceptibility on BiasMedQA
evidence.effect: Reasoning variants had higher overall performance (OR 4.0 Llama, OR 3.6 Qwen) but did not consistently prevent bias; frequency bias OR 0.6 (p = 0.006) and recency bias OR 0.5 (p < 0.001) worsened in Llama.
evidence.tradeoff: Increased vulnerability to several bias types in the reasoning variant of Llama-3.3-70B.
evidence.quote: In neither of the two models, reasoning capabilities were able to consistently prevent cognitive bias, although both reasoning models achieved better overall performance compared to their respective base model (OR 4.0 for Llama-3.3-70B, OR 3.6 for Qwen3-32B).

evidence.title: Beyond Accuracy: Multidimensional Evaluation of Large Language Models in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Management Emphasizing Prompting
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT-4o, Grok-3) compared against medical-domain LLMs, 10 models in total, on HCC questions
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated accuracy and local interpretability across HCC management stages
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4o and Grok-3 had the highest accuracy (2.62 ± 0.06, 93%; 2.60 ± 0.06, 95%) and interpretability (0.43; 0.43). General-purpose models outperformed some medical models.
evidence.quote: General-purpose models outperformed some medical models, revealing limitations in domain-specific fine-tuning.

evidence.title: Validating LLM judges for automated oversight of patient communication
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose LLM judges
evidence.outcome: Agreement with clinician ratings when used as judges
evidence.effect: Safety-specialized guard models underperformed general-purpose models (no numbers given in abstract)
evidence.quote: Safety-specialized guard models underperformed general-purpose models.

evidence.title: Large Language Models Generate Stigmatizing Language During Reasoning Over Real-World Clinical Data
evidence.comparator_used: Non-reasoning models (reasoning vs non-reasoning LLMs across 107 models)
evidence.outcome: Stigma rate in LLM-generated reasoning text
evidence.effect: Reasoning models 2.35% vs non-reasoning 1.70% stigma rate (p < 0.0001)
evidence.tradeoff: Reasoning-enhanced models produced more stigmatizing language, a new safety failure mode.
evidence.quote: Reasoning models showed higher stigma rates than non-reasoning models (2.35% vs. 1.70%; p < 0.0001), whereas medical models did not show significantly lower stigma rates than general-purpose models (1.80% vs. 2.00%; p = 0.26).

evidence.title: Simulating Clinical AI Assistance using Multimodal LLMs: A Case Study in Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose GPT-4o used zero-shot as the standard model, compared with the open-source medical model MedGemma on IDRiD and Messidor-2
evidence.outcome: Baseline diabetic retinopathy detection (sensitivity, AUROC, specificity)
evidence.effect: MedGemma had higher sensitivity and AUROC than GPT-4o. GPT-4o had near-perfect specificity but low sensitivity. The abstract gives no figures for this baseline comparison.
evidence.tradeoff: GPT-4o's near-perfect specificity came with low sensitivity. GPT-4o's performance also collapsed when given incorrect simulated AI inputs, while MedGemma stayed more stable.
evidence.quote: MedGemma outperformed GPT-4o at baseline, achieving higher sensitivity and AUROC, while GPT-4o showed near-perfect specificity but low sensitivity.

evidence.title: Clinician expertise and prompt engineering enhance cancer information extraction in electronic health records by small language models
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose small language models (e.g., LLaMA 3.1 8B) compared with biomedical models
evidence.outcome: Clinical information extraction performance from Italian EHRs, especially binary features
evidence.effect: General-purpose models outperformed biomedical models in most tasks, particularly binary features; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Multiclass variables (TNM staging, PD-L1, ECOG-PS) remained harder because of implicit language and lack of standardization
evidence.quote: We show that general-purpose models (e.g., LLaMA 3.1 8B) outperform biomedical models in most tasks, particularly in extracting binary features.

evidence.title: A Multimodal Large Language Model as an End-to-End Classifier of Thyroid Nodule Malignancy Risk: Usability Study
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose LLaVA (non-medical) model
evidence.outcome: Valid response rate
evidence.tradeoff: The medically fine-tuned variant produced many more invalid responses, which is a new failure mode.
evidence.quote: Overall, 88.4% (6110/6912) of responses were valid, with the o3 model producing the highest validity rate (2273/2304, 98.6%), followed by LLaVA (2108/2304, 91.5%) and LLaVA-Med (1729/2304, 75%; P<.001).

evidence.title: Can Large Language Models Reliably Extract Physiology Index Values from Coronary Angiography Reports?
evidence.comparator_used: Non-medical general-purpose LLMs
evidence.outcome: Extraction performance of physiology index values from CAG reports
evidence.effect: MedGemma showed similar results to non-medical models; MedLlama's results were out-of-format in the unconstrained setting and had significantly lower performance in the constrained one
evidence.tradeoff: MedLlama produced out-of-format outputs in the unconstrained setting
evidence.quote: While MedGemma demonstrated similar results to non-medical models, MedLlama's results were out-of-format in the unconstrained setting, and had a significant lower performance in the constrained one.

evidence.title: A Systematic Study of Retrieval Pipeline Design for Retrieval-Augmented Medical Question Answering
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose language models given the same retrieved evidence
evidence.outcome: Utilization of retrieved medical evidence in RAG medical QA
evidence.effect: Domain-specialized models better utilized retrieved medical evidence than general-purpose models (no numbers given in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Domain-specialized language models were also found to better utilize retrieved medical evidence than general-purpose models.

evidence.title: Domain Fine-Tuning vs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Multiple-Choice Question Answering: A Controlled Comparison at the 4B-Parameter Scale
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose Gemma 3 4B (4-bit quantized, via Ollama) vs. domain-adapted MedGemma 4B, same prompt, temperature and retrieval setup
evidence.outcome: Majority-vote accuracy on MedQA-USMLE 4-option test split (1,273 questions, 3 repetitions each)
evidence.effect: +6.8 pp majority-vote accuracy (53.3% vs. 46.4%, McNemar p < 10^-4)
evidence.quote: Domain fine-tuning yields a +6.8 percentage-point gain in majority-vote accuracy over the general 4B baseline (53.3% vs. 46.4%, McNemar p < 10^-4).

evidence.title: Performance of Large Language Models on the Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose models (ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek R1) without RAG, used zero-shot
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on 38 guideline-based ACS questions
evidence.effect: Med-PaLM 2 (medicine-specific) 68.4% vs DeepSeek R1 without RAG 78.9% and ChatGPT-4o without RAG 71.1%
evidence.quote: Med-PaLM 2 had the lowest accuracy (68.4%; 95% CI: 52.5%-80.9%).

evidence.title: Serialisation Strategy Matters: How FHIR Data Format Affects LLM Medication Reconciliation
evidence.comparator_used: Instruction-tuned general-purpose models (e.g., Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) used on the same task
evidence.outcome: Usable structured medication extraction output
evidence.effect: BioMistral-7B, a domain-pretrained model without instruction tuning, produced zero usable output in all conditions.
evidence.quote: BioMistral-7B, a domain-pretrained model without instruction tuning, produces zero usable output in all conditions, showing that domain pretraining alone is not sufficient for structured extraction.

evidence.title: Learning to Make Rare and Complex Diagnoses With Generative AI Assistance: Qualitative Study of Popular Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose LLMs (Bard, ChatGPT-3.5, GPT-4) compared against the medical-domain LLM MedAlpaca
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy on 30 diagnostic case challenge cases
evidence.effect: All general LLMs outperformed MedAlpaca by a minimum margin of 13% across all 30 cases. On the MIMIC-III multiple-choice prompts, Bard and GPT-4 scored 93%, ChatGPT-3.5 scored 73%, and MedAlpaca scored 47%.
evidence.quote: Notably, all LLMs outperformed the average human consensus and MedAlpaca, with a minimum margin of 5% and 13%, respectively, across all 30 cases from the diagnostic case challenge collection.

evidence.title: Evaluating Clinical Concept Extraction and Evidence-Bounded Terminology Linking: Multisite Model Comparison and Pilot Ablation Study
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose Gemma and other models (SciBERT, sci_md, Llama 3.3) for clinical concept extraction
evidence.outcome: Embedding-match F1 for concept extraction against human annotation in 66 notes
evidence.effect: MedGemma 0.55 vs Gemma 0.53, sci_md and SciBERT 0.43 each, Llama 3.3 0.32. Exact-match F1 for all automated pipelines ranged from 0.07 to 0.17.
evidence.quote: embedding-match F1 was highest for MedGemma (0.55), followed by Gemma (0.53)

evidence.title: Cross-Sensor and Cross-Population Generalization of Deep Learning Models for Digital Mammography: A Controlled Four-Country Benchmark of Five Backbone Architectures with Statistical Significance Testing
evidence.comparator_used: ResNet-50 (standard general-purpose backbone) and general-purpose DINOv2-B14, versus mammography/radiology-specific models (Rad-DINO, Mammo-CLIP B5, Mammo-FM)
evidence.outcome: AUC in-distribution (CBIS-DDSM) and at external transfer cohorts (CMMD, DMID, MIAS)
evidence.effect: In-distribution ResNet-50 AUC 0.867 vs 0.847, 0.846, 0.813, 0.703 for the four foundation models (all p_adj < 0.05). At transfer, Mammo-CLIP B5 and Mammo-FM significantly outperformed ResNet-50 on DMID and Mammo-CLIP on CMMD after BH-FDR; MIAS directional only. In the BI-RADS D4 subgroup, Mammo-FM AUC 0.870 vs ResNet-50 0.842 (CIs overlap, not statistically supported).
evidence.tradeoff: Every model lost 0.165 to 0.320 AUC points at transfer; sensitivity at 95% specificity fell from 0.31-0.47 to 0.11-0.22, so none was defensible for deployment without local validation.
evidence.quote: Within this single-source three-seed evaluation, ResNet-50 outperformed all four foundation models on CBIS-DDSM (AUC 0.867 vs. 0.847, 0.846, 0.813, and 0.703; all gaps p_adj < 0.05).

evidence.title: The Effect of Quantization on Clinical Benchmarks: Accuracy and Safety Across Model Families
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose 7-8B models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) compared with the clinically fine-tuned BioMistral-7B, at FP16 vs INT4 quantization
evidence.outcome: Accuracy retention on MedMCQA under INT4 quantization (compression robustness)
evidence.effect: BioMistral-7B (clinically fine-tuned) lost 19.7% on MedMCQA under INT4, more than any general-purpose model
evidence.tradeoff: Clinical fine-tuning gave no robustness to compression. The abstract also states that safety alignment is determined primarily by instruction tuning rather than clinical domain adaptation.
evidence.quote: BioMistral-7B, clinically fine-tuned, loses 19.7% on MedMCQA, more than any general-purpose model, showing clinical fine-tuning does not confer compression robustness.

evidence.title: MedMeta: A Benchmark for LLMs in Synthesizing Meta-Analysis Conclusion from Medical Studies
evidence.comparator_used: Standard general-purpose models (without domain-specific fine-tuning), in both Parametric-only and Golden-RAG settings
evidence.outcome: Quality of meta-analysis conclusions for domain-fine-tuned vs general models
evidence.effect: Benefits of domain-specific fine-tuning were marginal and largely neutralized when external material (RAG) was provided; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: In contrast, the benefits of domain-specific fine-tuning are marginal and largely neutralized when external material is provided.

evidence.title: When Medical Safety Alignment Fails: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on High-Risk Medical Queries
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose LLMs, without medical fine-tuning
evidence.outcome: Safety on high-risk medical queries, including harmful specificity of responses
evidence.effect: No numbers in the abstract; medical fine-tuning can amplify harmful specificity
evidence.tradeoff: Amplified harmful specificity in medically fine-tuned models
evidence.quote: Results reveal a substantial gap between apparent alignment and medical safety: aligned models can still produce unsafe or actionable responses, medical fine-tuning can amplify harmful specificity, and external guardrails reduce some failures while introducing brittle blocking and weak safe helpfulness.

evidence.title: Not One Size Fits All: The Selective Effect of Reasoning Processes for Multimodal Body Language Emotion Recognition in GAI
evidence.comparator_used: Generalist Gemini models (Pro 2.0, Pro 1.5, Flash 2.0)
evidence.outcome: Chance-corrected recognition (CCR) of emotion from body language
evidence.effect: FlashThinking CCR = 0.463, 95% CI [0.310, 0.621]. Gemini Pro 2.0, a generalist, reached CCR = 0.722, 95% CI [0.590, 0.838], and was on par with the human benchmark (0.717).
evidence.quote: The specialized reasoning model (FlashThinking) achieved a Chance-Corrected Recognition (CCR) score of 0.463, 95% CI [0.310, 0.621], failing to outperform generalist architectures.

evidence.title: Improving electronic health record processing of large language models via retrieval-augmented generation: A case study on dietary supplements
evidence.venue: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium
evidence.comparator_used: Smaller general-purpose models paired with optimized retrievers versus specialized (domain-specific) models
evidence.outcome: Dietary supplement information extraction performance across NLP tasks
evidence.effect: Smaller general models with optimized retrievers match or exceed specialized counterparts (no numeric values in the abstract)
evidence.quote: Smaller general models paired with optimized retrievers match or exceed specialized counterparts-structured retrieval aids complex tasks (e.g., triple extraction), while semantic retrieval improves classification.

evidence.title: Large-scale deep learning for metastasis detection in pathology reports
evidence.comparator_used: widely used general-purpose large language model
evidence.outcome: Recall for metastasis detection from pathology reports
evidence.effect: recall 0.894 for task-specific deep learning model vs 0.824 for general-purpose LLM
evidence.quote: Our deep learning architecture trained on task-specific data outperforms a general-purpose LLM, with a recall of 0.894 compared to 0.824.

evidence.title: Patient Cognitive Bias in Large Language Model-Supported Health Consultations: Simulation-Based Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Foundation conversational LLM performing both interaction and final diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy under biased consultations when a reasoning-oriented LLM (o1-mini) made the final diagnosis
evidence.effect: Gains of approximately 10 to 39 percentage points across most models
evidence.quote: By contrast, the dual-system framework substantially improved diagnostic accuracy under biased conditions, producing gains of approximately 10 to 39 percentage points across most models and recovering a large proportion of the performance lost due to bias, particularly in lower-capacity systems.

evidence.title: How DISCERNing is ChatGPT? An Evaluation of Models and Prompt Engineering in Assessing Patient Education Materials
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4o and GPT-5.2 general-purpose models
evidence.outcome: Agreement with human DISCERN scores and absolute error
evidence.effect: The o3 reasoning model consistently outperformed GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o, particularly with combined prompting. Numeric effect sizes are not given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Even o3 showed attenuation bias and poor repeatability, and was judged insufficient for reliable automated DISCERN scoring.
evidence.quote: Combined prompting modestly improved agreement and reduced absolute error, particularly for the o3 model, which consistently outperformed GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o.

evidence.title: From Attribution to Abstention: Training-Free Attention-Based Auditing for Clinical Summarization
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose MLLM (Qwen3-8B)
evidence.outcome: Reliability of attention-based hallucination detection
evidence.effect: Medical finetuning reported to substantially improve reliability of attention-based hallucination detection (0.77 AUROC reported for the medical-finetuned model); no numeric comparison given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Notably, medical finetuning substantially improves the reliability of attention-based hallucination detection, suggesting that domain adaptation produces more semantically structured attention patterns amenable to self-auditing.

evidence.title: LLM-based reconstruction of longitudinal clinical trajectories in chronic liver disease
evidence.comparator_used: General-purpose Llama models (Llama-3.3-70B and Llama-3.1-8B); the medically fine-tuned OpenBioLLM-70B and reasoning-model DeepSeek-R1-8B were the domain-specific variants
evidence.outcome: Accuracy across 70 information extraction tasks on the calibration set
evidence.effect: Llama-3.3-70B exceeded 90% accuracy on 59/70 tasks and outperformed OpenBioLLM-70B (medically fine-tuned) and DeepSeek-R1-8B; per-model figures not given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Llama-3.3-70B performed best, exceeding 90% accuracy on 59/70 tasks, outperforming Llama-3.1-8B (a smaller variant), OpenBioLLM-70B (a medically fine-tuned model), and DeepSeek-R1-8B.

controls.question: Should we add synthetic or model-generated data to training when real labeled data are scarce or imbalanced?
controls.control: Augment or pretrain with synthetic records, generated text, or simulated images, quality-filtered and mixed with real data.
controls.comparator: Training on available real data only
controls.aim: Improve performance and balance when real labeled data are scarce
variants: Quality filtering and real-synthetic mixing ratios
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment
tradeoffs: Synthetic data did not substitute for real data: zero-shot use of the synthetic-pretrained model performed worse, and the authors conclude synthetic data is a complement, not a substitute, for local clinical data.

evidence.title: Rural Medical Centers Struggle to Produce Well-Calibrated Clinical Prediction Models: Data Augmentation Can Help
evidence.comparator_used: Local real data only (local fine-tuning/recalibration at rural sites with limited patient volumes); other SDG approaches were also compared
evidence.outcome: Quality of local classifiers (prediction performance and calibration) at sites with small data volumes
evidence.effect: Deep learning approaches to SDG produced the best local classifiers; no numeric effect sizes reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Our results indicate that deep learning approaches to SDG produced the best local classifiers.

evidence.title: Evaluation of the Applicability of Synthetic Data in the Development of Colorectal Cancer Survival Prediction Models: External Validation of Advanced Machine Learning Models Based on National Cancer Data Center Data
evidence.comparator_used: Hospital-only baseline model trained on real hospital data only (vs. synthetic-pretrained zero-shot and domain-adapted models)
evidence.outcome: 7-year overall survival prediction, AUPRC and Brier score on held-out real hospital test set
evidence.effect: Domain adaptation (synthetic pretraining then local fine-tuning) improved AUPRC in 8/12 combinations, 4 statistically significant; best XGBoost+RUS+F1 AUPRC=0.5391 (Δ+0.1474; P<.001). Zero-shot use of the synthetic-pretrained model reduced AUPRC in most settings, with no significant gains elsewhere. Brier scores improved in most domain adaptation combinations.
evidence.tradeoff: Synthetic data did not substitute for real data: zero-shot use of the synthetic-pretrained model performed worse, and the authors conclude synthetic data is a complement, not a substitute, for local clinical data.
evidence.quote: In contrast, the domain adaptation model improved AUPRC in 8/12 combinations, with 4 statistically significant gains; the best setting (XGBoost+RUS+F1 optimization) achieved AUPRC=0.5391 (Δ+0.1474; P<.001).

evidence.title: Community medical centers struggle to produce well-calibrated clinical prediction models: Data augmentation can help
evidence.comparator_used: Recalibration using only available local real data (no synthetic augmentation), compared across several SDG methods
evidence.outcome: Calibration performance after local recalibration in smaller simulated hospitals
evidence.effect: Deep learning-based SDG was most effective at improving calibration performance; no numeric effect sizes given in the abstract
evidence.quote: In the simulation study, deep learning-based SDG was most effective at improving calibration performance.

controls.question: Should we lock the model's temperature and decoding settings low or deterministic for clinical use?
controls.control: Set decoding temperature to zero or a tuned low value and fix inference settings per clinical task.
controls.comparator: Default vendor temperature and sampling settings
controls.aim: Reduce output variability and hallucination in clinical tasks
variants: Fixed top-p and other sampling parameters
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment
tradeoffs: The improvement at T=1.0 was modest, and safety remained low at both settings.

evidence.title: Multi-model assurance analysis showing large language models are highly vulnerable to adversarial hallucination attacks during clinical decision support
evidence.comparator_used: Default vendor temperature and sampling settings across six LLMs, 300 vignettes
evidence.outcome: Rate of elaborating on fabricated clinical details (adversarial hallucination)
evidence.effect: Temperature 0 offered no significant improvement; overall hallucination rates ranged from 50% to 82% across models and prompting methods
evidence.quote: Temperature adjustments offer no significant improvement.

evidence.title: Assessment of Large Language Models in Colorectal Cancer Multidisciplinary Tumor Board Decision-Making: A Retrospective Single-Center Comparison of Guideline-Integrated General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specialized Models
evidence.comparator_used: MedGemma at temperature T = 1.0
evidence.outcome: Concordance with MTB decisions (kappa, accuracy) and safety rate
evidence.effect: T=0.0: κ = 0.566, accuracy 70.3%, safety 62.3%. T=1.0: κ = 0.610, accuracy 73.5%, safety 62.7%. Concordance improvement p = 0.038.
evidence.tradeoff: The improvement at T=1.0 was modest, and safety remained low at both settings.
evidence.quote: MedGemma showed moderate agreement at T = 0.0 (κ = 0.566; accuracy = 70.3%) and modest improvement at T = 1.0 (κ = 0.610; accuracy = 73.5%; p = 0.038), with lower safety rates (62.3% and 62.7%; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Large Language Models Are Highly Vulnerable to Adversarial Hallucination Attacks in Clinical Decision Support: A Multi-Model Assurance Analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Default vendor temperature and sampling settings
evidence.outcome: Rate of adversarial hallucination (elaboration on fabricated clinical detail)
evidence.effect: Temperature adjustments offered no significant improvement over default settings across six LLMs
evidence.quote: Temperature adjustments offered no significant improvement.

evidence.title: Drug or Pokémon? Large language model performance in identification of fabricated medications
evidence.comparator_used: Standard (default) decoding
evidence.outcome: Confabulation rate for fabricated medications
evidence.effect: Deterministic decoding (temperature = 0) did not substantially change confabulation rates; no specific numbers reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Deterministic decoding did not substantially impact confabulation rates.

evidence.title: Domain-Specific Knowledge Graphs in RAG-Enhanced Healthcare LLMs
evidence.comparator_used: Three decoding temperatures compared against each other (higher vs lower temperature)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy across decoding temperatures
evidence.effect: Temperature played a secondary role; higher values rarely helped. No numeric values reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Temperature plays a secondary role; higher values rarely help.

evidence.title: Dictionary-Augmented Large Language Model Postprocessing for Bilingual Code-Switched Medical Speech Recognition: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Different temperature settings (0.0-0.8) across six LLMs
evidence.outcome: Postprocessing performance (BERTScore, CER) across temperature settings
evidence.effect: All models had small temperature-related effect sizes (all |Cohen dz| ≤0.15); GPT-4o showed the largest dependency, with significant improvement at temperature 0.6 (Holm-adjusted P<.001 for BERTScore and CER); the 4 Claude variants and GPT-4.1 performed practically consistently across all settings.
evidence.quote: Temperature optimization showed that all postprocessing models had small temperature-related effect sizes (all |Cohen dz| ≤0.15), with GPT-4o exhibiting the largest dependency and statistically significant improvement at temperature 0.6 (Holm-adjusted P<.001 for both BERTScore and CER) and the 4 Claude variants and GPT-4.1 exhibiting practically consistent performance across all settings.

evidence.title: Rapidly Benchmarking Large Language Models for Diagnosing Comorbid Patients: Comparative Study Leveraging the LLM-as-a-Judge Method
evidence.comparator_used: The other of the 2 tested temperature settings
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic hit rate across LLMs
evidence.effect: Changes in temperature generally had little effect; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Significant variation in diagnostic hit rates was observed across different prompts, while changes in temperature generally had little effect.

evidence.title: The Impact of the Temperature on Extracting Information From Clinical Trial Publications Using Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Other temperature settings across nine levels (0.00 to 2.00) for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, with no vendor default arm reported
evidence.outcome: Correctly formatted predictions and other performance metrics for extracting the number of randomized participants and classifying abstracts as RCT and/or oncology-related
evidence.effect: Both models gave correctly formatted predictions for more than 98.7% of abstracts at temperatures 0.00 to 1.50. Formatted predictions then declined, with the most notable drop between 1.75 and 2.00. Other performance metrics remained largely stable.
evidence.quote: Temperature settings at or below 1.50 yielded consistent performance across text mining tasks, with performance declines at higher settings.

evidence.title: Case-matched retrieval improves textual alignment of LLM-generated radiology impressions
evidence.comparator_used: higher decoding temperatures (0.7 and 1)
evidence.outcome: Textual similarity of generated impressions to reference impressions (ROUGE, BERTScore F1)
evidence.effect: The highest scores were at temperature 0 (with k = 10); lower temperature was associated with higher similarity scores.
evidence.quote: The highest scores were observed at temperature 0 and k = 10.

controls.aim: Reduce unsafe, harmful, or rule-violating clinical outputs

controls.question: Should we adopt deep learning image reconstruction to enable lower-dose or faster imaging protocols?
controls.control: Use deep learning reconstruction, denoising, or synthesis to run lower-dose or shorter acquisition protocols.
controls.comparator: Current standard-dose or standard-duration protocol with conventional reconstruction
controls.aim: Reduce radiation dose and scan time while preserving diagnostic image quality
variants: Reconstruction-only comparison at matched acquisition settings

controls.aim: Improve accuracy, reliability, and efficiency on defined subtasks

Peak LLM performance was still slightly lower than the pure ML model on AUC and AUPRC.
The evidence gate converted some correct raw judgments into incomplete decision-basis entries

evidence.title: Automating standardization of prostate cancer biopsy and histopathology reports with privacy-preserving local large language models
evidence.comparator_used: Single-stage prompt with the LLM alone on procedure reports
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of structured data extraction from ultrasound-guided biopsy procedure reports versus human-extracted data
evidence.effect: Multistage mixed LLM-NLP pipeline 98.0% (1314/1341) vs single-stage 95.3% (991/1040 discrete data points)
evidence.quote: The multistage LLM-NLP pipeline reached 98.0% accuracy (1314/1341) for ultrasound procedure reports.

evidence.title: Large language models approach clinician performance in ESC cardiovascular risk stratification: a vignette-based benchmark study
evidence.comparator_used: Single end-to-end LLM performing extraction, SCORE2 calculation and risk classification (post hoc deterministic SCORE2 recalculation applied to model-extracted variables)
evidence.outcome: Agreement (quadratic-weighted kappa) with expert-assigned final ESC risk category
evidence.effect: End-to-end best model GPT-4o κw 0.69 (95% CI 0.44-0.84); with deterministic recalculation using model-extracted variables, κw 0.85-0.90 across all models
evidence.quote: this markedly improved agreement across all models (κw 0.85-0.90), demonstrating that extraction was largely intact and computational execution was the primary failure mode.

evidence.title: Reducing Under-Triage Risk in Large Language Model Based Clinical Triage Using UMLS-CUI Augmentation
evidence.comparator_used: Each LLM (GPT-4o-mini, MedGemma 27B) used alone without UMLS CUI augmentation. The CUIs came from a ClinicalBERT NER and rule-based lab-abnormality extraction pipeline.
evidence.outcome: Under-triage, over-triage, overall accuracy, emergency-case accuracy and sensitivity to anchoring statements
evidence.effect: Emergency-case accuracy rose from 73.0% to 80.7% for GPT-4o-mini and from 60.5% to 68.5% for MedGemma 27B. Under-triage decreased in both models. Overall accuracy increased for MedGemma 27B but decreased for GPT-4o-mini. Susceptibility to anchoring statements was reduced.
evidence.tradeoff: Over-triage increased in both models. Recognition of low-acuity cases fell. Overall accuracy decreased for GPT-4o-mini.
evidence.quote: CUI augmentation decreased under-triage but increased over-triage in both models tested (GPT-4o-mini and MedGemma 27B).

evidence.title: Improving Health Literacy through Lay Summarization of Radiological Reports: An Evaluation of BioNER and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence.comparator_used: Standard LLM-based generation without NER-based entity extraction
evidence.outcome: Readability and overall quality of lay summaries
evidence.effect: NER consistently improved readability and overall quality; fine-tuned BioBART with NER achieved the best overall performance (no numbers in the abstract).
evidence.quote: Results show that NER consistently improves readability and overall quality, while RAG alone offers no benefit and can introduce hallucinations from irrelevant retrieved terms.

evidence.title: Evaluating the accuracy of a state-of-the-art large language model for prediction of admissions from the emergency room
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Naive GPT-4 alone, without ML numerical probabilities
evidence.outcome: Prediction of ED admission (AUC, AUPRC, accuracy)
evidence.effect: Naive GPT-4: 0.79 AUC, 0.48 AUPRC, 77.5% accuracy. With RAG and ML probabilities: 0.87 AUC, 0.71 AUPRC, 83.1% accuracy. The pure Ensemble ML model reached 0.88 AUC, 0.72 AUPRC, 82.9% accuracy.
evidence.tradeoff: Peak LLM performance was still slightly lower than the pure ML model on AUC and AUPRC.
evidence.quote: The naïve GPT-4's performance (0.79 AUC, 0.48 AUPRC, and 77.5% accuracy) showed substantial improvement when given limited, relevant data to learn from (ie, RAG) and underlying ML probabilities (0.87 AUC, 0.71 AUPRC, and 83.1% accuracy).

evidence.title: A decision-basis contract for auditable LLM-assisted medical billing verification: deterministic rules, verbatim evidence, and fail-closed abstention
evidence.comparator_used: End-to-end baseline (single model performing the whole verification) versus the decision-basis contract with deterministic rule checks plus LLM documentation assessment
evidence.outcome: Outcome agreement on 36 curated billing cases across four open-weight models
evidence.effect: Outcome agreement varied across models and showed no consistent advantage over the baseline; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: The evidence gate converted some correct raw judgments into incomplete decision-basis entries
evidence.quote: Outcome agreement varied across models and showed no consistent advantage over the baseline.

controls.question: Should we invest in systematic curation and informed selection of training cases rather than using available or randomly chosen data?
controls.control: Audit label consistency, handle label noise, deduplicate, enrich clinically important cases, and select cases for expert annotation by model uncertainty.
controls.comparator: Available or randomly selected data with only basic cleaning, same labeling budget
controls.aim: Improve accuracy and robustness per unit of annotation effort by reducing noise and redundancy
variants: Active learning by uncertainty or informativeness
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment

evidence.title: Evaluating real-world deployment of an HL7-CDA-aligned LLM for ICD-10-CM coding
evidence.comparator_used: BioMistral trained on the full, non-deduplicated dataset (DischgDiag only)
evidence.outcome: Coding precision, recall and F-score, and training time
evidence.effect: Deduplicated model outperformed the baseline on precision, recall and F1 and cut training time by 10.2%. Full-code F rose from 0.780 to 0.786 on the internal test set, from 0.754 to 0.764 on the KMUH RCT data, and from 0.620 to 0.626 on TMMH.
evidence.quote: As shown in Fig. 5 , the deduplicated model consistently outperformed the baseline across precision, recall, and F 1 -scores, and reduced total training time by 10.2%.

evidence.title: Scalable Stewardship of an LLM-Assisted Clinical Benchmark with Physician Oversight
evidence.comparator_used: Original MedCalc-Bench labels (partly LLM-derived), used without the physician-in-the-loop audit and relabeling
evidence.outcome: Agreement with physician ground truth, and downstream accuracy of a model trained with RL on the labels, on physician-labeled instances
evidence.effect: Recomputed labels agreed with physician ground truth 74% of the time (95% CI 60-84%) versus 20% for the originals (95% CI 11-33%) on a 50-instance subset. The model trained on recomputed labels outperformed the one trained on originals by 13.5 percentage points (95% CI 10.6-16.6%). At least 27% of test labels were likely erroneous or incomputable. Evaluating frontier LLMs with the original labels underestimated their accuracy by 16-23 percentage points.
evidence.quote: In a controlled reinforcement-learning experiment, a model trained on recomputed labels outperforms one trained on originals by 13.5 percentage points (95% CI, 10.6-16.6%) on physician-labeled instances, and this advantage extends to related medical tasks.

controls.question: Should we let clinicians build their own models with no-code AutoML platforms?
controls.control: Provide code-free AutoML platforms so clinicians can label data and train task-specific models.
controls.comparator: Data-scientist-led conventional development for the same clinical task
controls.aim: Enable faster, lower-cost development of task-specific models by clinicians
controls.family_label: fine-tuning, domain-specific versus general models, model size, open versus closed, local deployment

controls.question: Should we use an LLM to rewrite existing patient materials, clinical reports and research summaries into plain language for patients?
controls.control: Use an LLM to rewrite existing patient education, discharge summaries, radiology or pathology reports, and research abstracts into plain-language versions for patients.
controls.comparator: Original, unsimplified clinical or research documents
controls.aim: Improve patient understanding of existing clinical and research documents without losing accuracy
variants: Share alongside the original rather than instead of it
Rewrite society-vetted materials instead of generating new content
Lay summaries of research abstracts and trial registry entries
controls.family_label: native-language processing, translation or back-translation, simplification, reading-level control
tradeoffs: Minimal hallucination rate of 1.7% in LLM-simplified reports; no hallucinations resulted in potential patient harm; all reports at least somewhat accurate

evidence.title: Patient-centric radiology: Utilising large language models (LLMs) to improve patient communication and education
evidence.comparator_used: Formal radiology report only (original, unsimplified)
evidence.outcome: Patient comprehension and report readability
evidence.effect: Reading level fell from university standard (11th-13th grade) to middle-school (5th-9th grade) (rank biserial correlation=0.83, p<0.001); 95% of patients with both reports reported understanding >50% vs 46% without the simplified report (rank biserial correlation=0.67, p<0.001)
evidence.tradeoff: Minimal hallucination rate of 1.7% in LLM-simplified reports; no hallucinations resulted in potential patient harm; all reports at least somewhat accurate
evidence.quote: Patients with both reports demonstrated a significantly greater comprehension level, with 95% reporting an understanding level greater than 50%, compared with 46% without the simplified report (rank biserial correlation = 0.67, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Provision of Radiology Reports Simplified With Large Language Models to Patients With Cancer: Impact on Patient Satisfaction
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified CT report impressions given to patients
evidence.outcome: Patient knowledge of primary site and disease extent, and confidence and understanding of the report
evidence.effect: Simplified report group had significantly better knowledge of primary site and extent of disease and significantly higher confidence and understanding (P < .05 for all); 100 patients randomized to two groups
evidence.tradeoff: Radiologist supervision was needed; 3 of 50 simplified reports required corrections by the radiologist.
evidence.quote: In phase II, simplified report group patients demonstrated significantly better knowledge of primary site and extent of their disease as well as showed significantly higher confidence and understanding of the report (P < .05 for all).

evidence.title: GPT-4 Enhances Readability of Online Patient Materials for Cardiac Amyloidosis
evidence.comparator_used: Original institutional patient education materials (unsimplified)
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level), accuracy and comprehensiveness of PEMs for cardiac amyloidosis
evidence.effect: Median FKGL 10.9 (IQR 9.2, 12.6) for institutional PEMs vs 7.8 (IQR 7.0, 8.8) for GPT-4 revised PEMs; 14/86 (16.3%) of revised PEMs reached at least 6th-grade level; 86/86 (100%) accurate; 9/86 (10.5%) more comprehensive, 3/86 (3.5%) less comprehensive
evidence.tradeoff: Most revised PEMs (72/86) still did not reach the 6th-grade target; 3/86 (3.5%) were judged less comprehensive than the originals.
evidence.quote: In comparison, GPT-4 revised PEMs reduced the median FKGL to 7.8 (seventh grade; IQR: 7.0, 8.8, p<0.001), with 14/86 (16.3%) achieving at least a 6th-grade reading level.

evidence.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence to Increase the Readability of Patient Education Materials in Pediatric Otolaryngology
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified AAO-HNS and children's hospital patient education materials
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of pediatric otolaryngology patient education materials
evidence.effect: AAO-HNS materials: 10.71 ± 0.71 to 7.9 ± 1.18 after ChatGPT (P < .01). Combined AAO-HNS and institutional materials: 9.32 ± 1.82 to 7.68 ± 1.12 (P = .0598).
evidence.tradeoff: ChatGPT did not reduce all materials below the recommended reading level; average output stayed around grade 7.7-7.9 despite a fifth-grade target. The reduction for the combined set was not statistically significant.
evidence.quote: After requesting the reduction of those materials to a fifth-grade reading level, ChatGPT converted the same materials to an average grade level of 7.9 ± 1.18 (P < .01).

evidence.title: Generating colloquial radiology reports with large language models
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified radiology reports
evidence.outcome: Readability measured by standard readability indices
evidence.effect: Translations were more readable than the original reports; no numeric index values given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy and readability traded off across reading levels; the eighth-grade level was judged the best balance
evidence.quote: Overall, translations were more readable than the original reports, as evaluated using standard readability indices.

evidence.title: Enhancing Health Literacy in Endourology: Using Artificial Intelligence to Improve Readability of Patient Education Materials
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unmodified AUA endourology patient education materials (21 documents)
evidence.outcome: Readability grade level and reading ease across six indices (FKGL, SMOG, GFI, CLI, ARI, FRE)
evidence.effect: Original PEMs were at about the 9th to 11th grade level; ChatGPT-4o-modified versions were at the 4th to 6th grade level (p < 0.001 for all comparisons). Variability across readability scores was also reduced.
evidence.quote: Unmodified PEMs were written at approximately the ninth to 11<sup>th</sup> grade level, whereas AI-modified versions were reduced to the fourth to sixth grade range (p < 0.001 for all comparisons).

evidence.title: Enhancing Readability of Surgical Patient Education Resources Using ChatGPT
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified online surgical patient education materials
evidence.outcome: Readability (SMOG index; also Coleman-Liau, Flesch-Kincaid, word count) of surgical patient education materials
evidence.effect: Mean SMOG decreased from 12.1 to 10.5 (P < 10^-9); Coleman-Liau -0.8 (P < 10^-5); Flesch-Kincaid -1.6 (P < 10^-8); word count reduced 55% on average (plastic surgery 66%, P = 0.008); accuracy maintained in all specialties
evidence.tradeoff: Key content such as risks and benefits was often omitted; the sixth-grade target was not reached (mean SMOG still 10.5)
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4o simplification significantly decreased mean Simple Measure of Gobbledygook score from 12.1 to 10.5 (P < 10-9), with similar reductions in Coleman-Liau index (-0.8, P < 10-5) and Flesch-Kincaid (-1.6, P < 10-8).

evidence.title: Online patient information on elective orthognathic surgery provided by UK National Health Services hospitals: assessment of readability and improvement using large language models
evidence.venue: The British journal of oral & maxillofacial surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified NHS orthognathic surgery patient information leaflets
evidence.outcome: Readability scores (FRES, FKGL, GFI, CLI, SMOG) against NHS standards
evidence.effect: All three LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) significantly improved readability on all five indices (p < 0.001). Original PILs met the standard only on FKGL (6.23 ± 1.26). Gemini performed best and met targets on 3/5 indices (FRES 80.35 ± 4.31, FKGL 4.73 ± 0.79, CLI 6.77 ± 0.59). No model met all NHS standards.
evidence.quote: Following revision, all three LLMs significantly improved readability across all indices (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Utility and Limitations of Large Language Models to Simplify Online Content on Generalized Pustular Psoriasis
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified online health information on generalized pustular psoriasis (top 20 search results)
evidence.outcome: Readability indices and enhanced DISCERN reliability/quality scores after LLM rewording to a sixth-grade level (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Gemini)
evidence.effect: All LLMs significantly changed readability scores (p<0.01), reported as improved readability. All LLMs also scored lower on DISCERN than the original text (p<0.01).
evidence.tradeoff: The simplified texts lost reliability and quality relative to the original content, as measured by lower enhanced DISCERN scores.
evidence.quote: While LLMs improved readability, they did not preserve the original content's reliability and quality.

evidence.title: Simplifying cardiology research abstracts: assessing ChatGPT’s readability and comprehensibility for non-medical audiences
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified Circulation cardiology research abstracts
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKGL, FKRE), word and character counts, and physician and layperson ratings of understandability
evidence.effect: Word and character counts fell significantly (p<0.0001). Readability improved from a college graduate level to an 8th-9th grade level (p<0.001), even though the target was 5th grade. Physicians and laypeople both found the simplified abstracts easier to understand (113 abstracts).
evidence.tradeoff: Some laypeople were concerned about oversimplification and missing details. The authors say further refinement is needed to ensure accuracy.
evidence.quote: The simplification significantly reduced word and character counts (p<0.0001) and improved readability from a college graduate level to an 8th-9th grade level (p<0.001).

evidence.title: Training a Bilingual Artificial Intelligence Model on Pediatric Orthopaedic Resources to Enhance the Readability of Patient Education Materials
evidence.venue: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified AAOS OrthoInfo pediatric orthopaedic patient education materials
evidence.outcome: Readability of patient education materials (grade level, Flesch Reading Ease, Fernández Huerta), with clinical accuracy reviewed on 10 English PEMs
evidence.effect: English mean grade level 9.8 to 5.8 (P < .001); Flesch Reading Ease 56.9 to 76.4 (P < .001). Spanish Fernández Huerta 81.0 to 100.7 (P < .001), grade level from fifth-sixth to fourth. All 10 reviewed English PEMs judged clinically accurate.
evidence.quote: The AI models significantly improved readability across all measures.

evidence.title: Large language model based simplification of ophthalmological clinical and ancillary results for patient readability
evidence.venue: International journal of retina and vitreous
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified ophthalmological fundus and ocular ultrasound reports
evidence.outcome: Readability (average Readability Grade Level, aRGL) of simplified vs original reports
evidence.effect: Original reports had a median aRGL of 13.8 overall, 11.6 for fundus reports and 15.4 for ocular ultrasound reports. All four LLMs improved readability to varying degrees, and Copilot, Gemini and GPT-4.0 reached median aRGL values closest to the recommended patient-facing level. Specific post-simplification values were not given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: After adjudication, 91% of simplified texts were factually accurate, 86% retained all critical information and 95% showed no potential for harm. So about 9% were not accurate, 14% omitted some critical information and 5% had potential for harm. GPT-3.5 performed weaker in some comparisons.
evidence.quote: All LLMs improved readability scores to varying degrees.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence Shows Limited Success in Improving Readability Levels of Spanish-language Orthopaedic Patient Education Materials
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified AAOS Spanish-language orthopaedic patient education materials
evidence.outcome: Readability (Fernández-Huerta and SOL grade levels) of AI-adapted vs original materials, plus surgeon-rated accuracy and usefulness
evidence.effect: Materials at a seventh- to eighth-grade level rose from 32% (25 of 77) originally to 53% (41 of 77) after a single AI simplification attempt (p < 0.001). Only 23% (18) and 16% (12) of adaptations reached the recommended sixth-grade level or below by Fernández-Huerta and SOL respectively. None of the originals met the sixth-grade target. 52% (40) of adaptations were rated accurate and 56% (43) useful.
evidence.tradeoff: Many adaptations were judged inaccurate (about 48%) or not useful (about 44%) by the orthopaedic surgeon reviewers. Adaptations rated accurate or useful had higher median word counts, so shorter outputs were more likely to be inaccurate or not useful.
evidence.quote: In comparison, after a single attempt at simplification, AI-adapted materials achieved this reading level in 53% of cases (41 of 77; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Use of ChatGPT to Accurately Simplify Patient-centered Information about Breast Cancer Prevention and Screening
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified responses to breast cancer prevention and screening questions
evidence.outcome: Reading ease and readability (Flesch Reading Ease, grade level) and word count of patient-facing responses
evidence.effect: Mean reading ease 46 original vs 70 simplified (P<.001); readability grade 13 vs 8.9 (P<.001); word count 193 vs 173 (P<.001); all 25 (100%) simplified responses met adequate reading ease vs 2 of 25 original (P<.001); only 2 of 25 (8%) simplified responses met sixth-grade readability
evidence.tradeoff: 2 of 25 simplified responses (8%) were not clinically appropriate (92% appropriate); potential to produce incorrect information necessitates physician oversight; most simplified responses still missed the sixth-grade target
evidence.quote: ChatGPT improved mean reading ease (original responses, 46 vs simplified responses, 70; P < .001) and readability (original, grade 13 vs simplified, grade 8.9; P < .001) and decreased word count (original, 193 vs simplified, 173; P < .001).

evidence.title: Large language models: a new frontier in paediatric cataract patient education
evidence.comparator_used: Original existing paediatric cataract patient education materials (before LLM rewriting)
evidence.outcome: Readability of existing PEMs after LLM rewriting to a sixth-grade level (SMOG)
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4 consistently rewrote materials to or below the specified sixth-grade reading level (SMOG: 5.14±0.3); all LLM responses had high quality (DISCERN ≥4), understandability (≥70%) and accuracy (Likert=1)
evidence.tradeoff: All LLM-generated responses were not actionable (<70%)
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4 generated more readable responses (lower SMOG and FKGL scores; 5.59±0.5 and 4.31±0.7, respectively) than the other two LLMs (p<0.001) and consistently rewrote them to or below the specified sixth-grade reading level (SMOG: 5.14±0.3).

evidence.title: The role of large language models in improving the readability of orthopaedic spine patient educational material
evidence.venue: Journal of orthopaedic surgery and research
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified AAOS OrthoInfo spine articles (baseline readability)
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and Flesch Reading Ease) of LLM-simplified text versus original articles
evidence.effect: Baseline mean FKGL 9.5 and Reading Ease 51.1, above the AMA sixth-grade recommendation. LLM summaries gave statistically significant readability improvement, largest at the first iteration. The three LLMs performed similarly, though ChatGPT showed significantly greater Reading Ease gains. Specific post-simplification scores are not given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: No accuracy cost reported: accuracy stayed stable across iterations with no evidence of hallucination. Gemini included disclaimers most consistently.
evidence.quote: LLM summaries provided statistically significant improvement in readability, with the greatest improvements in the first iteration.

evidence.title: Using GPT-4 to Automate the Generation of Lay Summaries for Cancer Publications
evidence.comparator_used: No comparison with the original unsimplified abstracts or papers; the study evaluated the LLM summaries on their own
evidence.outcome: Human-rated clarity and accuracy of LLM lay summaries of cancer research, and patient partners' view of their usefulness
evidence.effect: Summaries rated around 7 out of 10 by 18 volunteers; all patient partners said the summaries would help them decide whether to join research studies
evidence.tradeoff: Patient partners emphasized the need for summaries to be accurate and reliable; mean accuracy was about 7 out of 10.
evidence.quote: They were rated at around 7 out of 10 points.

evidence.title: Ability of Large Language Models to Answer Patients' Questions and Generate Educational Materials for Uncommon Retinal Conditions
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified LLM-generated patient education materials (before revision)
evidence.outcome: Reading grade level of patient education materials; accuracy preserved
evidence.effect: Reading levels reduced by 4.8 (ChatGPT), 6.9 (Gemini), and 3.8 (Copilot) grade levels (P < .001) without compromising accuracy
evidence.quote: When instructed to revise educational materials to improve understandability, all large language models significantly reduced reading levels by 4.8 (ChatGPT), 6.9 (Gemini), and 3.8 (Copilot) grade levels (P < .001) without compromising accuracy.

evidence.title: Large Language Models: Pioneering New Educational Frontiers in Childhood Myopia
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified online patient education materials on childhood myopia
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKGL, SMOG) of rewritten existing PEMs
evidence.effect: Prompt C improved readability across all LLMs; ChatGPT-4o (o1 Preview) showed the largest gains (FKGL 5.8 ± 1.5; p < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Prompt C improved readability across all LLMs, with ChatGPT-4o (o1 Preview) showing the most significant gains (FKGL 5.8 ± 1.5; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Enhancing readability and understandability of vascular surgery discharge summaries using artificial intelligence
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified vascular surgery discharge summaries
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and Flesch Reading Ease Score) of discharge summaries
evidence.effect: 39.6% reduction in Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and 106.37% increase in Ease Score; mean PEMAT-P understandability 77.71, actionability 52.12; accuracy mean 5.21 (6-point scale), completeness mean 2.61 (3-point scale)
evidence.tradeoff: 10.8% of summaries had omissions and 7.5% had hallucinations, with corrections made in some cases; actionability was only moderate (52.12).
evidence.quote: AI-generated summaries demonstrated significant improvements in readability, with a 39.6% reduction in Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and a 106.37% increase in Ease Score.

evidence.title: Optimizing Readability of Patient-Facing Hand Surgery Education Materials Using Chat Generative Pretrained Transformer (ChatGPT) 3.5
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified patient-facing hand surgery education excerpts
evidence.outcome: Readability (reading grade level) of simplified vs original excerpts
evidence.effect: Simplified excerpts' scores were lower than the originals, with a mean of 7.28, less than the maximum recommended 8
evidence.quote: The simplified excerpts' scores were lower than the originals, with a mean of 7.28, less than the maximum recommended 8.

evidence.title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
evidence.comparator_used: Original, unsimplified radiology reports (320 reports rated by 16 non-medical participants)
evidence.outcome: Layperson comprehension (5-point Likert) of LLM plain-language reports versus original reports
evidence.effect: Mean comprehension: original 4.32 ± 0.80; ChatGPT-4.0 4.55 ± 0.68; Grok-3 4.69 ± 0.56; DeepSeek-R1 4.80 ± 0.49. Effect sizes: DeepSeek-R1 r = 0.81, Grok-3 r = 0.74, ChatGPT-4.0 r = 0.49. All adjusted P < 0.05.
evidence.tradeoff: Radiologists found omissions and inaccuracies in the LLM versions. Omissions per report: ChatGPT 0.072, Grok 0.047, DeepSeek 0.093. Inaccuracies per report: ChatGPT 0.038, Grok 0.069, DeepSeek 0.05. Some anatomical location details were lost. Outputs were inconsistent across repeated runs. Musculoskeletal reports benefited less.
evidence.quote: Compared to the original reports, all LLM-generated versions demonstrated statistically significant improvements in comprehension (all adjusted P < 0.05 after Bonferroni correction), as illustrated in Fig. 1 .
