evidence.tradeoff: Even with patient-friendly prompting, responses stayed above the recommended reading level for patient information.
evidence.quote: Responses from patient-friendly prompting had a lower mean grade level (12.45 ± 2.32) than no prompting (14.15 ± 1.59), physician-level prompting (14.27 ± 2.09), and statistics/references prompting (15.00 ± 2.26) (P < .0001).

evidence.title: Comparison of AI chatbot-generated and web-based health information on the effects of radiation in fetuses and children
evidence.comparator_used: Standard reading-level prompt with no grade-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Understandability (share of texts with PEMAT-P score ≥70)
evidence.effect: At standard level, 46.7% of ChatGPT-4o texts and 78.6% of Gemini texts achieved PEMAT-P ≥70; at the 6th-grade level, all AI-generated texts exceeded this threshold.
evidence.tradeoff: Both AI and web content lacked sufficient actionable elements and visual support. Accuracy and reliability of the AI text were not assessed. Copilot showed limitations in coherence and clarity.
evidence.quote: At the 6th-grade level, all AI-generated texts exceeded this threshold.

evidence.title: Readability of custom chatbot vs. GPT-4 responses to otolaryngology-related patient questions
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4 default responses to the same 33 otolaryngology questions, with no plain-language customization
evidence.outcome: Readability of answers (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and Flesch Reading Ease)
evidence.effect: FKGL reduced by an average of 4.2 grade levels (95% CI 3.2, 5.1; p<0.001); FRE increased by an average of 17.3 points (95% CI 12.5, 21.7; p<0.001); improvements significant in three of four theme subgroups
evidence.quote: The custom GPT reduced FKGL by an average of 4.2 grade levels (95 % confidence interval [CI]: 3.2, 5.1; p < 0.001) and increased FRE by an average of 17.3 points (95 % CI: 12.5, 21.7; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Enhancing Readability of Surgical Patient Education Resources Using ChatGPT
evidence.comparator_used: Original unsimplified materials (no prompt-free LLM arm was compared)
evidence.outcome: Readability after prompting ChatGPT-4o to simplify to sixth-grade level
evidence.effect: Mean SMOG 12.1 to 10.5 (P < 10^-9); Flesch-Kincaid -1.6; Coleman-Liau -0.8; sixth-grade target not achieved
evidence.tradeoff: Key content such as risks and benefits was often omitted; achieving the sixth grade level may be challenging due to inherent complexity of medical information
evidence.quote: Achieving the recommended sixth grade reading level may be challenging due to the inherent complexity of medical information.

evidence.title: Enhancing Patient Education with AI: A Readability Analysis of AI-Generated Versus American Academy of Ophthalmology Online Patient Education Materials
evidence.comparator_used: Initial default prompt to generate PEMs with no reading-level instruction, versus a follow-up readability-optimized prompt asking for a 6th-grade reading level
evidence.outcome: Readability of LLM-generated patient education materials (grade level)
evidence.effect: Initial vs FRO grade level: ChatGPT 10.8 to 8.3, Copilot 12.2 to 11.2, Llama 13.2 to 9.3 (p < 0.001). AI PEMs were not statistically easier to read than AAO PEMs (8.0 Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level).
evidence.tradeoff: Most outputs stayed above the recommended 6th-grade level. A subjective review of one subtopic found AI content had less nuance than AAO, especially in areas of clinical uncertainty.
evidence.quote: While initially prompted ChatGPT, Copilot, and Llama outputs were 10.8, 12.2, and 13.2, respectively, FRO prompting significantly improved readability to 8.3 for ChatGPT, 11.2 for Copilot, and 9.3 for Llama (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: ChatGPT and low back pain - Evaluating AI-driven patient education in the context of interventional pain medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Neutral and reference/college-level wording of the same low back pain questions, with no reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Clinical accuracy and completeness of ChatGPT answers, plus Flesch-Kincaid readability
evidence.effect: Prompt wording influenced accuracy significantly. Over-simplified (4th grade) prompts degraded clinical completeness, while neutral and reference prompts preserved accuracy. No numeric values are given in the abstract. Readability stayed misaligned with health literacy standards whatever the prompt.
evidence.tradeoff: Simplified prompts produced clinically incomplete answers, and most errors were omissions rather than commissions. Outputs still trended technical, and word count was not a reliable proxy for completeness.
evidence.quote: Over-simplification of queries (e.g. to a 4th grade level) degrades ChatGPT's ability to return clinically complete responses.

evidence.title: Plain-language prompting improves readability of ChatGPT-generated patient education for meniscal surgery without loss of accuracy
evidence.venue: Journal of ISAKOS : joint disorders & orthopaedic sports medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline default ChatGPT responses with no reading-level instruction (pre-prompt vs post plain-language prompt targeting 6th-8th grade level)
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKGL and FRES) of ChatGPT-generated meniscal surgery patient education
evidence.effect: Baseline FKGL 11.4-12.1 and FRES 37-40; plain-language prompt reduced FKGL by approximately 5 grade levels and increased FRES by 30-38 points (P < 0.001), with no loss of accuracy, relevance, or depth
evidence.quote: The plain-language prompt significantly improved readability for both models, reducing FKGL by approximately 5 grade levels and increasing FRES by 30-38 points (P < 0.001), with no loss of accuracy, relevance, or depth.

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Generate Retina Patient Education Material: A Comparative Analysis With American Society of Retina Specialists Patient Brochures
evidence.comparator_used: General prompt with no readability instruction (prompt A); results were also reported relative to ASRS brochures
evidence.outcome: Readability of LLM-generated retina patient education materials
evidence.effect: Prompt B (sixth-grade target) significantly improved readability across all LLMs relative to ASRS brochures (mean ASRS grade level 14.17), but outputs still exceeded the sixth-grade level. The abstract gives no direct prompt A vs prompt B numbers.
evidence.tradeoff: Outputs still missed the sixth-grade target. The abstract reports no significant differences in misinformation or actionability, and the authors say expert oversight remains essential.
evidence.quote: Prompt B significantly improved readability across all large language models relative to ASRS but still exceeded the sixth-grade readability level.

evidence.title: Large language model based simplification of ophthalmological clinical and ancillary results for patient readability
evidence.venue: International journal of retina and vitreous
evidence.comparator_used: Basic command prompt and patient-oriented prompt without a specified grade level
evidence.outcome: Readability (aRGL) of LLM-simplified reports by prompt type
evidence.effect: The targeted 7th-grade reading level prompt gave the best readability results across the four models. Numeric differences between prompts were not reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Prompt engineering was a major determinant of performance, and the targeted 7th-grade prompt produced the best results across models.

evidence.title: Optimizing Ophthalmology Patient Education via ChatBot-Generated Materials: Readability Analysis of AI-Generated Patient Education Materials and The American Society of Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Patient Brochures
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no reading-level instruction (unprompted ChatGPT 4.0 and Bard output)
evidence.outcome: Readability of AI-generated patient education materials (Flesch Reading Ease, SMOG and other readability indices)
evidence.effect: Unprompted ChatGPT 4.0: FRES 36.5, SMOG 14.7; prompted ChatGPT 4.0: FRES 67.9, SMOG 10.2. Both ChatGPT 4.0 and Bard significantly improved readability scores with the 6th-grade prompt.
evidence.quote: When prompted to produce PEM at a 6th-grade reading level, both ChatGPT 4.0 and Bard were able to significantly improve in their readability scores, with prompted ChatGPT 4.0 being able to consistently generate content that was easier to read (Flesch Reading Ease Score: 67.9, Simple Measure of Gobbledygook: 10.2).

evidence.title: Evaluation of the Appropriateness and Readability of ChatGPT-4 Responses to Patient Queries on Uveitis
evidence.comparator_used: Standard ChatGPT-4 prompt with no reading-level instruction (and existing patient education websites)
evidence.outcome: Readability indices (grade level required for comprehension)
evidence.effect: Almost all readability indices showed standard ChatGPT-4 responses demanded a higher educational level, whereas simplified (sixth-grade prompt) responses required a lower level of education than the existing websites. Simplified responses matched almost all existing websites on preference, accuracy and comprehensiveness.
evidence.tradeoff: Simplified responses were not preferred over standard ones; standard responses were preferred and rated more comprehensive by specialists, with simplified responses only matching websites on these measures.
evidence.quote: Notably, almost all readability indices suggested that standard ChatGPT-4 responses demand a higher educational level for comprehension, whereas simplified responses required lower level of education compared with the existing websites.

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4o as a digital health tool for diabetes technology education: insights on reliability, quality, and readability
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT-4o responses before prompt modification, without a simpler-language instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability of patient-facing diabetes technology education responses
evidence.effect: Before simplification: mean FKGL: 10.5, GFI: 11.1; FRE: 37.8; after prompt modification: mean FKGL: 4.9; FRE: 79.0
evidence.quote: Prompting simplification improved readability significantly (mean FKGL: 4.9; FRE: 79.0), without altering content.

evidence.title: Large language models: a new frontier in paediatric cataract patient education
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt A (write a handout 'easily understandable by an average American') with no specific grade level or readability formula
evidence.outcome: Readability of LLM-generated paediatric cataract handouts (SMOG, FKGL)
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 prompt B responses were more readable than prompt A responses (p<0.001); ChatGPT-4 prompt B outputs had SMOG 5.59±0.5 and FKGL 4.31±0.7
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 prompt B responses were more readable than prompt A responses (p<0.001).

evidence.title: Accuracy and Readability of Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer-4 Omni in Answering Ophthalmology Patient Questions
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT-4o prompt with no reading-level instruction (same questions submitted without limitations)
evidence.outcome: Response quality (accurate and complete) and reading level
evidence.effect: Default: 220 (77%) accurate and complete, 49 (17%) incomplete, 16 (6%) unacceptable; mean Flesch-Kincaid grade level 12.1 ± 2.1. Sixth-grade prompt: 242 (85%) accurate and complete, 38 (13%) incomplete, 5 (2%) unacceptable. Authors report the LLM can respond at a sixth-grade level without compromising quality.
evidence.quote: When asked to respond at a sixth-grade reading level, 242 (85%) responses were graded as accurate and complete, 38 (13%) were incomplete, and 5 (2%) were graded as unacceptable.

evidence.title: ChatGPT: Is This Patient Education Tool for Urological Malignancies Readable for the General Population?
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT default structured question with no audience or reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT output (Flesch-Kincaid reading ease)
evidence.effect: Readability increased further when the question targeted a 16-year-old audience; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Ease of use of the information generated from ChatGPT was increased further when the question was modified to target an audience of 16 years of age, the average level of education attained by an Australian.

evidence.title: Chat Generative Pretraining Transformer Answers Patient-focused Questions in Cervical Spine Surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Original ChatGPT response with no reading-level instruction (default prompt)
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of ChatGPT responses to cervical spine questions
evidence.effect: Grade level 13.5 originally vs 11.2 after a second prompt asking for rephrasing at the sixth-grade reading level
evidence.tradeoff: Reading level remained well above the requested sixth-grade target; readability still not optimal for the average patient
evidence.quote: Readability was determined to be at the 13.5 grade level originally and at the 11.2 grade level after prompting.

evidence.title: Guidelines vs. generative AI in CKD patient education: the role of prompt engineering and expert blinded evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Initial AI responses with a default prompt, without a structured prompt targeting readability
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKGL and FRE) of AI-generated CKD patient education responses
evidence.effect: ChatGPT FKGL 11.34 to 7.87 and FRE 36.17 to 64.23; Gemini FKGL 9.62 to 7.13 and FRE 46.36 to 61.45 (about 7th-grade level)
evidence.quote: However, when a structured prompt was applied, AI responses demonstrated significant improvements in readability, reducing the required literacy level to approximately the 7th-grade (ChatGPT FKGL: 7.87, FRE: 64.23; Gemini FKGL: 7.13, FRE: 61.45).

evidence.title: Enhancing Patient Communication With Chat-GPT in Radiology: Evaluating the Efficacy and Readability of Answers to Common Imaging-Related Questions
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.comparator_used: Same ChatGPT questions asked without the short prompt requesting an easy-to-understand response for the average person
evidence.outcome: Readability measured by Flesch Kincaid Grade Level
evidence.effect: Unprompted 13.6 (CI 12.9-14.2) vs prompted 13.0 (CI 12.41-13.60), P = .2. No responses reached the eighth-grade level.
evidence.quote: The average Flesch Kincaid Grade Level was high at 13.6 [CI, 12.9-14.2], unchanged with the prompt (13.0 [CI, 12.41-13.60], P = .2).

evidence.title: Can ChatGPT Aid Clinicians in Educating Patients on the Surgical Management of Glaucoma?
evidence.comparator_used: Existing online patient information on glaucoma surgery (webpages), not a default no-instruction prompt
evidence.outcome: Reading grade level of patient handouts
evidence.effect: Online webpages 12th grade vs ChatGPT responses 11th grade, no significant difference; the 6th-grade target was not met
evidence.quote: There was no difference between the reading level of online webpages (12th grade) and the reading level of ChatGPT-generated responses (11th grade), despite the ChatGPT prompts asking for simple language and a sixth grade reading level.

evidence.title: Large Language Models: Pioneering New Educational Frontiers in Childhood Myopia
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt A (default prompt with no reading-level instruction) vs Prompt B (sixth-grade level using FKGL)
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKGL) of LLM-generated patient education materials on childhood myopia
evidence.effect: Readability improved with prompt B; ChatGPT-4o (o1) FKGL 6 ± 0.6 and ChatGPT-3.5 FKGL 6.2 ± 0.3 reached sixth-grade level; Gemini FKGL 7 ± 0.6 did not.
evidence.tradeoff: DISCERN quality declined from prompt A to B for ChatGPT-4o (p = 0.001) and ChatGPT-3.5 (p = 0.013); Gemini quality improved with prompt B (p = 0.02). All PEMs failed the 70% actionability threshold (40%).
evidence.quote: Readability improved with prompt B; ChatGPT-4o (01) and ChatGPT-3.5 achieved a sixth-grade level or below (FGKL 6 ± 0.6 and 6.2 ± 0.3), while Google Gemini did not (FGKL 7 ± 0.6).

evidence.title: GPT-4 as a source of patient information for cervical disc arthroplasty: a comparative analysis against Google web search
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4's initial responses without a reading-level instruction (and Google search answers)
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade level and Flesch Reading Ease) of CDA FAQ responses
evidence.effect: Flesch-Kincaid grade level 6.58 vs 13.06 (initial GPT-4) vs 12.24 (Google), P<0.001; Flesch Reading Ease 76.20 vs 36.87 vs 40.05, P<0.001
evidence.quote: Upon prompting GPT-4 to improve the readability of its responses, GPT-4 showed a lower Flesch-Kincaid grade level (6.58 vs. 13.06 vs. 12.24, P<0.001) and a higher Flesch Reading Ease score (76.20 vs. 36.87 vs. 40.05, P<0.001).

evidence.title: Optimizing Large Language Model Responses to Medical Queries: a Cross-sectional Study On the Effective Use of Chatgpt for Cancer-related Questions
evidence.comparator_used: Other prompt types without a reading-level instruction (e.g., default question prompt)
evidence.outcome: Readability indices (FKRE, GFI, FKGL, SMOG) of ChatGPT responses to cancer questions
evidence.quote: The 6th-grade prompt markedly improved readability over other strategies (ChatGPT-5: FKRE:64.92 ± 8.56, GFI:8.10 ± 1.13, FKGL:8.74 ± 1.73, SMOG:6.97 ± 1.26; ChatGPT-4o:65.44 ± 7.43, GFI:8.04 ± 1.48, FKGL:8.73 ± 1.80, SMOG:6.86 ± 1.53).

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Generate Educational Materials on Childhood Glaucoma
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt A, which asked for PEMs 'easily understandable by the average American' with no grade level or readability formula
evidence.outcome: Readability of LLM-generated childhood glaucoma PEMs (SMOG, FKGL)
evidence.effect: Prompt B (6th-grade level using SMOG) responses were more readable than Prompt A responses for all 3 LLMs (P ≤ .001)
evidence.quote: Prompt B responses were more readable than Prompt A responses for all 3 LLM (P ≤ .001).

evidence.title: Using large language models to generate child-friendly education materials on myopia
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt A (adult-directed prompt) versus Prompt B (child-directed prompt), same questions and LLMs
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid) of LLM responses
evidence.effect: Prompt B responses were significantly more readable than Prompt A responses across all LLMs (p ≤ 0.001); no scores given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Prompt B ratings were lower for ChatGPT 4o on correctness (83% vs 91%) and conciseness (63% vs 79%), and potential-harm ratings were slightly worse (97% vs 99%).
evidence.quote: The responses generated with Prompt B were significantly more readable than those generated with Prompt A across all LLMs (p ≤ 0.001).

evidence.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence to decipher gynecologic cytopathology reports: Insights from an exploratory study for possible use in patient portals
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt 2, a generic prompt with no audience or reading-level instruction ("What are the most important things I should know from my pathology report?"), versus prompt 1, which named a child audience
evidence.outcome: Pathologist Likert ratings of accuracy, completeness and potential harm of the simplified explanations
evidence.effect: Prompt 1 (explain to a child using simple language) was scored less favorably than prompt 2. No numeric values given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Explanations from ChatGPT for prompt 1 were scored less favorably.

evidence.title: Leveraging large language models to improve patient education on dry eye disease
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt A: generate DED PEMs with no reading-level instruction, compared with Prompt B specifying a 6th-grade level using the SMOG formula
evidence.outcome: Quality, understandability and accuracy of generated PEMs
evidence.effect: Outputs from both Prompt A and B had median DISCERN = 4, PEMAT understandability ≥70% and Likert misinformation score = 1. The abstract gives no readability scores for A versus B.
evidence.tradeoff: All LLM-generated PEMs were not actionable (PEMAT Actionability <70%).
evidence.quote: All LLM-generated PEMs in response to Prompt A and B were of high quality (median DISCERN = 4), understandable (PEMAT understandability ≥70%) and accurate (Likert Score=1).

evidence.title: Evaluating the efficacy of large language models in cardio-oncology patient education: a comparative analysis of accuracy, readability, and prompt engineering strategies
evidence.comparator_used: Same 20 questions posed with no prompt directive (default prompt), versus a directive to simplify language
evidence.outcome: Readability/complexity of responses versus expert-rated comprehensiveness, helpfulness and accuracy
evidence.effect: Simplification prompt reduced complexity (DouBao readability age 12.9 ± 0.8 to 10.1 ± 1.2 years, p < 0.01). Comprehensiveness (p = 0.03) and helpfulness (p < 0.01) declined significantly post-prompt, particularly for DouBao (accuracy: 57.5% vs. 7.5%, p < 0.01).
evidence.tradeoff: Simpler language came with reduced comprehensiveness and helpfulness and lower rated accuracy (notably DouBao), risking compromised clinical relevance.
evidence.quote: While simplifying language improves readability, it risks compromising clinical relevance.

evidence.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence to Improve Readability of Otolaryngology Patient Education Materials
evidence.venue: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Original articles before conversion; no prompt-without-reading-level arm was tested
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT4 output when prompted to rewrite to a sixth-grade reading level
evidence.effect: Prompting with 'translate this text to a sixth-grade reading level' produced an average FKGL of 5.80 and FRES of 77.27, versus 11.03 and 46.79 for the originals
evidence.quote: Articles were entered into ChatGPT4 with the prompt "translate this text to a sixth-grade reading level."

evidence.title: ChatGPT vs. web search for patient questions: what does ChatGPT do better?
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT prompt without additional readability prompting
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT responses (Flesch Reading Ease)
evidence.effect: Additional prompting improved FRE to 55.6 ± 13.6 (p < 0.01). The default ChatGPT responses scored 42.3 ± 13.1.
evidence.quote: Additional prompting improved ChatGPT response readability (FRE 55.6 ± 13.6, p < 0.01).

evidence.title: Assessing the accuracy and readability of ChatGPT 4.0's original and simplified responses to common patient questions regarding periacetabular osteotomy
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT 4.0 original responses with no reading-level instruction, compared with prompts asking to simplify and to respond at a 6th-grade level
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT 4.0 responses (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and Reading Ease)
evidence.effect: Grade Level: original 11.09 ± 1.47; simplified 8.16 ± 1.46; 6th-grade prompt 7.09 ± 1.23. Reading Ease: original 39.12 ± 8.25; simplified 51.53 ± 9.62; 6th-grade prompt 62.46 ± 7.48.
evidence.quote: Asking ChatGPT 4.0 to simplify or respond at a specific reading level may increase the readability of responses.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering with ChatGPT3.5 and GPT4 to improve patient education on retinal diseases
evidence.venue: Canadian journal of ophthalmology. Journal canadien d'ophtalmologie
evidence.comparator_used: Stand-alone question with no reading-level or audience instruction (also compared with prompt A, which had no length or grade-level limits)
evidence.outcome: Readability (average grade reading level) versus accuracy and comprehensiveness of LLM answers to retinal disease patient questions
evidence.effect: Average grade reading level 13.45 (stand-alone), 11.5 (prompt A), 10.3 (prompt B) (p < 0.001). Median accuracy 5.0, 5.0, 4.0 and median comprehensiveness 5.0, 5.0, 4.0 for stand-alone, prompt A, prompt B; prompt B accuracy and comprehensiveness lower (p < 0.001).
evidence.tradeoff: Specifying length and grade reading level (prompt B) lowered accuracy and comprehensiveness compared with stand-alone and prompt A.
evidence.quote: Prompt engineering can significantly improve readability of LLM-generated responses, although at the cost of reducing accuracy and comprehensiveness.

evidence.title: Accuracy, readability, and understandability of large language models for prostate cancer information to the public
evidence.comparator_used: Original ChatGPT prostate-cancer responses without a sixth-grade simplification instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability after prompting for sixth-grade layperson summaries
evidence.quote: Subsequently, these responses were re-inputted into ChatGPT to create simplified summaries understandable at a sixth-grade level.

evidence.title: Comparing the Readability and Content Quality of Online Patient Education Materials and ChatGPT-Generated Patient Education Materials for Breast Cancer Surgery and Reconstruction
evidence.comparator_used: Standard ChatGPT 4.0 prompting with no reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) of patient education guides
evidence.effect: Median FKGL 5.8 for simplified ChatGPT responses vs 10.0 for standard ChatGPT responses (and 10.8 for OPEMs); simplified responses significantly easier to read (p < 0.001)
evidence.quote: Simplified ChatGPT responses aligned with the sixth-grade level and were significantly easier to read than OPEMs and standard ChatGPT responses ( p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Assessing the Efficacy of ChatGPT Prompting Strategies in Enhancing Thyroid Cancer Patient Education: A Prospective Study
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT responses with no specific prompt (also compared with the 'statistics and references' prompt and a fourth prompt strategy)
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT patient education responses (Flesch-Kincaid grade level, Gunning Fog, SMOG, Fry)
evidence.effect: The 6th-grade-level prompt gave the most easily understandable text; responses without specific prompts were the most complex. No numeric values given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: The 6th-grade-level prompt produced the shortest responses.
evidence.quote: Prompts tailored to a "6th-grade level" generated the most easily understandable text, whereas responses without specific prompts were the most complex.

evidence.title: What Resources Are Available for Parents Online? A Readability, Quality, and Source Evaluation of Website and AI-Generated Content on Inherited Pediatric Orthopaedic Conditions
evidence.venue: Journal of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no readability request (same chatbots, standard prompt)
evidence.outcome: Readability of AI chatbot output (FRE and FKGL)
evidence.effect: With a readability-improvement request, average output readability fell by nearly six grade levels (FRE 69.0; FKGL 6.8), versus default AI output (FRE 36.1; FKGL 12.3); only 2% of default AI responses met the eighth-grade standard.
evidence.quote: However, when the input prompt included a request to improve readability, AI models lowered average output readability by nearly six grade levels (FRE 69.0; FKGL 6.8).

evidence.title: ChatGPT for improving postoperative instructions in multiple fields of plastic surgery
evidence.venue: Journal of plastic, reconstructive & aesthetic surgery : JPRAS
evidence.comparator_used: Prompting for a sixth-grade target versus a fourth-grade target, compared with the original instructions; no no-instruction prompt arm
evidence.outcome: Achievement of target reading level and actionability when prompting for specific grade levels
evidence.effect: Prompting for sixth grade lowered only one rewrite to sixth grade; prompting for fourth grade brought all rewrites to sixth grade or below but none reached fourth grade. Authors suggest prompting one to two grade levels lower than desired.
evidence.tradeoff: Fourth-grade prompts reduced actionability; the model overshot or undershot the target grade level.
evidence.quote: Of the fourth-grade ChatGPT instructions, all were reduced to the sixth-grade-level or below, but none achieved the fourth-grade level.

evidence.title: [Making prostate cancer research accessible: chatGPT-4 as a tool to enhance lay communication]
evidence.comparator_used: Basic prompt without readability optimization
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT-4 layperson summaries (readability indices); content quality
evidence.effect: Advanced prompt significantly improved readability vs basic prompt (p < 0.001); content quality comparable (p = 0.665); error-free LS 92% vs 76.1%
evidence.quote: The advanced prompt led to significantly improved readability compared to the basic prompt (p < 0.001) and the original LS (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Can artificial intelligence improve the readability of patient education information in gynecology?
evidence.venue: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology
evidence.comparator_used: Original ACOG/UpToDate materials before the sixth-grade instruction (no default-prompt arm reported)
evidence.outcome: Whether prompting for a sixth-grade target reading level achieved that level
evidence.effect: Explicit sixth-grade prompting improved readability for CoPilot and Gemini but no LLM reached the sixth-grade level; ChatGPT became harder to read.
evidence.tradeoff: Explicit prompting did not guarantee target readability; ChatGPT output increased in difficulty. Readability safeguards are needed.
evidence.quote: Even when explicitly prompted, no large language model achieved the sixth-grade reading level required for optimal patient comprehension.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence improves urologic oncology patient education and counseling
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT output with no reading-level or audience instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability (grade level) and quality of patient education content
evidence.effect: Default ChatGPT averaged grade level 12.16; the readability-adjusted prompt (ChatGPT-a) gave 7.50 and retained high quality, whereas Epic Easy to Read reached 3.53 but did not retain high quality.
evidence.quote: When adjusted for user education level (ChatGPT-a and Epic Easy to Read), readability improved (7.50 and 3.53), but only ChatGPT-a retained high quality.

evidence.title: The Use of ChatGPT-4.0 to Simplify Breast Pathology Reports: A Study on Readability and Accuracy
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt 1 (simple request to simplify the report) with no reading-level specification
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Level) and ease of reading (Flesch Reading Ease Score) of simplified breast pathology reports
evidence.effect: Prompt 2 (6th-grade-level specification) reduced FKRL (p < 0.001) and increased FRES (p < 0.001); the abstract gives no mean values for each prompt.
evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy was only mostly maintained: overall 3.59/4, with relevancy lowest at 3.27/4 and factual correctness 3.62/4. The abstract does not report accuracy by prompt. The authors recommend review before dissemination to limit inaccurate or misleading information.
evidence.quote: Prompt 2 demonstrated a reduction in FKRL (p < 0.001) and an increase in FRES (p < 0.001), demonstrating improved readability and ease of reading.

evidence.title: Empowering patients: how accurate and readable are large language models in renal cancer education
evidence.comparator_used: Default chatbot outputs with no reading-level instruction, compared with the same chatbots' outputs after being asked to simplify to a sixth-grade reading level
evidence.outcome: Readability grade level of chatbot-generated kidney cancer patient education text
evidence.effect: Default mean readability: ChatGPT-4.0 11.03 ± 1.76, Gemini AI 10.83 ± 2.31, Perplexity AI 12.66 ± 1.83. After the simplification request: ChatGPT-4.0 5.76 to 9.19, Perplexity AI 7.33 to 8.45, Gemini AI 6.43 to 8.43.
evidence.tradeoff: Most simplified outputs still did not reach the sixth-grade target. The study also reports that LLM outputs in general are prone to detail omission and some inaccuracies, but it does not separately assess the simplified versions.
evidence.quote: The Chatbots demonstrated the capability to simplify text lower grade levels upon request, with ChatGPT-4.0 achieving a readability grade level ranging from 5.76 to 9.19, Perplexity AI from 7.33 to 8.45, Gemini AI from 6.43 to 8.43.

evidence.title: Comparative Readability of Large Language Models Responses to Male Infertility Questions: Impact of Contextual Prompting
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no reading-level or audience instruction (no additional context)
evidence.outcome: Readability of patient-facing LLM output (FRE and SMOG)
evidence.effect: Readability improved across all models with a lay patient/couple audience prompt; Grok after prompting FRE 69.71±6.09, SMOG 9.96±1.04
evidence.tradeoff: Clinical accuracy was not evaluated; the authors state readability gains must be paired with ongoing verification of accuracy.
evidence.quote: After prompting, Grok generated the most readable responses (mean FRE 69.71±6.09; mean SMOG 9.96±1.04), and readability improved across all models.

evidence.title: Using ChatGPT-4 for Lay Summarization in Prostate Cancer Research to Advance Patient-Centered Communication: Large-Scale Generative AI Performance Evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Simple prompt based on the journal's guidelines (versus extended prompt refined to improve readability)
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKRE) and composite high-quality rate; accuracy and word count compliance
evidence.effect: Median FKRE 47 (IQR 42-56) extended vs 36 (IQR 29-43) simple (P<.001); high-quality 79.4% vs 54.9%; no significant difference in accuracy (P=.53) or word count compliance (P=.87)
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4-generated lay summaries showed an improvement in readability compared to human-written versions, with the extended prompt achieving higher scores than the simple prompt (median FKRE: extended prompt 47, IQR 42-56; simple prompt 36, IQR 29-43; original 20, IQR 9.5-29; P<.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating if ChatGPT Can Answer Common Patient Questions Compared With OrthoInfo Regarding Rotator Cuff Tears
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Global research & reviews
evidence.comparator_used: Standard ChatGPT responses with no reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade level) versus accuracy and appropriateness of responses, rated by five orthopaedic surgeons
evidence.effect: Sixth-grade responses scored lower on accuracy (3.6 ± 0.76 vs. 4.7 ± 0.47; P < 0.001) and appropriateness (3.7 ± 0.98 vs. 4.5 ± 0.57; P < 0.001). Standard responses had a higher Flesch-Kincaid grade level than sixth-grade responses (P < 0.001), so the sixth-grade prompt was easier to read. No grade-level values were given.
evidence.tradeoff: The sixth-grade prompt improved readability but lowered accuracy and appropriateness. Sixth-grade responses were also rated worse than OrthoInfo on both measures (P < 0.001).
evidence.quote: Despite being easier to read, sixth-grade level ChatGPT responses compromised on accuracy and appropriateness.

evidence.title: The quality and readability of patient information provided by ChatGPT: can AI reliably explain common ENT operations?
evidence.venue: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT standard question versus simplified question (default prompt with no simplification instruction)
evidence.outcome: Readability (FRES) and information quality (DISCERN) of ChatGPT answers
evidence.effect: Mean FRES 38.9 pre-simplification vs 55.1 post-simplification; simplified information 43.6% more readable (FRES) but scored 11.6% lower for quality. Readability remained poor.
evidence.tradeoff: Simplification came at the expense of quality, giving shorter answers with important omissions.
evidence.quote: Simplified information from ChatGPT was 43.6% more readable (FRES) but scored 11.6% lower for quality.

evidence.title: Ai-generated personalized informed consent for elective spinal surgery: a comparative study using retrieval-augmented generation
evidence.venue: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
evidence.comparator_used: None; single-arm measurement of readability against the recommended threshold after a sixth-grade prompt instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability of AI-generated consent documents (Flesch indices)
evidence.effect: Mean Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level 7.76; 95.8% of documents met the recommended reading level threshold
evidence.tradeoff: Mean grade level of 7.76 was above the sixth-grade level requested in the prompt
evidence.quote: Mean Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level was 7.76, with 95.8% of documents meeting the recommended reading level threshold.

evidence.title: A quality and readability comparison of artificial intelligence and popular health website education materials for common hand surgery procedures
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT prompted for a scientific reading level, with no simplification instruction
evidence.outcome: Reading grade level of ChatGPT-generated hand surgery patient education materials
evidence.effect: Mean reading grade level was 10th grade for ChatGPT at a 4th-grade prompt versus 14th grade for ChatGPT at a scientific level. Both exceeded the recommended 4th-6th grade by at least four grade levels.
evidence.tradeoff: The 4th-grade prompt did not reach the target level. The authors report that ChatGPT prompted for easier reading gave less robust information than patient-friendly websites, but this was measured against the websites, not against the scientific-level ChatGPT output.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT - 4th Grade Reading Level, ChatGPT - Scientific Reading Level, WebMD, and Mayo Clinic written materials on average exceeded recommended reading grade levels (4th-6th grade) by at least four grade levels (10th, 14th, 13th, and 11th grade, respectively).

evidence.title: Large language models: unlocking new potential in patient education for thyroid eye disease
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt A (brochure prompt without a sixth-grade reading-level instruction)
evidence.outcome: Readability of LLM-generated TED patient education brochures (FKGL, SMOG); also quality, understandability, accuracy, empathy
evidence.effect: Prompt B (sixth-grade instruction) was easier to understand than prompt A; no significant differences in quality (DISCERN >=4), understandability (PEMAT >=70%), accuracy (>=4) or empathy (>=4). Numeric readability scores not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Regarding readability, prompt B was easier to understand than prompt A, although the optimized version of prompt B still did not reach the ideal readability level.

evidence.title: Using ChatGPT to Improve the Presentation of Plain Language Summaries of Cochrane Systematic Reviews About Oncology Interventions: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.comparator_used: Original PLSs, and an alternative prompt asking only to make the text simpler and easier to read for a lay audience (prompt 3)
evidence.outcome: Readability (SMOG index) of ChatGPT-generated summaries
evidence.effect: Prompt with explicit SMOG target of 6: median SMOG 8.2 (95% CI 8-8.4) vs 8.7 (95% CI 8.4-8.8) for the 'simpler and easier' prompt and 13.1 for original PLSs
evidence.tradeoff: The requested SMOG target of 6 was not reached (median 8.2).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-generated PLSs using the first prompt (SMOG index 6) were the shortest and easiest to read, with a median SMOG score of 8.2 (95% CI 8-8.4), compared with the original PLSs (median SMOG score 13.1, 95% CI 12.9-13.4).

evidence.title: Evaluating if ChatGPT Can Answer Common Patient Questions Compared to OrthoInfo Regarding Lateral Epicondylitis
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT prompt with no reading-level instruction (standard level responses)
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade level) versus accuracy and appropriateness of ChatGPT responses
evidence.effect: Sixth-grade prompt lowered the Flesch-Kincaid grade from 14.06 to 8.48, matching OrthoInfo (8.98, no significant difference). Accuracy fell to 3.9 ± 0.87 vs 4.7 ± 0.43 (p = 0.046) and appropriateness to 3.7 ± 0.92 vs 4.7 ± 0.45 (p = 0.045).
evidence.tradeoff: The sixth-grade responses were oversimplified and less accurate and less appropriate than standard responses.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT's responses at the sixth-grade level scored lower in accuracy (mean = 3.9 ± 0.87, p = 0.046) and appropriateness (mean = 3.7 ± 0.92, p = 0.045) compared to the standard level (accuracy = 4.7 ± 0.43, appropriateness = 4.7 ± 0.45).

evidence.title: Evaluation of the artificial intelligence chatbots in frequently asked questions about retinitis pigmentosa: a comparative analysis between ChatGPT-4 and Gemini-2.0
evidence.venue: International journal of retina and vitreous
evidence.comparator_used: Standard prompt with no reading-level or audience instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability of chatbot answers (8 readability indices) for ChatGPT-4 and Gemini-2.0
evidence.effect: Almost all readability indices showed standard responses required a higher education level and simplified (sixth-grade prompt) responses a lower level; no numeric values given in the abstract. Accuracy p-values (0.557 standard, 0.090 simplified) compared the two chatbots, not the prompt types.
evidence.quote: In particular, almost all readability indices suggest that standard AI chatbot responses require a higher level of education for comprehension, whereas simplified responses require a lower level of education.

evidence.title: ChatGPT improves readability in validated spine patient-reported outcome measures
evidence.comparator_used: Original PROMs before revision (no comparison against a prompt without reading-level instruction)
evidence.outcome: Readability of PROMs after ChatGPT revision with a standardized prompt instructing a sixth-grade reading level
evidence.effect: 7 of 9 grade-level metrics achieved NIH/AMA sixth-grade compliance after revision; all readability indices improved (p < .001)
evidence.tradeoff: 59.7% of revised PROMs had at least one content-related error, including altered response scales (23%) and omitted recall timeframes (18%)
evidence.quote: About 7 of 9 grade-level metrics achieved NIH/AMA sixth-grade readability compliance following revision.

evidence.title: Readability versus accuracy in LLM-transformed radiology reports: stakeholder preferences across reading grade levels
evidence.comparator_used: Other target reading grade levels (7-17) specified in the same Gemini transformation of radiology reports; no default no-instruction prompt arm
evidence.outcome: Stakeholder preference, accuracy, readability and error rates (generalizations, omissions, hallucinations) across target reading grade levels
evidence.effect: Preferences peaked at grade 16 and declined at grade 17, especially among laypersons; higher grades were generally preferred (range 12-17). Accuracy was the strongest predictor of preference (OR 30.29, 33.05, 2.16 for radiologists, physicians, laypersons; p<0.001), followed by readability (OR 2.73, 1.70, 2.01; p<0.001).
evidence.tradeoff: Lower grade levels improved readability but increased errors (generalizations, omissions, hallucinations); higher grade levels improved accuracy but sharply reduced readability. Authors note the limits of unsupervised LLM transformation.
evidence.quote: Lower reading grades improved readability but increased errors, while higher grades improved accuracy but reduced readability.

evidence.title: Investigating the capabilities of advanced large language models in generating patient instructions and patient educational material
evidence.venue: European journal of hospital pharmacy : science and practice
evidence.comparator_used: Simple prompt versus detailed prompt for patient instructions and educational material; the abstract does not say what the detailed prompt contained, so the link to reading-level or audience specification is inferred
evidence.outcome: Reading grade level of patient-facing output
evidence.effect: Simple prompts: ChatGPT 4.0 at 10th-grade level, Gemini 1.0 Pro at 7th-grade level. Detailed prompts: both at 6th-grade level. ChatGPT 4.0 reached 85% readability with detailed prompts.
evidence.tradeoff: ChatGPT 4.0 produced longer outputs with detailed prompts. Outputs from both models lacked guidance on expiration dates and medication disposal, and the authors say healthcare professional oversight is still needed.
evidence.quote: Both LLMs produced outputs at a 6th-grade level with detailed prompts.

evidence.title: Comparing the Accuracy and Readability of Glaucoma-related Question Responses and Educational Materials by Google and ChatGPT
evidence.comparator_used: Original procedural explanations without a reading-level instruction (pre-revision baseline at grade 16.6)
evidence.outcome: Reading grade level and accuracy of procedural explanations when ChatGPT was instructed to write at specific reading levels
evidence.effect: Reading level fell from grade 16.6 to grade 9.4 (p < 0.001) with no loss of accuracy
evidence.quote: ChatGPT successfully reduced the reading level of glaucoma procedural explanations without sacrificing accuracy, with implications for the future of customized patient education for patients with varying health literacy.

evidence.title: Chatbots as Patient Education Resources for Aesthetic Facial Plastic Surgery: Evaluation of ChatGPT and Google Bard Responses
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no reading-level or audience instruction (no-prompt condition), alongside patient-friendly and references prompts
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of chatbot responses to patient education questions on aesthetic facial plastic surgery
evidence.effect: With eighth-grade prompting, mean grade level was ChatGPT 10.5 ± 1.8 and Google Bard 9.6 ± 1.3, still above the eighth-grade target; Google Bard was at a significantly lower grade level than ChatGPT for all prompts (p < 0.05). The abstract gives no numbers for the no-prompt baseline.
evidence.quote: Despite eighth-grade prompting, response grade level for both chatbots was high: ChatGPT (10.5 ± 1.8) and Google Bard™ (9.6 ± 1.3).

evidence.title: Physician Perspectives on ChatGPT-4o as a Patient Resource for Abdominal Cancer Surgeries: Cross-Sectional Survey
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT-4o responses to the same questions without prompting for reading level (baseline), plus a separate rephrasing condition
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Grade Level and Flesch Reading Ease) on a post hoc analysis of select questions
evidence.effect: Median FKRGL 15.6 (IQR 14.4-16.7) at baseline, decreasing to 7.1 (IQR 6.1-8.3) with prompting and 14.5 (IQR 13.2-15.4) with rephrasing; median FRE 18.1 (IQR 14.6-24.7) at baseline, increasing to 73.8 (IQR 66.6-79.3) with prompting and 32.0 (IQR 27.0-37.7) with rephrasing
evidence.quote: On a post hoc analysis for select questions, the median FKRGL was 15.6 (IQR 14.4-16.7), decreasing to 7.1 (IQR 6.1-8.3) and 14.5 (IQR 13.2-15.4) with prompting and rephrasing, and the median FRE was 18.1 (IQR 14.6-24.7), increasing to 73.8 (IQR 66.6-79.3) and 32.0 (IQR 27.0-37.7) with prompting and rephrasing.

evidence.title: The ethics of simplification: balancing patient autonomy, comprehension, and accuracy in AI-generated radiology reports
evidence.comparator_used: Different prompted target reading grade levels (1-17) within the same GPT-4 Turbo prompting approach
evidence.outcome: Correlation of readability scores with prompted reading level, and clinical accuracy by prompted grade level
evidence.effect: Readability scores correlated with prompted reading levels (r = 0.80-0.84); accuracy stable at grades 13-11 but declined significantly below grade 11; 11th grade identified as lower bound
evidence.tradeoff: Lower prompted grade levels reduced accuracy, with 20% of 7th-grade reports having potentially management-altering inaccuracies.
evidence.quote: Readability scores showed strong correlation with prompted reading levels (r = 0.80-0.84).

evidence.title: Comparing the Ability of Google and ChatGPT to Accurately Respond to Oculoplastics-Related Patient Questions and Generate Customized Oculoplastics Patient Education Materials
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT's initial patient education materials generated without a lower reading-level instruction (default output)
evidence.outcome: Readability (grade level) of ChatGPT-generated patient education materials, with accuracy also assessed
evidence.effect: Grade level reduced by approximately 4 (15.7 vs 11.7, p < 0.001) without sacrificing accuracy
evidence.quote: When instructed to rewrite patient education materials at a lower reading level, grade level was reduced by approximately 4 (15.7 vs 11.7, respectively, p < 0.001) without sacrificing accuracy.

evidence.title: Prompt matters: evaluation of large language model chatbot responses related to Peyronie's disease
evidence.comparator_used: Unprompted LLM responses (default prompt without reading-level instruction)
evidence.outcome: Reading level of patient-facing responses when prompted for a grade 8 level
evidence.effect: Chatbots could not reach grade 8 when prompted. Average Flesch-Kincaid reading level was grade 12.9 (SD 2.1). Overall information quality (DISCERN) rose from moderate to high with prompting, but the abstract does not say that prompt specified reading level.
evidence.tradeoff: Citations were appropriate only 42.5% of the time.
evidence.quote: Chatbots were unable to communicate at a grade 8 reading level when prompted, and their citations were appropriate only 42.5% of the time.

evidence.title: Evaluating ChatGPT Responses on Atrial Fibrillation for Patient Education
evidence.comparator_used: Form 1 (no prompt), with Form 3 physician-level and Form 4 references prompts also reported
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of ChatGPT answers to atrial fibrillation questions
evidence.effect: Form 2 (patient-friendly) mean grade level 12.80 ± 3.38 vs Form 1 14.23 ± 2.34, Form 3 16.73 ± 2.65, Form 4 14.85 ± 2.76 (p < 0.05). Proportion of responses at least correct did not differ by form (p = 0.350).
evidence.quote: Form 2 answers had a lower mean grade level (12.80 ± 3.38) than Forms 1 (14.23 ± 2.34), 3 (16.73 ± 2.65), and 4 (14.85 ± 2.76) (p < 0.05).

evidence.title: Prompting generative artificial intelligence to create plain language patient education materials
evidence.comparator_used: Basic prompt (without the plain-language instructions) given to the same AI programs (ChatGPT, Gemini)
evidence.outcome: Readability (grade level from a panel of readability indices), plus understandability and actionability (PEMAT) of patient education materials
evidence.effect: Advanced plain-language prompt documents had mean readability scores at or below 6th grade and were significantly more readable than basic-prompt documents. ChatGPT with the advanced prompt had the lowest mean grade level (5.8; SD 0.84) and the highest PEMAT scores (91% understandable, 84% actionable). Both AIs with the advanced prompt exceeded the 70% actionability threshold. Numeric basic-prompt scores are not given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Documents from generative AI using the advanced prompt and UpToDate had mean readability scores ≤ 6th grade, with significantly better readability than AI-generated documents using the basic prompt or HealthyChildren.org.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Responses to Patient Questions About Return to Activities of Daily Living After Knee Arthroplasty: A Multidimensional Evaluation Before and After Plain-Language Prompting
evidence.comparator_used: Original question submitted without simplification prompt (default prompt, same models, same 12 questions)
evidence.outcome: Readability, understandability, actionability, completeness and DISCERN treatment-information quality of Turkish LLM responses (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude)
evidence.effect: Understandability improved [F(1,11) = 55.633, P < 0.001, partial η²=0.835]; readability increased for all models; actionability remained 60%; completeness decreased for ChatGPT (P = 0.004) and Claude (P = 0.016) but not Gemini; total DISCERN decreased by 11.58 points for ChatGPT and 11.00 for Claude (both P < 0.001), Gemini's 4.00-point decrease not significant (P = 0.062); accuracy and safety maximal in all groups
evidence.tradeoff: Simplification reduced completeness and treatment-information quality (DISCERN) for ChatGPT and Claude; professional review and individualization still needed
evidence.quote: Simplification improved readability and understandability but could reduce completeness and treatment-information quality.

evidence.title: Leveraging Large Language Models for High-Quality Lay Summaries: Efficacy of ChatGPT-4 with Custom Prompts in a Consecutive Series of Prostate Cancer Manuscripts
evidence.comparator_used: Basic "simple" prompt without the enhanced instructions
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease), required reading level, and alignment with quality thresholds of ChatGPT-4 lay summaries of prostate cancer articles
evidence.effect: Median FKRE 40.9 vs 29.1 (p < 0.001); quality threshold alignment 86.2% vs 47.5% (p < 0.001); reduced required reading level; both prompts had median comprehensiveness Likert score of 5
evidence.quote: The extended prompt demonstrated significantly higher readability (median FKRE: 40.9 vs. 29.1, p < 0.001), better alignment with quality thresholds (86.2% vs. 47.5%, p < 0.001), and reduced the required reading level, making content more accessible.

evidence.title: Evaluation of large language models in generating and optimizing educational materials for neonatal home oxygen therapy
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompt (Prompt A) with no simplification instruction
evidence.outcome: C-DISCERN content quality, C-PEMAT understandability and actionability of generated texts
evidence.effect: Simplification prompt (Prompt B) significantly reduced C-DISCERN scores across all models (all p < 0.001) without meaningfully improving understandability or actionability.
evidence.tradeoff: Simplistic plain-language instructions risked compromising content quality; prompt optimization reduced lexical richness.
evidence.quote: The simplification prompt (Prompt B) significantly reduced C-DISCERN scores across all models (all p < 0.001) without meaningfully improving understandability or actionability.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of ChatGPT in simplifying information for Polish patients on cervical cancer screening using advanced prompting
evidence.venue: Annals of agricultural and environmental medicine : AAEM
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompting with no reading-level or audience instruction (STANDARD)
evidence.outcome: Readability of patient-facing ChatGPT cervical cancer screening information in Polish
evidence.effect: Average difficulty level 5.32 (at least 15 years of education) for STANDARD vs 4.15 (12 years of education) for EASY; 21 of 24 indicators significantly improved (p < 0.05)
evidence.tradeoff: Output still too difficult for patients with only primary education (8 years of schooling target not reached)
evidence.quote: The average difficulty level of STANDARD output was 5.32 (at least 15 years of formal education), while EASY output averaged 4.15 (12 years of formal education).

evidence.title: De novo generation of colorectal patient educational materials using large language models: Prompt engineering key to improved readability
evidence.comparator_used: Basic prompt and Iterative prompt (no grade-level or metric instructions) for LLM-generated materials, with existing institutional materials as the baseline
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Modified Grade Level, Reading Ease) of LLM-generated colorectal patient education materials
evidence.effect: ChatGPT with Metric-based prompt vs baseline: Grade Level 5.2 vs 8.1, Modified Grade Level 7.3 vs 10.3, Ease 70.5 vs 60.4, all P < .01. Perplexity with Metric-based prompt did not differ statistically from baseline, whereas Perplexity's other prompts were significantly less readable. Direct Metric-vs-Basic numbers were not given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: LLM-generated documents were much shorter than existing materials (170-313 words vs 863-956), which may mean less content. Most LLM output from non-metric prompts did not meet readability recommendations.
evidence.quote: Overall, ChatGPT materials were more readable than baseline materials with the Metric-based prompt: Grade Level 5.2 vs 8.1, Modified Grade Level 7.3 vs 10.3, and Ease 70.5 vs 60.4, all P < .01.

evidence.title: Evaluating ChatGPT Responses on Thyroid Nodules for Patient Education
evidence.venue: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no reading-level or audience instruction (no prompting), also compared with patient-friendly prompting and prompting for references
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of ChatGPT answers
evidence.effect: 8th-grade prompting mean grade level 13.43 ± 2.86 vs no prompting 14.97 ± 2.01 (p = 0.01) and prompting for references 16.43 ± 2.05 (p < 0.0001)
evidence.tradeoff: Even with 8th-grade prompting, output stayed well above recommended grade levels for patient information.
evidence.quote: Responses from 8th-grade level prompting were the lowest mean grade level (13.43 ± 2.86) and were significantly lower than no prompting (14.97 ± 2.01, p = 0.01) and prompting for references (16.43 ± 2.05, p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Improving readability in AI-generated medical information on fragility fractures: the role of prompt wording on ChatGPT's responses
evidence.venue: Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA
evidence.comparator_used: Keyword-only prompts with no plain-language instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT responses on fragility fractures (Flesch-Kincaid reading ease and grade level)
evidence.effect: FKRE median 34.35 with plain language prompts vs 23.60 with keyword-only prompts; FKGL median 12.05 vs 14.50; both differences statistically significant (Mann-Whitney U)
evidence.quote: The FKRE scores indicated significantly higher readability with plain language prompts (median 34.35) compared to keyword-only prompts (median 23.60).

evidence.title: AI-generated explanations in kidney transplantation: accuracy vs. readability and implications for patient education
evidence.comparator_used: Standardized prompt with no explicit reading-level instruction (first round)
evidence.outcome: Readability of GPT-5.1 plain-language explanations of kidney transplantation terms (Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level)
evidence.effect: Mean Flesch Reading Ease rose from 23.6 ± 23.4 to 62.4 ± 7.5; mean Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level fell from 13.4 ± 4.8 to 6.3 ± 1.1; 46% of explanations needed college-level reading in round 1 vs all at middle school level or below in round 2
evidence.quote: Explicit readability-focused prompting substantially improved readability without compromising accuracy, underscoring the importance of prompt design when deploying LLMs for patient-centered education in transplantation.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Model Adherence to Targeted Fifth-Grade Readability Standards in Patient Education on Chronic Conditions
evidence.comparator_used: Unprompted LLM outputs with no reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability scores of LLM-generated patient education materials on chronic conditions
evidence.effect: Prompting for a 5th-grade level consistently produced statistically lower readability scores than unprompted outputs; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Prompting LLMs to produce PEMs at a 5th-grade level consistently produced statistically lower readability scores than unprompted outputs.

evidence.title: Implementing Generative AI to Enhance Patient Education on Retinopathy of Prematurity
evidence.venue: Journal of pediatric ophthalmology and strabismus
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt A: default prompt asking for a novel ROP patient education material with no reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability of LLM-generated patient education materials (SMOG, FKGL)
evidence.effect: Prompt B (6th-grade target using SMOG) generated more readable PEMs than Prompt A (P < .001)
evidence.quote: Prompt B generated more readable PEMs than Prompt A (P < .001).

evidence.title: The Use of Large Language Models to Generate Education Materials about Uveitis
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt B, which asked for patient-targeted uveitis information easy to understand by an average American, with no grade level or FKGL instruction
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of generated uveitis patient information (lower is easier to read)
evidence.effect: Both models produced lower FKGL with prompt A (6th-grade/FKGL instruction) than prompt B, but the difference was significant only for ChatGPT (P < 0.0001). Mean FKGL with prompt A: ChatGPT 6.3 ± 1.2, Bard 10.5 ± 0.8.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT and Bard generated responses with lower FKGL scores (i.e., easier to understand) in response to prompt A compared with prompt B.

evidence.title: Quantitative Evaluation of Large Language Models to Streamline Radiology Report Impressions: A Multimodal Retrospective Analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Prompt 1, 'Simplify this radiology report.', with no reading-level or audience instruction
evidence.outcome: Reading grade level of LLM-simplified radiology report impressions
evidence.effect: Stating the patient context (prompt 2) or a 7th grade level (prompt 3) reduced reading grade level for all models and prompts except prompt 1 to prompt 2 for ChatGPT-4, P < .001
evidence.quote: Providing the context of being a patient or requesting simplification at the seventh-grade level reduced the reading grade level of output for all models and prompts (except prompt 1 to prompt 2 for ChatGPT-4) (P < .001).

evidence.title: Enhancing Patient Comprehension of Glomerular Disease Treatments Using ChatGPT
evidence.comparator_used: GPT-4 general explanations without an 8th-grade readability instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability, understandability, and accuracy of patient-facing explanations of glomerular disorder therapies
evidence.effect: Readability improved from 12.85 ± 0.93 to 8.44 ± 0.72; FRE increased from 25.73 ± 6.98 to 60.75 ± 4.56; PEMAT-P increased from 60.7% to 76.8% (p < 0.0001 for both); accuracy decreased from 4.56 ± 0.66 to 3.99 ± 0.39 (p < 0.0001).
evidence.tradeoff: Reduced accuracy/comprehensiveness for tailored explanations.
evidence.quote: The accuracy of GPT-4's tailored explanations was significantly lower compared to the general explanations (3.99 ± 0.39 versus 4.56 ± 0.66, p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Assessing the Application of Large Language Models in Generating Dermatologic Patient Education Materials According to Reading Level: Qualitative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no reading-level instruction (unspecified prompt), compared with fifth- and seventh-grade prompts
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid reading level of LLM-generated dermatology patient education materials
evidence.effect: Common conditions: FKRL 9.8-11.21 unspecified vs 4.22-7.43 (fifth-grade prompt) and 5.98-7.28 (seventh-grade prompt). Rare conditions: 9.85-11.45 unspecified vs 4.22-7.43 and 5.98-7.28. Current AAD PEMs averaged 9.35 (common) and 9.50 (rare).
evidence.tradeoff: Results varied by model and grade level. Not every model reached the fifth-grade target, and for rare conditions at seventh grade ChatGPT-3.5 and DocsGPT outperformed GPT-4.
evidence.quote: For common diseases, the FKRLs of LLM-produced PEMs ranged between 9.8 and 11.21 (unspecified prompt), between 4.22 and 7.43 (fifth-grade prompt), and between 5.98 and 7.28 (seventh-grade prompt).

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering and Follow-Up Questioning Improves the Readability of Spine Surgery Questions in Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline prompt with no reading-level instruction (phase 1) versus sixth-grade request, rule-based prompting and direct readability targeting
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT responses to spine surgery questions (SMOG, Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid, Gunning Fog, Coleman-Liau)
evidence.effect: Phase 2 (sixth-grade level request) yielded the most readable responses, with 51.11% meeting the sixth-grade level; simplified prompting was more effective than complex rule-based prompts; ChatGPT 4o was more readable than ChatGPT 5 in all phases except phase 1 (P < 0.001)
evidence.quote: Phase 2 yielded the most readable responses, with 51.11% meeting the sixth-grade level.

evidence.title: Comparison of ChatGPT and Traditional Patient Education Materials for Men's Health
evidence.comparator_used: Default ChatGPT responses to the same UCF patient questions with no reading-level instruction (also benchmarked against the UCF materials)
evidence.outcome: Readability of patient education responses (six validated readability formulae)
evidence.effect: Default ChatGPT was significantly worse than UCF on readability across all 6 topics (all P < .001). Adjusted ChatGPT readability typically surpassed UCF and met the recommended level for 2 topics. No numerical scores were given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Conversely, adjusted ChatGPT readability typically surpassed UCF, even meeting the recommended level for 2 topics.

evidence.title: Assessing the readability of AI-generated medication counseling for common Medicaid drug classes: metformin, lisinopril, and atorvastatin
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no reading-level instruction (default AI condition)
evidence.outcome: Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of AI-generated medication counseling passages
evidence.effect: Pooled default AI FKGL 12.19 ± 4.85 vs pooled sixth-grade-prompted AI FKGL 7.63 ± 3.16; decreased across all three models (all P ≤ 0.001)
evidence.tradeoff: Study addressed readability only; accuracy, completeness and comprehension were not assessed. Pooled sixth-grade AI FKGL (7.63) still exceeded the sixth-grade target.
evidence.quote: sixth-grade prompting markedly decreased FKGL across all three models (all P ≤ 0.001).

evidence.title: Readability of dermatology patient education materials: a comparative analysis of Turkish Dermatology Association brochures and texts generated by ChatGPT and Gemini
evidence.comparator_used: Default prompt with no specific instructions versus low-literacy prompt (write at a sixth-grade level)
evidence.outcome: Ateşman Readability Index score of AI-generated Turkish dermatology patient education texts
evidence.effect: Prompting significantly improved ChatGPT readability (p < 0.001); no significant change for Gemini, already high by default. Prompted Gemini had the highest mean score (68.98 ± 4.66). Default Gemini 66.63 vs default ChatGPT 62.66 (p = 0.004).
evidence.quote: While specific prompting significantly improved ChatGPT performance (p < 0.001), no significant change was observed in Gemini scores, which were already high in the default condition.

evidence.title: The Impact of Specific Prompt Engineering Techniques on the Readability of LLM-Generated Patient Materials in Gastroenterology and Hepatology
evidence.comparator_used: Zero-shot prompt without constraints (less constrained prompts: Zero-Shot, Contextualized, Meta, Persona)
evidence.outcome: Readability (SMOG index and FKGL) of LLM-generated gastroenterology and hepatology patient explanations
evidence.effect: More constrained prompts yielded significantly more readable outputs, and less constrained prompts yielded less readable outputs (p < 0.001). No prompt technique or model consistently reached a 6th grade level by SMOG.
evidence.quote: However, prompts with less constraints yield less readable outputs, while prompts with more constraints yield significantly more readable outputs (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Presentation suitability and readability of ChatGPT's medical responses to patient questions about on knee osteoarthritis
evidence.comparator_used: Original ChatGPT responses generated without a reading-level instruction; detailed versus simplified instruction prompts were also compared with each other
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT responses to knee osteoarthritis patient questions
evidence.effect: Readability improved slightly after the instruction intervention, with no significant difference between detailed and simplified instructions. Baseline responses significantly exceeded the recommended sixth-grade reading level (p < .001). No numeric post-intervention scores are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: After the intervention, readability improved slightly for responses related to knee OA; however, there was no significant difference in readability between the groups receiving detailed versus simplified instructions.

evidence.title: ChatGPT Provides Accurate but Incomplete Responses and Reliably Adjusts Readability to Prompts for Hamstring Injury Frequently Asked Questions
evidence.comparator_used: Unprompted (naïve) ChatGPT-4.0 query with no reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability (Flesch Reading Ease Score and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level) of responses to hamstring injury FAQs
evidence.effect: Unprompted: FRES 61.64, FKGL 10.28. Seventh-grade prompt: FRES 75.2, FKGL 6.1. College graduate prompt: FRES 12.08, FKGL 17.23.
evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy was graded only on the unprompted responses (2 of 10 grade A, 7 B, 1 C), so the effect of reading-level prompts on accuracy or completeness was not assessed.
evidence.quote: However, when explicitly prompted, ChatGPT reliably adjusted the complexity of its responses to both a seventh-grade and a graduate-level reading standard.

evidence.title: The Ability of Large Language Models to Generate Patient Information Materials for Retinopathy of Prematurity: Evaluation of Readability, Accuracy, and Comprehensiveness
evidence.comparator_used: The LLMs' original responses before reformulation; the P1 prompt (6th-grade level) was also compared with the P2 prompt (easier to understand, no grade level)
evidence.outcome: Change in readability after prompting for a 6th-grade reading level (P1) or easier text (P2)
evidence.effect: Readability improved for GPT-4.0 with both P1 and P2; no significant change for GPT-4o mini and Gemini. No numeric values are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Adjustments made in the P1 and P2 formats improved readability for GPT-4.0, while no significant change was observed for GPT-4o mini and Gemini.

evidence.title: Readability of Retina Patient Education Materials Generated With a Large Language Model
evidence.comparator_used: Default GPT-4 generated patient education text without a reading-level instruction
evidence.outcome: Readability (ARLCalc consensus grade level) of GPT-4 generated patient education text
evidence.effect: GPT-4 Enhanced (prompted for sixth-grade level) 8.66 (± 0.87) vs GPT-4 Response (default) 12.37 (± 0.97); significant difference across the 4 groups (P < .001)
evidence.tradeoff: Output still exceeded the requested sixth-grade level. Accuracy of the simplified text was not reported as assessed.
evidence.quote: The ARLCalc scores for the ASRS Fact Sheet, GPT-4 Response, GPT-4 Enhanced, and ASRS Enhanced responses were 12.85 (± 0.89), 12.37 (± 0.97), 8.66 (± 0.87), and 9.37 (± 1.09), respectively.

evidence.title: Utilizing Large Language Models to Simplify Radiology Reports: a comparative analysis of ChatGPT3.5, ChatGPT4.0, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing
evidence.comparator_used: Prompts without the added patient-recipient or 7th-grade reading-level context
evidence.outcome: Simplification/readability performance of ChatGPT models
evidence.effect: Specifying user as a patient or requesting simplification at the 7th grade level performed best for ChatGPT models; no numerical readability scores reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: The ChatGPT models performed best when additional context was provided (i.e., specifying user as a patient or requesting simplification at the 7th grade level).

controls.question: Should the AI adapt its language, format and depth to each patient's literacy, age or stated preference?
controls.control: Adjust AI output reading level, depth, format and tone to each user's literacy, education, age or preference, including on-request simplification.
controls.comparator: One fixed text-only output for all users
controls.aim: Make AI tools usable for low-literacy, older or cognitively impaired patients
variants: Follow-up 'explain more simply' request after first answer, monitoring information quality
controls.family_label: native-language processing, translation or back-translation, simplification, reading-level control
tradeoffs: Output readability fell into 3 broad tiers (easy, medium, difficult) rather than 4 distinct levels. GPT-3.5 largely failed to reach the lower-grade targets, and GPT-4 missed the 6th-grade FKRE target.

34.8% of Bard's simplified responses were graded as less comprehensive than its initial responses. Comprehensiveness was similar for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Some simplified responses still exceeded the 6th grade target.

evidence.title: ChatGPT-4o as a digital health tool for diabetes technology education: insights on reliability, quality, and readability
evidence.comparator_used: Original ChatGPT-4o responses to the same five questions, before the 'explain in simpler terms' prompt modification (one fixed output)
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKGL, FRE) of responses before vs after simplification prompt
evidence.effect: Mean FKGL fell to 4.9 and mean FRE rose to 79.0, versus baseline English responses with mean FKGL 10.5, GFI 11.1 and FRE 37.8 (college-level literacy); content reported as unaltered
evidence.quote: Prompting simplification improved readability significantly (mean FKGL: 4.9; FRE: 79.0), without altering content.

evidence.title: Evaluation of Generative Language Models in Personalizing Medical Information: Instrument Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Outputs across the different input education levels (6th grade, 8th grade, high school, bachelor's) for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, scored against target readability; no single fixed-output arm
evidence.outcome: Readability (FKRE and FKGL) of LLM output compared with the prespecified patient education level
evidence.effect: GPT-3.5 FKGL means were 9.08, 10.27, 13.4 and 13.74 for 6th grade, 8th grade, high school and bachelor's, and it aligned with the target only at the bachelor's level. GPT-4 FKGL means were 6.3, 6.7, 11.09 and 17.03 and it met the target for all groups except the 6th-grade FKRE average. Both models showed significant differences in FKRE and FKGL across education levels (P<.001 for most comparisons).
evidence.tradeoff: Output readability fell into 3 broad tiers (easy, medium, difficult) rather than 4 distinct levels. GPT-3.5 largely failed to reach the lower-grade targets, and GPT-4 missed the 6th-grade FKRE target.
evidence.quote: GLMs can change the structure and readability of medical text outputs according to input-specified education.

evidence.title: Is ChatGPT a trusted source of information for total hip and knee arthroplasty patients?
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT's original response to each question, before the follow-up request to simplify
evidence.outcome: Reading grade level of responses (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level)
evidence.effect: Easier responses had a mean FKGL of 11.14 (95% CI 10.57 to 11.71) versus 12.15 (95% CI 11.45 to 12.85) for original responses (t = 2.204; p = 0.029).
evidence.quote: There was a significantly lower FKGL (t = 2.204; p = 0.029) for easier responses (11.14; 95% CI 10.57 to 11.71) than original responses (12.15; 95% CI 11.45 to 12.85).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence Can Answer Postoperative Questions About Distal Radius Fractures-But Can Patients Understand the Answers?
evidence.venue: Journal of hand surgery global online
evidence.comparator_used: Original default responses to the same five questions, before the follow-up request to simplify the response
evidence.outcome: Reading level of AI answers (Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease Score and Grade Level) after a simplification request
evidence.effect: Default answers had Flesch-Kincaid Reading Ease Scores of 35.8-41.4 and Grade Levels of 10.5-12.1. After simplification, Gemini's reading level was unchanged, ChatGPT improved to a seventh-grade level, and Copilot improved to an eighth-grade level.
evidence.quote: After simplification, Gemini's reading level remained unchanged, whereas ChatGPT improved to that of a seventh-grade reading level and Copilot improved to that of an eighth-grade reading level.

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering and Follow-Up Questioning Improves the Readability of Spine Surgery Questions in Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline single response without follow-up clarification (phase 1)
evidence.outcome: Readability of ChatGPT responses after a follow-up clarification question (phase 1.5)
evidence.effect: Follow-up clarification questions were more effective than complex rule-based prompts; the abstract gives no phase 1.5 versus baseline numbers
evidence.quote: Follow-up clarification questions and simplified prompt engineering were more effective than complex rule-based prompts.

evidence.title: Large language models and bariatric surgery patient education: a comparative readability analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, and online institutional resources
evidence.comparator_used: Initial (unsimplified) LLM responses to the same bariatric surgery FAQs, before the follow-up prompt to improve readability
evidence.outcome: Readability of LLM-generated patient education responses (validated readability formulas)
evidence.effect: Initial LLM and institutional responses ranged from 9th grade to college graduate level; simplified LLM responses ranged from 6th grade to college freshman, a significant improvement. GPT-4 simplified responses were most readable (6th to 9th grade). Accuracy was similar between initial and simplified responses for all LLMs.
evidence.tradeoff: 34.8% of Bard's simplified responses were graded as less comprehensive than its initial responses. Comprehensiveness was similar for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Some simplified responses still exceeded the 6th grade target.
evidence.quote: Simplified responses from LLMs had significantly improved readability, with reading levels ranging from 6th grade to college freshman.
