controls.question: Should we use LLM or machine translation for written patient materials and questionnaires instead of professional translators?
controls.control: Use machine-generated (LLM or MT) translation of written patient materials, results and questionnaires, with back-translation or human checks.
controls.comparator: Professional human translation of the same written materials
controls.aim: Deliver accurate translated materials faster and at lower cost
variants: AI as one forward translation alongside one human translation
Prompts augmented with medical term definitions, synonyms and multilingual variants
controls.family_label: native-language processing, translation or back-translation, simplification, reading-level control
tradeoffs: The two radiologists differed substantially (poor inter-rater agreement), so the preference for LLM translation was not consistent across raters.

The ChatGPT-4 version needed human quality control (an expert corrected outdated terminology and grammar) and face validation to reach parity. Earlier prompt versions produced omissions, hallucinations and altered meanings. Participants noted improper abbreviations and slightly less detail. Authors say ChatGPT-4 saves time and cost, but this was not measured. Findings are from one language pair and a small sample.

evidence.title: Blinded Radiologist and LLM-Based Evaluation of LLM-Generated Japanese Translations of Chest CT Reports: Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Human-edited Japanese translation of the same chest CT reports
evidence.outcome: Blinded radiologist pairwise preference on terminology accuracy, readability, overall quality and authenticity of LLM-generated (DeepSeek-V3.2) versus human-edited Japanese translations
evidence.effect: Radiologist 1 rated terminology as equivalent in 59% of cases and favored the LLM translation for readability (51%) and overall quality (51%). Radiologist 2 rated readability as equivalent in 75% of cases and favored the human-edited translation for overall quality (40% vs 21%).
evidence.tradeoff: The two radiologists differed substantially (poor inter-rater agreement), so the preference for LLM translation was not consistent across raters.
evidence.quote: Radiologist 1 rated terminology as equivalent in 59% of cases and favored the LLM translation for readability (51%) and overall quality (51%).

evidence.title: Comparing ChatGPT-4 and Human Translation of an Outcome Questionnaire: A Randomized, Double-Blinded Non-inferiority Study
evidence.comparator_used: Traditional human forward-backward translation with expert committee review (English to Danish) of the Abdominal Hernia-Q questionnaire
evidence.outcome: Participant Likert ratings (1-5) of readability, comprehension, appropriate language and overall opinion; preferred version; ability to guess which version was AI-translated
evidence.effect: Before face validation (n=20), human translation was rated higher on all four outcomes. Medians were ChatGPT-4 4 vs human 5; p=0.008 readability, 0.004 understandability, 0.001 appropriate language, 0.002 overall. 18/20 (90%) preferred the human version and 18/20 (90%) correctly guessed which was AI. After face validation (n=18), there were no significant differences. Readability median 5 vs 5, p=0.341; understandability 5 vs 5, p=0.082; appropriate language 5 vs 5, p=0.359; overall 4 vs 5, p=0.100. 9 (50%) preferred human, 2 (11%) ChatGPT-4, 7 (39%) had no preference. 12/18 (67%) still correctly guessed the AI version.
evidence.tradeoff: The ChatGPT-4 version needed human quality control (an expert corrected outdated terminology and grammar) and face validation to reach parity. Earlier prompt versions produced omissions, hallucinations and altered meanings. Participants noted improper abbreviations and slightly less detail. Authors say ChatGPT-4 saves time and cost, but this was not measured. Findings are from one language pair and a small sample.
evidence.quote: After face validation, there were no significant differences between the assessments of the two versions of the questionnaire, their guesses were less accurate, and no significant difference in their preference was observed.

evidence.title: Patient-friendly simplification and translation of neuroradiology impressions using artificial intelligence
evidence.comparator_used: Manual translation of simplified impressions, assessed by certified interpreters
evidence.outcome: Translation quality of Spanish translations of simplified impressions, as rated by certified interpreters
evidence.effect: Machine and manual translations were statistically indistinguishable; no numbers given in the abstract.

tradeoffs: Benefit seen only with the interruptive display; noninterruptive CDS had a lower rate than baseline. Prior-year comparison was descriptive and non-randomized. No 30-day suicide events occurred in either arm, and the trial was not powered for them.
42.3% of called patients were not reached; model performance fell in the prospective test (AUROC 0.65 to 0.61) due to data drift

Algorithm PPV was only 0.18 (273/1512 presentations accepted by specialists). Each case needed specialist chart review, adding burden in busy primary care practices. Only 50.7% of notified patients had a consultation ordered and 26.1% completed one. Barriers such as patient disinterest and scheduling limited the effect on completed consultations.

Poor adherence to the enhanced hand hygiene component. Of 17 practitioners interviewed, 6 ignored the BPAs and 10 could not recall their content, with signs of alert fatigue. Pharmacists engaged consistently with the alerts. Residual confounding and concurrent stewardship initiatives cannot be excluded.

Algorithms using CXR and AI had the highest total cost, driven by ultraportable X-ray and AI licence costs (US$75000 and US$9000) and Xpert cartridges. Cost per case was higher than any-symptom screening in the main analysis. Asymptomatic TB was only about 10% of cases in this population.

Most of the gain came from workflow standardization (consistent prep/wrap time inclusion, vendor-recommended Epic settings), which alone approached ML-level accuracy. The ML model added only a small further MAE reduction (20.1 to 19.8 min), with the largest gains in high-variability services.

evidence.title: Risk Model-Guided Clinical Decision Support for Suicide Screening: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Prior-year baseline (standard of care) rate of documented suicide risk assessment in the same clinics, descriptive comparison; also compared with noninterruptive CDS, both of which used the risk-model trigger
evidence.outcome: Documented suicide risk assessment rate in model-flagged encounters vs the prior-year baseline
evidence.effect: 22% (63 of 289 encounters, interruptive arm) vs 8% (64 of 832 encounters) in the prior year; noninterruptive arm 4% (11 of 307), below baseline. Risk-model flagging limited screening prompts to 8% of all 7732 encounters.
evidence.tradeoff: Benefit seen only with the interruptive display; noninterruptive CDS had a lower rate than baseline. Prior-year comparison was descriptive and non-randomized. No 30-day suicide events occurred in either arm, and the trial was not powered for them.
evidence.quote: Compared with a study-period rate of 22% (63 of 289) encounters, the same clinical settings had a baseline suicide risk assessment rate of 8% (64 of 832 encounters) in the prior year.

evidence.title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial

evidence.effect: High-risk encounters: unadjusted SIC rate 3.4% (59/1754) in the control period vs 13.5% (510/3765) in the intervention period; aOR 2.62 (95% CI 1.84-3.72). All encounters: aOR 2.09 (1.53-2.87). Non-high-risk encounters: aOR 2.07 (1.52-2.82).
evidence.quote: The intervention was associated with significant increases in SICs among all patient encounters (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.09 [95% CI, 1.53–2.87]; P < .001), those with high-risk patients (aOR, 2.62 [95% CI, 1.84–3.72]; P < .001), and those with non–high-risk patients (aOR, 2.07 [95% CI, 1.52–2.82]; P < .001).

evidence.title: Randomized Pilot of a Clinical Decision Support Tool to Increase Suicide Screening for at-Risk Primary Care Patients With Opioid Use Disorder

evidence.quote: Over a mean follow-up of 249 days, 20.3% of intervention patients and 17.4% of control patients had at least 1 Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale completed in the next 14 days (p=0.70).

evidence.title: From prediction to practice: machine learning models and real-world interventions for magnetic resonance imaging appointment no-shows in a hospital setting

evidence.title: Using a Machine-Learning Algorithm to Identify Palliative Care Needs in a Primary Care Population: A Pilot Study
evidence.comparator_used: Usual care without a referral notification: patients in the control arm were also flagged by the algorithm and reviewed by palliative specialists, but their PCPs were not messaged, so they could still be referred through usual pathways.
evidence.outcome: Time to 0.1% of the primary care population receiving a palliative care consultation (primary outcome); time to consultation being ordered. Secondary outcomes were time to advance care planning note and time to palliative care ICD-10 code.
evidence.effect: Consultation completed: 60.9 (47.8–79.4) vs 71.8 (50.9–103.8) days, posterior probability of a shorter time with intervention 0.88. Consultation ordered: 42.8 (34.5–54.2) vs 63.9 (46.8–90.1) days, probability >0.99. Advance care planning note: median effect 1.04 (0.81–1.35), probability 0.64. Palliative care ICD-10 code: 1.03 (0.87–1.24), probability 0.64.
evidence.tradeoff: Algorithm PPV was only 0.18 (273/1512 presentations accepted by specialists). Each case needed specialist chart review, adding burden in busy primary care practices. Only 50.7% of notified patients had a consultation ordered and 26.1% completed one. Barriers such as patient disinterest and scheduling limited the effect on completed consultations.
evidence.quote: For the primary outcome of time to a palliative care consultation, the median (95% credible interval) time to 0.1% of the primary care adult population receiving the consultation was 60.9 (47.8–79.4) days for the intervention, as compared with 71.8 (50.9–103.8) days for the control (posterior probability of a shorter time with the intervention, 0.88; Fig. 2 ).

evidence.title: Prediction-Augmented Shared Decision-Making and Lung Cancer Screening Uptake
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation period under standard care (clinical reminders and USPSTF eligibility criteria), in an interrupted time series
evidence.outcome: Lung cancer screening uptake, and benefit-based uptake (high-benefit vs intermediate-benefit persons)
evidence.effect: Benefit-based LCS OR 1.03 (0.82-1.31) pre-implementation, 1.81 (1.34-2.46) during implementation, 1.55 (1.41-1.72) post-implementation. By the final month, predicted screening probability was 24.8% for high-benefit vs 15.8% for intermediate-benefit persons (mean absolute difference 9.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.6%-16.5%). Overall uptake rose 6% per month. This is an uncontrolled before-after design and other site initiatives may have contributed to the overall rise.
evidence.quote: The association between predicted benefit on LCS uptake was greater after tool implementation; that is, more benefit-based LCS.

evidence.title: Guiding Clostridioides difficile Infection Prevention Efforts in a Hospital Setting With AI
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-AI period (Sept 2021 to Aug 2022) without the AI-guided bundle, compared with the post-AI period (2023) after a 4-month rollout; pre-post quasi-experimental design with matching adjustment
evidence.outcome: CDI incidence (primary); CDI-associated antimicrobial use (secondary)
evidence.effect: CDI incidence 5.76 vs 5.65 per 10 000 patient-days, absolute difference -0.11 (95% CI -1.43 to 1.18; P = .85). Piperacillin-tazobactam -9.64 days of therapy per 1000 days present (95% CI -12.93 to -6.28; P < .001), clindamycin -1.04 (95% CI -1.60 to -0.47; P = .03), ampicillin-sulbactam -2.82 (P = .03). Piperacillin-tazobactam relative reduction 16.8% (95% CI 8.0%-24.6%) in AI-alerted high-risk patients, with no significant change in low-risk patients.
evidence.tradeoff: Poor adherence to the enhanced hand hygiene component. Of 17 practitioners interviewed, 6 ignored the BPAs and 10 could not recall their content, with signs of alert fatigue. Pharmacists engaged consistently with the alerts. Residual confounding and concurrent stewardship initiatives cannot be excluded.
evidence.quote: In this quality improvement study, although the implementation of an AI-guided infection prevention bundle for CDI was not associated with a significant reduction in CDI incidence, it was associated with reductions in the use of CDI-associated antimicrobials, demonstrating the potential of AI-guided antimicrobial stewardship.

evidence.title: Implementation costs and cost-effectiveness of ultraportable chest X-ray with artificial intelligence in active case finding for tuberculosis in Nigeria
evidence.comparator_used: Symptom-only screening algorithms (cough ≥2 weeks; any symptom) for deciding who gets Xpert testing
evidence.outcome: Bacteriologically-confirmed TB cases detected, cost per case detected and ICER in active case finding
evidence.effect: Abnormality ≥0.30 OR any symptom detected 85 cases at US$773 per case (total US$65704). Cough ≥2 weeks detected 34 cases at US$1198 per case (US$40740). Any symptom detected 77 cases at US$636 per case (US$48939). Versus the cough ≥2 weeks baseline, the ICER was US$191 per additional case for any symptom and US$2096 for Abnormality ≥0.30 OR any symptom. CXR-AI-only algorithms (≥0.30: 81 cases, ≥0.50: 76 cases) were dominated. CXR-AI cost per case fell below any-symptom screening only when asymptomatic TB exceeded about 30% of cases.
evidence.tradeoff: Algorithms using CXR and AI had the highest total cost, driven by ultraportable X-ray and AI licence costs (US$75000 and US$9000) and Xpert cartridges. Cost per case was higher than any-symptom screening in the main analysis. Asymptomatic TB was only about 10% of cases in this population.
evidence.quote: Compared to traditional symptom screening, using CXR and AI or combination with symptoms detects more cases at lower cost per case detected.

evidence.title: Development and Implementation of a Machine Learning Model for Prediction of Surgical Case Duration
evidence.venue: Joint Commission journal on quality and patient safety
evidence.comparator_used: Existing scheduling practices: originally scheduled duration, historical averages, and Epic's CDE tool (user-adjusted and vendor-recommended configurations)
evidence.outcome: Surgical case duration estimation accuracy (MAE, bias, proportion within ±30 min or ±10%)
evidence.effect: Baseline scheduling: MAE 35.3 min, MSE bias -31 min, f30min 0.52, f10% 0.09. Standardized workflow with vendor-recommended Epic settings: MAE 20.1 min, f30min 0.81, f10% 0.37. ORchestra ML model: MAE 19.8 min, bias +1.2 min, fewer overscheduling outliers.
evidence.tradeoff: Most of the gain came from workflow standardization (consistent prep/wrap time inclusion, vendor-recommended Epic settings), which alone approached ML-level accuracy. The ML model added only a small further MAE reduction (20.1 to 19.8 min), with the largest gains in high-variability services.
evidence.quote: The ORchestra ML model further reduced error (MAE = 19.8 min), eliminated systematic bias (+1.2 min), and decreased overscheduling outliers, with the largest gains observed in high-variability services.

evidence.title: Machine Learning for Targeted Advance Care Planning in Cancer Patients: A Quality Improvement Study
evidence.venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-intervention usual care without model-based identification of high-mortality-risk patients
evidence.outcome: Documented ACP conversations for patients flagged high-risk (increased) and end-of-life care outcomes (unchanged)
evidence.effect: ACP documented in 2.3% preintervention vs 80.5% postintervention (P<0.001); no differences in LOS, hospice referral, code status change, ICU use, readmissions, ED visits, or deaths
evidence.tradeoff: No impact on EOL care outcomes; single-site, small cohorts, before/after design
evidence.quote: ACP conversations were documented for 2.3% of hospitalizations preintervention vs. 80.5% postintervention (P<0.001), and if the attending physician notified was a palliative care specialist (4.1% vs. 84.6%) or oncologist (0% vs. 76.3%) (P<0.001).

evidence.title: Incidence of cardiac arrest following implementation of a predictive analytics display in a pediatric intensive care unit
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation period (18 months before the CoMET risk score display), with no risk score display
evidence.outcome: Incidence of PICU cardiac arrest events per 1000 patient days, and arrests with versus without return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC)
evidence.effect: Overall arrest rate fell from 3.0 (95% CI 2.0-4.4) to 2.4 (95% CI 1.6-3.5) per 1000 patient days, a non-significant decrease. Arrests without ROSC fell from 1.4 (95% CI 0.7-2.4) to 0.4 (95% CI 0.1-0.9) per 1000 patient days (incidence rate difference 1.0, 95% CI 0.13-1.8), about 7 fewer per year. Arrests with ROSC rose 50% (p = 0.025). Case fatality (42.5%) and ECLS use did not differ between periods.
evidence.tradeoff: Alert burden and protocol adherence were not measured. One or both scores exceeded 4 about 4.7% of the time, roughly 21 instances per day. The design was a single-centre, unadjusted pre-post comparison.
evidence.quote: The cardiac arrest incidence rate dropped from 3.0 events per 1000 patient days (95% CI 2.0–4.4) in the pre-CoMET period to 2.4 events per 1000 patient days (95% CI 1.6–3.5) in the post-CoMET period ( Fig. 2 ).

evidence.title: Continuous predicted risks should be retained when deploying clinical prediction models
evidence.comparator_used: Risk groups alone (categorized or dichotomized predicted risk, without ranking by continuous probability) under resource constraints
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value, sensitivity and mean rank of true positives when prioritizing patients under resource constraints (simulation, plus real data from a Singaporean emergency department)
evidence.effect: No numeric values in the abstract. Ranking by continuous predicted risk outperformed risk groups alone. The benefit grew with model discrimination and outcome prevalence, was robust to poor calibration, and was greatest when resource constraints were highest.
evidence.quote: Using predicted probabilities to rank patients by predicted risk led to model performance benefits when compared to risk groups alone.

evidence.title: Improving ART Retention Through Machine Learning–Guided Targeting of Interventions: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study in Lilongwe, Malawi
evidence.comparator_used: Simulated baseline retention among the same high-risk patients with no intervention (not universal or random allocation)
evidence.outcome: Twelve-month ART retention among patients classified as high risk by the ML model (n = 512)
evidence.effect: Baseline retention 44.1%. Combined package raised it to 64.0% (RR = 1.45; p < 0.001), an absolute gain of 19.9 percentage points. Individual interventions: Expert Client support 55.0% (RR = 1.25), two-way texting 52.7% (RR = 1.19). Among newly initiated patients retention rose from 43.0% to 58.9% (RR = 1.37), and among clinically unstable patients from 28.3% to 39.1% (RR = 1.38).
evidence.tradeoff: 46% of high-risk patients remained hard to retain after multiple interventions. Their expected retention rose only from about 0.15 to 0.20, and it was worst among patients who were virally unsuppressed, had depressive symptoms, or were younger. Effects among adolescents were more modest (34.3% to 45.6%; RR = 1.33). Results come from a simulation that used meta-analytic effect sizes.
evidence.quote: Machine learning–guided targeting of ART retention interventions can substantially improve retention outcomes, particularly when interventions are combined.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of screening protocols to reduce MRSA colonization in a pediatric hospital
evidence.venue: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
evidence.comparator_used: Adding universal biweekly screening to existing protocols (uniform screening allocation), in an individual-based model calibrated to an Italian pediatric hospital
evidence.outcome: Incidence of MRSA colonizations versus number of screening tests
evidence.effect: Biweekly screening reduced colonization incidence by about 33% with a 56% increase in screening tests; ML-targeted screening achieved comparable reductions with only a 20% additional screening effort.
evidence.tradeoff: Targeted screening still required about 20% more screening tests than existing protocols. Results come from a simulation model, not a prospective trial.
evidence.quote: However, a targeted screening of patients selected by a trained machine learning classifier would achieve comparable reductions with only a 20% additional screening effort.

evidence.title: Combining Machine Learning Models and Screening to Enhance Suicide Risk Identification for American Indian Patients: Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.comparator_used: ASQ screening alone (universal screening of ED visits), versus ML risk model at high/medium thresholds, and ML plus ASQ in parallel or in series
evidence.outcome: Identification of patients who went on to suicide attempt or death within 90 days (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV)
evidence.effect: ML medium-risk threshold alone: sensitivity 0.782, specificity 0.751, PPV 0.012, NPV 0.999. ML high-risk threshold alone: sensitivity 0.429, specificity 0.955, PPV 0.035. ASQ alone: sensitivity 0.178, specificity 0.970, PPV 0.022, NPV 0.997. Parallel ML medium-risk plus ASQ: sensitivity 0.795, specificity 0.742, PPV 0.012. Serial ML high-risk then ASQ: PPV 0.050, sensitivity 0.129.
evidence.tradeoff: The medium-risk ML threshold had lower specificity (0.751 vs 0.970) and very low PPV (0.012), which implies many false positives. Serial testing raised PPV but cut sensitivity to 0.129 and was described as often infeasible. Real-world workflow fit must be balanced against statistical accuracy.
evidence.quote: The ML medium-risk threshold alone identified the most true positives (sensitivity: 0.782, 95% CI 0.648-0.915; specificity: 0.751, 95% CI 0.725-0.777; positive predictive value [PPV]: 0.012, 95% CI 0.009-0.014; negative predictive value [NPV]: 0.999, 95% CI 0.998-0.999) in comparison to the ML high-risk threshold alone (sensitivity: 0.429, 95% CI 0.287-0.572; specificity: 0.955, 95% CI 0.948-0.961; PPV: 0.035, 95% CI 0.022-0.048; NPV: 0.998, 95% CI 0.997-0.999) or the ASQ alone (sensitivity: 0.178, 95% CI 0.073-0.282; specificity: 0.970, 95% CI 0.968-0.971; PPV: 0.022, 95% CI 0.010-0.034; NPV: 0.997, 95% CI 0.996-0.998).

evidence.title: A clinical prediction model to support risk-adapted fibrinogen monitoring during tigecycline therapy: multicenter development and validation
evidence.comparator_used: Uniform fibrinogen monitoring of all patients (decision-curve analysis of model-guided monitoring against default monitoring strategies)
evidence.outcome: Net benefit of monitoring-intensity stratification for fibrinogen deterioration (decline of at least 50% from baseline and/or nadir below 1.5 g/L) during tigecycline therapy
evidence.effect: Decision-curve analysis favored model-guided monitoring at prespecified threshold probabilities after recalibration. Optimism-corrected AUCs were 0.755 (development), 0.731 (external validation) and 0.714 (prospective validation); the AUC was 0.693 in the full prospective eligible cohort (N=319). No net-benefit figures were given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Discrimination attenuated in the full prospective cohort (AUC 0.693). Calibration drift meant local recalibration was needed before implementation or threshold-based use in new settings.
evidence.quote: After recalibration, decision-curve analysis favored model-guided monitoring at prespecified threshold probabilities.

evidence.title: Automated daily adaptation for breast cancer radiotherapy: benefits of deep learning-driven dose prediction workflow for CBCT-based adaptation
evidence.comparator_used: Non-adapted (original scheduled) plan on daily anatomy; selective replanning guided by a DL dose-prediction criterion, with daily replanning of every fraction discussed as the other alternative
evidence.outcome: PTV V38.05 Gy coverage and OAR doses when only fractions flagged by the DL-prediction criterion were replanned
evidence.effect: About 25% of fractions were flagged for replanning, giving a 1.2 pp increase in PTV V38.05 Gy and reduced OAR doses. Daily adaptation of all fractions raised the share of fractions meeting PTV V38.05 Gy >95% from 35% to 93%.
evidence.tradeoff: Daily adaptation may not benefit all patients on all fractions. Selective replanning of about 25% of fractions is proposed to optimize clinical resource use. The study did not report a direct head-to-head comparison of selective versus all-fraction replanning.
evidence.quote: Using an adaptation criterion based on DL prediction, approximately 25% of fractions were identified for replanning, resulting in a 1.2 pp increase in PTVV38.05 Gyand reduced organs at risk (OAR) doses.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-driven forecasting and shift optimization for pediatric emergency department crowding
evidence.comparator_used: Fixed, existing physician staffing schedule without forecast-based shift optimization
evidence.outcome: Patient-to-physician ratio during peak shifts
evidence.effect: Staffing adjusted in 69 of 84 shifts, physician allocation increased by up to 30.4% during peak hours, patient-to-physician ratio reduced by an average of 4.32 patients (8-16 shift) and 4.40 patients (16-24 shift)
evidence.quote: This adjustment reduced the patient-to-physician ratio by an average of 4.32 patients during the 8-16 shift and 4.40 patients during the 16-24 shift.

evidence.title: Decision Curve Analysis for Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Next-Day Transfer Out of ICU
evidence.comparator_used: Review-all, review-none, and a simple clinical rule
evidence.outcome: Net benefit (decision curve analysis) of model-triggered chart review for next-day ICU transfer, and feasible trial-recruitment yield under an 8-hour daily limit
evidence.effect: Model-guided strategies had higher net benefit than all comparators across thresholds (ROC AUC 0.80-0.84). At a feasible threshold of 0.23 the model flagged ~23 charts/day and yielded ~1.23 enrollments/day under conservative eligibility and consent assumptions.
evidence.tradeoff: Review workload had to fit an 8-hour daily time constraint covering chart review and consent effort; the threshold was chosen to be feasible within that limit.
evidence.quote: Across thresholds, model guided strategies outperformed review-all, review-none, and a simple clinical rule.

controls.question: Should the LLM do first-pass chart abstraction or coding with staff verifying it, rather than fully manual or fully automated work?
controls.control: Use the LLM for first-pass data extraction, abstraction, terminology mapping or code assignment, with trained staff confirming or correcting outputs.
controls.comparator: Fully manual or double-manual abstraction and coding, or unreviewed automated output
controls.aim: Cut abstraction and coding effort while keeping data and billing accuracy
variants: Humans review only discordant cases instead of double manual abstraction
AI-suggested ICD, DRG, CPT or SNOMED codes verified by human coders
Annotation and terminology mapping with human confirmation
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Satisfaction varied by model and coder background: HAN users were less likely to give positive or neutral ratings, and coders with <10 years of experience and Gen Y were the least satisfied. One late-career coder withdrew because they would not adopt the AI interface. Weekly rotation may be confounded by time, and the rotation was truncated by an ICD-10-CM version transition. Accuracy was not directly compared in the trial.

The comparison is indicative only. Manual sessions used easier, more frequent concepts from the training data (only 1.7 needed further data analysis versus 16.8 in ArcMAP sessions). There was a single informatician, three manual sessions, and considerable variation between ArcMAP sessions. The suggestions came from a small BERT-based embedding model, not an LLM.

Preannotation had a few false negative and false positive errors on PHONE (F1 0.9667 vs 1) and ADDRESS (F1 0.9231 vs 1). Overall precision was slightly lower (0.9958 vs 0.9985). The model was a BiLSTM-CRF with RoBERTa embeddings, not an LLM. A single annotator did the work, and rounds were not randomized (the first 5 were without preannotation, the last 5 with).
Residual risks of model hallucination, edge-case misclassification, and workflow overreliance, requiring continuous monitoring and human intervention
The MLLMs hallucinated often. ChatGPT-4o gave incorrect HPO IDs in 57.3% (67/117) of cases and fabricated terms in 34.2% (40/117). The open-source Llama models had incorrect IDs in 82-98% of cases.

evidence.title: Evaluating real-world deployment of an HL7-CDA-aligned LLM for ICD-10-CM coding
evidence.comparator_used: Manual coding by certified coding specialists without AI assistance (control workflow in a randomized weekly rotation)
evidence.outcome: Coding time per discharge summary (RQ1) and coder satisfaction
evidence.effect: Across 10,688 coded summaries, all three AI-assisted workflows (HAN, PubMedGPT-2, BioMistral) were faster than manual coding (Games-Howell, all p < 0.001). PubMedGPT-2 gave the largest time reduction, followed by BioMistral and HAN. The text gives no mean times in seconds. Workflow uptake rose from 37.26% to 90.59%.
evidence.tradeoff: Satisfaction varied by model and coder background: HAN users were less likely to give positive or neutral ratings, and coders with <10 years of experience and Gen Y were the least satisfied. One late-career coder withdrew because they would not adopt the AI interface. Weekly rotation may be confounded by time, and the rotation was truncated by an ICD-10-CM version transition. Accuracy was not directly compared in the trial.
evidence.quote: All three AI-assisted workflows yielded faster completion times than manual coding (Games-Howell, all p < 0.001).

evidence.title: An agentic AI system enhances clinical detection of immunotherapy toxicities: a multi-phase validation study
evidence.comparator_used: Manual annotation by clinical trial staff without agentic assistance (randomized crossover)
evidence.outcome: Annotation time, complete-match accuracy and inter-annotator agreement
evidence.effect: Annotation time reduced by 40% (P < 0.001); complete-match accuracy OR 1.45 (95% CI 1.01–2.09; P = 0.045); Krippendorff's α rose from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85
evidence.quote: In a randomized crossover study of clinical trial staff (17 participants, 316 observations), agentic assistance reduced annotation time by 40% (P < 0.001), increased complete-match accuracy (OR 1.45; 95% CI 1.01–2.09; P = 0.045), and improved inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff’s α from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85).

evidence.title: ArcMAP - ML assisted medical concept mapping to accelerate NHS data standardization
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual concept mapping in Microsoft Excel by the same informatician
evidence.outcome: Number of laboratory test concepts mapped per 30-minute session
evidence.effect: ArcMAP sessions mapped 64.6 ± 30 concepts on average, against 31.7 ± 0.9 in manual sessions, an estimated >2-fold efficiency increase.
evidence.tradeoff: The comparison is indicative only. Manual sessions used easier, more frequent concepts from the training data (only 1.7 needed further data analysis versus 16.8 in ArcMAP sessions). There was a single informatician, three manual sessions, and considerable variation between ArcMAP sessions. The suggestions came from a small BERT-based embedding model, not an LLM.
evidence.quote: In contrast, during the manual mapping sessions without ArcMAP, only 31.7 ± 0.9 ( Supplementary Table 2 ) concepts were mapped on average, resulting in an estimated >2-fold increase in efficiency when using ArcMAP.

evidence.title: Web-Based Application Based on Human-in-the-Loop Deep Learning for Deidentifying Free-Text Data in Electronic Medical Records: Development and Usability Study
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual annotation of PII without model preannotation (same annotator, same 200 notes split into 10 rounds)
evidence.outcome: Annotation time and annotation accuracy (PII tagging) against a gold standard
evidence.effect: Time for 5 rounds ~58 min with preannotation vs ~98 min without; 43% faster (95% CI 33.9-52.1; P<.001). Overall micro-average recall higher by 0.013 (0.9886 vs 0.9756) and F1 higher by 0.0053 (0.9922 vs 0.9869).
evidence.tradeoff: Preannotation had a few false negative and false positive errors on PHONE (F1 0.9667 vs 1) and ADDRESS (F1 0.9231 vs 1). Overall precision was slightly lower (0.9958 vs 0.9985). The model was a BiLSTM-CRF with RoBERTa embeddings, not an LLM. A single annotator did the work, and rounds were not randomized (the first 5 were without preannotation, the last 5 with).
evidence.quote: Using preannotation during the manual annotation process resulted in a time savings of 43% and a micro- F 1 -score improvement of 0.005 compared to manual annotation performed without preannotation.

evidence.title: End-to-End Pipeline Integrating Local Small Language Models and Machine Learning for Data Extraction and Stroke Outcome Prediction in Emergency Department
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automated multi-tiered validation output without human review
evidence.outcome: Data extraction accuracy
evidence.effect: 86.0% after fully automated multi-tiered validation vs 97.0% (95% CI, 95.7% to 98.3%) following human-in-the-loop review
evidence.quote: Baseline extraction accuracy was 64.9% (95% CI, 62.0% to 67.8%), improving to 86.0% after fully automated multi-tiered validation, and further to 97.0% (95% CI, 95.7% to 98.3%) following human-in-the-loop review.

evidence.title: Next-generation multicenter studies: using artificial intelligence to automatically process unstructured health records of patients with lung cancer across multiple institutions
evidence.venue: Annals of oncology : official journal of the European Society for Medical Oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Manual abstraction of real-world data by clinical research professionals
evidence.outcome: Data extraction error rate across 28 single-answer variables (8708 datapoints); also F1 for multiple-choice variables and interinstitutional variance
evidence.effect: Error rate 7.0% with LLM vs 14.2% manual (P<0.001); F1 gene alterations 0.97 vs 0.86, comorbidities 0.86 vs 0.76, metastatic sites 0.71 vs 0.69; interinstitutional variance 0.12% vs 0.39%
evidence.quote: Across 8708 datapoints for 28 variables with only one correct answer, the LLM achieved a 7.0% error rate, outperforming manual abstraction (14.2%, P <0.001).

evidence.title: Generative and Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Medical Coding and Billing: A Human-in-the-Loop Architecture and Evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: conventional manual pipelines and fully automated (unreviewed) pipelines
evidence.outcome: coding precision, turnaround time, and audit readiness
evidence.effect: Reported as measurable improvements in coding precision, turnaround time, and audit readiness; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Residual risks of model hallucination, edge-case misclassification, and workflow overreliance, requiring continuous monitoring and human intervention
evidence.quote: Results indicate measurable improvements in coding precision, turnaround time, and audit readiness when compared to conventional manual or fully automated pipelines.

evidence.title: Optimising the paradigms of human AI collaborative clinical coding
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual clinical coding by human coders
evidence.outcome: Coding time, correction rate of EMR mistakes, and coder F1 score
evidence.effect: Coding time reduced by 40% on average; correction rates on EMR mistakes about three times better for missing codes; senior coders' F1 raised from 0.72 to more than 0.93
evidence.quote: In human evaluations, compared to manual coding, CliniCoCo reduces coding time by 40% on average and significantly improves the correction rates on EMR mistakes (e.g., three times better on missing codes).

evidence.title: A workflow utilizing general-purpose large language models for efficient structuring and data mining of bone scintigraphy narratives
evidence.comparator_used: Unaided manual structured extraction by trainees using the template alone
evidence.outcome: Processing time and extraction accuracy (global quality score and per-tier error rate) for structuring bone scintigraphy reports
evidence.effect: Total time fell 82.6% for Trainee 1 (80.72 to 14.08 min) and 74.5% for Trainee 2 (110.48 to 28.12 min). Global quality score rose from 4.84 to 4.95 (Trainee 1) and from 4.88 to 4.98 (Trainee 2), F = 14.658, P <.001. Per-tier error rate fell from 3.2% (13/410) to 1.0% (4/410) for Trainee 1 and from 2.4% (10/410) to 0.5% (2/410) for Trainee 2.
evidence.quote: With LLM assistance, the time required for Trainee 1 to complete the task decreased from 80.72 min to 14.08 min, representing an 82.6% reduction in total duration.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Large Language Model Framework for Identification of Cutaneous Immune-Related Adverse Events
evidence.comparator_used: unassisted manual review
evidence.outcome: Human-in-the-loop LLM-assisted adverse event data extraction from clinical notes: accuracy, inter-rater agreement, and average review time.
evidence.effect: F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77; kappa = 0.82 vs 0.50; reduced average review time by approximately half.
evidence.quote: Compared with unassisted manual review, the LLM-assisted workflow improved accuracy (F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen's kappa (kappa = 0.82 vs 0.50), and reduced average review time by approximately half.

evidence.title: Enhancing the Accuracy of Human Phenotype Ontology Identification: Comparative Evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Manual search of the Chinese Human Phenotype Ontology website by junior physicians, with no MLLM prompts
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of HPO term identification from patient images, compared with an expert panel standard set
evidence.effect: MLLM-assisted 67.4% (182/270) vs manual 20.4% (55/270); relative risk 3.31, 95% CI 2.58-4.25; P<.001
evidence.tradeoff: The MLLMs hallucinated often. ChatGPT-4o gave incorrect HPO IDs in 57.3% (67/117) of cases and fabricated terms in 34.2% (40/117). The open-source Llama models had incorrect IDs in 82-98% of cases.
evidence.quote: The MLLM-assisted group achieved a significantly higher accuracy rate of 67.4% (182/270) compared to 20.4% (55/270) in the manual group (relative risk 3.31, 95% CI 2.58-4.25; P<.001).

controls.question: Should experts review LLM-generated code, research documents, evidence appraisals and teaching materials before use, rather than using them unreviewed?
controls.control: Require domain experts to review, fact-check and refine LLM-drafted code, queries, rules, evidence appraisals, research documents and education content before use.
controls.comparator: Using LLM-generated artifacts without expert review
controls.aim: Prevent errors in LLM-produced technical, research and educational artifacts
variants: Analysis code, phenotype queries and decision rules
Guideline syntheses, IRB and research documents
LLM first-pass triage for systematic review or decision aid appraisal with expert confirmation
Faculty edit and select LLM-generated questions, vignettes, concept maps and trainee feedback
Separate adoption comparison: reviewed LLM drafts versus experts producing artifacts from scratch
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Expert review and iterative refinement required reviewer time (review time was recorded). Interrater reliability fell after revision (ICC 0.965 to 0.7425).
Clinician approval reduced the number of recovered values relative to the unrestricted LLM-enhanced roadmaps, in exchange for clinical relevance; it still recovered more than expert chart review.
The expert-in-the-loop workflow was much slower (about 245 vs 68 min) and needed 19 recorded human expert interventions.

evidence.title: Can a Generative Artificial Intelligence Model Be Used to Create Mass Casualty Incident Simulation Scenarios? A Feasibility Study
evidence.comparator_used: Initial LLM-generated scenarios without expert review (pre-revision scores); publicly available human-authored scenarios served as an external benchmark
evidence.outcome: Simulation Scenario Evaluation Tool (SSET) score out of 100 for MCI simulation scenarios
evidence.effect: Median SSET 78.5 (IQR 74-82) for initial LLM scenarios vs 94 (IQR 93-96) after human revision; publicly available scenarios scored 94 (IQR 93-95). Interrater ICC 0.965 before revision and 0.7425 after.
evidence.tradeoff: Expert review and iterative refinement required reviewer time (review time was recorded). Interrater reliability fell after revision (ICC 0.965 to 0.7425).
evidence.quote: Following secondary human revision and iterative refinement, the LLM-generated scenarios improved, achieving a median SSET score of 94 (IQR 93-96) with an interrater reliability ICC of 0.7425.

evidence.title: Using large language models to enhance clinically-driven missing data recovery algorithms in electronic health records
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-enhanced roadmaps using LLM-suggested auxiliary diagnoses without restriction to clinician-approved additions (also compared with the original clinician roadmap and expert chart review)
evidence.outcome: Number of missing EHR values recovered (out of 413) by roadmap-driven algorithm
evidence.effect: Expert chart reviews recovered 49 (12%); algorithms with LLM-enhanced roadmaps recommended 83-89 (20%-22%); final algorithm with clinician-approved LLM additions recovered 73 (18%).
evidence.tradeoff: Clinician approval reduced the number of recovered values relative to the unrestricted LLM-enhanced roadmaps, in exchange for clinical relevance; it still recovered more than expert chart review.
evidence.quote: The final algorithm using clinician-approved LLMs' additions offered a balance (73, 18%), expanding the original roadmap with LLMs' suggestions but only when deemed clinically relevant.

evidence.title: Feasibility analysis of generative artificial intelligence tools as a means of medical science popularization on urological diseases
evidence.comparator_used: Initial unrevised ChatGPT 4.0 generated content (no expert revision)
evidence.outcome: Expert ratings of generated urological content on comprehensiveness and conciseness (also scientificity, recency, understandability, interest)
evidence.effect: Manual revision significantly improved comprehensiveness and conciseness; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Manual revision could significantly improve the comprehensiveness and conciseness of the generated content.

evidence.title: Strategic Governance of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Algorithm Development: Formative Evaluation of the Semiautomatic Clinical Algorithm Development Framework
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automated AI clinical algorithm development (F-ACAD) without human expert review, benchmarked in a single illustrative run
evidence.outcome: Safety and clinical quality of the AI-drafted febrile seizure algorithm, plus turnaround time
evidence.effect: S-ACAD with expert oversight took about 245 min. Two external specialists found no medically inaccurate sections or critical safety errors and rated clinical validity 9.0 and 9.5 out of 10. F-ACAD took about 68 min, and its own AI critics identified 17 issues (9 high-priority). The comparison is descriptive, from a single execution with one expert and one topic.
evidence.tradeoff: The expert-in-the-loop workflow was much slower (about 245 vs 68 min) and needed 19 recorded human expert interventions.
evidence.quote: By comparison, the fully automated approach (F-ACAD) completed the task in approximately 68 minutes, but its own AI critics identified 17 issues (9 high-priority), including concerns related to emergency response clarity and standard-of-care alignment.

controls.question: Should an LLM prescreen or rank records first, with humans reviewing only flagged or top-ranked cases rather than every record?
controls.control: Use an LLM or NLP to prescreen, triage or rank records, then have clinicians review flagged or top-ranked cases.
controls.comparator: Full manual review of all records by humans
controls.aim: Reduce manual review workload without missing eligible or positive cases
variants: LLM as first-pass screener with human review of flagged cases
Related scoring workflow: humans confirm LLM-generated scores, or LLM as second assessor of human scores, compared with fully manual scoring
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Imperfect sensitivity (98.0% on the selection benchmark, 96.7% on topic-matched validation); the approach relies on audit of AI-excluded records, human oversight and programme-specific monitoring.

Specificity 14.1% (61 false positives among 71 non-IBC cases) and NPV 33.3%; human-in-the-loop time commitment remains and the authors want to minimize it. Manual effort is described as lower than traditional surveillance, but no figures are given.
Per-nodule sensitivity was numerically lower (62.9% vs 64.2%), though not significantly. Radiologists read only AI-positive examinations, so any nodule the AI misses is not reviewed.

evidence.title: Audited large language model triage for systematic review screening in national clinical guideline production: validation and prospective deployment
evidence.comparator_used: Full manual first-pass screening of all records by humans (estimated effort; locked blinded human consensus in the audit)
evidence.outcome: First-pass screening effort and missed relevant records in systematic review title/abstract screening
evidence.effect: Estimated first-pass effort fell from 415 to 34 person-days; 63,858 of 74,679 records (85.5%) were placed in the AI-excluded pool; 0 of 600 sampled AI-excluded records were confirmed false negatives; in the 680-record audit all 38 final retained records had been AI flagged, whereas blinded human consensus missed seven.
evidence.tradeoff: Imperfect sensitivity (98.0% on the selection benchmark, 96.7% on topic-matched validation); the approach relies on audit of AI-excluded records, human oversight and programme-specific monitoring.
evidence.quote: Prospective deployment screened 74,679 records, placed 63,858 (85.5%) in the AI-excluded pool and reduced estimated first-pass screening effort from 415 to 34 person-days.

evidence.title: Use of natural language processing to identify patients with inflammatory breast cancer across a health-care system
evidence.comparator_used: traditional surveillance methods (standard clinical workflows)
evidence.outcome: Identification of confirmed inflammatory breast cancer cases
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 92.2% (235 of 255 confirmed cases); 57 (22.4%) identified solely through the NLP pipeline and would have been missed by traditional surveillance
evidence.tradeoff: Specificity 14.1% (61 false positives among 71 non-IBC cases) and NPV 33.3%; human-in-the-loop time commitment remains and the authors want to minimize it. Manual effort is described as lower than traditional surveillance, but no figures are given.
evidence.quote: Of these confirmed cases, 57 (22.4%) were identified solely through the NLP pipeline and would have been missed through traditional surveillance methods.

evidence.title: Unmet Needs in Acute Hepatic Porphyria Diagnosis: A Comparative Big Data Analysis of an AI-based Human-in-the-Loop Screening Versus Standard of Care
evidence.comparator_used: Standard of care: historically suspected and diagnosed AHP cases retrieved from the hospital records, with specialist review of plausibility
evidence.outcome: Rate of clinically plausible cases (precision) and number of de-novo plausible cases
evidence.effect: 74 of 191 (38.74%) HAI cases were clinically plausible vs 28 of 107 (27.72%) SOC cases. 46 of the 74 plausible HAI cases were de-novo cases missed by SOC. The difference in precision was not statistically significant.
evidence.quote: In our study, our proposed HAI screening approach showed a higher plausibility rate in suspected cases compared to the SOC and statistical testing could not find a statistically significant difference between the screening methods.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence for Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Comparison of Utilization Scenarios
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologist interpretation of all LDCT examinations without AI
evidence.outcome: Recall rate, per-examination specificity, per-nodule sensitivity, mean interpretation time and net benefit on decision-curve analysis
evidence.effect: AI as prescreener vs no AI: recall 20.8% vs 22.1% (p=.02); mean interpretation time 143 vs 164 seconds (p=.001); per-examination specificity 90.3% vs 88.8% (p=.04); per-nodule sensitivity 62.9% vs 64.2% (p=.16, not significant). Only the prescreener scenario showed higher net benefit than interpretation without AI.
evidence.tradeoff: Per-nodule sensitivity was numerically lower (62.9% vs 64.2%), though not significantly. Radiologists read only AI-positive examinations, so any nodule the AI misses is not reviewed.
evidence.quote: Among scenarios, only AI as a prescreener demonstrated higher net benefit than interpretation without AI; AI as an assistant had the least net benefit.

controls.question: Should a clinician or qualified linguist approve AI-generated patient materials, messages and translations before patients see them?
controls.control: Require clinician, bilingual professional or health literacy expert review and editing of AI-generated patient materials, translations, consent text and responses before release.
controls.comparator: Releasing AI-generated content to patients without human review
controls.aim: Prevent inaccurate, unsafe or unreadable content and translations reaching patients
variants: Clinician review of patient responses and consent text before release (drafting itself covered in llm_draft_documentation)
Professional linguist post-editing of AI translations
Health literacy expert review of patient education materials
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Clinician review time is still required, though 72% less than clinician rewriting. LLMs showed limited TCM conceptual depth, which expert oversight is meant to address.
Clinician-led refinements decreased readability, increasing the risk of poorer post-visit patient understanding.

evidence.title: Radiologist Detection of Deficiencies in LLM-Generated Patient Communications About Radiology Reports: A Multi-Reader Study
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.comparator_used: Single-radiologist review of LLM-generated patient answers (versus dual- and triple-reader review); no unreviewed-release arm was tested
evidence.outcome: Miss rate of deficient LLM-generated patient answers (clinically significant errors and incomplete/ambiguous responses) under radiologist review
evidence.effect: Single reader missed an average of 12.4% of deficiencies; dual-reader review reduced the average miss rate to 0.6%; triple-reader review detected all deficiencies. Individual reader sensitivity ranged from 81.4% to 96.5%, and readers missed 5.6-11.1% of clinically significant errors.
evidence.quote: A single reader missed an average of 12.4% of deficiencies, whereas dual-reader review reduced the average miss rate to 0.6%; triple-reader review detected all deficiencies.

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models for simplifying non-English medical consent with clinician involvement
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-simplified consent forms released without clinician revision
evidence.outcome: Content accuracy, clarity and layperson comprehension
evidence.effect: Clinician-revised version restored accuracy, maintained clarity and achieved the highest comprehension scores; no numeric values given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Clinician revision restored accuracy while maintaining clarity and achieved the highest comprehension scores.

evidence.title: Feasibility analysis of generative artificial intelligence tools as a means of medical science popularization on urological diseases
evidence.comparator_used: Initial unrevised ChatGPT 4.0 generated content (no manual revision)
evidence.outcome: Quality ratings of AI-generated patient education content on urological diseases after manual revision versus initial output
evidence.effect: Significant improvement in comprehensiveness and conciseness after revision; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: Manual revision could significantly improve the comprehensiveness and conciseness of the generated content.

evidence.title: Physician-revised AI-generated drafts are associated with higher ratings of written explanations in end-of-life care in the intensive care unit: a scenario-based single-center cross-sectional study
evidence.comparator_used: AI-only chatbot responses with no physician revision
evidence.outcome: Ratings of medical validity (healthcare professionals) and empathy (healthcare and nonhealthcare professionals) on 5-point Likert scales
evidence.effect: Physician-revised AI drafts were rated significantly higher than AI-only responses on all three prespecified primary outcomes. Differences were larger for empathy than for medical validity. No numeric values were reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: In the primary analyses, physician-AI collaborative responses received significantly higher ratings than both physician-only and AI-only responses across all three prespecified primary outcomes.

evidence.title: Large language models versus expert clinicians in optimizing Chinese patient education materials for temporomandibular disorders: a mixed-methods study integrating readability, accuracy, actionability, and cultural adaptability
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-rewritten texts released without clinician review (Group B), with clinician-only rewriting (Group C) as a second reference
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and actionability of patient education materials, plus clinician time
evidence.effect: Human-AI collaboration accuracy 4.49, matching clinician accuracy of 4.48 (p = 1.000) and above the 3.23 reported for the lower-accuracy comparison. Actionability preserved at 95.6%. Clinician time reduced by 72%.
evidence.tradeoff: Clinician review time is still required, though 72% less than clinician rewriting. LLMs showed limited TCM conceptual depth, which expert oversight is meant to address.
evidence.quote: The human-AI collaboration model matched clinician accuracy (4.49, p = 1.000) while preserving LLM actionability (95.6%), with 72% less clinician time.

evidence.title: Clinician-supervised large language AI model after-discharge instruction generation for common emergency department presentations
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-generated instructions before physician edits
evidence.outcome: Clinical accuracy and Flesch Reading Ease readability of LLM-generated after-discharge instructions
evidence.effect: Physician edits improved accuracy but reduced objective readability scores. No numbers given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Clinician-led refinements decreased readability, increasing the risk of poorer post-visit patient understanding.
evidence.quote: Physician edits improved accuracy but paradoxically reduced objective readability scores.

evidence.title: Evaluating human-in-the-loop strategies for artificial intelligence-enabled translation of patient discharge instructions: a multidisciplinary analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Unedited ChatGPT-4o translations released without professional linguist post-editing
evidence.outcome: Linguist, clinician and family caregiver Likert ratings of translation quality
evidence.effect: Unedited ChatGPT-4o performance was variable relative to professional translations, with the poorest ratings for Armenian and Somali; linguist post-edited (human-in-the-loop) translations were comparable or often better than professional translations in all languages (e.g., Armenian overall quality 3.9 vs professional 3.6). No direct numeric ChatGPT-vs-human-in-the-loop contrast is given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4o exhibited variable performance relative to professional translations, with poorest ratings for digitally underrepresented languages (Armenian and Somali).

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Responses to Retina Questions from Either Experts, Expert-Edited Large Language Models, or Expert-Edited Large Language Models Alone
evidence.comparator_used: Unedited LLM responses (five LLMs: ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Claude 2, Bing, Bard)
evidence.outcome: Quality and empathy of responses to retina patient questions
evidence.effect: Quality: Expert + AI 3.86 ± 0.85 vs top LLM GPT-3.5 3.75 ± 0.79. Empathy: GPT-3.5 3.75 ± 0.69 vs Expert + AI 3.73 ± 0.63. Significant differences among the groups (P < 0.001 for both).
evidence.quote: For quality, Expert + AI (3.86 ± 0.85) performed the best overall while GPT-3.5 (3.75 ± 0.79) was the top performing LLM.

evidence.title: Smart Pharmaceutical Monitoring System With Personalized Medication Schedules and Self-Management Programs for Patients With Diabetes: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Unreviewed system-generated (DUMS) outputs, and ChatGPT-4 outputs, rated by senior health care professionals on a 5-point Likert scale
evidence.outcome: Expert-rated medication schedule and self-management program quality (accuracy, safety, comprehensiveness, richness)
evidence.effect: Pharmacist-refined outputs (intervention group) scored higher than DUMS and GPT-4 groups on all indicator scores; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.quote: The intervention group outperformed the DUMS and GPT-4 groups on all indicator scores.

controls.question: Should AI output be embedded in existing clinical systems rather than provided through a standalone tool?
controls.control: Embed AI outputs in the EHR, LIS or nursing systems clinicians already use, displayed where the relevant task is performed.

Adoption default: AI use set default-on versus opt-in

The gain was confounded with the POHM curriculum and faculty calibration, which were named as key drivers of adoption. Completion varied by student group, reflecting the importance of consistent faculty leadership.

evidence.title: The Implementation of a Clinical Decision Support System for Managing Drug-Disease Interactions in Outpatients with Cardiovascular and Diabetic Comorbidities: An Interventional Study at a Tertiary Hospital in Vietnam
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-intervention phase (May-Aug 2024) before the HIS-integrated CDSS and pharmacist consultation; not compared against a standalone tool
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of drug-disease interactions (absolute and relative contraindications, use-with-caution) in outpatient prescriptions
evidence.effect: Absolute contraindication prevalence decreased significantly (P < 0.05); relative contraindication fell from 0.33% to 0.01% (P < 0.05); 'use with caution' interactions fell from 0.20% to 0.13% (P < 0.05). The effect is of the combined CDSS-in-HIS plus pharmacist intervention.
evidence.quote: The integration of CDSS into HIS and pharmacist interventions were associated with significantly reduced harmful DDSIs in high-risk CV-DM patients.

evidence.title: Integrated Implementation Strategies to Promote the Use of AI-Assisted Diagnostic Software for Lung Nodule Screening in China: Process Evaluation Based on the RE-AIM Framework
evidence.comparator_used: The non-integrated ESDR data transfer tool, accessed through an external web link outside hospital systems (an internal contrast within the study, not a randomized comparison)
evidence.outcome: Disruption of routine clinical workflow and physician burden
evidence.effect: AI software integrated with PACS: 93.3% (14/15) of secondary hospital physicians said it did not interfere with routine practice. ESDR tool, not integrated: 55.6% (5/9) of respiratory physicians reported a substantial burden on daily tasks, and 5/8 (62.5%) of tertiary physicians reported workflow disruption.
evidence.tradeoff: The non-integrated ESDR tool required manual uploads and retrieval. Only 28% (7/25) of referral records were complete. Only 44.4% (4/9) of secondary physicians reviewed the final diagnostic results. Only 50% (4/8) of tertiary physicians uploaded final results.
evidence.quote: With respect to integration into clinical workflows, 93.3% (14/15) of physicians at the secondary hospital reported that the AI-assisted diagnostic software did not interfere with routine clinical practice.

evidence.title: Shifting the Paradigm: CAMBRA Adoption and Medical-Dental Integration Leveraging an Electronic Health Record
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation baseline, before the EHR-integrated CAMBRA tool (July 2022), described only as under 5% completion. The abstract does not describe the earlier workflow.
evidence.outcome: Caries risk assessment (CRA) completion rate
evidence.effect: CRA completion rose from under 5% to a peak of 89% in March 2024. Provider agreement with algorithm-generated risk levels exceeded 96% after a mandatory confirmation field was introduced in November 2023.
evidence.tradeoff: The gain was confounded with the POHM curriculum and faculty calibration, which were named as key drivers of adoption. Completion varied by student group, reflecting the importance of consistent faculty leadership.
evidence.quote: Following EHR-integrated CAMBRA tool implementation in July of 2022, CRA completion rates rose from under 5% to a peak of 89% in March of 2024.

evidence.title: Perceived Trust and Professional Identity Threat in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems: Scenario-Based Experimental Study on AI Process Design Features

evidence.title: AI-Human Hybrid Workflow Enhances Teleophthalmology for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence.comparator_used: AI system alone for MTMDR-positive screening results, before referral for in-person examination.
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity after routing AI-positive cases to retina specialist overread.
evidence.effect: AI alone PPV was 47.7%; 2-step AI-human overread increased PPV to 95.5% (95% CI, 86.7%–100%), accuracy to 97.4%, sensitivity was 95.5% (95% CI, 86.7%–100%), and specificity was 98.2% (95% CI, 94.6%–100%).
evidence.tradeoff: Requires an experienced retina specialist to overread all AI MTMDR-positive encounters before referral; no cost or latency was quantified.
evidence.quote: Under this 2-step workflow, the positive predictive value increased to 95.5% (95% CI, 86.7%–100%), along with accuracy of 97.4%, sensitivity of 95.5% (95% CI, 86.7%–100%), and specificity of 98.2% (95% CI, 94.6%–100%) ( Figs 6 , 15 ).

evidence.title: Deep learning based semi-automated model can predict lineage in patients with pituitary neuroendocrine tumors
evidence.comparator_used: uniform IHC staining and manual review of all slides
evidence.outcome: diagnostic workload and accuracy when only low-confidence cases are routed to IHC and pathologist review
evidence.effect: 68.9% reduction in IHC workload with 95.9% accuracy in the prospective cohort (p=0.610 vs full IHC/manual). Functional cohort 74.4% reduction and 99.0% accuracy. External cohort 39.3% reduction and 95.1% accuracy at cutoff 0.9.
evidence.tradeoff: Savings shrink as the cutoff is raised to maintain accuracy; escalated cases still require IHC staining (about 1,000 CNY per three-antibody panel) and manual review.
evidence.quote: The pipeline employs a dynamic confidence threshold: samples below this threshold undergo confirmatory IHC staining and manual pathological review, while those surpassing it are classified automatically.

evidence.title: Revenue-sensitive evaluation of AI-assisted ICD-10-CM coding and human-AI collaboration under dual DRG payment systems
evidence.comparator_used: Random sampling of AI-coded admissions for human review at the same 20% review rate (simulated)
evidence.outcome: Reduction in Coding Reimbursement Score (CRS) gap from human review of AI-assigned ICD-10-CM codes
evidence.effect: 43.2% CRS reduction with revenue-targeted prioritization vs 20.0% with random sampling at 20% review rate; reached 91% of the oracle bound
evidence.quote: At a 20% review rate, revenue-targeted prioritization achieved 43.2% CRS reduction versus 20.0% for random sampling, reaching 91% of the oracle bound.

evidence.title: Implementation of Delineation Error Detection Systems in Clinical Practice: Do AI-Supported Optimization and Human Preferences Meet?
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline manual slice-by-slice QA of AI delineations without system assistance (simulated on 42 head and neck cancer patients)
evidence.outcome: Time required for delineation quality assessment (simulated)
evidence.effect: Potential time savings through error and dose information; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Savings depend on per-slice analysis time staying near the current baseline
evidence.quote: The simulation study results indicate potential time savings through error and dose information, contingent on per-slice analysis time remaining near the current baseline.

evidence.title: Human-AI collaboration enhances the performance of large language models in risk of bias assessment
evidence.comparator_used: Human review of LLM output without disagreement triggering (M1 and M2 modes, where humans judge each sample)
evidence.outcome: Human intervention rate (manual workload) while keeping accuracy
evidence.effect: M3 markedly reduced intervention rates; accuracy under M2 and M3 ranged from 0.633 to 0.900 (no per-mode intervention numbers in the abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: Disagreement Trigger Mode was cost-effective for structured and moderate-reasoning tasks, but Reasoning Support Mode was more stable and practical for open-ended and highly subjective tasks.
evidence.quote: M1 showed relatively limited performance in both accuracy and intervention rate; M2 achieved the highest accuracy in most tasks; M3 markedly reduced intervention rates.

evidence.title: Evaluating an AI-assisted triage workflow for retinal diseases
evidence.comparator_used: Direct ophthalmologist review of all fundus photographs / standard human interpretation without AI-negative cases being automatically classified as negative
evidence.outcome: Ophthalmologist review workload and diagnostic sensitivity/specificity for DR, RVO, AMD
evidence.effect: Review reduced to 7.3%-8.0% of images for DR, 11.7%-11.9% for RVO, and 13.5%-16.8% for AMD. DR sensitivity decreased from 0.9168 to 0.8838 (difference, -0.0330; 95% CI, -0.0495 to -0.0165; p < 0.001) with specificity not significantly changed (0.9961 to 0.9983; p = 0.183). RVO sensitivity was unchanged (0.9807) and specificity did not change significantly (0.9985 to 0.9988; p = 0.320). AMD sensitivity decreased from 0.8570 to 0.8445 (difference, -0.0124; 95% CI, -0.0215 to -0.0033; p = 0.008), with specificity not significantly changed (0.9685 to 0.9843; p = 0.324).
evidence.tradeoff: Reduced ophthalmologist workload, but reduced sensitivity for DR and AMD, meaning some true-positive cases would go undetected and diagnosis/treatment could be delayed.
evidence.quote: AI-assisted negative-screening can reduce ophthalmologist workload across multiple retinal diseases, but with disease-specific safety trade-offs: because AI-negative images are not reviewed, reduced sensitivity for DR and AMD means a small proportion of true-positive cases would go undetected, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment for sight-threatening disease.

evidence.title: A hybrid approach to scalable real-world data curation by machine learning and human experts
evidence.comparator_used: Uniform manual abstraction of all records by clinical experts
evidence.outcome: Error rate and manual abstraction effort when only low-confidence model outputs are routed to human abstractors
evidence.effect: The hybrid approach can reduce error rates relative to manual abstraction in some cases. A cohort defined with hybrid variables had demographics comparable to one curated conventionally. No numeric values are given in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Reference-standard labels are required to calibrate the tradeoff between abstraction effort and data quality.
evidence.quote: In fact, the hybrid methodology can even reduce error rates relative to manual abstraction in some cases.

evidence.title: Extracting Clinical Guideline Information Using Two Large Language Models: Evaluation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Uniform manual review of all guideline classifications
evidence.outcome: Number of cases needing priority manual review and residual error
evidence.effect: Priority manual review fell to 2.9% (11/385) of cases, with the error rate at 0.5% (2/374).
evidence.tradeoff: The error rate increased slightly, to 0.5%, and some manual review is still required.
evidence.quote: Applying a predefined agreement-threshold strategy further reduced the number of priority manual review cases to 2.9% (11/385), although the error rate slightly increased to 0.5% (2/374).

evidence.title: Use of artificial intelligence in triaging of chest radiographs to reduce radiologists' workload
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologists interpreted all chest radiographs without DLD (full radiologist reading/no worklist reduction).
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity for positive outpatient chest radiograph findings in a simulated 50% worklist reduction where the lower half by DLD probability score was regarded as negative and the remaining radiographs were read with DLD by radiologists.
evidence.effect: Sensitivity was 82.6% (195 of 236; 95% CI: 77.5%, 87.3%) with all radiographs read without DLD versus 83.5% (197 of 236; 95% CI: 78.8%, 88.1%) in the 50% worklist reduction scenario; difference 0.8% (95% CI: - 3.8%, 5.5%), noninferiority p = 0.01. Specificity increased from 86.7% (1498 of 1728) to 90.4% (1562 of 1728), p < 0.001.
evidence.tradeoff: Legal responsibility for incorrect diagnoses based on AI-standalone interpretation remains an issue.
evidence.quote: The sensitivity was 82.6% (195 of 236; 95% CI: 77.5%, 87.3%) when readers interpreted all chest radiographs without DLD and 83.5% (197 of 236; 95% CI: 78.8%, 88.1%) in the 50% worklist reduction scenario.

evidence.title: A Human-Centered AI Framework for Efficient Labelling of ECGs From Drug Safety Trials
evidence.comparator_used: Full expert review of all DL-based QT measurements (uniform manual review)
evidence.outcome: Expert effort for ECG QT labelling while maintaining QT accuracy
evidence.effect: Only 10% of the data were reviewed per trial, mostly high-uncertainty measurements, with high QT accuracy maintained; effort significantly reduced (no numeric accuracy values in abstract)
evidence.quote: We assess its effectiveness on 3 drug safety trials and show that it can significantly reduce effort required for ECG labelling-in our experiments only 10% of the data were reviewed per trial-while maintaining high levels of QT accuracy.

evidence.title: AI-clinician collaboration via disagreement prediction: A decision pipeline and retrospective analysis of real-world radiologist-AI interactions
evidence.comparator_used: Diagnostic model in isolation, with all predictions presented equivalently
evidence.outcome: Expected clinician burden, with second reads for predicted disagreements on urgent findings
evidence.effect: Average disagreement rate 6.5%; expected burden reduction 4.8%, even if 5% of disagreements on urgent findings receive a second read
evidence.tradeoff: Burden balance depends on reducing disagreement false positives; the authors conclude risk mitigation can be balanced with clinician burden only if they are reduced.
evidence.quote: The average disagreement rate is 6.5%, and the expected burden reduction is 4.8%, even if 5% of disagreements on urgent findings receive a second read.

evidence.title: Development and retrospective validation of SCOUT: scalable clinical oversight of large language models via uncertainty triangulation
evidence.comparator_used: Clinician review of every LLM output (uniform human review)
evidence.outcome: Volume of cases requiring human review, and projected final accuracy
evidence.effect: Human review volume reduced by 45% to 83%; projected final accuracy 99.1% to 100.0% assuming expert correction of all flagged cases
evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy is projected, not observed, and assumes experts correct all flagged cases. The validation was retrospective and prospective randomized validation is still underway.
evidence.quote: SCOUT reduced the volume of cases requiring human review by 45% to 83%, with projected final accuracy of 99.1% to 100.0% assuming expert correction of all flagged cases.

evidence.title: Neonatal Pain Detection from Facial Expressions Using Deep Learning
evidence.comparator_used: Uniform manual evaluation of all cases (implied by the claim of reduced manual effort)
evidence.outcome: Manual evaluation effort and recall of true pain events
evidence.effect: Reported qualitatively: the integration increases recall and reduces manual evaluation effort; no numbers are given for the effort reduction
evidence.quote: The integration of both machine detection and manual evaluation can increase the recall rate of true pain events, reduce the manual evaluation effort, and increase public trust in such applications.

controls.question: Should clinicians keep final decision authority, validating AI or LLM suggestions as a second opinion, rather than letting AI decide?
controls.control: Use AI or LLM suggestions as a second opinion to challenge differentials and orders, with clinicians validating all suggestions and making the final decision.
controls.comparator: AI-led decisions or AI acting alone
controls.aim: Gain AI benefit while avoiding automation bias and unchecked AI errors
variants: Presentation order, holding clinician authority constant: clinician assesses first then sees AI, versus AI-first presentation
LLM as diagnostic second opinion broadening differentials
AI framed explicitly as decision support
Separate adoption comparison: clinician with AI versus clinician without AI
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Reading time fell slightly (87·5 s vs 82·7 s). The model had a 0·51% (8/1570) error rate from poor-quality CTA images and recognition failure.

AI assistance altered grading in a sizeable minority of cases, including clinically relevant GG1/GG2 shifts; accuracy against an independent truth was not established because the unassisted pathologist was the reference
