evidence.title: A deep-learning model for intracranial aneurysm detection on CT angiography images in China: a stepwise, multicentre, early-stage clinical validation study
evidence.comparator_used: Clinicians reading CTA without AI assistance (same readers with vs without AI after a 4-week washout; randomised AI-assisted vs control group)
evidence.outcome: Clinician diagnostic performance (AUC, sensitivity) for intracranial aneurysm detection on CTA
evidence.effect: MRMC per-patient AUC 0·795 without AI vs 0·878 with AI (p<0·0001); randomised study AUC 0·858 vs 0·789 (p<0·0001); prospective AUC 0·787 to 0·909 and patient-level sensitivity 0·590 to 0·825 (p<0·0001); AI adoption rate 92·6%
evidence.tradeoff: Reading time fell slightly (87·5 s vs 82·7 s). The model had a 0·51% (8/1570) error rate from poor-quality CTA images and recognition failure.
evidence.quote: In the randomised open-label comparison study, clinicians in the AI-assisted group had a high acceptance of the AI model (92·6% adoption rate), and a higher AUC when compared with the control group (0·858 [95% CI 0·850-0·866] vs 0·789 [0·780-0·799]; p<0·0001).

evidence.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence Assistance on Gleason Grading and Prostate Cancer Detection by Uropathologists in Daily Practice: A Prospective Multicenter Study
evidence.comparator_used: Same pathologist's unassisted reading (reference standard); AI alone was run as a separate step but not scored against the AI-assisted reading
evidence.outcome: Gleason/grade group assessment, tumor detection agreement, and diagnostic confidence with vs without AI assistance
evidence.effect: GG assessments differed in 16.5% (30/182) of entries; 80.0% (24/30) were one-point changes and 20.0% (6/30) two-point changes; 36.7% (11/30) of discrepancies were shifts between GG1 and GG2; tumor detection agreement 98.6% (279/283), with differences limited to GG1 tumors; confidence rose from confident to high confidence
evidence.tradeoff: AI assistance altered grading in a sizeable minority of cases, including clinically relevant GG1/GG2 shifts; accuracy against an independent truth was not established because the unassisted pathologist was the reference
evidence.quote: In clinical practice, AI assistance influenced Gleason grading in 16.5% of entries.

evidence.title: Impact of real-life use of artificial intelligence as support for human reading in a population-based breast cancer screening program with mammography and tomosynthesis
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologist double reading without AI support (historical matched control cohort from the year before AI implementation)
evidence.outcome: Cancer detection rate and positive predictive value of recalls in population-based screening (DM and DBT combined)
evidence.effect: CDR 9.0 vs 5.8 per 1000 (+3.2, p<0.001); PPV 14.6% vs 10.6% (+4%, p<0.001); recall rate 6.1% vs 5.4% (+0.7%, p<0.001). For DM alone, the CDR, recall rate and PPV differences were not significant (p=0.055, 0.373, 0.25).
evidence.tradeoff: Recall rate rose slightly (+0.7%), described as acceptable. Interval cancers and false negatives were not yet known. Single site, one AI system, historical control group.
evidence.quote: The implementation of an AI system for concurrent decision support for reading DM and DBT screening exams increased the breast cancer detection rate (CDR) by 3.2‰ (9.0‰ vs 5.8‰; p < 0.001) and the positive predictive value (PPV) of the recalled women by 4% (14.6% vs 10.6%; p < 0.001) with an acceptable increase in recall rate (RR) by 0.7% (6.1% vs 5.4%; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Patient and dermatologists' perspectives on augmented intelligence for melanoma screening: A prospective study
evidence.venue: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
evidence.comparator_used: AI examination alone and dermatologist screening alone
evidence.outcome: Patients' subjective safety score (0-10) and screening preference after augmented intelligence versus AI alone or dermatologist alone
evidence.effect: mSSS 9.5 (AuI) vs 7.7 (AI), p < 0.0001; 9.5 vs 9.1 (dermatologist alone), p = 0.001. 83.4% of patients preferred AuI-based screening over AI or dermatologist alone (n = 199).
evidence.tradeoff: Dermatologists still relied largely on their own judgement: in divergent risk assessments only 1.5% (3/205) trusted a benign CNN classification over their own malignancy suspicion. Experts (20.9%) found AI less helpful to their clinical work than beginners (61.8%).
evidence.quote: Regarding SSS, AuI induced a significantly higher feeling of safety than AI (mean-SSS (mSSS): 9.5 vs. 7.7, p < 0.0001) or dermatologist screening alone (mSSS: 9.5 vs. 9.1, p = 0.001).

evidence.title: Prospective multi-centre evaluation of guideline-based artificial intelligence to streamline multidisciplinary tumour board
evidence.comparator_used: AI-only decision (group 2, LLM guideline-based algorithm acting alone); MTB-only also reported
evidence.outcome: Change in diagnosis and/or treatment plan after the decision (D+TP) at 1 and 6 months
evidence.effect: D+TP change at 6 months: MTB+AI 14.73% vs AI only 24.3% vs MTB only 28.08%; at 1 month: 4.86% vs 8.78% vs 13.12%. Treatment plan change at 6 months: 15.5% vs 22.84%. MTB+AI was significantly better than both other groups. Time to recommendation was 29.2 vs 22.4 min for AI only, but 36.9 min for MTB only.
evidence.tradeoff: MTB+AI took longer than AI alone: preparation time 26.9 vs 19.7 min, decision time 4.9 vs 2.1 min, time to recommendation 29.2 vs 22.4 min. Cases where MTB and AI disagreed had to go back to the MTB for a final decision.
evidence.quote: The combination of the MTB with AI gives the most effective result in reducing the change in D and TP from 28.08% to 14.73% within 6 months (13.12% vs 4.86% in 1 month).

evidence.title: Real-World Diagnostic Performance and Clinical Utility of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Interpretation for Detection of Lung Metastasis on CT in Patients With Colorectal Cancer
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional radiologist interpretation without AI (historical period); stand-alone AI output also evaluated
evidence.outcome: Radiologist diagnostic performance for lung metastasis on chest CT in colorectal cancer, with radiologists deciding whether to report AI-detected nodules
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 72.4% vs 32.1% (p = .008); accuracy 98.5% vs 96.0% (p = .005); management changes 55.2% vs 25.0% (p = .02); specificity 99.7% vs 98.9% (p = .11, ns); diagnostic yield 3.2% vs 1.4% (p = .30, ns); false-referral rate 0.3% vs 1.1% (p = .10, ns). Stand-alone AI had 381 false-positive detections in 634 patients without metastasis, and only one was reported as positive by radiologists.
evidence.tradeoff: Stand-alone AI produced many false positives (381 in 634 patients without metastasis), so radiologist filtering was needed. No significant change in specificity or false-referral rate was seen with AI assistance.
evidence.quote: AI assistance yielded increased sensitivity, accuracy, and frequency of management changes, without significantly changed specificity.

evidence.title: Standalone AI Versus AI-Assisted Radiologists in Emergency ICH Detection: A Prospective, Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
evidence.comparator_used: Standalone AI services (three commercial ICH detection tools) acting alone, versus radiologists who had AI results available as an auxiliary tool
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy for ICH detection on brain CT (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, diagnostic odds ratio, false positives, missed cases)
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 98.91% vs 95.91%, specificity 99.83% vs 87.35%, accuracy 99.53% vs 90.11% (p<0.001); diagnostic odds ratio 52,272 vs 162.0 (323-fold); false positives 4 vs 293 (0.17% vs 12.65%); missed ICH 12 vs 45 cases; kappa 0.776
evidence.tradeoff: AI use was optional, and radiologists may not have used the AI results. The radiologist arm is not a clean test of AI assistance, since it was not compared with radiologists reading without AI. Adding AI findings to radiologist reads could raise false positives from 4 to 297 cases, requiring extra specialist verification and workload and risking alert fatigue.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity was 98.91% vs. 95.91% for AI, specificity was 99.83% vs. 87.35%, and overall accuracy was 99.53% vs. 90.11%.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency skeletal X-ray: post-deployment monitoring and clinical impact of incorrect AI results
evidence.comparator_used: AI's initial suggestion alone (before radiographer supervision)
evidence.outcome: Patient pathway changes and overriding of incorrect AI results under radiographer supervision
evidence.effect: Radiographer supervision altered the subsequent patient pathway in 20% of cases, with overriding more likely when AI was later found incorrect (false positives or false negatives). Only one patient needing treatment was prematurely discharged.
evidence.tradeoff: One patient who required treatment was prematurely discharged and was recalled after the radiologist's report.
evidence.quote: Compared to AI's initial suggestion, radiographer supervision altered the subsequent patient pathway in 20% of the cases, with the likelihood overriding AI being higher when AI results were later found to be incorrect (i.e. false positives or false negatives).

evidence.title: The AI implementation gap in trauma radiography: standalone versus discretionary AI-integrated fracture detection
evidence.comparator_used: Standalone AI reading (same Feb 2024 cases) versus AI-assisted radiologists making the final decision
evidence.outcome: Fracture-level sensitivity, accuracy, specificity and PPV
evidence.effect: Standalone AI vs AI-assisted radiologists (Feb 2024, fracture level): sensitivity 93.5% vs 90.0% (McNemar p=0.049); accuracy 94.1% vs 93.4%; specificity 94.6% vs 96.7%; PPV 94.5% vs 96.4%; NPV 93.6% vs 90.7%. Patient-level sensitivity (p=0.871) and accuracy (p=1.000) did not differ significantly.
evidence.tradeoff: AI-assisted radiologists had lower sensitivity, so subtle fractures flagged by the AI may have been overlooked. AI use was discretionary and not recorded, which introduces reader and confirmation bias.
evidence.quote: In conclusion, this study demonstrates that a standalone AI system achieves high diagnostic performance in musculoskeletal trauma imaging, often statistically outperforming AI-assisted radiologists in both sensitivity and accuracy.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence guided physician directive improves head and neck planning quality and practice Uniformity: A prospective study
evidence.comparator_used: Phase I physician directives made without AI assistance (pre-AI, 60 retrospective cases), compared with Phase II AI-guided directives (60 prospective cases)
evidence.outcome: Plan achievability (achieved plan within ±3 Gy of physician directive), first-plan acceptance, plan iterations, and OAR dose
evidence.effect: Plan achievability rose from 52.9% to 80.4%. Physician acceptance of the first plan rose from 63.3% to 90%. Maximum plan iterations fell from 4 to 2. Spinal cord, inferior constrictor, larynx and oral cavity doses fell significantly (range 4.3 to 15.2 Gy).
evidence.tradeoff: Esophagus and contralateral parotid doses rose by 2.3 to 3.1 Gy, not statistically significant. Planning time data were not sufficient to measure efficiency. Phase I and Phase II used different cases, with systematic dose differences in some OARs. Oral cavity dose was slightly higher than the AI-guided directive.
evidence.quote: Overall, implementation of the AI assistant improved achieved increased plan uniformity and quality comparing to planning without AI guidance.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Intermediate Suspicion Category in Thyroid Nodules With Artificial Intelligence Assistance: A Comparative Analysis of C-TIRADS, ACR-TIRADS, and American Thyroid Association Guidelines
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologists interpreting thyroid nodules without AI assistance (same radiologists, three guidelines)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and FNA decision making for intermediate suspicion thyroid nodules
evidence.effect: Radiologists' accuracy rose from 66.4%-71.4% without AI to 74.1%-79.4% with AI (P < .001). FNA rates fell by 20.3%-34.7%, malignant detection rose by 15.0%-23.4%, and missed malignancy fell by 23.7%-36.8% (all P < .001).
evidence.quote: AI assistance reduced FNA rates by 20.3% to 34.7%, increased malignant detection rate by 15.0% to 23.4%, and decreased missed malignancy rate by 23.7% to 36.8% (all P < .001).

evidence.title: The effects of multitype prompt engineering for large language models in hypertension treatment decisions
evidence.comparator_used: Physician decision-making at baseline, without LLM assistance
evidence.outcome: Physician treatment decision accuracy and inappropriate regimen rate with LLM assistance
evidence.effect: Optimal LLM assistance raised accuracy: community hospital 73.4% to 82.5%, county hospital 84.0% to 87.9%, teaching hospital 91.5% to 92.0%. The worst LLM configurations pushed inappropriate regimen rates from 26.6% to 35.2% across all levels.
evidence.tradeoff: Poorly designed LLM configurations worsened physician performance below baseline and increased inappropriate regimens, so the benefit depends on prompt quality.
evidence.quote: Optimal LLM assistance consistently enhanced physicians' average accuracy across all levels (community hospital: 73.4% to 82.5%; county hospital: 84.0% to 87.9%; teaching hospital: 91.5% to 92.0%) and reduced inappropriate regimen rates.

evidence.title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologist diagnosis alone and AI-standalone (AI acting alone)
evidence.outcome: Missed fractures (FN) with clinical consequences, and false positives, using AI as a safety net when the radiologist diagnosis is negative
evidence.effect: AI-safety net: 0.07% FN (1/1508; 1 consequence), 7.6% FP (115/1508). Radiologist alone: 2.7% FN (40/1508; 28 consequences), 1.2% FP. AI-standalone: 1.5% FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), 6.8% FP.
evidence.tradeoff: False positives rose from 1.2% to 7.6%, although the authors say unnecessary treatments remain limited.
evidence.quote: Best results were obtained implementing AI as safety net, which eliminates missed fractures with serious clinical consequences; even though false positives are increased, unnecessary treatments are limited.

evidence.title: Safety of human-AI cooperative decision-making within intensive care: A physical simulation study
evidence.comparator_used: No AI-alone arm. Clinician decisions after unsafe AI recommendations were compared with decisions after safe ones, and with their own pre-AI plans.
evidence.outcome: Rejection of unsafe versus safe AI drug recommendations by clinicians making the final prescribing decision
evidence.effect: 92% of clinicians rejected unsafe AI recommendations vs 29% of safe ones; +37% gaze fixations on unsafe vs safe AI recommendations
evidence.tradeoff: Visual attention on AI explanations was not greater in unsafe scenarios. Clinicians did not look back at the patient monitor or chart after an unsafe AI reveal. Scripted nurse comments changed the dose only 5% of the time. 29% of safe recommendations were also rejected.
evidence.quote: 92% of clinicians rejected unsafe AI recommendations vs 29% of safe ones.

evidence.title: From tool to teammate in a randomized controlled trial of clinician-AI collaborative workflows for diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: AI alone (independent AI diagnosis without clinician)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of collaborative workflows vs AI alone
evidence.effect: Collaborative workflows 85% and 82% were not statistically different from AI-alone accuracy of 90%; performance was comparable across first- and second-opinion workflows
evidence.quote: Performance was comparable across workflows and not statistically different from AI-alone accuracy (90%), highlighting the potential of collaborative AI to complement clinician expertise.

evidence.title: AI-literacy training enhances physician-LLM diagnostic collaboration in a resource-limited setting: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.comparator_used: LLM alone (AI acting alone, without physician involvement)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic reasoning score (%) on expert-graded rubric
evidence.effect: LLM alone outperformed the trained physician plus LLM group by 11.5 percentage points (95% CI, 5.5 to 17.5; P < 0.001); in 38% of cases the physician plus LLM group surpassed the median LLM-alone performance
evidence.quote: While LLM alone outperformed the trained physician group by 11.5 percentage points (95% CI, 5.5 to 17.5; P < 0.001), in 38% of cases the physician plus LLM group surpassed the median LLM-alone performance, highlighting physician-AI complementarities.

evidence.title: Comparison of Artificial Intelligence Models and Human Experts in Managing Dyslipidemia: Assessment of Adherence to Clinical Guidelines
evidence.comparator_used: AI alone (GPT-4, Claude-3, DeepSeek-V2) and professors alone, in simulated dyslipidemia management
evidence.outcome: Simulated LDL-C target attainment
evidence.effect: 92% with combined AI-human approach vs 83% with AI alone and 64% with professors alone
evidence.quote: Simulated outcomes showed LDL-C target attainment of 83% with AI, 64% with professors, and 92% with a combined approach.

evidence.title: Multicentre external validation of a commercial artificial intelligence software to analyse chest radiographs in health screening environments with low disease prevalence
evidence.comparator_used: Same four radiology residents reading CXRs without AI assistance (AI alone also measured separately)
evidence.outcome: Reader diagnostic performance (AUROC) for detecting clinically significant lesions on chest radiographs
evidence.effect: Reader AUROC 0.534-0.676 without AI vs 0.571-0.688 with AI (all p < 0.05); AI alone AUROC 0.648, sensitivity 35.3%, specificity 94.2%; modest boost mainly for less-experienced readers
evidence.tradeoff: Mean reading time was 2.96-10.27 s longer with AI assistance (all p < 0.05)
evidence.quote: The readers' AUROCs ranged from 0.534-0.676 without AI and 0.571-0.688 with AI (all p values < 0.05).

evidence.title: The clinical value of artificial intelligence in assisting junior radiologists in thyroid ultrasound: a multicenter prospective study from real clinical practice
evidence.comparator_used: Junior and senior radiologists reading independently without AI (also compared with the AI system alone)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, AUC) of junior radiologists for benign vs malignant thyroid nodules on ultrasound
evidence.effect: Against the 2e criteria, junior radiologists' specificity rose from 0.837 to 0.921, accuracy from 0.833 to 0.895 and AUC from 0.829 to 0.871 (all p<0.001), with sensitivity unchanged at 0.820. Against pathology, accuracy rose from 0.745 to 0.798 (p=0.014) and AUC from 0.744 to 0.798 (p=0.012). Against the arbitration committee, AUC rose from 0.878 to 0.909 (p=0.006). AI-assisted juniors matched senior radiologists against pathology (all p>0.05). Senior radiologists showed no significant change with AI.
evidence.tradeoff: AI misled junior radiologists in 31 nodules (17 benign and 14 malignant that were originally correct), versus 193 corrected. Sensitivity did not improve. Against the arbitration committee standard, AI-assisted juniors still did not reach senior level (all p<0.05). AI and senior radiologists failed together on 140 nodules. The AI gave only binary outputs with no probability shown.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, AI assistance significantly improved the performance of junior radiologists in the diagnosis of thyroid nodules, and their diagnostic performance was comparable to that of senior radiologists when pathological results were taken as the gold standard (all p > 0.05).

evidence.title: MDT-guided language-model reasoning for spinal infection diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Same clinicians making decisions without AI advice (paired multi-reader, multi-case reader study)
evidence.outcome: Clinician diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: Accuracy 92.1% with fixed AI advice vs 89.1% without; difference 3.03 percentage points (95% CI 1.47 to 4.55); 93 incorrect-to-correct vs 41 correct-to-incorrect transitions
evidence.tradeoff: 41 correct-to-incorrect transitions, where clinicians changed a correct decision to an incorrect one after AI advice
evidence.quote: In the reader study, five clinicians made 1,716 matched reader–case–decision assessments; accuracy was 92.1% with fixed AI advice and 89.1% without advice (difference, 3.03 percentage points; fixed-reader case-bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 1.47 to 4.55), with 93 incorrect-to-correct and 41 correct-to-incorrect transitions.

evidence.title: Digital Pathology with AI for Cervical Biopsies: Diagnostic Accuracy at the CIN2+ Threshold
evidence.comparator_used: EagleEye AI alone, and the original pathologist sign-out (P1) without AI
evidence.outcome: Detection of CIN2+ (vs <CIN2) on cervical biopsies, including additional case-finding and correction of AI errors by pathologist adjudication
evidence.effect: EagleEye alone vs P1: sensitivity 93.3%, specificity 71.8%, kappa 0.67. With the AI-assisted consensus (EE + P2) as the comparator, P1 had 83.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity, so the workflow found additional CIN2+ cases signed out as <CIN2 by P1. EagleEye alone under-called ACIS but improved after adjudication. Several CIN3 cases flagged as SCC by EagleEye were confirmed by EE + P2 review.
evidence.quote: When the AI-assisted consensus (EE + P2) was used as an augmented internal comparator, P1 showed 83.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity, indicating that the human-in-the-loop workflow identified additional CIN2+ cases that had been signed out as <CIN2 by P1, particularly near the CIN1/CIN2 boundary.

evidence.title: A randomized controlled trial on evaluating clinician-supervised generative AI for decision support
evidence.comparator_used: Autonomous ChatGPT (and a paper guide) in a simulated CPR scenario with lay participants
evidence.outcome: Decision accuracy, cognitive load (LF/HF ratio), trust in AI, and scenario completion time
evidence.effect: Supervised-ChatGPT showed significantly higher decision accuracy than the paper guide and ChatGPT groups. It had a reduced LF/HF ratio, suggesting potentially lower cognitive load, and the highest trust in AI. No numeric values were reported in the abstract.
evidence.tradeoff: Scenario completion time was longer with supervision. In one instance autonomous ChatGPT suggested a risky option, which shows why clinician supervision is needed.
evidence.quote: Results indicate that the Supervised-ChatGPT group showed significantly higher decision accuracy compared to the paper guide and ChatGPT groups, although the scenario completion time was longer.

evidence.title: Peer perceptions of clinicians using generative AI in medical decision-making
evidence.comparator_used: GenAI used as a primary decision-making tool (AI-led) in the vignette; a no-GenAI control vignette was also included
evidence.outcome: Peer clinicians' rating of the depicted physician's clinical skill (1-7 scale)
evidence.effect: GenAI-verify mean 4.99 vs GenAI-primary mean 3.79; no-GenAI Control 5.93 (p < 0.001 for the reported contrasts)
evidence.tradeoff: Verification framing only partially mitigated the penalty. Peers still rated the physician lower than in the no-GenAI Control, and similar patterns appeared for perceived overall healthcare experience and competence.
evidence.quote: Framing GenAI use as verification partially mitigated this effect (4.99, p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Multimodal Generative Artificial Intelligence Model for Creating Radiology Reports for Chest Radiographs in Patients Undergoing Tuberculosis Screening
evidence.comparator_used: Standalone AI-generated reports without radiologist review
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and localization of TB-related abnormality detection, AI alone vs radiologists using AI reports
evidence.effect: Standalone AI accuracy 90.8% (sensitivity 95.2%, specificity 86.7%) vs 94.1% for reader 1 and 93.5% for reader 2 with AI reports. Standalone AI localization 63.3% vs 78.7% and 81.5% for readers with AI reports.
evidence.quote: Although AI-generated reports may augment radiologists' diagnostic assessments, the current model requires human oversight, given inferior standalone performance.

evidence.title: External validation of a commercial AI system for pulmonary embolism detection on chest CTPA: a multicenter study
evidence.comparator_used: AI alone (also compared with radiologist manual reading alone)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy (AUC) and number of diagnostic errors for PE detection on CTPA
evidence.effect: Combined manual + AI AUC 0.928-0.934 vs AI alone 0.807-0.810 (manual alone 0.888-0.914); diagnostic errors 7 with combined vs 43 for AI alone (29 for manual alone)
evidence.tradeoff: Combined reading took longer than AI alone (2.61 ± 0.69 min vs 0.19 ± 0.02 min), though it was shorter than manual reading alone (5.26 ± 0.94 min).
evidence.quote: The combined approach significantly reduced diagnostic errors to 7 cases compared to 43 for AI alone and 29 for manual reading alone.

evidence.title: Large language model as clinical decision support system augments medication safety in 16 clinical specialties
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-based CDSS alone and pharmacist alone (no LLM)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of detecting prescribing errors in medication chart review scenarios, including errors posing serious harm
evidence.effect: Co-pilot (pharmacist plus LLM-based CDSS) accuracy 61% (precision 0.57, recall 0.61, F1 0.59), the best of the three arms; for errors posing serious harm, accuracy was 1.5-fold higher than pharmacist alone
evidence.quote: The co-pilot arm demonstrated the best performance with an accuracy of 61% (precision 0.57, recall 0.61, and F1 0.59).

evidence.title: Comparative performance of LLMs and machine learning in predicting complications after percutaneous kyphoplasty for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures
evidence.comparator_used: Spine surgeons predicting complications without exposure to LLM responses
evidence.outcome: Surgeon prediction performance for BCL and NVF
evidence.effect: LLM explanations improved surgeon performance for BCL but not for NVF; surgeons alone had BCL F1-score 0.675-0.684, MCC 0.074-0.185; numeric values with LLM exposure not given in the abstract
evidence.quote: LLM explanations enhanced surgeon performance in BCL prediction but not in NVF.

evidence.title: Prospective quantitative analysis of hyperparameter and input optimization in GPT-5: comparative contribution to radiologist performance in abdominal radiology
evidence.comparator_used: Junior radiologists reading the same cases without GPT-5 assistance (washout between reads)
evidence.outcome: Radiologist diagnostic accuracy and differential diagnosis scores
evidence.effect: Accuracy 73% and 71% unassisted vs 87% and 86% with browser-based GPT-5 and 94% with optimal-settings GPT-5; median differential diagnosis score 4 (range 3-5) unassisted vs 5 (range 4-5) with optimal-settings GPT-5
evidence.quote: The radiologists' diagnostic accuracy increased from 73% and 71% without assistance to 87% and 86% with browser-based GPT-5 assistance and further to 94% with GPT-5 with optimal settings assistance.

evidence.title: Factors for Patient Trust and Acceptance of Medical Artificial Intelligence
evidence.comparator_used: AI-assisted diagnosis visit with no clinician present (AI acting alone)
evidence.outcome: Patient choice of a hypothetical AI-assisted diagnostic visit (the study also measured trust ratings)
evidence.effect: Clinician presence increased the probability of selecting a visit by 18.4% (95% CI, 17.3%-19.5%; P < .00025)
evidence.quote: The presence of a clinician was associated with increasing the probability of selecting a visit by 18.4% (95% CI, 17.3%-19.5%; P < .00025).

evidence.title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Independent reading by radiologists without DL-3DABUV assistance (also compared second-reading vs concurrent-reading modes)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance of novice radiologists (AUC, specificity) and reading time
evidence.effect: Novices in independent reading had lower AUC and specificity than DL-3DABUV (0.68 vs 0.82, P<0.001; 57.4% vs 81.5%, P<0.001), but novice performance reached parity with DL-3DABUV in both second-reading and concurrent-reading. No significant difference in diagnostic performance between second-reading and concurrent-reading.
evidence.tradeoff: Second-reading took longer: concurrent reading reduced reading time by 33.6 seconds compared with second-reading (P<0.001).
evidence.quote: DL-3DABUV achieves diagnostic performance comparable to experienced radiologists and enhances diagnostic accuracy for novices.

evidence.title: BiTNet: Hybrid deep convolutional model for ultrasound image analysis of human biliary tract and its applications
evidence.comparator_used: Healthcare professionals diagnosing without the AI assisting tool
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and precision of 11 healthcare professionals, with vs without BiTNet assistance
evidence.effect: Mean accuracy 0.74 vs 0.50 and precision 0.61 vs 0.46 (p<0.001); improvement seen at all four experience levels
evidence.quote: The mean accuracy and precision of the participants with BiTNet as an assisting tool (0.74 and 0.61, respectively) are statistically higher than those of participants without the assisting tool (0.50 and 0.46, respectively (p<0.001)).

evidence.title: Grounding Large Language Model in Clinical Diagnostics
evidence.comparator_used: ClinDiag-GPT alone and physicians alone
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and efficiency
evidence.effect: No numerical effect reported in the abstract; collaboration between ClinDiag-GPT and physicians enhanced both outcomes.
evidence.quote: Collaboration between ClinDiag-GPT and physicians enhanced both diagnostic accuracy and efficiency, demonstrating ClinDiag-GPT's potential as a valuable clinical assistant.

evidence.title: First, do NOHARM: a medical safety benchmark and randomized study of physician and AI teaming on clinical consultations
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional resources (physicians working without AI assistance)
evidence.outcome: Physician performance on clinical consultation cases in a randomized study of 101 physicians
evidence.effect: AI assistance improved physician performance compared to conventional resources; no numeric effect given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: AI-assisted physicians frequently omitted valuable AI-generated recommendations and still scored lower than many AI systems alone
evidence.quote: In a randomized study of 101 U.S.-licensed generalist physicians, AI assistance improved physician performance compared to conventional resources.

evidence.title: Grading of diabetic retinopathy using a pre-segmenting deep learning classification model: Validation of an automated algorithm
evidence.comparator_used: DL algorithm operating autonomously (Model 3)
evidence.outcome: Agreement with gold standard (weighted kappa), sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV for any DR
evidence.effect: Human grader with DL assistance (Model 2) vs autonomous DL (Model 3): weighted kappa 0.89 vs 0.72; sensitivity 94% vs 78%; specificity 84% vs 81%; PPV 64% vs 57%; NPV 98% vs 92%
evidence.quote: As compared to the gold standard, weighted kappa for Models 1-3 was 0.88, 0.89 and 0.72, sensitivities were 95%, 94% and 78% and specificities were 82%, 84% and 81%.

evidence.title: Quantifying the impact of a computer-aided diagnostic score on the clinical diagnosis of functional seizures
evidence.comparator_used: Clinician diagnosis from the text-based clinical history alone, before the FSLS score was shown
evidence.outcome: Reader accuracy in identifying functional/dissociative seizures versus epileptic seizures
evidence.effect: Groups containing 66% of readers improved accuracy by 12%-15% (p < .05). The other groups had no net change (p > .75).
evidence.quote: Data-driven groups including 66% of readers benefitted from the FSLS (accuracy improvement = 12%-15%, p < .05), including those in the reference and near highest baseline performance group.

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of medication recommendation workflows: Retrieval augmentation, physician-RAG collaborative workflow, and prescribing quality
evidence.comparator_used: Retrieval-augmented LLM workflow without physician collaboration (AI alone)
evidence.outcome: Prescription-parameter accuracy, recall, precision, and unsafe (AVOID) drug exposure against the expert reference standard
evidence.effect: All-correct rate 0.951 (Physician-RAG) vs 0.948 (RAG LLM), 0.945 (Physician) and 0.494 (Base LLM). Physician-RAG had CORE recall 1.000, overall recall 0.978, precision 0.963, the lowest case-level AVOID-hit rate (0.026), and AVOID hit@1/3/5 of 0.000/0.000/0.008.
evidence.quote: Prescription-parameter accuracy was highest in the Physician-RAG collaborative workflow (all-correct rate 0.951), compared with 0.948 for the Retrieval-augmented LLM workflow, 0.945 for the Physician workflow, and 0.494 for the Base LLM workflow.

evidence.title: Development and Testing of a Novel Large Language Model-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Medication Safety in 12 Clinical Specialties
evidence.comparator_used: LLM-based CDSS alone (fully autonomous mode)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, recall and F1 for identifying moderate to severe DRPs
evidence.effect: Junior pharmacist plus LLM-CDSS co-pilot optimized accuracy, recall and F1 scores, with notable improvements in detecting severe DRPs (no numeric values given in abstract)
evidence.quote: This study established that a RAG-LLM based CDSS significantly boosts the accuracy of medication error identification when used alongside junior pharmacists (co-pilot), with notable improvements in detecting severe DRPs.

evidence.title: Digitally Assisted Clinical Decision-Making in Traditional Chinese Medicine: Comparative Study of 5 Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Physician-only decision-making (AI-only arm also included in the design, but its result is not reported in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Clinical decision quality score and decision time across 5 TCM cases
evidence.effect: Quality 33.62 vs 28.97 (16.1% improvement; P<.001); time 162.6 s vs 479.2 s (66.1% reduction; P<.001); adoption of AI suggestions 74.25%, modification 24%, rejection 1.75%
evidence.quote: Human-AI collaboration achieved significant improvements compared with physician-only decision-making, with 16.1% quality enhancement (33.62 vs 28.97; P<.001) and 66.1% time reduction (162.6 s vs 479.2 s; P<.001).

evidence.title: Optical Biopsy of Dysplasia in Barrett's Oesophagus Assisted by Artificial Intelligence
evidence.comparator_used: Unassisted gastroenterologists interpreting endocytoscopic BE images without AI assistance (AI offered as an optional second assessor)
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and accuracy for identifying dysplasia in Barrett's oesophagus at follow-up
evidence.effect: AI-assisted gastroenterologists outperformed unassisted ones: sensitivity +20.0% (p = 0.025) and accuracy +12.22% (p = 0.05); they maintained high sensitivity and accuracy at follow-up
evidence.quote: Contrastingly, AI-assisted gastroenterologists maintained high sensitivity and accuracy at follow-up, subsequently outperforming the unassisted gastroenterologists (+20.0%, p = 0.025 and +12.22%, p = 0.05).

evidence.title: Quantitative assessment of myocardial fibrosis by digital image analysis: An adjunctive tool for pathologist "ground truth"
evidence.venue: Cardiovascular pathology : the official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Pathology
evidence.comparator_used: Pathologists' own blinded first quantification of myocardial fibrosis without AI output (pre-AI vs post-AI reassessment)
evidence.outcome: Inter-observer agreement among pathologists in quantifying myocardial fibrosis on endomyocardial biopsies
evidence.effect: Pathologist agreement improved significantly and no longer depended on fibrosis severity. Before AI, discordance was relevant, especially at higher fibrosis percentages. Median fibrosis was 8.33% (first pathologist) vs 13.60% (algorithm), R2 0.79, p<0.001. No agreement statistics were given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The knowledge of the automatic quantification significantly improved the overall pathologist´s agreement, which became unaffected by the degree of MF severity.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence algorithm improves radiologists' bone age assessment accuracy
evidence.venue: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologists assessing bone age independently without AI assistance (crossover design)
evidence.outcome: Bone age assessment accuracy (mean absolute difference from expert ground truth; proportion of estimates with MAD >1 year)
evidence.effect: MAD 0.74 vs 0.46 years without vs with AI (p < 0.001); proportion of assessments with MAD >1 year 24.0% vs 8.4% (p < 0.001); improved predictions with AI 16.8% vs less accurate predictions with AI 2.3% (p < 0.001)
evidence.tradeoff: Automation bias was prone to affect less experienced radiologists; 2.3% of predictions became less accurate with AI assistance. Senior radiologists disagreed with the AI more often. No consistent timing effect between early and delayed AI assistance.
evidence.quote: The AI algorithm improved the BA assessment accuracy of radiologists with varying experience levels.

evidence.title: Human-AI collaboration in clinical reasoning: a UK replication and interaction analysis
evidence.comparator_used: LLM alone (AI acting alone) answering the same vignette questions
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic reasoning score on structured vignette questions
evidence.effect: Physicians with LLM assistance scored lower than the LLM alone (mean difference 21.3 percentage points, p<0.001)
evidence.tradeoff: Physicians posed only 30% of case questions directly to the LLM, which suggests under-utilisation contributed to the gap. Improvement from LLM assistance varied widely between clinicians (SD 12.8%).
evidence.quote: Physicians with LLM assistance scored significantly lower than the LLM alone (mean difference 21.3 percentage points, p<0.001).

evidence.title: From Tool to Teammate: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Clinician-AI Collaborative Workflows for Diagnosis
evidence.comparator_used: Traditional diagnostic resources (clinicians without the custom GPT collaborative workflow)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: AI-first 85% and AI-second 82% vs 75% with traditional resources (p < 0.0004 and p < 0.00001; mean differences 9.8% and 6.8%; 95% CI 4.6%–15% and 4.0%–9.6%)
evidence.quote: Clinicians using either collaborative workflow outperformed those using traditional tools, achieving average accuracies of 85% (AI-first) and 82% (AI-second), compared to 75% with traditional resources (p < 0.0004 and p < 0.00001; mean differences = 9.8% and 6.8%; 95% CI = 4.6%–15% and 4.0%–9.6%).

evidence.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models in Infectious Disease Decision-Making: From Examination to Clinical Practice
evidence.comparator_used: LLMs alone (AI acting alone) on real-world infectious disease cases
evidence.outcome: Completeness of clinical decision responses (expert Likert ratings)
evidence.effect: Doctors supported by LLMs scored significantly higher than LLMs alone (p = 0.0010) and than doctors alone (p = 0.0015)
evidence.quote: Notably, for completeness, doctors supported by LLMs achieved significantly higher scores compared with both doctors alone (p = 0.0015) and the LLMs alone (p = 0.0010).

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Large Language Model-Augmented Diagnostic Reasoning in Thoracic Imaging: Impact of Radiologic Expertise
evidence.comparator_used: Reader's own initial interpretation without LLM output (session 1 vs session 2)
evidence.outcome: Reader diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: Thoracic radiologists 56.3% to 65.6%; residents 42.4% to 58.5%; gain greater for residents (16.1 vs 9.2 percentage points; p = .02)
evidence.tradeoff: New failure mode: residents accepted LLM-favored diagnoses more often than thoracic radiologists (73.2% vs 48.9%; p < .001). They also switched to an incorrect diagnosis more often after misleading LLM output (60.6% vs 32.4%; p = .009).
evidence.quote: From session 1 to session 2, accuracy increased from 56.3% to 65.6% for thoracic radiologists and from 42.4% to 58.5% for residents, respectively.

evidence.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Professional Expertise in Adapted Physical Activity Prescription for Orthopedic Rehabilitation
evidence.venue: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology
evidence.comparator_used: AI alone generating the adapted physical activity protocol without professional involvement (novice professional with AI support vs AI alone; expert-only protocols also rated)
evidence.outcome: Blinded panel-rated overall quality of adapted physical activity protocols (effectiveness, safety, appropriateness, clarity, progression) across five orthopedic conditions
evidence.effect: NAI protocols were rated significantly higher than AI-alone protocols in most conditions (p < 0.01), except osteoporosis (p = 0.362). Expert-only protocols scored highest, then NAI, then AI alone (all p < 0.05). EP vs AI differences were largest for safety (p < 0.01), appropriateness/tailoring (p < 0.01) and progression (p < 0.05).
evidence.tradeoff: NAI protocols still scored below expert-only protocols, so the expertise gap was only partly closed. AI-alone protocols varied more across pathologies. No benefit of NAI over AI alone was seen for osteoporosis.
evidence.quote: AI-generated protocols without human oversight are not yet suitable for autonomous APA prescription, supporting a complementary, expertise-dependent role of AI in exercise programming.

evidence.title: Improving the Real-Time Classification of Disease Severity in Ulcerative Colitis: Artificial Intelligence as the Trigger for a Second Opinion
evidence.comparator_used: Non-IBD-expert physicians scoring the videos without AI support (AI alone was also compared with experts)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of UC endoscopic severity (Mayo Endoscopic Subscore) classification by non-IBD experts, with expert scores as gold standard
evidence.effect: AI as a supporting system improved non-IBD experts' performance by 12%; AI alone reached 82% accuracy with no significant difference from experts; AI disagreed with the primary physician in 20%-39% of cases
evidence.tradeoff: The AI disagreed with the primary physician in 20%-39% of cases, which triggers second-opinion reviews. No other cost or burden was reported.
evidence.quote: When used as a supporting system, it improved non-IBD experts' performance by 12% and disagreed with the primary physician in 20%-39% of cases.

evidence.title: Locally Deployed Large Language Models for AI-Assisted Outpatient Prescription Review: Crossover Study
evidence.comparator_used: Pharmacist-alone unaided prescription review
evidence.outcome: Overall prescription review accuracy
evidence.effect: 97.2% (207/213, 95% CI 94.0%-98.7%) in the human-AI collaborative condition vs 82.6% (176/213, 95% CI 77.0%-87.1%) in the pharmacist-alone condition (P<.001)
evidence.quote: Overall review accuracy was 97.2% (207/213, 95% CI 94.0%-98.7%) in the human-AI collaborative condition vs 82.6% (176/213, 95% CI 77.0%-87.1%) in the pharmacist-alone condition (P<.001).

controls.question: Should patient-facing AI chatbots and prediction estimates be offered with clinician supervision and explanation rather than without clinician support?
controls.control: Offer AI chatbots or risk and prognosis estimates alongside clinician-led consent, counseling, therapy or shared decision-making, with clinician supervising and explaining.
controls.comparator: Unsupervised patient-facing AI tools or predictions shown without clinician support
controls.aim: Improve patient understanding and decisions while keeping clinician accountability and avoiding unwanted disclosure
variants: Predictions shared only with patients who want them
Separate adoption comparison: clinician-supported AI versus clinician-only care
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: QoR-15 postoperative recovery score was better in the physician-led group (p = 0.019); IC duration differed significantly between groups (p = 0.020) despite equal medians; baseline anxiety was higher in the AI-assisted group (p < 0.01)

RAG did not eliminate hallucinations, so a physician had to be present to identify and correct incorrect responses. Patients' attitude toward AI did not improve. The AI-only comparison was a hypothetical scenario question rather than a tested arm.

evidence.title: Physician-Supervised ChatGPT-Assisted Versus Physician-Led Informed Consent for Reducing Preoperative Anxiety: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional physician-led informed consent without ChatGPT assistance
evidence.outcome: Preoperative anxiety (STAI-1) after informed consent; also IC duration and postoperative quality of recovery (QoR-15)
evidence.effect: Adjusted postintervention anxiety mean difference 0.26 (95% CI -1.45 to 1.97), meeting the noninferiority margin of +5 STAI points; no between-group difference in ΔSTAI-1 (p = 0.533); median IC duration 10 minutes in both groups (p = 0.020 for the between-group difference); QoR-15 favored the control group (p = 0.019)
evidence.tradeoff: QoR-15 postoperative recovery score was better in the physician-led group (p = 0.019); IC duration differed significantly between groups (p = 0.020) despite equal medians; baseline anxiety was higher in the AI-assisted group (p < 0.01)
evidence.quote: After adjustment for baseline STAI-1 and STAI-2 scores, postintervention anxiety did not differ between groups (mean difference, 0.26; 95% CI: -1.45 to 1.97), confirming noninferiority.

evidence.title: Exploring Patient Perspectives, Engagement, and Output Quality in Doctor-Supervised Use of Artificial Intelligence During Informed Consent Consultation With ChatGPT and Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG): Quantitative Exploratory Study
evidence.comparator_used: Physician-only consultation (control arm); hypothetical AI-only assistant without a physician (scenario preference question)
evidence.outcome: Patient preference for physician-supervised consent vs an AI-only assistant, and satisfaction with the consent process
evidence.effect: Across all groups, patients preferred the physician-led scenario even when the AI-only alternative offered more accurate information. Mean preference ratings were 1.25-1.42 (human only), 1.75-2.33 (native ChatGPT) and 0.58-0.83 (ChatGPT+RAG). The preference did not change during the consent procedure. Satisfaction with informedness and information quantity was similar across arms after Q&A.
evidence.tradeoff: RAG did not eliminate hallucinations, so a physician had to be present to identify and correct incorrect responses. Patients' attitude toward AI did not improve. The AI-only comparison was a hypothetical scenario question rather than a tested arm.
evidence.quote: Results show that across all groups, participants preferred Scenario A (a human doctor with less accurate information) over Scenario B (an AI assistant alone with more accurate information).

evidence.title: Older adults' perceptions of artificial intelligence in healthcare: an exploratory quantitative analysis
evidence.comparator_used: AI used without clinician supervision for medication management, scheduling, prescription refills and patient portal messages
evidence.outcome: Older adults' self-reported comfort with AI use in patient-facing functions
evidence.effect: Medication management 74% vs 17%; scheduling 77% vs 64%; prescription refills 81% vs 54%; patient portal messages 55% vs 20% (all p < .001), supervised vs unsupervised
evidence.quote: Older adults were more comfortable with AI used under the supervision of a clinician rather than without supervision for diagnosis (75% vs 5%, p < .001), treatment (76% vs 5%, p < .001), medication management (74% vs 17%, p < .001), scheduling (77% vs 64%, p < .001), prescription refills (81% vs 54%, p < .001), patient portal messages (55% vs 20%, p < .001).

controls.question: Should AI take an independent reading role in screening, as an autonomous point-of-care test or as a second or backup reader?
controls.control: Use AI as an autonomous diabetic retinopathy test in primary care, or as an independent second or backup reader in breast screening.
controls.comparator: Specialist-read screening or standard two-radiologist double reading
controls.aim: Increase screening access and reduce reader workload without losing detection accuracy
variants: Autonomous AI diabetic eye exam at primary care visit, replacing specialist referral
AI replacing the second reader in double-read mammography
AI as backup reader added to human reading, not replacing a reader
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Sensitivity gain was not seen for in-situ cancer; no specificity gain or loss.

Additional arbitration reads on AI-flagged cases (arbitration rate rose from 3.0% to 13.6%, 3.0% to 14.2%, and 3.3% to 10.8%), equating to 4-6% additional overall reading workload; 0.16-0.30% additional recalls; specificity fell by up to 0.2 points; live-use PPV of additional arbitration was only 22.9%

About 35% of AI referrals were judged unnecessary by the over-reader (72 false positives). Median screening time was longer with AI (6:30 vs 5:38 min) because of image upload. AI false negatives included 3 severe NPDR cases and 1 cataract case. The authors say the two modalities had different workflows, no adjudicated gold standard, and no randomization, so results are trends only.

Lower specificity, with PPV under 50%, so many false-positive referrals. AI-ungradable rate of 36.5% in non-dilated patients, which can overwhelm referral pathways. The AI phase followed the human phase at the same sites. The in-person subset was not random, so PPV may be overestimated.
Recall rate rose among generalists by 14.79% relative (9.06% to 10.40%, P=.007).
Higher cost with no advantage in the base case. Any benefit appeared only in the trial-based scenario analyses.

evidence.title: Interval cancer, sensitivity, and specificity comparing AI-supported mammography screening with standard double reading without AI in the MASAI study: a randomised, controlled, non-inferiority, single-blinded, population-based, screening-accuracy trial
evidence.comparator_used: Standard double reading by two radiologists without AI
evidence.outcome: Interval cancer rate (non-inferiority), sensitivity and specificity
evidence.effect: Interval cancer rate 1·55 vs 1·76 per 1000 (proportion ratio 0·88, 95% CI 0·65-1·18; non-inferior); sensitivity 80·5% vs 73·8% (p=0·031); specificity 98·5% in both groups (p=0·88)
evidence.tradeoff: Sensitivity gain was not seen for in-situ cancer; no specificity gain or loss.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity was higher in the intervention group (80·5% [95% CI 76·4-84·2]) than the control group (73·8% [68·9-78·3]; p=0·031), an effect consistent across age and breast density, and for invasive cancer but not for in-situ cancer.

evidence.title: Prospective implementation of AI-assisted screen reading to improve early detection of breast cancer
evidence.comparator_used: Standard double reading by two radiologists without AI (AI as additional reader flagging no-recall cases for extra arbitration)
evidence.outcome: Cancer detection rate, sensitivity, recall rate and PPV across three prospective phases
evidence.effect: CDR increased by 1.6, 1.4 and 0.7 per 1,000 cases (13%, 10%, 5% relative) in the initial pilot, extended pilot and live use (all P<0.05); sensitivity rose by 10.3, 9.0 and 4.3 points; recall rate rose by 0.2, 0.2 and 0.3 points; PPV changed by +1.9, +1.3 and +0.1 points
evidence.tradeoff: Additional arbitration reads on AI-flagged cases (arbitration rate rose from 3.0% to 13.6%, 3.0% to 14.2%, and 3.3% to 10.8%), equating to 4-6% additional overall reading workload; 0.16-0.30% additional recalls; specificity fell by up to 0.2 points; live-use PPV of additional arbitration was only 22.9%
evidence.quote: The additional arbitration reviews resulted in six (initial pilot), 22 (extended pilot) and 48 (live use) additional recalled cases, increasing the recall rate by 0.16% (initial pilot), 0.23% (extended pilot) and 0.25% (live use), respectively.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence for breast cancer detection in screening mammography in Sweden: a prospective, population-based, paired-reader, non-inferiority study
evidence.comparator_used: standard-of-care double reading by two radiologists
evidence.outcome: screen-detected breast cancer within 3 months / cancer detection rate
evidence.effect: double reading by one radiologist plus AI: 261 [0·5%] detected cases vs 250 [0·4%] with double reading by two radiologists; relative proportion 1·04 [95% CI 1·00-1·09]
evidence.quote: Replacing one radiologist with AI for independent reading of screening mammograms resulted in a 4% higher non-inferior cancer detection rate compared with radiologist double reading.

evidence.title: Transforming Non-Digital, Clinical Workflows to Detect and Track Vision-Threatening Diabetic Retinopathy via a Digital Platform Integrating Artificial Intelligence: Implementation Research
evidence.comparator_used: Manual grading of retinal photographs by trained mid-level personnel at the primary care hospital, with positives referred or sent to a visiting general ophthalmologist. This was a non-randomized, alternate-week comparison, and AI results were over-read remotely by a retinal specialist.
evidence.outcome: Referral positives identified at point of screening, true positives, and referral adherence
evidence.effect: Referral positives 201/645 (31.2%) with AI vs 175/730 (24.0%) with manual grading, P=0.003. True positives 129/201 (64.2%) vs 11/116 (9.5%), P<0.001. Referral adherence for true positives 115/129 (89.1%) vs 17/22 (77.3%), P=0.158, not significant. AI false negatives were 5/444 (1.1%). Manual false negatives could not be assessed.
evidence.tradeoff: About 35% of AI referrals were judged unnecessary by the over-reader (72 false positives). Median screening time was longer with AI (6:30 vs 5:38 min) because of image upload. AI false negatives included 3 severe NPDR cases and 1 cataract case. The authors say the two modalities had different workflows, no adjudicated gold standard, and no randomization, so results are trends only.
evidence.quote: To observe the trends of the two screening modalities (Table 2 ), the proportions of patients with referral positive and TP were found to be significantly higher in the AI group.

evidence.title: AI-Human Hybrid Workflow Enhances Teleophthalmology for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence.comparator_used: Store-and-forward teleophthalmology read by retina specialists (human consensus overread), both compared against in-person retina specialist examination
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity, specificity and gradability for more-than-mild diabetic retinopathy (MTMDR) in primary care screening
evidence.effect: AI sensitivity 95.5% (95% CI 86.7-100) vs 69.5% (95% CI 50.7-88.3) for retina specialists; specificity 60.3% (95% CI 47.7-72.9) vs 96.9% (95% CI 93.5-100); gradability 62.5% vs 93.1%; AI PPV 47.7%; MTMDR detected in 19.0% of gradable encounters in the AI phase vs 5.6% in the human phase
evidence.tradeoff: Lower specificity, with PPV under 50%, so many false-positive referrals. AI-ungradable rate of 36.5% in non-dilated patients, which can overwhelm referral pathways. The AI phase followed the human phase at the same sites. The in-person subset was not random, so PPV may be overestimated.
evidence.quote: The AI algorithm had higher sensitivity (95.5% sensitivity; 95% confidence interval [CI], 86.7%-100%) but lower specificity (60.3% specificity; 95% CI, 47.7%-72.9%) for detection of MTMDR compared with remote image interpretation by retina specialists (69.5% sensitivity; 95% CI, 50.7%-88.3%; 96.9% specificity; 95% CI, 93.5%-100%).

evidence.title: Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Increases Access and Health Equity in Underserved Populations with Diabetes
evidence.comparator_used: Non-AI primary care sites where patients are referred to eyecare for DED testing (difference-in-difference, 2019 vs 2021)
evidence.outcome: Adherence to annual diabetic eye disease testing (HEDIS measure), including among Black/African American patients and the equity gap
evidence.effect: Odds ratio of adherence at AI-switched sites was 36% higher than at non-AI sites; Black/African American adherence increased 11.9% at AI-switched sites vs decreased 1.2% at non-AI sites; Asian American vs Black/African American gap shrank from 15.6% (61.1% vs 45.5%) to 3.5%
evidence.quote: First, after controlling for a wide range of potential confounders, our regression analysis demonstrated that the odds ratio of adherence at AI-switched sites was 36% higher than that of non-AI sites, suggesting that there was a higher increase in DED testing between 2019 and 2021 at AI-switched sites than at non-AI sites.

evidence.title: Closing the Performance Gap between Generalists and Breast Imaging Specialists Using a Nationally Deployed AI Workflow for Screening Mammography
evidence.comparator_used: Same radiologists' screening mammography interpretation before introduction of the AI workflow (no AI, no Safeguard Review); not a standard two-radiologist double-reading comparison
evidence.outcome: Cancer detection rate and PPV of recalls in generalists and specialists
evidence.effect: Generalists: CDR 3.76 to 4.99 per 1000 (P<.001); PPV of recalls 3.38% to 3.89% (P=.02). Specialists: CDR 4.47 to 4.76 per 1000 (P=.33), no change in PPV (P=.86). Generalist CDR with AI was similar to specialists (P=.53).
evidence.tradeoff: Recall rate rose among generalists by 14.79% relative (9.06% to 10.40%, P=.007).
evidence.quote: A multistage AI-driven workflow was associated with substantially improved CDR and PPV of recalls for generalists, which were on par with those of specialists.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in population breast cancer screening: A two-year cost-effectiveness analysis
evidence.comparator_used: Standard screening practice (two radiologists read independently, a third resolves discordance)
evidence.outcome: Cost-effectiveness (cost per additional cancer detected) of AI as independent reader alongside one radiologist, with a second radiologist for discordance
evidence.effect: Integrated strategy was dominated in the base case. Scenario analyses using randomized controlled trial estimates showed AI-supported screening was more effective but more costly than standard practice (ICER $1123 per additional cancer detected).
evidence.tradeoff: Higher cost with no advantage in the base case. Any benefit appeared only in the trial-based scenario analyses.
evidence.quote: Integrated and Triage Single were dominated.

evidence.title: Deep Learning Algorithms for Breast Cancer Detection in a UK Screening Cohort: As Stand-alone Readers and Combined with Human Readers
evidence.comparator_used: Standard double reading by two human readers
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of DL combined with a human reader versus double reading in UK mammography screening
evidence.effect: Sensitivity noninferior: 67.0%, 65.6% and 65.4% for DL-1, DL-2 and DL-3 vs 67.4% for double reading (P < .001 for all). Specificity superior: 97.4%, 97.6% and 97.6% vs 97.1% (P < .001 for all).
evidence.quote: Combining the DL algorithms with human readers achieved noninferior sensitivity (67.0%, 65.6%, and 65.4% for DL-1, DL-2, and DL-3, respectively; P < .001 for all) compared with double reading (67.4%), and superior specificity (97.4%, 97.6%, and 97.6%; P < .001 for all) compared with double reading (97.1%).

evidence.title: Grading of diabetic retinopathy using a pre-segmenting deep learning classification model: Validation of an automated algorithm
evidence.comparator_used: Certified human grader without DL assistance (Model 1), with all models compared against an expert ophthalmologist gold standard
evidence.outcome: Agreement with gold standard (weighted kappa), sensitivity and specificity for any DR, and NPV and PPV extrapolated to 23.8% prevalence
evidence.effect: Autonomous DL (Model 3) vs human grader (Model 1): weighted kappa 0.72 vs 0.88; sensitivity 78% vs 95%; specificity 81% vs 82%; PPV 57% vs 63%; NPV 92% vs 98%
evidence.tradeoff: Autonomous DL errors: incorrect detection of artefacts (n=49), missed microaneurysms (n=26), and inconsistencies between segmentation and classification (n=51).
evidence.quote: As compared to the gold standard, weighted kappa for Models 1-3 was 0.88, 0.89 and 0.72, sensitivities were 95%, 94% and 78% and specificities were 82%, 84% and 81%.

evidence.title: Population-wide evaluation of artificial intelligence and radiologist assessment of screening mammograms
evidence.comparator_used: First readers (breast radiologists) in a double-read screening programme, compared with standalone AI replacing the first reader at two cut-offs
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, recall rate, and screen-detected versus interval cancers detected
evidence.effect: AI_spec was comparable to first readers on all accuracy measures. AI_sens had lower specificity (97.5% vs 97.7%; p < 0.0001) and PPV (17.5% vs 18.7%; p = 0.01) and a higher recall rate (3.0% vs 2.8%; p < 0.0001). Both AI settings detected fewer screen-detected cancers (1166 AI_sens, 1156 AI_spec vs 1252; p < 0.0001) but more interval cancers (126 AI_sens, 117 AI_spec vs 39; p < 0.0001).
evidence.tradeoff: AI and first readers detected a different mix of cancers, with AI missing more screen-detected cancers. Matching at sensitivity gave a higher recall rate and lower PPV.
evidence.quote: AI<sub>spec</sub> was comparable to first readers in terms of all accuracy measures.

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
evidence.comparator_used: Current standard multi-reader (double reading) screening pathway, in retrospective simulation
evidence.outcome: Screening sensitivity, specificity, assessments and human reads
evidence.effect: Sensitivity +1.9-2.5%, specificity up to +0.6%, 4.6-10.9% reduction in assessments, 48-80.7% reduction in human reads (AI as second reader or high confidence filter)
evidence.tradeoff: Automation bias degrades performance in multi-reader settings (but improves it for single-readers); results are from retrospective simulation and need prospective studies before clinical adoption.
evidence.quote: Operating an AI reader as a second reader or as a high confidence filter improves current screening outcomes by 1.9-2.5% in sensitivity and up to 0.6% in specificity, achieving 4.6-10.9% reduction in assessments and 48-80.7% reduction in human reads.

controls.question: Should AI triage incoming work, ordering imaging worklists by urgency and routing patient messages and reports to appropriate staff?
controls.control: Use AI to prioritize imaging worklists and stroke workflows by urgency, and to route patient messages, complaints and incident reports by risk tier to appropriate staff.
controls.comparator: First-in-first-out reading order or manual triage and assignment
controls.aim: Speed action on urgent cases and messages and reduce triage workload
variants: Urgency ordering: suspected-positive studies read first, accounting for reader operating-point shift, versus first-in-first-out
Routing: messages, complaints and incident reports assigned to staff or expert templates versus manual assignment
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Total processing time after image acquisition including transmission and software analysis was less than 5 minutes on average; clinical care team had to download the mobile app and sites received onboarding/education.
Added cost to the NHS with no demonstrated reduction in time to diagnosis.

AI prioritized 29% of cases vs the 14% expected from retrospective testing, so more immediate reads were needed than planned. A radiologist was unavailable within 30 minutes for 6% (8/131) of prioritized cases. Same-visit imaging was not offered to 15% (5/33) for operational reasons, and 14% (4/28) declined it. Recall rate was 17.0% vs 14.3% (p=0.36, not significant). Immediate reads can disrupt workflow, and radiologists reported discomfort reading AI-prioritized cases as normal.
AI processing took about 70 s per slide; adenocarcinoma sensitivity was only 50.0% (PPV 100%); no turnaround benefit for neoplastic lesions; cost of deployment and operation described as reasonable

Post-implementation local CTA acquisition increased from 28% (n = 33) to 81% (n = 111); NCCT predictions had processing errors in 5 cases (4%) and CTA outputs were unavailable in 2 cases (2%) due to processing errors.

evidence.title: Blueprint for Safety: Implementing a Clinically Governed AI Digital Assistant for Patient Guidance
evidence.venue: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery
evidence.comparator_used: Randomized rollout to half of patients; the other half presumably had standard human-support handling of queries without the risk-stratified assistant (comparator arm not described in detail in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Human support workload, human response time, clinical safety and resolution of inquiries
evidence.effect: 65% fewer standard-risk queries routed to human support; average human response time 9.6 to 3.6 minutes; 96% accurate guidance, 0% critical safety events, no AI-generated diagnoses; improved resolution without additional visits
evidence.quote: Using a randomized rollout to half of the patient population, the authors found that the risk-stratified assistant maintained a high level of clinical safety (96% accurate guidance, 0% critical safety events, and no AI-generated diagnoses) while reducing standard-risk queries routed to human support by 65%, shortening average human response times from 9.6 to 3.6 minutes, and improving resolution of health inquiries without additional visits.

evidence.title: Automated Large Vessel Occlusion Detection Software and Thrombectomy Treatment Times: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-AI/unexposed standard stroke workflow before site activation; the LVO alerts were not sent and the mobile PACS and patient-level secure messaging were not available.
evidence.outcome: Door-to-groin time and CT initiation-to-EVT start time for LVO stroke patients treated with EVT
evidence.effect: Mixed-effects regression: DTG time −11.2 minutes (95% CI, −18.22 to −4.2; P < .01); initiation of CT scan to EVT start time −9.8 minutes (95% CI, −16.9 to −2.6; P < .01). Univariable medians: DTG 100 (IQR, 81-116) minutes pre-AI vs 88 (IQR, 65-110) minutes post-AI; CT-to-EVT 85 (IQR, 68-99) minutes pre-AI vs 72 (IQR, 55-90) minutes post-AI.
evidence.tradeoff: Total processing time after image acquisition including transmission and software analysis was less than 5 minutes on average; clinical care team had to download the mobile app and sites received onboarding/education.
evidence.quote: In mixed-effects linear regression, implementation of the LVO detection AI algorithm resulted in a reduction in DTG time by 11.2 minutes.

evidence.title: Cost-effectiveness of immediate prioritisation of chest X-rays using artificial intelligence in lung cancer in England: the LungIMPACT study
evidence.comparator_used: AI support in interpretation only (no worklist prioritisation); secondarily current practice with no AI support
evidence.outcome: Cost-effectiveness (incremental cost per day reduction in time from chest X-ray to lung cancer diagnosis or discharge from the lung cancer pathway)
evidence.effect: AI with prioritisation was not cost-effective vs AI without prioritisation; no AI was always more cost-effective. Budget impact was £2 million per year in England for AI with prioritisation vs AI without, rising to £16–35 million per year vs No AI. The underlying LungIMPACT trial found no reduction in time from CXR to lung cancer diagnosis.
evidence.tradeoff: Added cost to the NHS with no demonstrated reduction in time to diagnosis.
evidence.quote: AI with prioritisation was not cost-effective vs. AI without prioritisation and secondary analysis showed that no AI was always more cost-effective.

evidence.title: Triaging mammography with artificial intelligence: an implementation study
evidence.comparator_used: Standard-of-care batch reading workflow (delayed radiologist interpretation after the patient left) with no AI prioritization
evidence.outcome: Time to additional imaging (TA) and time to biopsy diagnosis (TB)
evidence.effect: Control mean TA 25.6 days vs experimental 19.1 days (25% reduction, ΔTA = -6.4 days, p<0.001). Control mean TB 55.9 days vs experimental 39.2 days (30% reduction, ΔTB = -16.8 days, p=0.003). In AI-prioritized participants, mean TA was 3.5 days (86% shorter) and mean TB 30.2 days (46% shorter). All 6 cancers were prioritized by AI.
evidence.tradeoff: AI prioritized 29% of cases vs the 14% expected from retrospective testing, so more immediate reads were needed than planned. A radiologist was unavailable within 30 minutes for 6% (8/131) of prioritized cases. Same-visit imaging was not offered to 15% (5/33) for operational reasons, and 14% (4/28) declined it. Recall rate was 17.0% vs 14.3% (p=0.36, not significant). Immediate reads can disrupt workflow, and radiologists reported discomfort reading AI-prioritized cases as normal.
evidence.quote: The AI-modified workflow resulted in significantly shortened diagnostic delays (Fig. 3 ).

evidence.title: AI triage of duodenal biopsies improves workflow
evidence.comparator_used: Routine reporting pathway (cases with even case numbers reported in standard order without AI prioritisation)
evidence.outcome: Reporting turnaround time for clinically significant duodenal biopsy diagnoses
evidence.effect: Coeliac disease reported in 6 days vs 10 days; non-neoplastic abnormalities as a group in 7 days vs 10 days (both p<0.005); neoplastic lesions not reported quicker
evidence.tradeoff: AI processing took about 70 s per slide; adenocarcinoma sensitivity was only 50.0% (PPV 100%); no turnaround benefit for neoplastic lesions; cost of deployment and operation described as reasonable
evidence.quote: In the AI triage workstream coeliac disease, and non-neoplastic abnormalities as a group, were reported quicker than in the standard workstream (6 days vs 10 days and 7 days vs 10 days, respectively, both p<0.005), but neoplastic lesions were not reported quicker.

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage of Incidental Pulmonary Emboli on Contrast-Enhanced CT Examinations of the Chest or Abdomen
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologist interpretation without AI assistance (widget inactive, phase 1) versus with the AI triage widget active (phase 2)
evidence.outcome: Radiologist sensitivity for incidental pulmonary embolism on contrast-enhanced chest or abdominal CT; report turnaround time for IPE-positive examinations
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 80.0% without AI vs 96.2% with AI (p = .03); specificity 99.9% vs 99.9% (p = .58); mean turnaround for IPE-positive examinations 78.3 vs 74.6 minutes (p = .26)
evidence.quote: An AI triage system improved radiologists' sensitivity for IPE detection on CECT examinations of the chest or abdomen without significant change in report turnaround times.

evidence.title: Towards clinical implementation of an AI-algorithm for detection of cervical spine fractures on computed tomography
evidence.comparator_used: Historic retrospective cohort with routine (non-AI-prioritized) worklist reading
evidence.outcome: Time to diagnosis (time from CT acquisition to scan first opened, DNT)
evidence.effect: DNT 18% (5 min) shorter overall in the prospective AI cohort; in fracture-positive scans DNT 46% (16 min) shorter
evidence.tradeoff: AI missed 22 fractures, 5 of which required stabilizing therapy; PPV 63.0%, sensitivity 89.8%
evidence.quote: A time gain of 16 min to diagnosis for fractured cases was observed after introducing AI.

evidence.title: CATalyze-AI: accelerating referral for thrombectomy in acute stroke patients using an AI-based software. A prospective, multicentre, quasi-experimental cohort study
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation tele-stroke usual-care workflow before Methinks Stroke Suite AI outputs were shared with vascular neurologists.
evidence.outcome: Primary workflow outcome: time from local stroke centre arrival to EMS transfer request.
evidence.effect: 59 [43–88] vs 61 [46–99] min; adjusted median difference: −2.40 min; 95% CI, −6.16 to 4.48.
evidence.tradeoff: Post-implementation local CTA acquisition increased from 28% (n = 33) to 81% (n = 111); NCCT predictions had processing errors in 5 cases (4%) and CTA outputs were unavailable in 2 cases (2%) due to processing errors.
evidence.quote: Time from arrival at the local-SC to EMS transfer request did not differ significantly between the pre- and post-implementation cohorts (59 [43–88] vs 61 [46–99] min; adjusted median difference: −2.40; 95% CI, −6.16 to 4.48) ( Figure 2A ).

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage of Intracranial Hemorrhage on Noncontrast Head CT Examinations
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologists interpreting head NCCT examinations without AI assistance (phase 1) versus with the AI triage and notification system (phase 2)
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround time for ICH-positive examinations, and diagnostic performance for ICH detection
evidence.effect: Mean turnaround 147.1 min without AI vs 149.9 min with AI (p = .11). Accuracy 99.5% vs 99.2%, sensitivity 98.6% vs 98.9%, PPV 99.0% vs 97.5%, NPV 99.7% vs 99.7% (all p > .01).
evidence.tradeoff: Specificity was significantly lower with AI (99.3% vs 99.8%, p = .004). The comparison was between sequential phases, not randomized.
evidence.quote: An AI triage system for ICH detection did not improve radiologists' diagnostic performance or report turnaround times.

evidence.title: Radiologist Worklist Reprioritization Using Artificial Intelligence: Impact on Report Turnaround Times for CTPA Examinations Positive for Acute Pulmonary Embolism
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-AI period worklist reading order without AI reprioritization (standard worklist prioritization)
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround time and wait time for PE-positive CTPA examinations
evidence.effect: Mean report turnaround time 47.6 vs 59.9 minutes (mean difference 12.3 min [95% CI 0.6-26.0]); mean wait time 21.4 vs 33.4 minutes (mean difference 12.0 min [95% CI 0.9-25.3]); read time no significant difference (26.3 vs 26.5 min). Routine-priority exams during regular hours: wait time 15.3 vs 43.7 min (mean difference 28.4 min [95% CI 2.2-64.7]); no significant difference for stat- or urgent-priority exams.
evidence.quote: For PE-positive examinations, the post-AI period, compared with the pre-AI period, had significantly shorter mean report turnaround time (47.6 vs 59.9 minutes; mean difference, 12.3 minutes [95% CI, 0.6-26.0 minutes]) and mean wait time (21.4 vs 33.4 minutes; mean difference, 12.0 minutes [95% CI, 0.9-25.3 minutes]) but no significant difference in mean read time (26.3 vs 26.5 minutes; mean difference, 0.2 minutes [95% CI, -2.8 to 3.2 minutes]).

evidence.title: Workflow improvements from automated large vessel occlusion detection algorithms are dependent on care team engagement
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-ML implementation door-to-groin time, compared across levels of care team software utilization (comment-to-patient ratio and number of users)
evidence.outcome: Door-to-groin (DTG) time reduction relative to pre-ML implementation, by hospital utilization level
evidence.effect: Each 1 unit increase in comment-to-patient ratio was associated with DTG decreasing by 2.6 min (95% CI -5.09 to -0.13). Number of users-to-patient was not associated with DTG reduction (β=-0.22, 95% CI -1.78 to 1.33).
evidence.quote: For every 1 unit increase in the comment-to-patient ratio, DTG time decreased by 2.6 (95% CI -5.09 to -0.13) min, while accounting for site-level random effects.

evidence.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Triage on Radiologist Report Turnaround Time: Real-World Time Savings and Insights From Model Predictions
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-AI period (standard reading order without AI triage prioritization) for PE-positive CTPA examinations
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround time (scan completion to first preliminary report) for PE-positive CTPA
evidence.effect: Work hours: mean TAT 68.9 min pre-AI vs 46.7 min post-AI, time savings 22.2 min (95% CI 5.85-38.6; P = .004). Off-hours: 44.8 vs 42.0 min, savings 2.82 min (-11.1 to 16.7; P = .345), not significant. Model predicted 29.6 min (work hours) and 2.10 min (off-hours).
evidence.quote: Clinically observed time savings during work hours (22.2 [95% confidence interval: 5.85-38.6] min) were significant (P = .004), while off-hour (2.82 [-11.1 to 16.7] min) were not (P = .345).

evidence.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Automated Triage of Breast Cancer Biopsies in Malaysia: A Pragmatic Trial to Reduce Resource Consumption and Diagnostic Turnaround Time
evidence.comparator_used: Standard first-in-first-out (FIFO) histopathology workflow in a discrete-event simulation
evidence.outcome: Average diagnostic turnaround time for suspicious cases (simulated one-year period)
evidence.effect: Reduced average TAT for suspicious cases by 38.2% (from 7.2 to 4.5 days)
evidence.tradeoff: Slightly increased TAT for benign cases; results come from a simulation using synthetic data, not real clinical deployment
evidence.quote: The simulation demonstrated that the triage system reduced the average TAT for suspicious cases by 38.2% (from 7.2 to 4.5 days) while slightly increasing the TAT for benign cases.

controls.question: Should the LLM draft notes, reports and patient message replies for clinicians to edit and sign, rather than clinicians writing from scratch?
controls.control: Generate LLM drafts of patient message replies, discharge summaries and report impressions that clinicians edit and sign.
controls.comparator: Clinician-authored documentation without AI drafts, with sign-off in both
controls.aim: Reduce documentation burden while keeping accuracy and clinician accountability
variants: Patient message reply drafts (release approval governed by review_patient_facing_content)
