controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Low uptake (11% of presented drafts used) and declining usage over time; drafts were less readable than final physician messages; workflow integration needs improvement

Use was optional and varied by APP, from 30% to 89% of encounters (66.7% overall). APPs kept a mean of 78% of AI-generated note content (range 20%-93%), so edits were still needed. The comparison was descriptive with limited generalizability.
Marginal increase in required steps (InBasket actions); drafts were generated for all messages, including the 80% that received no response, adding review burden; low utilization

Factual accuracy was not assessed and there was no draft-to-final audit, so transcription errors could propagate; accuracy rested on mandatory supervisor verification. Succinctness showed no significant gain (P=.31). Design was pre-post with voluntary, self-selected users (about 40% uptake), and the effect cannot be attributed to any single component. Several narrative-quality gains were format-dependent.

Only 41% believed InBasket time would fall. The initial-prompt drafts were less preferred than human replies, and 6% of training-set drafts contained hallucinated information. Cognitive load was not measured with a validated questionnaire.
New failure mode: clinician review often missed objective inaccuracies and potentially harmful omissions, creating patient safety risk

evidence.title: Poetic or Prosaic? Evaluating the Linguistic Quality of AI-Generated Draft Replies to Patient Portal Messages
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline physician messages with GDRs not shown (clinician-authored replies without AI drafts)
evidence.outcome: Draft usage, alignment with final physician messages, readability, and provider-reported time savings and cognitive load
evidence.effect: Of 66,200 GDRs generated, 21,073 were presented and 2,264 (11%) were used; used GDRs aligned with final messages (BLEU 0.49, ROUGE-L 0.60, BERTScore F1 > 0.9); final messages were longer and more readable; providers reported time savings and reduced cognitive load
evidence.tradeoff: Low uptake (11% of presented drafts used) and declining usage over time; drafts were less readable than final physician messages; workflow integration needs improvement
evidence.quote: GDR usage declined over time, yet providers reported time savings and reduced cognitive load.

evidence.title: Navigating Collective Bargaining Barriers to the Implementation of AI Scribe Technology Among Ambulatory Advanced Practice Providers: Mixed Methods Quality Improvement Study
evidence.comparator_used: Nonpilot APPs in the same organization documenting without the AI scribe (non-randomized, descriptive comparison)
evidence.outcome: Time spent in the note writer and same-day encounter closure
evidence.effect: Note writer time: mean 6 min (SD 2.2; median 6, IQR 5.0-8.0) in the pilot group vs mean 14 min (SD 11.2; median 11, IQR 8.4-18.5) in nonpilot APPs. Same-day encounter closure: 90% (7290/8100) vs 72% (23,682/32,983).
evidence.tradeoff: Use was optional and varied by APP, from 30% to 89% of encounters (66.7% overall). APPs kept a mean of 78% of AI-generated note content (range 20%-93%), so edits were still needed. The comparison was descriptive with limited generalizability.
evidence.quote: The time spent in the note writer for the pilot group was a mean 6 (SD 2.2; median 6, IQR 5.0-8.0) minutes vs a mean 14 (SD 11.2; median 11, IQR 8.4-18.5) minutes for nonpilot APPs.

evidence.title: Utilization of Generative AI-drafted Responses for Managing Patient-Provider Communication
evidence.comparator_used: Patient message replies without GenAI drafts (messages handled without AI draft assistance)
evidence.outcome: Message turnaround time
evidence.effect: AI drafts reduced message turnaround time by 6.76%; overall draft utilization 19.4%
evidence.tradeoff: Marginal increase in required steps (InBasket actions); drafts were generated for all messages, including the 80% that received no response, adding review burden; low utilization
evidence.quote: AI generated drafts reduced message turnaround time by 6.76% despite a marginal increase in required steps (InBasket actions).

evidence.title: Nurse-Led Ambient AI Scribe for Patient Safety Incident Investigation Reports (Project NARRATE): Retrospective Pre-Post Comparative Document-Quality Study
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional manual free-text supervisor investigation reports (pre-implementation, June-August 2025), without AI drafts
evidence.outcome: Report completeness (WHO MIM PS-aligned total completeness, primary) and narrative quality (adapted 8-domain PDQI mean, secondary), rated by blinded reviewers
evidence.effect: WHO total completeness 13.61 (SD 2.54) vs 11.81 (SD 3.39); cluster-adjusted mean difference 1.95 (95% CI 0.91-3.00; P<.001). Adapted PDQI mean 4.13 (SD 0.34) vs 3.61 (SD 0.52); cluster-adjusted mean difference 0.53 (95% CI 0.37-0.69; P<.001). After plain-paragraph deformatting, completeness difference 1.70 (95% CI 0.27-3.14; P=.02) and PDQI difference 0.25 (95% CI 0.06-0.43; P=.009).
evidence.tradeoff: Factual accuracy was not assessed and there was no draft-to-final audit, so transcription errors could propagate; accuracy rested on mandatory supervisor verification. Succinctness showed no significant gain (P=.31). Design was pre-post with voluntary, self-selected users (about 40% uptake), and the effect cannot be attributed to any single component. Several narrative-quality gains were format-dependent.
evidence.quote: Among voluntary early adopters, NARRATE use was associated with more complete reports and higher adapted PDQI mean scores after accounting for supervisor clustering.

evidence.title: Prompt engineering on leveraging large language models in generating response to InBasket messages
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: No direct comparator; clinicians' perceived effect of LLM drafts on InBasket workload, and patient blinded comparison of drafts against real human-written responses
evidence.outcome: Clinician perceived usefulness, cognitive load and InBasket time after production deployment of LLM draft replies
evidence.effect: 94% of surveyed clinicians would keep using and recommend the tool. 72% believed it can reduce cognitive load and 41% believed it can reduce InBasket time. 74% of drafts were rated helpful (761 rated messages). Survey response rate was 58% (40 clinicians).
evidence.tradeoff: Only 41% believed InBasket time would fall. The initial-prompt drafts were less preferred than human replies, and 6% of training-set drafts contained hallucinated information. Cognitive load was not measured with a validated questionnaire.
evidence.quote: Vast majority (94%) clinicians would like to keep using the ART technology and would recommend it to a colleague, 72% believe that LLM draft response can reduce cognitive load in dealing with InBasket messages, and 41% believe it has potential to reduce InBasket time.

evidence.title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
evidence.comparator_used: No non-AI comparator arm; simulation of PCP review of AI drafts, with self-reported perception of workload versus usual practice
evidence.outcome: Clinician error detection and correction in AI-drafted patient portal replies, and perceived cognitive workload and safety
evidence.effect: 80% of PCPs agreed AI drafts reduced cognitive workload and 75% found them safe; each of 4 seeded errors was insufficiently addressed by 13-15 of 20 participants; 35-45% of erroneous drafts were submitted entirely unedited
evidence.tradeoff: New failure mode: clinician review often missed objective inaccuracies and potentially harmful omissions, creating patient safety risk
evidence.quote: While 80% of participants agreed AI drafts reduced cognitive workload and 75% found them safe, uncorrected errors highlight patient safety risks, underscoring the need for improved design, training, and error-detection mechanisms for AI tools.

evidence.title: Surgeon, Trainee, or GPT? A Blinded Multicentric Study of AI-Augmented Operative Notes
evidence.comparator_used: Operative notes written by an attending surgeon alone or a surgical resident alone (human-only authorship); GPT-only notes were also compared
evidence.outcome: Blinded reviewer domain scores, 'as is' approval rate, and writing time for operative notes
evidence.effect: Hybrid attending+GPT notes had the highest average domain scores and the highest 'as is' approval (79%), versus 23% for GPT-only notes. Writing time was significantly reduced in both AI-assisted groups compared with human-only authorship.
evidence.quote: Hybrid notes written by an attending surgeon with GPT assistance received the highest average domain scores and the highest "as is" approval rate (79%), outperforming all other groups.

evidence.title: Physician-revised AI-generated drafts are associated with higher ratings of written explanations in end-of-life care in the intensive care unit: a scenario-based single-center cross-sectional study
evidence.comparator_used: Physician-only written responses (no AI draft)
evidence.outcome: Ratings of medical validity (healthcare professionals) and empathy (healthcare and nonhealthcare professionals) on 5-point Likert scales
evidence.effect: Physician-AI collaborative responses were rated significantly higher than physician-only responses on all three prespecified primary outcomes. Differences were larger for empathy than for medical validity. No numeric values were reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: In the primary analyses, physician-AI collaborative responses received significantly higher ratings than both physician-only and AI-only responses across all three prespecified primary outcomes.

evidence.title: Multimodal Generative Artificial Intelligence Model for Creating Radiology Reports for Chest Radiographs in Patients Undergoing Tuberculosis Screening
evidence.comparator_used: Same radiologists reading chest radiographs without AI-generated reports
evidence.outcome: Accuracy for TB-related abnormality detection and localization performance with vs without AI-generated reports
evidence.effect: Accuracy reader 1: 93.4% without vs 94.1% with AI reports (p=.47); reader 2: 91.3% without vs 93.5% with (p=.03). Localization reader 1: 79.8% vs 78.7% (p=.71); reader 2: 77.9% vs 81.5% (p=.23).
evidence.tradeoff: Radiologists accepted few AI reports for abnormal radiographs without modification (reader 1: 52.4%; reader 2: 37.0%), versus 91.7% and 83.2% for normal radiographs, so abnormal cases still need substantial editing.
evidence.quote: Accuracy was significantly lower for AI-generated reports than for both readers alone (p < .001), but significantly higher with than without AI-generated reports for one reader (reader 1: p = .47; reader 2: p = .03).

evidence.title: Evaluating an LLM-Assisted Workflow for Clinical Documentation:  A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial on Time and Quality
evidence.comparator_used: Clinician-only drafting from scratch using matched templates (unedited LLM-only drafts also analyzed)
evidence.outcome: Document creation time (primary) and expert-rated document quality (secondary) for discharge summaries and referrals
evidence.effect: Summaries: clinician-in-the-loop β = −59.4 seconds (95% CI −118.1 to −0.8; P = .047). Referrals: β = +94.8 seconds (95% CI 40.4 to 149.3; P<.001). Quality was higher with clinician-in-the-loop in most domains for both document types. LLM-only drafts were fastest but had the lowest quality.
evidence.tradeoff: Referrals took longer with the LLM-assisted workflow (+94.8 seconds). Unedited LLM drafts were the lowest quality.
evidence.quote: For summaries, Clinician-in-the-loop was associated with shorter creation time versus Clinician-only (β = −59.4 seconds; 95% CI, −118.1 to −0.8; P = .047).

evidence.title: Impact of an Ambient AI Scribe on Medical Student Objective Structured Clinical Examination Notes: Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Student-authored human-only note without AI input, compared with a hybrid note revised after reviewing an AI scribe draft (paired, same students, OSCE)
evidence.outcome: QNOTE element scores (0-100) rated by blinded raters across 10 note elements
evidence.effect: Little change across elements. The only notable shift was a chief complaint decline (median 50 vs 50, mean 69.1 vs 59.6, P=.05), with fewer fully acceptable (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more unacceptable (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes. All other elements were similar (P=.14-.97). Of 12 students in the bottom quartile of human-only scores, 9 (75%) improved; 5/47 (10.6%) declined by 20 points or more.
evidence.tradeoff: AI notes often omitted symptom duration (mentioned in the chief complaint of only 8/47, 17%). 26/47 (55.3%) agreed the AI note left out important details, and 10/47 (21.3%) agreed it may reduce their ability to learn note writing. Students wrote their own note first (cognitive forcing), so the AI was not a true first draft. The study was nonrandomized, with self-selected participants, preclerkship students and a single site.
evidence.quote: After writing high-quality “human-only” notes, interaction with notes generated by the AI scribe had little impact on the quality of the “hybrid” notes written by preclerkship medical students.

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Large Language Models, Human Experts, and Expert-Edited Large Language Models to Neuro-Ophthalmology Questions
evidence.venue: Journal of neuro-ophthalmology : the official journal of the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society
evidence.comparator_used: Expert-authored responses without an LLM draft (human experts answering the neuro-ophthalmology questions on their own)
evidence.outcome: Mean expert-rated quality and empathy of responses (1-5 scale)
evidence.effect: Quality: Expert + AI 4.16 ± 0.81 vs Expert 3.56 ± 1.01 (P < 0.0001). Empathy: Expert + AI 3.63 ± 0.87 vs Expert 3.26 ± 1.08 (P = 0.002).
evidence.tradeoff: No time cost reported: time taken for expert-created and expert-edited LLM responses was similar (P = 0.75).
evidence.quote: For quality ( P < 0.0001) and empathy ( P = 0.002), Expert + AI performed better than Expert.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Assistant for Emergency Department Discharge Documentation
evidence.comparator_used: Manual physician-written ED discharge notes (session 1) versus physician-edited LLM drafts (session 2)
evidence.outcome: Note quality (4C Likert scores) and documentation time per note
evidence.effect: LLM-assisted vs manual: completeness 4.23 vs 4.03, correctness 4.38 vs 4.20, conciseness 4.23 vs 4.11, clinical utility 4.17 vs 3.85 (all P < .001). Median time per note 69.5 s (95% CI, 65.5-78.0) manual vs 32.0 s (95% CI, 29.5-36.0) LLM-assisted (P < .001).
evidence.tradeoff: Physician editing of the LLM drafts lowered completeness (4.23 vs 4.34; P = .001) and correctness (4.38 vs 4.45; P < .001) relative to the unedited drafts. Clinical utility was equivalent (4.17 vs 4.16).
evidence.quote: The median documentation time per note dropped from 69.5 (95% CI, 65.5-78.0) seconds for manual notes to 32.0 (95% CI, 29.5-36.0) seconds for LLM-assisted notes (P < .001).

evidence.title: Consensus, dissensus and synergy between clinicians and specialist foundation models in radiology report generation
evidence.comparator_used: Unassisted AI-generated reports and clinician-written reports (the abstract does not say which comparator the synergy is measured against)
evidence.outcome: Quality of radiology reports that contained errors, in an assistive clinician-AI report composition setting
evidence.effect: Described only as a synergistic improvement across all clinical settings; no numbers are given in the abstract
evidence.quote: For reports that contain errors we develop an assistive setting, the first demonstration of clinician-AI collaboration for radiology report composition, and we observe a synergistic improvement across all clinical settings.

evidence.title: A Comparative Study of Responses to Retina Questions from Either Experts, Expert-Edited Large Language Models, or Expert-Edited Large Language Models Alone
evidence.comparator_used: Expert-created responses without LLM drafts (Expert alone)
evidence.outcome: Quality and empathy scores of responses to retina patient questions, plus time to produce a response
evidence.effect: Expert + AI quality 3.86 ± 0.85 (best overall); Expert ranked 4/7 for quality and 6/7 for empathy; Expert + AI better than Expert for quality and empathy (both P < 0.001); time savings for expert-edited LLM vs expert-created response (P = 0.02)
evidence.quote: For both quality (P < 0.001) and empathy (P < 0.001), expert-edited LLM responses performed better than expert-created responses.

controls.question: Should clinicians review and correct AI segmentations and image annotations before clinical use?
controls.control: Have clinicians review and edit AI-generated contours, segmentations, landmarks and karyotypes before clinical use.
controls.comparator: Fully automatic AI segmentation or analysis without human correction
controls.aim: Catch segmentation errors while saving time over manual contouring
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Small non-significant increases in median contouring time for left bronchial tree (+22.9%), esophagus (+10.3%) and trachea (+20.8%); missing slices in auto-segmentations of aorta and heart in 5 cases; manual USB file transfer step still needed; time savings could not be predicted from geometric metrics
Manual adjustment took about two hours per plan. Time spent was not formally recorded.
Manual revision is still necessary for lymph node delineation, adding clinician time. The 5 h to 2 h total segmentation time is reported for the combined DL and AB workflow, not for revision alone.
Auto-segmentation took 2.51 minutes on average, and manual correction added 6.24 minutes. DLS failed in 11 patients with significant anatomical challenges and artifact.
The authors note the model may not completely replace humans; stomach and duodenum DSCs were lower (0.67 and 0.73) and CTV DSCs were 0.75-0.80.
Manual correction of the DL contours was still needed, with a median of 10 min and up to 46.3 min per case. The abstract does not report any other cost or new error.

evidence.title: Accuracy and efficiency of artificial Intelligence-Assisted three-dimensional liver volumetry in living donor evaluation based on real world prospective data
evidence.venue: HPB : the official journal of the International Hepato Pancreato Biliary Association
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional 2D manual segmentation for liver volumetry (not fully automatic AI without human correction)
evidence.outcome: Turnaround time and accuracy of graft volume prediction against intraoperative graft weight
evidence.effect: Turnaround 1.5 ± 1.5 vs 4.2 ± 3.6 days (p < 0.001). After exclusions, R2 0.818 and median error 54.0 mL with AI-based volumetry vs R2 0.707 and median error 65.0 mL with conventional methods. AI and manually edited volumes agreed with R2 = 0.992 and a mean difference of 23.7 ± 39.5 mL.
evidence.quote: The AI group had shorter turnaround times (1.5 ± 1.5 vs. 4.2 ± 3.6 days; p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Implementation and clinical evaluation of an in-house thoracic auto-segmentation model for 0.35 T magnetic resonance imaging guided radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual contouring by physicians according to standard clinical workflow (Group 2, 11 cases)
evidence.outcome: Physician contouring time for 9 thoracic OARs at a 0.35 T MR-linac
evidence.effect: Median total contouring time reduced by 50.3% (12.6 min; 750 s vs 1509 s, p<0.01); significant reductions for right lung (90.7%), left lung (92.7%) and heart (52.9%); non-significant reductions for spinal canal, aorta and right bronchial tree
evidence.tradeoff: Small non-significant increases in median contouring time for left bronchial tree (+22.9%), esophagus (+10.3%) and trachea (+20.8%); missing slices in auto-segmentations of aorta and heart in 5 cases; manual USB file transfer step still needed; time savings could not be predicted from geometric metrics
evidence.quote: Statistically significant median time reductions – based on a p < 0 . 025 threshold – were observed for the right lung (5.7 min, a 90.7% reduction), left lung (5.9 min, a 92.7% reduction), heart (1.1 min, a 52.9% reduction) and total contouring time (12.6 min, a 50.3% reduction).

evidence.title: Quality assurance for deep learning-based proton therapy planning in routine clinical use for oropharyngeal cancer
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Standard deep learning optimization (sDLO) plans without manual planner adjustment
evidence.outcome: Clinical goal achievement and NTCP in DL-generated IMPT plans
evidence.effect: CTV therapeutic goal achievement 91% (sDLO) to 93.6% (mDLO); CTV elective 78.2% to 88.5%. All NTCPs significantly lower in mDLO (p<0.001), e.g. grade ≥2 dysphagia 15.9% to 15.5%, grade ≥2 xerostomia 37.9% to 37.6%. The authors judged the NTCP reductions small and likely not clinically relevant.
evidence.tradeoff: Manual adjustment took about two hours per plan. Time spent was not formally recorded.
evidence.quote: Manual adjustments resulted in an increase of clinical goal achievement from 91% (sDLO, n = 71) to 93.6% (mDLO, n = 73) in CTV therapeutic and 78.2% (sDLO, n = 61) to 88.5% (mDLO, n = 69) in CTV elective ( Fig. 1 , Supplementary Table S4).

evidence.title: The Impact of a Neuroradiologist on the Report of a Real-World CT Perfusion Imaging Map Derived from Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning-Driven Software
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automatic AI (RapidAI) CTP maps without neuroradiologist review or correction
evidence.outcome: Proportion of CTP maps rated reportable
evidence.effect: 65.2% reportable without artifacts from AI software alone vs 87.9% reportable after neuroradiologist review (n=132)
evidence.quote: The study found that CTP maps derived from AI software were reportable in 65.2% of cases without artifacts and improved to 87.9% reportable cases when reviewed by neuroradiologists.

evidence.title: Deep learning and atlas-based models to streamline the segmentation workflow of total marrow and lymphoid irradiation
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automatic atlas-based CTV_LN contours with no manual correction
evidence.outcome: Topological agreement (DSC) with manual lymph node CTV contours
evidence.effect: Median DSC 0.70 [0.66;0.74] for automatic atlas-based contours, rising to 0.94 [0.94;0.95] after manual revision, with minimal Dmean differences
evidence.tradeoff: Manual revision is still necessary for lymph node delineation, adding clinician time. The 5 h to 2 h total segmentation time is reported for the combined DL and AB workflow, not for revision alone.
evidence.quote: The AB model achieved a median DSC of 0.70 [0.66;0.74] for CTV_LN delineation, increasing to 0.94 [0.94;0.95] after manual revision, with minimal Dmean differences.

evidence.title: Geometric and Dosimetric Evaluation of a RayStation Deep Learning Model for Auto-Segmentation of Organs at Risk in a Real-World Head and Neck Cancer Dataset
evidence.venue: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
evidence.comparator_used: Unedited (fully automatic) deep learning auto-segmentation vs manually corrected DLS-edited OARs, with manual GT-OARs as reference
evidence.outcome: Geometric similarity (DSC, HD) and dosimetric difference (ΔDmean, ΔDmax) of non-edited vs manually edited auto-segmented OARs
evidence.effect: All DLS-nonedited OARs had DSC>0.8 and HD<4mm vs DLS-edited OARs. Mean ΔDmean and ΔDmax were within ±300 and ±3 cGyRBE, except oesophagus and larynx, where mean ΔDmean rose up to 837.14 cGyRBE. Conclusion: skilled manual editing needed for few OARs. Vs GT-OARs, non-edited DLS had good DSC (>0.8) in only 12 of 30 OARs and poor DSC (<0.5) in 8.
evidence.tradeoff: Auto-segmentation took 2.51 minutes on average, and manual correction added 6.24 minutes. DLS failed in 11 patients with significant anatomical challenges and artifact.
evidence.quote: Compared with manually corrected, DLS-edited OARs, all DLS-nonedited OARs demonstrated excellent similarity with DSC>0.8 and HD<4mm.

evidence.title: Comprehensive clinical evaluation of deep learning-based auto-segmentation for radiotherapy in patients with cervical cancer
evidence.comparator_used: Physicians from other institutions delineating contours manually without auto-segmented contours (not fully automatic segmentation without correction)
evidence.outcome: Inter-physician contouring heterogeneity and contouring time
evidence.effect: Auto-segmentation reduced heterogeneity and shortened contouring time by 30 min; median overall physician satisfaction 7/10; no auto-segmented contours had large, obvious errors
evidence.tradeoff: The authors note the model may not completely replace humans; stomach and duodenum DSCs were lower (0.67 and 0.73) and CTV DSCs were 0.75-0.80.
evidence.quote: Auto-segmentation reduced heterogeneity and shortened contouring time by 30 min among radiation oncologists from different institutions.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Enhances Machine Learning Inference in Intraoperative Optical Coherence Tomography Glioma Imaging
evidence.comparator_used: Standalone models-only SVM inference pipeline without surgeon HITL correction
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity for glioma detection
evidence.effect: HITL using segmentation maps: Accuracy 94% [95% CI: 88-98%], Sensitivity 98% [95% CI: 92-100%]; SVM baseline: Accuracy 84% [95% CI: 81-87%], Sensitivity 83% [95% CI: 78-88%].
evidence.quote: Compared to the standalone models, the HITL approach significantly outperformed the SVM baseline (Accuracy 84% [95% CI: 81-87%]; Sensitivity 83% [95% CI: 78-88%]).

evidence.title: How smart is artificial intelligence in organs delineation? Testing a CE and FDA-approved Deep-Learning tool using multiple expert contours delineated on planning CT images
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual contouring of volumes of interest by radiation oncologists (the abstract does not report a fully automatic, uncorrected arm)
evidence.outcome: Contouring time and inter-observer agreement (relative volume differences and similarity indices), plus clinician satisfaction
evidence.effect: Median time was 25.0 min (range 8.0-115.0) for manual delineation, versus 2.3 min (1.2-8) for DL segmentation plus 10.0 min (0.3-46.3) for manual corrections; the time difference was p<0.001. Satisfaction was 44% vote 4 and 43% vote 5, correlated with time saved (p<0.001). Manually adjusted DL-based VOIs showed better inter-agreement than manually segmented ones.
evidence.tradeoff: Manual correction of the DL contours was still needed, with a median of 10 min and up to 46.3 min per case. The abstract does not report any other cost or new error.
evidence.quote: The overall time for VOIs retrieving and modification was statistically significantly lower than for manual contouring (p<0.001).

evidence.title: OSAIRIS: Lessons Learned From the Hospital-Based Implementation and Evaluation of an Open-Source Deep-Learning Model for Radiotherapy Image Segmentation
evidence.venue: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
evidence.comparator_used: Unedited AI-generated contours containing deliberately inserted errors (mystery shopping), compared with the same contours after clinician editing
evidence.outcome: Proportion of inserted contouring errors removed by clinician editing
evidence.effect: 72% of head and neck errors and 81% of prostate errors were removed in the editing step
evidence.tradeoff: Anchoring bias was present when clinicians edited AI-generated contours, more pronounced for some structures than others. Some errors were not corrected (roughly 28% of head and neck and 19% of prostate errors remained).
evidence.quote: Most errors, however, were corrected by clinicians, with 72% of the head and neck errors 81% of the prostate errors removed in the editing step.

evidence.title: A prospective multicenter trial of deep learning auto-segmentation for organs at risk in thoracic radiotherapy
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automatic AI-generated delineation without physician correction (AI-generated) and fully manual delineation
evidence.outcome: Delineation accuracy (vDSC, HD95), revision workload (VRI), and dosimetric deviation versus ground truth
evidence.effect: Mean vDSC 0.902 AI-assisted vs 0.896 AI-only vs 0.857 manual; mean HD95 5.20 vs 5.62 vs 8.01 mm; AI-assisted significantly better than AI alone for 6 of 11 OARs; median VRI 0.168 vs 0.181 (AI) vs 0.221 (manual); mean DVH deviation 4.2% AI-assisted vs 5.8% AI vs 11.1% manual
evidence.tradeoff: Physician editing requires time (median 10.0 min); some physicians showed decline in manual accuracy over time (12% of less-experienced), raising over-reliance concerns; AI-assisted showed no advantage over manual for trachea in Center 4 and EC patients, and aorta in Center 5.
evidence.quote: AI-assisted delineation also achieved significantly higher accuracy than AI delineation for 6 out of 11 OARs (54.5%): the heart, aorta, liver, trachea, spinal cord, and esophagus (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 3 ).

evidence.title: Diagnosing growth in low-grade gliomas with and without artificial intelligence-measured longitudinal volume measurements: A retrospective observational study
evidence.comparator_used: AI segmentation without human review (fully automatic AI volumetry)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of tumor growth detection (false positive and false negative rates) from longitudinal volumes
evidence.effect: AI without human review gave similar results but with a 25% false positive rate and an 8.33% false negative rate. AI with physician review detected growth a median of 21 months earlier than visual inspection in the clinical progression group.
evidence.tradeoff: Physicians spent a median of 2 minutes reviewing, revising and approving each AI segmentation.
evidence.quote: AI without human review generated similar results but with a 25% false positive and an 8.33% false negative rate.

evidence.title: Multicenter validation and randomized crossover reader evaluation of deep learning-assisted tri-sequence three-dimensional MRI segmentation for hypopharyngeal tumor
evidence.venue: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Manual contouring by the same readers, without AI assistance (randomized double-crossover)
evidence.outcome: Contouring accuracy (DSC), contouring time, and inter-reader consistency (Fleiss' κ)
evidence.effect: Junior DSC 0.73 ± 0.16 to 0.86 ± 0.14; senior DSC 0.79 ± 0.13 to 0.84 ± 0.15; contouring time reduced by 55%; Fleiss' κ 0.69 ± 0.12 to 0.86 ± 0.12 (all p < 0.01)
evidence.quote: In the reader study, AI assistance increased mean DSC in juniors from 0.73 ± 0.16 to 0.86 ± 0.14 and in seniors from 0.79 ± 0.13 to 0.84 ± 0.15, reduced contouring time by 55%, and improved Fleiss' κ from 0.69 ± 0.12 to 0.86 ± 0.12 (all p < 0.01).

evidence.title: Real-world validation of Artificial Intelligence-based Computed Tomography auto-contouring for prostate cancer radiotherapy planning
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual contouring by the observers (automatic-only contours were also compared against manual)
evidence.outcome: Inter-observer variability (DSC) and contouring time for CTVs/OARs
evidence.effect: Inter-observer DSC for automatic + editing vs manual: seminal vesicles 0.83 vs 0.73; prostate 0.86 vs 0.83; rectum 0.96 vs 0.81. Editing improved DSC vs manual to 0.76-0.94. Contouring time fell from 17-24 min (manual) to 3-7 min (editing) for the two observers (p < 0.01).
evidence.tradeoff: Automatic contours needed some editing: median clinical score 4 (little editing), and score <4 in 3 and 2 patients for the two observers.
evidence.quote: Inter-observer variability of automatic + editing contours improved significantly, being lower than manual contouring (e.g.: seminal vesicles: 0.83vs0.73; prostate: 0.86vs0.83; rectum: 0.96vs0.81).

evidence.title: Volume of hyperintense inflammation (VHI): A quantitative imaging biomarker of inflammation load in spondyloarthritis, enabled by human-machine cooperation
evidence.comparator_used: purely manual segmentation / purely visual assessment by readers (no automated preliminary segmentation)
evidence.outcome: inter-observer segmentation overlap (Dice score); inter-observer agreement of inflammation measurement; response assessment
evidence.effect: Dice 0.84 for human-machine workflow vs 0.56 for purely manual segmentation; VHI inter-observer agreement similar or better than visual scoring, with similar response assessments
evidence.quote: The human-machine workflow showed superior inter-observer segmentation overlap than purely manual segmentation (Dice score 0.84 versus 0.56).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted delineation for postoperative radiotherapy in patients with lung cancer: a prospective, multi-center, cohort study
evidence.comparator_used: Unmodified AI auto-segmentation (also compared with fully manual delineation by junior radiation oncology residents)
evidence.outcome: CTV contouring accuracy (HD, MDA, DSC) against senior oncologist ground truth, plus inter-observer variability for OARs
evidence.effect: CTV median HD, MDA and DSC values of 20.03 vs. 21.55 mm, 2.57 vs. 3.06 mm, 0.745 vs. 0.703 (all P<0.05); OAR results were similar; CV for OARs reduced by approximately 50%
evidence.quote: AI-assisted delineation achieved significantly higher accuracy compared to unmodified AI auto-contouring and fully manual delineation by radiation oncologists, with median HD, MDA, and DCS values of 20.03 vs. 21.55 mm, 2.57 vs. 3.06 mm, 0.745 vs. 0.703 (all P<0.05) for CTV, respectively.

evidence.title: Dosimetric Impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Based Autocontouring Software, OncoStudio, in High-Risk Prostate Cancer Treatment Planning: A Three-Group Comparative Study on the Slice Ranges of Seminal Vesicles
evidence.comparator_used: Unadjusted AI autocontouring of seminal vesicles, with manual contouring as the Dunnett's test reference group
evidence.outcome: PTV and CTV dose coverage (Dmax, Dmin, Dmean, D95, D98, D99, V95%)
evidence.effect: CTV Dmean vs manual contouring: unadjusted AC -58.7 cGy (95% CI -123.0 to 5.5, p = 0.077, g = 0.78); slice-adjusted AC -41.3 cGy (p = 0.254, g = 0.63). PTV Dmean unadjusted AC -92.8 cGy (p = 0.075, g = 0.67). Dose differences <1% of prescription. No significant differences in any DVH parameter.
evidence.quote: No statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups in any dose volume histogram parameters.

evidence.title: Evaluation of a commercial deep-learning-based contouring software for CT-based gynecological brachytherapy
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual contouring by 4 radiation oncologists
evidence.outcome: Interobserver agreement across organs and metrics
evidence.effect: AI-assisted interobserver agreement was better than manual for all organs and metrics; numeric values not given in the abstract
evidence.quote: AI-assisted interobserver agreement was better than manual interobserver agreement for all organs and metrics.

evidence.title: Evaluation of segmentation accuracy and the improvement of time effectiveness using deep learning-based segmentation in 177Lu-DOTATATE dosimetry
evidence.comparator_used: Fully manual delineation of liver, spleen and kidneys by medical physicists and radiological technologists (manual contouring without AI)
evidence.outcome: Total time required for dosimetry (image reconstruction, segmentation, absorbed dose calculation)
evidence.effect: Reference method (AI-seg modified by the most experienced MP) took 47.0 [30.0-58.0] min vs. 54.3 [49.5-67.0] min for manual, p = 0.014; DSCs for AI-seg were liver 0.988, spleen 0.965, kidneys 0.994 vs manual 0.955, 0.929, 0.929; kidney absorbed dose from AI-seg differed significantly (1.4% increase)
evidence.tradeoff: AI-seg HD exceeded 30.0 mm in a few cases (liver 3/23; spleen 2/23) due to hepatomegaly, so segmentation errors occurred and required correction; kidney absorbed dose from AI-seg differed significantly (1.4% increase).
evidence.quote: Dosimetry using the reference method took significantly less time than the manual approach (47.0 [30.0-58.0] min vs. 54.3 [49.5-67.0] min, p = 0.014).

evidence.title: Evaluation of a convolution neural network for baseline total tumor metabolic volume on [18F]FDG PET in diffuse large B cell lymphoma
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automated AI lesion segmentation without physician review (method 1) versus fully automated with physician review (method 3); semi-automated method 5 as reference
evidence.outcome: Processing time to obtain TMTV and TLG (the abstract reports agreement for the reviewed method 3 against reference, not for unreviewed method 1)
evidence.effect: Mean processing time 20 s ± 9.0 for fully automated method 1 vs 178 s ± 125.7 for automated with physician review (method 3) vs 326 s ± 188.6 for semi-automated method 5 (p < 0.05). Method 3 vs method 5 ICC 0.99 for TMTV and 1.0 for TLG.
evidence.tradeoff: Physician review of the automated segmentation added roughly 158 s per case compared with fully automated processing, though it was still faster than the semi-automated reference method.
evidence.quote: Mean processing time (± standard deviation) was 20 s ± 9.0 for method 1, 178 s ± 125.7 for method 3, and 326 s ± 188.6 for method 5 (p < 0.05).

evidence.title: Accuracy of AI-Driven Cephalometric Tracing Systems in Orthodontic Analysis Including Patients With Cleft Lip/Palate
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automated AI cephalometric tracing (AC1, OD1, WC1) versus the same AI tracings manually corrected by researchers (AC2, OD2, WC2), each against computer-aided manual tracing as the reference
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of cephalometric landmark and measurement agreement with the computer-aided manual reference
evidence.effect: Method significantly affected 62 of 85 measurements. U1-NA° and U1-L1° remained clinically unacceptably different from the reference in all AI programs even after manual correction. Overall concordance with manual tracing was high, but the authors concluded use is not sufficiently reliable without human oversight.
evidence.quote: U1-NA° and U1-L1° showed clinically unacceptable differences from RV across all AI programs, even after researcher intervention.

evidence.title: Clinical evaluation of a deep learning segmentation model including manual adjustments afterwards for locally advanced breast cancer
evidence.venue: Technical innovations & patient support in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Uncorrected automatic DL contours, each compared against manual delineation
evidence.outcome: Contour agreement with manual delineation (DSC, 95%HD, sDSC) and clinical acceptability
evidence.effect: Mean DSC for right-sided CTVp was 0.92 ± 0.06 before correction; correction statistically significantly improved it by only 0.02 ± 0.05. 92% of auto-contours were scored clinically acceptable, with or without corrections.
evidence.tradeoff: Correction adds editing time. Even so, auto-segmentation including correction cut time versus manual delineation in 95% of cases (OARs 42.4% ± 26.5%, CTVs 58.5% ± 19.1%; mean absolute reduction 00:08:51 and 00:25:38).
evidence.quote: Good quantitative results were achieved before correction, e.g. mean DSC for the right-sided CTVp was 0.92 ± 0.06, whereas correction statistically significantly improved this contour by only 0.02 ± 0.05, respectively.

evidence.title: Potential of E-Learning Interventions and Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Contouring Skills in Radiotherapy: The ELAISA Study
evidence.comparator_used: Manual contouring by radiation oncologists without AI template (randomized, with or without teaching)
evidence.outcome: Contour quality (DSC vs expert consensus) and contouring time for organs-at-risk in head-and-neck cases
evidence.effect: Without prior teaching, AI-assisted contouring raised DSC for optic nerve (0.05 [0.01; 0.10]), oral cavity (0.10 [0.06; 0.13]), parotid (0.07 [0.05; 0.12]), spinal cord (0.04 [0.01; 0.06]) and mandible (0.02 [0.01; 0.03]). Contouring time fell for brain stem (-1.41 [-2.44; -0.25]), mandible (-6.60 [-8.09; -3.35]), optic nerve (-0.19 [-0.47; -0.02]), parotid (-1.80 [-2.66; -0.32]) and thyroid (-1.03 [-2.18; -0.05]).
evidence.quote: AI-assisted contouring without previous teaching increased absolute DSC for optic nerve (by 0.05 [0.01; 0.10]), oral cavity (0.10 [0.06; 0.13]), parotid (0.07 [0.05; 0.12]), spinal cord (0.04 [0.01; 0.06]), and mandible (0.02 [0.01; 0.03]).

evidence.title: Benchmarking robustness of automated CT pancreas segmentation: achieving human-level reliability through human-in-the-loop optimization
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automatic AI segmentation without human correction
evidence.outcome: Fraction of predictions reaching human-level performance (FT)
evidence.effect: FT increased to 0.99 after human revision of flagged outliers; 23-fold workload reduction
evidence.tradeoff: Average 1.54 minutes of human revision time per case
evidence.quote: Human-in-the-loop revision of acquisition-flagged outliers increased FT to 0.99, with an average time of 1.54 minutes per case, corresponding to a 23-fold workload reduction.

evidence.title: AI-assisted cardiomegaly screening via implicit morphological inference and human-in-the-loop validation
evidence.venue: Journal of X-ray science and technology
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automatic UBNet-Seg lung segmentation and CTR-based classification without expert correction
evidence.outcome: Cardiomegaly screening accuracy on external NIH and OpenI datasets
evidence.effect: Accuracy rose from 90.31% to 93.63% on NIH and from 76.07% to 91.21% on OpenI with expert-guided refinement (McNemar p<0.001)
evidence.quote: Crucially, the integration of a Human-in-the-Loop mechanism successfully neutralized domain shifts; the McNemar test confirmed that expert-guided refinement provided statistically significant accuracy improvements to 93.63% and 91.21% on NIH and OpenI, respectively (p<0.001).

evidence.title: Dosimetric comparison of autocontouring techniques for online adaptive proton therapy
evidence.comparator_used: Plans reoptimized on fully automatic contours (rigid registration, DIR, deep-learning, patient-specific segmentation) compared with plans on manual contours
evidence.outcome: Dosimetric effect on the daily reoptimized plan of using automatic versus manual OAR and target contours
evidence.effect: Automatic OAR contours: dosimetric influence small (<5% prescribed dose in most cases), best with DIR. Automatic target contour: effect larger (>5% prescribed dose in most cases), so manual verification remains necessary. Compared with non-adaptive therapy, dose differences from automatic target contours were small and target coverage improved, especially with DIR.
evidence.tradeoff: Manual contouring is too slow for online adaptation, so manual adjustment time must be prioritized (target over OARs) during time-critical sessions.
evidence.quote: The results show that manual adjustment of OARs is rarely necessary and that several autocontouring techniques are directly usable.

evidence.title: An Integral R-Banded Karyotype Analysis System of Bone Marrow Metaphases Based on Deep Learning
evidence.comparator_used: Fully automatic workflow of the karyotype analysis system without human correction
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy of the whole karyotype analysis system on the 885-metaphase test set
evidence.effect: Accuracy 99.06% with the semiautomatic strategy vs 93.33% with the automatic strategy
evidence.quote: The whole system achieved an accuracy of 93.33% with the automatic strategy and an accuracy of 99.06% with the semiautomatic strategy.

controls.question: Should AI and decision support medication alerts go to a pharmacist team first rather than straight to prescribers?
controls.control: Route AI or CDS medication alerts to pharmacists who review, refine and contact prescribers or patients.
controls.comparator: Alerts delivered directly to prescribers without pharmacist review
controls.aim: Reduce alert fatigue and improve action on medication safety alerts
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: A few gout-related interventions were only partially accepted.
Clinical pharmacists received 17.2 alerts per day to review. Acceptance was lower for pharmacist-reviewed alerts than for direct alerts, and the two groups were not randomized.

Many alerts resolved without any pharmacist action (27% at day 1, 48% at day 3), suggesting many alerts may be low value or 'false positive' and could cause distraction/alert fatigue; retrospective observational design; broad definition of 'action' may overstate the pharmacist effect.

evidence.title: The Implementation of a Clinical Decision Support System for Managing Drug-Disease Interactions in Outpatients with Cardiovascular and Diabetic Comorbidities: An Interventional Study at a Tertiary Hospital in Vietnam
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-intervention phase without CDSS and pharmacist consultation; not compared against alerts sent directly to prescribers
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of drug-disease interactions and acceptance of pharmacist interventions
evidence.effect: Relative contraindications fell from 0.33% to 0.01% (P < 0.05). Pharmacist interventions were largely fully accepted and none were rejected. The effect is of the combined CDSS plus pharmacist intervention.
evidence.tradeoff: A few gout-related interventions were only partially accepted.
evidence.quote: The rate of relative contraindication plummeted from 0.33% to 0.01% (P < 0.05).

evidence.title: Tackling alert fatigue with a semi-automated clinical decision support system: quantitative evaluation and end-user survey
evidence.comparator_used: Alerts sent directly to physicians without pharmacist review (compared within the same CDSS, retrospective, non-randomized)
evidence.outcome: Physician acceptance rate and physician alert burden
evidence.effect: Of 10,556 alerts, 619 went directly to physicians (acceptance 89.8%) and 2,231 reached physicians after pharmacist evaluation (acceptance 68.4%); overall acceptance 72.4%. All hospital physicians together received 7.8 notifications per day.
evidence.tradeoff: Clinical pharmacists received 17.2 alerts per day to review. Acceptance was lower for pharmacist-reviewed alerts than for direct alerts, and the two groups were not randomized.
evidence.quote: Involving clinical pharmacists proved a promising approach to limit the alert burden of physicians and thus tackle alert fatigue.

evidence.title: Clinical Decision Support Systems in Hospitalized Older Patients: An Exploratory Analysis in a Real-Life Clinical Setting
evidence.comparator_used: CDSS alerts with no pharmacist action (alerts reviewed by pharmacist but not acted on), i.e. natural course of alerts
evidence.outcome: Proportion of CDSS alerts resolved at day 1 and day 3
evidence.effect: Day 1: 36.1% vs 27.3% resolved (p<0.001); day 3: 62.4% vs 48.0% (p<0.001). Renal function category: 16.6% vs 10.6% (day 1) and 29.8% vs 19.4% (day 3), both p<0.001; other categories showed small non-significant positive effects.
evidence.tradeoff: Many alerts resolved without any pharmacist action (27% at day 1, 48% at day 3), suggesting many alerts may be low value or 'false positive' and could cause distraction/alert fatigue; retrospective observational design; broad definition of 'action' may overstate the pharmacist effect.
evidence.quote: In 4083 (51.6%) of the handled alerts, an action was performed by the pharmacist, resulting in 1297 (36.1% after excluding ‘unknown’) resolved alerts after day 1, while when the pharmacist did not perform an action, which was the case in 3824 alerts, 915 (27.3% after excluding ‘unknown’) alerts were resolved (36.1% vs 27.3%, p < 0.001).

controls.question: Should a predictive alert be paired with a defined response protocol, nudge or documentation tool rather than delivered alone?
controls.control: Pair predictive alerts with a defined clinical response protocol, behavioral nudges, team rounding process or documentation templates.
controls.comparator: Delivering the risk prediction alone without a linked action pathway
controls.aim: Turn risk predictions into consistent clinical action and better outcomes
variants: Behavioral nudges prompting the linked action
controls.family_label: draft versus autonomous modes, review designs, routing to humans, double review, workload timing
tradeoffs: Limited reach: 116 of 274 (42.3%) not reached, with no retry; calls added scheduling-staff workload

PRSS staff burden was high, at about 21 calls per week. Participants answered only 36% of first call attempts (175 of 483). Participants also bore a high burden from responding to numerous alerts. A program would need enough trained PRSS staff for extended hours, and the cost could be prohibitive. Differences were modest, which may temper clinical significance. Drug use recurrence was not examined as an outcome. Anomaly-based and random alerts could not be separated because identifiers were lost.

CDSS accuracy was only moderate (true positives 61.3% in System A, 70.4% in System B). Outreach required portal/mailed letters plus a phone call, and navigation required one or more additional calls. Navigation added no clear benefit over outreach alone.

The package could not be separated into its components, so the effect of the alert versus the workflow is unknown. Sensitivity analyses showed 95% CIs including 0 at bandwidths greater than 9 points. No specific preventive action was required.

The ADR reduction was not statistically significant (p=0.095). The design is single-centre and before-after, with no concurrent control, so the effect of the ML warning cannot be separated from the pharmacist-led process redesign. The study reports no workload or latency data.
NASA Task Load Index rose from 43 to 57 post-intervention (slight workload increase). Only 28% (555/1977) of huddles occurred without an alert firing, suggesting some automation bias.

evidence.title: Perioperative goal-directed therapy with artificial intelligence to reduce the incidence of intraoperative hypotension and renal failure in patients undergoing lung surgery: A pilot study
evidence.comparator_used: Control group with standard care and no specific hemodynamic protocol
evidence.outcome: Frequency, duration and severity of intraoperative hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg) during lung surgery with single lung ventilation
evidence.effect: Hypotensive episodes 0 [0-1] vs 1 [0-2], p=0.01; duration 0 min [0-3.17] vs 2.33 min [0-7.42], p=0.01; area under MAP 65 0 [0-12] vs 10.67 [0-44.16] mmHg*min, p<0.01; TWA of MAP 65 0 [0-0.08] vs 0.07 [0-0.25] mmHg, p<0.01. No significant difference in postoperative AKI (6.7% vs 4.2%, p=0.72); MINS trend 17.1% vs 31.8% (p=0.07); infection trend 16.0% vs 26.8% (p=0.16).
evidence.quote: The number of hypotensive episodes was lower in the intervention group compared to the control group (0 [0-1] vs. 1 [0-2]; p = 0.01), the duration of hypotension was shorter in the intervention group (0 min [0-3.17] vs. 2.33 min [0-7.42]; p = 0.01).

evidence.title: Long-term Effect of Machine Learning-Triggered Behavioral Nudges on Serious Illness Conversations and End-of-Life Outcomes Among Patients With Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Usual care (control period before rollout); the trial did not test the risk prediction alone
evidence.outcome: Sustained SIC rate and end-of-life systemic therapy over 40 weeks
evidence.effect: SIC rates for all encounters rose from 1.3% (158/12 356) to 4.4% (1262/28 665), about 4 times baseline after 6 months. End-of-life systemic therapy fell from 10.4% (24/231) to 7.5% (72/957); aOR 0.25 (95% CI 0.11-0.57). No effect on inpatient death, ICU use, hospice enrollment or hospice length of stay.
evidence.quote: First, our intervention led to a sustained increase in SICs, and rates remained nearly 4 times above baseline after 6 months.

evidence.title: From prediction to practice: machine learning models and real-world interventions for magnetic resonance imaging appointment no-shows in a hospital setting
evidence.comparator_used: High-risk patients flagged by the model but receiving no reminder call (control group)
evidence.outcome: MRI no-show rate
evidence.effect: 21.9% intervention (274 appointments) vs 22.0% control (460 appointments), P = .48; reached patients 18.4% vs not reached 26.7%
evidence.tradeoff: Limited reach: 116 of 274 (42.3%) not reached, with no retry; calls added scheduling-staff workload
evidence.quote: Overall, the phone call trial showed no significant reduction in the no-show rate between the control (22.0%) and intervention (21.9%) groups ( P- value: .48), as shown in Table 2 .

evidence.title: Identifying risk factors for drug use recurrence with ecological momentary assessment, wearable technologies, and machine learning: a feasibility trial of peer recovery support specialist intervention
evidence.comparator_used: Standard of care arm: participant received the push alert on their phone suggesting they contact their support system, with no PRSS call
evidence.outcome: Self-reported anxiety, depression, stress, angst composite and maximum craving (daily EMA, 0-10 scale) across study phases
evidence.effect: PRSS arm had modest but significant decreases in anxiety, stress, depression and angst composite (all p < 0.001) and maximum craving (p = 0.011) relative to SoC. In the PRSS arm all five variables were lower in Phase 2 than at Baseline, whereas in the SoC arm depression, stress and angst composite slightly increased. Among the upper-third responders, interaction p-values ranged from <0.001 to 0.027.
evidence.tradeoff: PRSS staff burden was high, at about 21 calls per week. Participants answered only 36% of first call attempts (175 of 483). Participants also bore a high burden from responding to numerous alerts. A program would need enough trained PRSS staff for extended hours, and the cost could be prohibitive. Differences were modest, which may temper clinical significance. Drug use recurrence was not examined as an outcome. Anomaly-based and random alerts could not be separated because identifiers were lost.
evidence.quote: Statistically significant reductions were noted in anxiety, depression, stress, angst, and cravings in the PRSS intervention arm relative to the SoC arm, though the extent of the differences was modest, therefore likely tempering the clinical significance.

evidence.title: Comparing clinical decision support systems for improving follow-up of abnormal cervical cancer screening test results
evidence.comparator_used: CDSS alone (identifying overdue abnormal results with recommended follow-up) and usual care, without linked patient outreach or navigation
evidence.outcome: Completion of recommended follow-up at 120 days after enrollment
evidence.effect: CDSS with outreach with or without navigation vs usual care: System A 38.2% or 37.2% vs 23.5% (p<0.001); System B 25.4% or 23% vs 19.7% (p=0.044). CDSS alone vs usual care did not improve outcomes in either system.
evidence.tradeoff: CDSS accuracy was only moderate (true positives 61.3% in System A, 70.4% in System B). Outreach required portal/mailed letters plus a phone call, and navigation required one or more additional calls. Navigation added no clear benefit over outreach alone.
evidence.quote: Both models with patient outreach with or without navigation - but not CDSS alone - increased recommended follow-up.

evidence.title: Spending Analysis of Machine Learning-Based Communication Nudges in Oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Standard of care (control arm, no behavioral nudges) among patients flagged high-risk by the ML mortality algorithm
evidence.outcome: Mean daily end-of-life spending in the last 6 months of life
evidence.effect: $377.96 vs $449.92 unadjusted; adjusted mean difference -$75.33 (95% CI -$136.42 to -$14.23; P=0.02); $13,747 adjusted savings per decedent; lower systemic therapy (-$44.59), office/outpatient (-$9.62) and other therapy (-$8.65) spending; no difference in acute care, long-term care or hospice spending
evidence.quote: The intervention was associated with lower unadjusted mean daily spending in the last 6 months of life for the intervention group versus controls ($377.96 vs. $449.92; adjusted mean difference, -$75.33; 95% confidence interval, -$136.42 to -$14.23; P=0.02), translating to $13,747 total adjusted savings per decedent and $13 million in cumulative savings across all decedents in the intervention group.

evidence.title: Impact of the National Early Warning Score-based sepsis response system on hospital-onset sepsis in a tertiary hospital in South Korea
evidence.comparator_used: Preliminary group: patients alerted in the first 6 months after implementation, compared with the SRP group from the second 6 months (propensity-matched, same NEWS alert system and 24/7 rapid response team)
evidence.outcome: 30-day mortality (secondary: blood culture ordering/performance and sepsis bundle compliance)
evidence.effect: 30-day mortality 25.0% (44/176) vs 15.3% (27/176); HR 0.56 (95% CI 0.36-0.86; P=0.017). Blood cultures 58.5% vs 45.5% (P=0.019). Antibiotics within 6 h 94.6% vs 88.3% (P=0.065). Survival benefit began to appear after about 4 months.
evidence.quote: The SRP group showed a lower 30-day mortality risk (hazard ratio, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.36-0.86; P=0.017) compared to the preliminary group.

evidence.title: Clinical Impact of a Sepsis Alert System Plus Electronic Sepsis Navigator Using the Epic Sepsis Prediction Model in the Emergency Department
evidence.comparator_used: Contemporaneous sites B-D using a SIRS-based sepsis alert without a sepsis navigator, and historical site A data before implementation
evidence.outcome: Time to initial antimicrobial delivery from ED arrival (and from threshold score to antimicrobial)
evidence.effect: Site A 3.33 h (IQR 2.10-5.37) vs sites B-D 3.22 h (IQR 1.97-5.60; p = 0.437); site A historical 6.20 h (IQR 3.49-11.61; p < 0.001). After matching-weight adjustment, no difference between contemporaneous sites; adjusted time improved by 2.87 h (p < 0.001) vs site A historical.
evidence.quote: Adjusted time to initial antimicrobial improved by 2.87 h (p < 0.001) at site A compared with site A historical.

evidence.title: Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Intervention for Detecting Clinical Deterioration
evidence.comparator_used: Patients just below the EDI threshold of 65.0 who did not trigger the alert or the collaborative huddle workflow (regression discontinuity)
evidence.outcome: Escalations in care (RRT activation, ICU transfer, or cardiopulmonary arrest)
evidence.effect: Absolute risk reduction of -10.4 percentage points (95% CI, -20.1 to -0.8; P = .03) at the threshold; secondary outcome including inpatient death -7.0 points (95% CI, -16.6 to 2.6; P = .15); inpatient death -0.4 points (95% CI, -6.4 to 5.6; P = .88)
evidence.tradeoff: The package could not be separated into its components, so the effect of the alert versus the workflow is unknown. Sensitivity analyses showed 95% CIs including 0 at bandwidths greater than 9 points. No specific preventive action was required.
evidence.quote: The RDD analysis estimated an absolute risk reduction of −10.4 percentage points (95% CI, −20.1 to −0.8 percentage points; P = .03) in the primary outcome for patients at the EDI score threshold.

evidence.title: Pharmacist-led surgical medicines prescription optimization and prediction service improves patient outcomes - a machine learning based study
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation periods (ML development and external validation periods) with pharmacist-led prescription review but no ML warning or SMPOP process nodes; uncontrolled before-after comparison
evidence.outcome: Prescriber acceptance of pharmacist recommendations, length of stay, hospitalization and medication costs, ADRs
evidence.effect: Acceptance 43.95% (ML development period) and 40.63% (external validation period) vs 71.30% post-implementation (p<0.001); median length of stay 15 and 13 vs 7 days (p<0.001); median total costs 36,160 and 32,263 vs 20,843 RMB (p<0.001); median medication costs 8,795 and 7,848 vs 4,713 RMB (p<0.001); ADRs 0.19% and 0.4% vs 0.18% (p=0.095)
evidence.tradeoff: The ADR reduction was not statistically significant (p=0.095). The design is single-centre and before-after, with no concurrent control, so the effect of the ML warning cannot be separated from the pharmacist-led process redesign. The study reports no workload or latency data.
evidence.quote: After the introduction of ML model, this study shows that the acceptance rate of pharmacists' recommendations increased from 43.9% to 71.3%, indicating that the model enhanced the scientific rigor and credibility of pharmacists' advice.

evidence.title: Pilot Study to Optimize Goal-directed Hemodynamic Management During Pancreatectomy
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation: patients monitored with the Hypotension Prediction Index monitor and managed per usual, without the GDHT decision algorithm
evidence.outcome: Intraoperative hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg), cardiac index >2, and stroke volume variation <12 during pancreatectomy
evidence.quote: There was a 33.3% reduction in IOH (5.2% ± 0.1% versus 7.8% ± 0.3%, P < 0.01, a 31.6% increase in cardiac index >2.0 (83.7% + 0.2% versus 63.6% + 0.5%, P < 0.01), and a 37.6% increase in stroke volume variation <12 (73.2% + 0.3% versus 53.2% + 0.5%, P < 0.01).

evidence.title: Human performance evaluation of a pediatric artificial intelligence sepsis model
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-intervention and post-intervention cases without a huddle, i.e. no linked huddle response to the sepsis alert
evidence.outcome: Antibiotic treatment of IPSO sepsis cases
evidence.effect: Without a huddle, treatment was similar pre- vs post-intervention (9.3% vs 10.5%); with the alert-driven huddle it was 22.7%.
evidence.tradeoff: NASA Task Load Index rose from 43 to 57 post-intervention (slight workload increase). Only 28% (555/1977) of huddles occurred without an alert firing, suggesting some automation bias.
evidence.quote: Treatment with antibiotics for IPSO sepsis cases was similar pre- and post-intervention without a huddle (9.3% vs 10.5%), though treatment doubled with huddle intervention (22.7%).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Algorithms Improve Care of Patients with AAA
evidence.comparator_used: Historical pre-AI standard of care (pre-AI group) without the AI-linked referral and evaluation workflow
evidence.outcome: Long-term AAA follow-up and scheduled monitoring appointments
evidence.effect: Long-term follow-up 45% vs 30%, P = 0.004; scheduled monitoring appointments 99% vs 65%, P < 0.001
evidence.quote: The implementation of the AI-assisted AAA detection and care protocol significantly increased proportion of patients receiving initial AAA evaluation and long-term follow-up care.

evidence.title: Optimizing deep learning-enhanced opportunistic osteoporosis screening from chest X-rays in Australia: Impact of follow-up and treatment adherence on clinical and economic outcomes
evidence.comparator_used: AI-enhanced opportunistic screening under baseline real-world DXA follow-up and medication persistence (modelled scenario analysis)
evidence.outcome: Clinical benefit (fractures prevented, QALYs gained) of AI-enhanced screening
evidence.effect: Optimizing follow-up and adherence could amplify clinical benefits by four- to five-fold; base case +0.0025 QALYs and -0.0043 fractures per patient, -AUD59 lifetime cost vs no screening
evidence.quote: Optimizing follow-up and adherence could amplify clinical benefits by four- to five-fold.

controls.question: Should we set the model's alert threshold for our clinical use, costs and team capacity rather than accept the vendor default?
controls.control: Choose the alert cutpoint on local data using clinical costs, false-alarm tolerance, prevalence, lead time and follow-up capacity.
controls.comparator: Vendor-fixed, default (e.g., 0.5) or purely statistical threshold
controls.aim: Balance missed cases against false alarms and keep alert volume actionable
variants: Tune for sensitivity versus high positive predictive value
Match flagged volume to staff, clinic or outreach capacity
Predefined alert budget per clinician-shift or patient-day
Prevalence-aware cutpoint selection for rare outcomes
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts
tradeoffs: Low precision at the optimal recall level (0.27%); higher recall levels exceeded the willingness-to-pay threshold
Choosing a threshold involves a trade-off between downstream provider workload (alert volume) and missed events; it also needs value judgments and stakeholder input.
Referral was also substantially higher for patients who did not need hospital assessment, and the cost of these unnecessary referrals offset savings at all cut-offs.
The cost-optimal operating point had lower specificity (80.4% vs 87.7%), which means more unnecessary referrals and possibly higher medical costs.

The conventional threshold gave high sensitivity but poor specificity. The abstract gives no numbers for the sensitivity change at the optimized cut-off, so any sensitivity loss is not quantified. The balanced accuracy gain was modest, and the Youden Index is a statistical criterion rather than one based on clinical costs.
CSBT-Untuned had the highest raw accuracy, so threshold tuning gave up some raw accuracy. The CDPS advantage was only numerical, not statistically significant against RUSBoost.

evidence.title: Clinical implementation of an AI-enabled ECG for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy detection
evidence.comparator_used: Initial algorithm operating point earlier in the study (before the optimised operating point was deployed)
evidence.outcome: Alert percentage of algorithm-screened patients; enrolment rate by alerts reviewed
evidence.effect: Alert percentage fell from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in the enrolment rate by alerts reviewed.
evidence.quote: During the study, deployment of an optimised algorithm operating point helped reduce the alert percentage of algorithm-screened patients from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in the enrolment rate by alerts reviewed.

evidence.title: Integrating economic considerations into cutpoint selection may help align clinical decision support toward value-based healthcare
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Alternative cutpoint selection approaches that optimize test-specific or purely statistical metrics (e.g., sensitivity/specificity-based methods), compared via Monte Carlo simulation of net monetary benefit
evidence.outcome: Expected net monetary benefit (NMB) of model-guided decisions for ICU readmission prevention and inpatient falls prevention
evidence.effect: The value-optimizing cutpoint approach was frequently NMB-maximizing; under realistic low-prevalence, modest-discrimination scenarios (ICU: prevalence 0.025, AUC 0.70; falls: prevalence 0.036, AUC 0.70) it was either the best or similar to the best of the compared methods, and was robust to model miscalibration. No numeric NMB values reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The proposed approach that considered expected downstream consequences was frequently NMB-maximizing compared with other methods.

evidence.title: Potential Cost-Effectiveness of Machine Learning-Enabled Primary Care Identification of Hepatitis C Virus Patients in the US
evidence.comparator_used: Other algorithm recall levels (5-100%) judged against a purely statistical or unconstrained operating point, within a $100,000/QALY willingness-to-pay threshold
evidence.outcome: Cost-effectiveness (ICER per QALY gained) across recall levels, used to identify the optimal cutpoint
evidence.effect: ML-enabled screening was cost-effective (ICER < $100k/QALY) for recall levels up to 30%; the optimal recall level was 30% with a mean ICER of $94,022/QALY gained
evidence.tradeoff: Low precision at the optimal recall level (0.27%); higher recall levels exceeded the willingness-to-pay threshold
evidence.quote: The optimal recall level was 30% (Precision 0.27%), which resulted in a mean ICER of $94,022/QALY gained.

evidence.title: Governing Decisions of Probability Cutoffs in Clinical AI Deployment: A Case Study of Asthma Exacerbation Prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Purely statistical 'optimal' cutoff selection, compared with a governance-informed threshold using prevalence-adjusted metrics and provider capacity modeling
evidence.outcome: Operational feasibility of alert volume and missed-event (miss) rate across candidate thresholds
evidence.effect: No numeric values given in the abstract; statistically optimal thresholds may produce operationally infeasible alert volumes or unacceptable miss rates
evidence.tradeoff: Choosing a threshold involves a trade-off between downstream provider workload (alert volume) and missed events; it also needs value judgments and stakeholder input.
evidence.quote: We demonstrate that statistically optimal thresholds may produce operationally infeasible alert volumes or unacceptable miss rates.

evidence.title: Diagnostic Performance of Fluorescence-Based Rapid On-Site Specimen Evaluation for  Helicobacter pylori  Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing Before and After Algorithm Optimization: A Two-Round Comparative Study
evidence.comparator_used: Uniform 50% fluorescence residual rate (FRR) threshold currently applied
evidence.outcome: Specificity of F-ROSE for H. pylori antimicrobial susceptibility (resistance detection)
evidence.effect: Drug-specific Youden-index cutoffs improved specificity 'appreciably' versus the uniform 50% FRR threshold, most evidently for levofloxacin; no numeric values reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: ROC analysis showed that drug-specific optimal cutoffs derived from the Youden index improved specificity appreciably compared with the uniform 50% FRR threshold currently applied, the gain being most evident for levofloxacin hydrochloride.

evidence.title: Potential impact of a new sepsis prediction model for the primary care setting: early health economic evaluation using an observational cohort
evidence.comparator_used: Four cut-off scenarios of the sepsis prediction model (low cut-offs of score 2 or 3 up to higher cut-offs) compared with observed GP referral behaviour
evidence.outcome: Cost per patient (healthcare perspective) and number of hospital referrals at different model cut-offs
evidence.effect: Referral rates at low cut-off (score 2 or 3) were 99% and 91% for patients with sepsis, versus 88% observed; no cut-off was likely to save costs.
evidence.tradeoff: Referral was also substantially higher for patients who did not need hospital assessment, and the cost of these unnecessary referrals offset savings at all cut-offs.
evidence.quote: As a consequence, cost-savings due to referral of patients with sepsis were offset by increased costs due to unnecessary referral for all cut-offs of the prediction model.

evidence.title: Economic evaluation for medical artificial intelligence: accuracy vs. cost-effectiveness in a diabetic retinopathy screening case
evidence.comparator_used: Status quo: the most accurate AI operating point (sensitivity/specificity 93.3%/87.7%), among 1100 simulated sensitivity/specificity pairs
evidence.outcome: Cost-effectiveness (ICER) of annual AI-based DR screening over 30 years
evidence.effect: Compared with the status quo, six scenarios were cost-saving and seven were cost-effective. The most cost-effective model had sensitivity 96.3% and specificity 80.4%. Cost-saving or cost-effective results needed minimum sensitivity of 88.2% and specificity of 80.4%. Higher DR prevalence and higher willingness-to-pay required higher sensitivity for optimal cost-effectiveness.
evidence.tradeoff: The cost-optimal operating point had lower specificity (80.4% vs 87.7%), which means more unnecessary referrals and possibly higher medical costs.
evidence.quote: The most cost-effective AI model exhibited higher sensitivity (96.3%) and lower specificity (80.4%) than the status quo.

evidence.title: From Notebook to Real World: Design and Deployment of a Web-Based Machine Learning System for PCOS Risk Screening
evidence.comparator_used: Default decision threshold (implied default, not stated numerically in the abstract)
evidence.outcome: Recall for the PCOS-positive class in a screening tool
evidence.effect: Decision threshold tuned to 0.40 raised recall for the PCOS-positive class to 0.89
evidence.quote: Decision threshold tuning at 0.40 raises recall for the PCOS-positive class to 0.89, appropriate for a screening tool where false negatives carry greater clinical cost.

evidence.title: Beyond AUC: The Clinical Impact of Threshold Optimization in COVID-19 Mortality Prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional (default) probability threshold, compared with a Youden Index-optimized cut-off of 0.23, on the same models
evidence.outcome: Specificity and balanced accuracy for COVID-19 mortality prediction
evidence.effect: Specificity rose from 29.0% to 82.3%; balanced accuracy rose from 61.1% to 65.6% at the 0.23 cut-off
evidence.tradeoff: The conventional threshold gave high sensitivity but poor specificity. The abstract gives no numbers for the sensitivity change at the optimized cut-off, so any sensitivity loss is not quantified. The balanced accuracy gain was modest, and the Youden Index is a statistical criterion rather than one based on clinical costs.
evidence.quote: The ideal cut-off discovered by threshold optimization was 0.23, raising specificity from 29.0% to 82.3% and balanced accuracy from 61.1% to 65.6%.

evidence.title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
evidence.comparator_used: Untuned cost-sensitive bagged trees (CSBT-Untuned) at its default threshold
evidence.outcome: Minority-class (opioid misuse) detection and Clinical Discriminative Performance Score under sensitivity-priority scenarios
evidence.effect: CSBT-Untuned had the highest raw accuracy (86.7%) but missed 61.5% of positive cases. Threshold-optimized CSBT-Tuned had enhanced minority class detection and numerically higher Clinical Discriminative Performance Scores, statistically comparable to RUSBoost given overlapping confidence intervals.
evidence.tradeoff: CSBT-Untuned had the highest raw accuracy, so threshold tuning gave up some raw accuracy. The CDPS advantage was only numerical, not statistically significant against RUSBoost.
evidence.quote: Conversely, the threshold-optimized CSBT-Tuned model achieved enhanced minority class detection and numerically higher Clinical Discriminative Performance Scores under sensitivity-priority scenarios, though its performance remained statistically comparable to RUSBoost given overlapping confidence intervals.

evidence.title: A Cost-Sensitive and Explainable Evaluation Framework for Chronic Kidney Disease Prediction Models
evidence.comparator_used: Default/non-optimized decision threshold (implied); cost-sensitive threshold optimization compared with standard evaluation
evidence.outcome: False negative predictions and overall misclassification cost in CKD prediction
evidence.effect: Ensemble models (Random Forest, XGBoost) eliminated false negative predictions at optimal thresholds, lowering overall cost; no numeric values given in abstract
evidence.quote: The ensemble models eliminated false negative predictions at their optimal thresholds, hence lowering the overall cost.

controls.question: Should the AI alert interrupt the clinician with a pop-up or hard stop, or appear passively in the chart?
controls.control: Present the AI alert interruptively, as a pop-up, hard stop or mandatory pause, rather than passively in the chart.
controls.comparator: Passive or on-demand display of the same alert
controls.aim: Get attention for critical findings while limiting alert fatigue and workflow disruption
variants: Mandatory pause or override prompt for high-risk decisions only
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts
tradeoffs: Among encounters with a decision to screen, documentation was lower in the interruptive arm (63 of 121 [52%]) than in the noninterruptive arm (11 of 12 [92%]). Authors note alert fatigue as a disadvantage of interruptive CDS, but it was not measured.

The threshold-alert group generated 5163 alerts among 117 of 177 participants. Alarm burden and alarm fatigue were not assessed. The authors note that responding needs adequate staffing, and the benefit was not seen in patients on intensive insulin therapy.
Among those who decided to screen, the proportion with documented assessment was lower in the Interruptive arm (52%=63/121) than in the Non-Interruptive arm (92%=11/12).

Only 60.13% of alerts were complied with within the BPA, and 32.19% of alerts were followed by the culprit medication being ordered anyway. Hospital stay was longer when the alert fired (IRR 1.08). Mortality was higher after deployment, though the authors suspect unmeasured confounding rather than a causal effect of the CDS.

evidence.title: Risk Model-Guided Clinical Decision Support for Suicide Screening: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Noninterruptive CDS (patient panel icon only, with the same pop-up on hover) in a 1:1 randomized trial
evidence.outcome: Decision to assess suicide risk in person (primary outcome)
evidence.effect: 121 of 289 encounters (42%) vs 12 of 307 (4%); OR 17.70 (95% CI 6.42-48.79; P < .001). Documented risk assessment: 63 of 289 (22%) vs 11 of 307 (4%); P < .001
evidence.tradeoff: Among encounters with a decision to screen, documentation was lower in the interruptive arm (63 of 121 [52%]) than in the noninterruptive arm (11 of 12 [92%]). Authors note alert fatigue as a disadvantage of interruptive CDS, but it was not measured.
evidence.quote: Accounting for cluster effects by individual clinicians, the interruptive CDS prompted higher rates of in-person screening compared with noninterruptive CDS (odds ratio, 17.70; 95% CI, 6.42-48.79; P < .001), consistent with the study alternative hypothesis.

evidence.title: Threshold and Predictive Alerts of Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Glycemic Control in Hospitalized Adults With Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: CGM with all alerts off (real-time glucose values and trend graphs still displayed passively on monitors and tablets, with a non-disableable 40 mg/dL alert)
