evidence.outcome: Percentage of time in range (70-180 mg/dL) during hospitalization
evidence.effect: TIR 75.1% (SD 16.6) with audible threshold alerts vs 71.2% (SD 18.1) with alerts off; adjusted mean difference 3.9% (95% CI 0.1% to 7.8%; Holm-adjusted P = .04). Time above range >180 mg/dL was lower (-3.9%, 95% CI -7.1% to -0.7%). Time below range <70 mg/dL did not differ (-0.04%, 95% CI -0.3% to 0.2%). The benefit appeared in the daytime (4.7%) but not overnight.
evidence.tradeoff: The threshold-alert group generated 5163 alerts among 117 of 177 participants. Alarm burden and alarm fatigue were not assessed. The authors note that responding needs adequate staffing, and the benefit was not seen in patients on intensive insulin therapy.
evidence.quote: The mean (SD) TIR was significantly higher in the threshold on and prediction off group than in the threshold off and prediction off group (75.1% [16.6%] vs 71.2% [18.1%]; adjusted mean difference, 3.9% [95% CI, 0.1%-7.8%]; Holm-adjusted P = .04) ( Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Randomized Controlled Comparative Effectiveness Trial of Risk Model-Guided Clinical Decision Support for Suicide Screening
evidence.comparator_used: Non-Interruptive CDS (passive display of the same risk-model-triggered alert)
evidence.outcome: Decision to screen for suicidal ideation (primary endpoint); documented suicide risk assessment
evidence.effect: Decisions to screen 42% (121/289) vs 4% (12/307), OR=17.7, p<0.001 adjusting for provider clustering; documented suicide risk assessment 63/289 vs 11/307 encounters, p<0.001
evidence.tradeoff: Among those who decided to screen, the proportion with documented assessment was lower in the Interruptive arm (52%=63/121) than in the Non-Interruptive arm (92%=11/12).
evidence.quote: Adjusting for provider cluster effects, Interruptive CDS led to significantly higher numbers of decisions to screen (42%=121/289 encounters) compared to Non-Interruptive CDS (4%=12/307) (odds ratio=17.7, p-value <0.001).

evidence.title: Impact of an Alert-Based Inpatient Clinical Decision Support Tool to Prevent Drug-Induced Long QT Syndrome: Large-Scale, System-Wide Observational Study
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation period, before the interruptive BPA alert was deployed (observational before/after); also alert fired vs not fired
evidence.outcome: Drug-induced QT prolongation (diLQTS) risk after deployment of the interruptive alert-based CDS
evidence.effect: diLQTS after CDS deployment vs before: OR 1.13 (95% CI 0.94-1.36; P=.21). Provider response to the alert had no effect on diLQTS (P=.79). Inpatient mortality after deployment: OR 1.43 (95% CI 1.09-1.88).
evidence.tradeoff: Only 60.13% of alerts were complied with within the BPA, and 32.19% of alerts were followed by the culprit medication being ordered anyway. Hospital stay was longer when the alert fired (IRR 1.08). Mortality was higher after deployment, though the authors suspect unmeasured confounding rather than a causal effect of the CDS.
evidence.quote: After adjustment for age, sex, race and ethnicity, location, laboratory findings, medication, and comorbidity clusters, there was no difference in risk of diLQTS based on CDS deployment (OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.94-1.36; P =.21; Table S10A in Multimedia Appendix 1 ), and no evidence of effect for any individual medication ( P =.98; Table S10B in Multimedia Appendix 1 ).

controls.question: Should we grade alerts into severity tiers instead of a single yes/no flag?
controls.control: Present AI output as graded risk or priority tiers rather than a single binary flag.
controls.comparator: Single binary alert at one threshold
controls.aim: Help clinicians prioritize patients and reduce fatigue from uniform alerts
variants: Continuous score to rank within tiers
Tiering by acuity, confidence margin and actionability
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-powered tiered early warning framework addressing high false alarm rates for in-hospital mortality prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline single-threshold model alerting (Stage 1 model without tiered risk stratification)
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value for in-hospital mortality alerts, with NPV in low-risk patients
evidence.effect: PPV rose from baseline 9.8-18.8% to 32.5-40.5% across sites; NPV stayed over 98% for low-risk individuals
evidence.quote: In Stage 2, AI-TEW implements a tiered risk stratification strategy by optimizing decision thresholds to prioritize high-risk patients, thereby increasing PPV from baseline levels of 9.8-18.8% to 32.5-40.5% across sites, while maintaining a high negative predictive value (NPV) of over 98% for low-risk individuals.

evidence.title: An interpretable machine learning tool for in-home monitoring of agitation episodes in people living with dementia: a proof-of-concept study
evidence.comparator_used: Binary agitation identification from the LightGBM model at a single threshold, without traffic-light stratification
evidence.outcome: Specificity and other performance metrics for identifying agitation over an 8-day period
evidence.effect: Specificity rose from 75.28% ± 7.38 (LightGBM without stratification) to 90.3% ± 7.55 with the traffic-light system; all metrics improved
evidence.quote: Implementing the traffic-light system for stratification increased specificity to 90.3% ± 7.55 and improved all metrics.

evidence.title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Tool for In-Home Screening of Agitation Episodes in People Living with Dementia
evidence.comparator_used: Single binary alert at one threshold (binary model output without traffic-light stratification)
evidence.outcome: Specificity and other agitation-screening performance metrics
evidence.effect: Traffic-light system for risk stratification increased specificity by 15% and improved all metrics
evidence.quote: Implementing the traffic-light system for risk stratification increased specificity by 15% and improved all metrics.

controls.question: Should we use different alert thresholds for different sites or patient subgroups?
controls.control: Set separate alert cutpoints by site, department or patient subgroup.
controls.comparator: One common cutpoint applied across all sites and subgroups
controls.aim: Improve accuracy and fairness across sites and vulnerable or understudied groups
variants: More conservative thresholds for paediatric, vulnerable or understudied groups
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts
tradeoffs: Net benefit depended significantly on compliance factors (noncompliance, treatment efficacy, tolerance for false alarms).

evidence.title: Optimizing the Implementation of Clinical Predictive Models to Minimize National Costs: Sepsis Case Study
evidence.comparator_used: Non-customized deployment of the sepsis model (a common policy across diagnostic categories); the abstract does not name the comparator explicitly
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic odds ratio and excess cost of sepsis care to CMS
evidence.effect: Significantly higher diagnostic odds ratio and reduced costs of sepsis care; potential US $4.6 billion in excess cost savings for CMS with powerful predictive models
evidence.tradeoff: Net benefit depended significantly on compliance factors (noncompliance, treatment efficacy, tolerance for false alarms).
evidence.quote: However, a customized deployment policy can achieve a significantly higher diagnostic odds ratio and reduced costs of sepsis care.

controls.question: Should alert thresholds adapt to each patient's own baseline and risk factors?
controls.control: Set alert thresholds from each patient's baseline, medications and cumulative risk.
controls.comparator: Fixed population cutpoint for all patients
controls.aim: Reduce false alarms and missed deterioration for patients with atypical baselines
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts

evidence.title: Automated Scan Region Classification and Patient-specific Dose Modeling for Enhanced Dose Management in Computed Tomography
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional fixed diagnostic reference level (DRL) exceedances applied to all patients
evidence.outcome: Number of cases flagged for dose review (alert burden)
evidence.effect: 60 statistical outliers from patient-specific models vs 170 DRL exceedances; manual analysis confirmed all flagged cases were clinically justified
evidence.quote: Crucially, the patient-specific models identified substantially fewer cases for review (60 statistical outliers) compared with the standard DRL-based method (170 exceedances).

controls.question: Should AI-detected high-risk findings automatically go to a named clinician or team?
controls.control: Automatically route high-risk AI detections in real time to defined recipients through established escalation pathways.
controls.comparator: No automatic notification, or alert visible to whoever opens the chart
controls.aim: Speed response to high-risk findings and ensure someone owns each alert
variants: Escalation from home or wearable monitoring to clinicians, caregivers or emergency services
Routing to primary team, rapid response or multidisciplinary group
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts
tradeoffs: 48 vs 35 potential AI false-positive cases (AF not confirmed by cardiologist); only 1 led to NOAC prescription, which was clinically justified. AF misdiagnosis remained high (55.1% vs 68.6%), so physicians often did not act on alerts. Effect on alert fatigue was uncertain.
Intervention patients were more likely to receive cardiovascular medication orders (16.1% vs 11.3%; IPTW adjusted RR 1.74; 95% CI 1.39-2.18). The IPTW adjusted escalation rate was higher with alerts.

Caregiver notification was bundled with other intervention components (daily risk summaries), so its effect cannot be isolated. The design was non-randomized and exploratory. Alert false positive rate was 8.2%.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled ECGs for Atrial Fibrillation Identification and Enhanced Oral Anticoagulant Adoption: A Pragmatic Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Heart Association
evidence.comparator_used: Usual care: control-group doctors did not receive AI-ECG results and interpreted ECGs themselves (no automatic notification)
evidence.outcome: NOAC prescription within 90 days after discharge (also new AF diagnosis)
evidence.effect: NOAC prescription 23.3% vs 12.0% (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.11-3.07); AF diagnosis 47.8% vs 36.0% (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.03-1.90); no significant difference in echocardiograms (HR 1.14), cardiology visits (HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.98-2.05), stroke, CV death or all-cause death
evidence.tradeoff: 48 vs 35 potential AI false-positive cases (AF not confirmed by cardiologist); only 1 led to NOAC prescription, which was clinically justified. AF misdiagnosis remained high (55.1% vs 68.6%), so physicians often did not act on alerts. Effect on alert fatigue was uncertain.
evidence.quote: The prescription rates of NOACs after discharge within 90 days after the index ECG were 23.3% in the intervention group and 12.0% in the control group, resulting in a HR of 1.85 (95% CI, 1.11–3.07).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence improves transfer times and ischemic stroke workflow metrics
evidence.venue: Interventional neuroradiology : journal of peritherapeutic neuroradiology, surgical procedures and related neurosciences
evidence.comparator_used: Prior system of passive CT perfusion software analysis with radiologist interpretation and notification
evidence.outcome: Door-to-puncture time and interhospital transfer time after real-time automatic LVO notification to the thrombectomy team
evidence.effect: Door-to-puncture time decreased 15 min (p = 0.009); transfer time from outside hospitals reduced by 37 min (p = 0.04); no significant change in transfer time at non-implementing hospitals
evidence.quote: Transfer time from outside hospitals that implemented Viz.ai was reduced by 37 min (p = 0.04).

evidence.title: Real-Time Machine Learning Alerts to Prevent Escalation of Care: A Nonrandomized Clustered Pragmatic Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Alerts generated but not sent to clinicians in control units, with standard RRT activation criteria used
evidence.outcome: Escalation rate per 1000 patient bed days (primary); cardiovascular medication orders; combined in-hospital and 30-day mortality
evidence.effect: Escalation 12.3 vs 11.3 per 1000 patient bed days (difference 1.0; 95% CI -2.8 to 4.7); IPTW adjusted IRR 1.43 (95% CI 1.16-1.78; p<0.001). Mortality 7% vs 9.3% (-2.4%; 95% CI -4.5% to -0.2%); IPTW adjusted RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.58-0.99; p=0.045).
evidence.tradeoff: Intervention patients were more likely to receive cardiovascular medication orders (16.1% vs 11.3%; IPTW adjusted RR 1.74; 95% CI 1.39-2.18). The IPTW adjusted escalation rate was higher with alerts.
evidence.quote: Real-time machine learning alerts do not reduce the rate of escalation but may reduce mortality.

evidence.title: Intelligent fall risk prediction and real-time warning system for elderly care based on multimodal deep learning and wearable sensor fusion
evidence.comparator_used: Passive-monitoring group with data logging only, no alerts or caregiver notification
evidence.outcome: Fall incidence over a three-month field deployment (exploratory)
evidence.effect: 0.82 vs 2.14 falls per person-month; RR 0.38 (95% CI 0.24-0.62); near-falls prevented (self-reported) 27 vs 8
evidence.tradeoff: Caregiver notification was bundled with other intervention components (daily risk summaries), so its effect cannot be isolated. The design was non-randomized and exploratory. Alert false positive rate was 8.2%.
evidence.quote: In a subsequent three-month deployment with 80 participants, the group receiving active alerts recorded 62% fewer falls than the passive-monitoring control group (0.82 vs. 2.14 falls per person-month; p < 0.01).

evidence.title: Impact of Deep Learning-Based Computer-Aided Detection and Electronic Notification System for Pneumothorax on Time to Treatment: Clinical Implementation
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.comparator_used: CAD-only (DL-based pneumothorax detection without the electronic notification system), difference-in-differences
evidence.outcome: Time to treatment (TTT) for pneumothorax: supplemental oxygen, aspiration or tube thoracostomy, and thoracic surgery consultation
evidence.effect: Oxygen therapy: -143.8 min (95% CI -277.8 to -9.9; P = .035). Aspiration or tube thoracostomy: 14.4 min (95% CI -35.0 to 63.9). Thoracic and cardiovascular surgery consultation: 86.3 min (95% CI -175.1 to 347.6).
evidence.quote: There was a significant reduction in TTT for supplemental oxygen therapy for the CAD and ENS group compared with the CAD-only group in the postimplementation period (-143.8 min; 95% confidence interval [CI], -277.8 to -9.9; P = .035).

evidence.title: Using an Artificial Intelligence Application Expedited ENRICH Trial Patient Screening: A Single Center Experience
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-implementation period without automatic VizAI notification (usual notification of the neurosurgical team)
evidence.outcome: Time from CT head to notification of the neurosurgical team for ENRICH trial screening
evidence.effect: Reduced by 50 minutes after VizAI implementation (p<0.002); 57 minutes when hemorrhages not identified by the ICH algorithm were excluded
evidence.quote: Active notification of the neurosurgical team by an artificial intelligence application significantly reduces the time from hemorrhage identification to trial screening.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Algorithms Improve Care of Patients with AAA
evidence.comparator_used: Historical pre-AI standard of care without automatic notification of AAA detections
evidence.outcome: Initial AAA evaluation after incidental detection (primary outcome)
evidence.effect: 42% vs 18% initial evaluation, P < 0.001; time to evaluation 22 vs 83 days, P = 0.1 (trend only)
evidence.quote: A greater proportion of patients underwent initial AAA evaluation after implementation of AI-assisted AAA care (42% vs. 18%, P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Prospective validation of clinical deterioration predictive models prior to intensive care unit transfer among patients admitted to acute care cardiology wards
evidence.comparator_used: Baseline event rate; no alternative alerting strategy such as a single-threshold alert was compared
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value of a hypothetical alert requiring a sustained rise in score
evidence.effect: PPV more than 10-fold the event rate
evidence.quote: A hypothetical alerting strategy based on a rise in score and duration of the rise would have had good performance, with a positive predictive value more than 10-fold the event rate.

controls.question: Should we suppress alerts when context shows they are not needed, such as patients already treated or scheduled?

Dialogue-context gating of conversational AI safety interventions

evidence.title: The effect of computerised decision support alerts tailored to intensive care on the administration of high-risk drug combinations, and their monitoring: a cluster randomised stepped-wedge trial
evidence.comparator_used: Standard CDSS potential DDI alerts (usual care; control period, with five ICUs already using potential DDI alerts) versus an adapted CDSS alerting only for high-risk DDIs
evidence.outcome: Administered high-risk drug combinations per 1000 drug administrations per patient
evidence.effect: Mean 26·2 (SD 53·4) in intervention (n=5534) vs 35·6 (65·0) in control (n=4353); adjusted 12% decrease (95% CI 5-18%; p=0·0008)
evidence.quote: Tailoring potential DDI alerts to the ICU led to a 12% decrease (95% CI 5-18%; p=0·0008) in the number of administered high-risk drug combinations per 1000 drug administrations per patient, after adjusting for clustering and prognostic factors.

controls.question: Should AI flags be pushed to clinicians by phone, text or email rather than waiting in the EHR?
controls.control: Push AI findings to clinicians via mobile notifications, texts or emails.
controls.comparator: Model output available only passively in the EHR or worklist
controls.aim: Speed clinician awareness and increase follow-through on flagged patients
variants: Mobile push with secure group messaging or image viewing
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts
tradeoffs: 48 vs 35 potential AI errors; only 1 patient with a false alert received NOAC (justified). The study did not test whether alert fatigue occurred. Cardiology visits rose numerically but not significantly.

Non-randomized, unblinded and confounded by daily risk summaries and caregiver notifications. The authors state it is not evidence of causal effect. Alert false positive rate was 8.2% (134 false alarms among 1,634 alerts).
No improvement in EOL care outcomes; small non-randomized before/after cohorts

evidence.tradeoff: 48 vs 35 potential AI errors; only 1 patient with a false alert received NOAC (justified). The study did not test whether alert fatigue occurred. Cardiology visits rose numerically but not significantly.
evidence.quote: The prescription rates of NOACs after discharge within 90 days after the index ECG were 23.3% in the intervention group and 12.0% in the control group, resulting in a HR of 1.85 (95% CI, 1.11–3.07).

evidence.title: Impact of Prognostic Notifications on Inpatient Advance Care Planning: A Cluster Randomized Trial
evidence.venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
evidence.comparator_used: No notification (control physicians received no email or page about high-risk patients; usual care)
evidence.outcome: ACP conversation documented in the EHR by the randomized physician during admission (primary outcome)
evidence.effect: 34.7% vs. 19.6%; OR 2.04; 95% CI 1.16-3.59. ACP documentation by any clinician (secondary) did not differ significantly: 52.8% vs. 42.8%, OR 1.31; 95% CI 0.81-2.13.
evidence.quote: Patients of physicians randomized to the intervention group were more likely to have a documented ACP conversation by the randomized physician compared to the control group (34.7% vs. 19.6%; OR 2.04; 95% CI 1.16-3.59).

evidence.title: Automated Large Vessel Occlusion Detection Software and Thrombectomy Treatment Times: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-AI (unexposed) period at the same stroke centers, before alerts were activated; images were analyzed but no alerts, mobile PACS or secure messaging were available
evidence.outcome: Door-to-groin (DTG) time (primary); CT initiation to EVT start (secondary)
evidence.effect: DTG reduced by 11.2 min (95% CI -18.22 to -4.2); CT initiation to EVT start reduced by 9.8 min (95% CI -16.9 to -2.6). No difference in IV tPA times (-3.5 min, 95% CI -9.1 to 2.2), length of stay (-0.4 d), or 90-day functional independence (OR 1.3, 95% CI 0.42-4.0).
evidence.quote: In mixed-effects linear regression, implementation of the LVO detection AI algorithm resulted in a reduction in DTG time by 11.2 minutes.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence improves transfer times and ischemic stroke workflow metrics
evidence.venue: Interventional neuroradiology : journal of peritherapeutic neuroradiology, surgical procedures and related neurosciences
evidence.comparator_used: Prior system of passive CT perfusion software analysis with radiologist interpretation and notification
evidence.outcome: Door-to-puncture time at the Comprehensive Stroke Center and interhospital transfer time for thrombectomy
evidence.effect: Door-to-puncture time decreased 15 min (p = 0.009); transfer time from outside hospitals that implemented Viz.ai was reduced by 37 min (p = 0.04); no significant change in transfer time at outlying hospitals that did not implement Viz.ai
evidence.quote: Door-to-puncture time decreased 15 min (p = 0.009) after the implementation of Viz.ai at our Comprehensive Stroke Center.

evidence.title: Intelligent fall risk prediction and real-time warning system for elderly care based on multimodal deep learning and wearable sensor fusion
evidence.comparator_used: Passive-monitoring group wearing identical sensors with data logging only (no alerts)
evidence.outcome: Fall incidence over a three-month field deployment (exploratory)
evidence.effect: 0.82 vs 2.14 falls per person-month; RR 0.38 (95% CI 0.24-0.62); total falls 12 vs 34; reported as 62% fewer falls
evidence.tradeoff: Non-randomized, unblinded and confounded by daily risk summaries and caregiver notifications. The authors state it is not evidence of causal effect. Alert false positive rate was 8.2% (134 false alarms among 1,634 alerts).
evidence.quote: In a subsequent three-month deployment with 80 participants, the group receiving active alerts recorded 62% fewer falls than the passive-monitoring control group (0.82 vs. 2.14 falls per person-month; p < 0.01).

evidence.outcome: Time from CT head to notification of the neurosurgical team for ENRICH trial screening
evidence.effect: Reduced by 50 minutes after VizAI implementation (p<0.002); 57 minutes when hemorrhages not identified by the ICH algorithm were excluded
evidence.quote: Time between CT Head and notification of the neurosurgical team for trial screening was reduced by 50 minutes after the implementation of VizAI (p<0.002).

evidence.title: Machine Learning for Targeted Advance Care Planning in Cancer Patients: A Quality Improvement Study
evidence.venue: Journal of pain and symptom management
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-intervention period without email notification of model output (before/after comparison)
evidence.outcome: Documented ACP conversations (increased) and end-of-life care outcomes (unchanged)
evidence.effect: ACP documented in 2.3% preintervention vs 80.5% postintervention (P<0.001); no differences in LOS, hospice referral, code status change, ICU admissions or LOS, 30-day readmissions, 30-day ED visits, or inpatient and 30-day deaths
evidence.tradeoff: No improvement in EOL care outcomes; small non-randomized before/after cohorts
evidence.quote: ACP conversations were documented for 2.3% of hospitalizations preintervention vs. 80.5% postintervention (P<0.001), and if the attending physician notified was a palliative care specialist (4.1% vs. 84.6%) or oncologist (0% vs. 76.3%) (P<0.001).

controls.question: Should we add a second AI layer, such as an LLM reading notes, to screen out false alerts before clinicians see them?
controls.control: Pass primary model alerts through a second AI model to suppress likely false positives.
controls.comparator: Primary model alerts shown without secondary filtering
controls.aim: Raise alert precision and reduce false alarms reaching clinicians
controls.family_label: alert thresholds, tiering, throttling, timing, and display of alerts
tradeoffs: "Will notify MD immediately" acknowledgements also fell, which the authors attribute to nurses using it interchangeably with "Sepsis Treatment/Workup in Progress". Median alert-to-initial-workup time rose from 104.1 to 132.3 minutes. 45% of nurses still agreed the BPA often identifies patients without infection. Authors note LLM infrastructure costs and a quasi-experimental design that cannot establish causality.

Sensitivity and missed true events were not measured in this study, and no downstream clinical outcomes were assessed. Effect size varied by site, and the study had no contemporaneous control. The effect is specific to a proprietary vendor algorithm.

evidence.title: Improving sepsis best practice utility and clinical acceptance using an LLM-enhanced prediction system
evidence.comparator_used: Pre-deployment baseline COMPOSER BPA without LLM augmentation (counterfactual estimated by Bayesian structural time-series from pre-deployment trends)
evidence.outcome: Proportion of sepsis BPAs acknowledged by nurses as "No Infection Suspected" (proxy for clinical acceptance); time to antibiotics as a safety check
evidence.effect: Model-predicted rate would have stayed around 25-30% without LLM; observed rate dropped approximately 18-22%, with pointwise deviations of roughly -5% to -15% and cumulative difference about -90% to -100%. Median BPA-to-antibiotics time went from 140.4 to 112.1 minutes. 2539 pre and 1978 post BPA events.
evidence.tradeoff: "Will notify MD immediately" acknowledgements also fell, which the authors attribute to nurses using it interchangeably with "Sepsis Treatment/Workup in Progress". Median alert-to-initial-workup time rose from 104.1 to 132.3 minutes. 45% of nurses still agreed the BPA often identifies patients without infection. Authors note LLM infrastructure costs and a quasi-experimental design that cannot establish causality.
evidence.quote: The causal impact analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in the percentage of BPAs acknowledged as “No Infection Suspected” following the deployment of COMPOSER-LLM.

evidence.title: Use of an Artificial Intelligence Algorithm to Increase Productivity in Implantable Loop Recorder Monitoring: A Multicentre Observational Study
evidence.comparator_used: Same ILR patients in the 12 months before AI activation, when primary device alerts for AF and pause were shown without secondary AI filtering (within-patient before-and-after)
evidence.outcome: Clinician-facing false AF and pause alert burden
evidence.effect: Of 1,007 alerts removed, 887 were false AF alerts and 120 were false pause alerts. Total viewed alerts fell from 4,261 to 2,509. Mean paired difference was -3.94 alerts per patient (95% CI -7.5 to -0.4; p=0.026), and the Wilcoxon signed-rank p=0.018.
evidence.tradeoff: Sensitivity and missed true events were not measured in this study, and no downstream clinical outcomes were assessed. Effect size varied by site, and the study had no contemporaneous control. The effect is specific to a proprietary vendor algorithm.
evidence.quote: During the post-AI period, a further 1,007 alerts were suppressed by the AI algorithm which would have otherwise entered the clinical workflow.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-powered tiered early warning framework addressing high false alarm rates for in-hospital mortality prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Stage 1 model alerts without LLM knowledge-based filtering
evidence.outcome: PPV in external validation after LLM filtering of SHAP-derived risk factors
evidence.effect: 11.53% increase in PPV in external validation (p = 0.0092 for MedGemma)
evidence.quote: Integrating explainable AI with clinical reasoning enhances contextual understanding and reduces spurious alerts, leading to an 11.53% increase in PPV in external validation (p = 0.0092 for MedGemma).

evidence.title: Evaluation of computer-aided detection for gastric cancer using white-light and linked-color imaging: a pilot study
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional EGD without CADe (propensity-matched controls)
evidence.outcome: Gastric cancer detection rate during EGD with real-time CADe detection boxes
evidence.effect: GC detection 4.8% (5/105) with CADe vs 1.8% (11/600) in unmatched controls (P = .07); vs 0.95% (1/105) in matched controls (P = .098). Biopsy rate 22.9% vs 16.2% (NS); exam time 12.1 vs 11.1 min (NS).
evidence.tradeoff: High false-positive rate: an average of 6.2 detection boxes per case at non-tumor sites. Biopsy rate and exam time were slightly higher with CADe, but not significantly. Possible downstream workload was noted as a concern.
evidence.quote: The GC detection rate in the CADe group was slightly higher than in the control group (difference, 3.0%; 95% CI, 0.3%-6.3%), although the difference was not statistically significant ( P = .07).

evidence.title: Machine learning and lean six sigma for targeted patient-specific quality assurance of volumetric modulated arc therapy plans
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: The same flagged plans before PSQA measurement and re-optimization; the deployed Poka Yoke system ran automated daily checks of approved plans and emailed planners when a plan was at risk.
evidence.outcome: Detection and remediation of VMAT plans at risk of PSQA failure.
evidence.effect: The Poka Yoke system analyzed 1722 VMAT plans; 29 (1.7 %) were marked at risk; after PSQA measurements, 9 out of 29 were actual failures and were re-optimized so that they were no longer ranked at risk.
evidence.tradeoff: False-positive workload was reported: only 9 of 29 marked plans were actual failures. The model sensitivity was low (0.39) despite specificity of 0.99; calculations took less than 30 s per plan.
evidence.quote: After the PSQA measurements, 9 out of 29 plans were found to be actual failures and were re-optimized such that they were no longer ranked at risk.

evidence.title: Improving Nurses' Management of Uterine Tachysystole
evidence.venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing

evidence.title: Optimizing efficiency of a custom clinical decision support tool improves adult congenital heart disease care
evidence.venue: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice

evidence.effect: Median true positive alerts rose from 47.3% (combined 2017 and 2019 baseline) to 78.9%. Median false positives fell from 35 (IQR 12) to 15 (IQR 7) per month. Median true positives rose from 27 (IQR 9) in 2019 to 54 (IQR 11) per month in 2021-2022. The last four months of 2022 met the 85% goal. Total alerts were 71 (IQR 6) per month. PFO/small ASD alerts fell from 30 to 0 per month.
evidence.tradeoff: Adding the department code created a new source of false positives: patients seen in the congenital cardiology department without CHD, about 7 (IQR 4) alerts per month or half of all false positives. evidence.quote: Following the changes implemented in August 2021, there was a significant increase in true positive CDS, which has sustained, and the median of percent true positives increased to 78.9 %, an improvement from the baseline median of 47.3 %.

evidence.title: Intelligent fall risk prediction and real-time warning system for elderly care based on multimodal deep learning and wearable sensor fusion

evidence.title: Clinical transportability, calibration drift, and local updating of a B-mode ultrasound radiomics-clinical prediction model for occult high-volume central lymph node metastasis in cN0 papillary thyroid carcinoma: development, temporal validation, and external validation

The locked combined model had AUCs of 0.823, 0.874, 0.866 and 0.870. The B-mode score accounted for most of the discrimination.
evidence.quote: Compared with the B-mode score-only model, adding clinical-ultrasound variables changed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) by +0.015 in development, +0.008 in temporal validation, -0.009 in Center 2, and -0.029 in Center 3.

evidence.title: Evaluating the clinical utility of multimodal large language models in rare maculopathy

evidence.title: Development and External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for 10-Year Ischemic Stroke Risk Prediction in Diverse Populations

evidence.title: Risk-Guided Atrial Fibrillation Screening With Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Electrocardiogram Models: A VITAL-AF Trial Analysis

evidence.title: Vision and Language Models for Classifying Maxillary Sinus Disease on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Transparent Multimodal Benchmark
evidence.comparator_used: Single-modality models: image-only vision models and language-only classifiers, compared with VLMs using image plus text
evidence.outcome: Maxillary sinus normal/abnormal classification AUC by input modality and label source
evidence.effect: On raw ChatGPT labels (n=300), language models reached AUC 0·992 to 1·000, vision models 0·799 to 0·880, and VLM image-only probes 0·63 to 0·69. On radiologist-confirmed labels (n=297), language and text-derived VLM performance fell (BERT-base AUC 0·999 to 0·837), while vision performance was stable or improved (DenseNet-121 0·867 to 0·891).
evidence.tradeoff: The text advantage reflects alignment with self-generated labels, not verified diagnostic content. A meaningful share of raw ChatGPT text was clinically uninterpretable or unsupported by the imaging, and the radiologist reclassified 62 of 297 cases (21%).
evidence.quote: We show that raw, unverified ChatGPT-generated text produces the highest classification performance of any modality evaluated (AUC up to 1·000), exceeding image-only and image-plus-text models—but that a meaningful proportion of this raw text is clinically uninterpretable, and that its apparent advantage collapses substantially once evaluated against a radiologist-confirmed reference standard on the same cases.

evidence.quote: The results showed a significant improvement in accuracy from 43 to 99% (p < 0.001), when guidelines were provided as context in a coherent corpus of text and non-text sources were converted into text.

evidence.quote: On average, summaries from highlighted notes (H-summaries) achieved 96% completeness, 8% higher than the summaries from unhighlighted notes (U-summaries).

evidence.title: Context-Dependent FHIR Serialisation Strategies for Clinical LLM Deployment: A Multi-Layer Benchmark on UK Core Data
evidence.comparator_used: Default raw FHIR JSON serialisation (raw_json) versus five other FHIR-to-text formats, including structured_markdown and hybrid_adaptive
evidence.outcome: Clinical LLM quality (scored 1-5) across clinical QA, clinical reasoning and summarisation tasks
evidence.effect: Format choice significantly affected quality (Kruskal-Wallis H=163.86, p<10^-33, Δ=0.24 on a 5-point scale). raw_json was suboptimal in 58% of model-task-complexity scenarios. raw_json was best for clinical QA, hybrid_adaptive for clinical reasoning, and structured_markdown for summarisation. Format sensitivity was 0.10 points for Claude Sonnet 4.5 versus 0.39 for Llama 3.3.
evidence.quote: The optimal format is context-dependent: raw_json dominates for clinical QA, hybrid_adaptive for clinical reasoning, and structured_markdown for summarisation.

evidence.title: Aligning Probabilistic Beliefs under Informative Missingness: LLM Steerability in Clinical Reasoning
evidence.comparator_used: Default input representation in which missingness is not made explicit (baseline without explicit serialization)
evidence.outcome: Alignment of verbalized probabilistic beliefs with the target distribution (log-loss) for ICU prognostic inference
evidence.effect: Reported qualitatively: explicit structural steering (serialization) can improve probabilistic alignment; no numbers given in the abstract
evidence.quote: Using a real-world intensive care testbed, we find that while explicit structural steering and in-context learning can improve probabilistic alignment, the models do not natively leverage informative missingness without careful interventions.

evidence.title: Serialisation Strategy Matters: How FHIR Data Format Affects LLM Medication Reconciliation
evidence.comparator_used: Raw FHIR JSON serialisation (also compared Markdown Table and Chronological Timeline) across five open-weight models
evidence.outcome: Medication reconciliation F1 on 200 synthetic patients (4,000 inference runs)
evidence.effect: Clinical Narrative outperformed Raw JSON by up to 19 F1 points for Mistral-7B (r = 0.617, p < 10^-10) in models up to 8B; the advantage reversed at 70B, where Raw JSON achieved the best mean F1 of 0.9956.
evidence.tradeoff: In all 20 model and strategy combinations mean precision exceeded mean recall, so omission of active medications was the dominant failure mode. Smaller models plateaued at roughly 7-10 concurrent active medications, underserving polypharmacy patients.
evidence.quote: We find that serialisation strategy has a large, statistically significant effect on performance for models up to 8B parameters: Clinical Narrative outperforms Raw JSON by up to 19 F1 points for Mistral-7B (r = 0.617, p < 10^{-10}).

evidence.title: FHIRBench: Benchmarking FHIR Clinical Data Serialization Strategies for Large Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: Raw FHIR JSON serialization (default format) vs. five alternative serialization strategies, including Narrative and Condensed
evidence.outcome: Downstream LLM quality on clinical QA, reasoning and summarization, measured by token-level F1 and LLM-as-judge clinical rubric score
evidence.effect: Condensed beat Raw JSON on F1 for 3/4 models (Wilcoxon p < 10^-17, N = 100), while Raw JSON scored higher on judge scores for 3/4 models (p < 10^-7). Narrative achieved 95% of Raw JSON's clinical quality at 83% fewer tokens. The Model x Serializer interaction was significant (Friedman p = 0.0009): GPT-5.4 favored Raw JSON, while Claude and the open-weight models favored compressed formats.
evidence.tradeoff: Raw JSON gave the highest judge-rated quality but used far more tokens. Narrative cut tokens by 83% with about a 5% quality loss. No universal best format exists, so the benchmark recommends model-aware serialization. Llama 3.1 70B failed on 100% of complex patients despite being within its nominal context window.
evidence.quote: The Pareto analysis resolves this tension: Narrative achieves 95% of Raw JSON’s clinical quality at 83% fewer tokens.

evidence.title: Assessing the Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Practice Guideline-concordant Treatment Decision-making on Real-world Data
evidence.comparator_used: Anonymized original medical reports as input (full record) versus manually generated case summaries
evidence.outcome: Agreement with Heart Team (Cohen's kappa), reliability (ICC) and bias toward TAVR (FBI) for guideline-concordant treatment decisions
evidence.effect: Original reports: kappa −0.47–0.22, ICC 0.0–1.0, FBI 0.95–1.51. Summaries plus guideline knowledge: kappa −0.02–0.63, ICC 0.01–1.0, FBI 0.46–1.23. The two changes were reported together, so the summary effect cannot be separated from the guideline effect.
evidence.tradeoff: Summaries were generated manually, so the approach needs extensively curated input. Hallucinations occurred in all LLMs, and some responses were unreliable and biased.
evidence.quote: The LLMs’ performance improved substantially when case summaries were used as input and additional guideline knowledge was added to the prompt (kappa: −0.02–0.63, ICC: 0.01–1.0, FBI: 0.46–1.23).

evidence.tradeoff: Summaries were manually generated, which is a curation burden. Hallucinations occurred in all LLMs tested, and the authors conclude that advanced LLMs still require extensively curated input.
evidence.quote: The LLMs' performance improved substantially when case summaries were used as input and additional guideline knowledge was added to the prompt (Cohen κ coefficient: -0.02 to 0.63; ICC: 0.01-1.0; FBI: 0.46-1.23).

evidence.comparator_used: Independent clinician re-review of a random sample of 100 triage-rated 'good' conversations, used as the reference standard. Flagged conversations also went to expert review.
