evidence.effect: Triage flagged 212/2035 conversations (10.4%). 45 went to specialist adjudication and 5 were confirmed critical, with 40 judged non-critical. In the random sample of 100 'good'-rated conversations, 4 (4%; 95% CI 1.6-9.8) had clinically critical errors the triage missed. Rated good: 1803/2035 (88.6%).
evidence.tradeoff: A conditional false-negative rate of about 4% within the 'good' stratum, from a single window and a small sample with a wide CI. 40 of the 45 conversations escalated for specialist review were false positives. The triage model had no prior disease-specific validation. The triage ran as one post-hoc batch, not in real time.
evidence.quote: Of 100 conversations randomly drawn from the AI-classified “good” stratum (1803 conversations), 4 contained critical safety issues after independent clinical review and adjudication (4%; 95% CI 1·6–9·8).

evidence.title: Can LLMs Accurately Score Medical Diagnoses and Clinical Reasoning?
evidence.comparator_used: Expert panel review of diagnoses without LLM-based flagging
evidence.outcome: Identification of diagnoses at high risk of error for targeted expert review, and panel efficiency
evidence.effect: The LLM Jury combined with LLM diagnoses could identify high-risk diagnoses, enabling targeted expert review and improved panel efficiency. No numeric values are given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: (iii) the LLM Jury combined with LLM diagnoses can be used to identify diagnoses at high risk of error, enabling targeted expert review and improved panel efficiency;

evidence.title: Economic costing of evaluating, deploying and monitoring an artificial intelligence-based reconstruction for acceleration of rectal MRI examinations
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologist scoring of repeated post-deployment quality control scans, versus automated image quality metrics
evidence.outcome: Monthly cost savings after deployment with ongoing quality control (cost analysis)
evidence.effect: Monthly saving of £2,636 with image quality metrics versus approximately £2,541 with radiologist evaluation of the quality control scans
evidence.quote: Quality control tests using image quality metrics would save radiological burden and reduce costs compared with conducting repeated image scoring by radiologists.

evidence.title: Validating LLM judges for automated oversight of patient communication
evidence.comparator_used: Clinician reference ratings (expert review) of the same outputs
evidence.outcome: Agreement of automated LLM-judge scoring with clinician ratings across rubric criteria
evidence.effect: Spearman ρ > 0.80 for safety screening and factual verification; ρ < 0.60 for communication quality
evidence.tradeoff: Weaker agreement on communication quality, and patient advocates rated it lower than clinicians and LLM judges, so recalibration is needed.
evidence.quote: LLM judges achieved strong clinician agreement for safety screening and factual verification (Spearman  ρ > 0.80) but weaker agreement for communication quality (  ρ < 0.60).

evidence.title: Automated Safety Testing and Reporting Application for Conversational Safety Monitoring of Generative AI Tools for Mental Health: Development and Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Human coder consensus ratings as reference standard (no head-to-head comparison against sampled-only human review)
evidence.outcome: Concordance of automated conversation-level risk classification with expert human ratings across 8 risk categories
evidence.effect: Accuracy >0.90 for all categories; specificity uniformly high; sensitivity range 0.55-1.00; kappa 0.65-1.00
evidence.tradeoff: Sensitivity varied by category, with a low of 0.55 for some risk behaviors; tested only on 100 synthetic conversations.
evidence.quote: ASTRA demonstrated consistently high concordance with expert human ratings across all categories.

controls.question: Should we run statistical drift detection on inputs and outputs so we can spot degradation without waiting for outcome labels?
controls.control: Test inputs, embeddings and output scores against a reference distribution and alert when shifts cross predefined control limits.
controls.comparator: Periodic labeled performance audits once outcomes become available
controls.aim: Detect data shift and likely model degradation early, before labeled outcomes accumulate
variants: Distribution shift tests on inputs, embeddings, output scores and feature importance
SPC or CUSUM control charts on metrics, alert rates or output proxies with predefined limits
Adding label-free accuracy estimation (uncertainty or pseudo-label discrepancy) between labeled audits
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards
tradeoffs: Thresholds for statistical significance remain unresolved, so flags may reflect practice change rather than malfunction and still need manual investigation.
Every alarm required manual investigation (93 outliers reviewed). Sensitivity and specificity were not tested. Control limits were fixed at one point in time, and the optimal sample size is unclear.

The 2σ criterion may be too general to detect all outliers and is limited with interobserver variability. The design was retrospective and single-site. Model A's original AI contours were not archived, so model B contours were used as the reference, which may confound the model comparison.

The reference came from one US region, so a different population could cause large significant differences without an AI problem. PCC detected shifts but could not measure their severity, so the Wasserstein distance was added. Alert thresholds and levels were not yet refined.
Flagged alerts needed investigation, and most were data quality problems or outliers rather than clinically meaningful drift. The study did not show any performance degradation.
Drift detection performance depends heavily on sample size and patient features, and gaps remain for practical application of existing methods.

evidence.title: Detecting atypical alert behavior through statistical process control: Clinical decision support alert frequency visualizations
evidence.comparator_used: No comparator; single-site descriptive implementation of an SPC dashboard on alert frequency (no comparison with periodic labeled audits)
evidence.outcome: Detection of atypical CDS alert behavior (alert frequency) using SPC control limits
evidence.effect: Dashboard pulled in data and flagged the alerts with greatest variation (June-August 2022). On investigation, the flagged alerts were functioning correctly, and the largest abnormalities reflected practice changes, not system errors. No head-to-head numbers were reported.
evidence.tradeoff: Thresholds for statistical significance remain unresolved, so flags may reflect practice change rather than malfunction and still need manual investigation.
evidence.quote: The most profound abnormalities detected during implementation reflected changes in practice and not system errors, though further investigation into thresholds for statistical significance will benefit this field.

evidence.title: Statistical process control for performance monitoring and continuous quality assurance of deep learning segmentations in radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: Previous less consistent QA that relied on end-users to report performance drops (informal comparison, no formal test of sensitivity or specificity)
evidence.outcome: Detection of a performance drop (humerus) after the software upgrade, and outlier flagging of DLS contours
evidence.effect: Rule 1 flagged 93 outliers (3.0% of 3093 ROIs), of which 12 were human errors. For the humerus, 4 trend shifts were reported for RayStation 2024B versus none for 12A, and the moving average moved outside the control limits. 12 other trend shifts and 1 drift caused only temporary deviations. End-users noticed the same humerus drop.
evidence.tradeoff: Every alarm required manual investigation (93 outliers reviewed). Sensitivity and specificity were not tested. Control limits were fixed at one point in time, and the optimal sample size is unclear.
evidence.quote: Simultaneously, end-users recognised the same performance drop in their daily practice, supporting the outcome of the CQA framework.

evidence.title: Establishing prospective performance monitoring for real-world implementation of deep learning-based auto-segmentation in prostate cancer radiotherapy
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.comparator_used: No comparison with periodic labeled audits; the study compared 2σ vs 3σ control limits and model A vs model B against baseline limits set from the first 150 cases
evidence.outcome: Detection of performance drift and model switching using statistical process control charts of auto-segmentation agreement (DSC, HD95, SDSC)
evidence.effect: Model A stayed mostly within 3σ limits (9-13 months per organ). Model B was flagged as a marked shift (p < 0.001), with all five organs outside both thresholds in all 7 months. 2σ limits were more sensitive to mild deviations in model A.
evidence.tradeoff: The 2σ criterion may be too general to detect all outliers and is limited with interobserver variability. The design was retrospective and single-site. Model A's original AI contours were not archived, so model B contours were used as the reference, which may confound the model comparison.
evidence.quote: The monitoring system using process behavior charts effectively detected out-of-distribution outliers for prostate, bladder, rectum, fem_head_l, and fem_head_r, providing a reliable and easy-to-use framework for quality assurance and early detection of clinical practice change.

evidence.title: Monitoring Methodology for an AI Tool for Breast Cancer Screening Deployed in Clinical Centers
evidence.comparator_used: Matched reference distribution vs deliberately unmatched reference (wrong manufacturer, modality or version) as simulated deviations; no comparison with labeled performance audits
evidence.outcome: Detection of simulated deviations in AI score distribution (PCC with 0.95 alert threshold; chi-squared test)
evidence.effect: With matched references, global PCCs were 0.998 (US-1), 0.975 (US-2), 0.995 (US-3), 0.994 (US-4) and chi-squared p-values were 0.346-0.853, so no deviation was flagged. With unmatched references, PCCs were 0.714 (US-1), 0.825 (US-2), 0.707 (US-3), 0.364 (US-4), all below 0.95. Chi-squared p-values were 0.026, 0.320, 0.221, 0.026, so it flagged only 2 of 4 centers.
evidence.tradeoff: The reference came from one US region, so a different population could cause large significant differences without an AI problem. PCC detected shifts but could not measure their severity, so the Wasserstein distance was added. Alert thresholds and levels were not yet refined.
evidence.quote: The low PCC value found when an unmatched manufacturer is used for the reference shows that finding a difference could be the source of an alert, which would facilitate the detection of software malfunctions or deviations (such as an unsupported manufacturer or a version of the tool that is not suitable for the analyzed mammogram).

evidence.title: Importance of model governance in clinical AI models: case study on the relevance of data drift detection
evidence.comparator_used: Monitoring model performance (AUC, Brier score) over the temporal validation period
evidence.outcome: Detection of data distribution shifts and data quality issues not visible in performance metrics
evidence.effect: Model performance stayed stable (AUC 0.82, Brier score 0.158). Univariate monitoring detected a significant shift in respiratory rate from January 2022, mainly at one hospital. PCA reconstruction error flagged three non-sequential months, with the highest in March 2021. Two alerts were data entry errors (saturation, heart rate) and one was an unusually long length of stay.
evidence.tradeoff: Flagged alerts needed investigation, and most were data quality problems or outliers rather than clinically meaningful drift. The study did not show any performance degradation.
evidence.quote: By tracking both model performance and data drift, this study identified shifts in data distributions and data quality issues in a clinical AI model.

evidence.title: Ensuring fair, safe, and interpretable artificial intelligence-based prediction tools in a real-world oncological setting
evidence.comparator_used: Monitoring model performance alone (lagging, label-dependent AUC), as a proxy for periodic labeled audits
evidence.outcome: Early detection of data drift and data quality problems before ground-truth outcomes were available
evidence.effect: Weekly PSI monitoring, with automated alerts on breaches, detected a 2-week period of incomplete data caused by an API/EHR feed outage. The issue was then resolved. No quantitative comparison with an audit-based approach was reported.
evidence.quote: We note that this issue would likely not have been noticed if we were monitoring for model performance alone.

evidence.title: Unsupervised Characterization of Temporal Dataset Shifts as an Early Indicator of AI Performance Variations: Evaluation Study Using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV Dataset
evidence.comparator_used: Annual labeled model performance (random forest and gradient boosting mortality models) embedded over time, used as the reference for the unsupervised shift clusters; not a head-to-head comparison with periodic audits
evidence.outcome: Association between unsupervised temporal data-shift clusters and temporal clusters of model performance (in-hospital mortality prediction, MIMIC-IV 2008-2019)
evidence.effect: Significant association between IGT shift clusters and model performance clusters (Fisher exact test, P<.05); 2 main temporal clusters corresponded to before and after ICD-10 implementation, and the ICD-9 to ICD-10 transition was associated with performance degradation
evidence.quote: Our results demonstrate a significant relationship between the unsupervised temporal shift patterns, specifically covariate and concept shifts, identified using the IGT projection method and the performance of the random forest and gradient boosting models (P<.05).

evidence.title: A quality assurance framework for routine monitoring of deep learning cardiac substructure computed tomography segmentation models in radiotherapy
evidence.comparator_used: Output (shape quality) detector alone, without input image domain shift detectors
evidence.outcome: Mean absolute error in predicted per-patient Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) for cardiac substructure autosegmentation
evidence.effect: MAE was lowest when combining input (image) and output (shape) detectors compared with output detectors alone; the best regression model (linear regression with bootstrap aggregation) reached an MAE of 0.041 ± 0.002 in predicted DSC. No separate MAE figure for output detectors alone is given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: MAE was lowest when combining both input (image) detectors and output (shape) detectors compared to output detectors alone.

evidence.title: Dynamic AI Risk Loop (DARL): A Continuous Risk Management Framework for AI-Enabled Health Information Systems in Medical Device Software
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional complaint-driven (reactive) surveillance, compared in a 12-month simulation with synthetic drift
evidence.outcome: Timing of detection of performance degradation (sensitivity decline)
evidence.effect: DARL detected degradation at month 5, when sensitivity had fallen only 2.5 percentage points from the 94.0% baseline. The DARL Risk Score crossed the High-risk trigger at month 10, before sensitivity reached its terminal 85.0%, an advance of about six weeks over reactive detection.
evidence.quote: A 12-month simulation study, conducted under controlled synthetic drift conditions based on published AI benchmarks, demonstrates that DARL detects early-stage performance degradation at month 5, when model sensitivity had declined by only 2.5 percentage points from the validated baseline of 94.0%, a point at which conventional complaint-driven surveillance systems would not generate a structured risk signal.

evidence.title: Empirical data drift detection experiments on real-world medical imaging data
evidence.comparator_used: Monitoring model performance alone (labeled performance metrics) as a proxy for detecting data drift
evidence.outcome: Detection of data drift (natural COVID-19 emergence in chest X-rays and synthetic drift)
evidence.effect: No numeric effect given in the abstract; performance monitoring alone was reported as not a good proxy for detecting data drift, whereas the three drift-detection methods could detect it.
evidence.tradeoff: Drift detection performance depends heavily on sample size and patient features, and gaps remain for practical application of existing methods.
evidence.quote: We find that monitoring performance alone is not a good proxy for detecting data drift and that drift-detection heavily depends on sample size and patient features.

evidence.title: Distribution shift detection for the postmarket surveillance of medical AI algorithms: a retrospective simulation study
evidence.comparator_used: Other distribution shift detection techniques (classifier-based vs deep kernel vs multiple univariate Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests) on simulated population and acquisition shifts; no periodic labeled audit comparator
evidence.outcome: Detection rate of simulated distribution shifts (sex, ethnicity, co-morbidity, image quality) in retinal images
evidence.effect: Classifier-based tests performed best overall, with perfect detection rates for quality and co-morbidity subgroup shifts at a sample size of 1000. It was the only method to detect patient sex shifts. All methods identified easier-to-detect out-of-distribution shifts with small (≤300) sample sizes.
evidence.tradeoff: Classifier-based test required large sample sizes (>30,000) to detect patient sex shifts.
evidence.quote: Classifier-based tests performed best overall, with perfect detection rates for quality and co-morbidity subgroup shifts at a sample size of 1000.

evidence.title: One-class support vector machines for detecting population drift in deployed machine learning medical diagnostics
evidence.comparator_used: No comparator; compared OCSVM inlier counts across three simulated noise levels (5%, 10%, 30%) against the training-data reference distribution
evidence.outcome: Number of simulated drifted records classed as inliers by a one-class SVM trained on the reference (Wisconsin Breast Cancer) data, used as a label-free population drift signal
evidence.effect: As noise increased, more inliers were detected: 5% (27 inliers), 10% (486), 30% (851), from 10,000 simulated records per noise level
evidence.quote: As noise increased, more inliers were detected: 5% (27 inliers), 10% (486), and 30% (851).

evidence.title: Detecting and Remediating Harmful Data Shifts for the Responsible Deployment of Clinical AI Models
evidence.comparator_used: No direct comparison with periodic labeled performance audits; the study measured the effect of the label-agnostic shift detection pipeline
evidence.outcome: Detection of harmful data shifts (age groups, admission source, hospital type, lab assays) in a mortality prediction model
evidence.effect: Significant data shifts were detected for younger age groups, admissions from nursing homes and acute care centers, community-to-academic hospital transfers, and changes in brain natriuretic peptide and D-dimer; no detection metrics were given in the abstract
evidence.quote: In this prognostic study, a proactive, label-agnostic monitoring pipeline detected harmful data shifts for a clinical AI system predicting in-hospital mortality.

controls.question: Should we automatically extract ground-truth labels from reports and records to measure the deployed model's real-world accuracy?
controls.control: Extract reference-standard outcomes from reports, EHR feeds or downstream diagnoses automatically, review discrepancies, and compare with model outputs on a rolling basis.
controls.comparator: Manual chart review or clinician panel labeling for periodic validation
controls.aim: Enable continuous, affordable real-world accuracy tracking of deployed models
variants: Rule-based or NLP extraction from EHR feeds and downstream diagnoses
LLM extraction of findings from radiology and clinical reports with human review of discrepancies
Audit of AI-generated labels against a maintained human-only labeled subset
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards
tradeoffs: Eligibility filtering showed high sensitivity but only moderate specificity and remains the main source of divergence from clinicians; no cost or time figures reported.
LLM labeling errors still occurred. Discrepant cases needed human adjudication, and performance metrics were recalculated after partial human correction of LLM errors.

Most alerts were false alarms (24 of 29 were CVPED false-positives), so human review of discrepancies was required; detection of a specificity drop took about 22 days; a 10% drop in sensitivity was needed to produce a discrepancy rise similar to a 2-3% specificity drop
EMR data undercapture deaths, causing informative censoring. This led to a false conclusion of miscalibration (survival underprediction).

evidence.title: Large language models for automatable real-world performance monitoring of diagnostic decision support systems: a comparison to manual doctor panel review in a prospective clinical study
evidence.comparator_used: Manual clinician panel review (reference standard) of eligibility and condition mapping
evidence.outcome: Agreement with clinician review on eligibility classification and condition mapping, and resulting DDSS diagnostic accuracy estimates
evidence.effect: Eligibility: GPT-5 reproduced clinician classifications with 84.7% accuracy (κ = 0.57). Condition mapping: in 347 encounters judged eligible by both, GPT-5 exactly matched clinician diagnoses in 93.6% and proposed clinically plausible alternatives in 3.5%. DDSS accuracy based on manual vs GPT-5 mappings was statistically indistinguishable at Top-1 and Top-3, with one significant difference at Top-5; no differences in the overlapping 346 cases.
evidence.tradeoff: Eligibility filtering showed high sensitivity but only moderate specificity and remains the main source of divergence from clinicians; no cost or time figures reported.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic accuracy estimates based on manual versus GPT-5 mappings were statistically indistinguishable at Top-1 and Top-3 across the full analyzable sets, with one significant difference at Top-5.

evidence.title: Post-deployment Monitoring of AI Performance in Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection by ChatGPT
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologists' manual review of 200 randomly selected cases as ground truth (manual chart review)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT-4 Turbo in extracting ICH status from radiology reports, used to monitor Aidoc
evidence.effect: PPV 1, NPV 0.988, AUC 0.996 against radiologist-established ground truth
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4 Turbo demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy in identifying intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) from radiology reports, with a positive predictive value of 1 and a negative predictive value of 0.988 (AUC:0.996).

evidence.title: Validating Radiology Artificial Intelligence Model Performance on Photon-Counting CT Images Using Large Language Models for Ground Truth Extraction
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.comparator_used: Human annotation: three human annotators adjudicated discrepant cases, and LLM-extracted labels were compared with the final human labels and with interrater agreement
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM-extracted ground truth labels with final human annotations in discrepant cases, versus agreement between human readers
evidence.effect: LLM vs final human annotation κ = 0.731; interreader agreement κ = 0.720. No statistically significant performance differences between PCCT and non-PCCT cohorts when using LLM labels.
evidence.tradeoff: LLM labeling errors still occurred. Discrepant cases needed human adjudication, and performance metrics were recalculated after partial human correction of LLM errors.
evidence.quote: In discrepant cases, the agreement between LLM labels and final human annotations (κ = 0.731) was comparable with interreader agreement (κ = 0.720), supporting the reliability of LLM labeling.

evidence.title: Using a Large Language Model for Postdeployment Monitoring of FDA-Approved Artificial Intelligence: Pulmonary Embolism Detection Use Case
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.comparator_used: No head-to-head comparator; the study simulated the LLM-report-classification framework against CVPED outputs, with human review of discrepancies, and did not compare it with manual chart review
evidence.outcome: Drift detection and incremental PE case detection when CVPED outputs were compared with LLM classification of radiology reports
evidence.effect: 373/11,999 (3.1%) discrepant classifications; 29 alerts among 111 CVPED-positive/LLM-negative cases, of which 24 were CVPED false-positives, 1 an LLM false-negative, and 4 true alerts for incremental PE; a 2.5% drop in LLM specificity gave a 1.7-fold increase in discrepancies, detected in 22 days; optimal retrospective assessment period 2 months
evidence.tradeoff: Most alerts were false alarms (24 of 29 were CVPED false-positives), so human review of discrepancies was required; detection of a specificity drop took about 22 days; a 10% drop in sensitivity was needed to produce a discrepancy rise similar to a 2-3% specificity drop
evidence.quote: Of those, 24 were CVPED false-positives, 1 was an LLM false-negative, and the framework ultimately identified 4 true-alerts for incremental PE cases.

evidence.title: Are Limited Electronic Medical Record Follow-Up Data Sufficiently Useful for Validating the Performance of Survival Prediction Models?
evidence.comparator_used: Higher-quality reference standard outcome data combining EMR and cancer registry, used to validate the same survival models
evidence.outcome: Model performance estimates (discrimination via C-index, integrated Brier score, calibration) when validating with EMR follow-up data alone versus EMR plus registry data
evidence.effect: All-features model: C-index 0.67 (95% CI, 0.65 to 0.69) and IBS 0.16 (95% CI, 0.15 to 0.17) with EMR only, versus C-index 0.66 (95% CI, 0.65 to 0.68) and IBS 0.17 (95% CI, 0.16 to 0.18) with reference standard data. With fewer features, performance estimates dropped similarly in both scenarios. The model was reasonably calibrated against the reference standard, but EMR-only data wrongly showed systematic underprediction of survival.
evidence.tradeoff: EMR data undercapture deaths, causing informative censoring. This led to a false conclusion of miscalibration (survival underprediction).
evidence.quote: EMR data were useful for validation of model discrimination, but not calibration.

controls.question: Should we keep a fixed regression test suite and rerun it whenever the model, prompt, vendor version or configuration changes, and on a schedule?
controls.control: Maintain a version-controlled panel of probe cases and benchmarks, and rerun it after every change and periodically to detect performance shifts.
controls.comparator: One-time validation at go-live, ad hoc spot checks or vendor release notes
controls.aim: Catch silent performance regressions from model, prompt, hardware or vendor updates
variants: Rerun after every model, prompt, build or configuration change
Scheduled re-benchmarking with repeated queries and consistency checks
Invariance checks on fixed probe cases
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards
tradeoffs: The calibration set was small (100 mammograms) and there was no external validation. The design cannot isolate the effect of specific updates from concurrent changes in data distribution and workflow, so gains cannot be attributed solely to the updates. No comparison against one-time validation was made.

evidence.title: Implementation of an artificial intelligence-based system for mammography in the compulsory medical insurance program: results of a 3-year study
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.comparator_used: No alternative arm; performance of the initial AI version at first calibration test compared with later versions re-tested after each architectural update
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance (AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity) across seven repeated calibration tests, with the fixed 100-case set rerun after architectural updates
evidence.effect: Over the testing and monitoring period AUC rose from 0.83 to 0.92, accuracy from 0.77 to 0.90, sensitivity from 0.84 to 0.88 and specificity from 0.70 to 0.91. Calibration tests 1 and 2 failed the predefined thresholds, test 3 passed, and test 6 failed again (accuracy 0.81, sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.81; relative deviation about 11-12%). Test 7 passed (AUC 0.92, accuracy 0.90).
evidence.tradeoff: The calibration set was small (100 mammograms) and there was no external validation. The design cannot isolate the effect of specific updates from concurrent changes in data distribution and workflow, so gains cannot be attributed solely to the updates. No comparison against one-time validation was made.
evidence.quote: Gradual improvements in calibration testing post-AI updates highlight the importance of iterative optimization and continuous monitoring for mammography AI.

evidence.title: Standardised evaluation and monitoring of site-specific AI performance with physical CT phantoms
evidence.comparator_used: No alternative monitoring approach compared; the same phantom test set was rerun over time on two CT systems and across scanner settings
evidence.outcome: Stability of AI liver lesion detection performance on repeated phantom scans (longitudinal monitoring) and sensitivity to scanner technology and operation
evidence.effect: Consistent results over fifteen months on both CT systems; the abstract gives no numeric values
evidence.quote: Next, we perform longitudinal monitoring, yielding consistent results over fifteen months on both systems.

evidence.title: Logit Fingerprinting: A Novel, Accuracy-Independent Method for Validating Large Language Model Stability in High-Stakes Clinical Applications
evidence.venue: AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science proceedings. AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional accuracy metrics on the benchmark, which the authors say miss behavioral volatility from quantization, distillation and sparse architectures
evidence.outcome: Detection of model compression and instability (quantized vs full-precision variants; Flip Rate across commercial API models in a longitudinal audit)
evidence.effect: 100% accuracy distinguishing full-precision from quantized variants across 11 local model families; distilled 'Nano' models had a 2.82% vs 1.58% Flip Rate compared with standard counterparts
evidence.quote: Validated on 11 local model families, our approach achieved 100% accuracy in distinguishing full-precision models from quantized variants.

controls.question: Should we withhold AI outputs from clinicians, silently before go-live or for a random fraction of live cases, to measure performance unconfounded by clinician action?
controls.control: Run the AI with outputs withheld from care, silently before activation or for a small random fraction after, and compare predictions with outcomes.
controls.comparator: Going live after retrospective validation; monitoring only labels observed after clinicians act
controls.aim: Obtain unbiased real-world performance estimates before and after outputs can change the outcomes predicted
variants: Silent mode: outputs hidden entirely until after clinical decisions, before activation
Prospective comparison of silent predictions against observed outcomes
Randomly withholding or varying display for a small fraction of live cases with causal weighting
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards
tradeoffs: Required a 13-month silent period before the intervention could begin

The silent run exposed a data-capture flaw: recorded live data differed from what the CDS actually used. Live and completed-care data differed in about 13% of encounters, mostly chief complaint changes, which made comparison harder. Standard CDS software limits live-data capture, so custom software is needed before deployment. The pilot took 5 months to accrue enough ACS cases.
Needs dedicated personnel (engineering, data science, EMR integration, networking/security). Cloud cost for the roughly 5-week silent deployment was under $300.
Some input and population data were not retained by the EPIC Nebula module, which limited cohort characterisation. The follow-up was only one year.
Required a 2-month silent pilot before activation; no other costs reported
Low specificity: 80% of examinations were classified abnormal. Missed findings were mostly subtle or overlapping lesions.

evidence.title: From prediction to practice: machine learning models and real-world interventions for magnetic resonance imaging appointment no-shows in a hospital setting
evidence.comparator_used: Retrospective hold-out validation performance before go-live
evidence.outcome: Prospective model discrimination (AUROC/AUPRC) detected in the silent live test
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.61 and AUPRC 0.24 in the silent live test (5882 appointments) vs 0.65 and 0.29 on the validation set; drop attributed in part to data drift
evidence.tradeoff: Required a 13-month silent period before the intervention could begin
evidence.quote: On this dataset, the model achieved an AUROC of 0.61 and an AUPRC of 0.24, a reduction in performance when compared to the validation data performance (AUROC: 0.65, AUPRC: 0.29).

evidence.title: In vivo clinical effectiveness of artificial intelligence screening for acute coronary syndrome: testing real-world performance
evidence.comparator_used: Retrospective in vitro model validation (completed-care data) and standard-of-care human ED screening
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity, specificity and PPV for ACS of the silent in vivo CDS versus the in vitro model and versus human screening; agreement between CDS and model decisions
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 81.7% (95% CI 77.1%-85.8%) for CDS vs 82.0% (77.4%-86.1%) for the in vitro model and 80.2% (75.4%-84.4%) for humans. Specificity 67.3% vs 67.3% vs 67.4%. Raw agreement between CDS and original model was 96.8%, Kappa 91.2%.
evidence.tradeoff: The silent run exposed a data-capture flaw: recorded live data differed from what the CDS actually used. Live and completed-care data differed in about 13% of encounters, mostly chief complaint changes, which made comparison harder. Standard CDS software limits live-data capture, so custom software is needed before deployment. The pilot took 5 months to accrue enough ACS cases.
evidence.quote: There was no notable difference between human performance and the CDS given overlapping CIs.

evidence.title: DEPLOYR: a technical framework for deploying custom real-time machine learning models into the electronic medical record
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: Retrospective validation alone (retrospective test-set estimates from the clinical data warehouse) as the basis for a go-live decision
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination (AUROC) of 12 lab-result prediction models, measured prospectively in a silent trial versus retrospectively
evidence.effect: Prospective AUROC was lower than retrospective for all 12 models, e.g. hematocrit 0.83 vs 0.86, white blood cell 0.69 vs 0.76, potassium 0.60 vs 0.67, sodium 0.71 vs 0.79, carbon dioxide 0.62 vs 0.69, magnesium 0.65 vs 0.70.
evidence.tradeoff: Needs dedicated personnel (engineering, data science, EMR integration, networking/security). Cloud cost for the roughly 5-week silent deployment was under $300.
evidence.quote: Across our 12 laboratory predictions tasks, AUROC in our prospective test sets were generally several percentage points lower than what is seen retrospectively.

evidence.title: Prospective validation of clinical deterioration predictive models prior to intensive care unit transfer among patients admitted to acute care cardiology wards
evidence.comparator_used: No direct comparator; silent prospective performance in the display-off arm was judged against the model's earlier development, before COVID-19 and five years earlier
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination and calibration for ICU transfer during silent prospective running
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.725 to 0.737 in 5184 display-off visits with 311 deterioration events; models well-calibrated
evidence.quote: We conclude that predictive statistical models developed five years before study initiation had good model performance despite the passage of time and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

evidence.title: Detecting changes in the performance of a clinical machine learning tool over time
evidence.comparator_used: Original retrospective validation results (AUC 0.75-0.81, AUPRC 0.19-0.38) from the model's earlier development and validation study
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC, AUPRC) and Brier score when the model ran silently in the live EHR for one year, compared with the original retrospective validations
evidence.effect: Average AUC 0.78 (SD 0.02) vs 0.75-0.81 in original validations; AUPRC 0.41 (SD 0.04) vs 0.19-0.38 previously; Brier score 0.10 (SD 0.01); no SPC control violations over 12 months
evidence.tradeoff: Some input and population data were not retained by the EPIC Nebula module, which limited cohort characterisation. The follow-up was only one year.
evidence.quote: The average AUC (0.78) during this follow-up is comparable to the original validations (AUCs ranging between 0.75 and 0.81), while the AUPRC (0.41) even is slightly higher (previous AUPRCs ranging between 0.19 and 0.38).

evidence.title: In vitro to in vivo translation of artificial intelligence for clinical use: screening for acute coronary syndrome to identify ST-elevation myocardial infarction
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.comparator_used: In vitro (retrospective) model validation alone, with the model's in vitro screening decisions used as the reference for the live CDS
evidence.outcome: Coding errors and discrepancies detected in the CDS before clinical activation, and fidelity of in vivo CDS decisions to the in vitro model
evidence.effect: Silent pilot processed 18,335 patient encounters; raw agreement 95.5% (CI 95.2%-95.9%), kappa 87.6% (CI 86.7%-88.6%); several small coding errors found in CDS components and additional coding errors found in the fidelity analysis, all corrected
evidence.tradeoff: Required a 2-month silent pilot before activation; no other costs reported
evidence.quote: Our structured framework for the in vitro to in vivo translation of our predictive model uncovered ways to improve performance in vivo and the validity of risk assessment decisions.

evidence.title: AI Triage of Normal Chest Radiographs: A Silent Trial and Failure Analysis
evidence.comparator_used: No direct comparator; AI ran silently with outputs withheld from care and predictions were compared with radiologist report labels and expert review (no retrospective-validation or go-live arm)
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance of AI for triaging normal chest radiographs and clinically significant misses
evidence.effect: 63,083 radiographs; 97% sensitivity, 35% specificity, 57% PPV, 94% NPV; 31 clinically significant AI misses (estimated miss rate 0.05%); 18.5% of examinations concordant normal and potentially deprioritized
evidence.tradeoff: Low specificity: 80% of examinations were classified abnormal. Missed findings were mostly subtle or overlapping lesions.
evidence.quote: Expert review of discrepant cases, after exclusion of 412 natural language processing labeling errors, identified 31 clinically significant AI misses, corresponding to an estimated clinically significant miss rate of 0.05%.

evidence.title: Avoiding Biased Clinical Machine Learning Model Performance Estimates in the Presence of Label Selection
evidence.venue: AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science proceedings. AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science
evidence.comparator_used: Naive performance estimates from labels observed only after clinicians act on the model (no randomization, unweighted)
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of estimated model performance (AUROC) during monitoring of deployed models under label selection feedback
evidence.effect: Naive AUROC estimates on the observed population undershoot actual performance by up to 20%; injected randomization combined with weighted estimates recovers true model performance
evidence.quote: We propose an altered deployment procedure, one that combines injected randomization with traditional weighted estimates, and find it recovers true model performance.

Continuous automated probing of live production endpoints

controls.question: Should we keep a complete, tamper-evident log of every AI interaction so incidents can be reconstructed?

evidence.title: Adaptive FHIR Native AI Governance for Clinical Decision Support: A Modular, Auditable Deployment Framework for Real World Clinical AI
evidence.comparator_used: None; no comparison against standard application logs without provenance was reported. Audit completeness was only measured for the framework's own artifacts, in simulation on synthetic FHIR data.
evidence.outcome: Audit completeness and deterministic reconstruction of deployment pathways
evidence.effect: All decisions (2,272 sequential decisions) generated complete FHIR AuditEvent and Provenance artifacts; 100% deterministic reconstruction of deployment pathways
evidence.quote: All deployment decisions generated complete HL7 FHIR AuditEvent and Provenance artifacts, enabling 100% deterministic reconstruction of deployment pathways.

controls.question: Should we track operational telemetry such as usage, prediction volume, missing inputs, latency, uptime and token cost as early warning signals?
controls.control: Continuously track label-independent operational signals: usage and adoption, prediction volume, input missingness, latency, uptime, energy and token cost.
controls.comparator: Tracking only lagging accuracy metrics such as AUC or calibration
controls.aim: Detect pipeline failures, adoption problems and degradation early using signals available immediately
variants: Usage and engagement dashboards built on interaction logs
Latency, uptime, energy and token-cost tracking
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards
tradeoffs: Associations are observational, not causal. The authors say outcome-based reassessment is still needed as confirmatory evidence, and telemetry is not an unbiased measure of clinical effectiveness.

evidence.title: Validation is not enough: Longitudinal evidence of post-deployment fragility in clinical AI systems
evidence.comparator_used: Outcome-label-dependent (lagging) performance monitoring such as AUROC and calibration
evidence.outcome: Early detection of emerging post-deployment degradation (timing relative to outcome-based monitoring)
evidence.effect: Input missingness was associated with lower calibration slope in every system (standardized beta -0.42 to -0.21). Data latency was associated in 3 of 4 systems (-0.35 to -0.08). Missingness and latency kept negative associations in 12/12 alternative specifications. Telemetry changes preceded or co-evolved with calibration degradation, while outcome labels lagged by 24-72 hours up to 2-8 weeks depending on system.
evidence.tradeoff: Associations are observational, not causal. The authors say outcome-based reassessment is still needed as confirmatory evidence, and telemetry is not an unbiased measure of clinical effectiveness.
evidence.quote: Label-independent operational signals, including input missingness and data latency, provided early indication of emerging fragility, whereas outcome-based monitoring was delayed by label latency and documentation processes.

evidence.title: Ensuring fair, safe, and interpretable artificial intelligence-based prediction tools in a real-world oncological setting
evidence.comparator_used: Monitoring model performance alone (lagging indicators such as AUC)
evidence.outcome: Detection of a data feed outage during the 77-day simulated production period
evidence.effect: Leading indicators (prediction volume, average predicted risk, PSI) showed a sharp drop in volume and a PSI spike in the weeks of May 16 and May 23, 2022. They flagged an EHR data feed outage that lagging performance monitoring would likely have missed. No numeric comparison was reported.
evidence.quote: We note that this issue would likely not have been noticed if we were monitoring for model performance alone.

controls.question: Should we use a dedicated monitoring platform and dashboard rather than ad hoc manual reports and one-off analyses?
controls.control: Deploy an integrated monitoring platform with automated data pipelines, performance dashboards, alerts and logging usable by clinical and technical teams.
controls.comparator: Ad hoc manual reports and one-off analyses by data scientists
controls.aim: Make ongoing model monitoring sustainable, timely and visible to both clinical and technical owners
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards

controls.question: Should we monitor calibration of predicted risks after deployment, not just discrimination?
controls.control: Track calibration across the range of predicted risks, such as observed-versus-expected, calibration slope and intercept, alongside discrimination.
controls.comparator: Monitoring discrimination (AUROC or accuracy) only
controls.aim: Catch miscalibrated risk estimates that discrimination metrics do not reveal
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards
tradeoffs: Evaluation was described as feasible with a part-time statistical analyst. The model was trained on a balanced dataset, so predicted probabilities were far above observed rates. Differential calibration was not detected by gender.
Confidence intervals for the calibration shifts were wide. The recalibration was apparent (fitted and assessed in the same temporal cohort) and only partly corrected the drift.

evidence.title: Validation is not enough: Longitudinal evidence of post-deployment fragility in clinical AI systems
evidence.comparator_used: Monitoring discrimination (AUROC) alone
evidence.outcome: Timing of detection of post-deployment degradation (calibration slope/intercept vs AUROC)
evidence.effect: Mean change from validation to the first 6 months of deployment: calibration slope -0.11 (-0.14 to -0.08) vs AUROC -0.02 (-0.03 to -0.01). Calibration changed earlier than AUROC with the 3-month definition (-0.08 vs -0.01) and the 9-month definition (-0.14 vs -0.03). In System A, early-deployment AUROC was 0.81 (validation 0.82) while calibration slope fell from 1.01 to 0.88.
evidence.quote: These findings indicate that discrimination metrics alone would have delayed detection of post-deployment degradation, particularly in Systems A and B, where calibration drift emerged before substantial AUROC decline.

evidence.title: Developing and Applying the BE-FAIR Equity Framework to a Population Health Predictive Model: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Study
evidence.comparator_used: Discrimination (AUROC) across groups, with no calibration assessment (no formal head-to-head comparison)
evidence.outcome: Detection of subgroup bias in model performance
evidence.effect: Calibration differed by race-ethnicity and HPI: predicted hospitalization probabilities were significantly lower for African Americans (0.129±0.051, p=0.016), Hispanics (0.133±0.047, p=0.004), AAPI (0.120±0.051, p=0.018), multi-race (0.245±0.087, p=0.005), and low-HPI areas (0-25%: 0.178±0.042, p<0.001). For hospitalizations, AUROC was similar across races (e.g., 0.781 white, 0.792 Black, 0.757 Hispanic) and across HPI quartiles (0.765-0.780).
evidence.tradeoff: Evaluation was described as feasible with a part-time statistical analyst. The model was trained on a balanced dataset, so predicted probabilities were far above observed rates. Differential calibration was not detected by gender.
evidence.quote: There was evidence of differential calibration by race-ethnicity for both ED visits and hospitalizations.

evidence.title: Explainable Machine Learning and Temporal Calibration Drift of a TyG- BMI-Based Model for Early Prediction of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
evidence.comparator_used: Discrimination (AUC) alone, as tracked across the same models and time periods
evidence.outcome: Detection of temporal performance drift in first-trimester GDM prediction models
evidence.effect: Calibration intercepts shifted downward from internal holdout to temporal cohort (XGBoost Δintercept -0.866; LightGBM -0.977), meaning more average overprediction, in all three models, while discrimination was largely preserved (temporal AUC: XGBoost 0.881, LightGBM 0.870, logistic regression 0.857). Logistic recalibration brought the intercept to about 0 and the slope to 1.0, and improved the XGBoost Brier score from 0.111 to 0.100.
evidence.tradeoff: Confidence intervals for the calibration shifts were wide. The recalibration was apparent (fitted and assessed in the same temporal cohort) and only partly corrected the drift.
evidence.quote: Calibration drift occurred despite stable AUC and was partly correctable by recalibration, underscoring the need for calibration monitoring before clinical deployment.

evidence.title: Silent calibration drift in a frozen clinical prediction model: a decade-long audit and an operational monitoring framework
evidence.comparator_used: Monitoring discrimination (AUC) only
evidence.outcome: Detection of model performance decay (calibration drift) in a frozen 2-year post-resection mortality model
evidence.effect: Discrimination stayed stable (optimism-corrected development AUC 0.76; later eras 0.74 and 0.75), but the calibration intercept drifted to -0.54 and -0.31 (both 95% CIs excluding zero), with over-prediction in both access strata. Predicted mortality was 19.2% against 15.6% observed, and intercept recalibration restored calibration-in-the-large without changing discrimination.
evidence.quote: Discrimination-based validation can conceal clinically meaningful calibration drift.

evidence.title: Calibration Drift Under Cross-Institutional Deployment: An External Validation Framework for ICU Mortality Prediction Across MIMIC-IV and eICU
evidence.comparator_used: Discrimination-only assessment (AUROC/AUPRC) of the same model, internally versus externally
evidence.outcome: Detection of performance drift under external deployment (calibration versus discrimination)
evidence.effect: Internal AUROC 0.847 vs external AUROC 0.819, so discrimination held up. Internal calibration was near-ideal (slope 0.982; intercept 0.001), but external validation showed systematic risk overestimation (intercept -0.678). An intercept-only adjustment reduced ECE by 26%.
evidence.quote: ICU mortality models exhibit transportable discrimination but clinically significant calibration drift under cross-institutional deployment.

evidence.title: Algorithmovigilance in AI-Based Oral-Health Surveillance: Temporal Drift, Cross-Survey Differences, and Predictor-Level Structural Stability in Population-Level Severe Tooth Loss Prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Monitoring discrimination (AUC) alone across chronological BRFSS cycles and external NHANES reference
evidence.outcome: Detection of drift and performance change not visible from discrimination alone
evidence.effect: AUC declined only modestly from 0.8638 in 2016 to 0.8495 in 2024, yet calibration and predictor-level changes were detected. Frozen unrecalibrated model in pooled NHANES: AUC = 0.8681, Brier Score = 0.1131.
evidence.quote: Aggregate discrimination alone did not capture calibration and predictor-level changes.

controls.question: Should we monitor error rates by class, demographic and acquisition subgroup at the deployed threshold, not just in aggregate?
controls.control: Report sensitivity, specificity and other error rates at the deployed threshold for each class, demographic group and acquisition subgroup.
controls.comparator: Monitoring aggregate performance across all patients only
controls.aim: Catch subgroup performance gaps and inequities hidden by aggregate metrics
controls.family_label: drift detection, automated evaluation, audit sampling, silent-mode runs, performance dashboards
tradeoffs: Small groups (e.g., AIAN) gave wide confidence intervals and unstable estimates. The operations team kept the 60% outreach threshold to balance reduced bias for some groups against outreach staff bandwidth.
Audit based on recorded demographics is blind to 30% of studies, since harm reached patients whose race was not recorded via the pixel shortcut

evidence.title: Developing and Applying the BE-FAIR Equity Framework to a Population Health Predictive Model: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Study
evidence.comparator_used: Aggregate performance across all patients (implicit; no aggregate-only arm was compared)
evidence.outcome: Subgroup differences in sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV at the deployed threshold of 60
evidence.effect: ED visit sensitivity: White 0.495, Black 0.599, Hispanic 0.402, Other 0.381. Hospitalization sensitivity: White 0.392, Black 0.511, AAPI 0.300, Other 0.282. Sensitivity was also higher in the lowest HPI quartile (hospitalization 0.462 vs 0.271 in the highest).
evidence.tradeoff: Small groups (e.g., AIAN) gave wide confidence intervals and unstable estimates. The operations team kept the 60% outreach threshold to balance reduced bias for some groups against outreach staff bandwidth.
evidence.quote: Test sensitivity for a decision threshold of 60 also varied among race/ethnicity group with sensitivity lowest among Hispanic and the Other race group and highest among African Americans (Table 3 ).

evidence.title: Demographic shortcuts as marker-free backdoors: silent subgroup underdiagnosis that only operating-point audits detect
evidence.comparator_used: Rank-based audit (AUROC) and aggregate overall performance monitoring
evidence.outcome: Detection of installed subgroup underdiagnosis backdoor failures
evidence.effect: Subgroup false-negative rate audit at deployed threshold flagged 96% of installed failures vs 73% for a rank-based audit; overall AUROC moved only 0.004
evidence.tradeoff: Audit based on recorded demographics is blind to 30% of studies, since harm reached patients whose race was not recorded via the pixel shortcut
evidence.quote: What works is auditing subgroup false-negative rate at the deployed threshold, which flagged 96% of installed failures compared to 73% for a rank-based audit.

evidence.title: EXHEART: A Fairness-Aware Explainable Stacked Ensemble for Cardiovascular Disease Classification with Cross-Instrument Disparity Attribution
evidence.comparator_used: single-attribute (sex-only) fairness auditing
evidence.outcome: Detection of subgroup disparities in true positive rate at the screening threshold
evidence.effect: Intersectional Sex × Age disparities reach 0.649 among adequately-powered cells, 5.2× the single-attribute gap (Sex TPR gap 0.124)
evidence.quote: The intersectional audit revealed disparities that single-attribute auditing missed, and the cross-instrument comparison indicated that much of the sex gap reflects how the outcome is measured in survey data rather than a substantive difference in risk.

evidence.title: When external validation isn’t enough: Simpson’s paradox, direction asymmetry, and calibration collapse in cross-continental perioperative mortality prediction
evidence.comparator_used: Aggregate cross-population AUC reported across all patients, versus within-stratum AUCs
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC) in external validation, aggregate versus within-stratum
evidence.effect: Simpson's paradox gap of 5.0–16.5 pp across the eight cross-population runs; worst case aggregate AUC 0.756 vs within-stratum AUCs 0.58–0.60
evidence.quote: Across the eight cross-population runs, aggregate AUCs concealed substantially lower within-stratum AUCs (Simpson’s paradox gap range 5.0–16.5 pp; worst case: aggregate AUC 0.756 vs within-stratum AUCs 0.58–0.60).

controls.question: Should we track downstream patient outcomes and balancing safety measures after go-live, not just model accuracy?
controls.control: Track patient outcomes, process measures, alert burden and balancing safety signals after AI deployment.
controls.comparator: Monitoring model accuracy metrics alone

controls.aim: Restore performance quickly after degradation while keeping model changes validated and governed

evidence.quote: During the COVID-19 pandemic, drift-triggered continual learning improved overall model performance (Delta AUROC [SD], 0.44 [0.02]; P = .007, Mann-Whitney U test).

Versioned deterministic skills or code tools
Clinician-authored rule engine, expert system or symbolic model makes the determination
LLM writes SQL or Python, runs it in a sandbox and debugs from execution feedback

Smaller models and distilled reasoning variants had more frequent formatting and execution errors

evidence.title: Closed-Loop Quality Assurance for Production Clinical AI Documentation
evidence.comparator_used: Multi-kilobyte LLM assembly-agent prompt (Chart_Builder) before replacement
evidence.outcome: H+P trace latency after replacing the LLM assembly call with a deterministic template plus sandboxed scripting
evidence.effect: Latency fell from 19.6 s to 10.8 s (−8.8 s, 95% CI [−10.5, −7.1] s; n = 100 pre, n = 100 post)
evidence.quote: a deterministic assembly-agent replacement cut H+P trace latency from 19.6 s to 10.8 s (−8.8 s, 95% CI [−10.5, −7.1] s

evidence.title: An LLM-Powered Clinical Calculator Chatbot Backed by Verifiable Clinical Calculators and their Metadata
evidence.venue: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium
evidence.comparator_used: Unassisted off-the-shelf LLM performing clinical calculations itself
evidence.outcome: Clinical calculation accuracy and calculation error rate on natural language conversation workloads
evidence.effect: Accuracy with complete sentences 86.4% vs 61.8%; with medical shorthand 79.2% vs 62.0%. Calculation errors with complete sentences 0% vs 16.8%; with shorthand 2.4% vs 18%.
evidence.tradeoff: Not yet ready for clinical use; residual calculation errors with shorthand (2.4%) and accuracy still below 100%.
evidence.quote: Our chatbot achieves 100% accuracy on queries interrogating calculator metadata content and shows a significant increase in clinical calculation accuracy vs. the off-the-shelf LLM when prompted with complete sentences (86.4% vs. 61.8%) or with medical shorthand (79.2% vs. 62.0%).

evidence.title: Large language models are poor clinical administrators: An evaluation of structured queries in real-world electronic health records
evidence.comparator_used: Direct prompting and chain-of-thought prompting, where the LLM answers directly in text
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on structured EHR table tasks and valid JSON output formatting
evidence.effect: Tool-based strategy (LLM-generated Python code, executed to retrieve answers) substantially improved accuracy over direct and CoT prompting; no numeric values reported in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Smaller models and distilled reasoning variants had more frequent formatting and execution errors
evidence.quote: The tool-based strategy substantially improved accuracy.

evidence.title: Trustworthy agentic genomics through versioned skill libraries
evidence.comparator_used: Model reasoning on its own (unguarded) and model reasoning grounded by guideline retrieval, across nine frontier LLMs and 110 pharmacogenomic cases
evidence.outcome: Correctness and determinism of the pharmacogenomic phenotype/clinical mapping, and lethal-class errors
evidence.effect: Executing the validated versioned skill as code made the mapping exact and identical across models, and removed the ancestry gradient from the clinical mapping. Model-only reasoning was stochastic and unsafe. The abstract gives no numeric accuracy figures for this comparison.
evidence.tradeoff: All residual error remains at the single input-interpretation step. The ancestry gradient moves to the completeness of the input caller. The authors do not claim full clinical validation.
evidence.quote: Encoding the validated decision logic as a versioned skill and executing it as code made the pharmacogenomic mapping exact, auditable and identical across models, confining all residual error to a single input-interpretation step.

evidence.title: Towards a Deterministic Math Solver for Clinical Language Models
evidence.comparator_used: direct model arithmetic (LLM calculating in free text) on MedCalc-Bench Verified, with formulas and gold variables supplied
evidence.outcome: Accuracy on clinical calculator cases (1,100 cases, 55 calculators)
evidence.effect: 7B: 75.31% vs 72.02%, paired +3.29 points, 95% calculator-cluster CI [-3.49, 10.38] (not a reliable advantage); 32B: 90.53% vs 83.47%, +7.05 [0.47, 14.60], clear of zero
evidence.tradeoff: Benefit depends on model size; not a substitute for verified formulas or reliable variable extraction. 16 of 55 benchmark formulas flagged with version, use or coefficient concerns.
evidence.quote: With formulas and gold variables supplied and both routes reading the whole note, handing off to the solver is not a reliable advantage at 7B (75.31% against 72.02%, a paired +3.29 points with a 95% calculator-cluster interval of [-3.49, 10.38]) but is one at 32B (90.53% against 83.47%, +7.05 [0.47, 14.60], clear of zero).

evidence.title: Large language model agents can use tools to perform clinical calculations
evidence.comparator_used: Unaugmented LLM (ChatGPT, LLaMa, GPT-based models) performing the medical calculations directly
evidence.outcome: Incorrect responses on medical calculation tasks
evidence.effect: 5.5-fold (88% vs 16%) reduction in incorrect responses for LLaMa and 13-fold (64% vs 4.8%) for GPT-based models with task-specific tools (OpenMedCalc) versus unimproved models
evidence.quote: Models with access to task-specific tools showed the greatest improvement, with LLaMa and GPT-based models demonstrating a 5.5-fold (88% vs 16%) and 13-fold (64% vs 4.8%) reduction in incorrect responses, respectively, compared to the unimproved models.

evidence.title: Benchmarking large language models for ACMG/AMP variant interpretation and variant calling
evidence.comparator_used: Model prior (LLM answering from its own knowledge) along a constraint gradient toward executed, validated code
evidence.outcome: Fabricated evidence, and trust properties (pinning, provenance, auditability, reproducibility) in variant calling
evidence.effect: No numbers in the abstract. Fabricated evidence is described as neutralised by execution. Trust properties climb monotonically toward validated execution. Dangerous misclassification is rare and model-invariant.
evidence.quote: First, dangerous misclassification is rare and model-invariant, a controlled precondition of the executed architecture rather than a frontier, while fabricated evidence is measurable and is neutralised by execution.

controls.question: Should we split the clinical task across specialized agents or sequential steps instead of one model doing everything in one prompt?
controls.control: Decompose the workflow into role- or stage-specialized agents or sequential LLM steps with defined responsibilities and information routing.

Chosen communication topology and limited pipeline depth
Sequential pipeline: screen, extract, check guidelines, synthesize, explain
Simulated patients built from separate disclosure, persona, tutoring and evaluation agents

evidence.title: Multi-Agent Dynamic Refinement Outperforms Static RAG in Clinical Reasoning for Complex Nephrology Cases
evidence.comparator_used: Single baseline frontier LLM (Model A) and LLM with static guideline RAG (Model B)
evidence.outcome: Overall clinical reasoning score, diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic management scores
evidence.effect: Human evaluation (20-point scale): Model C 17.2 (SD 1.2) vs Model A 16.1 and Model B 16.2 (P < 0.001). AI panel (15-point scale): Model C 14.7 vs Model A 14.2 (P < 0.001) and Model B 14.3 (P = 0.01). Diagnostic accuracy 17.6 (P = 0.019); therapeutic management 17.3 (P = 0.002).
evidence.quote: Distributing clinical workflows into a multi-agent dynamic refinement pipeline significantly improves reasoning completeness, intercepts error cascades, and safely resolves planning bottlenecks in complex patient care.

evidence.title: Representation Before Retrieval: Structured Patient Artifacts Reduce Hallucination in Clinical AI Systems
evidence.comparator_used: Artifact-augmented single-pass generation (C2)
evidence.outcome: Unsupported claims, contraindication miss rate, clinician utility
evidence.effect: Agent workflow had 21.1% unsupported claims, with the lowest contraindication miss rate (0.04) and the highest clinician utility scores; single-pass artifact generation had 8.4% unsupported claims
evidence.tradeoff: Unsupported claim rate (21.1%) was higher than in single-pass artifact generation (8.4%).
evidence.quote: The agent workflow achieved 21.1% unsupported claims with the lowest contraindication miss rate (0.04) and highest clinician utility scores.

evidence.title: OGA-AID: Clinician-in-the-loop AI Report Drafting Assistant for Multimodal Observational Gait Analysis in Post-Stroke Rehabilitation
evidence.comparator_used: single-pass multimodal LLM baselines
evidence.outcome: Error in structured gait assessment reports, rated by expert physiotherapists on real patient data
evidence.effect: OGA-AID, with 3 specialized agents, consistently outperformed single-pass multimodal baselines with low error. No numeric values are given in the abstract.

evidence.title: Emergent Misinformation Genesis in Multi-Agent LLM Clinical Pipelines

evidence.quote: Our four central findings: (1) emergence is universal, with 30-56% of network assertions absent from any individual agent and 85-100% of clinical vignettes affected; (2) two independent judges rate 70-87% of emergent assertions as clinically dangerous (n≥499 each), with a third judge (n=37) providing directional confirmation at 68%, and severity confirmed against published AHA/ASA/ADA guidelines (42/45, 93%); (3) the network exhibits collective delusion, where individual agents reject 70-90% of the assertions the network produces; (4) a 5-line confidence-calibration prompt reduces emergence by 25-28% (p<0.001), but FC cross-checking fails for 3 of 4 models, and depth ablation reveals two distinct emergence regimes.

evidence.quote: Multi-agent M1 and M2 also achieved zero observed false inclusion on the structured cohort with distinct uncertainty profiles (25.8% and 1.7% uncertain, respectively); in the PMC real-text validation, M1 maintained zero false inclusion (0/44; 95% CI 0.0-8.0%) while M2 produced one false inclusion arising from an anomalous Safety Agent label upgrade on ambiguous unstructured text.

evidence.title: Not All Uncertainty Is Equal: How Uncertainty Granularity Shapes Human Verification in LLM-Assisted Decision Making
evidence.comparator_used: LLM output shown without uncertainty information (baseline condition), and across different uncertainty granularities (output-level, relation-level, token-level)
evidence.outcome: User agreement with the AI, user confidence in own answers, and external verification behavior (internet searches, checking URLs)
evidence.effect: Token-level uncertainty increased agreement with the AI; output- and relation-level uncertainty did not increase agreement but reduced users' confidence in their own answers; relation-level uncertainty also reduced external verification.
evidence.tradeoff: Relation-level uncertainty steered users away from independent fact-checking toward reliance on the LLM and its uncertainty cues; token-level uncertainty increased agreement with the AI (risk of over-reliance).
evidence.quote: Token-level uncertainty increased users' agreement with the AI, whereas output- and relation-level uncertainty did not increase agreement but instead reduced users' confidence in their own answers.

evidence.tradeoff: Accuracy did not benefit when the AI was incorrect, or for pathological cases in the student group. Self-reported trust of all participants decreased from the beginning to the end of the study.

evidence.quote: In the decision-making study (n=21; 20 assessments per radiologist), recall increased with AI score in both conditions; however, recall was higher when AI scores were presented alone compared with scores accompanied by FDR/FOR (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI [1.331, 6.417], p=0.0077).

evidence.title: Auditable Emergency Triage for Maternal and Newborn Care in India
evidence.comparator_used: Opaque LLM-only triage classifier with rationale chains, compared with a decomposed pipeline whose decision path runs through canonical symptom/context extraction and a deterministic clinician-authored rule engine.
evidence.outcome: Emergency triage accuracy and auditability of the decision process.
evidence.effect: Recall raised from 0.565 to 0.810; F1 raised from 0.606 to 0.702; clinicians added 48 new rules since deployment; no increase in missed emergencies was reported.
evidence.tradeoff: Over-escalation rate was 17.8%; rule maintenance required clinician additions, but the study reports a faster correction loop and avoidance of costly full evaluations.
evidence.quote: We show that the new system raised recall from 0.565 to 0.810 and F1 from 0.606 to 0.702, with structured rules driving most of the accuracy gains while the decomposition provides auditability: clinical experts can inspect each stage of the new system to see whether the query was mistranslated, symptoms were incorrectly extracted, patient context was wrongly inferred, or the necessary rules were missing.

evidence.quote: Participants tended to have higher satisfaction with a human disclosure over AI disclosure, with a mean difference of 0.13 (95% CI, 0.05-0.22) points, and with no disclosure over AI authorship disclosure, with a mean difference of 0.09 (95% CI, 0.01-0.17) points.

evidence.title: Physician Ratings and Adoption of AI-Generated e-Consultation Advice: A Randomized Clinical Vignette Study
evidence.comparator_used: Same e-consultation advice labeled as written by a "specialist attending physician" versus a "medically specialized artificial intelligence system" (randomized label)
evidence.outcome: Perceived quality ratings and adoption of e-consult recommendations
evidence.effect: Mean perceived quality ratings 4.2-4.7 out of 5 with no significant differences between randomization groups (all p > 0.05); labeling did not significantly affect adoption (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.51-2.75; p = 0.70)
evidence.quote: Labeling the advice as human- or GAI-generated did not significantly affect adoption of e-consult recommendations (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.51-2.75; p = 0.70).

evidence.title: Acceptability of AI-Assisted Psychotherapy to Prospective Patients and Their Intent to Continue Treatment: A Vignette Study
evidence.comparator_used: Covert (undisclosed) therapist AI use, with a no-AI control scenario as reference
evidence.outcome: Perceived acceptability of AI-assisted psychotherapy and intent to continue treatment
evidence.effect: Covert use consistently produced the strongest declines in acceptability and continuation intent. Transparent disclosure reduced the penalty but did not eliminate it. All AI-use vignettes were rated lower than the no-AI control (all p<0.001). Older age and greater chatbot familiarity modestly reduced the penalty in transparent conditions.
evidence.tradeoff: Even with transparent disclosure, ratings stayed below the no-AI scenario, so disclosure only partly offset the negative reaction to AI use.
evidence.quote: Transparency reduced, but did not eliminate, negative reactions.

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence With Youth Codesign to Create Vaping Awareness Advertisements
evidence.comparator_used: Same vaping ads presented with no source label, or with other labels (made by WHO, made with AI by WHO), compared across four between-participant labeling conditions
evidence.outcome: Perceived message effectiveness (vaping perception, behavioral intent, attention, information, convincingness) of vaping awareness ads
evidence.effect: Labeling conditions did not differ significantly on PME scores; χ2 values ranged from 0.10 to 4.19, all P > .20
evidence.quote: Source labeling showed no significant association with PME scores (χ2 values ranging from 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20).

evidence.title: Effectiveness of Humanized AI Avatars and Messenger Gender for Dental Postprocedure Instructions: Two Randomized Experiments
evidence.comparator_used: Same avatar video instructions presented without disclosure of AI identity
evidence.outcome: Intention to comply with instructions and reported likelihood of returning to the same dentist
evidence.effect: AI disclosure did not affect intention to comply; it reduced the reported likelihood of returning to the same dentist (no numeric effect sizes given in abstract). Experiment 1, n=650.
evidence.tradeoff: Disclosure reduced patients' reported likelihood of returning to the same dentist, a trust or retention cost.
evidence.quote: AI disclosure did not affect intention to comply but reduced the reported likelihood of returning to the same dentist.

evidence.title: Should AI results be disclosed in mammography reports? A randomised survey study of patient responses to concordant and discordant interpretations
evidence.comparator_used: Radiologist Only report with no AI result disclosed
evidence.outcome: Trust in radiologist, anxiety, second-opinion intent and legal action intent when a discordant AI result is disclosed
evidence.effect: Trust 73.0 vs 90.1 (p < 0.001); anxiety 58.0% vs 16.0% (OR = 15.4); second-opinion intent 50.0% vs 8.7% (OR = 10.2); legal action consideration 60.7% vs 38.7% (OR = 2.49). AI approval stayed above 85% in all groups.
evidence.tradeoff: Disclosing a discordant AI flag lowered trust and increased anxiety, follow-up seeking and litigation intent.
evidence.quote: Disclosure of a discordant AI result significantly reduced trust in the radiologist (73.0 vs 90.1; p < 0.001), and increased anxiety (58.0% vs 16.0%; OR = 15.4), second-opinion intent (50.0% vs 8.7%; OR = 10.2), and legal action consideration (60.7% vs 38.7%; OR = 2.49).

evidence.title: Influence of believed AI involvement on the perception of digital medical advice
evidence.comparator_used: Identical medical advice labelled as from a "Human physician" (no AI label), compared with "AI" and "Human + AI" labels
evidence.outcome: Perceived reliability, perceived empathy and willingness to follow the advice
evidence.effect: AI-labelled and Human + AI-labelled advice was rated significantly less reliable and less empathetic than Human-labelled advice, and participants were less willing to follow it when AI was believed to be involved (two preregistered studies, N = 2,280; no numeric estimates in the abstract)
evidence.tradeoff: Labelling AI involvement produced an anti-AI bias, which persisted even when AI was described as supervised by physicians
evidence.quote: “AI” and “Human + AI”-labelled advice was evaluated as significantly less reliable and less empathetic compared to “Human”-labelled advice.
