evidence.title: Mitigating Automation Bias in Physician-LLM Diagnostic Reasoning Using Behavioral Nudges: A Randomized Controlled Trial
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT-5.1 recommendations alone, without the anchoring cue reporting ChatGPT’s benchmark accuracy to calibrate expectations
evidence.outcome: Physician diagnostic reasoning scored by blinded reviewers against an expert rubric
evidence.effect: mean difference, 7.6 percentage-points; 95% CI, 1.4-13.9; P =0.016
evidence.quote: The treatment group scored significantly higher (mean difference, 7.6 percentage-points; 95% CI, 1.4-13.9;  P =0.016) than the control, suggesting a scalable strategy to preserve clinical judgment in LLM-assisted care.

evidence.title: 'ChatGPT can make mistakes' warnings fail: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.comparator_used: ChatGPT-attributed diagnostic feedback shown without the warning ('ChatGPT can make mistakes. Check important info')
evidence.outcome: Diagnosis change rate after viewing disagreeing ChatGPT advice (advice-taking) among medical students
evidence.quote: The warning did not influence diagnostic changes (15.3% no-warning vs. 15.9% warning; OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 0.46-2.59, p = 0.84).

evidence.title: Facilitating Trust Calibration in Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnostic Decision Support Systems for Determining Physicians' Diagnostic Accuracy: Quasi-Experimental Study
evidence.comparator_used: Physicians reviewing the AI-generated differential diagnosis list without the trust calibration prompt (control group)
evidence.outcome: Physicians' diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: 41.5% in the intervention group vs 46% in the control group (95% CI -0.75 to 2.55; P=.27). Within the intervention group, accuracy of the trust calibration was a significant contributor to diagnostic accuracy (adjusted OR 5.90, 95% CI 2.93-12.46; P<.001).
evidence.quote: The physicians' diagnostic accuracy was 41.5% in the intervention group and 46% in the control group, with no significant difference (95% CI -0.75 to 2.55; P=.27).

evidence.title: Should AI results be disclosed in mammography reports? A randomised survey study of patient responses to concordant and discordant interpretations
evidence.comparator_used: Discordant (false-positive) AI flag disclosed without explanatory note (AI Flagged scenario)
evidence.outcome: Patient anxiety, trust, second-opinion intent and legal action intent after disclosure of a discordant AI result
evidence.effect: Anxiety 25.3% with explanation (OR = 0.26 vs flag without explanation). Versus Radiologist Only, AI Flagged + Explanation showed a modest anxiety increase (p = 0.04) and no significant trust reduction (p = 0.42).
evidence.tradeoff: Anxiety remained modestly higher than in the Radiologist Only scenario (p = 0.04) even with the explanation.
evidence.quote: Adding explanatory context significantly mitigated these effects (e.g., anxiety: 25.3%; OR = 0.26).

evidence.title: Designing Medical Chatbots where Accuracy and Acceptability are in Conflict: An Exploratory, Vignette-based Study in Urban India
evidence.comparator_used: Preferences for chatbot transcripts without context-aware nudges (baseline preference, in which a majority rejected guideline-aligned, norm-divergent advice)
evidence.outcome: User preference for transcripts containing guideline-aligned advice (expectation alignment)
evidence.effect: Nudges shifted preferences towards guideline-aligned transcripts; the abstract gives no numbers for the shift (a majority of the 200 participants rejected such advice at baseline).
evidence.quote: Through the design and introduction of context-aware nudges, we support expectation alignment that shifts preferences towards transcripts containing guideline-aligned advice.

evidence.title: Augmented reality microscopy to bridge trust between AI and pathologists
evidence.comparator_used: Pathologists scoring PD-L1 CPS on the microscope without the AI overlay (unassisted reads)
evidence.outcome: Interobserver agreement on PD-L1 CPS scoring of difficult gastroesophageal biopsy regions, and positive calls at CPS ≥ 5
evidence.effect: Agreement between any 2 pathologists rose by 14% (77% vs 91%). Agreement among 11 pathologists rose by 26% (43% vs 69%). Cases called positive by all 11 pathologists at CPS ≥ 5 increased by 31%.
evidence.quote: Using difficult to interpret regions on gastroesophageal biopsies, we show that AI-assistance improved case agreement between any 2 pathologists by 14% (agreement on 77% vs 91%) and among 11 pathologists by 26% (agreement on 43% vs 69%).

controls.question: Should LLMs that handle patient data run only in environments we manage or contractually govern, rather than through uncontracted external LLM services?
controls.control: Host open-weight LLMs on hospital servers or devices, or use commercial LLMs only in contracted, institutionally governed environments with access, logging, and retention terms.
controls.comparator: Consumer or commercial LLM services used without institutional contract or governance
controls.aim: Keep identifiable patient data from leaving institutional control or reaching uncontracted third parties.

Fully on-device, browser, or edge inference with no data leaving the device
Commercial LLM inside a contracted, institutionally governed cloud environment with authentication, logging, and retention limits

controls.question: Should we limit and de-identify the patient data sent to AI tools, rather than sending full identified records and raw media?

Client-side PHI redaction before external API calls
Pseudonymization with local re-identification of outputs
Blurring, cropping, or defacing images and video, or sending only derived features

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Abstract Complex Social Determinants of Health From Original and Deidentified Medical Notes: Development and Validation Study
evidence.comparator_used: Original (identified) clinical notes sent to GPT-4
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 precision and recall for identifying housing instability on deidentified vs original notes
evidence.effect: Precision 0.936 original vs 0.939 deidentified; recall 0.781 original vs 0.704 deidentified
evidence.tradeoff: Deidentifying notes before LLM abstraction lowered recall (0.781 to 0.704), so more cases of housing instability were missed.
evidence.quote: GPT-4's precision improved slightly (0.936 original, 0.939 deidentified) on deidentified versions of the same notes, while recall dropped (0.781 original, 0.704 deidentified).

evidence.title: Client-Side Ephemeral De-Identification of Protected Health Information (PHI) in Multi-Center Clinical Trial Analysis and Large Language Model Workflows: Validating Zero-Trust Data Sanitization Under HIPAA Safe Harbor Section 164.514(b)
evidence.comparator_used: Conventional cloud-based DLP proxy gateways (server-side intermediate processing), rather than sending full identified records
evidence.outcome: Processing latency of de-identification before transmission to AI APIs, with recall of HIPAA identifiers and outbound PHI bytes
evidence.effect: Client-side ZTDS: 99.94% recall on direct HIPAA 18 identifiers, average 1.84 ms per note vs 242.6 ms for cloud DLP proxy gateways (131-fold latency reduction); zero outbound bytes of PHI on packet inspection in connected and Airplane Mode states (2,500 synthetic notes)
evidence.quote: In comparison, conventional cloud-based DLP proxy gatewaysincurred an average latency of 242.6 ms (a 131-fold latency reduction)

controls.question: Should AI tools process patient data statelessly or delete inputs after a short window, rather than retaining them indefinitely?

controls.aim: Reduce exposure if an AI service or its stored data is breached or misused.

Deleting raw audio and other inputs after a defined window

Second-pass check by a reviewer agent, leakage detector, or human on the same pipeline

evidence.title: Institution-Specific LLM Prompting Recovers PHI That De-identification Systems and Their Gold Standards Both Miss
evidence.comparator_used: Purpose-built de-identification systems (Stanford TiDE, OpenMed PII) and pattern-based baselines
evidence.outcome: PHI de-identification F1, with the advantage concentrated in contextual categories
evidence.effect: Best LLM F1=0.918±0.001 vs TiDE 0.779
evidence.tradeoff: LLMs cost more to run than traditional methods
evidence.quote: LLMs outperformed the purpose-built systems (best F1=0.918$\pm$0.001 vs.\ TiDE 0.779), with advantages concentrated in contextual categories.

controls.question: Should we restrict AI tools and agents to role-based, least-privilege access with auditable identities and query limits?
controls.control: Give AI tools and agents role-based, read-only, least-privilege access with MFA, auditable identities, per-user query caps, and runtime policy-as-code rules.
controls.comparator: Broad service-account access without query caps or runtime policy enforcement
controls.aim: Limit unauthorized data access, model extraction, and misuse by users or agents.
variants: Read-only access scoped to each query's data needs
Machine-readable runtime policies with auditable agent identities
controls.family_label: PHI redaction and de-identification, on-premises models, prompt-injection defenses, access limits
tradeoffs: Model choice was highlighted as a necessary architectural consideration, which suggests results varied across LLMs.

evidence.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
evidence.comparator_used: Insecure agent workflow in which agents have access rights exceeding those of ordinary users
evidence.outcome: Security (attack success rate) and report accuracy of the least-privilege, defence-in-depth agentic workflow
evidence.effect: Attack success fell from 31% to 10% (RAG poisoning) and from 42% to 25% (data-field injection). Report accuracy rose 14 percentage points, from 72.5% to 86.5%.
evidence.tradeoff: Model choice was highlighted as a necessary architectural consideration, which suggests results varied across LLMs.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, report accuracy increased by 14 percentage points (72.5% to 86.5%) with the agentic workflow, demonstrating a secure design which provides more reliable outputs.

controls.question: Should we add dedicated defenses against prompt injection, jailbreaks, and adversarial image inputs at inference time?
controls.control: Defend inference inputs: build prompts server-side, label untrusted content, run injection and jailbreak classifiers, sanitize image text, and denoise adversarial image perturbations.
controls.comparator: Relying on the base model's built-in robustness with undefended inputs
controls.aim: Prevent malicious prompts or manipulated images from hijacking outputs, leaking data, or corrupting predictions.
variants: OCR sanitization of text embedded in medical images
Input denoising against adversarial image perturbations
controls.family_label: PHI redaction and de-identification, on-premises models, prompt-injection defenses, access limits
tradeoffs: All defenses preserved clean-image F1 within 0.6 percentage points of baseline on a high-prevalence benchmark; ProvDent is a fail-open mechanism that escalates suspicious cases for human review.

evidence.title: Image-embedded prompt injection vulnerability of vision-language models in dental radiology: a cross-vendor attack–defense evaluation
evidence.comparator_used: Undefended baseline VLM inference on images with embedded prompt injection (no defense); five defenses benchmarked including image cropping, OCR-based text sanitization, and ProvDent
evidence.outcome: Attack success rate of image-embedded prompt injection across four VLMs on dental panoramic radiographs
evidence.effect: OCR-based sanitization pooled ASR 0.2%, versus baseline paired attack success rates up to 62.6% (95% CI: 58.5–66.7%) for GPT-4o
evidence.tradeoff: All defenses preserved clean-image F1 within 0.6 percentage points of baseline on a high-prevalence benchmark; ProvDent is a fail-open mechanism that escalates suspicious cases for human review.
evidence.quote: OCR-based sanitization achieved the strongest attack reduction (pooled ASR: 0.2%), while ProvDent provided a complementary fail-open governance mechanism that escalates suspicious cases for human review.

evidence.title: Auto encoder-based defense mechanism against popular adversarial attacks in deep learning
evidence.comparator_used: Undefended CNN models (VGG16, VGG19, Stack Model) receiving adversarially perturbed chest X-ray images with no denoising
evidence.outcome: Classification accuracy of pneumonia detection models under FGSM and PGD adversarial attacks
evidence.effect: The autoencoder improves accuracy by up to 16% against PGD attacks in both the VGG16 and VGG19 models; PGD without defense reduced VGG16 overall accuracy by up to 67%.
evidence.quote: The autoencoder improves accuracy by up to 16% against PGD attacks in both the VGG16 and VGG19 models.

evidence.title: Balancing Safety and Educational Availability in a Large Language Model-Based Virtual Patient for Medical Interview Training: Robustness Evaluation Under Direct and Indirect Instructional Contamination
evidence.comparator_used: Undefended virtual patient (gpt-4o-mini with no input defense) under direct and indirect instructional contamination
evidence.outcome: Slot F1 excluding initial greeting (information recovery) and refusal rate under indirect contamination
evidence.effect: Indirect contamination without defense: slot F1 excl. init 0.489 (95% CI 0.398-0.581), refusal rate 0.047. With sanitizing defense: slot F1 excl. init 0.903 (95% CI 0.880-0.926), refusal rate 0.000. Clean baseline was 0.901. Direct contamination was not substantially harmful without defense (0.927), and the defended direct condition also returned to near-clean levels.
evidence.quote: Both defended conditions returned to near-clean levels, including indirect contamination plus defense (slot F1 excl. init 0.903, 95% CI 0.880-0.926; refusal rate 0.000).

evidence.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
evidence.comparator_used: Insecure agent workflow with undefended inputs, including client-side prompt construction, compared with the TRiSM-guided workflow
evidence.outcome: Attack success rate across RAG poisoning, data-field injection and client-side network injection (500 attack scenarios, 5 LLMs)
evidence.effect: Mean attack success fell from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection. The network injection vector was eliminated through server-side prompt construction.
evidence.quote: The TRiSM-guided agentic workflow reduced mean attack success rates from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection, while eliminating the network injection vector entirely through server-side prompt construction.

evidence.title: Robustness of a Large Language Model (LLM)-Based Virtual Patient for Japanese History-Taking Training Under Direct and Indirect Instructional Contamination
evidence.comparator_used: Direct contamination (prompt injection) without preprocessing defense
evidence.outcome: Case fidelity (slot-level F1) and turn-target hit rate under direct contamination
evidence.effect: Direct contamination without defense: fidelity 0.098 (95% CI 0.052-0.144), hit rate 0.077 (95% CI 0.034-0.119). With preprocessing defense: fidelity 0.945 (95% CI 0.938-0.952), hit rate 0.942 (95% CI 0.930-0.955). Clean baseline: fidelity 0.947, hit rate 0.946.
evidence.quote: With preprocessing defense, performance returned to near-clean levels (fidelity, 0.945; 95% CI, 0.938-0.952; hit rate, 0.942; 95% CI, 0.930-0.955).

controls.question: Should we keep raw patient data out of the LLM, letting it plan while controlled interfaces execute and return checked outputs or aggregates?

controls.aim: Reduce privacy risk of model development while preserving model performance.

Synthetic data for development pipelines before real-data validation

controls.question: Should every AI system handling PHI be required to meet a defined security baseline with automated intrusion detection and response?
controls.control: Require encryption, tamper-evident audit logs, network segmentation, penetration testing, and automated intrusion detection and response for AI systems and connected devices.
controls.comparator: No required security baseline or automated detection for AI systems
controls.aim: Prevent and detect breaches and attacks on AI systems, clinical networks, and medical devices.

AI-based intrusion detection and trust scoring for medical IoT

controls.question: Should we apply differential privacy when training or fine-tuning models or sharing federated updates?
controls.control: Add calibrated differential privacy noise during training, fine-tuning, or federated update sharing, under a defined privacy budget.

controls.aim: Limit memorization and reconstruction of individual patient records from trained models or shared updates.
variants: Differential privacy during training or fine-tuning
controls.family_label: PHI redaction and de-identification, on-premises models, prompt-injection defenses, access limits
tradeoffs: Monotonic privacy-utility trade-off: performance declined as ε decreased, with collapse to near-chance at ε=0.01.
Large utility loss: the lowest leakage came with a drop in utility from 3.87 to 3.03. The authors describe a pervasive privacy-utility trade-off.

evidence.title: A novel gradient inversion attack framework to investigate privacy vulnerabilities during retinal image-based federated learning
evidence.comparator_used: Federated training without differential privacy (undefended gradients); the abstract does not detail the comparison
evidence.outcome: Information recoverable from reconstructed retinal images under gradient inversion attack
evidence.effect: No numbers reported for the DP condition in the text. Without DP, over 92% of training-set participants could be identified from reconstructed retinal vessel structure. With DP, substantial information could still be extracted.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, even with the implementation of differential privacy countermeasures, we show that substantial information can still be extracted from the reconstructed images.

evidence.title: Impact of differential privacy on breast ultrasound image classification performance using vision transformer
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.comparator_used: Same ViT-B/16 fine-tuning without differential privacy (non-private baseline)
evidence.outcome: Breast ultrasound classification accuracy, F1 and AUC-ROC
evidence.effect: Non-DP: 94.9% accuracy, 93.4% F1, 99.2% AUC-ROC. DP at ε=10, δ=1e-5: 89.5% accuracy, 86.0% F1, 96.1% AUC-ROC. DP at ε=1, δ=0.1: 87.4% accuracy, 82.8% F1, 94.1% AUC-ROC. DP at ε=0.01, δ=1e-5: 48.3% accuracy, 43.5% F1, 48.6% AUC-ROC. ANOVA showed ε as the dominant factor (P<0.001).
evidence.tradeoff: Monotonic privacy-utility trade-off: performance declined as ε decreased, with collapse to near-chance at ε=0.01.
evidence.quote: Introducing DP produced a clear monotonic privacy-utility trade-off: performance declined as ε decreased.

evidence.title: MedPriv-Bench: Benchmarking the Privacy-Utility Trade-off of Large Language Models in Medical Open-Ended Question Answering
evidence.comparator_used: Unprotected Med42-v2-8B with no privacy-preserving method
evidence.outcome: Privacy leakage rate and clinical utility score (1-5) in medical open-ended QA
evidence.effect: Leakage fell from 72.8% to 20.5% with local differential privacy, but utility fell from 3.87/5 to 3.03
evidence.tradeoff: Large utility loss: the lowest leakage came with a drop in utility from 3.87 to 3.03. The authors describe a pervasive privacy-utility trade-off.
evidence.quote: Relative to unprotected Med42-v2-8B (utility 3.87/5; leakage 72.8%), supervised fine-tuning improved utility to 4.25 and reduced leakage to 38.9%, whereas local differential privacy reduced leakage to 20.5% but lowered utility to 3.03.

controls.question: Should we cryptographically protect model updates and computation, including inference, rather than processing them in plaintext?

controls.aim: Reduce exposure of individual updates and patient inputs to aggregators, servers, and interception.
controls.family_label: PHI redaction and de-identification, on-premises models, prompt-injection defenses, access limits
tradeoffs: Large utility loss, convergence degradation, approximately 24× ciphertext expansion, and uplink increase from 3.18 MB to 37.69 MB per round
Intermediate timing results were reported, but the abstract gives no figures for the computational overhead.

evidence.title: Security Analysis of a Federated Learning Framework for Medical Image-to-Image Translation
evidence.comparator_used: Federated updates without Secure Aggregation (plain FL, attacked by FedMIA)
evidence.outcome: Membership inference attack discrimination (AUC) and synthesis quality
evidence.effect: FedMIA AUC 0.92-0.99 without SecAgg; with SecAgg AUC fell to 0.23-0.56 across all centers, with no impact on synthesis quality
evidence.quote: The introduction of SecAgg reduced AUC values to near-random levels (0.23-0.56) across all centers without impacting synthesis quality.

evidence.title: Privacy Preserving Disease Prediction Across Multiple Hospitals Using CKKS Based Homomorphic Federated Learning
evidence.comparator_used: Plaintext federated learning (unencrypted model updates), also compared with centralised learning and differential-privacy baselines
evidence.outcome: Membership-inference attack AUC (privacy) versus predictive utility (F1, ROC-AUC) and communication cost
evidence.effect: HE-FL reduced membership-inference AUC to 0.5000 (random guess); plaintext FL had F1 = 0.9922 and ROC-AUC = 0.9996 versus HE-FL F1 = 0.4042 and ROC-AUC = 0.7714; uplink rose from 3.18 MB to 37.69 MB per round (~24× ciphertext expansion)
evidence.tradeoff: Large utility loss, convergence degradation, approximately 24× ciphertext expansion, and uplink increase from 3.18 MB to 37.69 MB per round
evidence.quote: Plaintext FL achieved the highest utility (F1 = 0.9922; ROC-AUC = 0.9996), whereas the proposed HE-FL configuration retained meaningful predictive capability (F1 = 0.4042; ROC-AUC = 0.7714) and reduced membership-inference attack performance to the random-guess level (AUC = 0.5000) under the evaluated protocol.

evidence.effect: Privacy-preserving XGBoost results identical to the plaintext model in both scenarios (A and B) in terms of prediction accuracy

evidence.quote: The privacy-preserving XGBoost model results are identical to the original plaintext model in the aforementioned two scenarios in terms of prediction accuracy.

evidence.title: Security Analysis of a Federated Learning Framework for Medical Image-to-Image Translation
evidence.comparator_used: Standard federated averaging (FedAvg) aggregation
evidence.outcome: Model performance under data poisoning (noise injection) relative to the no-poisoning baseline
evidence.effect: High-noise poisoning: FedAvg rendered the federation inoperative, while FedMedian restored performance close to baseline in most scenarios. Low noise: FedMedian's advantage was less consistent.
evidence.tradeoff: Significant residual degradation remained in specific center configurations. Low-level noise may be indistinguishable from natural heterogeneity across centers, potentially enabling stealthy degradation.
evidence.quote: Under high-noise poisoning, the standard federated averaging (FedAvg) aggregation rendered the federation inoperative, while FedMedian restored performance close to the no-poisoning baseline in most scenarios, with significant residual degradation in specific center configurations.

evidence.title: Impact of labelling inaccuracy and image noise on tooth segmentation in panoramic radiographs using federated, centralized, and local learning
evidence.comparator_used: Centralized learning (CL) on pooled data from the same 6 institutions
evidence.outcome: Tooth segmentation accuracy (Dice, ASSD) on a hold-out test set under baseline, label-manipulation, image-noise and faulty-client-exclusion settings
evidence.effect: Baseline median Dice 0.949 (ASSD 1.332) FL vs 0.947 (ASSD 1.371) CL; label manipulation 0.949 (ASSD 1.465) vs 0.942 (ASSD 1.757); image noise 0.949 (ASSD 1.311) vs 0.948 (ASSD 1.361); faulty client excluded 0.948 (ASSD 1.331) vs 0.946 (ASSD 1.393). With 2 noisy clients CL performed slightly better than FL.

evidence.title: When Patients Say “Do Not Share”: LLMs Misroute Sensitive Information in Clinical Documentation
evidence.comparator_used: Matched versions without an explicit patient request not to share sensitive information
evidence.outcome: Disclosure of sensitive information in documents for unrelated specialists or employers
evidence.effect: Requests reduced disclosure from 46.6% to 34.2%, a 12.5-percentage-point decrease; sensitive information was still disclosed in 722 of 2,113 documents (34.2%).
evidence.tradeoff: Residual inappropriate disclosure remained in more than one in three documents.
evidence.quote: Overall, requests reduced disclosure from 46.6% to 34.2%, a 12.5-percentage-point decrease, leaving sensitive information disclosed in more than one in three such documents.

evidence.title: Machine Unlearning for GDPR Right-to-Erasure in Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction Models
evidence.comparator_used: Full retraining (also Label-Flip Retraining, Influence Reweighting, and Selective Tree Pruning as alternative unlearning methods)
evidence.outcome: Unlearning time, accuracy cost versus 0.5% clinical threshold, and cumulative 12-month deletion cost for removing patient data from AMR prediction models
evidence.effect: SISA achieved an 8.9× speedup over full retraining on ARMD (7.5 s vs. 66.7 s) and 9.8× on PATRIC (1.4 s vs. 13.4 s), with accuracy costs of 0.024% and 0.048%. Over 12 months at 50 monthly deletions, cumulative overhead fell from 800 s to 90 s (ARMD) and from 160 s to 16 s (PATRIC). Label-Flip Retraining and Influence Reweighting gave no speedup (≤1.0×).
evidence.tradeoff: Small accuracy loss (0.024% ARMD, 0.048% PATRIC), below the 0.5% clinical threshold. Tree Pruning exceeded the threshold on EHR data (+0.648%).
evidence.quote: SISA achieved an 8.9× speedup over full retraining on ARMD (7.5 s vs. 66.7 s) and a 9.8 × speedup on PATRIC (1.4 s vs. 13.4 s), with accuracy costs of 0.024% and 0.048%, respectively, both below the 0.5% clinical threshold.

evidence.title: Factuality Beyond Coherence: Evaluating LLM Watermarking Methods for Medical Texts
evidence.comparator_used: Unwatermarked LLM-generated medical text (implied baseline; the abstract does not name it)
evidence.outcome: Medical factual accuracy and coherence of watermarked text, summarised in the Factuality-Weighted Score
evidence.effect: Watermarking methods 'substantially compromise medical factuality'; the abstract reports no numeric values.

evidence.quote: Our evaluation shows current watermarking methods substantially compromise medical factuality, with entropy shifts degrading medical entity representation.

evidence.title: Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts
evidence.comparator_used: Unwatermarked LLM/VLM output (same models without watermarking), across 5 watermarking schemes, 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on medical tasks
evidence.outcome: Medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations in watermarked versus unwatermarked generation
evidence.effect: Watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes; no numeric effect sizes given in the abstract
evidence.tradeoff: Watermark-induced lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings; aggregate metrics and general benchmarks can mask these failures
evidence.quote: Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings.
